Border police won’t publish Schiphol e-gate investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Border police won’t publish Schiphol e-gate investigation
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Hundreds of people missed their flights and thousands more faced long delays at Schiphol on Sunday after all 78 of the airport’s automatic passport gates went down at around 6am.
The Royal Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border checks, said the outage was caused by an IT malfunction and that there was “no indication whatsoever” of a cyberattack.
The exact cause is still being investigated, but the results will not be made public, Marechaussee head of press, Major Mike Hofman, told Dutch News.
“For operational reasons, we do not comment regarding the further configuration, operation and technical details of our systems,” he said.
With the e-gates down, everyone flying to or from a country outside the Schengen area had to be checked manually by hand, including passengers in transit. The Marechaussee opened every desk and carried out less thorough checks to keep the queues moving.
Passengers waited an hour on average, and some waited up to an hour and a half, Schiphol officials said. The gates were working again by around 3pm.
KLM held departures where possible, and Transavia said it would be flexible with rebookings. A claims specialist told the Telegraaf the number of people affected in some way could run into the tens of thousands.
Few are likely to receive compensation, experts told the paper, because the outage will probably count as force majeure since the e-gates are run by the Marechaussee, not the airlines. The Marechaussee said travellers who missed their flights should contact their airline.
The outage happened during one of the busiest weekends of the autumn, as the one-week October school holiday began in the middle and south of the country and ended in the north. The Amsterdam marathon on Sunday also attracted thousands of runners to the city from all over the world.

The third President of Ukraine, Viktor Yushchenko, emphasized that history and language form the core foundation of Ukraine's state agency and sovereignty.

Israel violating US-mediated framework agreement, Lebanese president says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:32:27 UTC
20:32:27 KST

Stephanie Rady and Sahin Demir
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Monday that Israel has failed to comply with a US-mediated framework agreement signed in June and continues daily violations in southern Lebanon, reaffirming his country’s commitment to a diplomatic solution.
Aoun made the remarks during a meeting with Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy at the presidential palace in Baabda, east of Beirut, according to a statement from the Lebanese presidency.
“The Israelis have not adhered to the framework agreement, and the south continues to face daily violations,” Aoun said.
He stressed that continued Israeli violations would not achieve their objectives but would instead strengthen the Lebanese people’s determination to defend their land and rights.
Aoun said the violations were obstructing the Lebanese state’s efforts to implement its stated objectives.
He reaffirmed Lebanon’s commitment to a diplomatic solution despite its difficulties, saying it was “far less costly than the devastating war” for which the Lebanese people, particularly residents of the south, continue to pay the price.
“It is time for Lebanon to have some peace,” he added.
The president also welcomed any efforts by the Arab League to help Lebanon overcome the difficult circumstances it faces.
For his part, Fahmy reaffirmed the Arab League’s support for the Lebanese state and its institutions, rejecting any infringement on the country’s sovereignty.
He expressed readiness to engage with Arab and Western countries to mobilize support for Lebanon and its people.
Fahmy stressed that the Arab position toward Lebanon remained united and that the organization was working to translate that support into practical measures and financial assistance.
Israel has carried out attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing and injuring thousands of people and displacing over 1.5 million residents.
On June 26, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-sponsored framework agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of Hezbollah.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued its attacks on southern Lebanon.
Israeli forces also continue to occupy Lebanese territory, including areas held for decades and others seized during more recent wars and military operations.

Women’s wheelchair basketball beat Cambodia at Asian Para Games
TEHRAN - Iran’s women’s wheelchair basketball team got off the mark at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games on Monday, beating Cambodia 52-39 in their third match of the tournament.
After back-to-back defeats to Japan and Thailand, Iran needed a response, and they delivered. It was a tight opening half, with the Iranians edging ahead 24-23 at the break.
The second half was a different story. Iran stepped up in brilliant fashion, pulling away from Cambodia to seal a comfortable 13-point win.
It is the team’s first victory of the 2026 Para Asian Games.
Iran still have China and Laos to face. The women’s wheelchair basketball event at the fifth edition of the Games is a round-robin featuring six teams: Iran, Japan, Thailand, China, Laos and Cambodia.

Contractors warned on deadline to submit bids for E1 tender

Contractors have until the end of the day on Monday to submit bids for the project. Their proposals must then be examined, winners selected, and building permits obtained before work can begin.

The fourth Türkiye-Belgium ministerial meeting will be held on Tuesday in Brussels, with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci, and Justice Minister Akin Gurlek attending.
According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, the three ministers will visit Belgium from Oct. 19 to 21 to participate in the meeting scheduled for Oct. 20.
Belgium will be represented by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot, Interior Minister Bernard Quintin, Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden, and Asylum and Migration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt.
The fourth round of the ministerial meeting, last held in Ankara in 2016, will address bilateral cooperation, particularly counterterrorism, judicial and police cooperation, the defense industry, consular affairs, visas, and migration.
The ministers will also exchange views on regional and international issues.
During his visit to Belgium, Fidan is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
He is also expected to deliver a speech at the European Policy Centre think tank and meet with representatives of the business community.
 
Bilateral relations
Increasing high-level contacts between Türkiye and Belgium in recent years have contributed to the development and deepening of bilateral cooperation in various fields.
Most recently, Belgium's Queen Mathilde paid an economy-focused visit to Türkiye on May 10-14, accompanied by a delegation that included the deputy prime minister and foreign minister, the defense and foreign trade minister, as well as the heads of regional governments.
Trade volume between Türkiye and Belgium reached $9.2 billion in 2025, with the two countries aiming to increase the figure to $15 billion.
Approximately 300,000 Turkish citizens living in Belgium also serve as an important bridge between the two countries.

Japan’s mega-quake that never was, and the danger of false alarms
A software error triggering a false magnitude 9.9 quake in Japan sparks fears that eroding public trust could cost lives in a real quake
3-MIN READ3-MIN

Julian Ryallin Tokyo
Kanako Hosomura was working in a clothing store in Yokohama when an alert on her phone warned of an imminent magnitude 9.9 earthquake.
“We all rushed outside,” Hosomura said, recalling how people poured out of nearby shops and offices to watch tall buildings and power lines for signs of shaking.
But no earthquake came. Eight minutes after issuing the warning on Friday, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) cancelled the alert, leaving residents to wonder what had gone wrong.
“These alarms do not go off very often – only maybe a couple of times a year – so when they do sound, everyone is worried that the quake is going to be really big,” Hosomura said.

The Domino Effect: How Strikes on Data Centers Paralyze Russian Businesses
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:25:58 EEST
20:25:58 KST

The Domino Effect: How Strikes on Data Centers Paralyze Russian Businesses
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian drones attacked the data centers of Yandex, Sberbank, and VK. Expert Oleksandr Hlushchenko explained that strikes on server infrastructure paralyze business processes and harm the Russian economy.
The massive attack by Ukrainian drones on St. Petersburg on the night of October 18 targeted an oil terminal, energy infrastructure, and a data center. After the strike, Russians began massively complaining about disruptions to the operation of the "VKontakte" social network. However, the consequences of further attacks on data centers could prove much more serious—from disruptions to banking payments to interference with the operation of businesses. Read about what this threatens for the Russian economy in the UNN article.
The Russians themselves effectively created the conditions under which their digital infrastructure is becoming vulnerable to such strikes. Russia spent years building a centralized digital system, moving an increasing number of services online, concentrating enormous amounts of data in large technology companies, and at the same time requiring that the personal data of Russian citizens be stored on Russian territory. In peacetime, this model makes it possible to centrally manage services, scale them, and control information flows. But during wartime, it creates serious risks. When a significant part of digital infrastructure is concentrated within a single state, and its operation depends on a limited number of large technology platforms, damage to individual elements can have consequences far beyond a single enterprise
In fact, this concerns a threat not only to social networks but also to the entire system of digital services on which Russians' daily lives depend. Data centers ensure the storage of enormous volumes of information and the operation of applications, cloud platforms, and financial and corporate services. Damage to such facilities can deprive companies of part of their computing capacity and users of access to their usual services.
Repeated strikes pose a particular danger. Large technology companies have backup data centers capable of taking over the load of damaged facilities. However, their capabilities are limited. If several complexes go offline at once, the load on the remaining ones increases, along with the risk of large-scale disruptions.
At a certain point, servers can no longer fully process all requests. Some services begin operating more slowly, others periodically become unavailable, and some operations end in errors. And the less reserve capacity remains, the harder it is for the system to withstand even ordinary technical failures
How will strikes on data centers affect the Russian economy?
The consequences of such disruptions will be felt most acutely by Russian businesses. Modern enterprises simultaneously depend on banking, cloud, logistics, and other digital services.
You may have goods, employees, and customers, but be unable to make a payment on time, process documents, or organize supplies. In other words, economic activity slows down not because the goods or enterprises themselves have disappeared, but because the mechanisms connecting them have stopped working properly
Why is it difficult for Russia to restore data centers?
Another problem for Russia is replacing damaged equipment. Data centers require not only servers but also complex information-storage systems, networking equipment, power-supply and cooling systems. Due to technological sanctions, purchasing the necessary components may turn into a lengthy and expensive process.
A data center cannot be restored simply because a company has enough money in its account. Servers, storage devices, network switches, optical equipment, power-supply systems, cooling systems, and other components are required
According to the expert's assessment, the additional costs of restoring the infrastructure may ultimately also be felt by Russians themselves. Technology companies will be forced to spend more money on equipment, reserve capacity, and maintenance. This creates the conditions for services to become more expensive for end consumers.
At the same time, several damaged data centers do not mean the immediate collapse of the Russian internet. Large companies have backup systems, but their capabilities are not unlimited.
This does not necessarily mean an immediate collapse, but it may mean a gradual degradation in the quality of digital services
Therefore, if the attacks continue, Russia’s main problem may no longer be the temporary unavailability of individual websites, but the gradual depletion of digital infrastructure, the increasingly costly restoration of that infrastructure, and growing risks for the entire economy.

Belgian Queen, Crown Princess targeted in AI-generated nude images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:25:30 UTC
20:25:30 KST

Melike Pala
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Queen Mathilde of Belgium, her daughter Crown Princess Elisabeth and several other prominent Belgian women have become targets of sexually explicit images generated by artificial intelligence (AI), renewing concerns over the growing spread of non-consensual deepfake pornography.
The fabricated images, which depict the women naked, have been circulating on social media platforms in recent days, the Belgian newspaper Le Soir reported on Monday.
The victims reportedly also include wives of politicians and government officials, as well as prominent female politicians.
According to an investigation by several Belgian news outlets, Flemish Vice-Minister-President Melissa Depraetere and former Belgian Defense Minister Ludivine Dedonder were among those targeted.
"As disgusting as it is, very little surprises me anymore," Depraetere said, adding that people needed to understand that the creation and distribution of such images was unacceptable and could destroy lives.
Dedonder announced that she intended to file a legal complaint over the fabricated images.
The Belgian Royal Palace also confirmed that action had been taken to have the images depicting the queen and the crown princess removed from the internet.
The controversy has once again drawn attention to AI-generated or manipulated images that make real people appear naked or engaged in sexual activity without their consent.
Civil society organisations and digital rights advocates have repeatedly warned that AI-generated sexual abuse disproportionately affects women and girls, with consequences extending beyond individual privacy violations.
The European Union prepares to introduce stricter measures against AI applications that generate non-consensual intimate images.
Under amendments to the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, AI systems designed to generate or manipulate realistic intimate images of identifiable people without their explicit consent are set to be prohibited.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has also become a prominent example of the risks posed by manipulated images and videos.
In 2024, Meloni sought 100,000 euros in damages in a case involving two men accused of producing and distributing pornographic deepfake videos featuring her face.
She also initiated a process to trademark her voice through the European Union Intellectual Property Office in an effort to protect her identity against AI-generated impersonations.

Ukraine and Russia are working to finalize arrangements to evacuate civilians from Russian-occupied Oleshky and six nearby settlements to Ukrainian government-controlled territory.
Speaking on Espreso television, Ukrainian human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said the Russian side had taken up all proposals previously submitted by Ukraine. Talks are continuing daily, he said, although difficult issues remain unresolved.

“We are now moving toward agreeing on the final details to secure a ceasefire and ensure the evacuation of everyone who wants to leave, not simply out of Oleshky, but directly to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government,” Lubinets said.
Ukraine estimates that about 6,000 civilians, including up to 200 children, may remain in the seven settlements covered by the proposed evacuation. Up to 2,000 people are believed to remain in Oleshky itself.
Lubinets expressed hope that the negotiations would soon produce concrete results but did not announce an evacuation date.

Earlier, Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said that Russian forces have turned the occupied city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region into a “death trap,” leaving approximately 1,700 remaining residents trapped under acute starvation, pervasive mining, and relentless drone surveillance
“Those who try to flee risk their lives. The adjacent river is also mined. Residents doubt they will survive this winter. The hospital has run out of medicine. Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in houses, as the Russians forbid residents from burying them,” Sybiha stated.
The foreign minister described extreme shortages of basic sustenance, noting that isolated civilians are struggling to endure on minimal rations while confronting harassment from occupation troops.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Sybiha added.
H2: Encirclement and isolation on the Dnipro left bank
Oleshky, situated on the east (left) bank of the Dnipro River approximately five kilometers (3 miles) southeast of the regional capital of Kherson, has been under Russian military occupation since the initial weeks of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The city has been completely cut off from authorized commercial freight convoys and organized institutional aid since late May.
While earlier demographic assessments by Ukrainian authorities indicated several thousand residents remained scattered across the wider river basin, civilian numbers within the municipal core have contracted to roughly 1,700 as conditions have deteriorated ahead of sub-zero winter temperatures.
Local municipal officials have confirmed that central utility grids – including drinking water supply, electrical networks, and municipal gas heating – have suffered significant damage.
With ground logistics paralyzed by dense minefields, destroyed bridge spans, and persistent Russian first-person view (FPV) drone patrols along the riverfront, Ukrainian defense units have intermittently deployed heavy multi-rotor transport drones to air-drop food and medical packages directly into residential yards.
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets previously reported that his office had documented hundreds of verified appeals from civilians trapped in the enclave, noting that residents desperate to flee have attempted to navigate active minefields on foot due to the absence of negotiated humanitarian corridors.
On Friday, Oct. 16, Pope Leo XIV held a telephone consultation with Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge an immediate localized ceasefire in Oleshky, calling for verified arrangements to permit emergency food and medical deliveries alongside the safe, voluntary evacuation of non-combatants.
The Vatican confirmed that the pope expressed deep concern over the grave humanitarian collapse in the municipality and pressed Moscow to facilitate unhindered relief operations.
In its official readout of the discussion, the Kremlin claimed that Putin offered what it described as a “detailed explanation” attributing responsibility for the municipal situation to Ukrainian authorities, while expressing general willingness to coordinate with Vatican initiatives.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has similarly characterized the humanitarian situation in Oleshky as desperate, appealing directly to the Russian Federation to fulfill its legal obligations under international humanitarian law as an occupying power by permitting the immediate evacuation of civilians and allowing international aid agencies unfettered access.

Development Road Project to contribute $55B to Türkiye's economy over 10 years: Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:23:17 UTC
20:23:17 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
The Development Road Project is expected to contribute around $55 billion to Türkiye's economy over 10 years, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu said Monday.
Speaking at a conference in Ankara, Uraloglu said the project would also provide employment opportunities for an average of 70,000 people annually while strengthening Türkiye's position in global trade and supporting Iraq's economic reconstruction.
The planned corridor will connect Iraq's Grand Faw Port in the Gulf to Europe through Türkiye, integrating railways and roads with energy transmission lines, fiber-optic infrastructure, and oil and natural gas pipelines.
“For our country alone, we foresee the project contributing approximately $55 billion to our economy over a 10-year period and, through the establishment of production and logistics centers, providing employment opportunities for an average of 70,000 citizens each year,” he said.
Uraloglu said tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and the Russia-Ukraine war had exposed vulnerabilities in global transport networks, prompting countries to seek safer, shorter and more predictable routes.
The Development Road would offer a strategic alternative that reduces dependence on the Strait of Hormuz, particularly for cargo moving from Gulf countries to Europe, he said.
He added that the route could cut journey times to approximately 25 days, compared with 45 days via the Cape of Good Hope and 35 days along the Southern Corridor.
 
Complementary trade routes
Uraloglu said Türkiye viewed the Development Road as complementary to existing trade networks, including the Middle Corridor linking China and Central Asia to Europe through the Caspian Sea and Türkiye.
“As Türkiye, located at the heart of the Middle Corridor, managing the Turkish Straits and building the Development Road, we are clearly demonstrating both at the negotiating table and on the ground: There can be no corridor without Türkiye,” he said.
Existing, ongoing and planned Turkish railway lines connecting to the Middle Corridor total 2,156 kilometers (1,340 miles) , with completed and planned investments amounting to $47.1 billion, he said.
The minister said the Development Road Project could help Iraq diversify away from oil revenues, generate transit trade income and strengthen its role as a regional commercial hub.
He recalled agreements signed by Türkiye and Iraq on July 28 this year, saying the two countries planned to secure parliamentary approval before beginning construction.
These include a memorandum on rail and road transport through the Fishkhabur-Ovakoy border crossing and a framework agreement to develop transport infrastructure in Iraq in exchange for natural resources.
Uraloglu also pointed to a recently signed railway cooperation memorandum with Saudi Arabia, saying efforts to revive the historic Hejaz Railway would create additional connections from the Gulf through Türkiye to Europe.
“The Development Road Project has the potential to reintegrate the Middle East's fragmented geoeconomic structure, transform Iraq into one of the crossroads of regional trade and strengthen Türkiye's position in global connectivity networks,” he said.

Singapore firm plans for up to 500MW AI data center capacity in Malaysia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:22:50 CST
20:22:50 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Singapore-founded neocloud provider Aolani has signed letters of intent to take up 500 megawatts (MW) of artificial intelligence (AI) data center capacity in Malaysia, with operations targeted to begin in the second half of 2027.
The capacity will be spread across multiple sites designed to Tier III standards and equipped with purpose-built AI data centers to support Aolani's expanding AI infrastructure and graphics processing unit (GPU) deployments, the company said in a statement on Monday.
Aolani plans to provide the AI infrastructure, GPU deployment and operational requirements for the facilities upon completion.
The latest commitment would bring its planned capacity in Malaysia to as much as 580MW by 2027, up from about 80MW committed in 2026.
The expanded capacity will serve global hyperscalers and AI-native companies, while supporting local demand for computing power. ■

US Treasury chief rebukes Zelensky for saying Ukraine must win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:22:46 UTC
20:22:46 KST

US Treasury chief rebukes Zelensky for saying Ukraine must win
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has rebuked Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky over his insistence that his country must defeat Russia, rejecting his all-or-nothing stance as a “false binary” and insisting that the conflict must end through a negotiated settlement.
Speaking to NBC’s ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday, Zelensky said Ukraine must win the conflict with Russia, calling victory essential to preserving the country’s independence, geopolitical alignment, and national identity. He lamented that Ukraine “will not prevail” if the US sides with Russia.
“Zelensky presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win,” Bessent told the show shortly after Zelensky’s appearance, arguing that the priority should be ending the conflict rather than determining a winner. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement.”
Bessent stressed that Trump made it clear “he wants to end this war,” noting that the president’s decisions are aimed at securing a negotiated settlement.
Zelensky’s remarks came amid a growing spat with Trump over sanctions on Russian and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities. Last week, Trump invoked a national-interest exemption to suspend the sanctions he signed into law last month, including 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
The move followed Trump’s decision days earlier to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports to ease rising fuel prices. According to US media reports, Trump eased the restrictions after Zelensky refused to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which the president blamed for global fuel shortages and soaring prices at the pump – a critical issue just weeks before the US midterm elections. The moves sparked outrage in Kiev, where they were seen as a betrayal of Ukraine’s efforts to maintain Western pressure on Russia.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump defended the moves, saying Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries are driving up prices, while stressing that he is focused on brokering a peace deal and does not want to “do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” Trump also argued that Zelensky does not want to end the conflict and probably never did, despite receiving billions in Western aid.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov echoed his criticism, suggesting on Sunday that Zelensky has “no desire” to reach a settlement because his government would collapse if Ukraine signed a deal that’s acceptable to both the US and Russia.
Zelensky, whose presidential term expired in 2024, has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law. Moscow maintains that Zelensky is illegitimate; Trump recently called for his resignation, saying Ukraine should get “a new president.”
Since returning to office, Trump has revived talks with Russia, which were largely suspended under his predecessor, Joe Biden. His efforts to broker peace have produced some results, including POW exchanges, but the diplomatic push has been overshadowed by the US war against Iran and has yet to yield a peace deal.
Moscow has said it would prefer a negotiated settlement. Last month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia expects to hold trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US in the foreseeable future. President Vladimir Putin, however, stressed that the conflict must end on terms that are acceptable to Russia – stressing that a settlement must address the root causes of the conflict and include the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Russian territory, protection for Russian-speakers in Ukraine, as well as denazification and neutral, non-nuclear status for Ukraine.

WFP cuts food aid to 500,000 people in Gaza amid funding shortages
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:22:13 CST
20:22:13 KST

GAZA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) announced on Monday that funding shortages had forced it to cut food assistance to around 500,000 people in the Gaza Strip, reducing its monthly beneficiaries from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
In a press statement, the agency warned that recent improvements in food security remained fragile as winter approaches and declining humanitarian funding threatens to reverse the gains.
Starting this month, the WFP has halved food rations, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, along with smaller quantities of wheat flour, according to the statement.
The agency has also reduced daily hot meal distributions from 250,000 to 150,000 and cut the value of cash assistance provided to 75,000 families.
Despite the cuts, the WFP will continue supporting bakeries that supply about one-third of Gaza's bread needs, providing nutrition assistance to 300,000 women and children, and distributing school snacks to 200,000 children.
According to the latest food security assessment cited by the WFP, around 1.4 million people, or 67 percent of Gaza's population, are experiencing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse, classified as Phase 3 or above under the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification.
The agency said it had received less than half the funding for its operations in Palestine in 2026 compared with previous years and urgently needed 450 million U.S. dollars to maintain operations in Gaza and the West Bank from October 2026 to March 2027. ■

====================================================================================================

Netanyahu unveils war doctrine, maps new regional threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:22:11 UTC
20:22:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's Netanyahu unveils war doctrine, maps new regional threats
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has unveiled a security doctrine advocating pre-emptive military strikes and buffer zones along Israel's borders, while displaying maps of supposed regional alliances that include Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan and Iran, just days before Israeli elections.
The three-page document, titled "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Security Concept", was published on the Israeli government's website on Sunday and outlines the country's alleged principal security threats and 10 central principles reportedly guiding its military strategy.
The proposals drew sharp criticism from Israeli opposition leaders, who dismissed the document as superficial, filled with hallow slogans and an attempt to distract from Netanyahu's security failures ahead of the 27 October parliamentary elections.
The document was released as Netanyahu struggles in opinion polls and has recently acknowledged being "very worried" about his prospects of winning another term.
Opposition figures accused him of manipulating public fears and using regional security threats to divert attention from his government's failures and increasingly divisive election campaign.
Pre-emptive strikes and military expansion
In the document's introduction, Netanyahu argued that the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023 had forced Israel into a wide-ranging war, claiming that Israeli military operations from Gaza to Yemen, Lebanon and Iran had averted what he described as the threat of imminent nuclear annihilation.
He also claimed that Israel had dismantled the "stranglehold" imposed by the so-called Iranian axis, despite the devastating consequences of Israel's military campaigns across the region, including its genocidal war in Gaza.
Netanyahu said the conflict had required a fundamental revision of Israel's security doctrine, prioritising offensive military action over containment and defence.
The document calls for "prioritising the prevention of threats and attacking them rather than containing them and defending against them", including pre-emptive strikes against emerging threats.
It identifies Iran, which Israel accuses of seeking nuclear weapons, as a principal threat, alongside what Netanyahu describes as its network of regional proxies, including Yemen's Houthis, Hezbollah in Lebanon and Palestinian armed groups in Gaza.
Precision-guided missiles, drones, electronic warfare and cyberattacks are also listed among Israel's major security concerns.
The document further identifies what it calls "domestic terrorism and internal enemies", international efforts to delegitimise and isolate Israel, and threats along its northern, eastern and western borders.
Among its central principles, the doctrine calls for maintaining Israel's military superiority, strengthening deterrence and early-warning capabilities, and preparing for preventive attacks.
It also advocates establishing buffer zones along Israel's borders where deemed necessary, although it does not specify their locations or which neighbouring countries could be affected.
Israel has already occupied additional territory in southern Syria and maintained military positions inside southern Lebanon, while continuing its occupation of Palestinian territory.
The document calls for strengthening Israel's domestic military industries to reduce dependence on foreign arms suppliers, while expanding its technological superiority in artificial intelligence, quantum computing and space.
It also seeks to deepen regional and international alliances and consolidate Israel's position as a regional power.
Under a section titled "Spirit of the People", the doctrine calls for strengthening national unity, preserving Israel's Jewish and democratic character, encouraging settlement in what it describes as the "Land of Israel", and strengthening ties with Jewish communities abroad.
The language on settlement comes amid continued Israeli expansion in the occupied West Bank, where settlements are illegal under international law.
The document does not provide a detailed operational strategy for confronting Iran.
According to Netanyahu's office, it was prepared with assistance from Israel's National Security Council and its head, Shmuel Ben Ezra.
Maps of regional alliances raise questions
During a presentation accompanying the document on Sunday, Netanyahu displayed a geopolitical map depicting what he claimed were emerging regional alliances and alleged threats to Israel.
The map, which carried the logo of Germany's Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung foundation, identified a grouping of Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan as the "Sunni Diamond".
It also depicted Iran and its regional allies as the "Axis of Resistance", alongside an Israel-UAE grouping described as the "Hexagon Alliance".
The graphic, originally published in May 2026 by researchers Marc Saxer and Marcus Schneider, also categorised countries and territories considered friendly to the competing blocs.
Somaliland and Puntland were depicted as territories considered friendly to Israel and the UAE, alongside Ethiopia, Djibouti and Greece. Somalia and its North East State, meanwhile, were shown as friendly to the Turkey-Egypt-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia grouping.
The presentation referred to an "Iranian-Shia axis" and a Turkey-linked Muslim Brotherhood axis as regional challenges.
Netanyahu also urged Israel to take advantage of the remaining two years of US President Donald Trump's administration to expand its alliances, warning that a future American government might be less supportive.
He acknowledged differences with Trump over Turkey and claimed Israel had acted to prevent Ankara from expanding its military presence in Syria.
"I hope we don't reach a direct confrontation," Netanyahu said.
The map also highlighted competing regional interests in the Horn of Africa, where Israel's growing relationship with Somaliland and the UAE's ties with Puntland have contributed to tensions with Somalia's federal government.
Israel recognised Somaliland as an independent state in December 2025, a move rejected by Mogadishu as a violation of Somalia's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Israeli opposition dismisses 'empty slogans'
The publication of Netanyahu's security doctrine prompted fierce criticism from opposition leaders Yair Lapid and Gadi Eisenkot, who accused the prime minister of attempting to conceal his government's failures, particularly those surrounding the 7 October 2023 attack.
In a post on X, Lapid described the document as "superficial and strange", saying it appeared to have been written using a free version of an AI chatbot.
He argued that the document offered no genuine national security strategy and instead sought to cover up Netanyahu's record.
Lapid criticised Netanyahu's refusal to establish an official commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding 7 October, as well as his inability to expand Israel's normalisation agreements with Arab countries.
He also accused the prime minister of contradicting his own security principles by allowing ultra-Orthodox Jews to avoid military service, damaging Israel's international relationships and deepening divisions within Israeli society.
Eisenkot, who leads the opposition Yashar party, described the document as "two empty pages filled with slogans", arguing that it exposed the strategic vacuum created by Netanyahu's leadership.
He questioned why the prime minister had waited until nine days before the elections, and three years after the 7 October attack, to publish his national security vision.
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of failing to achieve his stated military objectives, including dismantling the military and governing capabilities of Hamas and Islamic Jihad, deterring Hezbollah, maintaining stability in the occupied West Bank and preserving domestic unity.
He also argued that Hamas continued to maintain armed forces in Gaza while Hezbollah was rebuilding its military capabilities.
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of refusing to investigate the failures of 7 October or draw lessons from them.
He described the document's publication as another example of Netanyahu's political tactics, accusing him of "manipulating public consciousness, stirring fear and trying to divert attention from the series of lies and racism surrounding his election campaign".
Eisenkot pledged that an opposition-led government would prepare and approve a formal Israeli national security strategy within 150 days of taking office.

====================================================================================================

Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments plans tenfold capacity boost by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:20:58 UTC
20:20:58 KST

CEO Grzegorz Brona warned that Europe could remain reliant on US rockets to launch its satellites into orbit for years.
Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments plans to increase its production capacity tenfold by 2029, CEO Grzegorz Brona said in an interview with Reuters. He also warned that Europe will still need US rockets to launch its satellites into orbit for years.
The satellite maker is aiming to open a new factory in 2029 in Mazowieckie, Poland, capable of making 40 satellites a year across different models, or 100 of a single model. This compares with 10 at its current site in Piaseczno, just outside Warsaw.
The comments come at a time when Europe is trying to reduce its reliance on US technology.
Two days before the interview, reports emerged that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had been ordered to limit Ukraine’s access to Starshield, its military-grade version of the Starlink satellite network, by the White House.
Donald Trump has since said: “It wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon. I don’t know if it was anybody. From what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
The lack of clarity over who was responsible for the decision is one concern. But for European leaders, the prospect of the Trump administration using US technology as political leverage against its allies is even more alarming.
Europe lags far behind the US in rocket launches, accounting for just eight of the world’s 324 orbital launches last year, compared with 193 by the US. Starlink alone accounts for more than 60% of active satellites, according to European Space Agency data.
Asked whether European industry could build an alternative to Starlink, Brona said the continent could produce thousands of satellites and still have no one to launch them.
“Launch vehicles are now becoming a means of political pressure on the European Union in the hands of [US President] Donald Trump’s administration,” he said.
Creotech, which does not build rockets, has kept US technology out of its satellites to avoid US arms export rules. Under these rules, Washington can block sales of satellites containing even a small American component.
Yet the company still relies on US rockets. SpaceX carried all four satellites Creotech built for Poland’s MikroGlob military programme into orbit.
Europe seeks to increase launch capacity
Europe is trying to expand its launch capacity in several ways.
The European Space Agency (ESA) announced in September that it was considering increasing the number of launches of its Ariane 6 and Vega-C rockets in the coming years to overcome a potential bottleneck in satellite deployments.
ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said a decision was needed soon ahead of an expected sharp rise in demand.
Arianespace, the operator of the Ariane 6 rocket, is planning nine or 10 launches a year from 2027.
Meanwhile, European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius has said the EU wants to increase the number of government satellites from 80 to 630 and carry out 62 launches annually by 2034 from sites in Europe and Canada.
The plans are intended to meet anticipated demand from the EU’s Galileo navigation and Copernicus Earth observation satellite programmes.
Aschbacher has also proposed a €10 billion, 10-year plan to develop an independent European crew vehicle and launch recovery system before the International Space Station retires at the end of 2030 or early 2031.
In March, the ESA launched the European Launcher Challenge to support private companies and start-ups developing launch services.
These efforts include plans for commercial spaceports such as SaxaVord in Scotland and Andøya in Norway, while companies including Isar Aerospace and Rocket Factory Augsburg aim to expand small-to-medium-lift launch options.
Creotech plans further expansion
Creotech Instruments currently makes small satellites and microsatellites, typically weighing between 10 kg and several dozen kilos, using its proprietary Hypersat modular platform family.
Its satellites include the HyperSat Earth observation platform, its Seagull, Eagle 2.0 and Nano 2.0 models, the PIAST Constellation and the MikroGlob Constellation, built for the Polish Armament Agency and launched this month.
The company also works with the ESA and has contributed platforms and subsystems to missions including Comet Interceptor, JUICE (Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer), LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna), the Plasma Observatory and the Twardowski lunar mission to map the Moon’s surface.
Brona added that Creotech would start opening subsidiaries in France and Germany in the coming weeks and was aiming to build 500 kg satellites by 2032.

Library book finds its way back after 92 years
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:19:33 EEST
20:19:33 KST

Someone on Åland just closed out one of the longest library loans on record. A copy of If Winter Comes by A.S.M. Hutchinson was checked out in 1933 and has finally returned to Åland's Saltvik municipal library.
The due date stamped in the back of the book reads 17 September 1933.
"It was 92 years and 6 months overdue," said Malin Blomqvist, a librarian at Saltvik.
Tally up the overdue fees at 20 cents a day and the late charges would have come to 6,757 euros. Luckily for whoever had it on their shelf, that's purely hypothetical.
The borrower who returned the book was a little unsure and politely asked whether a fine was due.
Blomqvist put them at ease, saying: "I'm just glad it came back. Thanks for thinking to return it. Getting it back is like finding a treasure."
The novel dealt with controversial subjects for its day, including adultery, unwed motherhood and suicide.
The Saltvik return is the second-oldest overdue library loan in Finland. The all-time record is held by a book Turku City Library got back five years ago, which had been out for more than 140 years.

French police ‘lost control’ during riots, concedes interior minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:18:39 UTC
20:18:39 KST

France’s interior minister has conceded police “lost control” in some cities during violent protests at the weekend, as the country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting and looting.
Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for Saturday’s protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.
Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.
He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”. Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.
The protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential election and amid mounting economic pressures.
Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said. Nearly 2,400 people – 70% of them adults – were arrested and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured.
Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.
“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.
The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence, he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.
Macron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.
Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.
“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”
Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.
On Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.
A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”
In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.
Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.

Swedish appeals court fines ex-national security adviser for gross negligence

Swedish appeals court fines ex-national security adviser for gross negligence
STOCKHOLM, Oct 19 - A Swedish appeals court on Monday found former national security adviser Henrik Landerholm, a friend of the prime minister, guilty of mishandling secret information, overturning a lower court ruling.
The case, involving documents left at a hotel in 2023, has embarrassed Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson as it unfolded against the backdrop of a deepening security crisis in the Baltic Sea region following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Kristersson submitted his resignation after his right-wing government lost its parliamentary majority in a general election in September, but he is leading a caretaker government while a new government is being formed.
Last year, a district court found Landerholm not guilty, saying he had been negligent, but not gravely.
"Unlike the district court ... the court of appeal finds that the man disclosed the information contained in the documents through gross negligence," the Svea Court of Appeal in Stockholm said in a statement.
"The only reasonable explanation for the man having left the documents behind is that he was quite careless when emptying the safe-deposit box where he had kept them," it said.
The appeals court fined Landerholm, Sweden's first national security adviser, 52,000 Swedish crowns ($5,247).
Landerholm, who has pleaded not guilty, stepped down in January 2025 after the investigations began.
His defence lawyer was not immediately available for comment and Landerholm did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

PARIS – Protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre in Paris on Oct 19, as French authorities scrambled to stem public discontent fuelling mass cost-of-living demonstrations that over the weekend spilled over into some of the worst street violence in recent years.
President Emmanuel Macron ordered a security review as the country’s interior minister admitted that the police “had lost control” during the weekend’s unrest.
Undeterred, the Yellow Vests movement that organised the weekend’s rallies called for a new round of protests.
Italy, Spain and Portugal, where anger over rising prices has also led to protests, were keeping a nervous eye on the developments after smaller clashes broke out in Milan over the weekend and protests about housing costs persisted in Spanish cities.
Some half a million people turned out across France to protest the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with high school students demanding better conditions at their schools.
What started as peaceful demonstrations morphed into violence in some places, as masked groups on the sidelines of the protests attacked law enforcement, broke into town halls and other public buildings, setting many of them ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters on the streets.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered to resign on Oct 19 after more than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured. Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade.
“On (Oct 17), in some major cities, you couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn’t lost control,” Nunez said.
Macron refused Nunez’s resignation, even as he acknowledged security and intelligence failures in the government response, despite the some 60,000 law enforcement personnel deployed across France on Oct 17.
Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70% of whom were adults, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said Oct 19.
More than 2,000 shops were expected to have been affected by the weekend’s violence across France, with damage running into “hundreds of millions of euros”, according to chamber of commerce president Alain Di Crescenzo.
In an address to the nation late on Oct 18, Macron slammed the “unbridled” violence and said the local authorities would be able to ban – “if necessary” – certain rallies in the coming days.
But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew.
The city authorities in Marseille said on Oct 19 that public gatherings would be banned from noon to 08pm.
Discontent spreads
The public discontent showed no signs of subsiding on Oct 19, with demonstrators blocking the entrance to Paris’ iconic Louvre Museum, the most visited in the world.
“We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum,” read a leaflet posted outside the museum, as management and unions said the protest was led by students from Ecole du Louvre.
Rising prices have fuelled anger in France, where diesel prices have jumped nearly 40% and petrol by 25% since March, and where food prices have risen by 25% since 2021.
The unrest in France has flared just months before a key presidential election where centrist Macron cannot stand again and Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, is riding high in the polls.
Ministers have blamed “ultra-left” groups for the violence, while Le Pen claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Melenchon, has “legitimised the violence”.
The left has accused Macron of ignoring protesters’ demands, while the right is calling on him to take a firmer line.
With costs of living rising across Europe, smaller demonstrations have broken out in other countries.
During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan, with Mayor Giuseppe Sala warning: “I’m very worried because it’s a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself.”
In Spain, hundreds of tents have occupied Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square since September, when the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong flat sparked nationwide protests in a country with soaring housing costs.
Dozens of tents have also sprung up in Portugal’s main cities of Lisbon and Porto, with protesters demanding action over rising costs of housing. AFP

Settler violence threatens Israel’s rule of law, international standing, legal expert warns ‘Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:11:49 UTC
20:11:49 KST

Unchecked settler violence risks undermining Israel’s rule of law, damaging its international standing and weakening international support for its efforts to curb the Palestinian Authority’s payments to convicted terrorists, while increasing the risk of sanctions and travel restrictions against settlers, Professor Yuval Shany, the Hersch Lauterpacht Chair in International Law and a senior research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
Shany’s remarks came days after extremist settlers attacked a European delegation and an American photojournalist in two separate incidents. Though 10 suspects have been detained for the attack, the issue of growing violence from extremist settlers has been widely discussed by the international community as a cause of concern.
Settler violence in the West Bank has increased in both frequency and severity in recent years. The number of attacks by extremist settlers against Palestinians and Israeli security forces rose by 27% in 2025 compared with the previous year, while severe incidents of nationalist crime increased by more than 50%, according to IDF and Shin Bet data released in January 2026. The rise in violence comes amid a longstanding record of limited prosecutions. Between 2005 and 2024, 93.8% of the 1,701 police investigation files monitored by Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din were closed without an indictment, while just 3% resulted in a full or partial conviction, according to the organization.
“In principle, Palestinians could go to the Supreme Court and ask for enhanced state protection, and also for the state to compensate them for its negligence in providing them security. And in theory, they could also bring civil cases against identifiable settlers who have damaged their property. ... Many of these Palestinian families do not have the means to actually hire legal [representation]. ... There is a question of whether such legal assistance is available, and also the question of whether they have trust in the Israeli legal system to protect their interests…,” Shany said.
“Even when the court sides with Palestinians occasionally, it's very difficult to actually enforce these decisions. So, in theory, yes, there are legal avenues that can be utilized. They are sometimes being utilized, but so far the effect has been quite marginal on the ground.”
Violence can prevent implementation of court decisions
As Shany noted, even when Israeli courts rule in favor of Palestinians, violence on the ground can prevent those decisions from being implemented. He pointed to the case of the Tubasi family, whose home the High Court of Justice ordered the IDF to secure after the family was forced to leave in July following harassment by extremist settlers.
When the military attempted to facilitate the family’s return, more than 100 extremist settlers attacked IDF forces, preventing the family from returning home. “Due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their homes was not completed,” the military said at the time.
The refusal of extremist settlers to abide by the law led prominent Israeli journalist and lawyer Ben-Dror Yemini to describe them in a Ynet opinion article as “Israel’s homegrown Hezbollah.” The comparison drew on Lebanon’s struggle to disarm the Iran-backed group and prevent it from dragging the state into wars through attacks against Israel carried out without state approval.
While Shany rejected the characterization, he stressed that Israel’s failure to uphold the rule of law does not absolve other countries of their own obligations. Nevertheless, he said, “in the court of public opinion, it doesn't do Israel much favor to have anarchy in territories it controls and criticize other states for also having anarchy in their own territories.”
Shany stressed that Israel has an obligation under international law to curb the violence, regardless of its position on the legal status of the territories.
“If Israel continues to fail its obligations, it will increasingly face threats of sanctions by third states, which see this as an issue with humanitarian consequences and broader international peace and security implications, because this could send the whole region into a more explosive dynamic,” he said. “So we will probably see more attempts by European countries to sanction Israel, as we saw last month with the 12 states that took this position.”
In September, the United Kingdom announced a ban on goods imported from Israeli settlements, while 11 other countries said they intended to introduce national restrictions or support broader European measures against settlement-produced goods.
Such measures could have economic consequences for Israel by restricting access to foreign markets and affecting businesses operating in settlements. According to the Israel Policy Forum, Israel exported at least $15 billion in goods and services to the 12 countries in 2024. Goods originating in the West Bank, east Jerusalem and the Golan Heights accounted for just short of $45 million of Israeli exports to the UK in 2025.
Sanctions likely to be placed on Israel
Shany warned that further measures could follow, including initiatives at the UN to impose sanctions on Israel and restrict goods and services originating in the territories, as well as potential legal action through international courts.
Beyond the economic impact, the diplomatic fallout could affect how international actors view Israel’s efforts to curb the Palestinian Authority’s payments to prisoners and families of Palestinians involved in attacks, Shany said.
Israel has withheld clearance revenues collected on behalf of the PA, including deductions linked to payments to prisoners and their families, as well as amounts equivalent to funds previously transferred to Gaza. Israel has also enacted legislation providing for compensation to victims of terrorism through deductions from PA revenues and advanced plans for new housing units in the E1 area near Jerusalem.
“There would be a growing view among European countries that the combined effect of these measures is not to motivate the Palestinian Authority to take the allegations against it regarding support for families of terrorists more seriously, but rather to bring about its financial collapse and move further away from a two-state framework,” Shany said.
“The E1 construction plans, along with the violence, are seen as part of this pincer movement by Israel. I think this would encounter increasingly stronger resistance and perhaps efforts by European countries to find other ways to support Palestinian sovereignty.”
Shany also predicted growing efforts by grassroots organizations to pursue legal action against settlers abroad, drawing a parallel with the Hind Rajab Foundation’s efforts to bring complaints against IDF soldiers over alleged crimes in Gaza.
“I'm pretty certain that the weak response by the current Israeli government to this violence is going to also put some wind in the sails of those sorts of initiatives,” he said. “So we may see renewed attempts to go directly after settlers in terms of trying to freeze their assets and to introduce movement restrictions on them.”

Overland lifelines under pressure: Iran’s trade with its neighbours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:11:36 UTC
20:11:36 KST

Iran is turning to its land borders for ways to keep trade moving as the U.S. naval blockade constrains shipping. But these routes are best seen as a buffer, not a substitute for maritime trade. They can help move selected goods, give merchants more options, and support businesses in border regions. They cannot make up for lost oil revenue, and they depend on infrastructure and political cooperation that Iran cannot control alone. The recent suspension of trade at two crossings with Pakistan is a reminder that land routes, too, can be disrupted with little warning.
The blockade and the shift to land
The loss of crude exports is at the heart of the problem. Citing Vortexa, Reuters reported that Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September 2026 and were still at zero in early October. Vortexa estimated that 43 million barrels of Iranian crude were trapped west of the Strait of Hormuz. This is more than a shipping setback: oil exports bring in foreign currency, which road and rail trade in food or machinery cannot replace. The figures refer to seaborne crude, however, and do not mean that every kind of Iranian trade has stopped.
Some petroleum products have still made it out. Reuters, drawing on shipping intelligence, reported that eight LPG tankers and one jet-fuel tanker had left the Gulf of Oman since the blockade was reimposed in July. UANI estimated the LPG cargoes at 4.1 million barrels. These shipments show that the restrictions are not an airtight seal, but they are limited and irregular. U.S. officials also cautioned that a ship passing through does not necessarily mean the blockade was breached; vessels are reviewed individually, and some may be allowed through. For now, these cargoes look like exceptions rather than a dependable route for Iran’s energy exports.
Iran’s push to move more goods by land is already straining key crossings. At Gürbulak, on the Turkey–Iran border, the Associated Press reported that truck numbers had risen from about 200 to 1,200.
Waits on the Iranian side reached 12 to 25 days, and an Iranian trade official said the destination side could not process that many vehicles. Trucks can carry food, machinery parts, chemicals, and other goods, but shifting cargo from ships to roads takes more than finding another route. It requires enough lanes, customs staff, scanners, storage, and coordination on both sides of the border.
Corridors: capacity, not just geography
ISNA’s report on the Maku Free Zone shows why it matters to distinguish planned capacity from actual throughput. The zone’s managing director said it could handle 700 to 1,000 trucks a day, while around 300 to 400 trucks were leaving through the Bazargan crossing at the time. Those numbers describe different things: the zone’s stated capacity is not the same as the number of trucks cleared across the border. Raising the latter would require coordination with Turkey and enough capacity at the crossing itself. The figures point to room for growth, but they do not mean trade can immediately increase by the same amount .
ISNA also reports on the proposed Sarakhs–Cheshmeh Sorayya railway. The project could take 12 to 18 months to build if funding is secured and a contractor is selected; its projected capacity is 15 to 20 million tonnes of freight in its first year. These are estimates, not cargo already moving on an operational line. A separate report describes the railway as part of a planned east–west corridor connecting Iran’s network with Turkey’s. If completed, it could offer another way to move goods across the country. Its usefulness will depend on the project being built, border connections working smoothly, and freight costs being competitive.
West Azerbaijan could also benefit from a broader view of Iran’s border network. IRNA highlights the province’s links with Turkey, Iraq, and Nakhchivan, arguing that its role goes beyond a single crossing. With reliable roads, customs facilities, storage, and logistics services, border areas can connect local businesses to several markets and support employment as well as transit.
But geography alone does not make a region a trade hub. Businesses need goods to move predictably, without delays that make the route too costly to use.
READ: Vance acknowledges ‘failures’ in US handling of Iran war
Neighboring markets and political risk
Iraq shows both the promise of regional trade and its exposure to disruption. Reuters reported that Iran–Iraq trade exceeded $10 billion in 2025, driven largely by Iranian food, consumer goods, and other exports. Trade declined in 2026 as the conflict increased security risks, disrupted crossings, and raised transport costs. Iraq remains an important market, but it is not insulated from regional instability. Routes through the Caucasus and Central Asia could add options, though each has its own infrastructure and border constraints. Having more neighbors does not automatically mean Iran can redirect unlimited cargo to them.
The latest suspension of trade at Pakistan’s Gabd–Rimdan and Taftan crossings makes that point especially clear.
Dawn reported that Pakistan suspended commercial traffic through both crossings, with Balochistan officials citing security concerns, smuggling, and border management. Iran’s foreign ministry described the stoppage as temporary and technical and said talks were under way. Hundreds of trucks carrying LPG, rice, fruit, and other goods were reportedly stranded, although passenger traffic through Rimdan–Gabd continued.
The closure may be temporary, but even a short interruption can mean lost sales, delayed deliveries, and higher costs for traders.
Turkey’s incentives and constraints
Turkey has a clear commercial interest in keeping trade with Iran going, but the size and direction of that trade matter. Türkiye’s foreign ministry puts bilateral trade at $5.5 billion in 2025: Turkish exports to Iran were $3 billion, while imports from Iran were $2.5 billion. Turkish exports include machinery, plastics, chemicals, vehicles, and agricultural products; imports from Iran include natural gas, metals, and agricultural goods. The relationship is significant, but the figures show that the balance favors Turkey. Iranian customs figures may not match Turkish data because the two sides can use different periods, categories, and methods; those figures should not be combined as if they were directly comparable.
Turkey has good reasons to maintain commerce with Iran: Turkish firms gain access to a large neighboring market, and transit can bring further business. But commercial interest does not mean Ankara will accept any level of risk. In September 2026, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned a Turkey-based bank and subsidiaries, alleging that they facilitated transactions for Iranian entities. Later that month, Turkey’s banking regulator revoked the operating license of Iran’s Bank Mellat branch. Reuters noted that Turkey’s official notice did not explicitly link the decision to U.S. pressure. These actions do not show that Turkey is ending trade, but they help explain why banks and businesses may be reluctant to handle Iranian payments.
A buffer, not a substitute
The practical value of Iran’s regional corridors will depend on whether goods can move reliably, not simply on how many routes appear on a map. The Maku figures suggest unused capacity, while the railway remains a proposal with a conditional timeline. Keeping border procedures predictable, coordinating customs, improving transport links, and making payments possible are all necessary if trade is to grow. Otherwise, congestion or a temporary closure can erase the advantage of geographic proximity.
Trade with neighboring countries can keep some supply chains functioning and give merchants alternatives when one route is blocked. But it cannot replace seaborne energy exports or the hard currency they generate. Turkey is likely to remain commercially interested, yet any increase will depend on border capacity, payment access, and how much sanctions risk its firms are willing to take.
Iran’s land corridors can reduce dependence on any one crossing; they cannot, by themselves, offset the economic impact of the naval blockade.

“By any pragmatic or moral measure, Putin has no place at the table with presidents Trump and Xi. The only thing that could earn him that seat is a serious step toward peace, such as accepting a ceasefire proposal before any such meeting,” Sybiha emphasized.
Instead, the minister noted, we are seeing the opposite: an escalation of terror against civilians.
“As long as he [Putin] continues this terror, there should be no place for him at any table,” Sybiha stressed.
According to The Wall Street Journal, citing its sources, Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed that he, US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet next month to discuss the situation in Ukraine, with the aim of securing an end to the war on terms favorable to Moscow.

After MP 'attacked' in the street, our democracy is facing its biggest test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:09:35 UTC
20:09:35 KST

analysis
After Helen Haines 'attack' in the street, Australian democracy is facing its biggest test
"This wasn't an accident."
With those words, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese laid bare the horrifying nature of an attack that has sent shock waves through Australia.
Independent MP Helen Haines was going about her day in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta when a four-wheel drive struck her outside her electorate office.
The 65-year-old, who has represented the people of Indi since 2019, suffered critical injuries in an attack now under police investigation.
A man is in custody, and while it is too early to conclude whether his alleged actions were politically motivated, the possibility alone is deeply disturbing.
Australians are accustomed to seeing their local politicians in the supermarket, at the footy or simply walking down the street.
They knock on doors, hold mobile offices, attend community events and make themselves available to constituents who want to raise concerns or have a chat.
It's easy to be cynical about politicians, but their accessibility is one of the great strengths of Australia's democracy.
That will now be seriously tested.
Loading...
Shock across political spectrum
Albanese was understandably emotional as he spoke about the attack on Haines just hours later.
He was joined by voices from every corner of Australian politics in expressing his horror at the incident and wishing the MP a full recovery.
While careful not to pre-empt the police investigation, Albanese also took the opportunity to repeat his calls to turn down the temperature of political debate.
He has often said parliamentarians should be able to carry out their work without fear of threats or intimidation, and warned about the consequences of personal vilification and increasingly aggressive political commentary.
Those concerns are not confined to the prime minister.
For years, the Australian Federal Police has been highlighting an alarming rise in threats directed at politicians, their families and staff.
The latest figures show the AFP received 1,067 reports of threatening, harassing, nuisance or offensive behaviour involving federal parliamentarians, high office holders and protected locations in the past financial year.
That was a 12 per cent increase on the previous year and almost double the 555 reports recorded in 2021-22.
Not every report involves a credible threat of violence, and the figures cover more than MPs and senators alone.
But they demonstrate the scale of the hostility increasingly confronting people in public office.
Loading...
AFP's warning
In March last year, then AFP commissioner Reece Kershaw delivered a sober warning to a parliamentary committee about the threats facing politicians ahead of the federal election.
He revealed some male politicians had been sent bullets in the mail, while female parliamentarians were subjected to particularly disturbing abuse, including threats of sexual violence.
In some cases, the threats extended to their children.
Just this month, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC she expected "high office holders and politicians will continue to be targeted by those who hold grievances".
She said while terror investigators were increasingly seeing cases with "ideological" motivations, another factor was emerging: "grievance".
Barrett said people who were feeling distanced and alone were "looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose".
"We are seeing a bit of a shift there that the grievance is what's actually driving them and then they're looking for some sort of ideological motivation to attach to," she said.
Examples mount across parties
There has been no shortage of examples demonstrating why police are concerned.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has spoken publicly about the threats directed at her and her family, and the security arrangements she believes are necessary to protect her.
Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has faced threats serious enough to prompt additional security arrangements at his home and electorate office.
Just last week, Labor minister Anne Aly revealed she had received 19 death threats in a week.
Others have faced criminal threats serious enough to result in charges.
Earlier this year, a Sydney man was charged after allegedly threatening to kill a federal parliamentarian over the phone.
Last year, Victorian men were charged in separate cases involving alleged death threats against federal MPs, including antisemitic abuse.
These are not isolated concerns confined to one political party, one side of an ideological divide or one contentious policy debate.
Nor are they limited to the anonymous abuse politicians have long endured online.
The rise in incidents has raised the question of whether elected representatives can safely do their jobs.
Loading
Warnings come to pass
The AFP has established specialist investigative teams to respond to the growing threat, while security arrangements for individual politicians have come under greater scrutiny.
But there are limits to what even the most extensive protective measures can achieve without changing the way politicians interact with the public.
Police officers stationed outside every electorate office or security checks at every community event would represent a very different Australian democracy.
Voters are entitled to be angry with their elected representatives, but there is an important distinction between robust debate and intimidation or threats.
Police must now be allowed to establish the facts of the attack on Haines.
But the incident has brought into sharp focus the safety concerns that security agencies and parliamentarians have been warning about for years.
