Did an ancient Egyptian god inspire the Oscar statuette? A 2,700-year-old bronze offers a clue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:09:23 UTC
20:09:23 KST

A 2,700-year-old Egyptian statuette of the god Ptah, which recently sold at Frieze Masters in London, may hold a clue to the origin story of the Oscar statuette.
Could the iconic design of one of Hollywood’s most coveted awards owe a debt to an ancient Egyptian god?
A 2,700-year-old bronze figure of Ptah, the Egyptian creator god and master architect, has drawn attention at Frieze Masters in London, where an antiquities dealer has uncovered a possible link between the sculpture and the design of the Oscar statuette.
The figure was once owned by newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst, a friend of Cedric Gibbons, the art director who designed the Oscar statuette in 1928.
Antiquities dealer Rupert Wace says he discovered the connection while researching the object's provenance ahead of the fair. "We found out that this particular piece was with (Randolph) Hearst and the chap who designed the Oscar called Cedric Gibbons was a frequent visitor and friend of Hearst's, and would have visited him both in Saint Simeon in California and his place in New York where he had a specific Egyptian collection room."
Cedric Gibbons, who died in 1960, never confirmed directly what inspired his famous design - but the similarities are striking to see, and he was in the right place at the right time
"The whole thing is supposition in a sense. We put two and two together and either made four or five. We can't prove it. It's uncannily similar and was in the right place with the right people at the right time for it to be more than just a coincidence," explains Wace.
And even if its Hollywood connection remains a mystery, the statuette still remains a significant and fascinating piece of ancient Egyptian art. It dates back to the late period of ancient Egypt, shortly before it was conquered by the Achaemenid Persian Empire.
"Without the history, this piece would still be fantastic. It's a very fine bronze. It's got a very good history, collecting history. So the extra Hollywood angle is the cherry on the cake," says Wace.
The statuette was sold on the opening day of Frieze Masters for an undisclosed sum.
Frieze Masters 2026 ran from 14 to 18 October in Regent's Park London, hosting an estimated 60,000 people.

Majority of Ukrainians oppose ceding Donbas for security guarantees, ready to endure war – KIIS poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:08:51 EEST
20:08:51 KST

An absolute majority (61%) of Ukrainians continue to consider it categorically unacceptable to cede full control of Donbas to the Russian Federation in exchange for security guarantees, while 35% are open to such a concession, according to a survey conducted on October 8–16 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
It is noted that compared to late July–early August, when a similar survey was conducted, there were no statistically significant changes. However, on October 8–9, prior to the announcement of the "diesel deal" between the U.S and Russia and subsequent pressure on Ukraine, 57% were categorically opposed to giving up Donbas in exchange for security guarantees.
Across all macro-regions, a half or majority rejects the proposal to withdraw Ukrainian troops in exchange for security guarantees. The highest proportion of those willing to approve such an option is among residents of the East (primarily Kharkiv region), where 45% generally allow for approval, while 51% are categorically against. In other regions, including the South and Lower Dnipro region, 60–66% categorically reject the proposal. In Kyiv, 66% are opposed.
When asked how much longer Ukrainians are willing to endure the war, virtually the same percentage (62%) stated for as long as necessary. Another 4% spoke of 1 year. A shorter timeframe (several months to six months) was cited by 21%, while the remaining 13% were undecided. Among respondents surveyed on October 8–9, 60% answered that they were ready to endure as long as necessary.
Only 10% of respondents expect the war to end by the end of the current year, 2026. Another 13% expect the war to end in the first half of 2027, and 17% by the end of 2027 (bringing the total to 40%). Meanwhile, 39% expect the war to end in 2028 or later, with 21% holding no definite opinion on the matter.
"The results of our survey once again demonstrate that many in both the West and the East still have a limited understanding of Ukraine and Ukrainians (and still seem to view us through the lens of Russian expertise). As we can see, the Russian enemy, through its despicable ballistic missile and drone strikes, is unable to break the spirit and will of Ukrainians; Ukrainians still insist on continuing the resistance. The same applies to pressure from the other side—attempts by some of our partners to pressure Ukrainians into accepting terms of virtual surrender (blushing behind empty and unfulfillable promises of something in the future). Once again, Ukrainians want peace, but between surrender now with an almost inevitable risk of future Russian genocide and resistance now with the hope of achieving acceptable terms, Ukrainians choose to continue resisting," noted Anton Hrushetsky, Executive Director of KIIS.
The survey was conducted via computer-assisted telephone interviews (CATI) based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers across all government-controlled territories of Ukraine, surveying 1,031 respondents aged 18 and older. Under standard conditions, the formal statistical margin of error (with a probability of 0.95 and taking into account a design effect of 1.3) did not exceed 4% for indicators close to 50% and 1.7% for indicators close to 5%, though certain systematic deviations are added under war conditions.

Russia arrests two men who ran a website for train enthusiasts. Now they face up to 10 years in prison for allegedly compromising ‘critical infrastructure.’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:08:05 UTC
20:08:05 KST

Russia arrests two men who ran a website for train enthusiasts. Now they face up to 10 years in prison for allegedly compromising ‘critical infrastructure.’
Moscow’s Dorogomilovsky District Court has ordered the arrest of Denis Yeskov and Anatoly Nagornov, administrators of the train photo site RailGallery, the press service of Moscow’s courts reported on October 16.
Yeskov and Nagornov are charged under Russia’s criminal statute against unlawful interference with critical information infrastructure causing serious consequences, which carries a prison sentence of five to 10 years. According to investigators, Yeskov and Nagornov gained unlawful access to a trade secret belonging to an organization, copied information stored “in a critical infrastructure facility of the Russian Federation,” and posted it on their own site.
The specialized Telegram channel “1520. Vse o zh/d” (All About Railways) noticed on the evening of October 15 that RailGallery had stopped loading, and the site remains inaccessible. The court had already ordered the arrest of the site’s administrators on October 14, according to case files published on the court’s website.
Telegram channels also carried a statement from RailGallery’s editorial board confirming the detentions:
We are all in shock over what happened, and this news came as a complete surprise to us. I think each of us is now feeling confused and trying to make sense of what happened, understand what occurred, and what to expect going forward.
At the moment, the situation remains uncertain. It’s too early to say what will happen to the site going forward, whether its usual operation can be maintained, or who will take over its management. Right now we don’t have enough information to draw any conclusions or make assumptions about the future. For many, RailGallery is not just a resource, but part of daily life, a place to communicate, share experience, and bring together people with shared interests. So it’s only natural that what’s happening is causing concern.
RailGallery launched in 2022 after the popular railway photo site TrainPix shut down. the independent Russian news outlet Mediazona reported that TrainPix was created by Ukrainians, who announced its closure in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. TrainPix’s administrators deleted the site’s entire archive and urged people to support the Ukrainian army.
Yeskov spoke about RailGallery’s launch in August 2022, saying that within six months, the Russian community had restored half of TrainPix’s archive, or about 150,000 photographs. By the end of 2022, more than 3,200 users had registered on RailGallery and posted 194,000 photographs, including 161,500 restored images. According to “1520. Vse o zh/d,” the site became more than a photo gallery: an extensive database on the history and operation of railway equipment from various countries.
In 2023, Dossier Center published an investigation into an armored train that Vladimir Putin presumably rides. The investigation included a photo of a train belonging to the company Grand Service Express, taken from RailGallery’s site. Journalists found special communications antennas on the roofs of the train cars, and the train was pulled by three locomotives at once. Whether Putin actually rides the train pictured remains unknown.

'O Captain, my Captain': Should Congress make room for Amarinder Singh again?

Rahul Gandhi named Captain Amarinder Singh as his favourite BJP leader.
NEW DELHI: Can a party install a new captain, retain the old team and still leave the door open for a former captain who quit the dressing room five years ago? With the leadership chanting 'O Captain! My Captain!' the Punjab Congress seems to be attempting to navigate that question precisely ahead of the 2027 assembly elections.With Pargat Singh at the helm, Raja Warring and Charanjit Singh Channi 'promised' an active role in the campaign; Sachin Pilot has also left the door open to Captain Amarinder Singh's possible return. Can Congress accommodate its old captain without unsettling the new captain and the team?Congress general secretary Sachin Pilot, the party's Punjab in-charge, on October 15 offered a line that will keep speculation alive: "Politics mein 'kuch bhi ho sakta hai' (anything is possible in politics)."Asked about the possibility of former Punjab chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh returning to Congress, Pilot praised him as a leader who had served Punjab "well" and was "a man of a very tall stature". Amarinder Singh on his relationship with Congress leadership.
The remark came less than a fortnight after Congress appointed former India hockey captain Pargat Singh as Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) president, replacing Amrinder Singh Raja Warring on October 2. It also followed Amarinder's public criticism of the BJP, the party he joined in 2022, over its handling of Punjab.So, is Congress merely acknowledging political speculation, or could the old captain's name return to the party's calculations? The 'Uncle Amarinder' connection
The latest speculation began with an unexpected public greeting. The former CM responded that his personal relationship with the Gandhi family would remain, but his political commitment was to the BJP. In a September interview with The Tribune, he said he remained fond of Rahul, Priyanka and Sonia Gandhi, while distinguishing personal relationships from politics."My personal relationship with the Gandhis will always be there, but my political commitment is to the BJP," he said."If tomorrow I tell Rahul, Priyanka or Sonia personally that I'll be there for them no matter what, I mean it and I'm happy to help," he added.The indirect exchange was notable because Amarinder Singh's departure from Congress in September 2021 followed a bitter confrontation with the party's state leadership. "When you've been with somebody for fifty years, they remain your party. I never asked to leave them; they asked me to leave," Captain Amarinder Singh said recently.
Amarinder's BJP discontent
The former chief minister's recent criticism of the BJP has provided the immediate backdrop to the comeback speculation.In an interview published by The Tribune on September 25, Amarinder said the BJP had not consulted him on Punjab politics or policy despite his long experience in the state."I haven't had a single meeting on Punjab policy or politics with them in the last five years," he said.He was more direct about his decision to join the party: "I have gained nothing by joining BJP."
The political career of Captain Amarinder Singh.
Amarinder also argued that the BJP did not adequately understand Punjab and should consult leaders familiar with the state's political and social realities. He advocated an alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal, pointing to the BJP's historical position as the junior partner in that relationship.In the same interview, he described himself as going through "difficult times", without elaborating.Yet he has also made clear that dissatisfaction does not automatically mean departure. Amarinder Singh said it was his duty to tell the BJP what he thought about Punjab and that criticising the party's approach did not mean he was quitting.
From a 77-seat victory to a bitter exit
Captain Amarinder Singh's record in Congress spans decades, including two terms as Punjab CM, from 2002 to 2007 and from 2017 to 2021.In the 2017 assembly election, Congress won 77 of Punjab's 117 seats under his leadership, returning to power after a decade. But the relationship between Amarinder Singh and the state leadership deteriorated, particularly amid his prolonged confrontation with Navjot Singh Sidhu.Sidhu became Punjab Congress president in July 2021. The conflict intensified over leadership and the government's handling of election promises. On September 18, 2021, Amarinder resigned as chief minister after the Congress high command called a meeting of the party's legislators to discuss leadership.
Sachin Pilot kept the door open to Amarinder Singh's return to the Congress.
He subsequently left Congress and launched the Punjab Lok Congress (PLC). In the 2022 assembly election, the PLC allied with the BJP, but the alliance failed to win a seat for Amarinder Singh's party. AAP swept the election with 92 seats, while Congress was reduced to 18.Amarinder joined the BJP in September 2022, and his PLC was merged with it.The electoral record provides the context for the renewed speculation, but it does not establish that bringing Amarinder back would reverse Congress's fortunes. The party's 2022 defeat followed a wider political shift in Punjab, including AAP's rise and Congress's internal divisions.
Pargat Singh's leadership test
Meanwhile, Pargat Singh's appointment has put a new leader at the head of a state unit that has repeatedly struggled with factional disputes. A former India hockey captain and three-time MLA from Jalandhar Cantonment, he was associated with Sidhu during the 2021 confrontation with Amarinder Singh and had publicly questioned the previous government's delivery on election promises.Pilot called Pargat a "unifying captain", saying the new president has reached out to state leaders and received public support. He has also invoked the team metaphor to describe Congress's approach to the election."You are one captain who's got a fantastic team, and the captain is only as strong as his team," Pilot said he had told Pargat. His appointment, replacing Warring as state chief, was particularly important in the backdrop of an internal tussle between Warring and Channi camps.Punjab Congress has spent months grappling with a bitter power struggle between the camps of state chief Amarinder Singh Raja Warring and former CM Charanjit Singh Channi. The feud spilled into public view through rival sloganeering, poster wars, clashes at party events and boycotts during visits by then state in-charge Bhupesh Baghel. The high command's July compromise, retaining Warring while appointing Channi to head the campaign committee, failed to end the friction. After Sachin Pilot replaced Baghel as Punjab in-charge in September, Warring eventually resigned on October 2, and Pargat Singh was appointed the new state chief.With the Congress leadership now sending the open-door signal to Captain Amarinder, the question is how Pargat's team would accommodate a strong-headed former CM with a history in the party.Moreover, the issue is not limited to Amarinder Singh. In the upcoming months, Congress must also manage the transition from Warring, who led the state unit from April 2022 until October 2026.
No CM face, but several leadership questions
Congress has also decided against projecting a CM face for the 2027 Punjab election.Pilot said the party would fight as a team and decide who should lead the state after securing the mandate, following consultations with workers, leaders and MLAs."We are fighting together as a team. Let the team win. And then we'll decide who gets to do what job," he said.
In June, Amarinder Singh shared that Rahul Gandhi wished him on his birthday.
The party has several experienced leaders, including Partap Singh Bajwa, Sukhjinder Randhawa, Charanjit Singh Channi and Warring. Pargat's appointment adds a new organisational chief to that mix, while the question of Amarinder's possible return remains unconfirmed.For the high command, the practical issue would be defining the role of each leader without undermining the other.
What could Captain Amarinder's return mean
Amarinder Singh's long tenure in Punjab politics, his experience as CM and his association with national security and border-state issues are part of his public political profile. A return could give Congress another experienced voice in its campaign, while his criticism of the BJP could offer a new line of political debate. The Congress may gain from his name, polularity and political history but it is unlikely that he would have any active role owing to his age.But the political costs would depend on the terms of any return. His 2021 exit followed a major leadership confrontation, and Pargat was part of the state leadership aligned with Sidhu during that period. Reconciliation would therefore involve not just Amarinder Singh and the Gandhi family, but a state unit whose leadership has changed since he left.
It would also raise questions about the position of leaders who remained with Congress through the subsequent elections and organisational changes. Warring's emphasis on youth representation, Pargat's task of consolidating the state unit and Pilot's insistence on collective leadership all point to issues that would need to be addressed.For now, there is no confirmed proposal to bring Captain Amarinder back, no announced role for him and no indication that talks have taken place or are under way.Pilot's "anything is possible" may keep the question open, but the party's immediate task remains to get the current team working together before Punjab votes in 2027.

What do travellers want from AI? Room rates, not personalised itineraries, study says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:02:35 UTC
20:02:35 KST

Just 44% of travellers feel comfortable letting artificial intelligence plan out their holidays.
Conversations around artificial intelligence (AI) and its uses are going on in every industry, from health and transport to banking and art.
The travel industry isn’t immune to this, and you’ll no doubt already have encountered it when researching a trip, whether that’s through AI overviews, chatbots or even influencers.
But while plenty of us are happy to use the technology, what we’re willing to use it for only goes so far, with just 44% of travellers saying they would let AI plan out their itinerary.
That’s according to a survey from Mews, a hospitality management software used by hoteliers, with 3,250 tourists polled across France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, the UK and the US.
According to the poll, the most common uses for AI are watching hotel rates – with 63% of travellers using it for this purpose – and translating on the spot (56%).
Using data for customisation
One of the best uses for AI is letting it pull on various data sources to compile a complete picture without wasting time, and in the ultra-competitive world of travel, this means using it for customisation.
But, perhaps unsurprisingly, travellers aren’t a big fan of AI using data collected on them through online behaviour or social media data being used by hotels, with 43% consenting to the former and 34% to the latter.
Travellers are, however, happy with AI using stated preferences (61%) and past stay history (56%).
How comfortable a traveller is with the use of AI varies from country to country, too, with Italian travellers being the most optimistic about AI's role five years from now (51% vs. 39% on average), with Spain having the most positive attitude towards AI (58%).
“Having clever technology is great, but firstly, we should know whether guests want a task done for them or want to be part of it. Get that wrong and even good AI feels intrusive,” Josef Starýchfojtů, Chief Product and Technology Officer (CPTO) of Mews, said.
“We're building for human hospitality: technology handles the mundane, repetitive admin, and hotel teams have more time for their guests."

Women may be at greater risk of AI job losses. Telephone switch operators and PCs show why.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:02:34 UTC
20:02:34 KST

Decades before Siri or Alexa or ChatGPT, there was a real person, almost always a woman, at the center of the information world. She was so vital, most long-distance communication could not happen without her.
She was the telephone switch operator, and at one time she was part of the single largest occupation for white, U.S.-born women under age 20.
Today, that job doesn't exist.
The world is struggling to figure out what the dawn of artificial intelligence means for society, culture and the economy. A lot of ordinary Americans are just wondering what it means for their jobs.
The history of technological progress — from automated telephone switches to the introduction of the washing machine and the personal computer — can offer some guidance. And that guidance suggests women are likely to be among the most affected by AI.
"AI is focused on routine tasks and numbers and finding patterns, and those types of jobs are the clerical, administrative jobs that a lot of women hold,'' said Ariane Hegewisch, a senior research fellow at the Institute for Women's Policy Research. "It's still 90% of secretaries and clerical workers who are women."
New research backs this up. The International Labour Organization in March concluded that nearly one in 10 women in high-income countries works in occupations at the highest risk from AI.
The invention that made operators obsolete
In the 1940s, nearly 95% of America's telephone operators were female. It was a relatively well-paying job for women at the time, and a complicated one: It took months of training to be able to handle the several hundred calls an hour that could come in at peak times. Operators were expected to be speedy, precise — and polite.
These women were hit hard when AT&T introduced the automated telephone switch. It was one of the largest automation investments in history — a close analog to the massive AI investment now underway — and created one of the biggest technological shocks the nation had ever seen.
In the decades after the automatic switch was popularized, an estimated 75,000 operator jobs vanished.
Economists James Feigenbaum from Boston University and Daniel P. Gross from Duke University's Fuqua School of Business studied census and paycheck data from the time and followed local employment trends along the path of AT&T's rolling investment in switches across the nation.
"The effect of this shock on incumbent operators was to dispossess many of their jobs and careers," they wrote in 2020. Many switchboard operators wound up in lower-paying jobs — or dropped out of the workforce entirely, they found.
Economist David Autor says this outcome reflects the reality that many workers are already in their highest and best-paying occupation. When the job goes away, the next step is often down.
"Most people are not changing careers very often. They make their career decisions early, and they stick with those careers," he said. "If those careers, if the value of that work … suddenly goes out of fashion, becomes technologically obsolete, they're going to, in general, do something not as good."
But Feigenbaum and Gross also discovered that the next generation of women fared better.
"Future workers found work in other fields, often taking up similar-quality jobs," they wrote, as the younger workers were "more adaptive to an evolving labor market … Anxiety over the opportunities available to future generations proved to be somewhat misplaced."
In other words: One type of job went away, but other work emerged over time that was just as good.
'Engines of liberation'
By the 1950s, another technological innovation would come along and have a profound effect on women: the washing machine.
Dubbed "engines of liberation" in a seminal paper on the topic by University of Pennsylvania economist Jeremy Greenwood and others, washing machines and other appliances dramatically reduced the time women spent on unpaid housework. That meant time could be reallocated to a paycheck outside the home, even as women's responsibility for the home remained.
From 1950 to 1980, as gender norms changed, the number of employed women in the U.S. grew by more than 25 million. Their participation rate, or share of the female population in the labor force, grew to 52% from 34%. At the same time, 16 million more men found work, though the male participation rate dropped by 5 percentage points.
The relevant question for the AI boom today: How did the economy suddenly find jobs for these women? If AI creates a vast new pool of available workers, can the economy put them to work?
First, the very entry of women into the workforce meant demand for tasks once done at home moved into the paid economy, services like childcare and food preparation. Second, as the nation grew wealthier, other employment opportunities for women emerged in the service economy — in retail, restaurants, leisure and hospitality, and even some professional services. And third, as American businesses grew, they needed more people to handle the paperwork — everything from payroll to customer accounts.
Changes to the economy and businesses were partly related to the entry of women into the workforce, but it was also partly random luck that the U.S. was booming and businesses were changing to need more office workers.
"Between 1940 and 1980, there was a ton of new work created in the U.S. economy, and it was in office and clerical work that was accessible to people with a high school education,'' Autor said.
The rise of the PC
The next big revolution affecting women in the workplace was the personal computer.
Before PCs arrived on the scene, women were the backbone of office infrastructure. According to the 1980 U.S. census, nearly 4.7 million Americans worked as secretaries, stenographers and typists. More than 98% were women.
When IBM introduced the personal computer in 1981, followed by the advent of Microsoft Word just two years later, some of the middlemen, or in this case, middlewomen, became obsolete. It didn't eliminate writing, filing or editing. It simply shifted a big chunk of those tasks from dedicated clerical workers to others in the office — executives could type their own reports, book their own travel and print their own papers.
But the PC wasn't entirely bad news for women in the workforce. Studies show women were already more likely than men to be using a computer at work at the dawn of the PC era. The PC put new tools at their fingertips: spreadsheets and databases and general computing power. While many roles were eliminated, many women adapted and found new ways to use the emerging technology to make themselves indispensable to their employers.
That's a potential outcome for AI. In some cases, it will eliminate tasks but not entire jobs, enhancing the time and ability of a worker to do the remaining value-added jobs that only humans can do.
A 2022 paper by Marcus Dillender and Eliza Forsythe found that when companies adopted software to do office and administrative work, it resulted in a 1% decline in employment in the sector but a 3% increase in wages for college graduates.
Many more women have earned college and advanced degrees, and hold managerial jobs, than when other technologies ripped through the economy, offering some potential protection from automation. But maybe not for long: One of the promises of AI is that it will move up the value chain of the jobs performed by humans.
Whatever capabilities the new technology may have now, the outlook is unclear because, Hegewisch says, somewhat ominously, "AI can learn."

‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’: What does the French student protest slogan mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:01:55 UTC
20:01:55 KST

A Snapchat message, which students believe came from an undercover police officer, has become the rallying cry of a youth movement that has now spread to Belgium and Italy.
It has been scrawled on cardboard placards outside blockaded schools, shared in parody videos tens of thousands of times and repeated by Greta Thunberg. In the space of a few weeks, "Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres" has become the unofficial slogan of France’s high school protests.
Taken literally, the phrase means very little, and that is the point.
What does ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’ mean?
"Bismillah" is Arabic for "in the name of God". Muslims traditionally say it before beginning a task, and in everyday French slang it can mean something closer to "let’s go".
"C’est les ténèbres" translates as "it’s the darkness". Among young people it is slang for a situation that is catastrophic or grim.
Put together, the phrase is nonsensical - "In the name of God, it’s the darkness". Students say that is exactly why it caught on. They are mocking someone trying, and failing, to sound like them.
Where did the slogan come from?
The phrase comes from a screenshot of a Snapchat conversation that began circulating in early October, while students were using the app to organise school blockades.
In the message, a user named "Mamadou" asks to join a group: “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?"
The message was accompanied by Algerian flag emojis.
Other screenshots showed similar accounts asking students where blockades would take place and who was selling fireworks and smoke grenades.
To many students, the clumsy mix of Arabic, street slang and national flags gave the game away. They concluded that the messages were written by police officers posing as teenagers to infiltrate private protest groups.
Did police really infiltrate student Snapchat groups?
This has not been proven. Neither the police nor the interior ministry in France has commented on the screenshots, and nobody has independently verified who was behind the accounts.
Some internet users claimed to have traced the accounts to locations near police stations, but those claims have not been verified. Some of the circulating screenshots may themselves be hoaxes or parodies.
Why are French students protesting?
The movement began in Créteil, south-east of Paris, on 18 September and quickly spread nationwide. A range of student grievances lie at the heart of the movement, including long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down schools and teacher absences.
Many argue that these problems hit working-class suburbs and minority communities hardest. Around 400 schools were closed by blockades on 2 October alone.
The student protests fed into the nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living on Saturday 17 October, which ended in some of the worst rioting and looting France has seen in years.
Has the slogan spread outside France?
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg used it during a visit to striking students in Seine-Saint-Denis, north of Paris, on 13 October, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.
On 9 October, it appeared on placards at a union-led demonstration in Brussels against the Belgian government’s budget cuts. There, it was used as a gesture of solidarity with French students rather than a reference to the infiltration claims.
In Italy, ANSA reported that the phrase appeared at student demonstrations in Bologna on 15 October. It was heard again in Milan over the weekend of 17 and 18 October, when protests in Piazza del Duomo also turned to looting and students from a french school in Berlin were photographed holding a banner of the slogan.

BERLIN, October 19. /TASS/. A large oil tanker, the Sled, temporarily lost propulsion in the Baltic Sea due to an engine failure, the Bild newspaper reported.
The incident occurred between the German island of Ruegen and the Danish island of Moen. Late Saturday night into Sunday morning, at around 01:30 a.m. local time (11:30 p.m. GMT), the tanker dramatically reduced its speed and subsequently anchored half a nautical mile from the border of Denmark's territorial waters. Due to strong easterly winds drifting the disabled vessel toward Danish waters, the Vessel Traffic Service Center in Warnemuende dispatched the rescue tug VB Bremen Fighter from the German port of Mukran to the incident scene. By Monday morning, the tanker managed to restore its maneuverability and has currently resumed its westward transit.
The tanker was en route from the Russian port of Primorsk to Skagen in Denmark, the newspaper said.

Saudi Arabia is learning the hard way: they can’t count on Trump for protection | Mohamad Bazzi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:00:55 UTC
20:00:55 KST

For years, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump and his son-in-law and former top adviser, Jared Kushner. The prince understood the president’s transactional approach to power: he signed deals to buy billions of dollars’ worth of US weapons and invested billions more in American companies.
Days after Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, Prince Mohammed pledged to expand investment and trade with the US by $600bn over four years. He later promised to increase that investment to nearly $1tn, although it wasn’t entirely clear how Saudi Arabia would manage to plough a sum close to the kingdom’s entire annual GDP into a foreign economy over a few years.
On a visit to Washington last November, Prince Mohammed sealed a defense cooperation agreement with the US and signed a deal for the monarchy to buy dozens of F-35 stealth fighter jets, America’s most advanced warplane.
Behind this flurry of deal-making, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler expected the US to defend the kingdom if it was attacked, as Washington has done in the past. But Prince Mohammed, like the leaders of other Arab petrostates who have invested billions of dollars to appease Trump, is learning a hard lesson: never count on Trump to protect you.
Over the summer, Trump’s war against Iran rekindled a years-long conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen. Last month, as the Houthis intensified their attacks on Saudi territory and the kingdom’s Yemeni allies, the prince called Trump multiple times in September, urging him to launch US airstrikes against the Houthis, who are allied with Iran.
For now, Trump has resisted appeals from Prince Mohammed to drag American forces into the Houthi-Saudi battle – one of the best foreign policy decisions of an otherwise disastrous second term.
But the conflict is escalating in dangerous ways. On 10 October, the Houthis fired a cruise missile at the international airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300.
After that attack, when reporters in Washington asked Trump whether he would be more willing to order US strikes against Yemeni rebels, he was non-committal. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” he said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision.”
The Houthi-Saudi conflagration is the latest illustration of Trump’s decision to attack Iran spiraling into an unpredictable regional conflict, as Middle East experts and some US intelligence officials warned would happen. It also reveals that Saudi Arabia and other Arab Gulf countries can’t rely on the Trump administration to protect them, even after they have spent tens of billions of dollars to buy American weapons and build US bases – some of which were decimated by Iranian attacks over the past seven months.
Trump’s resistance to ordering US attacks on the Houthis has been particularly embarrassing for Prince Mohammed. Billions of dollars in Saudi investments have been directed into Kushner’s private equity firm and the president’s family business, the Trump Organization. Now Saudi Arabia is being rewarded with lukewarm US support against Yemeni rebels.
For now, Trump seems worried about expanding the US role in a regional war that is deeply unpopular among Americans, including segments of Trump’s own Maga base that believed his repeated promises not to start new wars. The Iran conflict has increased gasoline and other energy prices, driving up the US inflation rate to 3.7% in September, weeks before midterm elections where Republicans are facing widespread anger over the cost of living.
It’s unclear if Trump will continue to resist launching airstrikes against the Houthis after next month’s elections, when Democrats could win control of both houses of Congress. If the Houthis keep up their attacks on Saudi infrastructure and capture more territory held by Yemen’s Saudi-aligned government, Trump could face more pressure to intervene from the Saudis and hawkish Republicans. And he would be less constrained by worries about expanding the Iran war shortly before the midterms.
Prince Mohammed, who is reeling from the war’s impact on Saudi oil exports, could also ratchet up pressure on Trump by threatening to withhold Saudi investments in the US economy and the president’s family business. That’s another danger underlying Trump’s corrupt and transactional style of governing: US interests can be subsumed by wealthy autocrats who try to exploit Trump through his extensive business ventures. In this case, rather than bombing one side to help another, there’s a clear US interest in promoting diplomacy and de-escalating the Houthi-Saudi conflict.
Early in Trump’s first term, the Saudi leader developed a relationship with the president and his key advisers, especially Kushner. In May 2017, Trump upended tradition and chose Saudi Arabia as the first stop of his maiden overseas trip as president. The Saudis realized that Trump craved flattery: they feted him with banquets in gilded palaces and awarded him the kingdom’s highest civilian honor.
At the time, Prince Mohammed was consolidating power as the monarchy’s de facto ruler under his ailing father, King Salman. The prince had also presided over a series of destructive regional policies, including a Saudi-led invasion of Yemen in 2015, and a subsequent campaign to blockade the kingdom’s tiny neighbor, Qatar.
Trump and Kushner proved to be invaluable allies to the young, ambitious royal. In October 2018, Jamal Khashoggi, a dissident Saudi journalist, was assassinated inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul by a 15-member hit team, who dismembered his body with a bone saw.
US intelligence agencies quickly concluded that Prince Mohammed had ordered the killing, but Trump protected the royal from US sanctions and pressure from outraged members of Congress.
A few years later, the prince found a way to return Trump’s favor. In January 2021, after a mob of Trump supporters stormed the US Capitol in an attempt to overturn the presidential election results, US banks and several large companies distanced themselves from the Trump Organization. But Saudi Arabia stood by Trump while he was out of power, generating real estate deals and new golf partnerships that helped Trump’s family business at one of its weakest points.
After the uproar over Khashoggi’s assassination, the prince stayed away from the US for seven years – until Trump returned to office and invited him for a victory tour last November. Trump rolled out the red carpet, hosting Prince Mohammed for lunch with top administration officials at the White House. Trump also held a black-tie dinner with business executives who were eager to solicit new investments from the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund, which is controlled by the crown prince.
Beyond the extravagant welcome, Trump also defended Prince Mohammed when a reporter asked about Khashoggi’s killing. “A lot of people didn’t like that gentleman that you’re talking about,” Trump said, referring to the murdered journalist, who was a US permanent resident and contributor to the Washington Post.
“Things happen,” Trump added, as he sat next to the Saudi leader in the Oval Office. He insisted that the prince “knew nothing about” Khashoggi’s assassination – despite the CIA reaching the opposite conclusion during Trump’s first term.
Trump spent years defending and protecting his Saudi ally and benefactor. In the coming weeks, Trump risks expanding US involvement in a disastrous regional war to help the prince.
- Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Hagop Kevorkian Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

====================================================================================================

Researchers identify female-specific and male-specific genetic risks for anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:00:14 UTC
20:00:14 KST

Men and women share much of the underlying genetic risk for anxiety, but researchers have now identified distinct genetic pathways specific to each sex. These biological differences help explain why females and males often experience and report anxiety in different ways. The findings were published in Psychological Medicine.
Anxiety disorders, which include generalized anxiety, panic disorders, specific phobias, and agoraphobia, are among the most common mental health conditions worldwide. They affect nearly a third of the global population at some point in their lives. Females are diagnosed with anxiety disorders at roughly twice the rate of males.
Men and women also tend to display different symptoms. Females more frequently report internalizing symptoms and experience depression alongside their anxiety. Males often exhibit externalizing behaviors and are more likely to use substances as a coping strategy.
Past research on these differences has often focused on cultural norms, hormonal fluctuations, or differences in brain activation. Studies examining the genetic roots of anxiety have yielded mixed results, with some suggesting stronger genetic influences in females and others finding equal risk. Previous genome-wide studies generally combined data from men and women, an approach that can hide genetic risks applying exclusively to one sex.
Lead authors Jihua Hu and Brittany L. Mitchell, researchers at the QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute and The University of Queensland in Australia, conducted a massive study to see if common genetic factors operate differently in men and women. They analyzed genetic and health data from 455,487 individuals of European ancestry using the UK Biobank and the All of Us research programs.
The team first conducted a combined analysis of the entire group. They compared the genetic profiles of individuals with a history of anxiety against those without any mental distress diagnoses. In this group, the researchers identified 56 specific genetic variants associated with anxiety. Genetic variants are slight differences in the DNA sequence that occur naturally between individuals.
Following this initial analysis, the team separated the data to run distinct tests for males and females. The female group included 281,831 individuals, and the male group included 173,656 individuals. The researchers found 21 genetic variants associated with anxiety in females, compared to just five in males. Only a single genetic variant overlapped between the two groups.
The team then calculated the heritability of anxiety for both groups. They found that males exhibit a higher overall threshold for developing the disorder. This indicates that men generally require a greater accumulation of genetic vulnerability and environmental factors to cross the threshold into clinical anxiety. When calculating heritability based on real-world population prevalence, the overall genetic contribution appeared higher in females.
To understand the biological functions of these genetic variants, the researchers mapped them to specific genes. They discovered entirely different biological pathways associated with anxiety in men compared to women. In females, the identified genes were heavily involved in chromatin regulation and olfactory transduction.
Chromatin regulation is a cellular process that packages DNA and controls gene expression, which can influence how sensitive an individual is to environmental stressors. Olfactory transduction involves the body’s ability to process smells.
Evolutionarily, the sense of smell is tightly linked to threat detection and survival. Odor information is processed directly in the amygdala, a brain region central to stress responses. Previous psychological studies have shown that women with anxiety often report heightened sensitivity to smells, a finding that aligns with these genetic associations.
In males, the genes tied to anxiety were primarily involved in lipoprotein metabolism. Lipoproteins help transport and process fats in the body. When a person experiences stress, the body typically mobilizes energy resources, often increasing lipoprotein levels as part of a physical fight-or-flight response. Because male and female metabolisms process fats differently due to sex hormones, these genetic variations provide a biological rationale for why anxiety might manifest differently in men.
The researchers next compared the genetic risk for anxiety against the genetic profiles of 28 other mental and physical health conditions. They wanted to see if the genetic predisposition for anxiety overlaps with the predisposition for other traits. This analysis revealed several sex-specific correlations.
The genetic risk for anxiety in females was strongly correlated with the genetic risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and a higher body mass index (BMI). In clinical settings, ADHD and anxiety frequently co-occur in females. The researchers noted that female ADHD might manifest predominantly as anxiety symptoms, which can sometimes result in ADHD being overlooked or misdiagnosed in women.
The link to general body mass index also aligns with past epidemiological studies showing that obesity and anxiety are more strongly linked in women, as well as neuroimaging research finding that higher BMI is associated with stronger stress-related brain responses in women. Conversely, the genetic risk for male anxiety showed a stronger association with waist-to-hip ratio adjusted for BMI. This metric reflects central body fat rather than overall weight.
Central fat distribution is more closely tied to insulin regulation and the specific lipoprotein metabolism pathways identified earlier in the male genetic data. In a final step, the researchers used the genetic variants to create polygenic scores, which are numerical estimates of a person’s genetic liability for a trait. They tested these scores in three independent cohorts, which included a general population group, a symptom-based group, and a clinical cohort of patients with depression.
A score generated from the female genetic data proved best at predicting anxiety in other women within the general population. When attempting to predict male anxiety, the female-derived score and the male-derived score performed similarly. Once the researchers mathematically matched the sample sizes to account for the smaller number of men, the only statistically significant difference was that the female-derived score predicted anxiety in women better than the male-derived score in the general population cohort; the other predictive differences between the male and female scores were not statistically significant.
The study does have a few limitations that require context. The male sample size was smaller than the female sample size, which reduces the statistical power to detect genetic variants in men. The researchers note that larger samples will be needed to clarify sex differences or commonalities.
The dataset also relied exclusively on individuals of European ancestry. As a result, the findings might not accurately reflect the genetic architecture of anxiety in other global populations. The researchers recommend that future genetic studies include larger and more diverse groups of people. By continuing to analyze male and female data separately, scientists can build a more accurate understanding of psychiatric conditions.
Standard approaches that blend male and female data run the risk of oversimplifying human biology and masking important genetic signals. The study, “Unravelling sex differences in the genetic architecture of anxiety,” was authored by Jihua Hu, Michelle K. Lupton, Enda M. Byrne, Nicholas G. Martin, David C. Whiteman, Catherine M. Olsen, Jodi T. Thomas, Sarah E. Medland, Katrina L. Grasby, and Brittany L. Mitchell.

New Philosophy of AI Initiatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) and the University of Toronto have launched new initiatives to support and focus philosophical research on various aspects of artificial intelligence (AI).
The Department of Philosophy, Logic and Scientific Method at LSE has received a $5.3 million donation to launch a new research group—The Global Priorities Research Group (GPRG)—dedicated to “determining which problems matter most and what should be done in trying to realize the best outcomes for humanity and the wider world.”
It’s primary emphasis will be “philosophical research that helps us navigate the largest-scale challenges associated with the impacts of transformative AI.”
Funded by Good Ventures, a philanthropic foundation, the GPRG “will also consider how we should compare and weight the interests of different kinds of beings—be they human, animal, or perhaps even artificial—as well as pursuing foundational research on issues related to value and rational choice with the potential to reorient our priorities across a wide range of issues.”
The group will be led by philosophers Andreas L. Mogensen, who recently joined LSE from the University of Oxford, and Teruji Thomas (Oxford, LSE), and will be based at LSE’s Centre for Philosophy of Natural and Social Science.
Meanwhile, the Artificial Consciousness Initiative is a new project from the University of Toronto Department of Philosophy that “aims to advance foundational research connecting artificial intelligence and consciousness.”
The project’s director, philosopher Andrew Y. Lee, writes:
The initiative’s research agenda focuses on questions about the nature, structure, and indicators of artificial consciousness; the valence and character of potential artificial experiences; the welfare and moral status of artificial systems; and the ethical and safety risks raised by increasingly capable AI. The initiative does not presuppose that current artificial systems are conscious or that future ones will be. But it starts from the view that these questions are worth taking seriously.
The core team of the Artificial Consciousness Initiative includes Karina Vold, Christian Tarsney, and Gwen Bradford.
The initiative’s aims include basic research, partnerships with other institutions, and contributing to public and policy discussions related to AI consciousness. The project is supported by a large grant from Longview Philanthropy.
Both initiatives are currently hiring postdocs.

An Idaho ICE Raid Rounded Up Hundreds. The Fallout Could Change How ICE Operates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

People first noticed the black helicopter in the sky.
It was a chilly Sunday afternoon a year ago at La Catedral Arena, a popular track for horse racing outside the Idaho town of Wilder. Hundreds had gathered at the arena for a festival celebrating horse racing and Mexican culture.
As the military-style helicopter hovered above them, attendees from the rural, predominantly Latino community, began to get nervous.
“Something is wrong,” Ivan Popoca, who attended the festival with his two kids, remembers thinking.
Within minutes, the festival grounds descended into chaos. Backed by armored trucks and snipers, more than 200 members of law enforcement stormed the grounds, some shot rubber bullets into the crowd and hurled flash-bang grenades into vehicles where people had fled to hide. Hundreds of people, including teens as young as 14, were detained and zip-tied.
When it was all over, federal authorities had arrested 105 people for alleged immigration violations. Yet on paper, this wasn’t an immigration raid at all. The only warrant for the Wilder raid was secured by the FBI. Its target: the owner of the track and four others for alleged unlicensed gambling.
Twelve months later, the Wilder raid is at the center of a court fight that could shape ICE operations around the country. Advocates argue that in Idaho, ICE unlawfully piggybacked on an FBI operation, rather than securing their own warrant, as they would be expected to do on this type of operation. A lawsuit brought forth by the ACLU argues that federal authorities violated the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, by using an unrelated search warrant as a “cover to go fishing for immigration arrests.”
“That is not what a criminal search warrant execution looks like. That is what a massively violent
immigration raid looks like,” says Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, an ACLU attorney who helped bring the resulting lawsuit.
Trump Administration officials insist that the arrests made that day were lawful. “The facts haven’t changed: ICE helped dismantle an illegal horse-racing, animal fighting, and a gambling enterprise operation out of a property known as La Cathedral Arena in Wilder, Idaho,” a DHS spokesperson told TIME. Idaho Gov. Brad Little also defended the raid, saying in a statement at the time that it is “common practice” to detain others present while processing the scene.
For Wilder residents, the La Catedral raid remains an open wound that refuses to heal. Popoca still recalls with anger how he and his 16-year-old son were zip-tied for hours for no apparent reason.
The ACLU and some of the families involved in the case released a documentary online on Monday called Wild Raids in which they discuss the raid’s impact, and why the legal challenge matters beyond people in Wilder.
“Some community members don't even want to think about this anymore,” says Leo Morales, the executive director of the ACLU Idaho. “But there are also folks who are also realizing how critical it is to be able to push back, to organize and to demand fairness and justice.”
Recurring nightmares
Juana Rodriguez attended the festival with her three-year-old son. Despite both of them being U.S. citizens, they were zip-tied and detained for hours following the raid. Like many others who were detained, she described not being given access to food or water.
“For the longest time, my son begged me for food. He begged me for water,” Rodriguez says. She repeatedly asked the officers she could be untied so that she could feed and console her crying son, she says, but was rebuffed. “I wish I could have done more in the moment, but I couldn't.”
Detainees were eventually taken into a tent and questioned by ICE agents about their immigration status. Among the 105 people who were ultimately arrested, 75 are believed to have been deported to their home countries, according to local media, and 26 were released from ICE custody after their lawyers filed habeas corpus petitions. The whereabouts of the remaining four people are unclear. ICE did not provide an update on their case status.
The day after the raid, the Wilder School District reported absent rates soared, with 20% of students absent, according to The Idaho Statesman. More than half of the district’s student body is Hispanic or Latino.
A year later, Rodriguez says she is still scared to go to Latino cultural and other public events because of what happened at La Catedral. She also has nightmares about ICE officers taking her child away from her.
“I'm from here. My kids are from here,” she says. ”Why should I have to feel that? Like, I shouldn't.”
ICE’s Growing Legal Fights
The ACLU filed a class-action complaint in February, charging that a variety of local, state and federal agencies violated the constitutional rights of those at the festival. Both sides are now waiting for a judge to rule on a motion by ICE and other agencies to dismiss, in which it argued that federal and state law enforcement are protected by qualified immunity, a longstanding legal doctrine when executing a federal warrant.
The Wilder case is one of multiple lawsuits the Trump Administration is fighting over its immigration enforcement operations. In Minnesota, none of the federal agents involved in the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti have been criminally charged, but a string of civil lawsuits is beginning to emerge. Earlier this month, the family of Renee Good, who was killed last January by a federal agent during the immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed a pair of civil lawsuits against the federal government, according to their legal representative. Marimar Martinez, a U.S. citizen who was shot by a Border Patrol agent during a confrontation on a Chicago street last year, has also filed a lawsuit against the federal government.
Anyone seeking to hold federal agents accountable must be prepared for a long wait, says Borchetta. A lawsuit against the federal government can’t even be filed unless it’s been six months since a complainant filed a claim for compensation and the issue remains unresolved.
“If a federal employee is driving their car negligently on the job and hits you with their car, you can bring a claim for them for that negligence,” Borchetta says. “It also applies where an ICE agent is mistreating you or causing you harm.”
But the law itself imposes many limitations on suing the federal government. Victims can seek compensatory damages for actual losses, but not punitive damages. And unlike state authorities who can be sued for civil rights violations in state courts, federal law enforcement authorities are generally shielded from such lawsuits based on legal precedents.
But Borchetta says the impact of the lawsuits can be bigger than any verdict. She argues that the ongoing Wilder case has already helped change ICE’s conduct as well as how local governments collaborate with them.
“While we don't yet have a decision from the court, we haven't seen more raids like this in Idaho,” she says. “The lawsuit itself exposes both the state and the federal actors to liability, and that can change behavior itself.”

jenny holzer transforms musée d’orsay with monumental light projections and engraved stone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

jenny holzer transforms musée d’orsay with monumental light projections and engraved stone
the american artist digs into musée d’orsay’s archives to uncover the conflicts, contradictions, and uncomfortable truths of the past.
prefer designboom on google
JENNY HOLZER ILLUMINATES MUSÉE D’ORSAY WITH WORDS FROM THE PAST
The walls of Paris’ Musée d’Orsay have plenty to say, and Jenny Holzer is giving them a voice. For J’ai Vu (I Saw), opening October 20, 2026, the American artist transforms the former railway station into a vast canvas of illuminated words, moving texts, and engraved stone sculptures. Developed in collaboration with the museum, the exhibition draws on writings from the period represented in its collections, bringing together artistic correspondence, political commentary, and historical accounts. Rather than simply revisiting the 19th century, Holzer lets its voices confront the present, proving that some conversations are far from over.
The intervention begins outside, where the museum’s Seine-facing facade becomes the setting for ÉCLAIRÉ, a series of monumental light projections presented from October 18 to 22, between 7 pm and 11 pm. Drawing on approximately 250 excerpts by 34 authors, including writings by Vincent van Gogh, Paul Cézanne, Gustave Flaubert, and Émile Zola, Holzer covers the historic architecture with luminous words that can be experienced freely from the riverbanks. Letters, literary passages, and political reflections unfold across the building, temporarily turning one of Paris’ most recognizable cultural landmarks into a public display of history in motion.
MONUMENTAL LED INSTALLATIONS TRANSFORM MUSÉE D’ORSAY
Inside the Musée d’Orsay, a monumental, site-specific LED installation by Jenny Holzer carries the exhibition through four galleries dedicated to history painting, naturalism, symbolism, and Gustave Courbet. Streams of brightly colored text move through the spaces, introducing historical voices into rooms traditionally dominated by paintings and sculptures. The installation responds to the architecture and the circulation of visitors, recalling the building’s original function as a bustling 19th-century railway station. Once a place for moving passengers, the former Gare d’Orsay now finds itself transporting words instead.
Jenny Holzer also introduces 19 stone sculptures, comprising 17 benches and two columns, distributed throughout the museum’s ground-floor galleries and public spaces. Created specifically for the exhibition, these works feature engraved texts largely dating from 1848 to 1914. Their carefully selected varieties of stone, each researched for its origin and character, establish a material dialogue with the museum’s existing sculptures and pedestals. Unlike the moving LED displays, these inscriptions invite a slower encounter with language, transforming familiar architectural elements into objects that demand a closer reading.
HOLZER CONFRONTS WAR, SECRECY AND CENSORSHIP THROUGH ART
The exhibition takes a more explicitly political turn in the museum’s history painting gallery, where Holzer has developed a new presentation centered on war and conflict. Historical works from the permanent collection appear alongside her own paintings, made with gold, platinum, and palladium leaf, which reference recent international conflicts. Based on partially redacted documents, these metallic surfaces conceal substantial portions of their original texts, leaving visible fragments that raise questions about secrecy, accountability, and the boundaries between legitimate confidentiality and the concealment of wrongdoing. A separate gallery overlooking the Seine extends the presentation, allowing natural light to transform the reflective surfaces throughout the day.
Altogether, J’ai Vu brings together more than 750 distinct texts from 424 sources and 73 authors, potentially making it Holzer’s most extensive selection of written material for a single exhibition. The subjects range from the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune to colonialism, anarchism, labor movements, military corruption, and the everyday realities of Haussmann-era Paris. By bringing these competing perspectives into the same space, Holzer constructs a portrait of history that resists any single interpretation. Projected in light, carved into stone, or partially erased beneath precious metals, the words expose how closely the anxieties of the past resemble those of the present. History, it seems, has never been particularly good at keeping quiet.
project info:
name: J’ai Vu
artist: Jenny Holzer | @jennyholzerstudio
location: Musée d’Orsay | @museeorsay
dates: October 20, 2026 – February 21, 2027

Russia Keeps Attacking, but Ukraine Has Liberated More Territory Than Moscow Captured Since Autumn
Ukrainian forces have liberated more territory than Russian troops have managed to capture since the beginning of autumn, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said following a briefing on the frontline situation by Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi.
In a statement on October 18, Zelenskyy highlighted the results of Ukrainian military operations across several sectors of the frontline, particularly near Dobropillia in Donetsk region, where Ukrainian forces continue to eliminate Russian assault groups and prevent infiltration attempts.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the president, Ukrainian troops are also maintaining their defensive positions in other parts of Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions despite continued Russian offensive operations.
Zelenskyy specifically praised the effectiveness of Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces and the Third Army Corps, whose operations are being conducted as part of the country's active defense strategy.
He emphasized that Ukrainian forces have achieved territorial gains exceeding those made by Russian troops since the beginning of autumn, adding that a similar trend had been observed during earlier periods of the year.
“We continue to maintain pressure along the frontline. Dobropillia, Kostiantynivka, Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka, Orikhiv, Novopavlivka, Novoandriivka, and Velykomykhailivka are all under Ukrainian control. We are also defending areas near Kramatorsk,” Zelenskyy stated.
Addressing the situation in Zaporizhzhia region, he rejected Russian claims that Moscow’s forces had advanced to within five kilometers of the regional capital.
According to the president, Ukrainian troops are instead engaging and eliminating Russian forces approximately 20 kilometers from the city of Zaporizhzhia, contradicting Moscow’s assertions about its proximity to the city.
The president’s remarks follow the completion of Operation Vivaldi, a major Ukrainian offensive in Donetsk region that resulted in the recapture of 277 square kilometers of territory and at least 8,000 Russian troops killed or wounded.
The operation, conducted by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, involved drones deploying combat robots behind Russian lines, coordinated battlefield deception, and a series of strikes and maneuvers that significantly weakened three Russian armies.
During the fourth and final phase alone, Ukrainian forces reclaimed 101 square kilometers (39 square miles), killed more than 3,000 Russian soldiers, and destroyed hundreds of pieces of military equipment.

From delivery driver to global fame: A Korean writer's journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:55:00 UTC
19:55:00 KST

From delivery driver to global fame: A Korean writer's journey
October 19, 2026
For ten years, publishers rejected You Yeong-Gwang's book. Yet before it was even printed in South Korea, the once-abandoned manuscript had international publishers flocking to secure translation rights.
"I'm so grateful that the book has now been published in more than 20 countries. Even more astonishingly, it also appeared on the Der Spiegel bestseller list in Germany," he told DW while attending the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair.
For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and traditional Chinese.
The Rainfall Market tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. In the shop, visitors can exchange their deepest unhappiness for a ticket to a brand-new destiny. The plot revolves around Serin, a disheartened young girl who stumbles into the marketplace run by whimsical spirits, finding a warm, comforting space.
"In fact, Serin's story is my story," author You said. "For a long time, I even wondered how wonderful it would be if I could sell my unhappiness and use the money to buy happiness."
While writing the book, he was going through a difficult time himself.
"I had to care for my mother, who had been ill for a long time, and I had also been responsible for supporting my family financially for many years. Life felt incredibly heavy," he reflected.
"But when I was writing, I could immerse myself in the world of the story and, even if only for a short while, forget about those circumstances. That's why writing made me so happy. I truly enjoyed it."
On the creation of The Rainfall Market
The idea of rain is inspired by his own life. "At that time, my circumstances felt as though it were raining constantly," You said.
The story draws heavily on traditional Korean folklore, serving as a quintessential "healing fiction" tale in which its young protagonist must weigh the true cost of seemingly perfect lives.
"When I was writing, I wasn't consciously trying to write healing fiction. At the time, I didn't even really know that such a label existed."
He initially planned to publish a book independently and started crowdfunding. But as the funding failed, he used all his savings and printed 200 copies, which bookstores refused to take. In a month, he only sold five copies. "I thought that's it. I really have to give up now.”
"At the time, I had undergone eye surgery and due to complications, I couldn't see, so I started working at a call center, where I could work using my voice." You said. "During the week, I worked at a call center, and on weekends I went to a computer academy. I learned how to make books on my own for a few years."
He then taught himself how to use the software needed to create books on his own.
While running one of the crowdfunding campaigns, he started working as a food delivery rider. "The round trip between my home and the area where I delivered food took about four hours each day. So I wrote on my phone's memo app while traveling on the subway."
"Even when I was going through very difficult circumstances, I was able to keep writing because the moments when I was writing were so joyful. For a little while, I could forget about the difficult situation I was in," You explained.
Finally a breakthrough
"I gathered those pieces of writing together and launched what I intended to be my final crowdfunding campaign," he said.
The campaign was intended to fund the publication of The Rainfall Market.
"To my amazement, the campaign succeeded, and I was able to publish the book commercially for the first time," he said.
Following the crowdfunding success, the novel was acquired by Clayhouse, a prominent South Korean publishing company.
Before it was even published, he had received offers from publishers in five countries and signed international publishing contracts.
And in the first month after publication, the book sold 30,000 copies across all formats, ranking as the bestselling e-book and third-bestselling physical book.
"I still find it hard to believe that all of this has happened and that I'm here at the Frankfurt Book Fair. I'm incredibly grateful and happy," said You.
A new horizon for Hallyu, or the 'Korean Wave': K-Comfort Fiction
Korea's newest soft power is K-literature, which sold about 1.2 million translated copies abroad in 2025 for the second consecutive year.
And You's book belongs to a trending genre called Korean comfort fiction.
"When readers closed the book, I wanted them to feel a little warmth in their hearts," he said.
Although Korean literature was first known for darker, more pragmatic books about societal realities, K-comfort fiction is the child of South Korea's pressure-cooker modern society. It offers an answer to the human need for escapism and a transient antidote to the reality of a hyper-competitive education system, brutal job market, and intense corporate pressure.
"When I was writing, I was going through a very difficult time myself, and I wished someone would comfort me. So, I thought, why don't I try reading something like that myself? Why don't I write something that can comfort me?" You wondered.
With burnout on the rise globally, more readers are seeking soul-soothing literature with exhausted protagonists they can relate to. Usually without a need to defeat a villain, the stories follow protagonists with a deep desire for rest, community and emotional repair.
The whimsical fiction aspect is the missing element allowing them to step away from reality. The genre originally gained traction through indie productions, online crowdfunding and endorsements from high-profile K-pop artists.
Despite the Korean context, this style of storytelling quickly went global, capturing different international audiences, including those already familiar with cozy K-dramas or those simply looking for a gentle refuge from the anxieties of the modern world.
Last year, the bestselling Korean novel abroad was Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop, according to the Literature Translation Institute of Korea. This book also belongs to the same genre as The Rainfall Market.
While readers embrace the genre, critics view it with literary skepticism. They point out that it relies heavily on a predictable, repetitive formula, often built around a single magical space, with simplistic prose and low-stakes conflicts that prioritize cozy vibes over deep character development.
Reviewing The Rainfall Market for the Korea Times, Peter Juhl, a literary critic, described healing fiction as light, feel-good stories and argued the boom reflects a deliberate effort to write global novels for international markets.
On his future aspirations and message to readers
"Of course, I'm happy that my book is receiving so much love and that I'm able to write. But more than anything, I hope my mother gets better and regains her health," he said after mentioning that his mother underwent surgery a week before his arrival at the book fair.
Beyond the book itself, people seem to relate to and appreciate the story of his own life.
"If I have the opportunity, I'd like to share more stories about hope and dreams with people who are going through circumstances similar to mine," said You. "If my story can help one person even a little, in any way, I don't think anything could make me happier."

Young audiences theater festival Naks kicks off in Tallinn and Narva

Young audiences theater festival Naks kicks off in Tallinn and Narva
The Naks theater festival for young audiences takes place in Tallinn and Narva from October 19 to 24, offering a varied program for children, young people, families, teachers and theater professionals.
This year's Naks will take place mainly in the border city of Narva from October 20 to 24. On the festival's opening day, October 19, audiences can see productions by two internationally acclaimed companies specializing in theater for young audiences at Tallinn's Salme Cultural Center: Kompani Giraff from Sweden and Le Moana from New Zealand.
For the youngest audiences — babies and their parents — the festival program includes Draakonipesa's "Talvevõlu," ("Winter Magic") a wordless visual journey into an enchanted winter world inhabited by rabbits, goats and Arctic foxes. After the performance, children can get to know the puppets used in the production.
For preschoolers and children in grades one through three, Sweden's Kompani Giraff offers the magical circus production "ABC," in which performers help audiences learn letters and the alphabet through play.
Finnish-Czech company Krepsko brings a miniature world all its own to Narva. "Fabsurdia" is a small, richly detailed world that audiences can do more than simply watch: They can also explore it up close and touch it.
Estonia's VAT Teater brings "Luukere Juhani juhtumised," ("Juhan the Skeleton's Adventures") an adventure production for children based on Triinu Laan's book, to the festival.
For audiences in grades four through nine, New Zealand dance company Le Moana presents "Shel We," a playful tribute to writer and poet Shel Silverstein and his beloved children's book "The Giving Tree." The production brings together trees, ghosts, goats and mischief.
Contemporary circus company Kompani Giraff also brings its second production, "A Study of Losses," to Narva. Combining aerial acrobatics, object manipulation and music, this visual journey reflects on lost worlds, memories and objects. Its musical world was created by Zach Condon, who performs as Beirut.
For students in grades seven through nine and upper secondary school, the program includes Miksteater's "Oskar ja Roosamamma. Kirjad Jumalale." ("Oscar and Pink Momma. Letters to God") This heartfelt, thought-provoking production tells the story of Oskar, a boy with cancer who spends the final days of his life in a hospital with his caregiver, Roosamamma.
Kuressaare Theatre's "Koleda tüdruku päevaraamat" ("An Ugly Girl's Diary") is also suitable for audiences ages 12 and older. It is a moving, honest story about young people that speaks to anyone who has felt left out.
The festival also includes several workshops, educational programs and a play reading.
