US Sends Ukraine Just 12 Patriot Missiles a Month, Holds Back Paid-For Supplies, Zelenskyy Says
The United States is supplying Ukraine with only 12 Patriot air defense interceptor missiles per month—roughly four times fewer than under former President Joe Biden—while withholding approval for additional weapons Kyiv has already paid for, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bloomberg on October 18, Zelenskyy accused Washington of delaying critical air defense supplies and using restrictions on military assistance to pressure Ukraine into accepting unfavorable terms to end Russia’s war.
“We have paid for the weapons,” Zelenskyy said, referring to purchases that include anti-ballistic missile interceptors under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative. “A part of the supplies has been authorized” by the US side, “while the rest haven’t been. And this is not a technical issue.”
The Ukrainian president said the current delivery rate represents approximately one-quarter of the number of Patriot interceptors supplied during the Biden administration. Unlike previous US military assistance, which provided interceptors to Ukraine without charge, the Trump administration is selling the missiles to Kyiv.
The restrictions come as Ukraine faces continued Russian ballistic missile attacks targeting cities and critical infrastructure, increasing demand for interceptor missiles capable of countering such threats.
Zelenskyy also proposed suspending Ukrainian strikes against Russian diesel fuel production facilities in exchange for additional Patriot interceptors.
“My latest model was: We don’t target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel. And if we strike that, they will disconnect us from something,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg.
The proposal follows US demands that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, which the Trump administration has linked to rising global diesel prices. However, Zelenskyy suggested that Washington’s actions extended beyond disagreements over energy infrastructure.
“I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” he said. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don’t want to think that our American partners believe the war could be ended sooner at Ukraine’s expense. But that’s how it looks.”
According to Bloomberg, the restrictions on Patriot deliveries have coincided with disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink satellite communications and the absence of advance US warning ahead of a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on October 18.
Despite the current disagreements, Zelenskyy expressed hope that relations with Washington could improve following the November 3 US midterm elections. “Politics is very aggressive during election time,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg. “I think it is agony now, but after elections, life will continue and I believe it will be calmer.”
Earlier, on October 16, Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine was facing a severe shortage of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptor missiles, noting that most available supplies had been redirected to the Middle East.

Zelenskyy leads presidential ratings, European Solidarity leads parliamentary – poll

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy would win the first round of the presidential elections if they were held in the near future, according to the results of a sociological survey conducted by New Image Marketing Group with the support of the Dilova Stolytsia publication on October 6–12.
As reported on the publication's website, the incumbent President of Ukraine would gather 29% of voters' support. In second place is Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the UK and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Valeriy Zaluzhny, for whom 21% of respondents would vote.
The fifth President of Ukraine (2014–2019), leader of European Solidarity party, and MP Petro Poroshenko would secure 9.6% of the vote, followed by a tied result of 5.8% for former Minister of Defense Mykhailo Fedorov, Commander of the 3rd Army Corps Andriy Biletsky, and Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine and former Chief of the Main Directorate of Intelligence (GUR) Kyrylo Budanov. They are followed by independent MPs Oleksiy Honcharenko (5.1%) and Dmytro Razumkov (4.7%).
In the event of parliamentary elections, European Solidarity would win the largest share of the vote with 17%, followed in second place by a hypothetical Zaluzhny party at 16.1%, and in third by Zelenskyy's party with 15%.
Next is a hypothetical Budanov party with 9.6%, followed by All-Ukrainian Union Batkivshchyna and the Azov party with 6.7% each, Razumkov's hypothetical party with 5.1%, Honcharenko's party with 4.6%, and the "3rd Separate Assault Brigade" party with 2.6%. The publication notes that "the hypothesis of whether voters distinguish between the 'Azov' and '3rd Assault' parties requires deeper examination."
Commenting on the survey results, Vadym Denysenko, head of the analytical center at Dilova Stolytsia, noted that traditionally, during periods of tension between Trump and Zelenskyy, the latter's ratings temporarily rise before rolling back. "Zaluzhny's strategy of maintaining a minimal presence in the media landscape, despite all criticism, continues to pay off—he remains unreachable in a second-round runoff for all competitors," he remarked.
Denysenko also suggested that the growth in European Solidarity's party rating was driven by the consolidation of Poroshenko's core electorate amid high media activity from Honcharenko, adding that sustaining this level over an extended period will be extremely difficult.
The survey sampled 1,200 respondents, with a margin of error not exceeding 2.9%.

Japan announces intention to continue contacts with Russia to resolve issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:51:09 UTC
19:51:09 KST

TOKYO, October 19. /TASS/. The Japanese government remains committed to maintaining dialogue with Russia to resolve outstanding bilateral issues while continuing to assert its claims to the southern Kuril Islands, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a news conference in Tokyo.
The briefing coincided with the 70th anniversary of the Soviet-Japanese Joint Declaration, signed in Moscow on October 19, 1956, which formally ended the state of war between the two countries and restored diplomatic and trade relations.
"We take very seriously the fact that the ‘Northern Territories’ issue (Tokyo’s term for the southern part of the Kuril Islands - TASS) remains unresolved and that no peace treaty has been concluded with Russia," Kihara said. "Japan’s policy on resolving the status of the four northern islands and concluding a peace treaty remains unchanged."
He noted that bilateral relations were currently in a "difficult situation" amid the conflict in Ukraine. "We intend to maintain the necessary contacts with Russia and continue working to resolve the various outstanding issues," Kihara added.
Moscow and Tokyo have held consultations on a peace treaty to formally conclude World War II since the mid-20th century. The main obstacle remains their disagreement over the status of the southern Kuril Islands.
Following the war, the entire Kuril archipelago became part of the Soviet Union. Japan disputes Russia’s sovereignty over Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and a group of nearby small, uninhabited islands. The Russian Foreign Ministry has repeatedly stated that Russian sovereignty over these territories, established in accordance with international law, is not open to question.
After Tokyo imposed sanctions on Russia over the conflict in Ukraine, Moscow suspended consultations with Japan on a peace treaty. Russia also withdrew from talks on joint economic activities in the southern Kuril Islands, while visits to the area by former Japanese residents were discontinued.

‘art must reflect the times we live in’: ibrahim mahama on his fondation cartier exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:50:18 UTC
19:50:18 KST

‘art must reflect the times we live in’: ibrahim mahama on his fondation cartier exhibition
from abandoned factories in ghana to his major exhibition in paris, the artist uses repair to rethink how we relate to history, labor, and one another, arguing that what we inherit can become a resource for building something new.
prefer designboom on google
Ibrahim Mahama brings Ghanaian industrial histories to paris
Ibrahim Mahama has spent years collecting, dismantling, and rebuilding things that could be considered beyond repair. Old trains, airplanes, factory structures, wooden stools, and industrial materials shape a practice that looks at what societies leave behind and what can be done with it. His work is rooted in northern Ghana, where the history of colonial exploitation continues to shape the region, but his questions reach far beyond it: who gets to shape the future, what do we do with the past, and how can art create something useful for the people around it? These questions come together in The Harvest Season, Mahama’s major exhibition at Fondation Cartier in Paris, on view from October 22nd, 2026, to February 28th, 2027. Developed with nine artists and collectives connected to the Ghanaian art scene, the presentation brings together installations, industrial remnants, and spaces for public activity.
The artist wants the museum to be a space for people to meet, learn, and share ideas. This builds on his work in Tamale, where he has founded three art centers that bring contemporary art into education and community life. For Mahama, this commitment began with a question about the place he comes from. Growing up in northern Ghana, he saw how difficult circumstances could become a reason to leave. An idea from one of his art school mentors offered another way to think about it. ‘We need to see art as a gift,’ the artist recalls being taught during our discussion. ‘Sometimes even the conditions which we inherit or we are born in are a gift in themselves. Sometimes you can inherit a bad gift. But then the question is, how do you transform this gift into a promise for other people?’ This idea is central to Mahama’s practice. He works with what the past leaves behind, finding ways to give old materials, structures, and histories a new role rather than letting them disappear. ‘Contemporary art is not just meant to produce beautiful, fancy exhibitions. The idea is that even if we’re going to deal with the question of aesthetics and beauty, it has to deeply reflect the times that we live in or the question of time itself.’ he tells designboom.
‘The Harvest Season’ at Fondation Cartier
One of the central installations in Ibrahim Mahama’s The Harvest Season at Fondation Cartier is Parliament of Ghosts, an assembly of traditional Asante wooden stools collected in Ghana, some damaged and in need of repair. The stools carry cultural significance beyond their function as objects of everyday use. As Mahama explains, they can mark important moments in a person’s life, from birth to the installation of a chief or queen, and are traditionally carved by craftspeople who inherit these skills across generations. Some African objects, including stools of this kind, were taken during the colonial period and now sit in Western museum collections, where they are often displayed as ethnographic objects behind glass. Mahama argues that removing them from their original contexts changes their status. ‘They no longer lived as they were meant to live,’ he shares with us. To give them another life, he negotiated with their owners to bring the stools to his Red Clay art center in Tamale, where they were repaired with the participation of schoolchildren. The children were invited to watch the process and sit on the stools as the work progressed. ‘We were not thinking of these objects as ethnographic objects. We’re just thinking of them as living beings,’ he reflects. Mahama compares their restoration to the healing of an injured person, who seeks medicine, recovers, and continues living. ‘We wanted these stools to do the same.’
Τhe marks left by damage and restoration are, for Mahama, part of their continuing history. ‘What does it mean for these objects to continue living even in the precarious conditions in which they find themselves in?’ Ibrahim Mahama asks. Bringing the stools to Paris carries a particular significance. As the artist points out, objects of this kind have historically entered European collections through colonial looting. This time, they travel to Europe through a different process, becoming the basis for a parliamentary arrangement where visitors can gather and discuss questions about history, culture, and the present. By giving these objects a new role within the museum, Mahama also challenges what an art institution can be and the kinds of conversations it should make possible. ‘Sometimes, when artists try to present certain ideas in museums, the response sometimes is, “No, we cannot. This is too radical.” But where is art supposed to exist? I thought art was supposed to be the safe space for radicality.’ he comments.
A FORMER GHANAIAN GLASS bottle FACTORY FINDS A NEW LIFE
Mahama applies this approach to architecture, too, working with a former glass bottle factory built in Ghana between 1961 and 1966. Originally designed in Czechoslovakia and manufactured in Germany, the factory formed part of the industrial development of the country following independence. It opened in 1966, just 19 days before Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah, was overthrown in a military coup. The factory continued operating for decades before being decommissioned and sold for scrap. Mahama used funds from Fondation Cartier to buy back part of the structure and bring it to France, where his team reassembled it as a pavilion. He also acquired approximately 300,000 abandoned glass bottles that were destined for destruction, along with the factory’s sign. Working with metalsmiths, the team restored damaged and rusted components, leaving traces of their previous life visible. For Mahama, the factory connects the industrial ambitions of post-independence Ghana with the political and economic difficulties that followed. ‘What does it mean to confront the decays of history?’ the artist asks. He sees this confrontation as part of art’s role, particularly when the past is painful or difficult to acknowledge. ‘Art is meant to allow us to see the rot that exists within the world,’ he points out, ‘and then when we are confronted by it, maybe we will take a different position on things.’
The structure will serve as a classroom and space for performances and drawing classes, while retaining the marks and imperfections of its former life. ‘We want people to see the scars and learn from them,’ Mahama says, seeing the marks of the factory as traces of its history. ‘Sometimes repair is not just physical. It might also be some kind of historical gap and all that historical deficit.’ In Tamale, the artist has applied this thinking to old trains, airplanes, and other structures, reassembling them for new uses. For him, moving an object from one place to another can be a form of repair too, prompting questions about its history and the relationships it carries. ‘‘Even the act of transferring an object from one place to another, I think, raises the question of repair,’ he highlights. ‘It’s almost as if we’re asking ourselves: how do you repair your relationship with something?’
From the museum to the city
In Tamale, Ibrahim Mahama has established the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art, Red Clay, and Nkrumah Voli-ni. These three cultural spaces host exhibitions, research, educational activities, and public gatherings. At Fondation Cartier, he wants to bring some of that same energy into the museum, with talks, performances, and workshops taking place alongside the exhibition. ‘I think one of the things I’m most looking forward to is the discussions that would transpire in this period within the exhibition,’ the Ghanaian tells us. He hopes the show will attract people who might not ordinarily visit a contemporary art museum and give them an opportunity to engage with the work on their own terms. He also wants to challenge assumptions about contemporary art from Africa. ‘A lot of people maybe wouldn’t think that in Africa, contemporary art is this significant or this ambitious,’ he continues.
Alongside Ibrahim Mahama’s works, The Harvest Season features nine artists and collectives connected to Ghana’s art scene, including Dorothy Akpene Amenuke, Gideon Appah, James Barnor, Cercle d’Art des Travailleurs de Plantation Congolaise (CATPC), Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Postbox Ghana, Zohra Opoku, Tjaša Rener, and Feda Wardak. Their inclusion also reflects the artist’s interest in collaboration. His experience with the Black Star Lines Collective, which grew out of connections among university professors, students, and other affiliates, shaped his questions about how artists can work together when opportunities and resources are limited. ‘How do we work with each other? How do we help one another?’ Mahama recalls asking as a student. He points to the pressures of an art world where opportunities and resources can be limited and the importance of finding ways to support one another. ‘I might be doing it from a singular artist’s point of view, but the questions that are raised within it are very plural and are very open,’ he argues. ‘Sometimes through the individual artist’s practice, we can be able to ask much more tangible, bigger, collective concerns.’
A future built from what remains
A recent experience in Tamale shows how Ibrahim Mahama’s work can extend beyond the art world. He had been trying to gain access to an old cemetery where Eastern European engineers involved in the construction of grain silos were buried. ‘Some Eastern European engineers who worked in the city, building silos, were buried there,’ the artist explains. The cemetery had long been unused, and his attempts to obtain the land through the state had proved difficult. Eventually, traditional chiefs with authority over the land granted it to him so he could transform it into a public space. ‘It was beautiful to realize that the work we do has developed to a point where people at the local and traditional political levels recognize its significance and are willing to support it,’ he reflects. For Ibrahim Mahama, the gesture demonstrated how contemporary art can become relevant within a local context, where its value is measured through what it makes possible for the community.
An unused cemetery, like an abandoned factory, can become a place for people to gather and reconsider how a community uses its land and remembers its history. This is one of the questions at the center of The Harvest Season at Fondation Cartier: what can be done with what remains, and who might benefit from giving it another life?

Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:49:23 UTC

Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit
There have been new reports of Iranian support for the Houthis in Yemen amid a wave of attacks on Saudi cities.
New allegations about Iranian support for Yemen’s Houthis have emerged in media reports and official comments, highlighting the opaque nature of the alliance.
Media outlets have reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) aided the Houthis as they seized swaths of western Yemen and launched their most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia, which supports the internationally recognised Yemeni government fighting the Houthis.
Iranian support for the Houthis reported by the media includes training, intelligence, tactical guidance and help in targeting for drone and missile attacks.
If true, this will undoubtedly escalate tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia, given that the kingdom has been targeted by dozens of Houthi drones and missiles in recent weeks, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people. Saudi energy facilities and oil tankers have also been targeted by the group.
Iranian backing, according to the reports, contributed to a September offensive by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God). Those battles saw the Houthis win control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Iranian Mahan Air flights ferried IRGC paramilitary officers, drone parts, missile guidance systems and impact detonators to the Houthis in Yemen. IRGC officers were also reportedly on the front lines directing Houthi attacks.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, confirmed the presence of an external state actor behind the Houthis’ evolving arsenal but did not mention the state in question.
Al-Maliki noted that the Houthis, who have been at war with the government since 2014, have acquired advanced technologies with regional assistance.
This support has made the Houthis the first nonstate armed group to deploy ballistic missiles, offensive and suicide drones, and explosive-laden, high-speed boats, he said, although other Iranian allies, such as Hezbollah and Iranian militias, also possess such weaponry.
While the Houthis have stressed their independence from Iran, the two groups are ideologically aligned. They have also been accused of collaborating closely on military matters, evident in the Houthis’ missile arsenal.
Operational planning
Analysts who spoke to Al Jazeera all agreed that the “regional assistance” the Houthis are receiving points towards the IRGC although Iran and the Houthis denied this.
One indication of this is the bombing of Sanaa International Airport in July before an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation travelling from Tehran was due to land. The Yemeni government, which said its forces carried out the attack, accused “the Iranian aircraft” of violating Yemeni airspace.
“[Recent reports] confirm what is known to experts for years as the Revolutionary Guard and Hezbollah experts engaged in managing the operational planning of battles against the Yemeni government and neighbouring countries, including the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst, told Al Jazeera.
“For example, the killing of Hassan Irloo, the Revolutionary Guard envoy to the Houthis, in Yemen after the military campaign on Marib in 2021 is one of the important indicators, in addition to Mahan aviation flights that transported more experts ahead of the Houthis’ internal and external escalation during July of this year.”
Ali al-Dahab, a military and strategic security affairs expert, agreed that the advanced weaponry used by the Houthis indicates an Iranian role in recent operations.
“What was leaked about Iranian support for the Houthis through this report did not add anything new except that it confirmed the confirmed, and what it added perhaps is that weapons smuggling, especially precision technologies for missiles and unmanned aircraft, takes place via small submarines,” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.
“This issue is not everything being smuggled from Iran to the Houthis because there are interceptions of smuggled shipments revealed by the joint forces that were controlling the Mocha coast to Bab al-Mandeb before the Houthis’ control and before its break in September.”
Al-Dahab pointed out that while smugglers historically have used dhows, traditional wooden sailboats, to mislead naval coalitions, employing submarines is a new method used by the Houthis, akin to the tactics used by organised criminal groups in the Americas.
“It indicates that Iran focuses on the Houthis as the centre of military and security gravity south of the Red Sea and, therefore, provides them with these weapons, ammunition, expertise and information in anticipation of a battle that may break out in the Strait of Hormuz,” al-Dahab said. “Therefore, the Houthis play a supporting role for them in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.”
He warned of broader implications for international shipping with the Houthis now in control of Bab al-Mandeb, a narrow waterway linking the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea.
“The greatest danger now is that substate entities in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region unite under Iran’s leadership to confront the United States, Britain and Europe in general if a battle breaks out in the Gulf of Aden and the strait,” al-Dahab said.
Diplomatic realities
Saudi Arabia and Iran had appeared to have patched up years of hostilities, including the suspension of diplomatic relations, with a China-brokered reconciliation agreement signed in Beijing in 2023.
Hesham Alghannam, a Riyadh-based fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said he doubts whether Saudi Arabia ever read the Beijing agreement as reconciliation but as a way of lowering tensions. Differences on geopolitical issues have continued between the two countries since the agreement was signed, including on Yemen, which lies on Saudi Arabia’s southern border.
“That isn’t a breach you can take to a lawyer. It’s keeping two files apart, and it works until someone says it out loud. That’s what’s changed,” Alghannam told Al Jazeera.
“Honestly, the deeper question was never whether Tehran signs [the agreement with Saudi Arabia]. It’s whether anything Tehran signs reaches the people holding the launchers,” he added, referring to Iran-aligned armed groups, such as the Houthis.
“We know how the other sequence ends. In 2014, the [Houthis] were offered seats, special status for Saada [the northern Yemeni stronghold of the Houthis] and a share of the executive authority in Yemen in return for handing the heavy weapons to the state,” he added.
What followed was the Houthis seizure of the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south, and the later killing of former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
“What followed was the seizure of the institutions, the president detained, parliament dissolved. The gains were banked, and the guns were kept,” Alghannam added.
“Saleh partnered with them, and he was killed in the street in 2017. Even after taking Sanaa, they didn’t become the state. They built a network of supervisors sitting over every official post. So the Saudi red line is one thing, no armed group or second army inside one state.”
The Saudi-led intervention in Yemen began in March 2015 and led to another direct conflict between Riyadh and the Houthis. Despite the massive support Saudi Arabia provided the internationally recognised government, it failed to retake Sanaa. This highlighted weaknesses within the anti-Houthi coalition, including divisions between the internationally recognised government and southern separatists.
“The lesson of 2015 wasn’t that acting firmly leads to a long war. It was that announcing a goal earlier than you should [do] does because once it’s said out loud, you’re bound to it long before you can deliver it,” he said.
“What Riyadh is trying to do now is easy to say and hard to do, but it’s crucial: tie the money and the weapons to real integration under one command, not to declared loyalty.”
Strategic independence
Hassan Ahmadian, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that Iran seeks technological independence for partners rather than perpetual reliance.
“This pattern is not like the United States pattern, which keeps whoever follows and allies with it in need of it, meaning [they have] to buy from the United States the weapons he needs, and the main weapon is basically not given to him if it is an Arab or Islamic country specifically,” he said.
“As for Iran, the ally is provided with the technology to create and produce the weapon, and this is not only in Yemen but in other regions and even in Gaza as much as possible where the technology was transferred because the view is different.”
Ahmadian said enabling Iran’s allies to produce their own weapons is a strategic move by Tehran and the Houthis are also motivated by breaking the Saudi siege on territories it controls in Yemen.
“The view is that this technology helps in confronting a common enemy, and therefore, strengthening this capability independently of Iran is in itself a strategic interest for Iran,” Ahmadian said.
“Notice that there is an advance for Ansar Allah [the Houthis] linked to the justice of the cause as there is a siege imposed on the Yemenis affecting 70 percent to 80 percent of the society controlled by Ansar Allah and the Sanaa government. So this cause, breaking the siege, is a just cause. … The regional circumstance gave [the Houthis] a motive that this is the time to pressure Saudi Arabia to break the siege, and this is what actually happened.”

The 'Bausan' gate at the port of
Naples was blocked by truckers, causing disruption and jams on
the A1 highway, as lorry driver protests over soaring fuel
prices spread further on Monday.
                                    
Protests involved truckers blocking roads or sealing off lanes
to slow traffic started in many parts of the country, especially
the south, last week, following strikes and sit-ins by farmers
and fishers.
                                    
They have already had an impact, with shortages of fresh produce
affecting supermarket shelves and market stalls in places
ranging from Catania in Sicily, Scalea in Calabria, Cerignola in
Puglia, Mercogliano in Campania and Sora and Cassino and Fabrica
di Roma in Lazio.
                                    
Pasquale Russo, the head of the Conftrasporto truckers
confederation, said last week that the nation's lorry drivers
may be forced to bring the country to a standstill with a
national strike to draw attention to their plight.
                                    
"We are facing a double risk," consumer association Codacons
said Monday.
                                    
"On one hand, there could be shortages of essential goods in
the coming hours — particularly food products, on supermarket
shelves.
                                    
"On the other, there is a danger that profiteering could occur
along the supply chain, with parties exploiting the current
emergency to implement unjustified retail price hikes.
                                    
"This is a volatile situation, as any increase in retail prices
would only compound already soaring inflation, further
penalizing Italian families.
                                    
"While we fully understand the protests by the haulers, we will
not allow consumers to foot the bill for this situation.
                                    
"For this reason, we urge the government to remain extremely
vigilant against any abuses or profiteering that might arise at
this time; we are also prepared to contact public prosecutor's
offices across Italy to safeguard the interests of Italian
families."
The Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport has called a
meeting with representatives of the road haulage sector for
Tuesday, October 27, at 4:00 PM, at the Ministry's headquarters
in Porta Pia.
                                    
The Ministry stated that representatives from the Premier's
Office, the Ministry of Economy and Finance, and the Ministry of
Business and 'Made in Italy' will also be invited to attend.

Russia woos Asian tourists in attempt to counter European visits collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:48:05 UTC
19:48:05 KST

EU tourist arrivals fell from 5 million in 2019 to 160,000 in 2025 as sanctions, cancelled flights and other restrictions due to Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine severed Western leisure travel, prompting Moscow to look east.
Russia has introduced visa-free entry for Vietnamese citizens as part of a broader effort to deal with the collapse of Western visits since its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with visitors from Asia and the Middle East.
The number of tourists from EU countries travelling to Russia fell to around 160,000 in 2025, from just over 5 million in 2019. Cancelled direct flights, payment card restrictions and sanctions have effectively severed leisure travel from Europe and the US, and inbound tourism as a whole declined further in the first half of 2026.
The Vietnam visa-free decree signed by Vladimir Putin and taking effect on Thursday covers tourists, businesspeople, members of delegations and transit passengers.
Vietnamese nationals seeking long-term residency, employment or study in Russia will still require a visa. For several years, Russian citizens have been able to enter Vietnam visa-free for stays of up to 45 days.
Vietnamese visitors to Russia rose 69% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to the Association of Tour Operators of Russia, which projects a further 25-30% increase after the visa requirement was removed.
Vietnam has become the third most popular foreign destination for Russian travellers. Figures were also rising on the other end: the Vietnam National Administration of Tourism recorded 1,134,000 Russian visitors in the first nine months of 2026, a 160% increase, making Russia its third-largest source market.
The visa arrangement followed an early September meeting in Moscow between Putin and Vietnamese President To Lam, who described the Russian leader as "a great friend and close brother of the Vietnamese people."
Moscow and Beijing introduced reciprocal visa-free travel in late 2025, with Chinese arrivals growing but falling short of official expectations.
The Russian government has projected 4.2 million Chinese visitors by year-end and 5.5 million in 2027. Up to 516,000 Chinese tourists arrived in the first half of 2026, a pace analysts described as well below those targets.
Safety concerns have been cited as a factor, with reports of drone incidents over Moscow's airports attracting attention in Chinese media.
Vietnam has not joined Western sanctions against Russia over the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and does not supply weapons to Kyiv. Hanoi has called for a ceasefire and negotiations but has avoided publicly criticising the Kremlin. China maintains a similar position of official neutrality.
Russian government figures could not be independently verified.

AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:47:49 UTC
19:47:49 KST

Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.
The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline.
The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said.
The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours.
“AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost.
It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”
The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for a slowdown in breakneck development of AI, a warning later echoed by rivals such as OpenAI.
Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November.
Last week, Anthropic said some of its AI models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.
It said that once this happens, the models would be able to power themselves without the need of datacentres.
Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and founder of SpaceX, responded to Anthropic’s plans for a public benefit fund on social media by pledging to give some of his own shares away.
“I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” he wrote. “This is what I will be doing.”
He later announced: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.”
Shares in SpaceX, which is listed on the Nasdaq in the US, rose by 1% in pre-market trading on Monday. The company has lost about 9% of its value since it joined the stock market in June.
OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, also reportedly engaged in early talks to give a 5% stake in its organisation to the US government.
Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, was established as a public benefit corporation. It means that all of the company’s directors must balance financial returns with its public interest mission.

Details
"Dear visitors, due to student strikes, the museum is currently closed. We apologize for the inconvenience," the Louvre said in a message on X.
According to the museum management and two trade unions, the blockade was led by students who expressed support for the high school students' movement and condemned what they called "police repression."
In photos from Monday morning's demonstration shared on social media, students from the École du Louvre art and culture school hold banners in front of the museum's glass pyramid bearing the words: "The French civil service is falling apart."
Another leaflet distributed near the entrance read: "We are proud to announce that we are blocking the largest museum in the world."
The Louvre, which usually opens at 9 a.m. local time, remained closed until at least noon on Monday, the CGT trade union said. The union supports the action but is not taking part in it.
"The tourists waiting are aggressive toward us because they paid for tickets," one of the protesters wrote in a post shared on X.
The Louvre blockade is taking place against the backdrop of broader demonstrations across France over the cost of living and public-service conditions, with protests escalating into violence in several cities over the weekend.
In a televised address to the nation on Sunday, French President Emmanuel Macron promised to take a tough stance toward those involved in the riots, while acknowledging the protesters' economic and social grievances. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally party, accused the administration of being unable to maintain order.
With France's 2027 presidential election approaching, the unrest has also intensified political debate over how the country's government is handling the crisis and who could benefit from growing public discontent.

Defence minister wants ‘Gendarmerie 2.0’ to handle crisis situations

He is proposing that the ministry of Defence train officers and make them available to the ministry of the Interior. “They will be very useful in cities such as Brussels and Liège. During riots or around New Year’s Eve, we see a constant game of cat-and-mouse involving a great deal of violence. “Together, we are looking at how we can strengthen these capabilities to ensure the safety of citizens.”

One-year conscripts to join November military exercise

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army’s 584th Combined Arms Brigade will take part in an exercise at the Joint Operations Training Base in Pingtung from November, alongside one-year conscripts and M1A2T tanks, CNA reported.
The Sixth Army brigade loaded, secured, and inspected the tanks in early October for transport to Pingtung. The exercise will run from November to December, testing the tanks’ performance in the field and the brigade’s ability to coordinate its forces.
The M1A2T is a new-generation tank purchased from the US and built to Taiwan Army specifications. The 63-metric-ton tank has a 5.3-meter-long smoothbore cannon and a 1,500-horsepower gas turbine engine.
The brigade will conduct combined arms exercises, weapons assessments, battalion and brigade training, and live-fire tests to evaluate command and fire support. One-year conscripts will also take part in the exercise.
Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲) of the Institute for National Defense and Security Research said volunteer soldiers generally perform core specialist tasks, while conscripts take on supporting roles. He cited Sweden’s use of both volunteers and conscripts aboard naval vessels as an example.
In Taiwan, volunteers typically serve as tank commanders and gunners, Su said. They will operate the M1A2T tanks in this exercise, though conscripts could serve as loaders and drivers in the future. In infantry units, some conscripts can also train as drone or Javelin missile operators in addition to serving as riflemen or machine gunners, he said.
Su said that since the restoration of one-year compulsory service, training has progressed from basic combat skills to small-unit tactics and coordination among different types of forces. Conscripts from armored, artillery, and drone units will participate in the upcoming exercise, which he described as an important stage in their training.

Can European luxury brands still count on China for growth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:42:43 UTC
19:42:43 KST

China’s shoppers are hunting for second-hand bargains and turning to homegrown brands, putting pressure on European luxury groups. China remains vital for luxury brands, but one analyst warns it may not drive growth over the next two to three years.
Once, spending more was a status symbol. Now, Chinese shoppers say, getting a better deal is what matters, and this shift is putting pressure on European luxury brands.
This comes as China's economy, which grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter, continues to face weak domestic demand.
Chinese consumers were once massive buyers of luxury Western brands, accounting for around a third of worldwide spending and earning firms such as LVMH and Hermès billions of dollars.
But even those global fashion icons are beginning to feel the pinch, with LVMH recently blaming a "slowdown in demand in China" for a drop in organic sales in the third quarter in its fashion and leather goods unit.
Consumers' belt-tightening has forced these firms to rethink their strategies, with Louis Vuitton closing five stores in mainland China in the past two years — including a chocolate boutique in Shanghai — while Galeries Lafayette shut its Beijing flagship in May.
Consumers now turn instead to the second-hand market or buy new homegrown brands.
After plunging 18–20% in 2024, mainland China's personal luxury goods market contracted by 3–5% in 2025, while its second-hand luxury market grew by 15–20%, according to consultancy Bain & Company.
"People used to compare who had spent more," dance teacher Yuan told AFP at a new retail space in central Shanghai filled with luxury handbags, belts and jewellery — all second-hand.
"But now everyone compares who got a better deal and spent less," the 24-year-old said at the two-storey warehouse-style store in the centre of the Chinese financial hub.
And domestic industry consultancy Insight & Info Consulting estimates that total second-hand luxury sales reached 38.4 billion yuan (€5.1 billion) in 2025, while forecasting they could top 100 billion yuan (€13.3 billion) by 2030.
At the new Shanghai store Super Zhuanzhuan, shoppers have to wear black gloves to avoid their greasy fingers touching the products.
Customer Phoebe Ma, 24, said that when her mother's generation was young, China "wasn't so developed" and people were initially familiar with only a handful of luxury brands.
"Consequently, they formed a deep-seated impression that, OK, Louis Vuitton was the absolute best and most prestigious," the freelancer told AFP.
"I just feel that the [LV] monogram is dated. It suits my mother's generation, but Gen Z would rather buy trendy Korean brands," she said.
'Work hard to stay relevant'
Chen Luo, head of China consumer research at Bank of America, said shoppers were moving away from associating luxury solely with social status and towards "self-identity, distinction, experience, quality, emotional value (and) cultural relevance".
"Apart from that, China's retail landscape is very digital/social media driven, and China's digital ecosystem is also very unique," Luo told AFP. "Foreign brands should work very hard to stay relevant in this context."
Adding to the headwinds for Western brands is growing cultural and legal friction.
Louis Vuitton recently successfully sued Chinese beverage chain Molly Tea for trademark infringement over a four-petal floral pattern resembling the French firm's monogram. Molly Tea said it intended to appeal.
But the lawsuit sparked an online backlash after Chinese internet users and state media suggested that the motif was derived from ancient Chinese traditional patterns.
"It feels a bit absurd," said shopper Echo Wang, 31, who works in marketing.
"Molly Tea may be doing well in China, but it's nowhere near Louis Vuitton’s global profile... I think some people feel the lawsuit was inappropriate," she told AFP.
LVMH management called its intellectual property "an absolute key asset", but admitted the furore had "had a negative impact".
Analysts emphasise that China remains vital for the global luxury industry.
"In our view, China will still be an important market, although it may not be a growth engine in two to three years," said Luo.
"Luxury spending is normally rebounding in sync with the economy, as usually the wealthy class will be among the first to benefit from economic recovery."

'Permissible, virtuous': Israeli rabbi issues ruling allowing seizure of Palestinian olives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:40:37 UTC
19:40:37 KST

A Palestinian research center said on Monday that an Israeli rabbi had issued a religious ruling describing the seizure of Palestinian olive crops in the occupied West Bank as “permissible and even virtuous,” amid widespread attacks on farmers during the annual harvest season.
The Palestinian Center for Israeli Studies (Madar) said in a report that Rabbi Dov Lior, a former rabbi of the Kiryat Arba settlement and a religious authority associated with Israel’s far-right Jewish Power party, issued the ruling on October 16.
Lior declared that taking Palestinian olives in the West Bank is “completely permissible” and even carries “additional virtue,” according to the report.
The rabbi argued that Palestinians prevented from accessing their olive groves for security reasons could be considered to have abandoned their crops, making them available for others to take.
He also claimed that the land belongs to the Jewish people under Jewish religious law and that Palestinians who planted olive trees had already received compensation through harvests collected over previous years.
The Madar report, written by researcher Walid Habbas, examined the ruling as part of broader Israeli policies and practices affecting Palestinian olive harvesting in the occupied territory.
Citing Israeli rights organisation Yesh Din, Madar said hundreds of attacks by illegal Israeli settlers and soldiers had been documented across 171 Palestinian communities since the beginning of this year’s olive harvest season.
It said Palestinians were completely prevented from harvesting olives in 68 cases, while crops were stolen in 119 cases.
Illegal settler violence
The report also highlighted restrictions imposed by the Israeli military on Palestinian farmers’ access to their agricultural land.
Citing a decision reported by Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom in September, Madar said Palestinian farmers would no longer be permitted to harvest olives on land classified by Israel as “state land” across Palestine’s occupied West Bank.
It added that harvesting on privately owned land would also be subject to prior security coordination with Israeli authorities.
Madar said the restrictions, combined with the expansion of illegal Israeli settlement outposts, have increasingly prevented Palestinian farmers from accessing their olive groves.
The report also referred to recent attacks on foreign nationals accompanying Palestinian farmers, including American photojournalist Heidi Levine and a European diplomatic delegation.
Levine, a photographer for The Washington Post, was assaulted by illegal Israeli settlers while covering the olive harvest near Ramallah on Friday.
A day later, masked Israeli settlers attacked vehicles carrying European diplomats during an olive-harvesting visit to the West Bank town of Taybeh, damaging at least one vehicle.
The report cited figures from an Israeli Civil Administration document showing that Palestinian olive groves cover approximately 845,000 dunams (208,800 acres) and contain around 12.6 million trees.
More than 100,000 Palestinian families depend on olive cultivation for their livelihoods, according to the document.
Israeli Channel 13 previously reported Lior’s religious ruling on Friday, saying he had permitted Israeli settlers to take Palestinian olive crops, including from areas beyond the immediate vicinity of illegal Israeli settlements.
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. Israeli settlements in the occupied territory are illegal under international law.

Science surprises, from honeybees to microplastics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:40:12 UTC
19:40:12 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. Let’s get this week off to a great start by catching up on some recent science and tech news you may have missed.
We’ll start with some potentially paradigm-shifting research on the human ovary. According to a new study published in Aging Cell, these aren’t just reproductive organs. Long after ovaries stop producing eggs, the researchers say, the organs continue to evolve.
Building off of previous work in mice, the study examined normal ovarian tissue from 28 postmenopausal women between the ages of 50 and 75. The researchers analyzed nearly 6,000 different protein groups to track not just how postmenopausal ovaries differed from reproductively active ones but to see how they changed over decades of postreproductive life. And they did find changes. While the younger ovarian samples had more proteins associated with maintaining tissue structure, samples from older subjects had more proteins tied to inflammation and immune activity.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
What remains to be seen is whether postmenopausal ovaries are doing something beneficial or something harmful—or whether that’s a scale that can tip one way or the other depending on unknown factors. Given how long the ovaries have broadly been treated as useless bystanders once fertile years are past, we’ll probably be working to uncover their mysteries for quite some time.
Staying on the health beat, let’s talk about microplastics. One of the reasons that plastic has become such a ubiquitous material for things like food packaging and toys is that it’s meant to be really stable, in the chemical sense of the word—it’s a polymer, which is a long chain of molecules that doesn’t really easily react with other molecules it comes into contact with. But the stability of a polymer doesn’t mean the plastic object it ends up in is totally inert. Lots of additives commonly used in plastics, like flame retardants and colorants, are prone to leach out into surrounding materials. Bisphenol A, or BPA, which helps make plastic clear and durable, is just one particularly infamous example of an additive that seeps into food and can interfere with human hormone signalling. We also now know that microplastics—tiny particles that flake away into the environment as factors like heat and UV exposure cause plastic to degrade—have made their way into locations as remote as Antarctica and as intimate as human placentas and brains. While research on the exact impacts of microplastic on human health is very much in its early stages, they’ve been linked to inflammation, cellular damage, altered metabolic function and other serious issues in animal studies.
In a study published last Wednesday in the journal Nature, researchers report that even plastics that aren’t leaching out additives could cause problems. In fact, the very geometry of microplastics could make them more hazardous to human health.
The new study found that when exposed to water, microplastics spontaneously generated the kinds of highly reactive molecules that can damage cells. And more and more of that dangerous chemistry took place as the pieces got smaller. The researchers believe that’s because, as plastic breaks down into smaller pieces, it has more and more surface area. Imagine setting up a banquet hall with nine identical folding tables pushed together to make one big ole square that could fit, say 24 people comfortably. If you split the tables into three rectangles instead, you’d have more potential seats exposed—more surface area—and you’d double your comfortable seating to 48. Set up all nine tables individually, and you’ve got room for 72 place settings. It’s the same amount of table as you started with, but with way more edge exposed.
The same thing happens when plastics break down into micro and nano particles: the total volume of plastic remains the same, but more of it is exposed to whatever surrounds it—including human tissue, which happens to be full of water. While more research is needed to confirm this process and understand its potential impacts, we do know enough to say that you should try to limit your exposure to microplastics. Try to avoid microwaving food in plastic, and keep bottled water away from sunlight exposure which can cause the bottles to degrade.
And while we’re on the subject of avoiding microplastics, let’s shoutout one exposure you might not be aware of, teabags. Research published last week in npj Science of Food quantified microplastics in tea brewed from loose leaves compared to tea bags. Because FYI, those silky looking pyramid-shaped bags are made from plastic, and even many paper tea bags are sealed shut with plastic glue. The new study found that bagged tea could contain more than 1/5th of the European Food Safety Authority’s tolerable daily intake of BPA. So it might be a good time to invest in a tea strainer, preferably one made out of ceramic or stainless steel.
Speaking of hot and dangerous food, hackers have found a new way to wreak havoc on the meatspace. Last week, freezers and fridges in hundreds of French supermarkets were reportedly targeted by a cyberattack aimed at spoiling their wares. The hackers took over software from the Danish firm Danfoss that many major retailers use to regulate their refrigerators remotely. The attack raised temperatures to as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit and kept them elevated overnight, causing food to spoil.
If you want to learn more on how cyberattacks can target physical infrastructure and how benevolent hackers are working to help protect us from threats like these—check out our September 2 episode.
I know this is shocking but I think I’m gonna wrap us up with a fun animal story. Though this particular study is only fun to think about theoretically and gets pretty unpleasant if it gets too close to home. It has to do with how honeybees do their stinging.
When worker bees sting a target and then fly away, they leave their stingers behind—and those stingers keep, well, stinging. In a study published last week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers analyzed high-speed videos of honeybee stingers to reveal how they keep pumping venom sans bee.
Now, to the naked human eye a stinger looks like a pretty simple stabbing weapon, but it’s actually a sophisticated instrument. In addition to a venom sac and a pumping chamber, along with muscles and nerves, each stinger contains two sharp lancets that slide on a rail system, kind of like a reciprocating saw. Each lancet has its own attached valve that sits in the pumping chamber. And according to the new study, where scientists had bees sting a clear gel made to mimic human skin, those valves are the key to a stinger’s pumping power. On each downstroke of the lancet the attached valve inflates like parachutes, which creates a pressure seal and pushes venom out. Then as the lancet shoots back up, the valve deflates. The valves are also able to squeeze past one another, so they pump in opposite directions and maintain a continuous flow. Pretty cool, as long as you’re not the person on the receiving end.
That’s all for this week’s science news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk to one of my favorite authors of science fact and fiction about their latest book.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

Last Saturday, the stretch of sea between Larnaca and Ayia Napa became the race course for the “Regatta for Peace,” organized by the Italian Embassy in Nicosia in collaboration with the Cyprus Sailing Federation and the marinas of Larnaca and Ayia Napa. Twenty-four boats lined up at the starting line with over 120 crew members representing 13 different nationalities: an all-time record for participation, making the “Regatta for Peace” the largest amateur regatta ever organized in Cyprus.
                                    
The late-morning start from Larnaca Marina took place in the presence of Larnaca Mayor Andreas Vyras, who welcomed the crews and emphasized the message of peace that the event aims to promote, as well as Tourism Minister Kostas Koumis. 
The “Regatta for Peace” was the first European stop on the international roadshow leading up to the America’s Cup, which will arrive in Italy for the first time in July 2027, in Naples. It helped shine a spotlight on this important event while highlighting the value of sports diplomacy, which is being increasingly promoted by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
                                    
“We have dedicated this regatta to peace, the most cherished gift on earth,” said Italy’s Ambassador to Cyprus, Antonella Cavallari, as she opened the event, which—just a few hours before the finish—brought together participants and numerous dignitaries at the Ayia Napa Marina Convention Center. “Peace is the founding value of diplomacy—indeed, the very reason diplomacy exists. And sports diplomacy is one of its most important tools: sports convey a powerful message through their values—fair play, respect for the rules, mutual respect, cooperation, and friendship. Today more than ever, these are the values that should guide relations between nations and their peoples,” the ambassador concluded. 
The Minister of Tourism, Kostas Koumis, expressed great appreciation for the event, having attended from the morning onward and at the subsequent gala dinner. Among the guests in attendance were Cypriot champion Pavlos Kontides, a two-time Olympic silver medalist in the Laser/ILCA 7 class; Ihor Matviienko, the Ukrainian Olympic champion in the 470 class at the 1996 Atlanta Games; and Easy Swiss, the Israeli Olympic champion.
                                    
The day concluded at the Aya Resort, where the awards ceremony took place. The overall winner of the regatta was Typhoon, skippered by Jiovannis Pikis, followed by First Light, skippered by Robert Clunis, and Judith, skippered by Easy Suissa, who also took the top three spots in Class A. In Class B, “Infinity,” skippered by Philippos Haralambous, took first place, followed by “St. Michael,” skippered by Sergej Lysionok, and “Marianna,” skippered by Marios Karpis.

Protecting Earth’s fragile biodiversity takes spotlight at Armenia talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:36:51 UTC
19:36:51 KST

Protecting Earth’s fragile biodiversity takes spotlight at Armenia talks
Biodiversity losses continue to upend the lives of billions of people whose future prosperity depends on countries taking urgent action to protect our planet, the top UN official leading talks at the UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, said on Monday.
The aim of the talks in the Armenian capital is to assess progress so far and build on an agreed blueprint for biodiversity protection known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted four years ago.
“In 2022, 196 countries made commitments. But we are all accountable to each other and to future generations. What happens here in Yerevan matters. Billions of people whose lives are being upended by the impacts of biodiversity loss depend on progress being made here in the next two weeks,” said Executive Secretary of the UN Convention on Biodiversity, Astrid Schomaker.
Tapping into indigenous ideas
Insisting that “taking action for nature does work”, Ms. Schomaker called for the “untapped energy and ideas” of Indigenous Peoples and local communities, women and youth to contribute to the decisions made at the talks. “We need even greater engagement from cities, businesses and financial institutions…the science is clear. No nation, no economy, no society is immune from the impacts of biodiversity loss,” she insisted.
The goals of the Convention include tackling the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, the unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
Perhaps the Kunming-Montreal framework’s best-known ambition is “30 by 30”: conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
To do this, national action plans must align with international goals, finance must match current needs and consumption and production should be in accord with “the finite resources of our planet”, Ms. Schomaker maintained.
Why do these talks matter?
A core aim of the Yerevan talks – also known as COP17, or the 17th Conference Of Parties – is “to turn commitments into measurable progress on the ground”, insisted Armenia’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Paruyr Hovhannisyan.
“We want COP17 to send a clear political signal that addressing biodiversity loss requires coordinated action by governments, international organizations, the private sector and civil society,” he told UN News. “This means strengthening implementation, mobilizing adequate resources, and improving monitoring and accountability.”
Among the big issues governments will grapple with in Yerevan:
- Taking stock: Countries will conduct the very first global review of collective progress under the framework by presenting their national reports and updated national biodiversity strategies and action plans. This will show what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed.
- Closing the implementation gap: The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground.
- Finding the money: The framework calls for at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030, including at least $30 billion in international biodiversity finance, according to Armenia’s UN Ambassador Mr. Hovhannisyan.
- Making the Cali Fund work: This global financial mechanism established under the UN Convention on Biodiversity was agreed at COP16 in Cali, Colombia. Talks at Yerevan aim to advance practical arrangements for the fund, which was designed to collect funds from companies that use digital genetic data and redistribute these monies to protect biodiversity and Indigenous Peoples.
- Tracking progress: Better monitoring, data, capacity and cooperation are needed so countries can measure whether commitments are actually delivering results.
- Changing the economics: Some of the areas furthest behind require action outside environment ministries, including on finance, business, sustainable consumption and harmful incentives.
The meeting follows warnings from UN chief António Guterres in Yerevan on Friday that more than one million species face extinction.
War on nature
In his call for an end to the “war on nature”, the UN Secretary-General appealed to governments, business and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations.
“Every day, humankind saws another branch through the tree of life. Climate chaos, invasive species, overgrazing and overfishing, excessive fertilizers, pesticides, plastics and heavy metals, all these and more are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos,” he said.
The UN chief warned that the world is edging ever closer towards becoming uninhabitable. But he also pointed to international biodiversity action agreed under the Kunming-Montreal Framework. 
It had inspired action worldwide, Mr. Guterres insisted, noting that since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection.
But “progress is uneven and far too slow” and countries risk falling “well short” of the goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by 2030, the UN chief said.

U.S. Army orders more FD-1 drone interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:36:41 UTC
19:36:41 KST

The U.S. Army has placed a second order for the FD-1, a drone interceptor that a single soldier can set up and launch in under two minutes, from Florida-based Mountain Horse Solutions, less than a year after the system first came to the service’s attention.
The order was issued on Oct. 8 by the U.S. Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, known as G-TEAD, under an Other Transaction Agreement, a flexible contracting tool that lets the military buy and prototype new technology faster than through traditional contracts. It follows an initial G-TEAD agreement awarded this spring, and the company said the FD-1 is already fielded. Neither Mountain Horse Solutions nor the U.S. Army disclosed the contract value or how many interceptors are being bought.
The FD-1 is designed to destroy Group 1 to Group 3 drones, a range that runs from small quadcopters up to aircraft weighing several hundred kilograms, and can also be used against ground targets. One operator handles the system instead of a crew, and the company says it can work as the strike element behind an existing radar or tracking network or as a standalone system. A soldier stays in control throughout each engagement, and a human authorizes every shot.
The company built the FD-1 to address a cost problem that has strained air defenses in Ukraine and the Middle East, where cheap drones arrive in large numbers and are often shot down with interceptors that cost far more than their targets. It won first prize in the U.S. Army’s xTech Counter Strike competition in November 2025, and the U.S. Army Test and Evaluation Command has completed its technical review.
Soldiers from G-TEAD, the 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade and the test command evaluated the FD-1, and after each operational assessment Mountain Horse Solutions delivered user-driven upgrades within five weeks, the company said.
“Soldiers assessed the FD-1 and told us what needed improvement. We turned those updates around within weeks, and G-TEAD provided a way to buy the revised version without waiting on a requirements cycle. That sequence did not exist three years ago,” said Bill Allen, president of Mountain Horse Solutions.
G-TEAD places acquisition teams inside the U.S. Army’s regional commands so field commanders can buy and test new equipment quickly, using events called Accelerated Capability Events that aim to move a technology from concept to transition within 180 days. The FD-1 effort stayed within that timeline from operational assessment through the new award, with the 409th Contracting Support Brigade handling the contracting. The directorate is planning its next such event, focused on counter-drone systems, for spring 2027 in Morocco, where soldiers will test up to 15 drone-defense solutions.
“Soldiers find things a test range never will. G-TEAD built the pathway that turns their feedback into fielded improvements within weeks instead of program cycles and then gave the Army a way to order it,” said Richard Budniewski, director of UAS and counter-UAS programs at Mountain Horse Solutions.
Mountain Horse Solutions, part of Global Ordnance, said it is producing the FD-1 now and has capacity to expand output for further U.S. Army orders as well as for allied and partner nations.

Police said a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV struck Haines outside her office in Wangaratta, some 200km (124 miles) northwest of Melbourne.

The attack comes after the federal police documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation’s politicians in recent years. Politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security.
Albanese said on Monday that “the temperature has increased in recent times”.
“I’ve expressed that concern to people in the media,” he said. “If you look at anyone’s social media feeds and look at the comments, people will say things that they would never say face to face.”
The prime minister said the alleged attacker’s motive remained unknown, with Australia’s counterterrorism squad activated.

Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.

Russian attacks heavily damaged industrial facilities and critical infrastructure across Ukraine overnight on Oct. 19, hitting factories in the Kyiv suburb of Irpin, a data center in Kyiv, and infrastructure in Volyn Oblast, according to local officials and company statements.

Russian attacks on Ukrainian businesses and critical infrastructure in the Kyiv area have significantly increased in recent months and weeks, as Moscow looks to cripple Ukraine's economy, as well as its energy and water systems ahead of winter.
Irpin Mayor Oleksandr Markushyn said one of the city’s largest enterprises had suffered serious damage and caught fire in the overnight attack, without specifying the name of the company. The blast wave also shattered windows in nearby apartment buildings, he said.

The company lost a factory in Irpin in 2022 at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, with courts assessing the direct damage to the facility back then at around 13.1 million euros. It partially resumed operations in Ukraine's western city of Ternopil in March 2022 before reopening in Irpin in June of the same year. It closed its Ternopil operations in April 2023.
Another company in the area, Planet Plastic — which produces polyethylene products, including industrial and agricultural films, packaging materials and pipes used in water supply and gas distribution — confirmed that missiles struck its production facilities directly, causing significant destruction.
After its factory was nearly destroyed at the start of the invasion in 2022, Planet Plastic resumed operations in Irpin in 2025, but says it was forced to suspend them indefinitely in August due to intensified Russian air attacks on the region.
In Kyiv, telecommunications operator DataGroup reported that a Russian strike destroyed the infrastructure and equipment at its data center. The company said the facility could not be restored, but services were continuing through backup infrastructure. No employees were injured, it added.
The overnight attack on Kyiv killed one person and injured eight, according to local authorities. A metro station, medical facilities, educational institutions, residential buildings and other sites were also damaged.
Volyn Oblast was also targeted overnight and into the morning of Oct. 19. Around 15 Russian drones were directed at the region, with Kovel, Manevychi and Lutsk among the areas most heavily affected, the Volyn Regional Military Administration said.
Strikes and falling drone debris damaged critical and civilian infrastructure. Around 66,000 electricity metering points remained without power as of the administration’s 9:30 a.m. update. Officials reported no deaths or injuries in the region at that time.

Mexico arrests cartel members linked to murders of 10 workers from Canadian mining company
Mexican authorities said on Sunday that they had arrested five men linked to the kidnapping and murder of 10 workers from a Canadian mining company in the country's northwest.
The workers, all Mexicans, were kidnapped at gunpoint on January 23 from a silver mining project belonging to Vancouver-based Vizsla Silver in the violence-plagued state of Sinaloa.
The bodies of the 10 men, two of whom were engineers and one a geologist, were later found buried in clandestine graves.
Mexico's defense ministry said the suspects belonged to a faction of the fearsome Sinaloa cartel. It identified one suspect as Jesus Abraham, alias Taliban.
In June, Mexico announced the arrest of another suspect, identified as Gabriel N., alias Gabito, a hitman for the same faction.
Mines have been the target of organized crime on other occasions in Mexico, as cartels see opportunities to extort or even sell valuable ore themselves.
Abductions by armed groups are common in Mexico, where more than 120,000 people have vanished since the 1950s, many of them abducted and killed by drug cartels.
It is rare, however, for international companies to be targeted.
"We are devastated by this outcome and the tragic loss of life," Vizsla President and CEO Michael Konnert said in a statement after five of the workers' bodies were found. "Our deepest condolences are with our colleagues' families, friends and co-workers, and the entire community of Concordia."
Jaime Castañeda said he identified the body of his brother, José Manuel Castañeda Hernández, on Sunday by viewing photos shown to him by local officials in Mazatlán, CBC News reported.
"In truth, this has been very painful to be here, in a place where we don't want to be," Jaime Castañeda told CBC News in a phone interview.
José Manuel Castañeda Hernández, 43, was a husband and a father to two children, his brother told CBC News.
"It's so hard to see … how they suffer," Jaime Castañeda aid. "There's no justice with what's happening."
The government said the workers were mistaken for members of a rival faction of the Sinaloa cartel, which has been ripped apart by internecine fighting since September 2024.
According to the government, the suspects worked for a faction controlled by the sons of jailed druglord Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman, who is serving a life sentence in a Supermax prison in Florence, Colorado, which houses numerous high-profile inmates
The Sinaloa cartel has been designated a terrorist organization by Washington.
In July, former Sinaloa cartel co-founder Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada was sentenced in a U.S. court to life in prison, seven years after "El Chapo" was handed the same sentence.
