Military Engineering Showcase highlights UK defence innovation
Over 60 UK companies joined partners from over 20 nations to showcase military engineering solutions, strengthen collaboration and support UK defence exports.
- The NAD Group brought together a range of SMEs and Primes to showcase UK military engineering capabilities to international partners and UK Defence stakeholders.
- 66 UK defence companies demonstrated solutions across domains from combat engineering to demining and force protection.
- International delegations from more than 20 nations attended to discuss common military engineering challenges and opportunities for collaboration.
- The event supported UK defence exports, strengthened international partnerships and showcased innovation from the UK’s industrial base.
Hosted by National Armaments International (NA-Intl), the Military Engineering Showcase 2026 provided a forum for the UK Ministry of Defence, international partners and industry to share expertise, discuss common requirements and examine innovative technologies across the military engineering sector.
Taking place on 5 and 6 October 2026, the event highlighted the UK’s military engineering capabilities across combat engineering, infrastructure, counter-explosive ordnance, demining, force protection, survivability and deployable infrastructure.
Against a backdrop of increasing global instability and evolving security challenges, military engineering continues to play a vital role in supporting operational effectiveness, force protection, post-conflict recovery, and humanitarian assistance.
The showcase is designed to strengthen collaboration between the British military, overseas partners and the UK’s innovative defence industry, much of which is made up of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). These companies play a critical role in developing and manufacturing specialist capabilities for Defence, while export opportunities help sustain the expertise and resilience of the UK’s industrial base.
Lieutenant Colonel Andrew Teeton MBE RE, Military Advisor Counter-Explosive Ordnance and CBRN, National Armaments - International, said:
  The UK military engineering sector is home to world-leading companies, many of them SMEs, that are passionate about supporting Defence. Through collaboration and export opportunities, we can help sustain the skills, expertise, and innovation needed to meet current and future military engineering requirements.
  Events like the Military Engineering demo help us enhance capability, improve interoperability and support a resilient UK industrial base by strengthening partnerships and sharing approaches to common challenges.
The event featured presentations from UK military engineering specialists, networking opportunities with international delegations, capability demonstrations and industry briefings. Delegates had the opportunity to engage directly with the Export Support Team (EST), part of NA-International. Comprised of British Army officers and soldiers, the EST provides specialist military services and advice to UK defence and security companies and were on hand throughout the demonstration to share their expertise on current and emerging military engineering requirements.
The Military Engineering Showcase supported wider efforts to strengthen international partnerships, promote UK defence collaboration and exports, and ensure military engineering capabilities continue to evolve in response to operational demands around the world.

Can countries deliver on a deal to save the world’s plants and animals?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:16:09 UTC
19:16:09 KST

Passersby could smell the dead fish before they saw them. In August, more than 3,000 pike, roach, carp and rudd were found lifeless along the River Wensum in Norwich. Some gasped for air in their final moments, desperate for the oxygen that heatwave conditions had depleted in the water. Investigators believe that the die-off was triggered by heavy rainfall that flushed through high concentrations of pollution at a time when wildlife were already struggling.
The 45-mile (70km) chalk river is one of about 250 in the country. They are a geological accident almost unique to Britain – and one of Earth’s rarest habitats. They emerge from chalk aquifers and are home to species such as freshwater shrimp, otters and stoneflies, also providing drinking water for millions of people. But just 11 have formal protection, with many ravaged by sewage pollution and overextraction. The Norfolk river is one of the few that does have legal protection, but it is in poor ecological health.
“We are a world away from the crystal clear, free flowing and mineral-rich waters they could, and should be,” says Eliot Lyne, head of the Norfolk Wildlife Trust.
This decade was meant to signal a change in humanity’s relationship with the natural world. At the end of 2022, nearly every government on Earth committed to an ambitious deal to better protect the world’s rapidly disappearing biodiversity at a summit in Montreal, Canada. Negotiators shook hands on targets that included protecting 30% of the planet for nature, restoring nearly a third of the planet’s most degraded ecosystems, and reforming at least $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally harmful subsidies.
Some scientists say that we are living through the largest loss of life since the time of the dinosaurs, putting a million species at risk of extinction. This time, humanity is the meteor. The Montreal agreement was the response.
But four years later, governments look almost certain to miss nearly all of the deal’s targets – potentially continuing the record of never having met a single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. The UK, one of the loudest voices demanding ambition in Montreal, is on track to meet just three of the 23 targets by the end of the decade. This week, countries gather at Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, to decide what to do next.
On the eve of the summit, at the launch of a report showing just how far off track the world is on meeting those commitments, António Guterres, secretary general of the UN, warned that lack of progress means “the war on nature has not ended” and that “nature will not survive on good intentions”. Following this, in an address to leaders at an event in Armenia, Guterres once again emphasised the importance of action on subsidies in particular. “Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said.
“They are boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity. I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”
“There’s a massive gap between countries agreeing to do something and actually doing it,” says Zac Goldsmith, former UK government minister when the deal was reached. “That’s where we are today.”
British conservationists point to a growing gap between government rhetoric and action. “The UK is back on the international stage on nature,” then environment secretary Steve Reed declared while standing under the skeleton of a blue whale at the Natural History Museum in the first few months of the Starmer government. Since then, the government has weakened rules on biodiversity net gain in England, slashed tens of millions of pounds of funding for rainforest protection schemes as part of aid cuts, and rejected an outright ban on bottom trawling in marine protected areas. No new sites of special scientific interest have been designated by Natural England to protect rare wildlife and habitats since 2023.
“For us to go around the world telling other countries that they must achieve these targets without us having a plan how to deliver them at home is a form of neocolonialism,” says Craig Bennett, head of The Wildlife Trusts. “We’ve got to pull our socks up and get serious about delivery at home. We are the nation of Sir David Attenborough. We are animal and nature lovers.”
A UK government spokesperson said it has backed a nature recovery and climate resilience with £7bn of funding, and implemented new powers to tackle water pollution, fund species recovery and support international conservation work.
The UK has also reinstated its climate aid commitments, apparently abandoned earlier this year, pledging around £6bn of international climate finance from the aid budget over the next three financial years, with around a quarter expected to be spent on nature.
Jonathan Hall, managing director of Conservation International UK, told the Guardian: “Re-instating the ditched goal for international nature funding as part of UK climate aid is smart politics, given UK public support, and a smart investment in our global security and resilience in the face of ecosystem collapse. This very welcome re-commitment now needs to be accompanied with increased transparency so we can ensure this approximately £1.5bn is disbursed as impactfully as possible.”
But the urgency of the warnings has not changed. Earlier this year, a report by intelligence chiefs warned that ecological collapse is a national security risk, threatening the country with food shortages, economic strife and global disorder. But nature has been unable to escape the swirling global current of populist culture wars.
In the Netherlands, efforts by the EU, in 2019, to crack down on nitrogen pollution to protect vulnerable ecosystems sparked nationwide farmer protests. While the discontent predates this decade’s biodiversity targets, the nature restoration law, the EU’s flagship package of laws resulting from the deal, also became embroiled in a bitter disagreement with the rightwing bloc in the European parliament, who tried to block the regulations due to the impact on agriculture. It was eventually passed, but only after it was substantially watered down.
“In the Netherlands, they tried really hard and you saw this huge backlash. It’s an extremely sensitive issue politically,” says Steven Guilbeault, Canada’s former environment minister, who helped guide the 2022 negotiations alongside China’s environment minister, Huang Runqiu. “Governments are not always the best at communicating these complex policy pieces. It is easy for a critic to come up with a totally meaningless slogan that gets picked up on social media,” he says.
The second presidency of Donald Trump has also been catastrophic for the conservation sector. Hundreds of projects had previously received support from Washington DC – from stopping illegal fishing in the Galápagos islands to backing the restoration of Gorongosa national park in Mozambique after the civil war – but Trump’s brutal cuts to USAID and other government agencies have meant funding evaporated overnight for many schemes.
Many European nations have followed suit – despite signing up to a target to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade. The UK has cut back funding for the Darwin Initiative, removing eligibility for at least 89 countries earlier this year. Efforts to get the private sector to help have struggled; a new fund to get companies that use digital forms of biodiversity for commercial discoveries, which proponents had hoped would raise hundreds of millions each year, has so far raised just $6,000.
It is not a universally gloomy picture. A majority of countries have responded to significant parts of the agreement. One estimate shows that countries could come close to meeting the land portion of the 30x30 target, and the deal has seen the formalisation of more Indigenous territories in many countries.
Even bigger protected areas could come: places such as French Polynesia have established huge new marine parks. Countries such as Kazakhstan have used the agreement to drive a major rewilding effort, bringing back the Caspian tiger. But the gap between what the science demands to avert ecological crisis and the current pace of change remains huge – and an urgent task for negotiators in Armenia.
“Protection targets are falling short, promised national plans have yet to materialise, and committed finance is not reaching where it is needed. This is increasingly a shared dynamic across environmental processes: making commitments is the easy part; delivering on them is much harder,” said Li Shuo, director of China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
“Sustainable change will only happen when countries internalise the urgency to act and translate commitments into domestic action. More than halfway through this decade, most countries are still moving far too slowly.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features.

Ursula von der Leyen, António Costa and Emmanuel Macron will join Hungarian PM Péter Magyar in Budapest on Friday to mark 70 years since the 1956 uprising, signalling a reset in EU-Hungary ties after Viktor Orbán’s years in power.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will travel to Budapest on Friday to mark the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 anti-Soviet uprising. French President Emmanuel Macron will also attend, according to Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who is set to host the ceremony.
The event marks a major thaw in relations between Brussels and Budapest after years of acrimony under his predecessor, Viktor Orbán.
It will be von der Leyen’s first visit to Hungary since 2024, when she attended a European Political Community summit in Budapest.
Under Orbán, Hungary repeatedly blocked EU initiatives to support Ukraine, opposed financial and military assistance to Kyiv and maintained close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
But since Magyar’s Tisza Party swept to power in April, the new government has pledged to bring Hungary back into the European mainstream and settle its longstanding disputes with Brussels.
In a sharp break with Orbán’s policies, Magyar’s government has identified Russia as a security threat and approved the opening of four negotiating clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also been invited to the commemoration, but Magyar said he is unlikely to attend. The Hungarian prime minister has said he invited all European leaders except Putin. The full list of participants has not yet been released.
On 23 October 1956, Hungarian students took to the streets to protest against Soviet occupation. The demonstrations quickly grew into a popular uprising, which the Red Army later crushed. Zelenskyy’s presence would have drawn parallels with Ukraine’s defence against Russia’s full-scale invasion.
The commemoration could also allow European leaders to signal their support for Magyar after the Orbán era and to speak up against Russia's war in Ukraine.

Mother leaves children on Poland mountain trail for 'whining', hikes to summit alone
Unknown

Conditions on the trail were poor with a thick fog over the area, prompting shocked tourists to take care of the young boys.
A mother left her two children alone on the Bieszczady Mountains hiking trail in southern Poland on Saturday because they were "whining" and she wanted to reach the summit alone.
"We are near the point where the blue and yellow trails split above Muczne. We are hiking with a group from the PTTK branch in Rzeszow. Suddenly we hear a piercing sob and a child’s scream. We stop, and two boys – a crying eight-year-old and his fourteen-year-old brother – are standing, bewildered, by the side of the trail," the Rzeszow branch of the Polish Tourist and Sightseeing Society (PTTK) wrote on its Facebook profile.
"We find out that their mother has left them behind and gone on alone to reach the summit (which from this point is about an hour away). She told them that if they were whining and didn’t want to walk, they should wait for fifteen minutes," the post continued.
The boys were left waiting on their own for far longer than 15 minutes.
"No reflection, no sense of guilt"
Conditions on the trail were poor; as the author of the PTTK post notes, a thick fog had settled over the area, prompting shocked tourists to take care of the young boys.
"After about a quarter of an hour, a fit-looking woman appears. The younger son grabs her by the hand and stops crying. When we point out how she could leave underage children alone in high mountains, in such weather conditions, she responds coolly that she was gone only for a moment, that she wanted to go higher, and that they were forcing her to give up on achieving the planned goal," PTTK said.
PTTK criticised the women for showing "no sense of guilt."
"The forced word 'sorry' comes from her lips only when I say that this could amount to charges from the public prosecutor. My reply, that she should not be apologising to me but to the children, is met with no reaction..." the author of the post wrote.
The incident was reported to local authorities and has sparked widespread public outrage in Poland regarding parental responsibility and safety on mountain trails.

Russia calls its upgraded T-80 a stealthy ‘assassin’ tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:14:43 UTC
19:14:43 KST

- Rostec described its T-80BVM tank as an “assassin,” claiming its gas turbine engine and camouflage allow fast, unnoticed flanking maneuvers.
- The company also called the tank a battering ram and a drone-guided “sniper” able to hit targets about 10 km away.
Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec has described its T-80BVM main battle tank as an “assassin,” claiming the gas turbine-powered vehicle is quiet and well camouflaged enough to make fast, unnoticed flanking moves on the battlefield.
In a promotional statement, Rostec said the modernized tank can play several roles: a “steel battering ram” that breaks through enemy defenses while firing under swarms of FPV drones, a “sniper” that works with a spotter drone to hit targets about 10 km away with a couple of shots, and an “assassin” that relies on its engine and camouflage to slip around enemy flanks.
“It’s also an assassin which, thanks to a quiet and powerful gas turbine engine and camouflage, can make fast and unnoticed flanking maneuvers,” Rostec said, in remarks translated from Russian.
Rostec also called the T-80BVM a “flying” tank, a reference to the T-80’s well-known jumps off dirt ramps at Russian military shows, and said that same ability reflects the tank’s mobility, speed and performance on difficult ground.
The T-80BVM is an upgrade of the Soviet-era T-80BV and it is powered by a GTD-1250 gas turbine engine rated at 1,250 horsepower and armed with a 125 mm 2A46M-1 smoothbore gun, and Rostec listed a modernized fire control system, new all-around armor protection and guided missiles fired through the gun barrel among its main features. The company did not give further details, saying it would describe other features later.
Rostec’s claim that the gas turbine runs more quietly than diesel engines is the company’s own assessment. Gas turbine engines give the T-80 strong acceleration and help it start in extreme cold, but they burn considerably more fuel than the diesel engines used in Russia’s T-72 and T-90 tanks, and the T-80 family has long been criticized for its high fuel consumption.
The “sniper” role Rostec describes, in which tanks fire at targets well beyond line of sight with corrections from drones, has become common in the war in Ukraine, where both sides often use tanks as mobile artillery to avoid being spotted and destroyed by drones at close range.
Russia has used the T-80BVM extensively in Ukraine, where the T-80 family has suffered heavy losses to drones, anti-tank missiles and mines.
The open-source monitoring group Oryx, which counts only losses confirmed by photos or video, has documented 1,311 T-80-series tanks destroyed, damaged, abandoned or captured, including 264 T-80BVMs: 150 of the standard version and 114 of the 2022 model. The total also includes 712 older T-80BVs, 148 T-80BVs of the 2022 model, 107 T-80Us and 53 T-80s whose exact variant could not be identified. Uralvagonzavod, Rostec’s main tank maker, has continued to upgrade stored T-80BV hulls to the T-80BVM standard and deliver them to Russian forces, and Rostec has not said how many it has built.

Winter rains deepen Gaza&#8217;s humanitarian crisis as displaced families face severe shelter shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:11:24 UTC
19:11:24 KST

The return of winter rains is worsening humanitarian conditions in the Gaza Strip, where widespread destruction, repeated displacement and shortages of adequate shelter have left hundreds of thousands of Palestinians exposed to cold weather and flooding.
According to figures compiled by Arabi21 from government authorities and United Nations agencies, many displaced families are living in deteriorating tents or damaged buildings that provide little protection against rain and falling temperatures.
Field assessments indicate that more than 162,000 of approximately 270,000 tents in Gaza have become worn out or completely unusable because of prolonged use and exposure to harsh weather.
Gaza’s Ministry of Social Development has called for the urgent provision of 200,000 weather-resistant tents and 300,000 shelter kits, including thermal insulation materials, tarpaulins and reinforced plastic sheeting.
The ministry said the supplies were needed to assist more than 300,000 families facing increasingly difficult living conditions.
READ: Repeated displacement leaves Gaza shelters deteriorating ahead of winter: IOM
The shelter crisis has been compounded by extensive destruction of residential infrastructure. According to the reported figures, approximately 85 percent of housing units across the Gaza Strip have been completely or partially destroyed, leaving many families without viable alternatives to displacement camps.
Children remain particularly vulnerable to the deteriorating conditions. An estimated 800,000 displaced children are living away from their homes, many in makeshift shelters that offer inadequate protection against winter weather.
The humanitarian crisis has also placed additional pressure on children who have lost family members during the war.
According to the figures cited in the report, approximately 60,000 children in Gaza have lost one or both parents, with some assuming responsibilities for supporting their families while living in displacement.
The combination of inadequate shelter, damaged infrastructure and approaching winter conditions is expected to intensify the difficulties facing displaced Palestinians, particularly children and families without access to secure housing.

PRESS REVIEW – Monday, October 19: French and international papers discuss the anti-government protests that turned violent at the weekend and their aftermath across France.
Many French papers are using the word "chaos" to describe the protests over the weekend. Le Parisien writes: "After the chaos, the anger". It says that on Sunday France woke up to destruction following the protests. The headline of left-wing paper Libération reads "Questioning chaos". Libération says that due to an inadequate law enforcement strategy that failed to anticipate the widespread vandalism and looting, the protests spiralled out of control, although hundreds of thousands of people were attempting to march peacefully. The headline of right-wing paper Le Figaro reads "Shame and anger". The paper says that all across France "unprecedented scenes of violence" took place, which are causing consternation.
The headline of the Communist paper L'Humanité reads "Social explosion". The paper says that the day of protests was ruined by violence and vandalism, as well as by widespread police crackdowns on demonstrators. Catholic paper La Croix asks "How did we get here?" It says that the riots and looting are fuelling fears of widespread unrest, against a backdrop of social anger. L'Opinion asks: "Who benefits from the chaos?" The paper tries to summarise what happened: Public order has broken down. The prime minister is responding solely on a political level. The president is calling for calm. Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon continues to stir up conflict, while far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen is seeking to capitalise on both fronts: public order and social issues.
International papers are also reacting. German newspaper Der Spiegel asks "Is France descending into chaos and crisis?" Politically, this unrest is going to further polarise France, according to the paper. One woman is likely to benefit, it says: the far-right presidential frontrunner, Marine Le Pen. Le Pen and her National Rally party are skilfully presenting themselves as the guarantors of public order. This time, the right wing has refrained from actively supporting the movement, as it did in 2018 with the Yellow Vests, even though it expresses sympathy for the peaceful demonstrators; after all, many of their voters are among them. The headline of Spanish paper El País says "France sets Macronism ablaze". The paper calls President Emmanuel Macron's second term "out of touch with society" – but there are still six long months to go until the next presidential elections, during which the country must pass a budget and find answers to the unstoppable rise of the far right.
The New York Times says there's "shock and recrimination", a day after the "huge riots". The paper says that during his speech, Macron "offered no concrete concessions". It reminds us that government officials and far-right leaders accuse the far left of stirring up the unrest. The left wing, meanwhile, blames the government for budget decisions and policies they said have spurred public anger. British paper The Times says that Paris was "divided by protests". Many are pointing the fingers at those who rioted and looted, saying the level of violence was worse than during the Yellow Vest protests in 2018. Others say that police repression pushed people to become increasingly violent. A 20-year-old art student told The Times: "Instead of listening to us, the government sends in the police to attack us". "We no longer live in a democracy" is the headline in the independent Russian paper Novaya Gazeta. It's a quote from one of the protesters who spoke to the paper. She says that "the Republic has been shaken to its core – we no longer live in a democracy where we can assemble," adding that "the police are seizing power through violence".

At least 18 killed in Houthi attack on Yemeni government training camp in Shabwa, sources say

The conflict in Yemen has become another front line in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran as the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter, targeting Riyadh's international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco.
War broke out in Yemen in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south. A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate until the sides agreed a 2022 truce that held until this year.
Yemen is already one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with aid agencies warning of rapidly deteriorating conditions there. REUTERS

Advertisement

Such internet restrictions are more commonly associated with countries like China, Iran, Russia and, more recently, India. These countries either have permanent blocks on certain social media platforms or have more recently restricted them during protest movements, with India and Iran going so far as to block internet access completely.

EU eyes Arctic cable linking Greenland to Europe amid growing security threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:10:18 UTC
19:10:18 KST

Brussels wants to secure digital infrastructure in the Arctic as melting ice and growing geopolitical tensions turn the polar region into a strategic corridor for trade, communications and security.
The European Union is planning a secure submarine cable linking Greenland directly to Europe, with ambitions to extend the network through Canada to Japan and South Korea, according to a draft Arctic strategy seen by Euronews.
The project is part of a broader effort to strengthen Europe's digital infrastructure and security in the increasingly contested Arctic region.
"The EU is working on a Pan-Arctic Cable concept that will connect Europe to Japan and South Korea via Greenland and Canada. In the coming years, the EU will connect Greenland to the European Union with a sovereign and secure submarine cable," the document reads.
The plans, outlined in the EU's new Arctic strategy, due to be unveiled on 20 October, reflect growing concerns in Brussels that undersea telecommunications cables have become a matter of strategic security rather than simply commercial infrastructure.
The initiative comes amid a deteriorating security environment in the Arctic, where Russia has expanded its military presence and European governments are increasingly concerned about hybrid threats, including interference with satellite navigation and sabotage of undersea infrastructure.
Meanwhile, growing US interest in Greenland ,has added another layer of geopolitical tension to the region, underlining Europe's concerns about its dependence on infrastructure controlled by others.
The North Atlantic has roughly 17 submarine telecommunications cables, with US technology giants playing a dominant role in the wider infrastructure network.
Submarine cables carry the vast majority of international data traffic, underpinning everything from everyday communications to financial transactions. Their vulnerability to accidental damage or deliberate sabotage has become a major concern for European governments.
For Brussels, improving Arctic connectivity goes beyond bringing faster internet to remote communities. The EU is looking to create more resilient routes for data and reduce exposure to infrastructure that could be disrupted during a geopolitical crisis.
Greenland occupies a particularly sensitive position. Situated between Europe and North America, the autonomous Danish territory has become increasingly important to transatlantic security as competition intensifies over Arctic resources, shipping routes and military access.
A more direct digital connection with Europe could strengthen the territory’s links to the EU while giving Brussels a greater stake in the infrastructure underpinning the region’s future.
"The new submarine cable routes will enhance the access of Arctic communities as well as boost resilience and redundancy in Europe’s digital connectivity. Such connection is a pre-condition for further investments highly relevant for both competitiveness, inclusion, preparedness and defence," reads the document.
The proposed extension towards Asia through Canada would add a broader strategic dimension. Rather than treating Greenland as an isolated connectivity challenge, the EU is considering how Arctic infrastructure might form part of a wider network linking European and Asian economies.
Whether that vision becomes a viable project will depend on technical feasibility, commercial demand, financing and cooperation with Canada and other partners.
Who will pay?
The EU has already earmarked €107 million for connectivity projects involving Greenland, meaning the proposed cable would build on existing commitments rather than represent an entirely new area of investment.
The Commission had presented the idea of co-financing Far North Fibre, a route planning a subsea cable in the Arctic area, to EU member-state representatives. The project was estimated to cost around $1.15 billion, but the project received around €11 million.
The potentially significant development is the prospect of a wider strategic connection between Greenland, Europe and, through Canada, Asian partners.
Such a network would raise difficult questions about who pays for construction, who owns and operates the cables, how they would be protected and whether the route would be commercially viable.
Any extension towards Japan and South Korea would also require agreement and coordination with partners beyond the EU.
However, the strategy does not settle those questions. Nor does it establish a final route, budget or construction schedule for the proposed network.
Still, it mentions creating an Arctic Cable Hub for EU countries, Norway and Iceland, to monitor, protect, and support the repair of submarine cables in the North Atlantic-Arctic. The hub will likely require support from an enhanced icebreaker fleet.
Expanding the icebreaker fleet
The EU's Arctic ambitions extend beyond digital infrastructure to the ships needed to operate in the region's increasingly contested waters.
At the Arctic Summit in September, the EU's special envoy for the region, former Finnish Prime Minister Jyrki Katainen, warned of a critical shortfall in European icebreaker capabilities.
“This is not just an issue for Finland, for Norway, for Sweden. This is something for the entire European Union, for the entire European continent. And that's the reason why we are talking about that. And you have my support on that to do that jointly,” German Chancellor Friederik Merz said at the summit’s press conference.
Indeed, the strategy goes in this direction, and vows to put in place an EU Industrial Maritime Value Chains Alliance meant to map icebreaking needs, available manufacturing capacity in Europe and the technical specifications required.
“The EU, together with member states and like-minded partners, will develop options for joint procurement, pooling and sharing icebreaker capabilities and other capabilities relevant for the Arctic,” reads the strategy.
The intent is to pool together funding and technological resources with Nordic countries and examine whether it is possible to facilitate the operational viability of nationally owned assets, while respecting the national command structure.
The strategy explicitly mentions “assets with special focus on icebreakers for extreme high North environments utilising advanced, high-endurance propulsion systems, including nuclear.”

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. The T-80BVM tank is the result of a comprehensive modernization carried out even before the start of Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine, and it has also undergone hundreds of modifications during combat operations, Rostec reported.
"The vehicle was created no less than 50 years ago. Today, it remains recognizable externally, but has evolved into something completely new. Even before the special military operation, the T-80 underwent a comprehensive upgrade to become the T-80BVM. During the course of combat, it has been adapted to the environment, receiving hundreds of additional modifications, including enhanced armor protection and upgraded systems," the state corporation stated.
Rostec noted that today the tank is capable of carrying out a wide range of tasks - from breaking through enemy defenses with direct-fire strikes during a massive attack by FPV drones to sniper operations in coordination with a spotter drone and stealthy flanking maneuvers enabled by its quiet and powerful gas turbine engine and camouflage systems. "And, of course, it’s still a ‘flying’ tank that can leap into the air with its entire multi-ton mass from an earthen ramp. This capability isn’t just for show - the tank boasts excellent cross-country mobility over difficult terrain, as well as high maneuverability and speed," Rostec added.
It noted that the combat vehicle’s multi-mission capability is ensured by a 1,250-horsepower GTD-1250 gas turbine engine, a modern 125-mm 2A46M-1 gun, a modernized fire control system, new all-aspect protection, and a guided weapons system with gun-launched missiles.

Russia Admits Its Air Defenses Cannot Shield Vast Industrial Empire From Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Russia cannot provide comprehensive air defense coverage for its vast industrial infrastructure, with many of the country’s largest factories and production complexes too extensive to be fully protected against Ukrainian drone strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), acknowledged these limitations, according to Russian state news agency TASS on October 17. He explained that the scale and layout of Soviet-era industrial facilities present significant challenges for Russia’s air defense systems.
Many of Russia’s largest industrial enterprises were originally designed during the Soviet period with the possibility of nuclear war in mind. Production facilities were deliberately spread across large areas to reduce the risk of an entire industrial complex being destroyed in a single attack.
However, the same design principles have created vulnerabilities in modern warfare, particularly as Ukraine continues using long-range drones to strike industrial and military-related infrastructure deep inside Russian territory.
Metallurgical plants, chemical factories, and other major industrial facilities can stretch across several kilometers, making it difficult to establish comprehensive protection over their entire territory.
Shokhin noted that Soviet planners placed individual workshops far apart to improve the chances of maintaining production following a nuclear strike. While this approach offered certain advantages, it also required extensive infrastructure connecting different sections of industrial complexes.
These dispersed facilities now present a major challenge for Russia, as protecting individual production buildings does not necessarily guarantee the security of the wider industrial site.
The acknowledgment comes amid Ukraine’s continuing campaign of long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries, military production facilities, airfields, chemical plants, and other strategically important infrastructure.
In September, five Russian oil refineries, including the Moscow Oil Refinery, suspended processing operations following damage and fires.
On October 18, Ukrainian drones also struck the Petersburg Oil Terminal, triggering a fire, while separate attacks targeted a VKontakte data center and electrical infrastructure in the surrounding Leningrad region.

Russia Bombards Kyiv and Surrounding Region With Missiles and Drones, Killing Two and Injuring 14
Russian forces launched a large-scale missile and drone attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight on October 19, killing at least two people and injuring 14 others, including three children.
The attack involved ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and hundreds of drones, damaging residential buildings, medical facilities, educational institutions, and transport infrastructure across the capital and Kyiv region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, one person was killed and eight others were injured in the capital, where damage was recorded in the Desnianskyi, Dniprovskyi, and Solomianskyi districts.
In the Desnianskyi district, the strikes damaged a private medical facility and a metro station. Authorities subsequently announced the temporary closure of the Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations on Kyiv’s left bank.
Debris from the attack damaged both the running and power rails near one of the stations, disrupting metro operations in the affected area.
In the Dniprovskyi district, falling debris damaged educational institutions and a sports facility, while additional debris landed on nonresidential premises.
Meanwhile, in the Solomianskyi district, a fire broke out inside a medical facility located on the third floor of a 25-story residential building. Emergency services extinguished the blaze, while the attack also damaged windows in nearby buildings and a shopping center.
The missile strikes also raised concerns about the lack of advance warning for residents. According to sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu, the ballistic missile attack on Kyiv once again occurred without any warning, a situation that has reportedly happened on previous occasions.
Beyond the capital, Russian strikes caused casualties and extensive damage in several communities across Kyiv region, particularly in Irpin, Bucha district.
According to Head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration Tymur Tkachenko, six people were injured in Irpin, including three children, while three others were reported missing. Deputy Mayor Oleksandr Pashchynskyi also confirmed that a woman had been killed in the attack.
In the wider Bucha district, the strikes damaged 11 private houses, six vehicles, an industrial facility, a warehouse, and an educational institution. Windows were also shattered in several apartment buildings.
In the Vyshhorod district, authorities reported damage to a private residence, five vehicles, and an infrastructure facility.
The overnight assault formed part of a broader Russian aerial attack involving multiple types of missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles launched from Russian territory and occupied Ukrainian regions.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Smolensk, Bryansk, and Kursk regions, as well as Iskander-K cruise missiles from the airspace over the Kursk region.
The attack also involved 269 drones, including Shahed-type attack UAVs, S-8000 Banderol drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoys. Of the total, 59 were jet-powered drones.
As of 9 a.m. on October 19, Ukrainian air defenses had intercepted or suppressed 247 aerial targets, including four Iskander-K cruise missiles and 243 drones of various types. Among the intercepted drones were 43 jet-powered UAVs, according to the Air Force’s preliminary assessment.
The latest attack comes amid renewed attention to Ukraine’s access to intelligence needed to detect incoming Russian missile strikes. On October 18, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that the United States had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine following a temporary suspension, restoring a key channel of military cooperation amid concerns over the availability of early warnings about Russian missile attacks.

WFP cuts aid to ‌500,000 Palestinians in Gaza amid funding shortages

WFP cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza amid funding shortages
The UN agency says funding shortages threaten to reverse ‘modest and fragile’ progress on food security.
The World Food Programme (WFP) has announced major cuts to its Gaza response due to a funding shortage, leaving about 500,000 people without critical support as much of the population of the war-ravaged Palestinian territory struggles to get enough to eat.
In a statement on Monday, the United Nations agency said it received less than half as much funding for its Palestine operation in 2026 as in previous years. It said it urgently needs a further $450 million to maintain critical operations in the occupied Palestinian territory over the next six months.
As a result, the WFP said it would reduce the number of people receiving monthly assistance in Gaza from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. Rations will be cut from two food parcels per family to one, and bags of flour will be smaller.
The UN agency said it would also reduce the number of hot meals provided, from 250,000 to 150,000 a day. Families living in hard-to-reach areas, including near the so-called “yellow line” demarcating Israeli military control, will receive a hot meal every other day instead of daily.
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, have brought the collapse of education, healthcare and the economy, while access to food, water, shelter and other basic necessities has become a daily struggle.
More than 74,245 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
UN estimates show more than 80 percent of people are unemployed and unable to afford fresh or protein-rich foods when they are available. Only one in five children consumes a sufficiently diverse diet while access to health services remains limited.
An estimated 1.4 million people, or 67 percent of Gaza’s population, are experiencing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. This figure is down from 1.6 million people, or 77 percent of the population, at the end of 2025, however the WFP said the improvement “remains modest and fragile.”
Funding shortfalls had already affected operations in the occupied West Bank, where the number of people receiving assistance was halved in September, from 400,000 to 200,000.

Ancient revenge porn: When sex became a weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:07:13 UTC
19:07:13 KST

Where modern culture relies on social media feeds and comment threads to communicate, the Romans turned to their architecture. The plastered walls of Roman cities served as an open-access billboard for public commentary, carrying everything from political slogans and advertisements to declarations of affection, poems, jokes, obscenities, and, inevitably, personal attacks.
Although the graffiti did not usually descend to private intimate images, nor was every sexual insult an act of revenge, these ephemeral inscriptions reveal a persistent feature of human behavior: the deliberate use of sexual information, or sexual allegations, to shame another person before a public audience.
A wall of shame
In some respects, the similarity to social media is striking. "Tagging" names on city walls resembles today's social media realities. While these ephemeral inscriptions lacked the digital infrastructure of today's platforms, they illustrate a persistent psychological reality: using sexual allegations to inflict public humiliation. With a bit of charcoal or a sharp stone, anyone could insult an enemy or expose a former lover's alleged transgressions.
Much like a digital post today, an ancient comment in a high-traffic area reached an audience far beyond the creator's immediate circle. To make matters worse, the readers often added their own observations below the original text, turning a single act of venom into a collective exchange that reads remarkably like an online comment section.
Of course, these inscriptions lacked the speed, extent, or reproducibility of digital communication. An accusation on a wall could not reach thousands of people within seconds or be replicated across multiple platforms with a click, leaving a long-term footprint. Nevertheless, its public visibility created a similar containment problem: once an accusation entered the public domain, its target could not know who encountered it or whether it would be repeated. Even if an inscription was later concealed, the damage was done, for the content's disappearance rarely means the end of its social consequences.
The humiliation arose not merely from being insulted, but from becoming the object of collective laughter. In this sense, Roman graffiti's significance lay not in the insult itself, but in the conditions of its exposure. In the tightly interconnected world of Roman public life, the existimatio, or reputation, was everything. It was a currency that dictated legal rights, eligibility for public office, and even financial creditworthiness. To dismantle a citizen's sexual standing was to strike not only at their civic identity but also potentially at their livelihood.
Albanus is a perv
The surviving graffiti of Pompeii and Herculaneum reveal how sexual insults could turn a wall into a public forum of humiliation. Some inscriptions mocked alleged sexual behaviors, while others used crude sexual labels to ridicule men and women, making them objects of public mockery.
These attacks were not necessarily based on personal knowledge; they might have been fabricated. Some may have been regarded as jokes, provocations, or were just the product of a bored mind. Yet even if written in jest, such insults drew on cultural assumptions about sex, and the strict social expectations that were attributed to gender. Their existence points to a universal urge that continues to this day: the need to humiliate others using vocabulary that thrives to this day in locker rooms, restrooms, and other public spaces where anonymity invites vulgarity.
The aim is not simply to accuse a man of sexual misconduct, but to portray him as sexually deviant, effeminate, and fundamentally unworthy of respect. One such accusation was immortalized on a public building in Pompeii: "Gaius Valerius Venustus, a soldier of the 1st cohort, was here. He is a cinaedus and sucks dicks".
The term cinaedus, used to mock men who engaged in passive homosexual acts, was particularly offensive. The same logic of dominance and degradation extended beyond penetration to other sexual acts, particularly oral sex. Another inscription near a street corner of the ancient city reads: "Theophilus, don't perform oral sex against the city wall like a dog."
For the Romans, performing fellatio or cunnilingus was seen as an act of submission and lacked dignity, especially for a man. In the Greco-Roman world, the mouth carried significance that extended well beyond the bedroom. It wasn't just a body part reserved for speech, prayers, eating, and breathing: it also carried profound philosophical and moral symbolism. Hence, spoiling it with a sexual organ was seen as deeply degrading, especially when fluids were involved.
Also, the act of going down on one's "knees" was not to everyone's taste, for the posture was associated with a servile spirit. Sexual insults thus drew their force not simply from the acts themselves but from the broader cultural meanings attached to bodily position, status, and gender.
Other examples of graffiti from Pompeii tell a similar story. An inscription found in different locations throughout Pompeii labels a certain Albanus a pervert; another inscription on the exterior of the city's amphitheater directs a similar insult at a man named M. Titinius, calling him a deviant. While the wording might sound mild to modern ears compared to the broader range of available profanity, their force lay in what they implied about the men to whom they were attached: masculinity meant dominance and control and the insults implied they didn't have it.
In the Roman imagination, the bedroom was inseparable from public life, and so it all came down to two things: active vs. passive. Penetration was synonymous with authority, while being penetrated carried the stigma of the "weaker sex" and slaves. Inviting entry by taking the passive role was seen as the height of unmanliness. To willingly relinquish the active role was more than a matter of personal preference; it was seen as a failure to embody the virtus (manliness and civic virtue) that distinguished a respectable citizen from those Roman society deemed barbarian.
Of course, it doesn't mean every Roman accepted these ideals, or that every insult produced lasting consequences. The graffiti rarely tell us how the targets of the inscriptions reacted or how seriously their audiences took them. Their significance lies instead in the shared cultural vocabulary in which sexual submission was synonymous with social inferiority.
Below the belt
In the higher tiers of Roman hierarchy, sexual shaming became a calculated political weapon. Roman orators routinely attacked their rivals' private lives to undermine their public credibility. Allegations involving adultery, sexual misconduct, incest, effeminacy, and other forms of sexual deviance could become part of a broader campaign to destroy someone's dignitas. It was a below-the-belt tactic that abandoned substantive political debate in favor of personal humiliation, but it worked.
Of course, the accusations did not necessarily need to be true to be effective, but they needed to be "memorable", needed to fit an existing social prejudice, and above all, needed to attach themselves to a person's identity. The objective was to create a story people would "buy" and repeat.
Cicero was particularly skilled at this. In his "Philippics", he portrayed Mark Antony as morally corrupt and sexually deviant. Antony was accused of "un-Roman" conduct, meaning youthful prostitution and passive homosexual acts for political gains. The Roman statesman delivered a series of public speeches claiming that, as a young man, Antony had acted as a male prostitute for the famous politician Gaius Curio: "You took the adult toga, which you immediately turned into a prostitute's gown. At first, you were a common whore, with a fixed price for your shameful favors... then Curio took you into a lasting marriage, as if he had given you a veil."
Julius Caesar faced similar attacks. The above, Gaius Scribonius Curio, referred to Julius Caesar as "every woman's man and every man's woman" in one of his speeches. Preserved by the historian Suetonius, the phrase compressed a much broader sexual reputation into a single, memorable insult: Caesar was portrayed as the lover of women and the sexual subordinate of men.
We do not know the precise occasion for Curio's speech, or whether Caesar was present, but the allegation followed Caesar throughout his political career. His enemies also repeatedly circulated rumors about his relationship with Nicomedes IV, king of Bithynia, during his youth, earning him the mocking nickname "the queen of Bithynia." Whether true or not, the rumor became a persistent way to ridicule one of Rome's most powerful men. Even his military victories could not silence the whispers.
For women, sexual accusations carried a different kind of weight. Just as modern revenge porn and non-consensual image sharing disproportionately target women to inflict moral judgment, Roman society vigorously weaponized accusations of female promiscuity.
Since a woman's chastity was inseparable from her family's honor and the legitimacy of its heirs, allegations of sexual misconduct could have catastrophic consequences for the entire household.
Even poets were not above shaming women. The poet Catullus famously used explicit verse to air intimate details and settle personal frustration against his former lover, Clodia Metelli. Following the bitter end of their affair, he publicly targeted the once cherished in his poetry, accusing her of engaging in casual sexual encounters in the back alleys of Rome.
Similarly, the elegiac poet Propertius weaponized verse against his former lover, Cynthia. After she rejected him, he decided to punish her by exposing her secret affairs, accusing her of nightly promiscuity, and broadcasting her private habits to his readers.
In "The Art of Love", Ovid documented a common form of post-breakup retaliation among men: public defamation. Rejected lovers frequently fabricated lies about their sexual behavior, boasted about intimate details, and spread malicious gossip within local taverns. For these men, as Ovid noted, the objective was clear: if they could no longer be with the woman, they would ensure her social standing and marriage prospects were destroyed.
Emperors and senators alike transformed accusations of female adultery into public spectacles of state-enforced shame. When women were described engaging in sexual acts, adopting supposedly shameful positions, or displaying excessive sexual desire, the details were often less important than the message the story was designed to convey. The historian Tacitus, for example, portrayed Messalina, the wife of Emperor Claudius, as the embodiment of uncontrollable female lust. In his "Annals", the historian recounts the sensational story of the empress who enjoyed going blonde when sneaking out at night to Rome's red-light district. Not only did she frequent brothels to offer her royal services, but she also competed with a very motivated prostitute in a sexual marathon that lasted all night. The empress came out on top with a score of 150 men, officially "endorsing" prostitution.
It's impossible to establish whether any of the stories were true. What matters is how effectively it reduced a politically influential imperial woman to a prostitute.
The list of dirty women goes on. Accusations of adultery and sexual excess became recurring features of Roman political life, particularly when powerful families were involved.
Whether through graffiti, political speeches, or poetic verses, the Romans became exceptionally good at weaponizing sexuality. In the end, the means have changed, but the appetite for turning private intimacy into public ruin endures.

NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19

19:06:55 KST

NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan"
Local studio NM3 looked to Vienna's iconic 20th-century American Bar by Adolf Loos when designing the bespoke red-hued interior of Milan's Bar Bardo.
When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos's famous bar, an early modernist landmark finished in 1908.
"The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference," studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen.
"The ambition was never to recreate Loos's bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann's Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project," he explained. "Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character."
Located just across the road from the city's popular Bar Basso, Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom.
Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020.
The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics.
A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect the globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni.
The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains with longer black ones.
The perimeter of the space features built-in red velvet banquette seating, which matches crimson curtains and a series of bright red speakers fitted across the bar to accommodate a stainless steel DJ booth and metal shelving for vinyl records.
Bar Bardo was purposefully designed to be a flexible space. Every interior element is movable, with the exception of the bar and the banquettes.
"By simply removing the furniture, the cocktail bar can easily be transformed into a club," said Zorzi. "The flexibility of the space is therefore achieved through a simple architectural arrangement rather than complex spatial interventions."
At the back of the space, the striking bathroom was covered with bright red 10-centimetre-by-10-centimetre tiles, from floor to ceiling.
Utilitarian stainless steel was once more selected for the toilet, sink and other fixtures, while pared-back sconce lights illuminate the cubicle.
Bar Bardo marks a softer design direction for NM3. The studio previously conceived a "raw" interior for Milan's Galleria Montegani, as well as a similarly metal-heavy store in the city for fashion brand Miss Sixty.
Ahead of Milan design week in April, NM3 was among the studios that spoke to Dezeen about what it's like to be a contemporary designer in Italy's design capital.
The photography is by Piercarlo Quecchia.

Two Serbian opposition figures targeted with spyware, research group says

Two Serbian opposition figures targeted with spyware, research group says
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 - Two Serbian opposition figures were recently targeted with powerful cyberespionage tools, according to one of the men and a report issued on Monday by the Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab.
The incident was the latest of several in which researchers say surveillance technology was used against students, opposition politicians and others in Serbia, which will hold a parliamentary election on Sunday.
Citizen Lab said on Monday that a joint investigation with the Share Foundation, a digital rights group, determined that Serbian academic Vladan Djokic's iPhone had been hacked using the Pegasus spyware tool made by Israeli group NSO.
At the same time, former prosecutor Rade Bajic told Reuters he received a warning from Apple on August 13 that his phone had been targeted using "mercenary spyware," although he and Citizen Lab both said they had been unable to establish with certainty whether he was hacked or how a hack might have happened.
Serbia's Interior Ministry did not return messages seeking comment. Officials there have previously dismissed allegations of cyberespionage. NSO, which was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 following years of reports of alleged human rights abuses, did not return emails. NSO, which says it only sells to governments, has previously said it would terminate commercial relationships that result in serious wrongdoing.
Apple confirmed having sent a batch of warnings to users on August 13 but did not directly address questions about Bajic's or Djokic's cases.
Both men have crossed Serbia's ruling party, which has been buffeted by two years of student-led anti-corruption protests.
Djokic, the rector of the University of Belgrade, has been under pressure from authorities following his expressions of solidarity with the students. Bajic said he was involved in prosecuting senior government officials over allegations that they improperly removed cultural protections on a historic Belgrade army compound that an investment company founded by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, had planned to redevelop. Kushner's company pulled out of the plan late last year, saying it was doing so out of respect for the people of Serbia and the city of Belgrade.
"In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack," Bajic said.
Last month, the Share Foundation said that at least 14 people, including students, activists and opposition party members, had been targeted with advanced spyware ahead of local elections in March. At least one of the devices was compromised using Pegasus, it said. REUTERS

- Ukraine’s 92nd Separate Assault Brigade said its specialists evacuated a wounded 30th Brigade soldier from the front line using a modified heavy hexacopter.
- The Gurzuf Defence drone was used because enemy drones and mines made evacuation by ground vehicle impossible.
Ukrainian troops have flown a wounded soldier off the front line with a heavy multirotor drone, in what the unit that organized the mission called the world’s first aerial evacuation of a casualty from the battlefield.
The operation was carried out by the unmanned ground systems company of Ukraine’s 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, working with other units and drone maker Gurzuf Defence, the brigade said on social media. The wounded soldier, an infantryman from the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade, survived and is now receiving treatment and rehabilitation, and his life is no longer in danger, according to the unit. The brigade did not say when or where the evacuation took place.
The soldier was hit while holding a position that could not be reached by the uncrewed ground vehicles Ukrainian units now routinely use to pull out wounded troops. Russian drones were highly active over the area and the ground around the position was mined, the brigade said, leaving no safe route for a ground vehicle.
Instead, the team turned to a heavy hexacopter from Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence, a type normally used as a bomber drone to drop munitions, which the company provided free of charge. Specialists from the 92nd Brigade’s company worked with the manufacturer to modify the aircraft so it could carry a person while staying stable in the air, without flipping or swinging excessively, and tested the setup at sites provided by Gurzuf Defence before planning the mission with neighboring units.
A drone operator from the 30th Brigade flew the aircraft during the evacuation itself. The brigade credited the 92nd and 30th brigades, the 14th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the 10th Army Corps and Gurzuf Defence for making it possible.
“This is a historic event, at least for our unit for sure,” said Napalm, a squad leader and programmer in the 92nd Brigade’s unmanned ground systems company, who was identified only by his call sign. The quote was translated from Ukrainian.
The brigade did not disclose the drone’s specifications, how far the soldier was carried, or how the casualty was secured to the aircraft. In the footage it published, the drone itself is blurred out, a step Ukrainian units take to keep a system’s configuration and control equipment secret so that Russian forces cannot develop ways to jam or suppress its control link.
Heavy drones have been used to lift people in civilian emergencies such as floods and fires in parts of Asia, but moving a wounded soldier by air from a front-line position under enemy drone surveillance is a new step for Ukraine’s military. Until now, Ukrainian units have relied mainly on ground drones and armored vehicles for casualty evacuation, because helicopters cannot safely operate near the front and the constant presence of Russian reconnaissance and attack drones makes it extremely dangerous for medics to reach the wounded on foot.

Alberta votes on leaving Canada; separatist movement likely to outlast expected defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:06:07 UTC

Alberta votes on leaving Canada; separatist movement likely to outlast expected defeat
CALGARY, Oct 19 - Oil-rich Alberta holds a nonbinding referendum on Monday on whether the western province should secede from Canada, a debate many believe will not be settled by what is widely expected to be a defeat for the separatist cause.
Polls have consistently shown that a majority of Alberta voters oppose splitting from Canada. Economic grievances have fueled the independence campaign in the province, which is home to 5 million people and slightly smaller than Texas despite having one-sixth the population.
The Alberta separatist movement adds to the pressures on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has made defending Canada's sovereignty a central mission as he confronts US tariffs and President Donald Trump's repeated calls for Canada to become the 51st state.
Many Alberta separatists believe the Liberal Party-led federal government in Ottawa has constrained the Conservative-governed province's oil industry through environmental policies, and that Alberta, the country's energy heartland, contributes more to Canada's economy than it receives in return.
"Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation advertising organization called Pathway to Independence.
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" side, urging supporters to vote and appealing to national pride.
Polls are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. MDT on Monday (0200 GMT on Tuesday) with results published as they arrive.
An Angus Reid poll released Friday showed 66% of Albertans plan to vote to remain in Canada, but three in five believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement" in the province.
"This issue is not going away now. Because the separatists are mobilized. They've networked. They're connected," said Mount Royal University political scientist Duane Bratt in Calgary.
While separatist sentiment has existed in the province for decades, Premier Danielle Smith is the first Alberta leader to put the question to voters. Smith, who has urged Albertans to remain in Canada, called the referendum after months of pressure from a small but vocal flank of her governing United Conservative Party.
If a majority votes in favor, Smith has said she would seek a binding referendum on separation.
"Separating, to my point of view, is completely ridiculous," said Ross Watson of Calgary after casting his ballot in favor of "remain" in an advance poll last week.
"I think the grievances that people have are completely unfounded. But I also think these people will probably never shut up."
SENDING A MESSAGE
Monday's referendum is the first time a vote on separation from the rest of Canada has been held in a province outside majority French-speaking Quebec, where separatist sentiment derives from language and cultural differences.
In Alberta, the issue is more about dollars than identity. Carney has appealed to national pride in arguing Alberta should remain part of Canada.
"Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," Carney said Friday in Red Deer, Alberta.
Partly to address the grievances that have driven separatist sentiment in Alberta, Carney has overturned some environmental policies and supported a proposed oil pipeline that would increase Alberta's exports to Asia.
Among the one-third of Albertans who would vote in favor of a future binding referendum on separation, 60% told pollsters their motivation was to "send a message" to Canada's federal government. Only 37% of respondents to the Angus Reid poll said their motivation was an independent nation.
Separatist groups have published transition plans, but key questions about how independence would work on issues such as defence, currency and border controls remain unresolved.
Bratt said the real question is where the movement goes from here.
"Do they focus on generating support for a future referendum? Or do they splinter off and create their own party — a real, powerful separatist party?" Bratt said. REUTERS

UN experts warn Palestinian farmers face escalating violence by occupiers as olive harvest underway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:05:43 UTC
19:05:43 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
UN experts warned Monday that Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank face escalating violence, land destruction and access restrictions by Israeli occupiers as the annual olive harvest begins.
"Palestinian farmers must be protected and able to access their land safely. Yet, year after year, the violence, destruction and restrictions intensify," the experts said in a statement, urging Israel to ensure their protection.
During the 2025 olive harvest, 178 occupier attacks linked to the harvest were documented across 88 Palestinian towns and villages, the highest number of affected locations since 2020, according to the experts.
More than 6,000 olive trees and saplings were vandalized, nearly double the 2024 figure and the highest number in six years, they said.
The experts also raised alarm over Israeli military orders issued in September 2026 to remove vegetation from approximately 339,000 square meters (84 acres) of Palestinian agricultural land, including olive groves in Jenin, Qabatiya and Beit Rima.
The orders allow olive trees to be uprooted and give landowners extremely limited time to remove vegetation or file objections, according to the experts.
They also warned that Israeli authorities have increasingly denied farmers permits to access their land.
A revised military policy also prevents Palestinians from harvesting olives on land Israel classifies as "state land," including plots cultivated for generations, they said.
"The olive harvest is an essential source of food, income and livelihood for thousands of Palestinian families, and is deeply rooted in Palestinian cultural and agricultural heritage," the experts said.
They urged Israel to protect farmers from attacks by occupiers, guarantee access to agricultural land and comply with its obligations under international law.
"The international community, especially States with power and influence, must exercise maximum pressure to protect Palestinian civilians, halt and reverse the rapidly expanding policies and practices of annexation and ensure accountability for decades of violations of Palestinian rights under international law," they concluded.

Türkiye’s mobile subscriber base expected to reach 105 million by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:03:00 UTC
19:03:00 KST

The number of mobile subscribers in Türkiye is expected to reach 105 million in 2027, up from 102.2 million as of the second quarter of this year.
According to the 2027 Central Government Budget Bill, efforts are continuing to improve technologies and service quality in the information and communications sector.
To support these goals, the budget allocated to the information and communications program has been increased by 39 percent to 32.34 billion lira for next year.
As investments rise and Türkiye’s technological infrastructure continues to develop, the number of users in the sector has also been increasing steadily.
Türkiye had 102.2 million mobile subscribers as of the second quarter of this year, while the figure is expected to reach 103 million by year-end, according to the program performance data included in the budget proposal.
Subscriber growth accelerated following the rollout of 5G technology this year and is expected to continue in the coming years.
Accordingly, the total number of mobile subscribers served by authorized mobile communication operators is projected to rise to 105 million in 2027, 107 million in 2028 and 109 million in 2029.
The government also aims to increase mobile broadband penetration across the country.
Mobile broadband penetration, defined as the ratio of total mobile internet subscribers served by authorized operators to the population, is expected to reach 94 percent this year.
With continued efforts to expand communication services nationwide, the rate is forecast to increase to 96 percent in 2027, 97 percent in 2028 and 98 percent in 2029.

Musk’s tech used in strike that killed Russian students – investigators
Two of at least seven Ukrainian drones used in a strike on a Russian college which killed 21 people earlier this year were equipped with Starlink terminals, investigators have established.
The nighttime attack on a college dormitory in Starobelsk in the Lugansk People’s Republic took place in May and was classified as a deliberate terrorist attack by Russia’s Investigative Committee. Its chairman, Aleksandr Bastrykin, discussed findings from the investigation in an interview with RIA Novosti published on Monday.
“The Ukrainian armed forces used at least seven drones identified as Fire Point 1, Fire Point 2, Sichen and RZ-100, two of which were controlled via the Starlink satellite communication system,” he said.
The strike also injured scores of civilians and caused an estimated $14.5 million in damage, according to Bastrykin. Investigators identified Robert Brodi, commander of Ukraine’s drone forces, Oleg Ivashchenko, head of Ukrainian military intelligence, and Andrey Klimenko, commander of the 414th drone brigade, as the main suspects, he added.
Kiev’s use of Starlink in territory that Washington recognizes as part of Ukraine became a source of friction with the US this month after Ukrainian officials claimed new restrictions had been imposed on faster-moving platforms. If true, the limitations would disrupt so-called “middle-strike” operations against targets behind the front line but within Starlink’s permitted coverage area, including Starobelsk.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied imposing such restrictions, accusing Vladimir Zelensky of making false claims and suggesting the Ukrainian leader does not know “what he’s talking about.” Starlink owner Elon Musk has also rejected the Ukrainian allegations.
Rubio further stated that Ukraine has no access to Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade sister service.
Bloomberg reported that Kiev had obtained access to Starshield years earlier, with a contract signed in 2024 to expand connectivity through regular Starlink terminals. Recent Reuters reporting suggests Starshield access remained active as of last week, albeit with new restrictions affecting its use in Ukrainian drone operations.

A vocabulary for the future: nature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

For the French philosopher Bruno Latour, ‘nature’ can’t exist in isolation, but only in relation to the ‘artificial’ or the ‘human-made’. In drawing a solid line between these two domains, he argues, we’re making a moral judgment rather than an ontological one: nature as good, its opposite as bad. Thinking outside that binary, he suggests, means rethinking the world not only as something acted upon by human agents, but as populated by other beings with agency of their own. Paired with visuals by the Barcelona-born, London-based filmmaker Gerard Ortín Castellví, this video gives shape to the divide Latour questions, showing the boundary between the natural world and the human one collapsing, to suggest the two are far more entangled than we tend to assume.
This video is part of the series A Vocabulary for the Future, produced by the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona. In it, notable thinkers reflect on a single word and are matched with filmmakers who give their writing a visual interpretation, inviting viewers to see familiar language anew.
