stefan sagmeister, neri&hu, and dani garcía lead interihotel MAD26’s creative rebellion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:44 UTC
19:00:44 KST

stefan sagmeister, neri&hu, and dani garcía lead interihotel MAD26’s creative rebellion
the madrid event combines an exhibition, talks, and experimental spaces to challenge conventions in hotel and restaurant design.
prefer designboom on google
rethinking the future of hospitality design
From November 17 to 19, 2026, IFEMA Madrid transforms into a hub of optimistic innovation as interihotel MAD26 returns for its sixteenth edition. Organized by the AMBIT Living Spaces Cluster, the event brings together around 350 exhibiting brands and over 200 international speakers. Under the theme of ‘Creative Rebellion,’ this year’s program directly challenges established hospitality conventions, using radical creativity and material experimentation to spark fresh paradigms for hotels and restaurants worldwide.
the anatomy of a rebellion
Uniting craftsmanship and industry insights, interihotel MAD26 structures its narrative across three dedicated thematic days. Day one, The Inside Rebellion, dives into design identity and human emotion, headlined by Stefan Sagmeister’s presentation No Doom, no Gloom, which blends data visualization with design to champion optimism, alongside discussions with Nini Andrade Silva and Astet Studio. Day two shifts toward The Green Rebellion, where Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu of Neri&Hu join designer Lucas Muñoz Muñoz, Studio Animal, and Rockwell Group to reframe circularity, environmental responsibility, and wellbeing. On the final day, The Future Rebellion, Michelin-starred chef Dani García leads the discussion on reinventing guest experiences, accompanied by industry disruptors including Luca Pronzato of We Are Ona, Laura Vall of Axel Hotels, and Kike Sarasola of Room Mate Hotels.
concept rooms and material labs explore new guest experiences
Beyond the forum talks, interihotel MAD26 translates theoretical discourse into tangible, spatial experiences. At the core of the floor plan sits the Interiors Living Lab, featuring two full-scale, walk-through physical prototypes. HBA presents The Sensory Explorer Concept Room, an immersive guest room installation inspired by Barceló Hotel Group, while Livit unveils The Social Playful Concept Restaurant, designed for hospitality brand Lamucca.
Specialized interactive hubs further expand the experimental footprint. The Materials Lab showcases sustainable material innovation via AMBIT Cluster and ‘Materialidad adaptable,’ an installation curated by MATTER dissecting six evolving material families. Nearby, Craft Lab — curated by Tachy Mora — highlights contemporary studio ceramics through eight selected makers, while the Xperience Lab offers hands-on interaction with spatial AI co-creation agents, Virtual and Mixed Reality modeling, and industrialized modular building configurations. Extending the event beyond the trade fair bounds, the interi-off satellite program activates Madrid from November 16 to 20 with architectural visits, installations, and evening gatherings across the city.
Admission to interihotel MAD26 is reserved exclusively for industry professionals, including hoteliers, restaurateurs, architects, interior designers, and real estate developers. To join the event and secure your professional accreditation pass, register directly on the official interihotel website.

The company has also announced a further £12 million of investment in the Fife facility, covering training infrastructure, new machinery, site improvements and technology. That takes total investment at Methil to £26.7 million since Navantia acquired the yard in January 2025.
Employment at the site has grown from 180 people at the point of acquisition to 275, while 75 apprentices are now undergoing training there. The additional 60 posts would further increase the permanent skilled workforce as new vessel work moves through the yard.
According to a news update from Navantia UK, Steve Chisholm, General Manager at Methil, said: “Winning another export contract shows the progress being made at Methil and the confidence customers are placing in the yard.
“With Seahorse completed, new work coming in and investment going into the site, we are now recruiting more skilled people to help build the yard’s future workload.”
The Methil facility has a long history of heavy engineering and offshore fabrication, with the latest recruitment drive intended to add experienced trades alongside the company’s apprentice intake.
Navantia UK included comments from several long-serving workers at the site. Allan Lister, a plater who began working at the yard in 1985, said: “I’ve worked all over Britain, and the guys you worked with here, nine times out of ten, were better than anybody else.”
Peter Ednie, who started as a burner in 1982, said: “I’ve cut steel over 300 millimetres thick.” Welder Willie Gibson, who also joined the yard in 1982, added: “We’ve got some really good apprentices.”
Katherine Thorn, Head of Talent and Culture at Navantia UK, said: “These are good skilled jobs, with the opportunity to work on significant programmes, develop long-term careers and contribute to the future of shipbuilding in Fife.
“We are looking for experienced welders and platers who want to join a growing team at a yard with a proud industrial heritage and a stronger pipeline of work.”
The company also pointed to potential future work connected with the floating docks programme for HM Naval Base Clyde. Navantia UK said Methil is well placed to support the programme following an announcement by the Chancellor earlier this month that the infrastructure would be built and delivered through UK shipyards.
The yard is already involved in work connected with the Fleet Solid Support programme through construction of the Seahorse barge, which is supporting delivery of the new replenishment ships for the Royal Fleet Auxiliary.
Navantia UK acquired the Methil facility in January 2025 and has since been investing in its workforce and industrial capability as it seeks to build a broader order book spanning domestic and export work.
Rhea Wolfson, GMB Scotland secretary, said: “Under new ownership, this shipyard is going from strength to strength with new investment being reflected in orders and recruitment.
“The importance of these skilled jobs and quality apprenticeships to the communities of Fife and Scotland’s industrial capability cannot be overstated.”
The new export order is the second secured for Methil during 2026, while the recruitment campaign will add welders, platers and other specialist trades to a workforce that has already increased by more than 50 per cent since Navantia UK took control of the site.

Arms manufacturers, miners and MPs oppose reducing the reservation quota: will the government listen?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:00:15 EEST
19:00:15 KST

Arms manufacturers, miners and MPs oppose reducing the reservation quota: will the government listen?
Kyiv • UNN
The Cabinet of Ministers has postponed a resolution to reduce the reservation quota for employees of critical enterprises from 100% to 85%. Businesses warn of staffing risks.
The government’s proposed reduction of reservation quotas for conscript-eligible employees has caused concern not only among representatives of the defense-industrial complex and related industries, but also among representatives of the energy sector. The Cabinet of Ministers is being warned of the risks of a staffing crisis in companies, disruptions to the fulfillment of defense contracts, and destabilization of the energy sector, UNN writes.
The reduction in reservations will jeopardize the production of Ukrainian weapons
The debate surrounding the government’s proposed initiative to change the rules for reserving conscript-eligible employees of critically important enterprises is gaining momentum. As is known, on October 13, the Cabinet of Ministers considered amendments to the resolution regulating the procedure for reserving conscript-eligible employees. The draft resolution proposed reducing the percentage quotas for reservations for enterprises in the defense-industrial complex and energy sector—from 100% to 85%, and for the utilities sector—from 75% to 60%.
The proposed reduction in quotas for companies in the defense-industrial complex and related industries, the fuel and energy complex, and the utilities sector has drawn sharp criticism from businesses, trade unions, and parliamentarians.
Representatives of businesses, think tanks, and parliamentarians stated that the government had not held the necessary consultations regarding the proposed changes, and that the draft resolution contained no calculations of the consequences of their introduction. In addition, the National Agency on Corruption Prevention reported that the document contained a number of corruption risks.
Representatives of strategic industries warn that in wartime, even a partial loss of qualified personnel can have much more serious consequences than an ordinary reduction in production capacity. After all, these are enterprises that directly determine the army’s supply of weapons, the stability of the energy system, the functioning of critical infrastructure, and the fulfillment of government orders.
Weapons manufacturers reacted particularly strongly to the government’s initiatives. Ukrainian company Skyeton, which operates in the defense-industrial complex, stated that reducing the reservation quota could trigger an outflow of specialists, halt promising developments, and disrupt the fulfillment of existing contracts.
Reducing the quota from 100% to 85% is a loophole for the outflow of personnel from critical defense enterprises, not a solution to the issue of staffing the military. The most realistic scenario to which it will lead within just a few months is a dead domestic defense industry in a country at war
Skyeton explains that defense enterprises are already operating amid an acute personnel shortage. Finding a single highly qualified specialist can take six months, with approximately the same amount of time needed for their adaptation to a specific project. At the same time, the complexity of modern defense developments has increased significantly compared with the beginning of the full-scale invasion.
According to the company’s assessment, for certain technological fields, the number of specialists with the required competencies may be limited to just a few dozen people across the entire country. Therefore, the loss of even one employee can affect the work of an entire team.
The industry is already facing an acute personnel shortage. If the reservation quota is reduced, manufacturers will be unable to work on developing new solutions that the military needs today. Moreover, under such conditions, companies will be unable to fulfill their current contractual obligations
The company sees a separate risk in the loss of competitiveness of Ukrainian manufacturers compared with foreign companies, which have more stable working conditions and access to personnel resources.
It is worth noting that earlier the Ministry of Defense categorically opposed reducing reservation quotas for defense companies. Skyeton supports the ministry’s position. The company emphasizes that developing its own weapons production enables Ukraine to reduce its dependence on the political decisions of international partners and strengthens its position on the international stage.
Miners warn of risks to energy security
Representatives of the energy sector were no less critical of the possible reduction in the reservation quota.
The Trade Union of Coal Industry Workers of Ukraine calls on Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi and the relevant ministry to preserve 100% reservation for enterprises in the fuel and energy complex.
The trade union emphasizes that the stable operation of coal enterprises is directly linked to the state's energy security, in particular, to supplying thermal power plants with fuel.
According to the Trade Union, the reduction in the reservation quota from 100% to 85% envisaged by the draft resolution could create additional risks for staffing in the coal industry and the stable operation of the energy sector
The main problem lies in the specifics of the industry. The operation of mines requires specialists with appropriate professional training, experience, and qualifications. It is impossible to replace such workers quickly. Therefore, reducing the number of reserved employees could lead not only to a decline in coal production, but also to additional risks for workers due to hazardous production processes.
In addition, representatives of the coal industry propose holding a discussion of the government's changes with the participation of trade unions.
The risks identified are particularly important against the backdrop of systematic Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Under such circumstances, the staffing resilience of enterprises becomes not only an economic issue, but also a security matter.
Risk of paralysis of critical infrastructure
The proposed changes have also raised concern in the Verkhovna Rada.
MP Larysa Bilozir said that the new reservation rules could paralyze the work of enterprises and territorial communities that provide the population with essential services.
Strengthening the Ukrainian army is an unconditional priority; at the same time, we must do everything to ensure that the country continues to function, people have heat, water, and electricity, and communities can provide essential services
In her view, the problem lies not only in reducing the reservation limits, but also in the simultaneous revision of the criteria for enterprises to be deemed critical and the need to reissue documents. Taken together, this could lead to an additional administrative burden and destabilize the operations of enterprises that must function continuously.
It cannot be allowed for them to face a simultaneous review of the criticality criteria, a change in quotas, and the need to urgently reissue documents
According to her, the parliamentary group "Dovira" sent the Prime Minister proposals regarding the final version of the government resolution.
In particular, the parliamentarians propose preserving the status of critically important enterprises that have already received it until the expiration of the relevant decision. A similar approach is proposed for previously approved reservation volumes.
According to her, this will allow businesses to adapt to the new requirements without a sharp reduction in staff and the risk of production processes being halted.
The ball is in the government's court
MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak reported that the government removed from the agenda of Friday's Cabinet of Ministers meeting the issue concerning the resolution on reservation. Following strong criticism, the Cabinet of Ministers agreed to hold additional consultations with businesses.
Virtually all sectoral associations, as well as representatives of 16 Ukrainian analytical centers, have declared their readiness to participate in drafting the government resolution of October 13.
It is currently unknown whether the relevant consultations with business representatives have begun.

====================================================================================================

People who score higher on intelligence tests tend to rate their own attractiveness slightly lower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:13 UTC
19:00:13 KST

People who rate themselves as more physically attractive tend to differ in certain demographic traits, beliefs, and workplace personality characteristics. Recent research suggests that being male, having a university degree, and possessing high levels of optimism and emotional stability are all linked to higher self-ratings of physical beauty. These findings, published in Evolutionary Psychology, provide evidence about how people perceive their own looks, which the authors interpret as being intertwined with personal confidence and status signaling.
The central subject of the research is self-assessed physical attractiveness. This concept refers to how good-looking a person believes they are, measured on a simple numerical scale, regardless of how an outside observer might rate them.
The investigation was led by Adrian Furnham, a professor emeritus in the Department of Leadership and Organisational Behaviour at the Norwegian Business School, alongside David S. Semmelink, who is affiliated with the University of Pretoria and test publisher Thomas International. The researchers wanted to explore the personality traits, cognitive abilities, and demographic factors that predict a person’s belief in their own beauty.
“I have long been interested in how well calibrated most people are with respect to their intelligence by looking at the relationship between IQ test scores and personal estimates,” Furnham told PsyPost. “I have done the same for emotional intelligence.”
“This paper is simply an extension to physical attractiveness, which is clearly an important asset as we know a lot about the ‘beauty premium,'” he continued. “Our primary interest was in personal correlates of PA [physical attractiveness], as it is difficult (but possible) to get more objective measures of PA (both face and body).”
Research on the “beauty premium” suggests that physical attractiveness can be an asset for occupational success and mate selection, providing advantages ranging from hiring decisions to earnings. Because confidence itself can be an attractive quality, people who rate themselves highly may project a social self-assurance that benefits them in competitive environments.
How people rate their own looks appears to reflect more than their actual features. A 2023 review found evidence that people’s ratings of their own looks tend to be boosted by self-esteem and confidence, not just their physical features.
Self-perceptions of attractiveness have also been linked to people’s values. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 indicated that higher self-perceived physical attractiveness was associated with greater materialism through an increased tendency to engage in social comparison. Earlier research by Furnham and a colleague covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that men tend to prioritize physical appearance in a partner more than women do, providing context for why self-evaluations might differ by sex.
To investigate these dynamics, the researchers divided their work into two separate studies. The first study included 799 working-age adults recruited from individuals who had completed workplace assessments through Thomas International. The sample was 58 percent women, had an average age of 47, and was predominantly British (54 percent).
Participants rated their own physical attractiveness on a scale from 0 to 100. They also reported demographic details, ideological beliefs such as religiosity and political orientation, and general optimism. In addition, they completed a workplace personality questionnaire measuring six traits (conscientiousness, emotional adjustment, curiosity, approach to risk, ambiguity acceptance, and competitiveness) and a behavior-style assessment measuring dominance, influence, steadiness, and compliance.
Across the first sample, the average self-rating of attractiveness was approximately 58 out of 100. Men rated themselves roughly 3 to 4 points higher than women, and university graduates scored about 3.5 points higher than nongraduates. The authors noted that education tends to be associated with occupational status and income, which are valued in a mate.
Ideological factors were also linked to self-ratings, with more religious, optimistic, and politically left-leaning participants giving higher scores. In terms of personality, the strongest positive associations were for competitiveness and for emotional adjustment, which refers to emotional resilience and stable moods. In contrast, ambiguity acceptance, meaning comfort with unclear or unpredictable situations, was linked to lower scores.
The workplace behavior-style assessment added little. Two of its four scales were dropped before the main analysis because they overlapped heavily with the others, and the remaining two were not related to self-ratings once the other factors were considered.
The authors had hypothesized that religious participants would rate their appearance higher, suspecting that faiths emphasize the unique worth of individuals and promote self-assurance. The link with liberal politics was weaker. They had expected it based on proposed connections between politics, intelligence, and attractiveness, but it runs against a 2017 study suggesting that conservatives tend to be rated as more attractive, and they note it needs replication.
Furnham noted that this religious connection was one of the more eye-catching patterns in the data. “I was intrigued by the association between religion and PA, more religious people believing they were more PA,” he said.
The researchers then conducted a second study with 292 working-age adults to examine whether these findings held up and to introduce an objective test of cognitive ability. Participants completed the same demographic, ideological, and six-trait personality surveys (without the behavior-style assessment), alongside a timed cognitive assessment measuring speed and accuracy in reasoning, spatial visualization, and perceptual tasks.
The second study replicated several key findings from the first. Holding a university degree, possessing higher optimism, and scoring high on trait emotional adjustment were again linked to higher self-ratings of physical attractiveness.
Several other links did not hold up. In the second study, sex, political views, competitiveness, and ambiguity acceptance were not related to self-ratings in the final analysis, and religiosity stopped being a reliable predictor once intelligence scores were added. Altogether, the measured factors accounted for about 15 percent of the differences in self-ratings in the first study and 23 percent in the second.
Cognitive ability showed a negative association with self-rated looks, meaning participants who performed better on the mental ability test rated their appearance slightly lower. In statistical terms, cognitive ability added only about 1 percent to the explained variation.
The authors suggest that people with higher general intelligence may simply be more realistic, or more honest, about their looks. They also note the puzzle that holding a degree was linked to higher self-ratings even though measured intelligence was linked to lower ones, and they suggest degrees serve as a more visible, socially recognized signal of ability than test scores. This negative relationship stands in contrast to a 2011 study, which found that objective intelligence is positively associated with other people’s ratings of physical attractiveness.
The researchers also conducted an exploratory analysis of nationality differences, which accounted for about 8 percent of the variation in attractiveness scores. British participants reported lower self-ratings than American, Canadian, Australian, and South African respondents, though the authors cautioned that the national groups differed greatly in size.
“Although it was not the focus of this study, there was considerable press interest in the fact that the British sample, compared to others … gave significantly lower estimates,” Furnham explained. “We did not have a big enough sample to really test this, which was not the focus of the study. We thought it may be a form of ‘humble bragging’ which the British are known for.”
The authors offer a similar explanation in the paper, suggesting that British respondents may lean toward modesty or understatement, but they describe the idea as speculative.
Furnham pointed out that cultural standards often dictate how people describe themselves in public. “We noted that there are various social conventions about self-descriptions and evaluations of personal characteristics including attractiveness,” he said. “Many cultures require people, more often women, to be publicly demure. Modesty is valued and hubris condemned.”
“Equally, it is important to ‘maintain a good appearance’ through diet, self-grooming, etc.,” he continued. “Clearly there are also socio-cultural, as well as individual difference factors, that impact on PA.”
The broader patterns align with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that higher self-perceived attractiveness was associated with a greater willingness to share ideas at work, though only among employees who saw appearance as a useful tool for influence. That study focused on communication behaviors on the job, whereas the current paper examined broader traits and outlooks such as optimism and emotional adjustment.
Furnham sees practical stakes in the findings. “Being self-aware of your personal characteristics like ability, EQ [emotional intelligence], and attractiveness is important,” he emphasized. “There is a massive literature on ‘the beauty premium’ which suggests PA has many consequences in life. People who both under- and over-estimate their abilities and attractiveness can experience a number of negative consequences.”
One outside researcher said the findings complement established work on the “beautiful is good” effect. “The classic ‘beautiful is good’ halo means that people perceived as attractive are often judged more favorably in other domains, which can shape social relationships and workplace opportunities, including hiring and promotion,” explained Antonio Olivera-La Rosa, a full professor at Universidad Católica Luis Amigó in Colombia specializing in social perception, judgment, and decision-making, who was not involved in the research. “These findings raise a complementary possibility: a favorable view of ourselves and our prospects may also influence how attractive we think we are, although the study cannot establish that direction of influence.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding these conclusions. The project relied on a single question to capture self-rated physical attractiveness, which cannot differentiate between facial beauty and body characteristics like shape or fitness.
“As we all know, statistical significance is not the same as social significance,” Furnham pointed out. “None of our effects were ‘large’ in terms of statistics, but we did replicate the findings in two studies.”
The studies also lacked objective ratings from outside observers. Without external evaluations, researchers cannot determine whether participants were evaluating themselves accurately or simply misjudging their appearance.
“Given the self-fulfilling nature of under-estimating your PA it would be a good idea to get a number of ‘observers’ (not only friends and family) to give detailed feedback on all aspects of personal physical attractiveness to be more informed and better calibrated,” Furnham advised.
Future research could explore how these self-evaluations develop over time and whether they can be adjusted. Researchers might also examine people whose self-ratings differ sharply from how others see them.
Olivera-La Rosa suggested linking self-ratings to research on perceived creepiness, which examines why some people come across as unsettling and how that leads others to avoid them. “I would test whether appearance-based acceptance or rejection gradually becomes part of our self-image,” he told PsyPost. “Comparing self-ratings with observers’ impressions and following real interactions over time could connect these findings with research on perceived ‘creepiness’ and social avoidance, helping clarify how others’ reactions might shape how attractive we feel.”
The authors are already looking to apply this research model to other personal beliefs. “We have collected a lot of data of self-estimates of personal characteristics like health, wealth and happiness,” Furnham said. “We intend to explore the data in the same way: notably individual difference correlates of these estimates.”
The study, “Self-Estimated Attractiveness: Demographic and Personality Correlates,” was authored by Adrian Furnham and David S. Semmelink.

After the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really is | Owen Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists? As the head of MI5 warns that anti-migrant haters are increasingly considering terrorist attacks, it is surely a question we must ask. After all, the role of hate preachers in Islamist terrorism has long been debated.
After the London Bridge Islamist terrorist attack in 2017, Nigel Farage demanded that Sadiq Khan – “as the first Muslim mayor of London” – declare that he would do all he could “to work with the Muslim community to drive out the extremist preachers from our mosques” and to fight radicalisation in schools and prisons. More recently, he suggested that Muslim parents in the United Arab Emirates feared sending their children to study in British universities “given the risk of radicalisation here”. His colleague Suella Braverman agrees. “There should be zero tolerance for hate preachers in mosques or radicalising imams in prisons,” she says.
And what of Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s self-styled shadow chancellor, who warns of “terrorist influencers and radicalising inmates” in prisons and demands “complete zero tolerance on hate preachers”?
Yet on the very day of MI5’s warning, Jenrick declared that Royal Marines would be deployed to turn back migrants in the Channel – and that “if they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so”. Here was one of Britain’s most prominent politicians injecting violence into our already deeply toxic debate about immigration.
Farage sought to backtrack on Jenrick’s behalf, claiming force “would be used only if soldiers were fired at” and insisting that Jenrick had been “utterly misconstrued”. This made little sense: the Home Office said last year that it had no record of firearms being brought in via small boats over the previous seven years.
Not that long ago, there was supposed to be a strict demarcation between the mainstream right and extremists. No longer. Consider the ITV investigation, screened last night, that exposed Reform councillors describing Asian families as “parasites” and Black children as “animals”. Another spoke of training young men to round up migrants “street by street, house by house”. One spoke of holding asylum seekers in “concentration camps”. Another Reform figure spoke of criminals facing “Sunday morning rose garden executions”. Some of these individuals have since stood down. But while the leaders of Reform have not yet plunged to such extreme depths, what effect might their own words have on impressionable people?
Consider that last week, Jenrick appeared on the YouTube channel of former GB News presenter Dan Wootton, a supporter of both Tommy Robinson and the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, the latter of whom he calls “a British hero”.
Take the anti-migrant protests outside hotels housing asylum seekers. Last August, Jenrick turned up to such a demonstration in Epping, Essex, where far-right activists were also present, praising the “peaceful, patriotic protesters”. A month earlier, following clashes which left eight police officers injured, Braverman insisted the protests had been “largely … peaceful”. Farage, meanwhile, warned that Britain was close to “civil disobedience on a vast scale” and said he understood the anger in Epping: “You bet your life I do.”
Asked about Thomas’s group, Patriot Platform, Jenrick sympathised with masked protesters, arguing that, without a face covering, “you can lose your job, you can be cancelled”. When he was pushed on whether he would accept Robinson supporters into Reform, Jenrick’s response was telling. “Ultimately [it’s] not my call who comes into the party, that’s for Nigel and others in the party to determine,” he said. “But look, I want to build as broad a coalition as possible of people who share my values, who want us to fix this country.” How to square this with Jenrick’s denunciation of Islamist hate preachers?
In the recent past, Reform politicians – Farage, Jenrick and Braverman among them – have described migrants arriving in small boats as an “invasion”. It is the language of war: a nation under siege, an enemy to be repelled. It is hardly a leap for fearful people to conclude that those who resort to violence are not really dangerous extremists, but patriots defending their country.
We can hardly forget that Farage called for “pure, cold rage” in response to alleged police failings over the murder of Henry Nowak. Hours later, violence erupted on the streets of Southampton. He increasingly embraces the language of white resentment, claiming that “anti-whiteness is institutionalised into every aspect of public life”, calling diversity policies a form of “social cleansing” and warning of white Britons becoming a minority by the end of the century. Such rhetoric echoes the “great replacement” conspiracy theory, which argues that white people are being deliberately displaced by mass immigration.
Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, meanwhile, describes Conservative and Labour politicians as “traitors to their country”, warning – without elaboration – that a “reckoning is coming”.
None of these statements constitute a direct incitement to violence. But taken together, they can conjure up a terrifying picture in impressionable minds: a nation and a people under attack, its own political leaders conspiring in its destruction and time running out to save it.
This can’t be divorced from rightwing media outlets echoing and amplifying such rhetoric. We’ve already had the far-right uprising of August 2024, when racist mobs assaulted people of colour in the streets, attacked mosques and migrant-owned businesses, and tried to burn down hotels housing asylum seekers. We’ve had far-right terrorist attacks, such as the neo-Nazi attempted murder of an Eritrean man in 2024, the firebombing of an immigration centre in Dover in 2022, the attack on the Finsbury Park mosque in 2017 and the murder of Jo Cox a year earlier.
None made a dent on the national discourse. It has only become cruder, more toxic and more inflammatory. So, with all we know, time to ask again. Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists?
- Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West, is out now. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Tourists are avoiding York, my home town – but I know how to get them back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

York may be falling out of fashion with tourists. The BBC reports January-to-June visitor numbers to my home town fell 8% compared with 2025, with visits to city attractions down by 17%.
This inspires a cocktail of conflicting emotions – selfish relief, a bit of huffiness (how dare they reject the birthplace of the Chocolate Orange and the KitKat?) and consternation. Slaloming through unpredictable, slow-moving tourist hordes in narrow medieval streets is far from my favourite activity (albeit probably good for my cognitive reserve), but tourists keep this city afloat. Our main economic activities in 2026 are “dressing up”, “tea and cake”, and “hen/stag night services (sub-categories: booze, kebabs, feather boas)”. This city runs on genteel treats and big, messy nights out: two things that are, yes, deeply incompatible. I wonder if that’s part of the problem – the bookshops, churches and scones crowd are put off by the inflatable-penis-toting, kebab-throwing party people, and vice versa – but most residents blame the £5-an-hour parking.
Anyway, time to work out – selflessly – how to increase footfall. New York has been having a moment recently (the World Cup, the Knicks win, a general optimistic buzz). Since they stole our name, why not steal their ideas? I’ll do my bit by shouting “I’m walkin’ here!” when someone stops dead in front of me to photograph a Viking handing out flyers.
We could also maybe Mamdani-fy our mayor, David Skaith. He’s already fairly online – let’s teach him Mandarin, get him to smile charmingly at more children and ask his team to work up some double entendres about filling potholes. And (with apologies to longtime supporter Richard Herring) York City FC needs more glamorous celebrity fans. I want paparazzi lurking outside the stadium Costa and stretch limos clogging the Park and Ride.
Then we need a banging tagline. I toyed with “York: so good they named a new one after it”. But I think we’re better off resurrecting the Yorkie Bar-inspired slogan that used to greet travellers on a billboard near the train station: “Where the men are hunky and the chocolate’s chunky”. Still true! Bring that back and surely visitors will follow.
Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

US teens can access ‘nudify’ apps despite Apple and Google’s parental controls, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

In December 2025, Morgan Dorfman received distressing news: a student at her daughter’s Pennsylvania high school was making AI-generated pornographic material using the daughter’s image.
He was using an artificial intelligence image-editing app called Movely to create sexual videos from pictures of her daughter and five other girls.
What Dorfman’s daughter experienced is not an anomaly: students in high schools across the US are reporting similar cases. Their classmates are generating nonconsensual pornographic or nude imagery using so-called “nudify apps”.
Governments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores, and most US states have implemented laws that criminalize possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
However, in spite of regulations prohibiting them, nudification apps are still proliferating and remain accessible to teens, according to a report from the digital advocacy group Tech Transparency Project (TTP) shared exclusively with the Guardian and released on Monday.
TTP researchers created four test accounts, two Apple accounts and two Google accounts, indicating the account holders were 13 years old. They searched for image-editing or face-swapping apps using terms such as “AI video generator” or “adult AI”. Using these accounts for a purported 13-year-old, the researchers were able to download 135 apps with features enabling them to strip people of their clothes or swap their faces on to nude bodies. The researchers disrobed women in AI-generated images in their tests rather than using photographs of real women.
At the time of her daughter’s distress, Dorfman didn’t know it was possible to create pornographic material of an everyday person so easily.
“All the girls were very scared and confused about what to do next,” Dorfman said. “I knew what a deepfake was, but I thought it was like Taylor Swift and people using celebrities’ [images],” Dorfman said. “I didn’t know it was possible to take any picture or any screenshot of anybody that you have and do this.”
Dorfman, a mother of four, spent weeks trying to figure out how the app worked and compiling material to educate other parents. She downloaded Movely and was immediately prompted to create suggestive videos using any image. The free version promoted sexually suggestive templates including “clothes explosion”, “brassiere unfasten” and “underwear drop”, according to a demonstration Dorfman put together for parents that the Guardian reviewed. In the paid version, it became more explicit: she saw templates for the types of pornographic situations in which, according a classmate, her daughter had appeared.
Both Apple and Google prohibit these types of apps from being distributed on their platforms. The companies also will often age-gate apps with adult content, restricting or blocking minors’ access. However, TPP researchers found that the companies largely rely on the developers to determine whether their apps are appropriate for certain ages.
“Many nudify apps identified in the investigation were inaccurately rated as suitable for minors – meaning the teen users could access them even when parental controls were activated,” the report said.
Researchers found that one face-swapping app, which was advertised to them with an image of a woman performing oral sex, was rated appropriate for ages four and up. The free version of the app prompted users to superimpose real women’s faces on to templates of women in lingerie or, if users paid, in pornographic situations. The researchers were able to buy a subscription to the app from a 13-year-old’s account without an alert to a linked parental account.
Google said the company regularly takes “proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content”.
“When violations are detected or reported to us, we investigate and take swift action, which in this case included suspending violating apps and restricting related search terms on our store,” Google spokesperson Dan Jackson said in a statement.
After TTP contacted Apple seeking comment on the findings of their study, Apple implemented changes that strengthened content moderation guidelines. The company now requires developers to preemptively prevent and remove nonconsensual intimate imagery including AI-generated images. Apple also said that the company reviews every app before it is published and that if a developer misrepresents any features, the company removes the app and its developers. The company said in addition to apps they already removed before the TTP report was shared with them, the company has also “taken action” on the remaining apps mentioned in the report.
“A number of the apps in this report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities,” said Apple spokesperson Adam Dema. “We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process – a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch.”
Of the four accounts the researchers created, two were placed under parental controls that only allowed users to download apps marked suitable for 13-year-olds and only then with a parental signoff. However, the researchers found that neither Apple nor Google required or suggested parental signoff to acquire any of the nudification apps.
One app, Image to Video Maker-Vidou AI, was rated appropriate for users aged nine and older. Upon opening the app, users were greeted by an image of a topless woman on a bus, according to the TTP study.
“The app had a feature that promised to digitally undress any person – and to demonstrate, it showed nude images of female celebrities,” the report read.
Age restrictions were also not entirely effective, the study found. In one case, when the researchers tried to download an adult-rated app from the Apple App Store, they came across a pop-up warning that the app contained “age-restricted material”. But all they had to do was confirm they were 17 or older, which Apple allowed the account to do despite its registered age being 13. The Google account without parental controls was blocked three times from downloading an age-restricted app but otherwise allowed the researchers to download nudification apps that were self-reported to be age-appropriate.
The Apple account that TTP set up parental controls for was still able to find and download 24 so-called “nudify” apps because they were all rated as appropriate for 13-year-olds. The Google account with parental controls was able to download 51 of these apps.
Removing image and video editing platforms from app stores was also not enough to prevent its use. In the course of TTP’s research, Apple took down 25 of the nudify apps, and Google took down six. However, the researchers were able to continue using the app since they had already downloaded it.
Dorfman had a similar experience with Movely, she said. While preparing a presentation for parents and law enforcement officials, she returned to the app and App Store to take screenshots when she realized it was no longer available to download. However, the app was already on her phone and it remained entirely functional. She was also still being charged for her paid subscription.
Once these nonconsensual images and videos are created, accountability proves evasive, Dorfman has found. “I just wanted someone to make him delete all of these videos,” she said.
In her daughter’s case, Dorfman feels her school has downplayed what happened. In a school-wide email the Guardian reviewed, the principal wrote that her daughter’s classmate did use the app to animate images of other students but that there was no evidence he had done anything inappropriate.
However, days later, Radnor police criminally charged him with harassment.
“The whole thing was dismissed as ‘it’s not real’,” Dorfman said. “The haunting trauma as a mom is that I can’t tell [my daughter] those videos are gone or who had them. We can’t search everyone’s phones, and he deleted the app.”

Press review: Trump seeks Ukraine talks revival as French unions join nationwide protests

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. US leader Donald Trump is eager to bring Kiev back to the negotiating table with Moscow, as trade unions and yellow vests take part in nationwide protests in France. Meanwhile, the United States could draw European businesses to joint projects with Russia. These stories topped Monday's newspaper headlines in Russia.
Izvestia: Trump seeks to bring Kiev back to negotiating table with Russia
US President Donald Trump opted not to use the bill on "sanctions from hell" against Russia to avoid disrupting a peaceful settlement: a senior Russian senator told Izvestia this step could be seen as a return to common sense. At the same time, the Western press is increasingly discussing a new US peace plan, which envisages the resumption of Russian gas purchases by European countries. Meanwhile, the Russian Army completely cleared pockets of encirclement near Volchansk and Dobropolye in the special military operation zone. These two major setbacks for the Ukrainian armed forces may increase pressure on Vladimir Zelensky both from Washington and within Ukraine itself.
The successful completion of this operation enabled Russian forces to significantly expand the security zone for the Belgorod Region and push the threat farther from the Russian border, military expert Viktor Litovkin told Izvestia.
The elimination of the pockets of encirclement will also free up a considerable number of Russian assault units. They will soon be redeployed to other sectors of the front line, increasing pressure on the enemy and accelerating the advance of Russian troops, another military expert, Alexey Leonkov, told Izvestia.
The Ukrainian defeats will serve as a strong argument for the White House to step up pressure on Kiev. The latest changes on the battlefield further confirm the US administration’s stance that Ukraine has no strong trump cards left. Trump told Newsmax television in an interview that Ukraine, among other things, is at a significant disadvantage in terms of manpower compared to Russia. In this situation, Washington will push more forcefully for the Ukrainian leadership to show greater flexibility and a greater willingness to compromise, Andrey Kortunov, a member of the Valdai Discussion Club, argued.
In addition, the elimination of the pockets of encirclement may worsen the political situation in Ukraine, as military failures will lead to more criticism of Zelensky from the opposition and those who support peace with Russia. He may also face pressure to hold a presidential election, a scenario he has persistently rejected. It is worth recalling that Zelensky’s term as president expired in 2024.
In these circumstances, Zelensky will step up his demands for additional financial and military assistance from the EU. However, European countries’ capabilities have been severely depleted. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for example, said after last week’s EU summit that the bloc had not made any specific decisions on support for Kiev. Meanwhile, Berlin itself has openly stated that Germany has exhausted its domestic reserves of new air defense systems to supply Ukraine.
Vedomosti: Trade unions, yellow vests join nationwide protests in France
On October 17, nationwide mass protests accompanied by widespread unrest and looting swept France. The unrest began several weeks ago with student-led protests. Approximately 800,000 people, mostly students, trade union members, and supporters of the Yellow Vests movement, took part in the October 17 protests, according to the General Confederation of Labour (CGT). The Ministry of the Interior put the number of protesters at 550,000, including 110,000 in Paris, with 1,200 people detained. Unrest broke out in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, and other major cities. Young people looted numerous retail outlets and various public and private facilities. In Limoges, rioters set fire to the town hall. Police have been using stun grenades, tear gas, and water cannons to disperse the demonstrators.
On Saturday, protests also spread to neighboring European countries as hundreds of youths, inspired by French protests, held rallies in Brussels to protest against the rising cost of university education. Tens of thousands of Portuguese people took to the streets in Lisbon to express their discontent with a doubling of housing prices since 2017. Similar marches that soon escalated into clashes with police took place in Italy’s Milan and Bologna. Clashes between students and police were reported in Albania too.
The protests in France could benefit both far-right politicians, including the National Rally and Marine Le Pen, the front-runner in the election campaign, and the ultra-left camp, represented by another presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of La France Insoumise (LFI), Alexey Chikhachev, an associate professor in the European Studies Department at St. Petersburg State University, told Vedomosti. On the one hand, right-wing politicians adopted a winning stance by condemning the rioting. On the other hand, Melenchon could theoretically leverage the situation to garner support from various minority groups and mostly left-leaning education employees, the political analyst noted. The migration issue could also work in favor of the far-right, Chikhachev observed. "Conversely, the ruling center-right parties are losing ground against this backdrop. Edouard Philippe, seen as a potential successor to [French leader Emmanuel] Macron in the upcoming 2027 presidential election, can currently count on the votes of about 10-12% of the electorate only," he argued.
Macron and his allies, who demonstrated an absolute inability to ensure the security of citizens and property, have been clearly weakened by the political unrest, Arnaud Dubien, director of the Franco-Russian Observatory think tank, agreed. Right-wing politicians, including Le Pen and Eric Zemmour, leader of the political party Reconquete (Reconquest), have earned additional brownie points against this backdrop, he maintained.
According to Chikhachev, the main political outcome of the latest protests will be increased attention to education-related issues within the political platforms of both the ruling forces and the opposition. "The CGT trade union is actually partially coordinating its activities with Melenchon. In France, trade unions have traditionally served as a link between protesters and political leaders," the expert said.
The CGT trade union’s ability to directly influence the country’s political processes is limited, Dubien argued. However, he continued, most French people are in a state of shock, including because of a fire at the town hall in Limoges, a city otherwise known for being very quiet. "All this can be called a manifestation of the death throes of 'Macronism.' Macron will leave office no earlier than in seven months. In the meantime, much could still happen in France, including a recurrence of major protests and unrest," Dubien warned.
Izvestia: US could draw European businesses into joint projects with Russia
The United States could attract European capital to joint projects with Russia, Robert Agee, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Russia, told Izvestia. Restarting Nord Streams could be one of these projects in principle. According to some data, US investors are interested in such a prospect. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party stressed that Washington's participation would provide reliable guarantees of European energy security and protect infrastructure from further acts of sabotage. However, even amid mutual business interest, full-fledged cooperation is hampered by the EU’s tough sanctions policy, although this could change as the opposition strengthens.
European investors can join projects if these steps are approved by EU governments, Mikhail Kucherov, a political analyst, told Izvestia. However, there is now a consensus to reject Russian energy among the elites in the leading countries, including Germany, France, and Britain as a key partner of the EU.
Even the lobbying capabilities of German businesses, for example, are not strong enough to pressure political elites on sanctions, as this has been a pan-European policy rather than a purely German one, Maria Khorolskaya, a researcher at the World Economy and International Relations Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized. In any case, all this could probably materialize after the Ukraine conflict is resolved, she concluded.
Meanwhile, European countries led by Germany have been focused exclusively on protecting Ukraine’s interests. "Continued military confrontation with Russia provides them with a convenient scapegoat to blame for the collapse of their own economies, a collapse that essentially has little to do with Russia and to a greater extent stems from their own policy in the fields of energy, migration and industry," former MEP Gunnar Beck told Izvestia.
Voters who back parties that are ready to restore ties with Moscow will be businesses’ key allies in this effort, Kucherov argued. Beck also stressed that Europe needs major political changes, such as the rise to power of right-wing politicians in France or Germany.
Kommersant: Russian stocks climb to three-month high after Trump moves to suspend `sanctions from hell’ bill
Reports about Trump’s move to suspend the `sanctions from hell’ on Russia sent the MOEX Russia Index close to 2,450 points. Investors expect that the two sides will be able to reach a diesel supply deal that could pave the way for further sanctions relief and a new era of economic cooperation. However, further stock market gains are constrained by the lack of results from the previous round of talks between Moscow and Washington, while the market will need confirmation of shipment volumes and no signs of sharp escalation, including from the EU.

According to him, the previous talks between Moscow and Washington did not yield any material results, prompting Washington to increase sanctions pressure on Russia. Thus, last fall, the White House announced sanctions against Lukoil and Rosneft and blacklisted 30 Russian partners in China, India, Turkey, and the UAE.
The market will need confirmation of actual Russian diesel supplies to the global market and possibly an extension of the relevant contracts, noted Oleg Abelev, head of analytics at the Ricom Trust investment company. If positive news is followed by a sharp escalation, including from the EU, investor optimism will also fade, AVI Capital argued. Kommersant: Russian metallurgical coal exports to India may rise to 52 mln tons by 2030
Russian metallurgical coal exports could increase at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 0.8% through 2030, reaching 52 million metric tons, according to a report from NEFT Research. Analysts estimate that this growth rate may exceed the rates for Australia (0.4%) or Canada (0.7%), but remain lower than those for Mongolia (1%) or the United States (0.9%). In 2025, Russia exported 50 million metric tons of metallurgical coal, experts say.
According to the NEFT Research report, Russian coking coal exporters may strengthen their position as key beneficiaries of the expected rise in demand in India and Southeast Asia, particularly Vietnam.
Dmitry Baikov, director for corporate ratings at the National Credit Ratings agency, also sees significant potential for Russian exports to India, where demand for coking coal could rise by more than one-third in the next five years. Russia has overtaken Indonesia and the United States in this market as the second-largest supplier after Australia. In certain months of this year, Russian coking coal supplies to India saw multiple-fold growth, and the annual figure could exceed last year’s 8 million metric tons, Baikov told Kommersant.
Akhmed Aliev, a leading analyst at T-Investments, stressed that the global coal industry has been severely underfunded for environmental reasons, leading to declining output even as demand has remained stable. A structural shortage of quality coal in Asia could drive a further 20% to 30% increase in prices for premium-grade metallurgical coal across Asia, Baikov predicts. The expert sees risks of a correction in the winter of 2026 and spring of 2027, when supply from Australia recovers, although he does not expect prices to plunge. The current potential for Russian coal exports is constrained by the throughput capacity of southern ports rather than by coal prices or availability, he explained.

The Story of Billy Evans and ‘Theranos 2.0’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Warning: Light movie spoilers below. Read at your own risk.
Even before becoming the stars of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s much-buzzed-about new documentary, Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans were a special kind of couple. Holmes “may have ultimately failed to change the world in the way she set out,” Evans wrote in a letter at the time of Holmes’ sentencing in 2022, “but she has undeniably changed mine.” The Theranos founder, in the hardest years of her life, taught her husband “a patience” that he “would have previously dismissed as unnecessary and soft.”
She brought out his inner light, another sentencing letter from a friend of the couple reports: When they returned from a “monthslong camping trip,” Evans “displayed a new level of compassion in his demeanor, a strong sense of intention with his actions, and a heightened desire to listen to and look at others with purpose.” Whatever others might think, Evans was saying, Holmes wasn’t the only one of the pair that had been given a second chance. And they might get a second second chance with Haemanthus, a company that Evans is keen to reassure social media followers is absolutely—most definitely— “not Theranos 2.0.” A person familiar with the business told The Wall Street Journal that Holmes is not involved.
But viewers of You Can See Everything will watch Evans agreeing to the characterization that he and Holmes are making Theranos 2.0. They discuss the trajectory to make a working prototype of something on camera; they talk about collaborating on product ideas from prison. “To meet her, to spend time with her, that was the intention of the film,” the Austin, Texas-based Evans told David Friedberg, a cohost of the podcast All-In. “I haven’t seen it yet. I might think this is the dumbest thing that I have done.”
So who is Evans? And what is he building?
Long before fathering two children—son William and daughter Invicta—with Holmes, Evans grew up in San Diego in one of the city’s more prominent families, heir to midcentury pioneers in the Southern California tourism industry. His grandparents, William and Anne Evans were “two young hoteliers [who] saw the future,” according to the family’s company website, and opened up what would become a popular resort hotel on a mudflat in Mission Bay in 1953. They added a second nearby, and today own a third in La Jolla. This brought generational wealth. The business passed in part to Billy’s father, also named William.
Billy went to the Francis Parker School, one of the most prestigious private schools in the city. “The Evans family is very well respected in San Diego,” said a contemporary of Evans’ who worked for the family as a teenager, but Billy ““always a source of drama, would try to fight to start fights.” He had “affluenza” and was “just your classic spoiled rich kid” in a way that was not true of all his relatives. The inner light would come around later. (Evans did not want to be interviewed for the story and did not answer specific questions.)
After graduating from MIT with a bachelor of science in economics, Evans reportedly tried to launch a startup offering medical concierge services. This failed. He then took jobs in a handful of tech companies, including LinkedIn and Luminar Technologies, a self-driving car company. In 2017, at a “Fleet Week charity event” in the Bay Area, the then 25-year-old met Holmes and was “captivated,” he later wrote the judge at her sentencing, “by her childish wonder and authenticity.”
There was some reporting in the early years that the Evans family was not entirely enthused by this courtship, but doubts seemed to have dissipated by the time of the Holmes trial. Billy’s father, William Evans, showed up to the courtroom incognito, under the alias “Hanson,” identifying himself as a kind of mechanic. (He owns an enormous classic car collection.) To journalists, he defended Holmes’ honor. In court, he turned heads by unwrapping a “large Rice Krispies Treat” whose crinkling foil drowned out the judge on the first day of jury selection, NPR reported.
While in the film Evans and Holmes are both shown on fundraising calls, her name doesn’t appear in any of the incorporation documents of Haemanthus, the company Evans founded in 2022. There is little publicly available information on the company; to date, it has released no products and barely has a LinkedIn page, let alone a website. Yet its name can’t help but conjure up Theranos, and, indeed, its stated goal is to bring blood, urine, and saliva testing to American homes in the form of a countertop-size machine, which was more or less the goal of Theranos.
But the technology of Haemanthus seems to be a bit different than that of Theranos. Where the earlier company’s machine hoped to perfect the “miniaturization” of existing diagnostic techniques such that they could fit in a box on a counter, using a very small blood sample, Haemanthus’ machine uses “light.” To employ a cooler word, it uses lasers. The company’s Raman Spectroscopy System, a patent for which was granted January 21, 2025, suggests a machine capable of firing high-power light sources into biological samples and reading the resulting information accurately.
Raman Spectroscopy is a real and promising diagnostic tool and the subject of research since its discovery by, among others, C. V. Raman in 1928. Shine a light source at a material and perhaps one in 1 million photons will shift in frequency in relation to the molecular vibrations of the material it bounced off of. That shift can be measured and analyzed, and a century of work has gone into making this process a little easier and a little more useful, carried out today by specialists at research universities and hospitals.
It may someday be even more useful. WIRED contacted Eric Potma, a professor of chemistry at UC Irvine, to shed some light on the technology. “Given that I act as one of their consultants, I am not sure if it is appropriate for me to delve much further into this,” he wrote back. “All I can say is that from an engineering perspective, they have some interesting ideas that are worth exploring.”
“It is not a technology concept pulled out of thin air, as people may be inclined to think based on the fact that the company is run by Elizabeth's husband (and thus an automatic repeat of the Theranos story),” he continued over email. “My own assessment is that Haemanthus is not Theranos. The engineers at Haemanthus are legit, and they are really trying to push the Raman detection technology into interesting directions.”
The challenges of putting this highly sensitive and difficult diagnostic technique into home appliances able to assess human health markers with a level of accuracy in seconds that will pass regulatory scrutiny—as promised in the company’s promotional materials—are great, though. Last year, The New York Times said that the company had garnered a $3.5 million investment from “friends and family.” It now reports as much as $20 million in funding.
Press accounts of the company’s marketing materials seem to promise investors that the company faces “no regulatory oversight,” in part because the machine would only be developed to test veterinary diseases at first. The New York Times, though, confirmed with the USDA that the agency had regulatory oversight over “vet diagnostics.”
Evans told the Times, which had other questions, that the company was “in stealth” and would remain so: “They aren’t going to find anything associated with the name Haemanthus.” There are a few things out there, among them the patent, but stealth mode continues. The addresses that turn up are mostly connected to private homes in one of Austin’s more desirable neighborhoods, near Barton Springs. Contacted by phone, a few folks who seem likely to be employees of the company declined to talk or even confirm or deny their role.
The desire for “stealth,” though, is a little discordant with the desire to participate in a yearslong documentary project with a graduate of one of Canada’s top business schools. Perhaps it will help raise money: Once the laser system is perfected, the company hopes, according to materials reviewed by the Times, to put the whole thing in a stamp-size wearable device, a research process it told investors will take “three years and $70 million.” Holmes will be reportedly moving from prison to a halfway house next summer. The world may yet be changed.

How Elizabeth Holmes Tricked WIRED—and Everyone Else
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of the fraud-ridden blood-test company Theranos, made her national press debut in The Wall Street Journal in 2013. The article—“A Drop of Blood, an Instant Diagnosis”—wasn’t a science story, or even a business story. It ran in the Opinion section, by a writer on the Journal’s editorial board named Joseph Rago, winner of a Pulitzer Prize for critiques of the Affordable Care Act.
He wrote that he was impressed by the prospect of individuals having more direct control of their health care; no less an eminence than former secretary of state George Shultz, a Theranos board member, had told Rago that Holmes was the next Steve Jobs or Bill Gates.
By 2014, Holmes was the youngest woman billionaire ever, and the mid-2010s were electric with tech-industry success stories—the iPhone, Tesla, Airbnb, Twitter. I was an editor at WIRED back then, and Theranos-as-presented felt very WIRED. It looked like evidence that a Silicon Valley approach to innovation would work in every industry, including medicine. And at the magazine that first published the idea of the “quantified self,” Theranos’ pitch validated the notion that individuals could take charge of their own health with innovative tech and access to data.
One of my colleagues, an editor named Caitlin Roper, saw a story in Theranos and in Holmes, but no one was sure what shape it should take. The executive editor suggested Roper just go talk to Holmes and see what was what. The result was an influential long-form Q&A headlined “One Drop, Infinite Data: How Elizabeth Holmes Built a Better Blood Test.” Because print magazines move with the agility and speed of a post-Panamax cargo ship, the story didn’t run until the March 2014 issue.
Over the next few months, other publications followed. Fortune put Holmes on the cover. The New Yorker did a profile. In October 2015, Inc. put her on the cover, calling her “the next Steve Jobs”—and a couple of weeks later, The Wall Street Journal did another article on Theranos, by the reporter John Carreyrou. The headline was deceptively humble: “Theranos Has Struggled with Blood Tests.”
Uh-oh.
The speedy and accurate blood tests were fake, the innovative tech didn’t exist, and Walgreens, a major partner, terminated its deal with Theranos. It was a grift. A new documentary film, out this week, follows Holmes in the weeks leading up to her incarceration.
Get a bunch of old WIRED editors together these days and it doesn’t take more than one drink before we start asking each other whether we enabled the worst parts of the tech world’s rise to power. Sometimes it seems like every antichrist-lecturing, panopticon-building, machine-god-bothering weirdo with $100 billion and a government contract made his debut in our pages. So, with Theranos and Holmes back in the news, the current administration at WIRED wondered what we were thinking back then.
It was a long time ago. I called Caitlin.
As always, we were looking for good stories. “I was interested in this female founder, but also the idea that her actual goal was disruption of health care, that there could be more transparency and reduced costs,” says Roper, who today is executive producer for scripted film and TV at The New York Times. “I was going through some medical stuff at the time and having constant blood tests, and I was curious about what this could do.”
Roper got a go-ahead to report and write something, execution to be determined. In the house jargon: Green light, format TK. She and I talked it through separately. “The conversation I remember with you, which I thought of many years later, was looking at the board of directors, her board, which was just completely batshit. It had military figures and government officials, and just seemed very odd,” Roper says. “You said there was something weird about that. It raised your suspicious hackles.”
It did—a few of us thought we saw hints of red flags. The company hadn’t published any peer-reviewed data. Colleagues had heard unconfirmable rumors of shenanigans inside the company. But that didn’t mean it wasn’t a story. We’d just have to figure out how to handle all that. WIRED had been, in years past, overly credulous, especially of scientific claims. But primarily WIRED covered innovation and stuff that sounded futuristic. This felt like it qualified.
“I remember that with dramatic irony, looking back,” Roper says.
Holmes agreed to an interview, and Roper went down to the Valley, to Theranos’ offices. She was only the second reporter to be there, and she got the performance that Holmes would become famous for. “There’s a lot of weird things about her. She was speaking in this strange, low voice. She was wearing a Steve Jobs outfit—black turtleneck,” Roper says. “She seemed like she was very precisely trying to project something.” (That first WSJ story ran with an illustrated caricature; WIRED shot a photo, professionally styled, of Holmes in her signature look.)
They spent an hour talking. Roper got her blood drawn, a tiny pinprick from the tip of her finger. “I said, ‘I’d love to see the box, can I follow my blood sample?’” Roper says. “They said, absolutely not.” Company reps implied it was a health-and-safety issue.
Instead, Holmes took Roper to the Palo Alto Walgreens, one of the few where Theranos had actually set up shop. “That part seemed like a snow job,” Roper says. “It was clear even from my own basic research that it hadn’t rolled out.” The booth at Walgreens was not in service. Holmes told her the company was going to open Walgreens labs across the Southwest.
Roper’s blood results came back. “The panel they took was similar to a panel I’d just had. I looked at them, and they matched,” Roper says. That seemed roughly confirmatory, at the time. It’s impossible to know now how it pulled that off, but later it turned out Theranos maintained a fully kitted-out lab in its Palo Alto offices, in addition to the lab for the company’s supposed new tech.
Interview done, Roper drove back up to San Francisco, to WIRED. “It didn’t feel like there was a feature to do,” she says. The Walgreens stuff wasn’t happening yet; it was too hard to report out how the technology worked. What was hard, in retrospect, was validation. Roper and the bosses weren’t sure that investment money from bold-faced names made up for an absence of hard scientific evidence.
So Roper wrote it up as an interview—a Q&A. “It seemed more like an interesting founder story,” she says. Roper asked every hard question, and got answers. They just turned out to be lies. But Roper acknowledges some cracks in the story’s origin. “If she had not been a woman, I would have been less motivated. That was part of what compelled me,” she says. “I felt sympathetic to the idea of her outfit and her weirdness, because I related to the idea that she was passing in some way in that environment, needing to assert herself.”
It’s tempting to see in that a DEI-run-amok story. It isn’t. All of us at WIRED were trying to wrestle with sexism in the world we covered, and at our magazine. Holmes’ board was all non–Silicon Valley types—was that because venture investors and scientists had identified her as a bad risk, or was it because Silicon Valley venture capitalists don’t support women founders?
Just a month after Roper’s Q&A ran, a team of researchers at the Harvard Business School and MIT Sloan School published a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that investors were far more likely to fund the same pitch if it came from a man than if it came from a woman—and that conventionally attractive men did even better. Today, roughly 75 percent of venture investors are men, and the proportions were worse a decade ago. There’s even research showing that male venture investors are more likely to promote women to partner if the men have daughters. Roper and WIRED were trying to fight that tide and ran aground on a grifter instead.
“Partially, yes, it’s a woman founder, and that’s a nice change of pace. It would’ve been nice if you guys could have beaten John Carreyrou and figured it out,” says Dave Karpf, an associate professor at George Washington University who has read every issue of WIRED and uses them to teach a class about Silicon Valley’s visions of the future. “But it wasn’t a new, untested claim. It was an active fraud.”
It’s fair to imagine a timeline where WIRED dug in deeper and was more critical, or at least didn’t further drive the hype cycle. “That story and the way we photographed her was absolutely fuel to lauding her and drawing attention,” Roper says. “I do feel partially responsible for that.”
We probably were, but I’m not sure WIRED’s Q&A was any more or less credulous than stories other magazines did. I know I sound defensive here, but even WIRED’s rigorous fact-check process wasn’t designed to unmask fraud. We all got got; it’s easy to see red flags when they’re in the rearview mirror. Was it weird to believe a 19-year-old college dropout had noticed something about pathology and microfluidics no one else had? Sure, but as Karpf points out, the system valorizes those kinds of iconoclasts. Steve Jobs was a dropout, man!
“If she had done all the graduate work, she wouldn’t have been nearly as fundable. They would just find someone else to tell them the stories they want to fund,” Karpf says. “It’s the people promoting it who, I think, have a bunch of answering to do.”
In 2019, as Sam Altman was leaving his role leading the tech incubator Y Combinator to become CEO of OpenAI, he wrote a blog post extolling the virtue in founders with “too much self belief … almost to the point of delusion.” Venture investors will tell you they invest in people as much as ideas, and the ideas are sometimes early-days, or half-baked. The system encourages exaggeration—right up to the line of deception. It can favor charismatic hucksters. If Theranos’ technology didn’t quite work yet, well, that’s a core tenet of Silicon Valley: Fake it till you make it.
And for a long time, WIRED helped. The magazine touted big ideas, and sometimes those ideas turned out to be dumb. Sometimes we were too early; sometimes we were wrong. Pitch meetings for stories big and small were a bit of a Thunderdome, actually. Eventually we developed some heuristics to encode skepticism in the process. For architecture stories, renders weren’t enough—ground had to have been broken. Physical objects had to exist in physical space; reporters had to be able to visit a thing. A flying car had to, you know, fly. In stories about new drugs or medical devices, the gating rule became “phase 3 trials or get the fuck out.”
Today, every responsible tech journalist has had to don new kinds of armor to prepare for the future that WIRED helped create. It’s possible to marvel at robot cars navigating cities as if driven by ghosts—while acknowledging the ways they sometimes fail, are often remote-piloted by humans, and pose new questions about regulating Big Tech. It’s possible to be awed by generative artificial intelligence’s capabilities while also interrogating the motives and practices of the companies that build it. And, yes, the personal politics of tech trillionaires matter when they’re donating more than a quarter of a billion dollars to support one political party over another. All of that was probably WIRED’s responsibility back then; it’s everyone’s responsibility now.
The tech business hates all that, reasonably. Not rarely, some longtime Silicon Valley dude will learn I spent most of my career at WIRED and say something like, “What happened to that place? I miss the old, optimistic WIRED.”
But you know, in the same issue of the magazine that carried the Holmes Q&A, another of our colleagues, Bill Wasik, wrote an opinion piece touted on the cover as “Silicon Valley’s Douchebag Problem.” Wasik, today the science editor at The New York Times, wrote then that dead-eyed misbehavior in pursuit of profit would kill tech’s magical status. Peter Thiel–derived ideas about secession and business models that relied on surveillance capitalism risked a backlash that would burn it all down, Wasik warned. The Valley and its toys, he wrote, would end up “a punch line—a hallucination of a future that no one believes in anymore.”
Science and tech journalism have to be about more than investors and returns. The future is too important; the stakes are too high. Case in point: As part of Joseph Rago’s reporting on Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos, he got his finger pricked. Rago’s blood test results were back “by the time I walked out the door,” he wrote. “(Phew: all clear.)” Four years later, Rago, 34, died alone in his New York apartment.
The city medical examiner said the cause of his death was sarcoidosis, a rare (and rarely fatal), hard-to-diagnose inflammatory disorder. Doctors usually figure it out by excluding other possibilities. Rago didn’t even know he had the disease. But among its signs are elevated levels of vitamin D and angiotensin-converting enzyme. Maybe an honest blood test would have spotted it.
