====================================================================================================

Far right blames migrants for France unrest, but look at these photos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:21:39 UTC
18:21:39 KST

Even before the smoke had cleared over France's scarred city centres, the far right had found its favourite target to pin the blame on. Nationalist commentators and online accounts rushed to allege that migrants were behind the looting and arson that followed the weekend's nationwide protests, and that immigration had set the country alight.
The evidence does not support the claim. French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting. Instead, they have blamed "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals".
Fact-checkers reached the same conclusion, finding that the available evidence does not show immigration caused the protests, even though immigration remains a contested political issue in France.
The unrest grew out of a mass movement. Organisers put turnout at about 800,000, with demonstrators answering calls from a labour union, student organisations and activists hoping to revive the "yellow vest" movement. That is hardly a migrant-led uprising.
Even the political camp most closely tied to the marches has distanced itself from the violence. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the left-wing leader who joined the Paris march, insisted that "those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction".
The far-right leader Marine Le Pen, for her part, aimed her fire at the government, describing it as "exhausted, disoriented" and powerless.
Across the political spectrum, the argument in France is about the state's failures, not about who arrived in the country.
The protests began on September 28, driven by rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. Students complained of a shortage of professors and "dilapidated buildings", and accused the government of trying to push young people out of higher education.
Petrol, energy and food prices have meanwhile spiked in recent months. With a presidential election about six months away, anger over living standards and crumbling public services has been building.
On Saturday, hundreds of thousands of mainly peaceful demonstrators took to the streets. The mood turned when groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared. An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted or destroyed, and the interior ministry says about 1,000 police officers were injured, seven of them seriously.
At least 2,400 people were arrested. In Saint-Etienne, a 17-year-old lost his right hand after being hit by a crowd-control grenade.
A state that lost control
The most damning verdict has come from inside government. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez admitted on Monday that police "lost control" in some cities during the weekend's violence.
He blamed a "lack of anticipation" in preparations and said he had tendered his resignation to President Emmanuel Macron "because I felt responsible for everything that happened". Macron did not accept it, with the Elysee citing the need for continued leadership of law enforcement.
Macron himself condemned the "failures" that led to the violence, saying: "Nothing can justify this. Nothing can explain it. Nothing can excuse it."
Macron asked Nunez to ensure transparency over "failures in planning and intelligence" and to introduce new operational methods for security forces. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu convened a crisis cabinet to assess one of the worst weekends of public disorder in modern French history.
Macron has also authorised regional prefects to ban demonstrations nationwide, a move likely to inflame tensions among the peaceful majority who marched.
Macron's televised address on Sunday, in which he called for national unity and promised the perpetrators would be punished, was widely criticised. Opponents and social media users said it lacked concrete detail to address the grievances.
The picture is of a government that missed the warning signs, failed to protect peaceful protesters, and now faces public anger over living costs it has yet to address.
Its own interior minister has admitted that the state lost control. Blaming migrants may be politically convenient, but it explains nothing about what happened on France's streets.

Qatar warns global energy shockwaves from Iran war have yet to peak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:18:24 UTC
18:18:24 KST

Qatar warns global energy shockwaves from Iran war have yet to peak
Deputy PM calls for dialogue with Tehran, highlights US defence ties and rejects Strait of Hormuz transit fees.
Doha, Qatar — Qatar’s deputy prime minister has warned that global energy shockwaves from the US-Israel war on Iran have yet to reach their peak, raising concerns about further disruption to supplies, international trade and economic growth.
Speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who also serves as Minister of State for Defence Affairs, identified several threats facing Qatar and the wider Gulf, including risks to sovereignty and disruptions to energy supplies.
“We haven’t reached the peak with respect to energy,” he said, warning of further repercussions “in the coming days and months”.
His remarks come amid continued instability in the Strait of Hormuz – a vital waterway for global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments – following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28, and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes across the region.
Iranian strikes on Qatar’s Ras Laffan industrial complex in March damaged facilities, with repairs expected to take several years.
“We were surprised,” Al Thani said when asked about the attack, adding that there had since been “a lot of discussion with Iran”.
He said Qatar had drawn lessons from the strikes, “to make sure that all of our assets will be protected from any unexpected attack”.
Al Thani also warned against imposing tolls on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
“Transit fees should not be applied,” he said, adding that uncertainty over the waterway would ultimately affect consumers worldwide.
‘We never stop our communication’
Despite the attacks, Al Thani said Qatar continued to maintain contact with Tehran.
“We never stop our communication,” he said, adding that the two countries remained in touch at different levels despite their disagreements.
He described Qatar’s relationship with Iran before the attacks as one of trust, pointing to their shared offshore gasfield and longstanding economic interests.
Al Thani expressed hope that mediation efforts involving Qatar, Pakistan and Oman would help produce an agreement between the United States, Iran and other parties, including Israel.
He said a sustainable settlement would require broader regional dialogue involving Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, Pakistan and Turkiye, in consultation with international allies.
“We need to build this on trust,” he added.
Al Thani also suggested developing economic ties with Iran to prevent future conflicts, citing cooperation between France and Germany following decades of hostilities.
“Iran is our neighbour. We need to find ways to live with them,” he said.
US defence ties
Al Thani also highlighted Qatar’s longstanding defence partnership with Washington, saying that “more than 90 percent” of attacks had been prevented through shared expertise and military capabilities developed over the past three to four decades.
He said Qatar was continuing to develop Al Udeid airbase, which hosts US forces and military personnel from other partner countries.
The base was itself targeted by Iran during the conflict, with Qatar reporting that it had shot down two Iranian warplanes during an attack in early March.
Al Thani also announced plans for a new regional defence partnership, saying Qatar was prioritising several aspects including air defence, counter-drone measures and cybersecurity.
“I’m happy to announce today also that soon we’re going to announce a new partnership,” he said, without naming the regional partners involved.
The deputy prime minister stressed that Qatar’s mediation efforts did not diminish its commitment to defending its territory.
“Mediation doesn’t mean that we should not be ready for any defensive action from our side,” he said.

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines was critically injured Monday after being struck by an SUV outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, in the southeastern state of Victoria, in what police are investigating as a possible deliberate attack. A 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and officers found a knife inside his vehicle.
Haines, 65, an independent member of Australia's federal Parliament since 2019, was struck by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her office. She was rushed to hospital with critical injuries, police said.
According to authorities, a passerby detained the driver after he exited the vehicle. Police subsequently arrested the man and seized a knife found inside the SUV. Investigators are working to determine whether the collision was intentional and what may have motivated it.
Police said they were unaware of any previous threats specifically directed at Haines. Authorities had not established whether the lawmaker and the detained man knew each other.
The incident comes amid growing concern in Australia over threats and harassment directed at elected officials. Authorities have recorded more than 1,000 reports of threatening behavior toward public figures over the past year, highlighting an increasingly hostile political environment.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese expressed shock over the incident and urged greater restraint in public discourse, while cautioning against speculation about the circumstances before investigators establish what happened.
"We can disagree," Albanese said in an interview with Australian broadcaster ABC. "In a democracy, those disagreements should be resolved through discussion, not personal resentment or questioning people's motives without good reason."
Asked whether he believed the incident was connected to previous episodes of political intimidation, including vandalism targeting election-related offices, Albanese said public debate had become increasingly confrontational.
"There has been too much shouting, too little dialogue and too little respectful conversation and disagreement," he said. He added that democracy requires people to debate political differences while maintaining mutual respect.
Albanese also linked the increasingly heated political climate to social media and what he described as a culture of chasing clicks, in which provocative content is rewarded over thoughtful discussion.
Police are continuing their investigation into the circumstances of the collision. No motive has been established.

How a grass fire at a Canadian military base killed four soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:12:31 UTC
18:12:31 KST

How a grass fire at a Canadian military base killed four soldiers
The cause of grass fire remains unknown as PM Carney describes it as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil.
On Saturday morning, Canadian military officials at a base in Alberta province observed a grass fire that appeared sufficiently contained, allowing soldiers to conduct live-fire combat training. Then, the officials say, the wind shifted.
In less than a minute, Canadian soldiers went from training drills to being engulfed in flames, said Major-General Wade Rutland, describing the incident that killed four soldiers and injured 39 people, 19 of them critically.
“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 36 seconds,” Rutland said at a news conference in Edmonton, the capital of Alberta, on Sunday.
While the cause of the grass blaze remains unknown, Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil.
So how did the grass fire spread so fast, and why is this base significant?
What is a grass fire?
A grass fire spreads through dry grass, weeds, shrubs and other low-growing vegetation. Unlike forest fires that burn through trees and woodland, grass fires spread across open fields, grasslands and plains.
They can move exceptionally quickly because dry grass ignites easily and provides a continuous source of fuel, and wind can play a pivotal role in how the fire develops.
Strong winds push flames rapidly across open terrain, change their direction with little warning, and carry burning embers ahead of the main fire, potentially igniting new fires.
The uncertainty of winds makes grass fires difficult to predict and contain, particularly in dry conditions.
They may burn for a shorter time than a forest fire, and while they are easier to contain, the speed at which they can spread in dry conditions can make them lethal.
Grass fires can start naturally but can also be ignited by human activities, such as discarded cigarettes or equipment sparks.
What happened at the base?
The fire spread on Saturday afternoon during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, western Canada, about 210km (130 miles) southeast of Edmonton.
The area lies in the prairies, a landscape of wide, open grasslands, rolling plains and scattered groves of trees. The base is also one of the Canadian Army’s largest training centres and a key facility for preparing troops for operational deployment.
About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practised attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.
Rutland said investigators would examine whether the wind drove the fire towards the soldiers or whether flames spread unseen through vegetation before suddenly overtaking them.
Large areas of Alberta were hit by a windstorm, with gusts up to 100km/h (62mph). The winds toppled trees, sent signs flying and pushed flames beyond the base into surrounding rural areas.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.
On Sunday, the Canadian media reported that the fire could have worsened after a gas facility was struck during a live firing exercise. However, the military later clarified that investigators do not believe any explosions were caused by oil or gas infrastructure.
Were there initial warnings?
Global News, a Canadian publication, reported that an armed forces memo obtained by it noted the fire risk was assessed as low for the scheduled live-ammunition exercise, greenlighting soldiers to train.
However, Environment Canada had issued a strong-wind warning earlier that day, forecasting gusts of up to 100km/h in parts of Alberta.
The memo also noted that blazes jumped a fire guard and spread outside the base, forcing the evacuation of one family home.
“During training, a grass fire ignited, and strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction; the fire shifted toward the personnel on the range and overtook their admin area,” the memo states.
Global News reported that the memo warned that the situation was “fluid” and the casualty figures “may change over time with ongoing assessments” of status.
Why is the base significant?
The Wainwright base is one of the country’s largest and most used military facilities, especially for training soldiers. It spans 609sq km (235sq miles) and is home to 25 weapons ranges.
During the final months of World War II and for several months in 1946, the base was used as an internment centre for German prisoners of war.

American F-22 stealth jet controls combat drone
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:11:23 BST
18:11:23 KST

A US Air Force F-22 Raptor has directed a YFQ-44A Collaborative Combat Aircraft during an airborne tactical-control demonstration, with the fighter pilot issuing commands that were interpreted and executed autonomously by the uncrewed aircraft, according to the US Air Force.
The demonstration took place earlier in October and was intended to test in-flight command and control between a crewed fighter and an autonomous combat aircraft as the Air Force continues development of its Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCA, programme. During the flight, the F-22 pilot acted as what the service described as an airborne “quarterback”, issuing high-level tactical instructions to a single YFQ-44A rather than directly flying the uncrewed aircraft.
The YFQ-44A’s onboard autonomy software then interpreted those instructions in real time and carried out dynamic manoeuvres and simulated combat tasks, allowing the F-22 pilot to direct the aircraft at the mission level rather than control individual flight inputs.
According to a US Air Force news update, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said: “This achievement demonstrates what is possible when we are aligned with industry on a shared imperative: delivering capability to the warfighter at unprecedented speed.”
He added: “We are driving urgency into every part of acquisition from rapid integration and flight learning to disciplined assessment, so we can turn promising technology into combat capability at the pace the threat demands.”
The test involved personnel from the 412th Test Wing, 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron, 309th Software Engineering Group, Experimental Operations Unit, F-22 System Program Office and the CCA Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch. Data gathered during the flight will now be used to support further software integration and developmental testing, as well as the Air Force’s work on future operational concepts for Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
The demonstration is focused on one of the central ideas behind CCA: allowing crewed combat aircraft to command groups of semi-autonomous aircraft without requiring pilots to manually control every movement.
Under that model, an F-22 or another crewed aircraft could assign tasks to uncrewed platforms, with onboard autonomy handling the detailed execution of those instructions while the human pilot retains tactical command.
U.S. Air Force Chief of Staff General Ken Wilsbach said: “This flight shows the power of crewed-uncrewed teaming and the advantage it provides our warfighters.”
He added: “We must test often, learn fast and give commanders what they need, when they need it.”
The YFQ-44A is one of the aircraft being developed under the US Air Force’s CCA programme, which is intended to introduce lower-cost uncrewed combat aircraft capable of operating alongside crewed fighters.

Over 60% Ukrainians strongly opposed to withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Donbas – survey
Over 60% of Ukrainians strictly disagree with the withdrawal of the defence forces from Donbas in exchange for security guarantees from the US and Europe. Only 7% easily agree to such a condition.
Source: a survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) conducted on 8-16 October
Quote from KIIS: "Thus, 61% of respondents consider it categorically unacceptable to transfer the entire Donbas under Russian control in exchange for security guarantees. At the same time, 35% are ready for such a concession (although most of them admit that this is a difficult condition). Another 4% could not express an opinion."
Details: The KIIS notes that compared to late July and early August, no statistically significant changes occurred.
Meanwhile, sociologists emphasise that among respondents surveyed on 8-9 October, prior to the announcement of the "diesel deal" and subsequent pressure on Ukraine, 57% were strongly opposed. Among respondents surveyed on 10-16 October, this figure rose to 62%.
Quote from KIIS: "Formally, the difference is within the margin of error, but we see that [at least] for now, the pressure campaign on Ukraine has not led to any greater readiness to accept this proposal."
Details: This situation applies across all regions – half or a majority reject the proposal to withdraw Ukrainian troops in exchange for security guarantees.
For reference: The study took place on 8-16 October. Using the telephone interview method based on a random sample of mobile numbers across all regions of Ukraine (territory controlled by Ukraine), 1,031 respondents aged 18 and older were surveyed. The sample did not include residents of territories temporarily not controlled by the Ukrainian authorities (at the same time, some respondents are internally displaced persons who moved from occupied territories), nor was the survey conducted among citizens who went abroad after 24 February 2022.
Under normal circumstances, the formal statistical margin of error for such a sample (with a probability of 0.95 and taking into account a design effect of 1.3) did not exceed 4.0% for indicators close to 50%, 3.4% for indicators close to 25%, 2.4% for indicators close to 10% and 1.7% for indicators close to 5%.
Under wartime conditions, in addition to the specified formal error, a certain systematic deviation is added. However, sociologists believe that the obtained results still retain high representativeness and allow for a fairly reliable analysis of public sentiment.

Leading Lithuanian histologist Albertas Vitkus dies aged 97
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:08:00 UTC
18:08:00 KST

Professor Albertas Vitkus (February 5, 1929 – September 16, 2026), a distinguished Lithuanian scientist and habilitated doctor of sciences, died on September 16 at age 97, the family announced in a press release on Sunday.
Professor Vitkus devoted his life to medicine, scientific research, and educating future generations of physicians.
He graduated from the Kaunas Medical Institute in 1954. From 1956 to 2003, he taught at the institutions that eventually became the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences (LSMU). He was appointed professor in 1971 and served as head of the Department of Histology and Embryology from 1971 to 1994.
Professor Vitkus combined his academic career with extensive clinical experience. He worked for ten years as an internal medicine physician at Kaunas Railway Hospital and spent four years as an emergency medical physician.
His clinical background continued to inform his scientific work throughout his career, as he believed that research findings should ultimately contribute to medical practice.
His principal research interests included experimental approaches to preventing myocardial infarction, the study of cardiac tissue, and other processes associated with heart function. In addressing questions in cardiology, he sought to move beyond the boundaries of individual disciplines, bringing together biochemists and researchers from other fields of medicine in collaborative studies.
In 1987, Professor Vitkus received the Lithuanian State Prize for a series of scientific studies conducted in collaboration with biochemist Professor Antanas Praškevičius, anatomist Professor Rimvydas Stropus, and other researchers.
His scientific legacy includes more than 250 research articles, books, textbooks, and educational materials. He authored and published four textbooks for students, as well as four educational publications.
He devoted considerable attention to the development and standardisation of Lithuanian medical terminology, which served generations of Lithuanian medical students and physicians.
His scientific contributions also extended to practical inventions. In 1989, he developed devices for preparing histological specimens and for coronary artery occlusion as part of his research.
Over nearly five decades of teaching, countless future Lithuanian physicians attended Professor Vitkus's lectures.
His colleagues and students will remember him not only as a scholar of histology and embryology, but also as a physician, educator, and mentor who dedicated his professional life to medicine, scientific research, and the education of future generations of medical professionals.
A farewell ceremony for Professor Albertas Vitkus will take place on October 19, 2026, from 13:00 to 20:00 in the main hall of the Good Shepherd Parish (Gerojo Ganytojo Parapija), V. Krėvės Ave. 95A, Kaunas.
On October 20, 2026, a funeral Mass will be held at 09:00 at the Good Shepherd Parish Church. The funeral procession will depart for Petrašiūnai Cemetery at 13:00.

Conversely, only 19% of coalition voters said that economic issues were their top priority, and only 28% of opposition voters said the same about security.

Finally, 33% of respondents to Sunday's KAN news poll said that if neither major bloc could muster a majority in the Knesset after the elections, they would be content with forming a unity government comprising members from both sides.
Just over a quarter of voters said they would prefer to hold another election in that case, and 20% said they would support a minority-run government.
Eisenkot pulls ahead of Netanyahu, Winter falls below electoral threshold

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party, however, lost one seat, bringing it to eight. Shas also landed on eight, gaining one seat from the previous week.
United Torah Judaism also lost one seat from the previous week, per KAN News, bringing it to seven. The Arab Joint List remained at eight seats, as did Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu. Ra'am remained at five seats.
Benni Gantz's Blue and White, Moti Leitner's Haredi Public, and Ofer Winter's People of Israel parties all fell below the electoral threshold in the KAN poll.

Traditional Thai lanterns inform blue-and-gold Bangkok cafe interior
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:00:51 UTC
18:00:51 KST

Traditional Thai lanterns inform blue-and-gold Bangkok cafe interior
Japanese studio I IN drew on traditional Thai festivals, where thousands of paper lanterns are released into the sky, when creating the interior for the first Blue Bottle Coffee cafe in Bangkok.
The interior of the cafe is dominated by the large Blue Lantern installation above the coffee counter.
"The main idea came from Thailand's traditional lantern festival," I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen. "We wanted to capture the feeling of a lantern floating in the sky and bring that into the space in a contemporary way."
"This became what we call the Blue Lantern, a large sculptural element extending from the ceiling above the drip station," he continued.
As it is the brand's first cafe in Bangkok, the studio wanted to design a "bold and dramatic" space that would also nod to local culture.
"The lantern idea came from the local culture, and from the beginning, we wanted to make it as large and impactful as possible," Terui said.
"We placed it at the location where customers first enter the cafe, so it would immediately catch their attention and become a symbol of the store."
The furniture and fixtures in the 178-square-metre cafe were made from teak wood, a material that is often avoided in the West due to concerns about illegal logging, but which is local to Thailand.
"Every country has their own approach to natural materials, depending on what is locally available and traditionally used," Terui said.
"In Thailand, especially in the north, teak is a very familiar material and commonly used in the interiors and architecture."
Blue Bottle Coffee cafe Bangkok is drenched in blue hues, with the brand's signature colour used for the lantern and coffee counter.
For the rest of the space, I IN chose a pale blue colour to "give guests a sense of brand identity and the feeling of a sky," Terui explained.
After visiting the city, the designer also decided to add gold details to the cafe interior.
"The idea of bringing gold into the interior actually came from my personal experience of walking around Bangkok," Terui said.
"As you walk through the city, you suddenly come across these beautiful, strong gold colours, and I found this contrast very unique," he continued.
"It was something that stayed in my memory of Bangkok, and I wanted to bring a little of that feeling into the cafe."
I IN also recently designed the concrete Andersson Bell store in Tokyo and clad the Human Made store in Seoul in handcrafted tiles.

Insta360 Luna Ultra and Luna Pro Review (2026): Steady Does It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Excellent gimbal and subject tracking. Detachable screen with recording controls. Superior image quality compared to action cameras and smartphones. The Ultra's dual lenses allow for more versatility.
TIRED
Small screen makes accessing advanced settings somewhat fiddly. Non-replaceable battery.
Not long ago, the idea of a compact, capable, and affordable camera gimbal seemed unfathomable. But then DJI pioneered this space with the Osmo Mobile, a gimbal for filming with your phone, and the Osmo Pocket, a gimbal-camera combo that's proved extremely popular. Now, Insta360 has joined the party with two competing gimbal cameras, the Insta360 Luna Ultra and Luna Pro.
You'd be forgiven for mistaking these Insta360 cameras for the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 and 4 Pro. In fact, the two companies are currently butting heads in a US court over these and other cameras. Oddly, given the lawsuit, neither of DJI's cameras is currently available in the US, which makes Insta360's Luna series a more compelling buy. Throw in great gimbal performance, excellent 4K footage, and, with the Luna Ultra, a zoom lens, and you have probably the best gimbal camera you can buy in the US.
Ultra Mega Pro
Insta360 launched the Luna Ultra in June. Looking like Wall-E, the Ultra features two lenses: one wide-angle main lens (developed with Leica) and one zoom lens. In September, Insta360 added the Luna Pro, which is largely identical to the Ultra but lacks the second zoom lens. Think of the Pro as the Ultra's budget-friendly version for those who don't mind sacrificing the zoom feature for cost savings.
The two cameras have more in common than they do different, so I'll highlight what they share before I get into what makes the Ultra a touch nicer than the Pro, and, for that matter, the DJI Osmo Pocket 4.
Both Luna models use a 20-mm equivalent lens with a wide, bright f/1.8 aperture. That main lens records to a 1-inch sensor, which means you're effectively shooting at the equivalent of a 20-mm f/5 lens on a full-frame (35-mm) camera.
The main sensor is the same 8K-capable 1-inch sensor found in the Insta360 X6 camera, but the Luna cameras deliver significantly better image quality because of the lens (or lenses, in the Ultra's case). In fact, the video from the Luna is vastly superior in almost every situation I tested, except in bright sunlight, where the Luna Ultra and X6 are roughly equivalent. The Luna's narrower field of view makes for sharper, clearer video. That 8K also means you can shoot with the main camera's digital 2X zoom and still get pretty dang nice 4K footage. On the other hand, the more durable X6 can handle shots you wouldn't want to risk with the more fragile Luna cameras, plus 360-degree photos and videos.
The Ultra's design mirrors what DJI has done for years with the Osmo Pocket series: a handle grip that houses most of the internals, a flip-out screen to turn it on, and a gimbal that holds the camera head at the top. It's a design that works well for filming both yourself and the world in front of you.
The three-axis gimbal not only keeps shots steady, but, as you'd expect, lets you smoothly pan, tilt, and roll without physically moving the entire camera or your body. You can set auto-tracking so the lens follows a subject automatically. The gimbal performed well in my testing, delivering stable shots. I occasionally had to recalibrate if I bumped or jarred it too much, but the process is quick and easy.
What sets Luna apart from the Osmo Pocket 4 is a detachable front panel with the OLED screen, buttons for record, zoom, and pan, plus a microphone. This means you can set up the camera and then use the screen remotely to frame yourself properly and control it from afar (up to approximately 66 feet, according to Insta360). This is extremely useful for anyone filming themselves.
The Luna cameras top out at 4K/120 frames per second (fps) for slow motion, which lags behind the Osmo Mobile 4's 4K/240 fps, but—and this is a big but—the Luna Ultra can shoot 4K/120 fps in log, whereas the Osmo Mobile cannot. If you color-grade and want slow motion, the Luna Ultra is the clear winner.
All of Insta360's advanced filming modes can be found in the Luna cameras, along with the usual color options, including the default 10-bit color profile and I-Log (Insta360's proprietary log format) recording for those who want to do their own color grading. In the default color profile, you can choose from about a dozen different filters. I find the default color mode oversaturated, especially in blue skies, which look extremely fake much of the time. I shoot almost exclusively with the Leica Natural color filter or in log and color-grade later.
Battery life seems pretty even for both Luna models. I recorded 4K/24-fps footage outdoors for two hours and 55 minutes. Ambient temps were about 65 degrees Fahrenheit, and I kept the camera out of direct sun for the test. The handle got pretty warm, but it didn't overheat. Even indoors, in a continuous shooting scenario like an interview, I don't think you'd have any issues with battery life or overheating on either camera. Sadly, the battery isn't replaceable, so you can't quickly swap one when it's dead. You can use a portable battery to keep it charged, but that makes the setup cumbersome.
Ultra Zoom
The Ultra's telephoto (zoom) lens uses a second but smaller 1/1.3-inch sensor. It has a 3X optical zoom (60-mm equivalent on a full-frame lens) but can reach up to 15X via digital zoom (300-mm equivalent). The Ultra launched with 12X digital zoom, but a firmware update increased it to 15X.
At first, I was somewhat underwhelmed by the zoom lens. If you're filming yourself (which I am loath to do, but never mind that), you don't need a zoom lens; the 20-mm is just about perfect. The zoom really comes in handy when shooting B-roll. Another scenario Insta360 touts is recording concerts or other live events from far away.
As you'd expect, image quality suffers considerably with the digital zoom. The processor does its best to keep the image sharp, but even in the best scenarios, the loss of quality is noticeable.
If your videos benefit from a zoom lens, consider the external zoom attachment Insta360 recently released, which adds 1.5X to the optical zoom (4.5X total), or the equivalent of a 90-mm lens. Unlike digital zoom, the image remains much sharper, but in my testing, I found almost no discernible loss of image quality when I used both optical and digital zoom with the telephoto attachment, at up to 200 mm. If you max out the digital zoom, you'll be shooting with the equivalent of a 450-mm lens, but the image does start to get softer.
When it launched, the Luna Pro featured 4K vertical video, while the Ultra did not. But now Insta360 has added 4K vertical video to the Ultra with a firmware update.
Over the Moon
First, who needs the Luna or the Osmo Pocket products? The target users include solo filmmakers, journalists, and content creators. That's why you often see them used by YouTubers and multimedia journalists.
Second, which Luna should you buy? The Luna Pro is probably the better value for most users. You do lose the zoom lens, but that's about it, and you save $170. The Ultra only makes more sense if you want to shoot with a longer focal length, but I don't think going beyond the 3X optical zoom is worthwhile.
If you're primarily interested in shooting yourself while moving—think walking, riding, skateboarding, etc.—it's also fair to consider Insta360's X6 in this equation. It can shoot similarly stable video by cropping its 360 footage. While both Luna cameras produce marginally better-looking video, the X6's 360-degree footage lets you pan around the shot in post, offering considerably more flexibility. Coupling the X6 with the folding selfie handle gives you an experience similar to the Luna. The X6 is also waterproof and virtually indestructible, so it can function as an action camera and 360 camera. To my mind, the main question is, do you need the higher-quality video of the Lunas? If you do, then the Luna cameras are the clear winner.
Finally, there's the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 and 4 Pro (the latter also called the 4P). Neither is officially for sale in the US, but you can find them on Amazon through third-party resellers. However, if registration, repair, support, and warranty matter to you, the Insta360 Luna series is your safer bet. If you want the absolute max dynamic range, the Osmo Pocket 4P boasts 17 stops of dynamic range and supports DJI's D-Log 2 log format. That's better dynamic range than all but one or two other cameras on the market. If that's what you're after, there's no competition, though remember color grading will crush much of that range anyway.
Beyond dynamic range, the Luna and Osmo Pocket cameras are pretty evenly matched, and since only one is officially available in the US, this is an easy choice.
Scott Gilbertson is Operations Manager for the WIRED Reviews Team. He was previously a writer and editor for WIRED’s Webmonkey.com, covering the independent web and early internet culture. You can reach him at luxagraf.net. ... Read More

Disney Asked Character.AI to Go Bankrupt for a Get-Out-of-Lawsuits Card
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand—potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology, and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations.
In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.
The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.
The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “reverse acquihire,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.
Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.
In the case of Character.AI, a motion filed by Character.AI’s legal counsel says that Disney required that the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy proceedings because of the startup’s “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.”
A spokesperson for Character.AI referred WIRED to Disney for comment on whether the deal was contingent on the startup declaring bankruptcy. Disney declined to comment on this story.
According to court filings, the deal involves “two interrelated and integrated” transactions—one before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, and one after.
As part of the first transaction, which occurred in September, Disney paid the startup $5.5 million, along with a refundable “good faith deposit” of $2 million. Disney also hired the “majority” of Character.AI’s employees, including the CEO, and agreed that it would let some of the now-Disney employees help keep Character.AI operational for five months.
Character.AI filed a petition for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12. Through the bankruptcy proceedings, court filings show that Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license for a huge range of Character.AI’s code, documentation, frameworks, tools, and “other artifacts,” including those produced for its trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure, and age-prediction technology. The list of IP included in the filings does not include users’ data (which can get additional protections in bankruptcy proceedings) or Character.AI’s website.
That license will be auctioned off in the coming months. If Disney is chosen as the winning bidder by Character.AI and a committee of unsecured creditors—and courts approve the deal—it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment. If Disney is not selected, the company will be refunded the $2 million deposit and receive a breakup fee.
In order to “preserve a competitive process,” Disney also agreed to permit the winning bidder to interview and potentially extend offers to up to 80 percent of “certain newly hired employees” that Disney already hired from Character.AI. Disney has the right to select which employees.
However, experts worry that bouncing Character.AI employees from one company to another in the span of months is unrealistic, and that the deal Disney and Character.AI have struck cannot be easily unwound.
In addition, Disney prepared a draft of a court order referred to as the “363 Free and Clear Order” in the filings, a version of which would be approved by the court at or before closing, that would clarify that this process should not be viewed as a merger of the two companies and that Character.AI would remain responsible for “any liability or other obligation” it might have, including any legal claims against it.
A spokesperson for Character.AI said they were unable to speculate on the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings and referred WIRED to the docket.
“There's decades of corporate law that developed to deal with the problem of a buyer who always wants to take on all the assets and never wants to take on any of the liability,” says John Newman, a law professor at the University of Memphis School of Law and a former deputy director of the Federal Trade Commission’s Bureau of Competition. But the Disney-Character.AI deal is extremely unusual and structured in a way, he says, that “all those corporate law safeguards really weren't built to guard against.”
Not Its First Rodeo
This isn’t even Character.AI’s first reverse acquihire.
In August 2024, Google reportedly paid the startup $2.7 billion to license its technology. A spokesperson tells WIRED that that license was for the existing AI technology at the time of the deal, and that Google also hired Character.AI’s founders and other members of its ML pre-training research team, but that the “vast majority” of the startup’s employees remained at the company.
In the following years, Google was named alongside Character.AI as a defendant in multiple lawsuits, including one that alleged a 14-year-old boy committed suicide after Character.AI’s chatbot “cultivated an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship.”
Google argued that because it was still a separate company from Character.AI, it was not responsible for the teen’s death, which it said occurred prior to Google’s licensing deal. The judge was not persuaded, determining that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged that Google was liable for aiding and abetting.
Google declined to comment for this story.
In January of this year, Google and Character.AI agreed in principle to settle that and a slew of similar lawsuits. “Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards,” Character.AI said in a statement at the time.
According to an order of dismissal in one of the cases, the overall settlement was approved by a California probate court in July, and the court tasked a referee to hear out all the issues pertaining to each individual settlement. On October 11, a day before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, the referee approved each settlement.
The Tech Justice Law Project and Social Media Victims Law Center, which represented plaintiffs in many of the lawsuits, declined to comment.
Despite losing key staff after the Google transaction and, according to the current CEO, struggled with profitability “at all times,” Character.AI continued to develop AI tools, including “real-time audio-driven FaceTime-style video generation with fictional characters,” according to the current CEO’s declaration.
In August 2025, Character.AI worked with an investment banker to try to find either a strategic buyer or investor. According to the bankruptcy filings, Character.AI and the banker received “consistent feedback” that its product and user base were “impressive,” but that the surrounding litigation and “regulatory overhang” made it unbuyable.
That November, Character.AI learned that a coalition of state attorneys general had started investigating the company. When the company filed for bankruptcy, the number of states and territories involved in the multistate investigation had climbed to 46.
According to a notice of interest filed in the bankruptcy proceedings by the National Association of Attorneys General on behalf of 40 states, those states’ investigations uncovered “serious issues” with Character.AI, including screenshots of Character.AI chatbots encouraging minors to hide their self-harm injuries and kill their parents.
A spokesperson for Character.AI says that the filing “is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform.”
The filings say that Character.AI was in the process of negotiating with the states over how to address the issues they identified, but did not reach any agreements before declaring bankruptcy.
If the deal is completed and approved by the courts, Disney will have both Character.AI’s staff and much of its technology stack, but will be able to sidestep the ongoing legal issues that contributed to Character.AI’s downfall, including the multistate investigation.
The states who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy have made it clear that they reserve their rights to challenge any bankruptcy plan, potentially setting up a fight over the ultimate outcome of the bankruptcy.
“It’s bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility,” says Newman. “And that’s what it looks like.”

Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine
Ukraine relies on US intel provided through Starshield system to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia fires at its cities.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied any suspension of intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Washington has resumed providing critical intelligence to help Kyiv defend against Russian missile strikes.
“There has been no pause,” Rubio told reporters while on a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday. “What [Zelenskyy] should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war.”
Ukraine has relied on US intelligence through Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, to detect the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities.
Asked about a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the more than four-year Ukraine war, Rubio said: “There’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know whether it’s been finalised, but the president [Trump] has been clear. He’d like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end.”
The comments were made after Ukrainian officials said some Russian strikes had occurred without warning. Speaking to the NBC TV network’s Meet the Press programme on Sunday, Zelenskyy said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but was later “deblocked”.
“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”
Waiving sanctions on Russia
Zelenskyy also said other US actions, such as signing a deal to import Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russia that had been slated to take effect this week, will hurt Ukraine.
“If the United States will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course, we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand,” he said.
Trump on Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia while accusing Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.
“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He claimed that “Zelenskyy doesn’t care” about ending the conflict. “Frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
Trump has temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing large quantities to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices.
The US president also reiterated his accusation that Ukraine was purposefully targeting Russian refineries to try to hurt Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 midterm elections.
Polling has suggested Trump’s party is heading for a likely defeat in the elections as many voters are upset by fuel costs, which have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke with Meet the Press after it aired Zelenskyy’s interview, saying the Ukrainian president “presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win”.
“The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement,” he said.
Bessent slammed the claim that the US government was behind the slowing of the SpaceX satellite communications. “President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that,” he said. “And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian missile attack killed a woman and wounded several people in the capital, Kyiv, overnight, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday.
The attack also damaged a metro station, a medical facility, an educational institution and a nonresidential building, according to the State Emergency Service.

Swiss research test radar drone to detect natural hazards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:56:52 UTC
17:56:52 KST

Swiss research test radar drone to detect natural hazards
Researchers at the Swiss federal institute of technology ETH Zurich are testing a radar drone to accurately measure and predict landslides before they happen.
The permafrost is thawing, which means monitoring the Alpine region to predict landslides and rockfalls has become increasingly important. To ensure forecasts are as accurate as possible, ETH Zurich researchers are testing a radar-equipped drone for the first time.
A large drone takes off in the Lötschental valley in Valais and then flies over the Oigschtchummun glacier above Blatten. Attached to the bottom of the drone is a radar device that scans the terrain using electromagnetic waves.
In this way, they want to measure the glacier’s movement, says Felix Seidel, managing director of the Swiss Geolab. “If we measure the glacier again 20 minutes later, we already see a very small difference,” he said. This means that the glacier has moved during this time, and the researchers can measure this movement.
More
The seven worst landslides in Swiss history
Radar gives more information
Lasers are normally used to detect rock movements. However, radar has an advantage over lasers. “With radar, we can also measure through clouds, which is difficult with lasers,” said Seidel.
The first test flights have been very promising, says the managing director of Swiss Geolab. The test flights were deliberately located in the Lötschental valley. The Oigschtchummun glacier is currently well monitored because it is moving. This allows the researchers to compare the measurements from the radar drones with regular monitoring data.
+ How to protect people and villages from landslides in Switzerland
However, drones are only one element in monitoring the Alpine region. Swiss Geolab also advocates satellite-based surveillance. From space, the entire Alpine region can be regularly observed to detect movement.
“While satellites can cover large areas, they don’t provide detailed views or allow you to see into steep slopes,” said Felix Seidel. However, it’s sufficient to identify areas that warrant closer inspection. “The next step involves deploying a drone to observe a rock face or valley slope.”
The drone could also be used to place sensors in the terrain for even more precise and continuous monitoring of movements.
Researchers want to process all this data using artificial intelligence so that it can be used as easily as possible by the authorities. “The goal is to provide the right person with the data in the right format at the right time so that they can make a decision,” said Felix Seidel. In the coming months, the researchers at Swiss Geolab plan to send more drones to glaciers and scree slopes.

Wind bands to play a bigger role in 2028 Song Celebration

Wind bands to play a bigger role in 2028 Song Celebration
Wind orchestra conductors from across Estonia gathered in Türi on Sunday to rehearse the repertoire for the 2028 Song Celebration.
Joonas Neumann is a young composer who has arranged two excerpts from Evald Aav's opera "Vikerlased." Neumann will make his Song Celebration debut at the next event.
"Two themes have been woven into one piece. First comes the warriors' chorus, followed by a duet between Ülo and Juta in the middle of the chorus, forming the B section," he explained. Neumann said the feedback had been positive and only minor adjustments would be needed.
On Sunday, participants in Türi familiarized themselves with the entire wind orchestra repertoire for the 2028 Song Celebration.
Kersti Perandi, conductor of the Väägvere brass band, said the repertoire is diverse. "It's very important for smaller orchestras that they can also perform pieces from the Song Celebration repertoire with their own ensembles afterward," she said. Perandi believes the current selection includes pieces that orchestras could add to their regular repertoire.
Gunnar Pettaig, conductor of the Tartu Tamme High School wind orchestra, said it is motivating for young musicians to experience classic works from the past. "Well-known pieces such as 'Kuldrannake' and other themes presented in a contemporary style," he added. Pettaig said this is both exciting and educational for young musicians.
The Song Celebration conductors gathered feedback from the orchestra leaders performing in the combined orchestra so that adjustments could be made before the sheet music goes to print.
Bert Langeler, head of the wind orchestra section, said the sheet music would be ready early next year, after which recordings of the repertoire would begin so that orchestra conductors would have them available. Wind orchestras will play a much more prominent role at the 2028 Song Celebration than at previous celebrations.
Riivo Jõgi, artistic director of the 2028 Song Celebration, said that in addition to performing at the Song Festival Grounds' main stage, wind orchestras will give a gala concert at Kalev Sports Hall. Registration for orchestras, as for choirs, remains open until October 31.
"I would say the wind orchestra repertoire is very beautiful, captivating and certainly offers something for the soul," Jõgi said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) announced Monday that Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) would chair his re-election campaign, with KMT Taipei lawmakers serving as vice chairs.
Explaining his choice, Chiang emphasized that “residents first” is a shared value between him and Lu, per UDN. He added that they had worked closely together both during his tenure in the legislature and since he became mayor.
Lu said Chiang had approached her for the role, suggesting that his administrative duties left him with little time for campaigning, per ETtoday. She said that with DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) actively campaigning across the city and the DPP reportedly focusing its attention on Chiang, he needed assistance with his campaign.
Lu added that no Taichung mayor had ever served as campaign chair for a Taipei mayor, calling Chiang’s move bold and innovative, per UDN. Lu said that although she was also busy with city governance, she felt compelled to help given the importance of Taipei.
Regarding key campaign positions, Lu said the campaign would include lawmakers who faced the DPP’s recall campaigns against KMT legislators. Wang Hung-wei (王鴻薇), Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀), Lo Chih-chiang (羅智強), Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯), and Lai Shyh-bao (賴士葆) would serve as vice chairs and secretary-generals.
Hsu commented on the partnership in an interview, calling Lu’s involvement a rallying call to encourage greater participation among KMT supporters. She noted that Lu was one of the party’s most experienced campaigners.
Hsu said that if the KMT failed to unite in response to what she described as the DPP’s coordinated campaign against the party in the November election, the public would have less confidence in the KMT’s ability to work together in the 2028 general election, per Z.Media. She cited Lu’s remarks to emphasize the importance of collective effort during election campaigns.
KMT Taichung mayoral candidate Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) also commented on Lu chairing both his and Chiang Wan-an’s campaigns, per NOWNews. He said that, as fellow National Chengchi University graduates, they should work together during the election season.
Former KMT Legislator Chen Hsueh-sheng (陳學聖) said the cooperation might run counter to conventional political calculations because Chiang Wan-an could compete with Lu for the party’s presidential nomination, per ETtoday. Chen pointed out that Lu could have allowed the DPP to target Chiang, potentially bringing his political career to an end.
Chen said both mayors had chosen cooperation over conventional political calculations. KMT Taipei City Councilor Chin Huei-chu (秦慧珠) said the move could pave the way for Lu’s potential 2028 presidential bid by connecting supporters in Taipei and Taichung, per Liberty Times.
DPP Taichung mayoral candidate Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純) urged Lu to honor her promise and focus on Taichung, per UDN. Ho argued that Lu was prioritizing campaigning over governing the city during the remainder of her term.

‘No early warning’: Zelenskyy says allies failed to alert Kyiv before Russian strikes; Rubio says US intel sharing never paused
Unknown

Zelenskyy says Ukraine received no early warning from partners before Russian strike
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Kyiv received no early warning from its international partners ahead of Russia’s latest ballistic missile attack on Monday. The overnight strikes across 11 Ukrainian regions damaged more than 10 energy facilities and left at least 5,50,000 households without electricity.The comments come as US secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the US had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine.The attack, which involved ballistic missiles and drones, also killed one person and injured eight others in Kyiv, according to local authorities. The strikes damaged residential buildings, a medical facility, a school and a metro station, highlighting the continued threat to civilian infrastructure as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine’s energy network.In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles in what he described as a deliberate attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region, alongside more than 200 drones, including jet-powered Shahed drones.
“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” he said.He added that the attacks extended beyond the capital, with strikes reported across regions ranging from Kharkiv and Dnipro to Volyn, Rivne and Odesa.“Overnight and this morning, Russia attacked energy facilities in the Vinnytsia, Volyn, Kirovohrad, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Kharkiv, Ternopil, Odesa, and Rivne regions,” Zelensky said.“In this one night alone, more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, and the lights went out for at least 550,000 families. Repair crews are working at the sites,” he added.
Rubio on Monday denied that intelligence-sharing with Ukraine had been interrupted. “There's been no pause,” Rubio told NBC in Uzbekistan, adding, "I don't know where he's getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There's been no pause."Ukraine’s Air Force said Russian forces had launched a large-scale overnight assault involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and 269 drones. Ukrainian air defences destroyed or suppressed 243 drones and four missiles, while strikes were recorded at 25 locations and debris fell at eight others, the force said.According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, the attack damaged a private medical facility and a metro station in the Desnianskyi district. Educational institutions and a sports facility were damaged in the Dniprovskyi district, while a fire broke out at a medical facility inside a 25-storey residential building in Solomianskyi district. Emergency services extinguished the blaze.Russia’s defence ministry also said it had carried out a “massive strike” using “ground-based high-precision weapons and strike drones”. It claimed to have hit military-industrial facilities, cruise missile storage sites and data centres in Ukraine, including locations in and around Kyiv allegedly linked to drone production and logistics.Ukraine’s deputy energy minister Artem Nekrasov said Russian attacks had targeted energy facilities in 11 regions. Rolling blackouts and electricity restrictions for industry and businesses had been introduced, he said in a post on Telegram.
Zelensky also criticised what he described as inadequate support from Ukraine’s partners, particularly over air defence supplies and sanctions on Moscow.“Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end,” he said, adding that Ukraine had responded positively to every ceasefire proposal.“Putin not only doesn't want to end this war – he doesn't even want to take any steps toward de-escalation. EVERY ONE of our partners has experienced this firsthand when they heard Russia's refusals. And it is crucial to call things what they are. To call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine defend lives. When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defense are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners", he said.

Her work combines breaking news with in-depth analysis, offering readers context and clarity on the stories shaping the world.

Taiwan Railway to ban political ads at stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:53:46 UTC
17:53:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Railway announced Monday that it will ban political advertising at its stations starting Jan. 1, 2027, to preserve its image of political neutrality.
The decision followed complaints about a campaign advertisement at Douliu Station in Yunlin County, CNA reported. The advertisement raised concerns about political neutrality ahead of Taiwan’s Nov. 28 local elections.
Taiwan Railway said political advertisements are permitted at stations under existing rules. Advertising spaces leased to private operators are treated as commercial rentals and do not represent the company’s political position.
Current contracts require advertisers to treat candidates fairly, regardless of party affiliation. They also limit the amount of space that can be used for political advertising, per CTS News.
To address public concerns, Taiwan Railway said it would introduce stricter rules covering election advertisements, political messages, and advertisements featuring political figures, per TVBS News.
Political advertisements already displayed at stations may remain under existing contracts. The new restrictions will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Juventus boss Luciano Spalletti
lamented his side's lack of hunger after their poor form
continued on Sunday with a 3-0 defeat to surprise-package Lazio
in Turin.
                                    
Goals by Danish defender Oliver Provstgaard, his compatriot
Gustav Isaksen and Nigeria midfielder Fisayo Dele-Bashiru
enabled the Rome side to keep pace with champions Inter, who won
3-1 at Bologna on Saturday, at the top of the table with 19
points from seven games in their best-ever start to the season.
                                    
Juve, on the the other hand, are eighth with 11 points after
winning only one of their last five Serie A games.
                                    
"What matters is the tempo you set in a match, the energy and
the heart you put into it," former Italy boss Luciano Spalletti
said.
                                    
"Tonight, we showed fragility, and that starts in the mind.
                                    
"You end up chasing events rather than anticipating them.
                                    
"What makes the difference is what you see and think ahead of
time, because at this level everyone is technically gifted.
                                    
"Tactical systems change nothing if there is no hunger, passion,
courage or character...
                                    
"We looked tired, because to some extent we were. Today, we took
a step backwards".
                                    
Lazio have made a strong start despite most of their fans
boycotting their home games in protest at how Chairman Claudio
Lotito is running the club and widespread initial scepticism
about the appointment in the close season of coach Gennaro
Gattuso, who failed to lead Italy to qualification for the 2026
World Cup in his previous job.
                                    
Roma, meanwhile, remain two points behind the leading duo thanks
to a 2-0 home win over third-from-bottom Genoa on Saturday.
                                    
Milan are fourth with 15 points after beating Atalanta 3-2 at
San Siro on Sunday, while Como are fifth with 14 after a 3-1 win
at second-bottom Fiorentina.
                                    
Another surprise package, Cagliari, can climb to 16 points and
regain fourth place if they beat Monza away later on Monday.

Israeli media: 110,000 people evading military service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:48:37 UTC
17:48:37 KST

The number of people classified as evading military service in the Israeli army has risen to around 110,000, up from about 75,000 at the beginning of 2026.
Israeli public broadcaster Kan reported on Sunday evening that the increase followed the activation of tens of thousands of military call-up orders, with the number expected to rise further in the coming period.
According to Israeli army estimates, ultra-Orthodox Jews, known as Haredim, account for around 80 per cent of those currently classified as evading military service.
Despite the unprecedented number and a Supreme Court ruling stressing that the law must be enforced against draft evaders, enforcement measures remain largely frozen, with only limited exceptions.
READ: Thousands of Haredim protest in Jerusalem against Israeli military service
In addition to those arrested at Ben Gurion Airport, the authorities arrested, during random campaigns, 14 Haredi Jewish evaders from service, and 13 other non-Haredim.
A large-scale enforcement operation was planned for this month but was cancelled following a dispute between the police and the army over the division of responsibilities.
The police requested 300 soldiers to assist with the arrests, but the army rejected the request, arguing that the task did not fall within its remit.

The war of attrition with Iran: What happened to US patriots?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:46:40 UTC
17:46:40 KST

The issue is not only the missiles the US military has consumed on the battlefield, but the time it needs to replace them; a time that can affect Washington's ability to confront potential crises in other regions, especially East Asia.
According to a report attributed to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, in seven months of confrontation with Iran, Washington used approximately the equivalent of 19 years of Patriot missile purchases of these interceptors. In the same assessment, restoring US missile stockpiles to prewar levels has been stated to take at least three years. These figures indicate the gap between the speed of munitions consumption in an intense conflict and the ability of the US defense industry to compensate for it.
The importance of this issue increases when we know that military power is not measured merely by the number of aircraft, ships, or advanced systems. The ability to sustain operations in a prolonged conflict and to quickly replace consumed equipment is also a determining factor. An army may possess advanced technology and extensive firepower, but if its munitions stockpiles decrease at a rate faster than production capacity, it will face more serious limitations in continuing operations.
Patriot; An Important Link in US Air Defense
 
The Patriot system is one of the important air defense equipment of the United States and its allies, used to counter certain aircraft and missile threats. The interceptor missiles of this system play an important role in protecting forces, bases, and military facilities. The extensive consumption of these missiles can force commanders to make more difficult decisions about how to allocate munitions, the priority of defending targets, and the level of risk acceptance.
Compensating for this reduction in stockpiles is also not simply a matter of increasing government orders. The production of advanced missiles depends on specialized components, raw materials, skilled manpower, and industrial capacity. Developing production lines and increasing delivery speed is a time-consuming process, and one cannot expect an increase in demand to immediately lead to a proportionate increase in supply.
For this reason, even after the intensity of the conflict decreases, pressure on the US military can continue. Washington must simultaneously meet the needs of forces deployed in the Middle East, maintain its commitments in Europe, and be prepared for potential crises in East Asia. The longer the rebuilding of stockpiles takes, the more difficult it will be to manage these commitments.
A Window of Vulnerability for Washington and a Possible Opportunity for China
 
One of the most important strategic consequences of the reduction in US munitions stockpiles is its connection to the competition between Washington and Beijing. China is considered America's most important strategic rival, and any potential conflict in the Indo-Pacific region could require extensive consumption of precision munitions and defense systems.
Under such circumstances, the reduction in interceptor stockpiles can complicate US military planning. Washington will be forced to strike a balance between meeting current needs in the Middle East and maintaining readiness for potential crises in East Asia. This situation may be what analysts refer to as a "window of vulnerability"; a period in which the replacement of consumed munitions has not yet been completed, but America's security needs in other regions still persist.
Of course, these conditions do not mean China's definitive superiority or America's inability to defend its interests. Washington's military power is not limited to Patriot missiles, and this country still possesses a naval fleet, air force, base network, and regional allies. However, in a prolonged confrontation, the depth of stockpiles and the speed of replacing munitions can become as important as technology and the quality of weapons.
A Cost Beyond the Battlefield
 
The consequences of this situation are not limited to the US military either. Washington's allies, who depend on American systems and munitions for air defense, may face delays in the delivery of orders if demand increases. Under such conditions, the US government must prioritize between the needs of its own forces and the requests of its security partners; a decision that can affect military relations and the security calculations of allies.
For Iran too, this issue has strategic importance; because it shows that the assessment of a military confrontation should not be made only on the basis of the number of equipment or the firepower of the parties. The capacity to withstand pressure, the continuity of operations, and the cost of replacing weapons also play a role in determining the course of a conflict. Of course, the reduction in US interceptor stockpiles alone is not sufficient to prove this country's military defeat and must be examined alongside the operational results and the extent to which the declared objectives of both sides have been achieved.
Ultimately, the extensive consumption of Patriot missiles and the time needed to rebuild America's stockpiles will be the possible restriction of Washington's strategic freedom of action in the post-conflict period. The war may end on the battlefield, but its effects on weapons stockpiles and military readiness will remain for years; an issue that takes the real cost of a prolonged confrontation beyond the days of military operations.

Six suspects arrested in connection with murder of police officer in Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:44:20 UTC
17:44:20 KST

Six people have been arrested following the murder of police officer Nordine El Talbi while he was on a reconnaissance mission, the Brussels public prosecutor has told a press conference. They are accused of the murder of a person holding a public office and of forming a criminal organisation.
Six suspects arrested in connection with murder of police officer in Brussels
Two suspects were arrested in Belgium, one at a railway station in Paris and three in the southern Spanish city of Almería. Belgium has requested the extradition of the four arrested in France and Spain.
The suspects are five adults and one juvenile. According to public prosecutor Julien Moinil, they are all Belgian citizens from Brussels who are known for drug trafficking. The arrests took place “in the hours leading up to the press conference”. Those arrested in Spain were likely fleeing to Morocco.
El Talbi was killed during a police operation on the night of 12 October following a violent carjacking in Tubize, Walloon Brabant. The stolen car was located in the Brussels municipality of Jette, with drugs and weapons found inside. Officers from the Anti-Robbery Brigade were dispatched to the scene.
El Talbi went to reconnoitre the location in plain clothes, as is customary in such operations. Shortly afterwards, colleagues found him shot by a bullet to the head.
According to Brussels police chief Michel Goovaerts, the 41-year-old was a highly experienced and respected colleague who had been an officer in Brussels for more than 15 years. He joined the Anti-Robbery Brigade, a specialist unit deployed for high-risk operations, in 2019.
He was commemorated by police forces across the country last Friday, including with a ceremony in Brussels’ Jubelpark.

"The liberation of Dobropolye has become a very important event. Dobropolye was one of the few remaining major Ukrainian army defensive areas in the Donetsk region.

Türkiye unveils tourism route linking east to Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
08:43:45 UTC
17:43:45 KST

This photo shows the eastern province of Erzurum’s Narman Fairy Chimneys.
Türkiye’s Culture and Tourism Ministry has created a four-day route linking eastern Anatolia with the Black Sea to expand domestic tourism, combining castles, monasteries and natural landmarks across four provinces in one itinerary.
The Anabasis Northern Route connects the eastern province of Erzurum with the Black Sea provinces of Bayburt, Gümüşhane and Trabzon. Run by the Türkiye Tourism Promotion and Development Agency (TGA), it is the third route in this year’s Ancient Cities Path project, following Batman-Şırnak and the ‘Unknown Cappadocia’ circuit through Aksaray, Niğde and Kayseri. Travel agencies are preparing to offer it as a package tour.
The route draws on Anabasis, in which Greek writer Xenophon, a student of Socrates, recounts the retreat of mercenaries hired by Cyrus the Younger in 401 B.C. After Cyrus died fighting for the Persian throne, the soldiers retreated north through hostile territory, winter weather and mountains. Their cry of ‘thalassa, thalassa’ (‘the sea, the sea’) on seeing the Black Sea links the ancient account to the tour’s coastal finale.
Day one starts at Erzurum’s Narman Fairy Chimneys, called the ‘Land of Red Fairies’ and designated a natural monument in 2018; wind and rain shaped the formations, colored red by oxidized iron. Stops include the Rainbow Hills, Engüzek Castle and Pirinkayalar Viewing Terrace before the 10th-century Öşvank Monastery in Uzundere’s Çamlıyamaç village. Built under Georgia’s Bagratid dynasty, it retains colored stone carvings, reliefs and frescoes; visitors stay in Erzurum.
Day two covers Bayburt Castle above the Çoruh River, known as Çinimaçin for its Seljuk-era tiles, then the Seljuk-era Ulu Mosque, with its cut-stone walls and brick minaret, Aydıntepe Underground City and Aydıntepe Plateau. The underground galleries and vaulted rooms may have provided shelter in different periods.
In Gümüşhane, Satala in Kelkit’s Sadak village preserves walls, baths and aqueducts from a Roman legionary base. The day ends in Süleymaniye, a former mining settlement shared by Turks, Armenians and Anatolian Greeks, with an overnight stay in Gümüşhane.
Day three covers Santa in Dumanlı village, a protected archaeological and natural site that grew through mining in the 16th-18th centuries. Its seven neighborhoods contain over 300 stone houses alongside churches; its Greek Orthodox residents left after the 1923 population exchange. Harmantepe Martyrs’ Cemetery, Mount Madur and Forapark’s mountain coaster precede a night in Trabzon.
The final day includes Atatürk Pavilion, Çal Cave with its stalactites, stalagmites, underground stream and waterfalls, Tonya’s forested Canikdere Waterfall and Beşikdüzü Cable Car. Furtuna Mansion in Araklı and the Girls’ Monastery, with its rock church on Boztepe’s slopes, complete the itinerary. Modern Türkiye founder Mustafa Kemal Atatürk decided at the pavilion in 1937 to donate his property to the nation.
