Philippines summons Chinese ambassador over ‘use of force’ remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:58:04 UTC
16:58:04 KST

The Philippines has summoned China’s ambassador to Manila after he said Beijing could “easily win” a conflict between the two countries, prompting calls from Philippine lawmakers for his expulsion.
Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro conveyed Manila’s “serious concern and strong objection” to Ambassador Jing Quan over his public remarks on October 15, which the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs said amounted to a threat to use force.
The dispute follows a series of incidents involving the two countries’ militaries and coast guards in contested areas of the South China Sea.
China claims most of the strategic waterway, despite an international ruling that found no legal basis for its expansive claims.
Jing made the remarks last week after Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro described Beijing as a regional “troublemaker”.
Speaking to reporters after a speech at a school in Manila, the Chinese envoy said the Philippines should “feel fortunate” to have China as a neighbour.
“If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace,” he said.
The comments prompted calls from politicians, including at least two sitting senators, for Manila to expel the ambassador.
In its statement on Monday, the Philippine foreign ministry described Jing’s remarks as “provocative and unacceptable”.
“The Department reserves the right to take further diplomatic action as it deems necessary,” it added.
Jing called for peaceful resolution
Earlier, speaking at the Second Diliman Dialogue in Manila, Jing called for a peaceful approach to maritime disputes, urging both sides to maintain a safe distance, avoid deliberate provocations and prevent incidents from escalating tensions.
He said China and the Philippines should manage their differences through dialogue and consultation, warning against a cycle of reciprocal countermeasures.
Jing also argued that maritime disputes should not define the entirety of bilateral relations, pointing to continued trade, people-to-people exchanges and cooperation in other areas.
“We must not allow a small group of people, backed by forces from outside the region, to steer bilateral relations into a dangerous and uncertain course, or even toward confrontation and conflict,” he said at the dialogue.

Daycare prices outpace benefit cap, hitting low earners hardest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:57:09 UTC
16:57:09 KST

Daycare prices outpace benefit cap, hitting low earners hardest
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Seven in 10 daycare centres now charge more than the hourly rate covered by childcare benefit (kinderopvangtoeslag), and parents have to make up the shortfall, parents’ association BOinK reported.
The average hourly rate at the 400 organisations BOinK surveyed is €11.82, while the government only subsidises up to €11.23. The cap goes up to €11.60 in January, which is still less than most centres are already charging, and prices are set to rise again next year.
Low earners will get hit hardest, NU.nl reported on Monday. The state covers 96% of the capped rate for the lowest incomes, leaving them with a bill of a few cents an hour – until the surcharge above the cap is added.
A family on a low income with a child in daycare two days a week could be paying €80 a month next year, up from €70.
“For many parents, this means their own contribution keeps rising,” BOinK chairman Gjalt Jellesma said in a statement.
A social affairs ministry spokesperson told NU.nl that childcare is becoming more affordable overall and that the gap between the cap and actual prices has narrowed since 2023.

World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza, cites funding shortages

World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza, cites funding shortages
- WFP says funding shortages are forcing Gaza aid cuts, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support and halving rations for many others.
- The agency says 1.4 million people in Gaza face crisis-level food insecurity or worse, while 200,000 are in emergency conditions.
- WFP needs US$450 million over six months and warns life in Gaza remains “brutal” as winter nears and basic services stay scarce.
AI generated
CAIRO/GAZA – The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has said funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid programme in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance to 1.1 million people from 1.6 million.
In addition, food rations have also been halved, cash assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and the number of daily hot meals for those unable to cook has fallen to 150,000 from 250,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now receiving a hot meal only every other day.
The WFP said about 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza’s population, face crisis levels of food insecurity or worse, including roughly 200,000 people in emergency conditions.
The US-brokered Gaza ceasefire in 2025 calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
Life is still brutal in Gaza, says acting head of WFP
“It’s a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter. There is no basic services. There is no safety, no security,” acting executive director of the WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.
“These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I’ve been through the winters here, absolutely brutal,” he added.
The WFP said it urgently needs US$450 million (S$575 million) over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
“We tell the world now is not the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery,” said Skau.
Israeli forces still hold more than 60% of the territory and conduct almost daily air strikes, while Hamas controls most of the area where more than two million Palestinians live, mostly in temporary shelters with what aid agencies call inadequate aid supplies.
The Hamas-run Gaza government media office described the WFP announcement as “catastrophic” and said it might accelerate famine in the enclave, calling for more fund to aid agencies to prevent it.
“On top of the circumstances and the difficult life, you want to make it even harder on us,” said Palestinian woman Sabrine Kuhail, standing by a tent shelter at a displacement site in Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza Strip.
“You made us hungry for three years with war, destruction, siege, and the bloodshed that is not stopping. What do you want from us? Enough, enough, we are tired.” REUTERS

Singapore sets aside 92 mln USD for bio-based chemicals research
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:55:19 CST
16:55:19 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Singapore has set aside 118 million Singapore dollars (about 92.23 million U.S. dollars) for research into producing chemicals from biological materials, the largest public funding commitment of its kind to date, the Economic Development Board (EDB) said on Monday.
The Bioeconomy Funding Initiative, launched under the 37-billion-Singapore-dollar Research, Innovation, Enterprise 2030 plan, aims to address industry challenges and support the transformation of Singapore's energy and chemicals sector, which accounts for one-fifth of domestic manufacturing output, the EDB said in a statement.
The initiative will target chemicals made from biological alternatives to petroleum-based feedstocks, such as yeast and oil palm, the EDB said.
Initial research will focus on converting industrial by-products, or "sidestreams," into usable materials, developing microbe- and enzyme-based production methods, and improving processing efficiency.
Research and development projects will also explore combinations of biological and chemical processes to produce commercially viable goods, including high-grade synthetic rubber.
"There are opportunities for Singapore to grow our capabilities in innovation and production of higher-value specialty chemicals and advanced materials, while supporting the transformation of our existing industrial base towards more sustainable production," said Jermaine Loy, managing director of the EDB.
The latest initiative builds on previous funding commitments and will bring government spending on bioeconomy-related initiatives to about 200 million Singapore dollars over the next five years. ■

ATHENS, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- An infant was among six people killed after a speedboat carrying migrants collided with a Greek coast guard patrol vessel off the eastern Aegean island of Lesvos on Monday, Greek authorities said.
The incident occurred in the early hours when the speedboat made dangerous maneuvers while attempting to evade a coast guard inspection, authorities said.
The bodies of four men, a woman and the infant were recovered after the boat capsized and sank, the coast guard said. Eight people, including four men, two women and two children, were rescued and taken to hospital for treatment.
The search and rescue operation was completed, with no other people reported missing, the coast guard said. The 37-year-old Turkish operator of the boat was arrested on suspicion of people smuggling.
Greek Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy Vassilis Kikilias expressed grief and anger over the deaths. He reiterated the government's zero-tolerance stance on smugglers, calling them criminals who risk the lives of desperate people for profit. ■

China's GDP expands 4.5 pct year on year in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:55:09 CST
16:55:09 KST

A drone photo taken on Oct. 14, 2026 shows the Yangzhou Port in Yangzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province. China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed Monday. The country's economy expanded 4.6 percent year on year in the first three quarters. The world's second-largest economy generated about 107.11 trillion yuan (about 15.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in output during the January-September period, according to the NBS. (Photo by Ren Fei/Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed Monday.
The growth rate was higher than the second quarter's reading of 4.3 percent, the data showed. The country's economy expanded 4.6 percent year on year in the first three quarters.
The world's second-largest economy generated about 107.11 trillion yuan (about 15.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in output during the January-September period, according to the NBS.
"The national economy forged ahead against pressure and continued to shift toward innovation-driven, high-quality development, with growing positive changes in major indicators," the NBS said in a statement.
Noting the GDP growth of 4.6 percent in the first three quarters is in line with the country's annual growth target, NBS deputy head Mao Shengyong told a media conference that the economy added 5.7 trillion yuan in output during the period, the largest increase for the same period in the past five years.
In the third quarter, GDP growth picked up 0.2 percentage points from the second quarter, while some international institutions forecasted that major economies were expected to grow more slowly compared to the previous quarter, Mao said.
New growth drivers continued to expand in China, contributing more than 40 percent to the country's economic growth in the first three quarters, according to preliminary estimates. Value-added industrial output rose 5.3 percent year on year, with equipment manufacturing up 10.2 percent and high-tech manufacturing up 14.3 percent. Output of industrial robots, lithium-ion batteries and 3D printing equipment jumped 29.1 percent, 39.5 percent and 62.5 percent, respectively.
Monday's data also showed that the services sector expanded 5.2 percent year on year in the first three quarters, with information transmission, software and IT services up 10.4 percent and leasing and business services up 12.3 percent.
Goods imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan in the first three quarters, with imports up 22.3 percent. In September alone, trade grew 27.5 percent.
The surveyed urban unemployment rate averaged 5.2 percent in the first three quarters, unchanged from a year earlier, while September figure stood at 5.2 percent, down 0.1 percentage points from August. In the first nine months, per capita disposable income rose 5.3 percent nominally and 4.4 percent in real terms year on year.
In the first three quarters, retail sales of consumer goods rose 1.1 percent year on year, while retail sales of services grew 5 percent. Mao added that energy consumption per unit of GDP fell 3.1 percent during the period.
China will step up efforts to expand domestic demand, improve supply and make macro policies more effective to sustain the positive momentum of innovation-led and high-quality development, the official said. ■

Feature: Wuhan Open offers glimpse into blossoming Chinese women's tennis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:54:57 CST
16:54:57 KST

WUHAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- When China's top player Zheng Qinwen announced to withdraw from the 2026 Wuhan Open due to a right shoulder injury, many home fans were left disappointed.
The 24-year-old had just lifted the China Open trophy and was expected to spearhead the home challenge in central China. Her absence, however, turned attention to the depth and resilience of Chinese women's tennis.
SHI HAN: GROWING THROUGH THE LOWER TIERS
Ranked outside the world's top 200, 21-year-old Shi Han was hardly a household name when she arrived in Wuhan.
She earned her place in the main draw the hard way, qualifying by beating top-seeded American Peyton Stearns and top-100 player Kamilla Rakhimova.
Drawn against 13th seed and world No. 19 Solana Sierra in the first round, Shi admitted she was taken aback by the challenge.
"I had finally made it through qualifying, only to get such a tough draw," Shi recalled after the match.
With little to lose, she decided to give it everything she had. After dropping the opening set 6-4, Shi fought back to win the next two 6-3, 6-3. Her first serve remained reliable, with speeds still reaching around 180 kph deep into the decider. The win was Shi's first over a top-20 opponent and her first main-draw victory at a WTA 1000 event.
Shi then pushed former US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez in the second round, taking a 4-1 lead in the second set before Fernandez closed out the match in straight sets. Shi left Wuhan encouraged rather than disheartened.
"As everyone jokes, maybe I came here to take tuition," she smiled. "The players I've met in Wuhan are all ranked much higher than me. I'll give everything I have, then look back and see where the gaps are between me and them."
This season, Shi has spent much of her time competing on the ITF circuit, away from the WTA spotlight. Yet she has quietly compiled 64 match wins this year, eight more than world No. 1 Elena Rybakina, even though victories at lower-tier tournaments yield relatively few ranking points.
Starting the year outside top 400, Shi has climbed into the top 200 and secured a place in the 2027 Australian Open qualifying draw.
"I've played a lot of tournaments this season. I wanted to improve my ranking as quickly as possible and get back to the Grand Slams," Shi said. "I'm quite satisfied with the effort I've put in. I have nothing to lose. I hope to go further and play better tennis."
GUO HANYU: FIGHTING BACK AGAINST ADVERSITY
Wild card Guo Hanyu, ranked No. 240 in singles but fresh from Wimbledon doubles glory, arrived in Wuhan with modest expectations. Facing 12th seed and world No. 16 Sorana Cirstea in the opening round, Guo lost the first set 6-1 and trailed 0-4 in the second.
"Until the match was over, I didn't think I was going to win," Guo said. "I just wanted to stay on court a little longer and enjoy the atmosphere on the center court. I didn't expect my form to keep getting better."
Trailing 6-3 in the second-set tiebreak, Guo faced three set points. She then seized control, winning five straight points to take the tiebreak 8-6. Trailing 3-5 in the decider, she broke Cirstea when the Romanian served for the match and reeled off four consecutive games to complete a remarkable 1-6, 7-6(6), 7-5 comeback.
She followed that with another marathon win over American Katie Volynets, prevailing 6-4, 4-6, 7-6(3) after more than three hours on court. Guo's run ended against fifth seed Elina Svitolina in the third round, but reaching the last 16 was her best singles result at a WTA 1000 event and made her the only Chinese player to reach that stage in Wuhan.
Her achievement carried extra significance amid personal turmoil. Shortly after returning from Wimbledon, where she partnered Kristina Mladenovic to claim the women's doubles title, Guo learned her father had been admitted to intensive care. She has since struggled to focus and broke down at her post-match press conference when discussing him.
"I can't stand on court and enjoy the match happily like I used to. There has always been a feeling of sadness around me," she said. "I've tried very hard to pull myself out of it, but it's difficult."
"I keep telling myself to leave it to fate. If this is something I have to go through, I can't escape it. All I can do is play point by point, give my best and see where fate takes me."
Last year, Guo recorded her first WTA 1000 main-draw victory in Montreal. At the time, she described it as feeling as if she had "hit the jackpot" by suddenly producing an exceptional performance.
After winning two main-draw matches in Wuhan, she now carries greater confidence into future tournaments.
"At least against players ranked in the top 100, whoever I'm facing, I feel I have a way to compete," she said. "Maybe I won't win every time, but I believe every match brings progress and something to learn."
ZHANG SHUAI: DEFYING AGE TO DREAM BIG
On Oct. 13, 37-year-old Zhang Shuai walked onto center court to face 22-year-old American Ashlyn Krueger.
Zhang began her professional career in 2006, meaning her time on tour almost matches the age of her young opponent.
But on this night, fatigue was evident.
Zhang struggled with her movement, her shots lacked their usual power, and she repeatedly bent over her racket to catch her breath. She eventually lost 6-3, 6-0.
Zhang's heavy workload this year helps explain her fatigue. Since the US Open, she has played at the Billie Jean King Cup, won an Asian Games silver in Nagoya, reached the China Open doubles final and then arrived in Wuhan two days later. Counting singles, doubles and mixed doubles, she has played 128 matches this year.
"At this intensity and at my age, I think I must be a superhero," she said. "Even though I played like this today, I'm still very proud of myself."
As she left Wuhan, the veteran was already looking ahead.
"I'm not young anymore, but I'll give everything I have over the next year and try to come back to the Wuhan Open," Zhang said. "I hope I can perform better next year." ■

China unveils new measures to boost technology-driven innovation in commerce
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:54:55 CST
16:54:55 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China has released new guidelines to promote the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and other advanced technologies in commerce, as part of efforts to upgrade consumption and improve commercial distribution efficiency.
These guidelines, jointly issued by nine government departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, outline 18 measures covering goods consumption, services consumption, commercial distribution, innovative business applications and policy support.
To upgrade consumer goods, the guidelines call for integrating AI into product development, design, manufacturing and marketing, expanding the supply of smart devices and robots, and encouraging flexible manufacturing and AI-powered customization.
In the services sector, these guidelines support the application of AI in healthcare and smart elderly care services, the digital transformation of catering businesses, and pilot applications of AI in culture and tourism.
In commercial distribution, the measures include promoting smart warehouses, intelligent logistics equipment and unmanned delivery, alongside digital upgrades in wholesale and retail businesses.
The guidelines also call for developing commercial AI agents for shopping assistance, business operations and logistics, expanding applications of embodied intelligence, and creating virtual shopping experiences. They additionally outline support for technology standards, digital infrastructure and financing.
In June, the Ministry of Commerce and seven other government departments released guidelines containing 17 measures to promote "AI plus consumption," focusing on smart products, AI-enabled services and new consumption scenarios.
China's retail sales of consumer goods rose 1.1 percent year on year to 37 trillion yuan (about 5.5 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of 2026, while retail sales of services increased 5 percent, outpacing the 1-percent growth in retail sales of goods, official data released on Monday showed. ■

Australian teens more likely to disclose online sexual harm to AI chatbots than authorities: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:54:53 CST
16:54:53 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Australian teenagers who experience online sexual abuse are more likely to disclose it to artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots than to authorities, a national study has found.
The study of almost 2,000 Australians aged 16 to 18, conducted in early 2026 by Adelaide University's Australian Cybercrime Observatory, found that 18.7 percent of victims told an AI about their experience, compared with 13.2 percent who reported it to a teacher, doctor, counsellor, police officer or helpline, according to a university statement released on Monday.
More than one in four cases of nonconsensual sharing of sexual images involved AI, while at least one in 25 Australians had experienced, or had a close friend who had experienced, AI-related online sexual victimization before the age of 18, showed the findings published in Child Abuse & Neglect.
Girls experienced higher rates of online sexual victimization overall, but boys were significantly more likely to be targeted when AI was involved, it said, adding that more than one-third of adolescents also expressed concern that AI could be used to create fake images of themselves or people they cared about.
The findings highlighted the need for reporting pathways accessible through AI tools, peer-focused prevention and broader efforts to protect children, researchers said.
"AI involvement in this abuse is worryingly common, and victims are now more likely to tell an AI than teachers, doctors, police or reporting services. We must adapt quickly to protect children," said Associate Professor Timothy Cubitt from Adelaide University, also the study's co-author. ■

boonserm premthada builds coastal office in thailand with reclaimed timber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:45:36 UTC
16:45:36 KST

boonserm premthada builds coastal office in thailand with reclaimed timber
the project combines traditional thai building principles, woven bamboo screens, and a design that allows the structures to be dismantled and rebuilt elsewhere.
prefer designboom on google
reclaimed timber carries its history forward
Designed by Boonserm Premthada of Bangkok Project Studio, Traces by the Sea is a 440.7-square-meter office for Matalay in Khao Lak, Phang Nga, Thailand. The project brings together timber reclaimed from an old rice cooperative building in Phatthalung and a wooden school building in Phang Nga, preserving the paint, joints, and surfaces accumulated through years of use. The architecture makes these traces part of its identity, allowing the histories of the materials to remain visible in their new coastal setting. Differences in dimensions, existing notches, and remnants of painted surfaces guide how each piece is put together. Premthada makes only the changes needed to reuse the wood, allowing its original features to shape the design.
The carpenters assemble the timber by hand on site, examining each piece to find the right position and adapting the connections to fit its existing features. Old joints remain visible alongside new ones, showing how the wood has been worked on before and how the carpenters give it a new purpose.
a cluster of buildings shaped by the climate
The office consists of four timber buildings connected by decks and walkways, drawing on the layout of traditional Thai house clusters. The spaces between the buildings allow breezes to pass through and keep views of the sea open, while the raised floors create shaded areas beneath the structures. Supported by rows of columns, the buildings stand above the sand, providing shelter while remaining open to the surrounding landscape.
The layout draws on traditional Thai architecture, where raised floors and open spaces help keep buildings cool in a hot climate. The design by Boonserm Premthada and his team adapts the principles of a traditional house to a contemporary workplace, allowing familiar ways of building to respond to the needs of an office by the sea. The decks and walkways take people outdoors as they move between workspaces, bringing them into contact with the trees, sea breeze, and changing light. This connection to the landscape makes the coastal setting an everyday part of working at Matalay.
woven bamboo turns traditional craft into a screen
Large woven bamboo trays from northeastern Thailand are used as sunscreens, giving everyday objects a new role in the building. Traditionally used for silkworm rearing, the trays retain their original shapes and woven patterns, keeping their connection to the craft and practices from which they come. Sunlight filters through the weave and the gaps between the trays, casting patterns of light and shadow across the interior. Although their purpose has changed, the trays remain recognizable as traditional tools, showing how local craftsmanship can be incorporated into architecture.
The timber and bamboo elements build on ideas that Boonserm Premthada explored in his artwork at Triennale Milano, now adapted to a building designed for everyday use. Here, the materials must respond to the coastal climate while retaining traces of their previous lives. Throughout the project, the approach is to change as little as possible. Old paint and marks remain on the timber, new joints sit alongside existing ones, and open spaces allow air and views to pass through.
The timber buildings are designed to be dismantled and reassembled elsewhere, extending the project’s interest in reuse beyond its current function. The wood has already moved from a rice cooperative and a school into an office by the sea. Its next life may take it somewhere else, adding another layer of use to its history.
elephant dung bricks extend the material exploration
The wider Matalay development also includes a public toilet building made from elephant dung bricks, extending the project’s exploration of materials and their potential for reuse. The toilet building is a long, low structure with brick walls and timber doorways. Openings above the walls let in natural light and air, while variations in the color of the bricks give the facade a sense of texture. Trees remain visible through the openings and above the roofline, keeping the building connected to its surroundings. Although the toilet building and timber office serve different purposes, both reflect Premthada’s interest in finding value in materials that might otherwise be overlooked. The reclaimed wood retains traces of its previous uses, while the elephant dung bricks turn a natural byproduct into a building material for an everyday public facility.
Visitors arriving at Matalay first encounter Goya Tower, built with the same elephant dung bricks used in the public toilets, before continuing toward the timber buildings by the sea. Together, the structures reflect Boonserm Premthada’s approach to materials, combining reclaimed elements and craftsmanship with new architectural uses.

Herzog heads to Hungary for first Israeli visit since Orbán's defeat

16:44:35 KST

President Isaac Herzog will travel to Budapest on Tuesday for a 12-hour diplomatic visit, becoming the first senior Israeli official to visit Hungary since the election defeat of longtime Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and the rise to power of his successor, Péter Magyar.
The Israeli government held a telephone vote Monday morning to approve the trip, which comes just ahead of Israel's upcoming elections and marks the first high-level diplomatic engagement between Jerusalem and Budapest since Hungary's historic political upheaval.
During the visit, Herzog will be received at Sándor Palace by Hungarian President András Baka. The two presidents are expected to discuss strengthening bilateral relations and expanding cooperation between their countries.
Herzog will then hold talks with Magyar, Hungary's new prime minister, focusing on advancing bilateral cooperation and maintaining ties between the two countries under Budapest's new leadership.
A central event of the visit will be Herzog's address to the international Voice of the People (VoP) conference. The gathering is part of a global initiative led by the Israeli president that brings together Jewish leaders and young people from Israel and the Diaspora to strengthen connections and encourage dialogue about the challenges facing Jewish communities worldwide.
Herzog is expected to conclude his brief visit with a meeting with leaders of Hungary's Jewish community.
The trip comes after a major political transformation in Hungary, where Magyar and his Tisza party defeated Orbán, ending the veteran prime minister's long rule. Orbán had been regarded as one of Israel's closest allies in Europe, regularly supporting Jerusalem in international forums.
Following Magyar's election victory, Herzog was quick to congratulate the incoming prime minister and expressed hope that the two countries would maintain their longstanding relationship. Magyar, for his part, said his government would pursue "pragmatic relations" with Israel.
The change in government has already brought significant adjustments to Hungarian foreign policy, including efforts to rebuild ties with the European Union and international institutions.
Among the most consequential changes was Magyar's decision to reverse Orbán's planned withdrawal from the International Criminal Court in The Hague. Orbán had initiated the withdrawal in response to the court's arrest warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new government subsequently halted the process, keeping Hungary within the ICC.
Against that backdrop, Herzog's meetings with Magyar and Baka will mark an important early diplomatic encounter between Israel and Hungary's new leadership, as the two countries seek to maintain cooperation despite Budapest's changing foreign policy.

Mystery European buyer signs $235M Israeli rocket deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:39:55 UTC
16:39:55 KST

- Elbit Systems won a $235 million contract to supply PULS launchers and EXTRA-MR guided rockets to an unnamed European customer.
- EXTRA-MR is designed to hit high-value targets at up to 80 km, and the deal includes additional launchers and logistics support.
Israel’s Elbit Systems has won a contract worth about $235 million to supply PULS rocket artillery launchers and EXTRA-MR precision-guided rockets to an unnamed European country, along with additional rocket artillery platforms and integrated logistics support, the company said.
Elbit did not identify the customer or say how many launchers and rockets the deal covers, and it gave no delivery schedule.
EXTRA-MR is a medium-range member of Elbit’s EXTRA family of guided rockets, designed to hit high-value targets at up to 80 km (50 miles), and the company says it can work with the command-and-control systems armies already use to find and assign targets.
PULS, short for Precise and Universal Launching System, is a truck-mounted launcher that carries two interchangeable pods, each loaded with a different munition, so the same vehicle can fire 122 mm and 160 mm Accular rockets out to about 35 to 40 km, full-size EXTRA rockets out to 150 km, or Predator Hawk missiles out to 300 km. The launcher can be fitted to a range of wheeled and tracked platforms, which lets armies put it on trucks they already operate.
The system has become one of the main European competitors to the U.S.-made HIMARS. The Netherlands ordered 20 PULS launchers in a $305 million deal, The Defence Blog reported, while Denmark received eight launchers under a 2023 contract and Germany placed a $57 million order in early 2025 for its EuroPULS version, developed with KNDS.
Greece became the latest major buyer in April 2026, when Elbit announced a $750 million contract covering launchers, rockets, loitering munitions and ten years of support for the Hellenic Armed Forces under a defense agreement between Israel and Greece. Outside NATO, Serbia ordered PULS launchers in 2024 in a deal worth about $335 million.
Elbit has kept European customers anonymous before, including in 2025, when it announced a $130 million contract to supply training rockets and precision-guided Accular, EXTRA and Predator Hawk munitions to an unnamed European PULS operator.
Israel’s ground forces have used PULS since 2020 under the name Lahav, mounted on a U.S.-made HEMTT heavy truck.

Twelve migrants drowned in two separate incidents off the Greek islands of Lesbos and Samos in the northeastern Aegean Sea on Monday, after their boats capsized as the coast guard chased them, authorities said.
Five men and one woman died after a speedboat carrying migrants from Turkey made a sudden maneuver and overturned roughly four nautical miles north of Samos, the Greek coast guard said.
Fourteen men survived, and a search-and-rescue operation was underway. Authorities arrested one of the survivors, an Iranian national, on suspicion of migrant smuggling.
Earlier, four men, one woman and an infant died when their boat collided with a Greek coast guard vessel and overturned off the area of Agrilia in Lesbos. Eight survivors were taken to hospital.
Authorities arrested a 37-year-old Turkish national who was among the eight survivors and identified him as the suspected smuggler and operator of the boat.
Zero tolerance for smugglers
The government vowed "zero tolerance" towards migrant smugglers, whom it blamed for the deaths.
On the incident off Lesbos, Greece's shipping minister Vassilis Kikilias said evidence so far indicated the speedboat struck the left side of a coast guard vessel with its bow, adding that the exact circumstances were under investigation.
"The tragedy that unfolded last night in the maritime area of Lesbos fills us with sorrow and rage. Six people lost their lives, including an infant, due to the criminal actions of modern-day traffickers," Kikilias wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
"Our position is non-negotiable: zero tolerance for smugglers, those ruthless criminals who, in their pursuit of wealth, do not hesitate to lead desperate people, families and innocent children to their very deaths," he stated.
Greece, for years a favored gateway to Europe for migrants and refugees from the Middle East, Africa and Asia, was at the front line of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-2016 and nearly 1 million people landed on its islands, mainly from Turkey.
It has since toughened its stance and has been accused by human rights groups of forcibly returning migrants and asylum-seekers on its sea and land borders, a practice it denies, saying its coast guard acts with full respect for human lives and rights.

U.S. soldiers fly Ukrainian-designed Stork drone in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:26:59 UTC
16:26:59 KST

- A U.S. Army soldier assembled a U&C UAS Stork drone during Combined Resolve 27-01 at Hohenfels, Germany, on Oct. 16, 2026.
- U&C UAS, founded by DeViRo co-owners, signed a contract in May 2026 to supply ISR drones to U.S. Army units in Europe.
A U.S. Army soldier has been spotted assembling a Stork reconnaissance drone, built by Czech-Ukrainian company U&C UAS, during a major training exercise in Germany, showing the battle-tested design in American hands.
The U.S. Army released the image from Combined Resolve 27-01 at the Hohenfels Training Area, part of the Joint Multinational Readiness Center in Bavaria. It shows a soldier from the 1st Battalion, 4th Infantry Regiment preparing the drone on Oct. 16, 2026. The battalion is based at Hohenfels and usually plays the opposing force for units training there, and the 7th Army Training Command runs the center to prepare formations for large-scale combat.
The Stork family traces back to the Leleka, or “Stork” in Ukrainian, reconnaissance drones made by Ukrainian manufacturer DeViRo and used widely by Ukraine’s military since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Co-owners of DeViRo founded U&C UAS in the Czech Republic in July 2022 to expand production, and the company now builds Stork drones and Mace strike drones at its plant in Kolín, east of Prague.
The company’s main reconnaissance model, the Stork LR, is a fixed-wing electric drone with a 3.4 m (11 ft) wingspan and a maximum takeoff weight of 14 kg (31 pounds). It launches from a pneumatic catapult, lands on its belly, can stay airborne for up to five hours and sends live video over encrypted links up to 135 km (84 miles), using another Stork as a relay when needed. U&C UAS says it carries satellite navigation hardened against jamming and is designed for scouting, mapping and spotting targets for artillery.
The appearance at Hohenfels follows a U.S. Army purchase. In May 2026, U&C UAS announced a contract to supply ISR drones to U.S. Army units in Europe for scouting and base protection, delivered in partnership with Illinois-based ATP Gov, after the systems were evaluated in exercises that included electronic warfare and degraded communications.
The Stork is one of several Ukrainian-designed drones the U.S. Army has bought or tested this year. In September, the U.S. Army awarded Skyeton Inc., the American arm of Ukrainian drone maker Skyeton, a $10.6 million contract for Raybird long-endurance reconnaissance drones, which have flown more than 350,000 combat hours in Ukraine. During the Bayonet Quest 26 exercise in Michigan, which ended Oct. 6, soldiers from the 7th Infantry Division used Ukraine’s MV7 uncrewed surface vessels as floating launch pads for aerial drones.
U&C UAS says it has delivered more than 7,500 drone systems and can build about 500 drones a month across two production sites, and that its drones are used by most Ukrainian brigades. It also signed a deal earlier this year to supply drones to India, with plans for technology transfer and joint production.
Russia’s defense ministry listed the Kolín company in April 2026 among European firms it described as potential targets because of their drone production for Ukraine.

‘We lost control’: France riots leave over 2,500 arrested as Macron rejects minister's resignation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:24:04 UTC
16:24:04 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron rejected the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Monday after another night of rioting and looting in Paris, as the number of arrests across France climbed past 2,500 and authorities acknowledged serious failures in their preparations for the unrest.
The Élysée Palace said Macron had refused Nuñez's offer to step down because the minister needed to remain in office to maintain continuity of command within the police and security forces. The decision followed mounting pressure from both the left and right over the authorities' handling of widespread violence that erupted on the sidelines of mass demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services.
Police said approximately 350 people had been arrested Sunday evening and overnight, some on suspicion of looting and others for additional offenses. The latest detentions brought the total since the weekend to more than 2,500. According to official figures, 997 security personnel were injured during the unrest, seven of them seriously, along with numerous protesters and rioters.
In its statement Monday morning, the Élysée acknowledged what Macron described as failures of preparation and intelligence ahead of the violence. The president instructed Nuñez to develop new approaches as quickly as possible to confront looters and violent rioters.
Nuñez also admitted shortcomings in the security response, saying that although the government had deployed 60,000 police officers to the streets, security forces had been overwhelmed in certain areas.
"There was an imbalance in some areas, and we lost control of them," Nuñez said when asked whether authorities had correctly anticipated the scale of the disturbances.
"I acknowledge my share of responsibility, but we must not forget that there were looters, vandals and far-left activists," he added. Nuñez was expected to visit the southern city of Marseille later Monday, where widespread destruction and looting also occurred over the weekend.
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said the unrest had exposed weaknesses in the security services' ability to respond to violent far-left groups. He argued that French security forces were effective in combating terrorism and organized crime but less capable of handling threats posed by radical left-wing demonstrators.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was expected to convene an interministerial crisis task force Monday morning, focusing on three areas: the economic and commercial consequences of the violence, insurance claims and criminal proceedings against those responsible.
Lecornu told French media that most of those arrested in Paris over the weekend were not individuals with extensive previous records known to police. "We will ensure that these acts receive the criminal response their seriousness warrants," he said.
The association representing French mayors also called on residents to gather outside their local town halls Monday afternoon to condemn what it described as serious attacks on democratic institutions.
‘Those who destroyed must pay’
Macron's decision to keep Nuñez in office came hours after the French president addressed the nation Sunday evening, following a weekend in which masked rioters attacked police officers and passersby, set government buildings ablaze and looted hundreds of businesses.
In his televised speech, Macron accused violent groups of attempting to undermine the French Republic but urged the public to distinguish between the hundreds of thousands of people who had taken to the streets to voice legitimate grievances and those responsible for the destruction.
He specifically condemned what he called unrestrained violence by radical far-left groups joined by numerous criminals.
"We all feel anger and shame tonight," Macron said, referring to the images of destruction across the country. "Those who destroyed must pay, and those who looted must compensate."
The president also announced that regional prefects would receive powers to prohibit certain gatherings when necessary to maintain public order. The measure stopped short of a nationwide state of emergency, despite growing criticism that the government had failed to respond forcefully enough to the violence.
The speech came as French media reported renewed looting in Paris. Broadcaster BFMTV aired footage Sunday evening showing several people smashing the storefront of a Petite Mendigote shop before entering and ransacking the premises.
According to Le Parisien, young men with uncovered faces were filmed walking through the streets carrying sweaters apparently taken from stores. Clashes continued shortly before Macron's address, with police using tear gas and stun grenades along Boulevard Voltaire and near Place de la République.
A Le Parisien reporter described groups of young people gathering in the area, including one person who could be heard shouting, "Come on, guys, let's loot something."
As the violence spread, the mayor of central Paris urged shop owners to close their businesses to protect themselves from further vandalism and arson, particularly around the Les Halles shopping district.
In Lyon, approximately 50 young people, many wearing masks, attempted to smash the window of a Lacoste store, but police intervened before they could enter and dispersed the group using tear gas.
A historic town hall destroyed, hundreds of businesses damaged
The latest disturbances followed Saturday's nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs, worsening public services and higher fuel prices, which drew hundreds of thousands of people into the streets.
Although the demonstrations began as protests over economic conditions and education, violence erupted in several cities as masked groups clashed with security forces, vandalized public buildings and looted stores.
Among the most dramatic incidents was the destruction of the historic city hall in Limoges, central France, where masked rioters set fire to the 19th-century building.
The ornate structure, inaugurated in 1883 and having survived both world wars, was devastated by the blaze. Much of its roof collapsed, and its clock tower came crashing down in footage widely circulated on social media. Authorities said the building had been largely destroyed.
In Marseille, Lille, Angers and Bordeaux, rioters attacked municipal buildings and regional government offices, causing extensive damage. In Lyon, the city's tourist office was set ablaze, with footage showing one of the rioters waving a Palestinian flag.
The French Chamber of Commerce estimated that at least 1,500 businesses had been affected by the unrest, with damage running into hundreds of millions of euros.
The weekend's violence also intensified scrutiny of the government's handling of a broader protest movement that began several weeks earlier among high school students in poorer suburbs north of Paris. Those demonstrations, sparked by teacher shortages and deteriorating conditions in schools, had already led to repeated confrontations with police and inspired related protests elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium.
Students, labor unions and members of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 in opposition to Macron's economic policies, joined Saturday's nationwide mobilization.
Macron, whose second and final presidential term ends in May 2027, had largely responded to the demonstrations in recent weeks with statements acknowledging protesters' frustrations while condemning violence. Critics accused his administration of failing to take sufficient preventive action as the disturbances escalated.
Far-left groups, meanwhile, accused police of using excessive force against demonstrators, adding to the pressure on the government from both sides of the political spectrum.
Le Pen attacks Macron: ‘A government without direction’
The president's handling of the crisis drew fierce criticism from opposition politicians, including far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, who accused his administration of losing its authority.
Le Pen said Macron's government was exhausted, disoriented and apparently incapable of doing anything beyond acknowledging its own inability to govern effectively. She accused the administration of condemning events without being able to prevent, control or manage them.
Jordan Bardella, president of Le Pen's National Rally party, dismissed Macron's televised address as a "pathetic speech."
"This cowardly and directionless government has nothing left to say to the French people and nothing left to offer them," Bardella said.
The political confrontation comes as France prepares for its next presidential election in 2027, in which Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking another consecutive term.
The unrest has also drawn attention from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly attributed France's social tensions to immigration and Islam.
About two weeks earlier, amid protests over education and public services, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the demonstrations were not really about schools but reflected what he described as mass immigration spiraling out of control. He claimed that Islam was seeking to take over a country that had once been great.
Following the weekend violence, Trump issued another statement, declaring, "France is burning!" He blamed immigration for the country's troubles and urged French authorities to close their borders and restore control before it was too late.
Macron's government now faces the challenge of restoring order while responding to the economic and social grievances that brought hundreds of thousands of demonstrators onto the streets. With the opposition intensifying its attacks and the scale of the destruction still being assessed, the president's refusal to accept Nuñez's resignation has left the interior minister responsible for repairing a security response that both men acknowledge failed.

The department also noted that operators had installed clear signages and facilities to help people queue in an orderly manner as well as deployed service ambassadors and operational staff at key locations to assist travellers.
The Immigration Department recorded more than 1.32 million crossings – more than 690,000 departures and nearly 630,000 arrivals – through all checkpoints on Sunday, with departures by Hong Kong residents exceeding 530,000. 
Of the inbound arrivals, mainland visitors numbered over 98,000.
Huanggang port recorded about 152,000 arrivals and departures – the highest since the crossing opened — with Hong Kong residents accounting for more than 66,000. 
The busiest crossing remained Lo Wu with nearly 260,000, followed by Lok Ma Chau Spur Line with more than 200,000.

The El Niño backdrop that could spell trouble off Australia's coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:17:54 UTC
16:17:54 KST

In Brief
- A new study is helping experts better understand how weather systems impact the Great Barrier Reef.
- Experts say the active El Niño is raising the risk of coral bleaching events this summer.
A combination of atmospheric conditions and weather patterns is increasing the risk of coral bleaching in the Great Barrier Reef, adding to the challenges of a summer that already has experts concerned.
A new study has investigated the relationship between atmospheric patterns and weather systems on a phenomenon known as the doldrums, which could spell danger for the UNESCO World Heritage site.
Doldrums are characterised as areas of calm winds, with reduced cloud cover and dry, descending air. They've been linked to coral bleaching events, as when doldrums stay in a particular location for longer, natural cooling systems are suppressed, which keeps ocean temperatures higher.
Dr Yi Huang, a chief investigator with the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century, says "all the bad things all happen at once" when it comes to weather systems so it's important for researchers to understand how each element interacts.
"A lot of research has looked at the local weather and how the local weather such as wind and local sunshine is related to the ocean temperature," she said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"This research is really looking at how the weather systems developed elsewhere could link to these coral bleaching conditions."
The doldrums are not caused by the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and can happen at any time.
But a prolonged spell could lead to a marine heatwave.
While there are several potential triggers for corals to bleach, heat stress is the main one. Temperatures of the relatively shallow waters where coral grows are heavily influenced by the surrounding weather patterns.
Dr Neal Cantin is a senior research scientist from the Australian Institute of Marine Science. He says there are already two different processes happening at the same time to raise the threat of a coral bleaching event.
The first is ongoing global warming, which is increasing the maximum temperatures experienced across the reef each summer, although the intensity varies season to season based on local weather.
"What we're starting to see in the recent decade is that it doesn't necessarily require an El Niño to drive coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef," he said.
In 2022, there was a mass bleaching event during a La Niña phase, where there is generally increased rainfall.
Cantin said it was "a clear sign that ocean warming is pushing reefs up to their upper thermal limit".
On top of human-induced climate change, El Niño periods tend to impact monsoon activity. Rainfall and winds contribute to increasing cloud cover and mixing warmer water at the surface with cooler temperatures below, which are beneficial for keeping temperatures more stable for coral.
Cantin says these changes can be the difference between a period of normal summer heat and an anomaly that will cause corals to bleach.
In 1998, 2016, and 2024, mass bleaching events occured at the Great Barrier Reef during El Niño periods.
"The likelihood of bleaching during an El Niño is a lot higher, and this is setting up to be the biggest El Niño that's ever been recorded," he said.
"We're preparing to coordinate to respond to this event with both science and monitoring, so that we can fully understand how these systems and how climate change are continuing to impact the Great Barrier Reef."

Civil society groups call for law to protect native-language rights in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:16:41 UTC
16:16:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Civil society groups on Monday urged the government to introduce an official languages law to protect people’s right to education in their native languages.
CNA reported that the call followed a June report by the Control Yuan, which found that Mandarin continues to dominate government offices, schools, and examinations. The Control Yuan urged authorities to review language policies and address unequal treatment of Taiwan’s languages.
Representatives of the Taiwan Official Languages Conference and the Su Beng Education Foundation held a press conference outside the Cabinet offices. Joined by physician Wu Hsin-tai (吳欣岱), they later submitted a petition calling for legal reforms and measures to address past language discrimination.
The petition said decades of policies promoting Mandarin had contributed to the decline of other languages and restricted people’s language rights. The groups called for an official languages law to give native languages stronger protection in education, government, and public services.
DPP Legislator Chang Ya-lin (張雅琳) said Taiwan must acknowledge its history of suppressing native languages under authoritarian rule. She said the government should help restore their use in everyday life, per UDN.
The groups proposed making native languages the main languages of instruction in schools. They also called for changes to education policies that give Mandarin priority over other languages.
Beyond education, the groups urged the government to promote Taiwanese Hokkien, Hakka, and Indigenous languages in diplomacy and overseas education. Mandarin, they said, should no longer be treated as the only language representing Taiwan internationally, per Liberty Times.
The groups also proposed giving native languages greater priority in government offices and courts. They said people should be able to use their preferred languages when accessing public services and the justice system, per Rti.
Taiwan passed the National Languages Development Act in 2018 to preserve and promote its national languages. The law supports language education and equal access to public services but does not establish official languages.
The Control Yuan’s June investigation also found continuing inequalities in language education. Mandarin receives far more classroom time than other national languages, which are generally taught for only one period a week.

====================================================================================================

Likud open to Liberman joining coalition, Education Minister Kisch tells ‘Post’ - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:13:40 UTC
16:13:40 KST

Likud could seek to bring opposition parties into a Netanyahu-led government, with Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman a possible partner, Education Minister Yoav Kisch told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday, while categorically ruling out a coalition with Democrats leader Yair Golan.
“Maybe he can join us,” Kisch said. “But he needs to understand that this government is going to continue to lead Israel’s agenda with force and strength, and make sure that nobody threatens us.”
Kisch said a potential partner would have to support controlling Israel’s borders, preventing threats from developing, and using military force when necessary.
“So if he will change and understand that he goes with the right to a really clear path of controlling our borders, making sure that nobody threatens us, and using force when needed, then he could be a partner in that sense as well.”
Kisch said Likud would pursue a broader coalition even if its existing partners secured enough seats to govern independently, arguing that opposition parties’ refusal to serve under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had deepened Israel’s divisions.
“I think that if we, as a right-wing government, with the current parties of the coalition, have 61, we’ll do all we can to enlarge this coalition, to join other parties from the other side,” he said.
“I think boycotting Netanyahu and Likud did huge damage to the State of Israel. I think this should stop now.”
Asked about other opposition parties that could join a Likud-led government if its current partners fell short of a majority, Kisch drew an immediate red line around Golan.
“I think the one who’s not relevant is Golan, by no chance.”
He was more open to Liberman, although he made clear that joining would require agreement with the government’s security approach.
Kisch details Likud's red lines for forming possible coalition
For Kisch, however, broadening the next government would still require agreement on substantive red lines. He listed opposition to a Palestinian state, maintaining security zones, and strengthening Jewish education among the principles Likud would insist on.
“These are for sure the red lines we’re not going to cross.”
Although Kisch called broadly for parties across the political divide to join, he did not specifically name Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot or B’Yachad leader Naftali Bennett as a prospective coalition partner.
Instead, he presented an Eisenkot-led government as the principal alternative to Netanyahu, arguing that it would depend on Golan and the Arab parties.
“It’s a simple issue of numbers,” he said.
Kisch’s appeal for a broader coalition also raised the question of whether parties demanding an equal military draft could govern alongside the haredi parties.
He argued that increasing haredi enlistment required cooperation with the community, alongside incentives and penalties, rather than an approach centered on imprisonment.
“Whoever is really learning in the yeshiva will learn, and the rest must join the army,” he said, and maintained that such an arrangement could bring tens of thousands of recruits into military service.
“You need to have carrots and sticks, but you need to work together in order to get them into the army.”
Kisch's plans to improve education in next government
On his own political future, Kisch said he wanted to remain education minister in the next government and pursue a NIS 15 billion education plan, including reducing class sizes to 20 pupils and moving to a five-day school week.
He said the war had constrained investment in education as resources went toward military needs, while the ministry had concentrated on maintaining schooling for displaced children and communities under fire.
“Because of the war, we couldn’t get new investments in the education system because most of the money went to the army and the war effort,” he said. “Now I think we need to change it.”
Kisch also described plans to expand personalized learning through artificial intelligence, including English instruction for seventh- and eighth-grade pupils.
Under that model, he said, students would practice individually with AI using phones and headphones while teachers remained in the classroom to help pupils and oversee their learning.
“You cannot replace the teacher, because the kid needs to learn how to behave in society and be responsible for what he’s doing,” he said.
On haredi education, Kisch rejected proposals to withhold all public funding from schools that do not teach a full core curriculum. He argued that funding tied to the extent of core studies offered an incentive to expand those subjects, while cutting support entirely could have the opposite effect.
“What’s going to happen in that case is that many kids who are studying today at 50% or 75% will drop to nothing,” he said.
Kisch opposes Supreme Court President-appointed October 7 inquiry
Echoing Likud’s stance, Kisch also opposed an October 7 inquiry whose members would be selected by Supreme Court President Isaac Amit, arguing that it would not command public confidence across the political divide.
He instead advocated an inquiry established jointly by the coalition and opposition, citing the US investigation into the September 11 attacks as a model.
“We have to investigate,” he said. “But it has to be an investigation that most of the people will accept.”
While the national investigation remains politically contested, Kisch said his own ministry had already conducted an internal review of its response to the war, identifying shortcomings in its ability to track displaced students and coordinate with local authorities.
The review, conducted approximately a year after the outbreak of the war, examined what the ministry could have handled differently as tens of thousands of children were evacuated from their homes.
"One thing is, for example, that the database was an issue in the beginning," Kisch acknowledged.
As families were relocated to hotels and temporary accommodation across the country, the ministry struggled to establish where individual students were staying, which communities they had come from, and how to maintain continuity in their education.
"The kids moved and we had to figure out who is where and where is he staying, where is he from," he explained.
Kisch said building a system capable of tracking displaced students required close cooperation with local authorities, an effort that took time to organize.
The ministry also confronted situations it had not previously been equipped to handle, including providing support to children who had lost parents or siblings in the attacks.
According to Kisch, the ministry established a support mechanism modeled on the military's casualty and bereavement assistance systems.
"For us, it was the first time to deal with real terror casualties in this sense," he said, describing the challenge of supporting bereaved families and particularly their children.
Kisch cited the rapid establishment of schools and kindergartens for evacuees in Eilat, where the population swelled following October 7, as one of his ministry's achievements during the war.
Additional investments necessary to improve education
Nevertheless, he acknowledged that the conflict had prevented the government from making the additional investments he believed were necessary to improve education.
The consequences of prolonged disruption to schooling have become a pressing concern following the publication of Israel's 2025 PISA results, which showed the country's lowest recorded scores in reading, mathematics, and science.
The results also showed a deterioration in Israel's international rankings compared with the previous assessment in 2022.
Kisch acknowledged that the findings were poor but argued that the decline should be understood in the context of a broader international deterioration in academic performance.
"The last PISA results were very bad for Israel," he said, but noted that Israel was not alone, and pointed to falling scores in other European countries.
He suggested that the effects of the coronavirus pandemic could also have contributed to the decline, although he emphasized that this was his own assessment.
Kisch maintained that Israel's relative standing had changed little compared with 2018 - where Israel also ranked below the developed world average - despite the fall in absolute scores.
Asked what his ministry intended to do to reverse the decline, he pointed to a new NIS 15 billion program launched in 2025-2026 to strengthen mathematics, science, and English education, alongside additional investment in language instruction.
He also outlined plans to expand the use of artificial intelligence in classrooms, including personalized English instruction for seventh- and eighth-grade students nationwide.
Under the model he described, students would use phones and headphones to interact individually with AI systems while teachers supervised the classroom and provided additional assistance.
Kisch insisted that the technology was not intended to eliminate the role of human teachers but rather to shift their responsibilities toward mentorship, personal guidance, and identifying students' individual difficulties.
"The teacher is in the classroom, but the kid is studying with his phone and he's with headphones and he's speaking and he's one on one with the AI," he explained.
Kisch discusses October 12 field trip explosion
The question of whether the education system has learned sufficient lessons from the war took on renewed urgency following the devastating October 12 explosion of Hezbollah ordnance during a school trip in northern Israel.
The blast killed 14-year-old Elazar Yair Wilensky and wounded more than 20 others, prompting questions over why students had been permitted to hike in an area where unexploded munitions remained a danger.
The Education Ministry has maintained that the planned route had been approved and did not pass through an area closed by Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF), despite the organization's warnings about the surrounding area.
In the interview, Kisch defended the ministry's approval procedures, explaining that schools must submit their proposed routes to a designated center responsible for checking whether they pass through restricted areas.
He said the approved route followed the Israel Trail, which had remained open at the time, while a parallel route had been closed.
However, Kisch acknowledged that investigators had yet to establish which route the students actually followed.
“I don't know exactly which route they took, actually. This is still under investigation," he said.
He confirmed that the rules had since changed, with new restrictions preventing school trips along the previously permitted section of the Israel Trail.
Asked whether ministry officials would face consequences if the investigation identified failures in the approval process, Kisch stopped short of committing to specific disciplinary measures.
"Whatever the consequences are will depend on what the findings will be," he said.
Kisch described visiting wounded students in hospital, meeting members of the school community, and attending the shiva following Wilensky's death.
He said the ministry was examining its own planning and approval procedures while police investigated what happened during the trip.
"We are fully investigating both the planning, which is what we did in the ministry, and what actually is going on, which the police are checking," he said.
The findings, he added, would determine what further lessons needed to be implemented.

Ukraine turns its Bars strike drone into a Shahed hunter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
07:11:29 UTC
16:11:29 KST

- Video shows a ground-launched interceptor version of Ukraine’s Bars jet drone destroying a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered attack drone.
- Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in September, and Ukraine has fielded several new interceptors against them.
Video published online shows Ukraine using an interceptor version of its Bars jet-powered drone to destroy a Russian Geran-5, the first footage of the Ukrainian missile-drone being used against Russia’s own jet-powered attack drones.
The clip, shared by the Ukrainian military, shows the interceptor launched from a ground launcher before it strikes the Geran-5.
The interceptor is based on the Bars strike drone, a small turbojet-powered weapon that Ukraine has used for long-range attacks on Russian targets, including oil refineries. Upgraded strike versions of Bars can reportedly fly at up to 700 km/h (435 mph) and travel up to 1,000 km (620 miles), carrying warheads of 22, 60 or 105 kg (49, 132 or 231 pounds).
The Geran-5 is a Russian jet-powered strike drone that looks and flies more like a small cruise missile than the propeller-driven Shahed-type drones Russia launches in large numbers. It can fly at up to about 600 km/h (370 mph), and at higher altitudes than older models, which makes it hard to catch for the small quadcopter interceptors Ukraine relies on against slower Shaheds.
Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in September alone, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that month that Ukrainian forces were shooting down only 57% of them.
Ukrainian manufacturers have rushed several faster interceptors into service in response. Wild Hornets’ Sting S, SkyFall’s P1-SUN JetKiller and a jet-powered interceptor supplied by the Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation have all been shown destroying Geran-5s since late September, and former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on Oct. 12 that a new interceptor developed by his team had downed two Geran-5s heading toward Kyiv.
Many of those interceptors were hit by a speed cap that SpaceX placed on Starshield satellite terminals used by Ukrainian forces overnight on Oct. 13-14, which cut connections on drones moving faster than about 160 km/h. A larger, faster jet interceptor such as Bars, launched from the ground against fast targets, could give Ukraine another option for reaching Geran-5s before they reach cities.
In July 2026, Germany and Ukraine signed an agreement on joint production of Bars drones.

Arab voter turnout could make or break Netanyahu in Israeli election

Arab voter turnout could make or break Netanyahu in Israeli election
- Arab leaders are urging high turnout to help defeat Benjamin Netanyahu and support an anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
- Polls show Eisenkot ahead but short of a majority, so Arab support could decide whether a new government forms or deadlock continues.
- Mansour Abbas is seeking influence through partnership with Jewish parties, while Arab voters are angry about demonisation, crime, and far-right policies.
AI generated
NAZARETH, Israel – Israel’s Palestinian leaders are urging people in the minority Arab community to vote in big numbers in next week’s election as they seek to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and topple the most right-wing government in the country’s history.
High turnout by the 21% Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by citizenship, could nudge Israel’s complex coalition arithmetic in favour of an anti-Netanyahu bloc led by a former military chief, Gadi Eisenkot.
“We can ensure the formation of a new government of change,” Mansour Abbas, an Islamist dentist-turned-politician who heads the United Arab List party, told Reuters in his office in Nazareth, Israel’s most populous Arab city.
Polls show Eisenkot short of majority without Arab support
Abbas and other Arab leaders face one big obstacle to their goal of playing a role in any future administration without Netanyahu.
Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties that most Palestinian Israelis will vote for, citing a lack of shared values.
But Abbas thinks there will be room for manoeuvre, perhaps after the vote, largely thanks to the cold, hard realities of electoral maths.
Opinion polls suggest Eisenkot’s patchwork bloc of centrist, right- and left-wing parties will get the most votes, but fall short of a majority, and will need Arab support, either as coalition partners or from outside, to prop up a minority government.
“We want to replace the right-wing government... to end the wars and these policies, to stop the expansion of settlements and to address the failure to stop settler attacks,” Abbas said.
“We also want a government that brings shared security and peace for Palestinians and Israelis.”
For now, Eisenkot is sticking to his position. “I will not align myself with any Arab party,” Eisenkot said in a podcast in October, citing among other issues their refusal to label Hamas a terrorist organisation.
If any bloc fails to form a workable government, that could lead to a period of political deadlock, then fresh elections in 2027, with Netanyahu left in charge in the meantime.
But Netanyahu, for one, appears to be taking the threat of some sort of Eisenkot-Arab alliance seriously, or at least sees it as an opportunity to rile up his base. His campaign has used doctored images and AI-generated videos to depict his rivals embracing Arab leaders.
One fake video, released over the summer, shows Eisenkot running through a meadow into the outstretched arms of Abbas.
Abbas’ own career shows such alliances can be made. In 2021 he became the first Arab Muslim to join an Israeli coalition as a minister, in a government led by Naftali Bennett, now a right-wing member of Eisenkot’s bloc.
That government collapsed after 18 months, partly over disagreements between the two men on the occupied West Bank.
This time round, Abbas said he could paper over those differences. To win over Jewish parties, he has taken the unprecedented step of giving the number two spot on his slate to a Jewish former police official, Yoav Segalovitz.
“It sends a message of partnership with the Jewish community and with Jewish citizens,” Abbas said.
Arabs frustrated with demonisation by Israel right, crime
Israel’s election will be the first since the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack, and is being viewed as a referendum on the leadership of Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader.
Polls show Eisenkot’s bloc would win 52 of the Knesset’s 120 seats if elections were held today. Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist bloc would win 50 seats.
Abbas’ party is projected to win five seats, with a further eight going to the Joint List, a coalition of three Arab parties.
Ahead of the vote, Bezalel Smotrich, Netanyahu’s far-right finance minister, proposed a plan to “Judaize” areas around Nazareth in the north and in southern Israel where most Arabs live, describing it as similar to settler expansionism in the West Bank.
Party organisers in Nazareth are hoping to capitalize on Arab anger with Netanyahu, Smotrich and far-right police minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, as well as frustration with rising crime in their communities.
Last week, canvassers with Abbas’ party handed out flyers near Nazareth’s massive Church of the Annunciation.
“There is a greater need this time than ever before to go out and vote in large numbers,” said one of the people they approached, 74-year-old Gassan Bsoul. “The danger is greater than in the past,” he added.
Arab turnout expected to be high
Israeli pollsters expect Arab voter turnout to be higher than in previous rounds of elections in 2022 and 2020. The Stat-Net Research Institute, based in an Arab Druze town near Haifa, projects turnout of 63%, compared with 56% in 2022.
While Abbas has tried to position his party to potentially join government, leaders of the Joint List have said they could wield just as much influence by staying in opposition.
Ahmad Tibi, a Joint List leader, said his group was ready to form “a preventive block to support (a government) from the outside”.
He said the Joint List would join an Eisenkot-led government in voting “to establish an official commission of inquiry into Oct 7”, a stated priority of the former military chief and his partners.
“We are placing as our top priority getting rid of the extreme right-wing government of Netanyahu, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir,” Tibi said. REUTERS
