Ghost Sharks to be armed with aerial drones and advanced sea mines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:17:06 UTC
15:17:06 KST

Australia's fleet of Ghost Sharks will carry armed aerial drones and sea mines
In short:
Australia's Ghost Shark submarines will carry advanced sea mines and launch armed aerial drones, according to newly declassified details.
While it was previously known the Ghost Sharks were armed, until now it has not been clear exactly how they could strike potential adversaries.
What's next?
The sea mine and drone capabilities are being offered to the UK and US under AUKUS technology-sharing arrangements.
Australia's fleet of lethal Ghost Shark underwater drones will be armed with explosive aerial drones and advanced sea mines.
Dozens of Ghost Sharks are being delivered to the Royal Australian Navy over the next few years under a $1.7 billion contract signed last year.
While it was previously known to carry lethal capabilities, until today the specifics of exactly what sort of payload it could carry were heavily classified.
Defence today revealed three of the autonomous submarines' key capabilities.
One is an ability to launch swarms of Anduril Altius aerial drones which can be used for reconnaissance or carry four kilograms of explosives to target enemy vessels.
It can also carry up to 12 sea mines at a time, which Defence says can be used to quickly close access to critical waterways.
And it can also carry special supply caches, essentially dropping supplies for special forces units in hard-to-reach locations.
Contracts for the supply of Ghost Shark drones were only signed last September, and while the total number is not being revealed, "dozens and dozens" are expected to be delivered to the navy.
The first was delivered in January this year, and Ghost Sharks are in service this month at joint Maritime Big Play exercises with the United States and United Kingdom off Southern California.
Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said the Ghost Sharks carried a different threat to potential adversaries.
"Those Ghost Sharks now have teeth,"
he said.
"Teeth with the ability to deny areas through them through mining. Teeth with the ability to strike targets thousands of nautical miles away from Australia."
Fleets of uncrewed subs
The Ghost Shark is described as a "force multiplier", designed to operate alongside crewed submarines and take on dangerous, difficult or mundane workloads.
It is built with a modular design, meaning it can be fitted out with different capabilities for different missions, including carrying torpedoes, reconnaissance equipment and personnel.
David Goodrich from Anduril Australia said it was designed to free up naval personnel from the worst tasks.
"Ghost Shark will do the dull, dirty and dangerous missions previously tasked to our sailors, leaving them to do the high-value missions and jobs,"
he said.
He said mine laying was a clear example.
"Ghost Shark will autonomously, accurately and securely deploy naval mines at significantly lower cost and risk than using a surface ship or crewed asset," he said.
The new Ghost Shark capabilities are being offered to the US and UK under AUKUS Pillar Two technology sharing arrangements designed to be interoperable with whatever autonomous systems they choose to use.
Questions over global appetite
The Ghost Shark and its aerial counterpart, the uncrewed Ghost Bat, are two of Australia's most significant defence innovations in recent years.
Both carry significant hopes for export, with countries such as Germany actively exploring options like the Ghost Bat.
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius visited Australia in March, addressing the National Press Club.
He later said Germany was formally investigating the possibility.
But news outlet Politico recently reported that Germany had dropped plans to directly acquire the Ghost Bat, and would instead consider it among other European-developed alternatives.
Mr Conroy today sought to downplay the German shift.
"My understanding is the German government has adopted a slightly different procurement strategy where they intend to run an open competition," he said.
The Ghost Shark is one of a number of similar uncrewed submarines in development or production around the world, including the United States Navy's Orca.
Mr Conroy said the US and UK would get the chance to see the Ghost Shark at upcoming exercises, and he "hasn't given up hope" they would take an interest.
But he said payloads were the export focus under AUKUS Pillar Two.
"The decision around marquee projects was to invest in common payloads and sensors," he said.
"We all have a range of our own platforms to deliver them."

China’s economy grows 4.5 percent, beating expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:13:40 UTC
15:13:40 KST

A worker stocks up plush toys for sale at a souvenir store during the China Open tennis championships in Beijing, Sept. 30, 2026. (AP File Photo)
China's economy grew slightly more than expected in the third quarter, but Oct. 19's figures still came in at the lower end of the government's full-year target, as the global energy shock and weak domestic demand counter surging exports.
The world's second-largest economy has charted a diverging path in recent years, with an AI-fuelled export boom masking the impact of a persistent real estate crisis and gloomy consumer sentiment.
Gross domestic product expanded 4.5 percent in July-September, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.
The reading was an improvement on the previous quarter's 4.3 percent expansion and just ahead of the 4.4 percent predicted in an AFP poll of economists.
Beijing is hoping for annual growth this year of 4.5-5 percent, its lowest goal in decades.
"Exports seem to be the only outperformer," Guo Shan of Hutong Research told AFP ahead of the data release.
She said China risked missing its official target for the year, spurring a recent roll-out of mortgage subsidies for certain home purchases and support for infrastructure investment.
Beijing "will need to work faster to deploy the funds so as to hit the growth target," she added.
While consumer activity has been a drag this year, separate data on Oct. 19 showed retail rose 1.1 percent last month, the fastest pace since March.
The Chinese economy is also under pressure from the high cost of energy caused by the Iran war, which has stymied shipping from the oil-rich Gulf.
China is the world's largest importer of crude.
Higher energy prices and "protracted uncertainty and structural headwinds" led the International Monetary Fund to last week slightly downgrade its projection for China's annual growth this year to 4.5 percent.
IMF officials gathering in Bangkok for its meetings with the World Bank described Beijing's recent support measures as "limited."
Economists say China's economy must shift towards a more sustainable growth model powered more by domestic consumption than traditional drivers like construction, property development and exports.
That long-awaited "rebalancing" of the Chinese economy has yet to materialize, IMF Asia and Pacific department director Krishna Srinivasan said.
Exports — for decades the engine of China's economy — remain a bright spot.
Figures released last week showed a surge in overseas shipments put the country on course for another record trade surplus that would top last year's $1.2 trillion.
That export boom has been underpinned in large part by insatiable global demand for AI-related products including computers, semiconductors and data center equipment.
But elsewhere, China's soaring surpluses are stoking tensions with key trading partners, including the European Union and the United States.
Talks this month between EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao ended with an agreement to limit exports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to Europe.
Many critics contend that Beijing's extensive subsidies doled out in recent years to domestic industries have given them an unfair advantage in foreign markets.
Domestic demand woes have also exacerbated the problem, as manufacturers increasingly look overseas for new growth.

UN survey shows rising fears of major war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:13:17 UTC
15:13:17 KST

Some 76 percent of respondents in a United Nations survey expected the effects of a large-scale war to be felt by a significant share of humanity within seven years.
Thirty-six percent expected those effects within 12 months. Compared with the first survey in 2024, large-scale war climbed 16 places in the ranking of how soon risks were expected to materialize — the biggest upward shift recorded.
The 2026 Global Risk Report, released on Sept. 15, draws on about 1,300 responses collected between Feb. 19 and April 24. Participants from government, business, civil society, academia and international organizations assessed 28 global risks.
“The rankings in this report measure perceptions of risk,” the report said.
Geopolitical tensions, disinformation and the breakdown of the rule of law were among the most interconnected threats.
The strongest link identified was between geopolitical tensions and large-scale war.
Resource shortages, economic fragmentation, disinformation and weakening international institutions were seen as factors that could increase geopolitical tensions.
Respondents still ranked failure to address climate change as the most important risk overall. Pandemics and biological threats received lower importance ratings than in 2024, while a global financial crisis and supply chain breakdowns featured among near-term economic concerns.
Priorities varied by region. War and geopolitical tensions featured prominently among respondents in Europe and North America, while financial instability and artificial intelligence risks stood out in East and Southeast Asia. Inequality, disinformation and climate change were among the main concerns in Latin America and the Caribbean.
International institutions were viewed as stronger at detecting risks and issuing warnings than at reducing them. Respondents rated them least prepared for technological threats.
Eighty-six percent said funding for risk reduction and prevention was inadequate.

Vanuatu says it expects fall in China police presence after deal with Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:10:01 UTC
15:10:01 KST

Vanuatu says it expects fall in China's police presence after signing Nakamal Agreement with Australia
In short:
Vanuatu has flagged it expects China's police presence there to reduce "over time" following the Pacific nation's landmark Nakamal Agreement with Australia.
It signals a potentially significant strategic win for the Australian government, which believes Beijing is using police training to embed itself as a legitimate security partner in the Pacific.
China has maintained a small police training team in Vanuatu since 2023, and its embassy there has made substantial donations to the police force.
The federal government has notched a potentially significant strategic win in the Pacific, with Vanuatu saying China's police presence there was "expected to reduce over time" following its signing of the Nakamal Agreement with Australia.
China has expanded policing ties with several Pacific nations in recent years, but this is only the second time a Pacific nation has made an on-the-record commitment, albeit with a caveat, to wind back Beijing's police presence on the ground.
Fiji's prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said in 2024 that Chinese officers in his country's police force had been "repatriated" because the two countries had different legal systems.
China has maintained a small police training team in Vanuatu since 2023, and its internal affairs minister, Andrew Napuat, travelled to Beijing last month to renew its policing cooperation pact with Beijing.
The Chinese embassy in Vanuatu has also made substantial donations to Vanuatu's police force, including multiple surveillance drones, dozens of motorcycles, patrol boats, uniforms, minibuses, riot gear and forensics laboratory equipment.
That is a source of anxiety for Australia, which believes Beijing is intent on establishing a military foothold in the region and that it is using police training teams to embed itself as a legitimate security partner for Pacific nations.
Last week Vanuatu's deputy prime minister and finance minister, Johnny Koanapo, met Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Pacific Minister Pat Conroy in Canberra to discuss implementation of the high-profile Nakamal Agreement, which was finally signed in June after months of sometimes tough negotiations.
The two governments said in a joint statement that the agreement recognised Australia as "Vanuatu's longstanding primary policing partner" and "reaffirmed its commitment in the Nakamal Agreement that it would prioritise any policing requests to Pacific Islands Forum members".
"Vanuatu said its police arrangement with China had been in place for some time, is time-limited and expected to reduce over time, whereas the Vanuatu-Australia Nakamal Agreement is legally binding and has no expiry date," they said.
The joint statement was quietly uploaded to DFAT's website early this afternoon, but has not been heavily publicised by either government.
Vanuatu's government did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The ABC has also sought comment from the Chinese embassies in Port Vila and Canberra.
Issues around police cooperation remain highly sensitive in Vanuatu, and disagreements over China's role in the sector have sparked up before.
Last week Vanuatu's prime minister, Jotham Napat, pushed back when a senior Australian Federal Police officer, David McLean, told a parliamentary committee that the eight-strong AFP team in Vanuatu would soon increase due to growing cooperation under the Nakamal Agreement.
"I expect that number could nearly double in size over the coming years as we increase the frequency and intensity of program delivery and advisory support,"
he said.
He said the cooperation would cover "everything from the fundamentals of modern organisational design and administration through to professional standards, investigative policing, community policing, general duties policing, forensics and the centre of excellence we're delivering".
But Mr Napat cautioned last week that his country had yet to give any approval for an increase in Australian police officers, and that any request would need to be signed off by his government.
"Anything where we allow them to come, that's a matter where our government with the government of Australia sits down and agrees to that," he said.
"But I'm not aware of any arrangement."
The two countries also provided some basic details about the early implementation of the Nakamal Agreement, which is expected to funnel about $500 million into Vanuatu's key priorities over a decade.
In their joint statement, the two countries said the early priorities would include "strengthened policing cooperation, budget support, climate cooperation and assistance for ni-Vanuatu communities affected by El Niño and volcanic ash".
They also said Australia had committed to "early delivery of two renewable energy and water projects", including providing "renewable electricity, lighting and clean water to schools and community facilities in remote communities, and solar-powered water supply systems to improve access to water".
Vanuatu also flagged investment in key infrastructure priorities, including maritime and aviation infrastructure and rebuilding efforts in Port Vila, Santo and Tanna, in meetings with representatives of the Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific.

World Insights: Cost-of-living anger fuels protests across Europe amid deepening social-economic strains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:08:09 CST
15:08:09 KST

PARIS, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Tens of thousands of people flooded streets across major European cities over the weekend, venting mounting anger over surging living costs, housing shortages, and strained public services.
From violent clashes in France and Italy to widespread rallies in Portugal, the simultaneous wave of social unrest underscores a deepening socio-economic divide and growing public frustration across the continent.
PROTESTS GO VIOLENT
In France, nationwide demonstrations on Saturday drew some 550,000 participants, uniting farmers, trade unions, climate activists and students demanding relief from high fuel prices, inflation and public service cuts.
The gatherings rapidly descended into violent clashes. According to the French Interior Ministry, 997 police officers and gendarmes were injured, seven of them seriously, while 2,397 people were arrested nationwide.
Protests against the rising cost of living also swept northern Italy. In Milan, hundreds of black-clad demonstrators besieged Piazza del Duomo, throwing firecrackers and bottles at police. At least four officers and 20 protesters were injured, while about 50 demonstrators were detained, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.
Clashes between police and protesters also broke out in Belgium's capital Brussels as students and their supporters took to the streets to protest education reforms and rising costs.
Also on Saturday, tens of thousands of people demonstrated in Lisbon, Porto, Coimbra and other Portuguese cities to demand affordable housing and action to curb the rising cost of living.
According to the police, protesters pitched dozens of tents in Lisbon's central square and carried banners calling for laws to "ban vulture real estate funds," which they accused of fueling property speculation, while chanting "Down with speculation" and "We want housing and jobs."
European leaders condemned the violence, vowing action against rioters.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday on the social platform X that there is no place for violence in France.
"Those who have engaged in destruction, attacked government offices and businesses, and even looted our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished," he said.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni also strongly condemned the chaos on Saturday, writing on social media: "Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not."
Calling the demonstrators thugs who exploited protests to sow chaos, attack those tasked with keeping people safe and hold entire cities hostage, she said: "Faced with scenes like these, the rejection must be unanimous. Any reticence amounts to justification. Silence is unacceptable."
SYSTEMIC CHALLENGES BEHIND PROTESTS
The unrest highlights systemic challenges that continue to pressure households across the continent.
Although tactics varied from peaceful occupations of public squares to violent street clashes, protesters shared common grievances: declining purchasing power, unaffordable housing, high energy prices and weakening social safety nets.
Eszter Sandor, a senior research manager at Eurofound, warned that the benefits of macroeconomic stability are failing to reach the bottom half of the income distribution.
This growing divide is also reflected in public trust, with unemployed people, low-paid workers and people with disabilities reporting the lowest levels of trust in national governments and the legal system, she said. "A gap is opening between the rhetoric of a resilient Europe and the reality of daily life."
Niek Pas, a scholar at the University of Amsterdam, told Dutch public broadcaster NOS on Saturday that in France, the protests came as the government faced severe fiscal and economic constraints, reflecting widespread public discontent and deeper structural problems in France's governance.
Analysts point out that as European governments struggle with fiscal deficits and economic uncertainty, balancing budget constraints with public welfare has become an increasingly delicate task.
The widespread protests signal that failure to address these economic hardships risks further eroding public trust, deepening social divisions and fueling continued unrest across Europe. ■

OpenAI bugging suspect WhatsApp'ed Saudi royal days before arrest, feds reveal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:06:58 UTC
15:06:58 KST

The Saudi national charged with planting a recording device in a sensitive OpenAI executive conference room in San Francisco was "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026, prosecutors revealed in a bombshell court filing Sunday.
The defendant, Abdulrahman Alfozan, communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, the U.S. Attorney's Office in San Francisco said in the filing, which requests that he be detained without bail.
Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal, or say in the filing how Alfozan, who then was working as an engineer at OpenAI, knew that person.
"Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," prosecutors wrote in their filing.
"In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote.
"The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. " At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested."
The filing does not say that the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from that AI giant.
Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm. Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, joined the firm as a venture partner in 2025. In their filing Sunday, prosecutors did not mention that prince by name, or say that the unidentified royal who communicated with Alfozan had ties to Raed.
Prosecutors in the same filing said that the Saudi government and then, shortly afterward, a member of the Saudi military, booked separate flights for Alfozan's wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their three-month-old baby son to fly out of the United States after his Oct. 9 arrest upended plans for the three of them to fly as a family to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.
The wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar, on Oct. 10 on a business-class flight paid for by the unidentified member of the Saudi military, the filing said.
The filing asks that a judge order Alfozan, 35, detained without bail when he appears in U.S. District Court in San Francisco on Monday morning.
Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted. OpenAI fired him after his arrest.
Alfozan's lawyer, William Pernik, in a separate filing asked that the defendant be released with home detention and GPS monitoring, and a bond co-signed by others, and "supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia."
The Saudi embassy in Washington, D.C., has not responded to CNBC's requests for comment on Alfozan since his arrest was announced on Oct. 13
Prosecutors said that in the days around the time that Alfozan allegedly installed the recording device on Sept. 28 in the back of a television in the conference room, "OpenAI executives met with government officials in that very room."
"Defendant's conduct could pose a danger to the national security of the United States," prosecutors said in the filing.
FBI Director Kash Patel, when Alfozan's arrest was announced on Oct. 13, said he allegedly concealed the recording device to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's artificial intelligence technology.
Prosecutors in their new filing also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk because of his access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said.
"He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote.
Alfozan has spent about 15 years in the United States, working at various tech companies, including Meta, and obtaining a master's degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 2025. He is a legal permanent resident of the United States and has applied to become a naturalized citizen.
For his most recent job, as an OpenAI engineer, Alfozan was hired in July 2025 with an annual base salary of $325,000, which was later increased to $385,000, prosecutors said in their filing. He also received a new hire equity grant of $2.2 million in profit participating units, the filing said.
Alfozan planned to take two months of parental leave after the birth of his son, according to the filing. He and his family were scheduled to fly one-way to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.
"On or about September 28, 2026 — about two weeks before their scheduled flight—the defendant inserted a surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days," the filing said.
The conference room is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the filing said.
The filing also says that Alfozan's iPhone, after his arrest, was found to contain photographs dated Sept. 22 to 28 depicting "at least one additional concealed device as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on televisions and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including another conference room where sensitive meetings frequently occurred."
"The defendant's residence contained several electronic components similar to those in the
customized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room," the filing said.
OpenAI also found another recording device in a bag Alfozan inadvertently left behind in a printer room on Oct. 5, the same day he was seen on camera checking behind the TV where the first recording device had been left in the conference room, prosecutors have said. The camera was installed after OpenAI discovered the recording device on Sept. 30, prosecutors said.
His cellphone also contained a deleted note from September 2026 "with links to various recording devices, including devices made by Seeed Studio, the manufacturer of the devices OpenAI found in its offices and the devices FBI agents found in the defendant's residence," the filing said.
Another note, entitled "OpenAI leave," suggests that Alfozan planned early pickup "of the devices he had installed or intended to install and then extending his planned parental 'leave to full,' " the filing said.
In addition to being in contact with a Saudi royal, Alfozan "was pursuing other opportunities in Saudi Arabia, including participating in the Misk Foundation's '2030 Leaders' program, which would have required his in- person participation in Riyadh," prosecutors said.
A day before she left the U.S. with her baby, Alfozan's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her U.S. visa was expiring and that she and her son were permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia — and that her husband, the defendant, eventually intended to do the same," the filing said.
Alfozan's lawyer, Pernik, in his request that Alfozan be released into home detention, said, "nationality is not evidence of flight," and that his planned travel to Saudi Arabia was for "family and immigration reasons."
Alfozan's wife's 60-day post-employment grace period for her own visa was expiring on Oct. 12, the originally scheduled date of their flight, the lawyer said.
"Mr. Alfozan was made aware of OpenAI finding the device per its own filings and OpenAI's
public statements, approximately eight to ten days before he was arrested," Pernik wrote. "If his intention was to flee, he would have done so at that time."
The lawyer also said that Alfozan, who had booked a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia for himself and his family, regularly bought one-way tickets because he has learned they are more cost-effective than changing his flights at the last minute.
Pernik also wrote that the Saudi Consulate General confirmed in writing to the U.S. Pretrial Services Office on Thursday that it "'will not issue any travel documents' to Mr. Alfozan during his release and that, if he requests one, it 'undertakes to promptly notify U.S. Pretrial Services.'"
The attorney argued that prosecutors have not shown that Alfozan is a serious flight risk.
"Mr. Alfozan has lived in the United States for fifteen years and in the Bay Area for roughly ten," Pernik wrote. "Fifty-four people, at least twenty-seven of them in the Bay Area, have written to the Court, and they describe someone who organizes dinners, welcomes newcomers, mentors students, and shows up for friends' weddings, birthdays, and moves."
"That is not the profile of a person with one foot out the door," Pernik said.

Officers are examining CCTV footage and forensic evidence, while checking the authenticity of messages attributed to Anil Pandit and Harman Sandhu.Investigators are also looking into whether Shroff had received any threats before the incident.The probe will need to establish whether the attackers acted on behalf of an organised group or whether someone claimed responsibility after the shooting to exploit the incident.For now, the alleged Bishnoi gang link remains under investigation.

Egypt’s constitution requires approval from two-thirds of lawmakers before troops can be sent on combat missions abroad, following consultation with the National Defense Council.
The Iran-backed Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi airports and energy facilities since fighting with the Saudi-led coalition resumed in July. The coalition supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

How a US$110 million fishing harbour in Tanzania serves China’s food and security goals

About 300km (186 miles) south of Dar es Salaam and near the ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani, the fishing town of Kilwa Masoko has a new port designed to accommodate fishing vessels far larger than the boats that have long worked this stretch of Tanzania’s coast.
The fishing port had passed its completion inspection, China’s ambassador to Tanzania Chen Mingjian said last week, while hailing it Tanzania’s first large-scale modern fishing harbour.
Designed to land 60,000 tonnes of fish a year, it aims to boost Tanzanian fish markets, cut spoilage and create jobs – Tanzania’s labour minister Deus Sangu expects about 30,000 direct and indirect jobs.
Some of the catch could reach Chinese buyers as China’s appetite for seafood grows. In recent years, Beijing has signed agreements allowing more African countries to export fish and other aquatic products to its market.
China imports live lobster from Namibia and Comoros, and crab and dried anchovies from Kenya. It agreed to import requirements for Tanzanian wild aquatic products, while a separate protocol provides for Somali tuna, lobster and other wild seafood to enter the Chinese market.

Parliament to debate fund repayment bill this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Parliament is set to debate a bill this week allowing interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to eligible investors in funds ordered into liquidation.
The proposal, approved by the Plan and Budget Commission on Oct. 14, covers funds the Capital Markets Board (SPK) ordered liquidated on Sept. 17 whose liquidation remains incomplete when the legislation is published.
Investors with net investments below 1 million liras could receive up to that amount, while those at or above the threshold could receive a maximum of 1 million liras.
Interim payments would be calculated without inflation adjustments, depend on available fund assets and be deducted from final entitlements.
Liquidation would proceed under SPK supervision.
People and institutions identified by the board as having participated in insider trading, market manipulation or other market-disrupting acts involving the funds would be excluded from payments.
The board would determine each fund’s losses, identify those responsible and notify the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) of the amounts to be recovered. Primary liability would rest with the portfolio management company that founded or managed the fund.
Assets could also be seized under the Criminal Procedure Code during investigations linked to the funds.
After necessary expenses are deducted, the TMSF would transfer recovered money to the institution handling liquidation.
If liquidation has been completed, the money would go to the Investor Compensation Center (YTM), which would distribute payments in proportion to investors’ fund holdings.
The General Assembly will first resume debate on the Turkish Red Crescent bill when it reconvenes on Oct. 20. Its first three articles have already been approved.
That proposal would make the organization the sole body authorized to receive and use aid sent to Türkiye by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, the International Committee of the Red Cross and national societies.
Budget discussions also begin this week. Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz is due to present the 2027 central government budget bill and the 2025 final accounts bill to the Plan and Budget Commission on Oct. 21.
Some 41 billion Turkish lira liquidation completed in troubled funds
A liquidation process worth approximately 40.8 billion Turkish lira ($828 million), covering 66 investment funds, has been completed, with more than 45,000 investors receiving cash and in-kind payments, according to a statement released by the Communications Directorate following the sixth meeting of the Fund Coordination Board chaired by Yılmaz on Oct. 18.
Ziraat Bank finalized the liquidation of 66 investment funds managed by A1 Portfolio Management, Bulls Portfolio Management and Pardus Portfolio Management, reducing the number of funds under liquidation from 131 to 65.
Under a decision issued by the Capital Markets Board (SPK) on Oct. 15, liquidation proceedings for funds established by Hedef Portfolio Management were brought under the same framework previously adopted for funds founded by those 3 portfolio management companies, said the statement.
Within this framework, authorities plan to make payments to the largest possible number of investors this week, with priority given to those holding money market funds, it added.

Macron signals protest bans after unrest across France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:59:00 UTC
14:59:00 KST

AA photo.
French police “lost control” during nationwide protests marred by violence over the weekend, the interior minister admitted on Oct. 19, with President Emmanuel Macron calling for a security review.
Macron also refused Interior Minister Laurent Nunez’s resignation even as he acknowledged security and intelligence failures in the government response.
Oct. 17’s demonstrations saw some half a million people turn out across France to protest the cost of living, but morphed into some of the worst violence to rock the country in years, with town halls and shops looted and set ablaze.
More than 2,500 people were arrested, while almost 1,000 members of the security forces were injured. Injuries were also reported among protesters, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade.
“On Saturday, in some major cities, you couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn’t lost control,” Nunez said.
Nunez acknowledged a “lack of anticipation” in the deployment of security forces on Oct. 17, whose numbers were insufficient to deal with the large crowds of rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.
He estimated that some 60,000 law enforcement personnel had been deployed across the country that day.
“Given the damage that has been caused, it was only right that I should hand in my resignation,” Nunez said.
The presidency said in a statement that Macron had rejected the resignation, however, citing “the necessity for continued leadership of law enforcement.”
Instead, Macron ordered Nunez to “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence.”
To end the “barricades and looting, he also requested that the interior minister promptly implement new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters,” the statement added.
Looting continued on Oct. 18, with Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire saying on Oct. 19 that around 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, describing the scenes as “unbearable.”
Nunez said some 350 people had been arrested in Paris on Oct. 18 and overnight.
Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70 percent of whom were adults, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said on Oct. 19.
More than 2,000 shops were expected to have been affected by the weekend’s violence across France, with damage running into “hundreds of millions of euros,” according to chamber of commerce president Alain Di Crescenzo.
In an address to the nation Oct. 18 evening, Macron slammed the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban, “if necessary,” certain rallies in coming days.
But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew.

The kingmakers who could determine Israel’s election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:58:46 UTC
14:58:46 KST

The kingmakers who could determine Israel’s election
Israel’s Arab-led and ultra-Orthodox parties face attacks but could hold the balance of power after October 27 vote.
In the run-up to Israel’s high-stakes election, few parties have featured more often in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s attacks on rivals than Ra’am and the Joint List.
Together, the two parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats. If this is confirmed at the October 27 polls, the Arab-led lists could be critical to any post-election coalition, regardless of its political stripe.
They have been here before.
In 2021, Ra’am made history by becoming the first Arab party to enter an Israeli government after joining a broad coalition that briefly removed Netanyahu from power. Netanyahu had previously shown himself ready to negotiate terms for a potential government with Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List. But instead, Abbas joined forces with the coalition of Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid to try to drive through some of the measures he had campaigned for.
This time, both the Netanyahu camp and most leaders of the self-styled Zionist opposition bloc have ruled out forming a government with the parties representing Palestinian citizens. Still, Netanyahu and his allies have sought to portray their political opponents as beholden to the Arab-led lists, while the opposition has been attacking them for their reliance on the minority ultra-Orthodox parties to maintain their own power base.
Opinion polls have consistently indicated that Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads are running neck-and-neck with the Zionist opposition bloc, with neither side on track to win an outright majority in the 120-strong Knesset.
“Netanyahu would work with Ra’am in a heartbeat, if it meant staying in power,” said Yossi Mekelberg, a Middle East analyst at Chatham House.
“The opposition, too, don’t seem to understand the consequences of their actions,” he said of repeated attempts across the opposition bloc to undermine the credibility of what may be a future plank in any government.
“If it came down to it, of course they’d accept the support of the party they’d previously vilified without thinking of how that will undermine their government, and undermine the votes of the large numbers of Arab Israelis who support them,” added Mekelberg.
In the lead-up to the polls, Likud has repeatedly used hard-hitting attack adverts to warn that if Netanyahu is voted out, it will be the Arab parties that would emerge as kingmakers in a new government potentially led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party.
“There is no Gadi without [Ahmad] Tibi,” said a Likud campaign slogan in reference to the leader of Ta’al, one of three parties comprising the Joint List.
The alliance, which also includes the Hadash and Balad factions, has said it could provide a so-called safety net to the anti-Netanyahu coalition by agreeing not to stand against it in a confidence vote, even if the alliance does not join the government. In return, it has said it would demand certain conditions, including a path to Palestinian statehood and fighting organised crime.
Combatting the wave of violent crime that has been allowed to engulf Palestinian communities, as well as addressing discriminatory government policies, including on housing, have also been the focus of Ra’am ahead of the election.
Established in 1996, the party has already distanced itself from its religiously conservative foundations. In December 2025, Abbas said the party’s political decision-making body would separate from its religious council. Eight months later, it selected its electoral list independently for the first time and placed the Jewish Zionist Yoav Segalovitz, a former senior police commander and deputy public security minister in the Bennett-Lapid government, second on its slate.
Describing Ra’am as “one of the most interesting parties” of this year’s election, Mekelberg said: “Through Mansour Abbas, they are continually reinventing themselves without appearing opportunist.”
The upcoming election is the first since the Hamas-led attack in southern Israel of October 7, 2023 that led to the killing of an estimated 1,200 people, and triggered Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The war has also sped up a political shift to the right, with Arab-led parties increasingly targeted by right-wing figures seeking to cast them as complicit in the October 7 assault.
In May, Bennett apologised for going into government with Ra’am, while in September, Netanyahu’s Likud and the Otzma Yehudi party of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir petitioned to bar Ra’am and the Joint List from the election.
On September 23, the Central Elections Committee, whose members are drawn from the Knesset’s parties, voted to disqualify both lists, as well as two individual candidates.
Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh was to be barred over an article he wrote on October 8, 2023 describing the Hamas-led attack of the previous day as an “important historic event”. Ofer Cassif, a Jewish politician with Hadash, was targeted in a petition filed by Likud that cited legal prohibitions on candidates who support “an armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organisation against the State of Israel”.
On October 2, the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the disqualifications of the Joint List and Ra’am, as well as Cassif’s, by a 7-2 majority. Abu Shehadeh had withdrawn his candidacy a day earlier, after it became clear the court was likely to uphold his disqualification.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Cassif later called it “a political decision far more than a judicial one”, driven by “fear that they’re going to need us”.
Orly Noy, a Balad candidate and the first Jewish politician to be voted onto the party list’s top five, said it was “safe to say” that the alliance is not going to be part of the next ruling coalition.
“It depends if the other parties want to prioritise the wishes of their voters or their own racism. However, even if we’re excluded, we can still gain concessions from any coalition in return for our support,” she added. “That might not mean ending the occupation, which of course would be ideal, but there’s a lot we can still do that will make people’s lives better.”
Fallout
The taint of October 7 has not only extended to Arab parties unconnected to the events of that day, but also to ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
As routine partners in Likud’s governing coalitions, they have faced accusations by many leading opponents of draft-dodging, while drawing heavily on what many regard as a generous state welfare package.
Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community is largely represented by two parties: Shas, which draws on Jews of Spanish, North African and Middle Eastern descent; and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), comprising Jews of central and eastern European descent. Each is polling at about seven or eight seats.
Rather than focusing on foreign policy and taxation, their core aims tend to be shielding ultra-Orthodox students from military service, securing welfare support for the large families common in the community, where many men study rather than work, and protecting state funding for their schools and institutions.
Long seen as Netanyahu’s most dependable allies, they broke with Likud last year over its failure to legislate an exemption to the draft. The UTJ left the coalition altogether, while Shas quit the government but did not pull its 11 politicians out of the parliamentary coalition. Shas later gave up its coalition committee roles, and both parties boycotted coalition bills.
Nevertheless, the support of the ultra-Orthodox has come with a political price tag. In January, opposition leader Yair Lapid accused the government of sending billions “to the corrupt and [the] draft dodgers” while another possible contender for the premiership, the right-wing Avigdor Lieberman, who heads the Yisrael Beytenu list, likened Shas and UTJ to the Taliban over their lack of female representation.

Is college worth it in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:57:25 UTC
14:57:25 KST

In our twenties, when there is still so much time ahead of us, time that seems ample for a hundred indecisions, for a hundred visions and revisions—we draw a card, and we must decide right then and there whether to keep that card and discard the next, or discard the first card and keep the second. And before we know it, the deck has been played out and the decisions we have just made will shape our lives for decades to come.
Rules of Civility, Amor Towles
Many years ago, I went to my parents expressing my wish to drop a year to prepare for IIT-JEE. It was a particularly stressful time for us financially, and yet, my parents did not think twice before fully supporting me in this risky endeavour. As grateful as I am to my parents, I am probably not unique. As I entered IIT Kharagpur the following year, I met several others who came through very humble backgrounds, students whose parents had pledged their land, or taken an extra job or a loan to provide the best opportunities to their children. For most parents, the choice was self-evident. A good undergraduate degree was a way to move up the social ladder.But lately, people have started questioning the worth of a university education. They contend that the university model is outdated today due to rapid technological advancements. In particular, given that we can now learn everything online using AI, we do not need a university degree. And in any case, the pay gap between those with a degree and those without no longer justifies the ever-rising costs.This view is wrong on three counts. First, it overstates the challenge that awaits us because it ignores the harsh reality of people’s ability to learn on their own.
Second, it misses what learning at a university entails. And finally, the pay gap it disputes is still very much there.
First, questions like whether our existing methods of teaching, working, and thinking are suited to the looming changes are hardly new. When computers arrived, apocalyptic prophecies about employment prospects were ubiquitous. Those arguing that the knowledge from a university degree is redundant over a person’s career miss the point that this is how it has always been. A person graduating in 1980 would have barely seen a computer. In 2005, they might not have known how to work without one. A person graduating in 1990 in India would most likely not have known what an email was; in 2020, their entire workflow would have been online. It is tempting to think this time is different. But, as they say, the more things change, the more they stay the same. A good university education teaches us how to learn and not what to learn. Neither AI nor most jobs will teach that.And what is the historical track record of self-learning? Top scholars from the world’s best universities like Stanford and MIT have made knowledge freely available for nearly two decades now. Gilbert Strang, one of the giants of linear algebra (the field that is at the heart of machine learning and AI), has a course on Linear Algebra on YouTube. The first lecture has 4.9 million views. By the last lecture, we have about 200K-250K views. A macroeconomics course drops from 860K to 15K, a deep learning course drops from 518K to 4.7K, you get the drift. In short, the fraction of people who manage to complete a course delivered by some of the best scholars in the world is anywhere from 1 in 20 to 1 in 100. After all, self-discipline and the art of learning have to be acquired. Universities allow the students to learn them the hard way by failing, struggling, and catching up. If being an Eklavya was so easy, Eklavya would not have made it into history in the first place!Recent evidence makes this concrete. David Strömberg and his co-authors tracked some 27,000 Chinese schoolchildren aged 12 to 18, roughly 80% of whom had taken to using models like DeepSeek. Within six months their homework scores had risen by 18%, and the time spent on each assignment had fallen from 64 minutes to 45. So far so good. But at exam time, those same pupils scored 20% below classmates who had never used AI. Most telling of all, the old relationship inverted: homework scores used to predict exam performance, and now the pupils with the best homework are the likeliest to stumble in the exam. A randomised experiment in Turkish classrooms points to the remedy—the damage largely disappears when the AI is set up to give teacher-designed hints rather than answers. In short, the irresistible temptation to fetch an answer immediately—much like scrolling reels to kill time—sounds the death knell of learning. Since much of the payoff in the labour market lies precisely in the harder skills, the relevance of the university is likely to persist.There is another challenge with self-learning. Most academics at good universities have far better information about their students than any online platform and can and do design courses that are better suited to their tastes, abilities, and contexts. For example, at ISB, a course on antitrust policies covers a range of cases from the US and India; a course on Indian National Financial Systems goes deep into the Indian economy through the lens of cutting-edge research in economics. I am yet to come across a place outside the university system where one can learn the foundational principles of these topics without wasting hours on obscure and irrelevant material.
Why do we go to university?
Second, there is a fundamental question: Does one attend a university only to be taught by professors? Here, I cannot do better than ancient Sanskrit wisdom.आचार्यात्पादमादत्ते पादं शिष्यः स्वमेधया। पादं सब्रह्मचारिभ्यः पादं कालक्रमेण च॥You learn a quarter from the teacher, a quarter through your own intellect, a quarter through fellow classmates, and a quarter from the passage of time. The internet at its best replaces only the teacher’s quarter—and even that I doubt; the other three quarters are what the campus is for. If one switches to a self-learning model, would it be so easy to find fellow classmates who are driven by shared interests, passions, and energy to learn?VS Naipaul once wrote, in A Bend in the River, “we make ourselves according to the ideas we have of our possibilities.” A good university reveals to us our possibilities, our challenges and limitations; it exposes us to people better than us and opens our horizons to the opportunities that await us. Skipping university education comes at the cost of denying yourself the opportunity to learn seemingly unrelated and unimportant subjects, the opportunity to engage in intellectually stimulating conversations with your classmates, and above all, the opportunity of discovering yourself. The unstructured time, the enduring friendships and debates, transform us from adolescents to adults, to people. As Oreopoulos and Salvanes show:
Schooling may not only affect income but also the degree to which one enjoys working or the likelihood of not being able to find work. Schooling could also lead individuals to make better decisions about health, marriage, and parenting style. It may have significant consumption value too. And, as we argue in this paper, schooling may affect preferences in a way that makes individuals more patient, more goal-oriented, and less likely to engage in risky behavior. In short, schooling may have important nonpecuniary returns.
— Philip Oreopoulos and Kjell G. Salvanes, “Priceless: The Nonpecuniary Benefits of Schooling”
Schooling creates adults of the kind we need; the robots who’d maximise productivity can be provided by technology.The obsession with finding the “use case” for every course, every lecture, is rather counterproductive. As Steve Jobs, the patron saint of dropping out, said in his famous Stanford commencement speech:Again, you can’t connect the dots looking forward. You can only connect them looking backwards, so you have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future.
The pay gap between having a university degree and not having one
And finally, even if one accepts all these benefits, are the costs—time lost and the tuition paid—worth it? Do graduates get paid significantly more? To slightly paraphrase the apocryphal quote of Mark Twain, the reports of the death of the college premium—the additional salaries that college graduates receive relative to their non-college peers—are greatly exaggerated. For example, in a recent article in the Financial Times, John Burn-Murdoch highlighted how the hourly wage premium for university graduates in the US has begun to slip: from a peak of roughly 85% to below 80% today. Unfortunately, such statistics are not available for India, so we must base the arguments mostly on estimates from the West.
-
Focusing on the decline, though, risks losing the bigger picture: a university education still pays a significant premium, and is likely to keep doing so.Still, I must concede one point. The perception that university education has stopped being useful is shaped by recent studies showing rising graduate unemployment in the US and a collapsing graduate job market in the UK. Over the past few decades, as the belief about the “college-premium” got cemented, universities floated several “soft” undergraduate programmes to earn quick money. It is no surprise that people graduating from such degrees would eventually struggle in the labour market. The median early-career salary (ages 22–27) of computer science graduates in the US is $87,000 (NY Fed data), while it can be as low as $43,000 for some other disciplines. Indeed, the falling average premium may say less about the democratisation of technical knowledge than about the rapid rise of degrees whose worth the labour market is yet to discover. Several empirical studies establish that even taking the costs into account, most undergraduate education in rigorous fields
pays off heavily. The problem is not university education; it is the choice of discipline!Echoing Towles’ protagonist in the opening quote, it may be seductive to embrace a paradigm shift after listening to the confident predictions about the demise of the university model. But it would be rather foolish to play the deck of one’s life, to make choices that will shape your life for decades to come, listening to confident projections about a very uncertain world. It is natural to feel encumbered by the gravity of looming changes in the world that awaits us. We must take comfort in the fact that people have always felt it, in 1960, 1980, 2000, and today. As I was graduating, my PhD advisor David Pearce from New York University gave me a piece of advice that has remained the mantra of my life. One evening in his office, discussing my plans for the years ahead, David said, “Aditya, just take care of the pennies, and the pounds will take care of themselves.” The chances are, if I had not gone to a university, I wouldn’t have learned this, let alone practised it. This was not a part of any curriculum. And that is the beauty of university education: the chance interactions that shape our lives are likely to remain important as long as humans continue to teach humans.

China’s economy grows 4.5 percent in Q3, beating forecasts

China’s economy grows 4.5 percent in Q3, beating forecasts
GDP growth picks up from Q2 amid AI-driven boom in exports.
China’s economy has grown faster than expected in the most recent quarter amid booming exports underpinned by artificial intelligence, according to official figures.
China’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 4.5 percent in the July-September period from the same quarter a year earlier, picking up from 4.3 percent growth in the second quarter and beating most analysts’ forecasts, figures released on Monday by the National Bureau of Statistics showed.
During the first nine months of the year, GDP grew 4.6 percent year-on-year, according to the preliminary figures.
While China’s technology-related exports have surged during the AI boom, growth in the world’s second-largest economy has been dampened by weak domestic demand and a sagging property market.
China’s ruling Communist Party has set a GDP growth target of 4.5 to 5 percent for 2026, which would be among the slowest expansions in decades, excluding during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Chinese exports surged more than 16 percent in the first three quarters of the year to reach 23.19 billion yuan ($3.47bn), according to the official data, largely due to strong demand for semiconductors and other tech-related goods.
Retail sales, a key measure of domestic consumption, increased 1.1 percent year-on-year in September and 2.6 percent during the first nine months of 2026.
Industrial production, which measures output in sectors such as manufacturing and mining, rose 5.5 percent in September, taking growth in the first three quarters to 5.3 percent.
Investment in fixed assets, which covers spending on real estate, factories and machinery, edged up 0.7 percent last month but contracted 7.2 percent during the January-September period.
Zhiguo He, a finance professor at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business who studies the Chinese economy, said that while China’s economy is on track to hit official targets, Beijing will be wary of the continuing reliance on export-driven growth.
“I expect Beijing is getting 4.5 percent as wanted,” He told Al Jazeera.
“A managed slow slowdown is the best Beijing can hope for,” he said.
“Real estate is still shrinking. This is what Beijing wanted and a good thing, and China’s households have been adapting their expectations based on this.”

Voting among IDF soldiers will begin on Tuesday and continue for seven days, until Election Day itself.
The idea behind the early voting is to allow soldiers to vote even if they are serving on ships and submarines deployed away from Israel, or at distant outposts.
Roughly a quarter of polling stations in the army will be mobile, traveling between different IDF units according to a schedule approved ahead of time.
Explained: A brief history of Israel's last elections
Despite the crises of the years since the last election in 2022, Israel's current government has been relatively stable by recent standards. It follows an unusually turbulent period in which Israel held five Knesset elections in just three and a half years: April 2019, September 2019, March 2020, March 2021 and November 2022.
The deadlock stemmed largely from the refusal of the main political blocs to sit together in a governing coalition, leaving no clear path to a majority. In the two elections of 2019, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was tasked with forming a government but failed both times.
After the first election, Likud moved to dissolve the Knesset to prevent the mandate from being passed to a lawmaker other than Netanyahu. At the center of the crisis was a bill to exempt ultra-Orthodox men from military conscription.
Following the second election, Benny Gantz's Kahol Lavan party emerged as the largest faction, but the mandate was still given to Netanyahu. Gantz's party had refused to serve in a government with Netanyahu once he was facing trial for criminal corruption charges.
After he failed to form a coalition, Gantz was tasked with doing so, but also could not put together a government, inducing another round of elections.
The March 2020 election produced another stalemate. Although Likud won the most seats, President Reuven Rivlin gave Gantz the mandate after a majority of lawmakers recommended him. Gantz ultimately abandoned his pledge not to serve under Netanyahu, joining a national unity government because the COVID-19 pandemic constituted a national emergency. The agreement included a rotation arrangement for the premiership, but the government collapsed later that year after failing to pass a budget.
After the March 2021 election, Netanyahu once again failed to form a coalition. The mandate then passed to Yair Lapid, who assembled a broad and ideologically diverse alliance that installed Naftali Bennett as prime minister in what became known as the "government of change." It was the first time since 2009 that Netanyahu was not in office. That government, too, proved short-lived, collapsing in June 2022.
Netanyahu returned to power following the November 2022 election, forming the most right-wing government in Israel's history, which is currently in office.
IDF chief orders freeze on soldiers' leave ahead of election
Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir ordered a freeze on soldiers' leave starting on Thursday, as part of the army's preparations for next Tuesday's Election Day, according to a statement released by the IDF Spokesperson's Unit.
October 7? War? The cost of living is the secret key issue of Israel's election
In the 2022 election campaign, then-opposition leader Benjamin Netanyahu stood in a supermarket and filmed a TikTok video. "Milk is going up, fruits and vegetables are going up, bread is going up, everything is going up, meat is going up, mortgages are going up, gasoline is going up," Netanyahu said in the campaign ad.
"Do you want to lower prices?" the man who would return as prime minister asked, and his audience in the video responded with an enthusiastic "yes." He replied: "Then you have to go out and vote so we can lower prices. We will lower prices – that is my commitment."
In those days, Israelis were naive; they also received a promise for free daycare up to age 3. Israel ended up with a government that tried to weaken the judiciary and didn't listen to defense officials' warnings, leading to Hamas' massacre and a three-year war – and a 20 percent surge in prices.
Four years have gone by. According to the OECD's Price Level Index, which measures the cost of a basket of goods and services for an average household in different countries, Israeli prices are 34 percent higher than the average in the organization. In the Israeli basket, the lion's share is for housing and food – 44 percent of all spending.
Can Tel Aviv's hipster heartland resist Israel's generational shift to the right?
In Tel Aviv's Florentin, it is not uncommon to find voters who – bucking national trends – have moved even further left since October 7. Even so, fear for Israel's future is testing old loyalties and pushing voters toward unlikely choices.
Netanyahu unveils new 'security concept' for Israel as October 7 failures remain unchecked
On Sunday, just nine days before Israel's general election, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu presented an updated plan for Israel, in the form of a document outlining the "Prime Minister's Security Doctrine" for Israel – without any independent state probe or inquiry formed to examine his decision-making in his previous terms as prime minister.
In a press conference, Netanyahu claimed he had significantly modified his previous plan – unveiled in 2018 under the title "Security Concept 2030" – which he drafted in 2018 and which guided him on the eve of Hamas' attack on October 7, 2023.
Explained: Why not every vote will count in Israel's next election
Thirty-eight parties will be on the ballot when Israelis head to the polls in exactly two weeks, but polls project that only 11 to 13 will win seats in the next Knesset, largely because of an election law requiring parties to receive a minimum share of the vote to enter parliament.
Known as the electoral threshold, this minimum currently stands at 3.25 percent of all valid votes cast. In Israel's last election, in 2022, that translated to 154,855 votes.
With the number of eligible voters having risen by more than 540,000, and turnout expected to increase, the number of votes needed to enter the Knesset is projected to reach a record high.

The mushy plants dividing Australians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:53:29 UTC
14:53:29 KST

IN BRIEF
- Crepe myrtles have become a familiar feature of new Australian housing developments.
- One botanist says they're better suited to gardens and courtyards than urban streetscapes.
The crepe myrtle — a medium-sized tree often covered in an explosion of white, pink, purple or red flowers — lines many an Australian street.
Lots of people love them, but others think of them as an inadequate and over-planted species.
Some even refer to them as "crap myrtle", which is a little harsh.
In the right numbers, these small trees can be a good choice and do well in a small urban courtyard.
But perhaps large-scale planting in urban streetscapes is not the best place for them — they can shed large volumes of flowers, which can get mushy and slippery as they decay.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Getting to know the crepe myrtle
Crepe myrtle is the common name for a number of Lagerstroemia species. There are about 50 different species: one native to northern Australia.
That native, Lagerstroemia archeriana, is also known as the Queensland or native crepe myrtle; it's also just crepe myrtle to many.
It is a purple or pink flowering species found in Queensland and Western Australia, and occurs naturally in drier forests. It has been cultivated for a long time but tends to be better suited to northern Australia.
However, the specimen that most people are familiar with is Lagerstroemia indica, the common crepe myrtle — also known as crape myrtle or crapemyrtle.
The name crepe is thought to relate to the crinkled nature of the flower petals resembling a crêpe (a type of French pancake).
Lagerstroemia indica is a small tree up to about five metres in height, with lovely smooth, silver to coppery coloured bark. But it is best known for its impressive and abundant flowering in white, pink, purple or red.
In full flower and en masse, it's a stunner. It has been very widely planted in the streets of new urban developments where small blocks, large houses and narrow roads are de rigeuer.
However, Lagerstroemia indica can be prone to some fungal diseases like powdery mildew, to which hybrid crepe myrtles are more resistant.
There are also hybrid crepe myrtles — usually a cross between Lagerstroemia indica and the Japanese crepe myrtle Lagerstroemia fauriei, which only produces white flowers.
These hybrids have the advantages of the more robust vigour, mottled bark and disease resistance of the Japanese species but retain the full colour range and magnificent flowering of Lagerstroemia indica. They also have great mottled bark — overall a magnificent combination.
A common street tree — but not always loved
Local governments love to plant crepe myrtle as a street tree — it's compact, boasts impressive flowers and reaches structural maturity in five to 10 years. It tolerates a variety of soils and climates and lives for up to 100 years
However, these trees can look or feel a bit small in dense housing estates with big houses; they are just not large enough to give an appropriate sense of scale to this kind of streetscape.
Crepe myrtles also provide less shade and cooling than larger trees, and fewer habitats for organisms such as birds, insects and fungi. Apart from the native version, most crepe myrtle species provide little food source (for humans or animals).
Compared to elms, oaks or eucalypts, the crepe myrtle is a modestly sized tree; there are no vaulted, cathedral-like ceilings of branches with crepe myrtle.
In some places, residents top or lop the trees to promote more prolific flowering. This treatment, which shortens the lifespan of trees, is known colloquially as crape murder and is not recommended in Australia.
And people often pile clippings high around the trunks, which can result in trunk damage from pests and diseases.
It is better to mulch under trees (but don't let the clippings touch the trunk). You can prune young trees to shape their canopies for appearance.
Tree fashions come and go
Perhaps, to some people, the crepe myrtle just feels out of fashion.
Municipal horticulture has always had an element of fashion, even fads attached to it.
In the past there have been mass plantings of elms, palms, even southern conifers, and more recently of the ornamental pear (Pyrus calleryana) or Manchurian pear (Pyrus ussuriensis).
There were doubts about the pears from the start, given their history of weediness in the US. But now, despite some great spring flowering, they are going out of fashion, and many people strongly dislike them.
Crepe myrtle seems to be on a similar trajectory to the pears.
Despite some staunch support for this tree and its lovely flowers, they do not meet the long-term aspirations many people have for urban street trees.
Some people fell out of love with them; others wanted them gone altogether.
They have their virtues
Despite the hate, crepe myrtles are likely to be climate change hardy, as they tend to occur in hotter and drier regions of northern Australia and across Asia.
In the right place and in the right numbers, these small trees can be a good choice. They can look lovely in a garden or courtyard — but perhaps they are not the best pick for large-scale planting in urban streetscapes.
In the longer term, only time will tell how successful crepe myrtle will be as street trees and in winning over the hearts and minds of residents.
Gregory Moore is a senior research associate at the University of Melbourne's School of Agriculture, Food and Ecosystem Sciences. He does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

Oil-rich Alberta votes on Canada breakup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:47:00 UTC
14:47:00 KST

Oil-rich Alberta votes on Canada break-up
- Alberta votes on Oct 19 on whether to start a binding referendum on leaving Canada, as Mark Carney warns of “dangerous uncertainty” during a trade war with the United States.
- Support for independence is below 25%, but turnout may decide the result. Danielle Smith says Alberta should stay in Canada, yet she will act if separatists win.
- The vote is shaped by anger over oil policy, a deadly base fire, and fears of AI manipulation and foreign influence. Results on question 10 are expected early on Oct 20.
AI generated
EDMONTON, Canada – Alberta decides on Oct 19 if it wants to pursue a binding referendum on leaving Canada, with Prime Minister Mark Carney warning a separatist win would bring dangerous uncertainty during a trade war with the United States.
Polls indicate less than a quarter of people in the western Canadian province support independence.
But attention has focused on turnout in the days before the vote, and whether a motivated separatist camp could defy the polls, helped by complacent federalists.
“Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a rally on Oct 15.
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has called the referendum “a dangerous bluff” as US President Donald Trump imposes punishing tariffs and levels annexation threats aimed – the Prime Minister says – at breaking Canadian resolve.
“Vote like Canada depends on it because it does,” Carney said.
Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves and separatist momentum has been driven by anger over Ottawa’s management of the sector.
Many Albertans loathed Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, whom they accused of trying to suppress oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda.
“If you want me to pinpoint who is responsible for the separatist sentiment, I think it’s Justin Trudeau,” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told the Canadaland podcast in October.
At a separatist rally in Edmonton on Oct 17, 61-year-old Sandy Martel said people connected to the oil industry feel “robbed, cheated (and) mistreated”. She told AFP: “It’s time to stand up and say stop.”
The vote comes days after a fire at a military base in the province left at least four soldiers dead and wounded dozens, prompting a national outpouring of condolences.
‘Huge uncertainty’
Smith, a conservative, says she wants Alberta to remain in Canada, but called the referendum to settle the divisive issue.
If a majority votes to separate, she has pledged to move forward with a binding referendum. If the federalists win, Smith says the secession question should be considered closed.
Analysts have compared Smith’s tactics with those of former British prime minister David Cameron, who had hoped to resolve the debate over Britain’s European Union membership with a vote.
Carney led the Bank of England through the turmoil that surrounded Brexit, and issued a warning to Albertans about that experience on Oct 15.
“It wasn’t clear what ‘Brexit’ meant at the time,” he told a Calgary television station.
“For the next few years, while that was being determined, there was huge uncertainty, investments stopped, the economy started to underperform,” he added, cautioning over unintended economic consequences.
AI influence
The referendum on Oct 19 features 10 questions, including several related to immigration. But the focus is on question 10, which asks whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or it should take the legal steps required for a definitive independence vote.
Alberta’s election authority says ballots for question 10 will be counted first, with results expected in the early hours of Oct 20.
The pre-referendum period was clouded by avalanches of manipulated AI content.
Carney has urged “a decisive result”, but experts are concerned about a contested outcome no matter the numbers.
“A very likely result of this referendum is going to be a community that sees this election as stolen or at least unfair,” said Aengus Bridgman, director of the Media Ecosystem Observatory at McGill University.
Close Trump allies have also inserted themselves into the discussion, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who in January described Alberta as a “natural partner” for the US.
After a separatist party won Quebec’s provincial election on Oct 5, tech billionaire Elon Musk posted on X that “they would be better off” if they seceded. “Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too,” he added.
Asked about alleged foreign interference, Carney said on Oct 15 that foreign governments, including the US, should not “get themselves involved in our elections”. AFP
