Israeli police propose 800-officer force to tackle nationalist violence in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
23:15:38 UTC
08:15:38 KST

Rising incidents of friction, violence and nationalist crime in Area C of the West Bank, along with coordination gaps between the police, IDF and Shin Bet security agency, have prompted Judea and Samaria District police commander Moshe Pinchi to develop a new operational plan. The proposal comes amid growing concerns that the police and military, with their limited forces deployed in the area, are unable to adequately respond to the increasing number of incidents. It aims to address extremist violence while improving security and police services for law-abiding residents of the West Bank.
At the heart of the proposal, which has yet to receive approval from the police commissioner and national security minister, is the establishment of "Brigade C," a joint interagency force designed to provide an effective, rapid and comprehensive response in areas where existing security arrangements have left gaps. As part of the planning process, police conducted an extensive survey of Area C, identifying flashpoints where a permanent presence could prevent violence before it occurs and ensure a rapid response when incidents do take place.
Under the proposal, which was presented to several security officials during its development, the force would not handle criminal offenses within Jewish communities but would focus instead on clashes in open areas. This would allow regional IDF brigade commanders to concentrate on combating terrorism, while Brigade C personnel would manage incidents of friction and violence. In effect, the plan would expand police capabilities under military authority.
The broader strategic concept of establishing a dedicated force in Area C was originally proposed by Maj. Gen. Yoram Halevi, head of the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), and was previously reported. However, no suitable framework was developed because such a force would have to operate under the military, which exercises governing authority in the West Bank. While Halevi's proposal focused primarily on the division of responsibilities, Pinchi's plan translates the concept into concrete operational measures.
The proposed force would include approximately 700 to 800 police officers and combat personnel, deployed across the West Bank from the southern Hebron Hills to northern Samaria.
The brigade would operate within territory under military jurisdiction and be administratively subordinate to the head of IDF Central Command, while providing full civilian policing capabilities. It would combine combat and police units with advanced investigative and intelligence capabilities, operating together from a joint command center. The arrangement is intended to establish, for the first time, a rapid and continuous operational, intelligence and investigative response to incidents ranging from public disturbances to terrorist attacks and nationalist crime.
One of the most significant changes in the proposed approach is the emphasis on maintaining a permanent presence on the ground to improve response times. Under the plan, the West Bank would be divided into several key operational zones covering major flashpoints, grazing areas and agricultural farms. Rather than dispatching forces from distant locations only after violence has escalated, brigade officers would conduct regular patrols around farms and grazing areas.
The new force would be established in stages, initially drawing personnel from existing Border Police companies operating in the West Bank. These officers would undergo accelerated training and transition to conventional district policing duties, alongside the recruitment of additional patrol officers and combat personnel.
Funding remains a point of disagreement. Police officials are demanding that the new unit be financed through the military budget, while the IDF maintains that the initiative is a national undertaking and should therefore be funded directly by the state.
The Israel Police said in response: "The plan, which has not yet been approved by the police commissioner and the minister, was developed in consultation with all relevant parties, from a national, interagency and institutional perspective. Its purpose is to present an effective proposal based on existing areas of responsibility under the law, integrating capabilities and authorities while addressing all the gaps identified during interagency discussions."

Balkan unrest: Albania burns as protests threaten its path to EU membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
23:01:40 UTC
08:01:40 KST

The wave of anti-government protests in Albania, a Balkan country hoping to join the European Union in the coming years, entered its sixth day Sunday, with Prime Minister Edi Rama refusing to resign as protesters demand. Rama insists the demonstrations threaten not his government but Albania's hopes of joining the EU, a move expected to dramatically improve living standards in the country.
The protests sweeping Albania since last Tuesday have been led by students angry over what they see as government corruption, a lack of job opportunities and poor education standards. The demonstrations began in the center of the capital, Tirana, but have since spread to other cities. Protesters demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings and banks, smashed storefront windows and torn up paving stones to throw at police officers.
The riots erupted after months of largely peaceful demonstrations that began over the summer and became known as the "flamingo protests." The pink bird became a symbol of the movement, whose participants protested a luxury real estate development along Albania's coastline led by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, the son-in-law and daughter of U.S. President Donald Trump. The current wave of demonstrations grew out of that earlier protest movement and now poses the greatest challenge yet to Rama's rule. He has governed Albania since 2013 and won a fourth term in office last year.
Violence flared again Sunday when thousands gathered outside Albania's Education Ministry and hurled stones at police, who responded with tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets. Protesters later dispersed across the city center, where clashes continued for several hours. Demonstrators set trash bins ablaze, smashed windows, including at the headquarters of the ruling Socialist Party, and set fire to a police station and the entrance to the Interior Ministry. Since the riots began last Tuesday, 272 people have been injured, including 169 police officers, and charges have been filed against 388 people.
Responding to the protests Sunday, Rama warned that the violence would harm neither him nor his government but rather Albania's prospects of joining the European Union, a process in which the country has made significant progress.
"I am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged," Rama said. "Albanians need to think very clearly: Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the European Union?"
As on previous days, Rama again accused groups serving foreign interests, which he did not identify, of being behind the protests. He also referred to what he described as an attempted drone attack on his office last week. Rama claims that an attack involving an explosives-laden drone intended to strike the prime minister's office and set fire to an inner courtyard containing a wooden structure was thwarted several days ago.
Rama did not identify those allegedly responsible for the attempted attack but blamed foreign actors. On Friday, he said the protest movement was "not a student phenomenon" and that "foreign hands that do not want Albania to be peaceful" were operating behind the scenes. His claims have not been independently verified, and neither police nor security officials have released details about the circumstances surrounding the alleged thwarted attack.
The European Commission, the EU's executive arm, has condemned the violence in Tirana and other Albanian cities in recent days. In a statement issued over the weekend, the Commission stressed that the authorities' response must remain proportionate.
"In a candidate country firmly committed to the EU accession process and making important progress on its EU path, grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner," the statement said.
Alongside Montenegro, Albania is among the leading Balkan countries seeking EU membership and aims to join the bloc by 2030.
One of the key requirements for EU membership is a determined fight against corruption. Corruption scandals have repeatedly tarnished Albania's reputation, and analysts say the country has become a hub for criminal gangs seeking to launder proceeds from drug and arms trafficking. Rama, however, insists that his government is fighting corruption more aggressively than ever before.

“It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say,” Obama said in his post.
“But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing.”
Federal agents searched Omar’s Washington home and issued subpoenas to relatives in October, scouring her family’s history for evidence of fraud and false statements in immigration paperwork.

She has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing on immigration matters.
In the weeks before elections, federal law enforcement officials typically avoid taking overt investigative steps, like executing search warrants and issuing subpoenas, that could be seen as trying to help or hurt a candidate.
The search and subpoenas, coming weeks before the midterm elections and as US President Donald Trump has issued attacks against Omar, have raised questions about whether the investigation was ramping up because of political pressure from the White House.
Obama said it was. “The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticise the president,” he wrote. NYTIMES

FATF Has Declared War on Fraud. Not All Its Allies Can Afford to Fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

FATF Has Declared War on Fraud. Not All Its Allies Can Afford to Fight
The UK is right to put fraud at the heart of its FATF presidency. Success will require source countries to have the means to act.
In the week commencing 26 October, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) will meet in Paris for its first plenary under UK leadership. The organisation’s founding is inextricably linked to the 1980s cocaine boom, which saw unprecedented flows of dirty money pour into the legitimate financial system. In response, FATF drew up 40 Recommendations for countries to implement to protect the global financial system from criminal actors. The more than 200 jurisdictions which have committed to uphold these Recommendations are assessed by their peers through periodic ‘Mutual Evaluations’. Countries found during their assessment to have fallen short of their obligations risk being placed on the ‘grey list’, which can deter investment and raise the cost of banking with other economies.
Over the years, FATF’s Recommendations have helped countries build and use their anti-money laundering infrastructure to make it harder for drug traffickers, terrorists and kleptocrats to abuse the financial system. Yet, in almost four decades of existence, no presidency has built its agenda so explicitly around a single underlying crime as the UK is doing now with fraud.
FATF’s emphasis on fraud reflects the scale of the current global scams industry, which cost an estimated $442 billion in 2025 and now generates profits to rival those of the drugs trade. But whether the UK’s agenda succeeds will depend less on the capabilities of the advanced economies around the table in Paris, and more on the countries outside the room which represent jurisdictions where fraudsters often set up shop. These countries are not FATF members but are held to its standards all the same, and following unprecedented reductions in development assistance many are facing the sharpest fiscal squeeze in decades.
A Threat Rooted Overseas
Fraud is among the most pressing threats developed countries such as the UK, the US, Australia and Singapore face. Sophisticated criminal networks are siphoning billions of pounds from their citizens each year, and in so doing fuelling their ‘polycriminality’ which spill into human trafficking, corruption and even terrorism. Some countries, the UK included, have penned impressive and all-encompassing domestic strategies, but they can only go so far. The UK Home Office estimates that two-thirds of fraud targeting Brits originates overseas, much of it from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with the conditions the UN says allow scam operations to take root: high economic informality, weak institutions, established criminal groups and fast-growing use of digital platforms. Dismantling the networks behind the fraud epidemic, therefore, means working with the governments and police forces of the countries where fraudsters operate.
Aid Cuts and Competing Priorities
However, the steepest fall in the history of official development assistance has left many governments in the developing world reeling, and all but crippled their ability to respond to other, more existential crises. By one estimate, LMICs are projected to suffer an additional 9.4 million deaths by 2030, and this year the World Food Programme estimates 266 million people are at risk of acute hunger. No minister worth their salt would divert scarce resources to anti-fraud policies favouring the priorities of the world’s wealthiest economies while facing malnutrition on such a scale.
This is not to say that developed countries are the only victims of fraud; far from it. The Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA) estimates citizens of developing countries are more likely to lose money to scams, and that their economies lose a larger relative share of GDP to fraud. Speak to officials in these countries and they know all too well how scams are damaging their economies and shaking their citizens’ faith in institutions. Often, what they lack is not political will, but rather, the means to fight back. Asking them to prioritise fraud without offering tangible support risks producing the kind of box-ticking (whereby countries pass laws in a bid to satisfy assessors without changing much in practice) which FATF has spent most of the past decade trying to stamp out.
Building on Existing Foundations
As our research at RUSI has shown, taking the first steps towards building a more effective anti-fraud response in these countries need not incur massive costs. The financial intelligence units, reporting obligations and central bank powers which FATF itself has spent nearly four decades persuading countries to build can be turned towards fraud, a crime which is far more visible and politically salient than many of the other offences which FATF has exhorted countries to consider.
That said, while the infrastructure FATF has encouraged countries to build provides the means to get started, scaling up efforts is another matter entirely. Freezing the mule accounts moving stolen money is one thing; dismantling the complex web of criminal networks running scam campaigns is quite another. For most jurisdictions, mounting an effective national response capable of plugging into international efforts will require drafting new laws, training specialist investigators and creating new channels for banks, telcos and police to share information safely. It is in these more substantive reforms where the true costs lie, and where cuts to government budgets are likely to hamper ambitions.
Who Should Foot the Bill?
So when FATF asks jurisdictions to treat fraud as a priority this month, it should ask something of its richer members too: help the countries struggling to confront this global epidemic with the associated costs. This is not charity. When the scams emptying British, American and Australian bank accounts are run from abroad, building other countries’ capacity to fight fraud is among the most cost-effective ways to protect people at home.
The mechanism could be a dedicated fund along the lines of the World Bank’s Cybersecurity Multi-Donor Trust Fund. Alternatively, FATF could encourage members to expand their use of bilateral partnerships, such as those the UK already has with Vietnam and Nigeria. To get started, the new presidency should use this month’s plenary to secure a joint commitment from members to put a share of the proceeds they recover from fraud towards building other countries’ capacity, making the scammers pay for their own undoing.
FATF cannot command its members to write cheques, nor should it try; but it can use its influence and importance in the global anti-financial crime community to drive forward the necessary response. If the UK uses its presidency to make the case to its FATF peers that funding other countries’ fight against fraud is one of the greatest acts of self-defence, it will have done more than any domestic strategy could alone. If, however, it declares a ‘war on fraud’ without helping to arm its allies, it risks getting only the bare minimum in return, and the scammers will continue to drain both bank accounts and trust in the financial system along with them.

Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with top US envoys Sunday to try to ease tensions, as Donald Trump accused his counterpart of not wanting to end the war with Russia.
Zelensky spoke to US officials Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other's energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Saint Petersburg since the start of the war in 2022.
Trump and Zelensky have clashed as the US president blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow.
On Sunday Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating a peace between Russia and Ukraine and making "great progress," but claimed: "Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him... he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said.
Earlier, after speaking to Trump's business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelensky said "a lot depends" on the US position in the war but that "it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end."
Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly", he said. "We expect exactly this approach from all our partners -- both from the Europeans and, of course, from the American side."
He said he discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defence systems, as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
Zelensky earlier told US broadcaster NBC it would be a "historic mistake" if Washington formally supported Russia and that he hoped Trump would "change his decisions."
But he also said he was "thankful" the US resumed intelligence sharing after a pause that left his country vulnerable to Russian missile strikes.
Thousands without power
A US-led push to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II has so far not brought about a breakthrough and Trump has in the past grown frustrated with both Zelensky and Russia's Vladimir Putin because of their lack of progress.
Zelensky spoke to the American officials as he accused Russia of breaking Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warning Moscow planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power in several regions, he said, with Ukrainian officials reporting three people had been killed.
Ukraine's army launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg's historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit and Ozon -- Russia's second largest retailer -- also reported a strike on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the war.
'Dreadful routine of war'
The Kremlin, however, said Ukrainian attacks on its cities will not change its war aims.
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine and, in a fifth year of war, few see a way out of the conflict.
"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking -- it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
Sergei, another Saint Petersburg resident who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
"I don't know if I was scared, what must be will be," he said.
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.

Venezuela opposition renews support for Maria Corina Machado as leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:41:49 UTC
07:41:49 KST

Venezuela opposition renews support for Maria Corina Machado as leader
The exiled Nobel laureate has petitioned for new elections in Venezuela and for the country to allow her return.
An alliance of Venezuelan opposition parties has reaffirmed its commitment to exiled Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado as its leader.
On Sunday, members of the opposition’s Unitary Democratic Platform (PUD) agreed in a meeting in Caracas to “recognise and support the leadership of Maria Corina Machado”.
The coalition also renewed its demand for free elections in Venezuela, following a series of contested presidential votes in 2024 and 2018.
Sunday’s statement included 14 proposals for a democratic transition, including freedom for political parties, the release of all political prisoners and the safe return of those who went into exile.
The announcement also increases pressure on authorities to allow Machado’s return. She has been living in exile since leaving Venezuela last December to receive her Nobel Prize.
“The will of the Venezuelans must once again govern the destiny of our nation,” the opposition’s former presidential candidate Edmundo Gonzalez wrote on social media supporting the proposals.
“We will not accept political prisoners, persecution or a governing power that disregards the mandate of its citizens. Living in freedom and under a genuine constitutional order is a legitimate demand of our society.”
No election set
Venezuela has yet to declare a date for a new presidential vote. Since January 3, the country has been led by interim President Delcy Rodriguez of the long-governing United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV).
PSUV leaders have been accused of carrying out human rights abuses against political dissidents, including arbitrary arrest, imprisonment and torture.
Still, after the United States launched a military operation to abduct and jail former President Nicolas Maduro, the PSUV has remained in power with the support of the White House.
US President Donald Trump has backed Rodriguez’s leadership, despite her having been Maduro’s vice president.
His administration has maintained an active role in Venezuela, exerting control over its oil resources and pressuring the Rodriguez government for reforms.
But critics point out that Trump has been reluctant to push Rodriguez for new elections, opting instead for a three-phase plan that focuses first on stabilising the country and economic recovery before pursuing a political transition.
Machado, meanwhile, has told The Financial Times she would like to see Venezuela hold elections by July next year.
“The US government and the Venezuelan people all agree that the only way to make this sustainable and a real victory is to turn Venezuela into a stable democracy,” she told the newspaper earlier this month.
A thwarted return
Venezuelan authorities blocked Machado’s repeated attempts to return to the country, according to her party, Vente Venezuela.
Machado has also reportedly attempted to petition the Trump administration for help re-entering Venezuela.
Separately, she gifted Trump her Nobel Peace Prize in January, during a visit to Washington, DC. Media reports, however, have suggested friction between the Trump administration and Machado.
In interviews with Reuters and Axios, US administration officials have anonymously expressed frustration with the opposition leader’s repeated efforts to return home, particularly after a pair of deadly earthquakes in Venezuela last July.
Axios quoted one official as calling Machado’s push “political opportunism”.
Machado, however, remains one of the most popular figures in Venezuela’s opposition.
In October 2023, Machado won the opposition coalition’s presidential primary, but in January 2024, Venezuela’s courts blocked her from running in the upcoming race.
The courts upheld a 15-year ban on her holding public office, reportedly due to her support of US sanctions against the Maduro government.
Gonzalez ultimately replaced Machado as the opposition candidate in the 2024 race. Maduro claimed victory for a third term as Venezuela’s president in that election cycle, despite widespread criticism that the vote did not meet democratic standards.
The opposition released vote tallies that appeared to show Gonzalez had won the race.
The US had recognised Gonzalez as the country’s rightful president-elect and denied the legitimacy of Maduro’s election claims.
Machado was previously removed from the National Assembly in 2014, due to her activism against the Venezuelan government.
A third round of talks between the Rodriguez government and the opposition began in Venezuela this month.
But instead of including Machado, the negotiations have involved members of the 2015 National Assembly, which was led by the opposition and dissolved under Maduro.
Still, in a statement this month, the US State Department praised the talks as aiding the Venezuelan government’s reform.
“Political reconciliation talks between the interim Venezuelan government and 2015 National Assembly representatives are producing tangible reforms in civil liberties and political rights, laying the groundwork for credible elections and a democratic transition,” the State Department said.

Roundup: Houthis, Saudi-led coalition trade fresh strikes as Egypt pledges support for Saudi Arabia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
06:25:59 CST
07:25:59 KST

RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Fighting between Yemen's Houthis and government forces intensified on Sunday, as a Houthi attack injured six people in Saudi Arabia and Egypt pledged support to the kingdom amid rising regional tensions.
INJURIES, DAMAGES IN SAUDI ARABIA
The Saudi Civil Defense said Sunday that six Saudi citizens were injured, and three houses and three vehicles were damaged after a projectile launched by Yemen's Houthi group struck a residential area in Najran, southern Saudi Arabia.
The civil defense noted that attempts to target civilian objects constitute a "flagrant violation of international humanitarian law."
In separate statements earlier on Sunday, Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said three drones were intercepted and destroyed, two over the Riyadh region and one over the Eastern Province. He also confirmed that two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis targeting the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted and destroyed.
INTENSIFIED FIGHTING IN YEMEN
Fighting between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government has intensified on several fronts.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said in a statement posted on social media platform X that a total of 110 strikes targeted areas in Sanaa and the provinces of Hodeidah, Taiz and Marib over the past 24 hours, leaving more than 30 people killed or injured.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia or the Saudi-led coalition on the Houthi claims.
Majid Al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the government forces, said in a statement posted on X that the government forces had carried out 1,326 strikes against Houthi targets across several battlefronts over the past 24 hours, as they pressed ahead with a major offensive against the group.
Government troops and allied fighters captured several positions in the southwestern province of Taiz and seized heavy weapons and other military equipment, according to Al-Nuzaili.
The spokesperson claimed that "about 370 Houthi fighters had been neutralized" and dozens of military vehicles destroyed during the operations.
The figures could not be independently verified, and the Houthis have not immediately commented on the claims.
EGYPT PLEDGES SUPPORT
The escalating hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia continue to raise growing concerns across the region.
Egypt's National Defense Council decided on Sunday, during a meeting chaired by President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, to provide Saudi Arabia with "all necessary and possible" forms of support to defend the kingdom's security and stability, the Egyptian presidency said.
The council pledged to help safeguard the kingdom's resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites, according to the presidency's statement, adding that the "escalating" attacks against the Kingdom were unacceptable.
Meanwhile, the council decided to continue and intensify political and diplomatic efforts, in coordination with relevant regional and international parties, to contribute to "de-escalating tensions across the entire region and achieving peaceful resolutions to ongoing regional crises."
On Saturday, Sisi said Egypt was prepared to take "any measures" requested by Saudi Arabia to defend the kingdom's security and sovereignty, calling for an emergency parliamentary session to authorize intervention if requested.
On Sunday, the House of Representatives concluded its session, chaired by House of Representatives Speaker Hisham Badawi, with deliberations set to resume on Monday, according to the local news website Masrawy.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Sunday on X that he and his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah Al Saud discussed current regional developments and the importance of de-escalation during a phone call.
President of the United Arab Emirates Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan received Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, with the two sides exchanging views on regional developments and ways to strengthen security and stability and achieve lasting peace in the region, the Emirates News Agency reported.
Also on Sunday, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi called for effective international action to halt Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia at a meeting of the GCC Ministerial Council in the Bahraini capital Manama.
In the final communique issued after the meeting, the GCC reaffirmed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and support for all measures taken by the kingdom to safeguard its sovereignty, security and interests, stressing that the security of GCC member states is indivisible. ■

TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- The navy of Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) announced early Monday that a "violating" oil tanker suffered a blast within the preceding hours after hitting a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement published on the IRGC's official news outlet Sepah News, the navy said the blast caused a fire in the oil tanker's engine room.
It added that the vessel had turned off its GPS and navigation systems and, in disregard of the regulations, was seeking to exit the strait through the "unauthorized" route south of the waterway.

Jacqui Lambie slams 'nasty' One Nation cartoon mocking vaginal prolapse

Jacqui Lambie slams 'nasty' One Nation cartoon mocking vaginal prolapse
In short:
A new One Nation cartoon ridicules outspoken independent senator Jacqui Lambie by mocking her vaginal prolapse.
Senator Lambie says Pauline Hanson's videos are full of "hatred" and "spitefulness".
What's next?
Politicians have condemned the cartoon, while One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says Senator Lambie should "get over it".
Jacqui Lambie has hit back at Pauline Hanson's "nastiness" after a One Nation cartoon mocked the independent senator's health condition.
Senator Lambie gave an emotional speech in the Senate in August, revealing she had a vaginal and bladder prolapse, which required surgery and five months of leave from parliament.
The One Nation cartoon is one in a series of satirical videos that mock politicians and take aim at recent political events.
The latest cartoon uses Senator Lambie's vaginal prolapse as a punchline.
The Tasmanian senator said people were welcome to watch Senator Hanson's videos "if you want more hatred, more spitefulness in your life".
"But what I do know is this: decent leaders don't stir up hatred, pushing us towards bloody anarchy, because that's exactly what she's doing," Senator Lambie told ABC's Radio National.
Senator Lambie said she would not be demanding One Nation remove the video, but called on Senator Hanson's team, especially the men, to ask her to remove it immediately.
"If you think it's a laughable matter about women having problems with their reproductive system, then you be my guest and you stand by her,"
she said.
"But seriously, enough is enough."
Senator Lambie had previously said the condition was directly linked to back injuries she sustained in the army.
On Monday, Senator Hanson said Senator Lambie should "get over it", insisting the video was satirical.
Asked whether the cartoon was appropriate, Senator Hanson said it had "opened" the eyes of women who "may be suffering" and helped raise awareness of women's health issues.
"I think she is taking it to heart, which she shouldn't be," she said.
"Have a bit of a laugh, Jacqui, and lighten up."
Loading...
Politicians stand with Lambie
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Liberal senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price are among a number of politicians who have publicly condemned the One Nation cartoon.
All praised Senator Lambie's courage in talking about a deeply personal health issue to raise awareness.
In a comment on social media, Mr Albanese thanked Senator Lambie for her "courage which will help others".
Senator Nampijinpa Price said the attack was in "bad taste", and said politicians should "play the ball, not the person".
"I don't like women being ridiculed for very personal issues," she said.
Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy called for the video to be taken down.
"Senator Lambie, who's a fine public servant committed to serving the public, has been open and honest about her health challenges in a way to raise awareness [of] … these conditions. That's incredibly brave of her," he said.
"So for her to be mocked by One Nation just shows, quite frankly, what they stand for."
Independent MP Monique Ryan said pelvic organ prolapse affected many women and was often linked to physical strain, heavy lifting or past childbirth.
"One Jacqui Lambie is worth 1,000 Pauline Hansons," she wrote.
It is not the first time One Nation's cartoons have sparked a political firestorm.
Last month, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie slammed One Nation for a cartoon that repeatedly described him as a "traitor".
Mr Hastie, a veteran like Senator Lambie, criticised Senator Hanson and called for the cartoon to be removed, a move that was backed widely across the political spectrum.
"I think that shows Pauline Hanson's hypocrisy. She cried a river for Gina Rinehart when the ABC had a satirical skit played on one of your programs and demanded that it be taken down," he told ABC.
"I think the double standard is ridiculous. It's a cheap, nasty and vulgar attack on Jacqui Lambie's health condition and if she had any decency, she would apologise and pull it down."
Mr Hastie also questioned whether taxpayer funds would be used to roll out cartoons to attack One Nation's political opponents if the party won government.
Pelvic health issues 'not a punchline'
Women's health advocates have slammed the "absolutely disgusting" cartoon, arguing it reinforces stigma surrounding pelvic health issues.
Birth Trauma Australia CEO Amy Dawes said hundreds of thousands of Australian women were impacted by pelvic floor dysfunction.
"Women's health conditions cannot become a subject of public ridicule … [or] a punchline of a joke," Ms Dawes said.
"[This cartoon] sends a message to women that their pain, that their bodies and their health concerns are acceptable targets for humiliation.
"We're working so hard to increase awareness … but this just seems like a gigantic step back."
Health experts have said prolapse and pelvic floor disorders affect as many as one in four women.
Ms Dawes said pelvic organ prolapse and bladder incontinence could have a "profound impact" on a woman's physical health, confidence, quality of life and relationships.
"This is about dignity, it's about health awareness and the message we send to women everywhere," she said.
"If we start to make fun of these conditions, we further exacerbate this stigma, we further increase barriers to people seeking support."

Macron denounces ‘unbridled’ violence as France hit by new clashes
President Emmanuel Macron on Oct 18 slammed the “unbridled” violence that erupted in cost-of-living protests across France, as police battled protesters and looters in new clashes in Paris.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested on Oct 17 in unrest that represented some of the worst urban violence in France in years, with almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, seven seriously, the interior ministry said.
In an address to the nation, Macron said local authorities would be able to ban – “if necessary” – certain rallies in coming days. But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew.
“Tonight, we all feel anger and shame,” Macron said of the devastation brought by the protests that include town halls burned down and hundreds of businesses looted or damaged.
Milan police clash with protesters on second day of unrest
Youth and police clashed for a second day on Oct 18 in Milan, where mostly black-clad assailants hurled bottles, ransacked stores, and destroyed property around the central Duomo plaza.
Police in the northern city have arrested more than 200 people since Oct 17, according to Ansa news agency.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called for a security meeting on Oct 19 to address the violence, which resembled some scenes of chaos and looting in Paris.
Kenya confirms eighth Ebola case as regional outbreak spreads
Kenya has confirmed one more Ebola case, bringing the total number of infections in the country to eight, Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said on Oct 18.
“Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive for Ebola,” Amoth said in an interview on Kenya’s Citizen TV.
“He is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker. He developed fever, headache and muscle pain.”
Trump says Washington golf course renovation to start in November, despite judge’s order
President Donald Trump on Oct 18 unveiled his plans for overhauling a beloved municipal golf course in the US capital, a project already mired in a contentious legal fight.

“When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the US Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” Trump said.
McLaren to sell five F1 cars, all driven by champions and one by Brad Pitt

The cars, to be sold through high-end dealer Tom Hartley Jr and expected to raise tens of millions of dollars, will be prepared by the reigning constructors’ champions for their next owners.

Alberta independence referendum: Will separatists survive a loss?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
21:53:13 UTC
06:53:13 KST

Alberta independence referendum: Will separatists survive a loss?
Alberta’s independence movement faces likely defeat, but history suggests losing a referendum may not end the fight.
Cory Morgan has spent more than 25 years fighting for Canada’s oil-rich province of Alberta to become an independent country. On Monday, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on the issue for the very first time. But even if the answer is no, Morgan said he’s in it for the long haul.
“I would respect the will of the voters,” he told Al Jazeera. “If they’ve decided it’s not time to go that route yet, then so be it. But that doesn’t mean I’ll stop.”
Morgan, the founder of the advocacy organisation Pathway to Independence, is among a group of longtime separatists who have managed to push what was once a fringe idea onto the ballot.
Monday’s provincial referendum asks Alberta residents to weigh whether they would like to pursue a binding resolution in the future on the question of independence.
Polls indicate the pro-independence side has little chance of succeeding, with four of five people in the province saying they want Alberta to remain a part of Canada. But Morgan’s focus is on the one in five who don’t.
“That’s not a movement that’s leaving,” he said.
What the referendum will mean for the separatist movement and for Canada as a whole, however, is a more complicated question.
What exactly are Albertans voting on?
Monday’s ballot gives Albertans two options: to remain part of Canada or begin the legal process for holding a future referendum on separation.
A vote in favour of the second option doesn’t mean Alberta immediately becomes an independent country.
Any province that tries to secede would first have to go through complex negotiations with the federal government in Ottawa, other provinces and Indigenous peoples who live in and around Alberta.
Some separatist organisers have been using that distinction to encourage people to vote for the referendum — even if they don’t necessarily want independence.
“Strategic separatists and their leaders have been using that ambiguity, that lower-bar threshold, to entice folks to vote not to leave, but rather to send Ottawa a message that Albertans need to be heard,” said Jared Wesley, a political science professor at the University of Alberta.
He told Al Jazeera that the message may be resonating with some voters.
Data collected by Viewpoint Alberta, a University of Alberta-based research initiative, suggests that two-thirds of voters who support the referendum say they’re doing so for strategic reasons, to send a message to Ottawa.
These are people Morgan calls “reluctant separatists”, people who are “at the end of their rope” and simply want Ottawa to pay attention.
But Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned Albertans against this strategy.
“Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote,” he told a pro-Canada rally in Calgary on Thursday. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.”
What’s driving Alberta’s separatist movement?
Monday’s referendum has been decades in the making. Separatists have long felt that Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, sends too much money to Ottawa, subsidising the rest of the country while receiving little in return.
They also take issue with federal energy policies that they feel limit the potential of the province’s oil industry.
For Morgan, the resentment stretches back to the 1980s when the National Energy Program was introduced by the government of Pierre Trudeau, former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s father.
The policy used price controls, taxes and ownership rules to keep Canadian energy affordable while directing more of Alberta’s revenues to Ottawa.
It has since become a central symbol of “Western alienation”, a term used to describe the sense of disenfranchisement felt among Canada’s westernmost provinces.
Those tensions resurfaced decades later under Justin Trudeau, whose term began in 2015. His climate policies, including a national carbon tax and a limit on emissions, angered Alberta’s oil sector.
“We’ve been fighting about the same things for 50 years,” said Morgan.
Then came the COVID-19 pandemic. Experts say demonstrations against health restrictions mobilised a new generation of conservative activists, breathing new life into Alberta’s separatist movement.
Trudeau ultimately resigned as Liberal Party leader and prime minister in 2025, amid sinking poll numbers. Carney was elected his replacement.
Last year, under growing pressure from separatist groups, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s government made it easier to start referendums, helping bring the question of Alberta’s independence onto the political agenda.
For Wesley, the moment is less about growing public support for independence and more about pressure from within Smith’s governing United Conservative Party, whose members show higher support for separation than Albertans generally.
“We’re having a referendum because Danielle Smith wants us to have a referendum,” Wesley said. “She is looking to solve internal party matters by throwing a question to the broader public.”
Though she called Monday’s referendum, Smith has said she opposes the independence effort, and on October 14, she announced she had voted against seceding.
“In my view, now is not the time to give up hope in our country, not when we have fought so long and come so far,” Smith said in a social media video, explaining her vote.
Could defeat make the movement stronger?
Smith’s political gamble has drawn comparisons with the 2016 Brexit referendum in the United Kingdom, including from Carney.
At the time, then-UK Prime Minister David Cameron called a vote over whether the country should leave the European Union, in hopes of settling a debate dividing his own Conservative Party.
Voters ultimately chose to leave the bloc, triggering years of political unrest.
But Ian Cooper, a political scientist who grew up in Alberta and now lives in Ireland, says a more useful comparison might be a different UK referendum in 1975, when British voters chose overwhelmingly to stay in what was then known as the European Economic Community.
That vote, he said, did little to deter those who wanted the country out.
“The activists who were in favour of Brexit — this is before anybody called it Brexit — they really played the long game,” he said. “It took them 25 years, but they finally achieved it.”
Cooper suspects that, even if Alberta separation is roundly defeated, separatists could take a similar approach, pursuing the issue over the long term to gain prominence and support.
“My impression is that they really are true believers, and it’s really ideologically driven,” he said.
If Monday’s separatist vote fails, Morgan said separatists would need to take a hard look at why they had fallen short and work towards making a stronger case for independence in the future.
He does not believe the underlying grievances can be resolved by working within the Canadian system or by electing a more sympathetic federal government.
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, acknowledged at Thursday’s rally that “the frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real”. He added that Ottawa had made people in the province feel “like our resources weren’t our own”.
The prime minister has tried, amid an ongoing trade war with the United States, to improve relations with Alberta, including through commitments to building a new pipeline to Canada’s west coast and major infrastructure projects.
Morgan admits that, for those whose goal is simply to get more leverage in Ottawa, “it’s pretty clear the movement has been effective”.
“We’ve seen more love from a federal prime minister in the last year than we’ve seen in the last 10,” Morgan said. “The problem though, when it comes to stubborn independence folks like me, is nothing has changed in the system.”
Prime ministers come and go, he added. “We’re just one election away from another hostile one.”
Why the other referendum questions matter
But the referendum could also offer an opportunity to challenge the premise that Alberta’s grievances cannot be addressed within Canada.
The independence question is just one of 10 on Monday’s ballot. Other proposals include restricting temporary residents’ access to healthcare and education, as well as allowing Alberta to choose its own judges.
Smith has encouraged Albertans to vote in favour of the nine other proposals, arguing that they will give her more negotiating power in Ottawa.
“Many Albertans I speak with tell me they want to send Ottawa a message, and I would suggest the best way to do that is to give us a strong mandate on the other nine questions,” she said on social media.
If Albertans back those proposals but Ottawa refuses to make concessions, Cooper, the political scientist, said the movement would have fresh ammunition to argue that meaningful change within the current system is impossible.
“Buried in the nine other questions are the seeds for a future referendum,” Cooper added.
What could keep the movement alive?
Not everyone agrees, however, on whether the separatists can emerge from the vote as a united force.
Wesley explained that people have been drawn to the separatist cause for a variety of reasons.
If there’s a sense that independence is not a realistic prospect, there may be little to keep that group of activists together, he said. They could turn their attention to other conservative issues, such as immigration.
Other experts question whether Alberta’s separatist movement, which is united more by economic grievances than by a shared cultural identity, can endure the way Quebec’s has.
Just two weeks ago, the largely French-speaking province elected the separatist Party Quebecois, which has promised a third referendum on independence after Trump leaves office.
Morgan, however, argues that Alberta does have a distinct culture, shaped by generations of people who have moved to the province in search of prosperity.
“The type of person drawn to do that is often an individualistic type of person,” he said. “They want the opportunity to go out and succeed or fail on their own.”
“And that builds a kind of a distinct culture on its own, even if it’s not a long-built one, as you would see in a distinct area like Quebec with a linguistic difference or in another country.”
Even if Albertans reject separation, he believes the movement has succeeded in forcing Ottawa to take the province’s frustrations more seriously.
“Hopefully some people understand that eventually something has to give,” he said. “So whatever the results are … I do hope, at the very least, they’ve served as a wake-up call to a lot of people.”

Bomb threat forces airliner from Tel Aviv to divert to Bulgaria
SOFIA – A bomb threat against an Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Oct 18 forced the plane to divert to Bulgaria, according to the Bulgarian authorities and the airline.
The Austrian Airlines crew decided to make an emergency landing in Sofia after reportedly receiving a bomb threat as they neared Romania, Bulgaria’s transport ministry said in a statement, adding that the passengers were evacuated from the aircraft after landing.
The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner as part of established procedures, the transport ministry said.
The airline told AFP that 51 passengers and six crew were aboard the flight, and that a security search of the aircraft – an Airbus A320 – was launched after it safely landed in Sofia about a half hour after the threat.
“Once the search of the aircraft is complete, the passengers will be rebooked onto alternative flights as quickly as possible,” the airline said.
According to Flightradar24 data, the aircraft, registered OE-LZE, entered Romanian airspace at around 9.10pm local time before turning south and heading back towards Bulgaria, where it landed in Sofia.
Data from another flight-tracking platform, ADS-B Exchange, indicated that the aircraft was transmitting squawk code 7700 – a signal for a general emergency – at around the same time.
The transport ministry said a crisis response team has been set up and the relevant authorities have launched an investigation into the incident.
In a separate incident in late September, the co-pilot aboard a flydubai flight headed to Tel Aviv from Dubai attacked the captain and allegedly planned to crash the plane, but was stopped by the captain, passengers and crew.
Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert. AFP

Drone crash prompts Lithuania to launch security meeting
China
Unknown Publisher

05:36:29 CST
06:36:29 KST

VILNIUS, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius called a meeting of the National Security Commission for Monday after a drone crashed in the northern region and damaged a civilian vehicle on Sunday, public broadcaster LRT reported.
Media reports said the drone entered the country from Poland and caused no casualties. Lithuanian authorities began tracking it around 6:00 a.m. local time (0300 GMT) as it flew north across much of the country. Air alerts were issued in parts of Lithuania shortly after 7:00 a.m. (0400 GMT), with red alerts subsequently declared in Siauliai and Panevezys counties.
NATO air-policing fighter jets responded from Siauliai Air Base to intercept the drone, but poor weather conditions prevented the pilots from locating the target.
For unknown reasons, the drone crashed, with its debris striking the door of a moving civilian vehicle. The driver escaped unhurt, according to Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre.
After the incident, Sinkevicius announced the meeting plan, demanding that investigators examine the possibility of sabotage and establish the drone's origin, flight path and the circumstances surrounding its detection by military radar.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said he had contacted his Polish counterpart and asked Poland to join the investigation. ■

Macron vows legal action against perpetrators of violence in France protests
China

Glass shattered during a protest is seen on a street in Paris, France, Oct. 18, 2026. French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday vowed legal action against those responsible for violence during protests across the country on Saturday. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo)
PARIS, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday vowed legal action against those responsible for violence during protests across the country on Saturday.
"Those who destroyed must pay. Those who looted must reimburse," Macron said in a televised address, pledging judicial proceedings over offenses committed during the violence.
He voiced support for law enforcement officers, elected officials and shopkeepers affected by the violence, adding that Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu would chair a crisis unit Monday to mobilize "the fastest possible assistance" and support those affected.
He called on the government to draw all the lessons from Saturday's violence, particularly regarding intelligence gathering and anticipation, to ensure such incidents "cannot happen again."
Meanwhile, Macron said he understood the "deep anxiety" expressed by young people in recent weeks at high schools and universities, adding that over the coming week, the government would work with students, teachers, trade unions, employers' organizations and officials to develop responses to young people's concerns.
Macron said the protests also reflected public concerns over the cost of living and fuel prices. He said the government was doing its utmost to address the key issue of residents' purchasing power.
Around 550,000 people took part in protests across France on Saturday. According to local media reports, the demonstrations brought together farmers, climate activists, trade unions and students, who voiced demands concerning fuel prices, the cost of living, education and public services.
A total of 2,397 people were arrested during the protests, which were marred by violence, according to figures released by the French Interior Ministry on Sunday. A total of 997 police officers and gendarmes were injured, seven of them seriously.
Since September, France has witnessed multiple rounds of mass student protests demanding better educational conditions. ■

Chinese FM holds talks with Montenegrin counterpart
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
05:36:23 CST
06:36:23 KST

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, holds talks with Montenegrin Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic in Podgorica, Montenegro, Oct. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Shi Zhongyu)
PODGORICA, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said here on Sunday that China is ready to expand practical cooperation and elevate ties with Montenegro to a higher level.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks during talks with Montenegrin Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic in Podgorica, the capital of Montenegro.
Wang said China and Montenegro are good friends despite the geographical distance. China was among the first countries to recognize Montenegro's independence and establish diplomatic relations with it, demonstrating China's respect for Montenegro and the importance it attaches to bilateral ties, he added.
Over the past 20 years, China-Montenegro relations have maintained sound and steady development, bringing benefits to both peoples and setting an example of win-win cooperation between countries with different sizes, national conditions and social systems, Wang said.
Wang said both countries share a history of anti-fascism and a national spirit of resilience and defiance in the face of aggression, noting that China is helping restore the Tara River Bridge featured in the famous Yugoslav film "The Bridge," which he believes will also connect the hearts of the two peoples.
Wang said China is ready to take the 20th anniversary of diplomatic relations as an opportunity to review the success of bilateral cooperation, elevate bilateral ties to a higher level on that basis, and explore an even better future for both countries over the next 20 years.
Wang said China supports Montenegro's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, supports the path of development and revitalization chosen by the Montenegrin people, and supports Montenegro in playing an active role in international affairs.
China has both the willingness and the capability to help Montenegro achieve development and stands ready to be a reliable and long-term partner, he said.
China appreciates Montenegro's commitment to the one-China principle and believes that the two countries will continue to support each other on issues concerning their respective core interests and major concerns, thus consolidating the political foundation for bilateral relations and creating important conditions for deeper cooperation, Wang said.
He added that China encourages Chinese enterprises to actively participate in Montenegro's infrastructure development and is ready to expand cooperation with Montenegro in tourism, energy, green transition and other areas.
On China-EU relations, Wang said China understands Montenegro's efforts to join the EU and hopes that Montenegro will become another good friend of China within the EU in the future.
China and the EU have maintained relations for more than half a century, and the essence of their cooperation is mutually beneficial and win-win, he added.
He said current differences in economic and trade areas have arisen in the course of cooperation and can be properly resolved through dialogue in the spirit of mutual respect, mutual understanding and mutual accommodation as China-EU relations continue to deepen.
Noting that the China-CEEC cooperation mechanism was established in response to the development needs of Central and Eastern European countries (CEECs), Wang said China pursues such cooperation without geopolitical considerations, does not interfere in the internal affairs of regional countries, and looks forward to mutually beneficial outcomes.
China welcomes Montenegro, as the lead country of the China-CEEC environmental protection cooperation mechanism, to play its due role in developing the mechanism, he said.
Noting that all Balkan countries are good friends of China and maintain sound cooperation with China, Wang expressed hope that countries in the region will live in harmony, build mutual trust and achieve common development.
For his part, Ibrahimovic said Montenegro and China enjoy a long-standing friendship, and despite the geographical distance, the two peoples share a strong sense of friendship, with the Tara River Bridge symbolizing their shared historical memories.
Noting that this year marks both the 20th anniversary of Montenegro's independence and the establishment of diplomatic relations with China, he said China's prompt recognition of Montenegro's independence demonstrated a solid foundation for the development of bilateral relations.
Ibrahimovic said Montenegro warmly welcomes the first-ever visit by a Chinese foreign minister, adding that frequent visits to China by Montenegrin representatives from various sectors have sent a positive signal of the country's commitment to exchanges and cooperation with China.
Montenegro firmly adheres to the one-China policy, and no official from any Montenegrin government institution will engage in exchanges with Taiwan, he stressed.
Ibrahimovic said bilateral relations have maintained sound momentum and yielded fruitful results in practical cooperation, with Chinese enterprises playing an important role in major infrastructure projects, including Montenegro's north-south expressway.
Montenegro welcomes continued support from Chinese enterprises for its infrastructure development and in exploring cooperation on major projects involving power plants, railways, airports and ports, he said.
Montenegro also stands ready to expand cooperation with China in tourism, film, education and scientific research, carry forward traditional friendship and open up broader prospects for bilateral relations, he added.
Ibrahimovic commended China's important role in promoting world peace and development and expressed Montenegro's willingness to further strengthen coordination with China in multilateral and international affairs. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has reaffirmed its continued support to Kenya following the confirmation of four additional Ebola cases, bringing the country's total caseload to seven.
Kenya's Ministry of Health on Saturday confirmed that all four new cases were detected among individuals already under quarantine following exposure to the initial case, as efforts to prevent community transmission of the hemorrhagic fever gather momentum.
In a statement issued late Saturday, the Africa CDC said that Kenya's early identification demonstrates the critical role of contact tracing, surveillance, and timely isolation in interrupting transmission and protecting communities.
The African Union's specialized continental public health agency also commended the Kenyan authorities for their "leadership, swift public health measures and transparent communication throughout the response."
"Africa CDC stands firmly alongside the government and people of Kenya, healthcare workers and all those affected by this outbreak," it said. "Protecting lives requires sustained vigilance, public trust, community engagement and coordinated action."
Noting that the evolving Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo reinforces the urgency of strong regional preparedness, the Africa CDC called on countries and partners to strengthen cross-border surveillance, information sharing, early detection and coordinated public health action across the continent.
The agency further encouraged communities to remain vigilant, follow guidance from national health authorities, and report symptoms promptly.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or bodily fluids of an infected person, or through contaminated materials. Early detection and access to appropriate care improve the chances of survival and help prevent further transmission, it said. ■

Netanyahu thanked Trump for his support in a post on X.
Trump told U.S. news outlet Axios in a phone interview on Sunday that he had begun planning the endorsement earlier this week.
Asked whether he could work with another Israeli leader, Trump said: "Maybe I will, maybe I won't. Who wants to take the chance?"
Israel is scheduled to hold parliamentary elections on Oct. 27, the country's first national vote since the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023.
Trump's endorsement came as Netanyahu faces a closely contested election. Most polls show his coalition falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government, according to Axios. ■

====================================================================================================

How much will Trump’s endorsement help Netanyahu? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
21:36:05 UTC
06:36:05 KST

Within minutes of President Donald Trump endorsing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a post on Truth Social Sunday, Netanyahu’s campaign team had released a 30-second clip showing all the times Trump has lavished praise on the Israeli leader over the past few years.
With polls showing that Netanyahu and his governing coalition are slipping in their struggle to retain power in the upcoming Oct. 27 election and lag behind the opposition bloc, an endorsement from the president of the United States is a powerful statement.
But is it enough to tip the scales?
“I don’t think it will change anything,” said Ilana Shpaizman, a senior lecturer in the Department of Political Studies at Bar-Ilan University.
Of course, she said, “Netanyahu will say this is the proof that I’m a leader and all that, and I can speak to Trump … But so what? His followers already know that and they believe in him. They don’t need the endorsement.”
Those who oppose him, Shpaizman continued, “know that Trump forced him (Netanyahu) to accept the ceasefire in Gaza and accept the hostage deal, and that Trump runs the show around Iran. So they also don’t need the endorsement either,” Shpaizman said.
Trump criticized for election interference
Some pundits speaking on Israeli news outlets criticized Trump for “interfering” in Israel’s election, while others put it down to the fact that Trump does not want America to return to fighting Iran alone if Netanyahu, who is hawkish on Iran, is replaced by someone less willing to act militarily. If Netanyahu loses, that is a scenario that could play out.
“This is the first time ever that the president, at least publicly, endorses a candidate in Israel’s election,” Bushinsky, a political commentator and former adviser to Netanyahu, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Bushinsky said he remembered Netanyahu complaining about US intervention in previous elections in 1999 and 2001, when presidents less enamored of him were in office. He even pushed for an initiative that would block foreign funding for election campaigns.
Now, Bushinsky said, “I guess he is not complaining,” adding that the endorsement serves Netanyahu in two ways.
First, it signals that Trump thinks that Netanyahu is the most suitable guy for the job. Second, it puts Netanyahu’s election campaign back on track, refocusing attention on an issue where Netanyahu is strong – Iran.
“It lets him say ‘I can now finish a job, and I can finish a job with Trump,’ and ‘without Trump or without me, the job will not be finished,’” said Bushinsky.
He said that in the last few days, the political debate had pivoted to other issues such as Ashkenazim vs Sephardim, the draft law and the contentious efforts by the outgoing government to overhaul the judiciary.
“This [endorsement] is the ultimate campaign boost for Netanyahu,” Bushinsky said.
But that boost might not be enough.
Opposition still polling ahead
Most of the polls taken in recent days show the opposition bloc led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot pulling ahead of Netanyahu’s ruling coalition, but give neither bloc enough seats to gain the necessary 61 of 120 seats in Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, to form the next government.
“I think this might give Netanyahu one more seat, one more mandate, but not more than that,” said Bushinsky.
Prof. Tamar Hermann, director of the Israel Democracy Institute’s Viterbi Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research, said that the timing of Trump’s support for Netanyahu in this election race had come both “too late and too early.”
“It’s too late because people have already decided electoral preferences. They may shift within each bloc, but will not move between the blocs because of this,” she said. “And it’s too early because there are nine days to go to the elections, and we can already see other American leaders spilling some cold water over what he said, even on the Republican side of the aisle.”
This criticism, Hermann continued, will be transmitted to Israeli voters, and they will see that Trump is facing a huge battle in the upcoming midterm elections.
“The image of President Trump has deteriorated significantly since April 26, when he started the negotiations with Iran,” she said, pointing to one of the IDI’s recent public opinion surveys that found the president’s popularity had plummeted after he stopped the war with Iran without totally removing the threats against the State of Israel.
According to that poll, the Israeli public’s confidence in Trump as someone dedicated to Israel’s security fell from around 70% to just 42%.
“In my view, the endorsement will not make a big change,” Hermann added. “It will just strengthen Netanyahu’s political supporters, who will see it as a sign that he is still the internationally known figure that even the president of the United States is endorsing.”
She concluded, “The meaning of endorsement in Israel is totally different than in the United States … we are not that used to this kind of move, and it will not make people change their minds.”

YEREVAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) opened on Sunday in Yerevan, the capital of Armenia, with countries set to conduct the first global review of collective progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF).
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan declared the conference open, calling for countries to translate their commitments into concrete actions and measurable results as the 2030 deadline for the framework's targets approaches.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, expressed hope that COP17 would demonstrate the multilateralism works and that the international community can fulfill its commitments.
She said the assessment of the KMGBF and countries' national reports would help identify implementation gaps and guide efforts to address them.
Adopted in 2022, the KMGBF aims to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030, with a vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050. The global review will assess progress, identify gaps and help determine priority actions to accelerate implementation.
COP17 will run from Oct. 19 to 30 under the theme "Taking Action for Nature." ■

According to an investigation by TIME magazine, based on official correspondence and testimony from senior Israeli, American, and Arab officials, successive Israeli governments helped establish, operate, and preserve the Qatari assistance mechanism for Hamas-controlled Gaza for years.
Among the documents uncovered in the investigation is a 2020 letter sent by then-Mossad director Yossi Cohen to Qatar's Emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. Cohen expressed Israel's gratitude for Qatar's humanitarian assistance to Gaza, writing that the aid had played a crucial role in improving humanitarian conditions in the Strip and ensuring regional stability and security.
Another letter from the same year, sent by a National Security Council official identified in the investigation as "R.L. Maoz," explicitly requested that the payments continue. The official emphasized the importance of maintaining Qatari humanitarian financial assistance through the existing mechanism and asked that the money be transferred through Ambassador Mohammed al-Emadi, chairman of the Qatari Committee for the Reconstruction of Gaza, rather than through intermediaries or other countries.
According to TIME, the requests reflect a contradiction that angered Qatari officials: While senior Israeli figures publicly condemned Doha for financing Hamas, they privately urged Qatar to continue transferring funds. A senior official from the first Trump administration described the arrangement to the magazine, which reported that Qatar demanded written documentation of Israel's involvement in 2018.
Israel helped establish Qatari aid mechanism for Gaza
Qatar began transferring funds to Gaza following Hamas's takeover of the territory in 2007. According to the investigation, by 2012, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government had approved a mechanism giving Israel a direct role in facilitating assistance, including food and medical supplies, determining which families qualified for financial aid, distributing payments, and allowing Qatari funding to expand electricity supplies.
The cooperation was subsequently formalized through a mechanism involving Israel, Qatar, and the United Nations. On October 2, 2018, the parties signed an agreement to finance fuel shipments to Gaza.
In August 2021, Qatar committed $40 million to a program intended to provide nearly 100,000 Palestinian households with $100 per month for four months. The arrangements were subsequently extended.
According to diplomats familiar with the mechanism, Israel vetted eligible recipients and supervised the distribution of funds. Payments were transferred through the World Food Programme, with families receiving text messages before collecting assistance at designated distribution points.
A July 2019 letter disclosed in the investigation shows that Qatar notified Netanyahu's government of a $6 million transfer to 20,000 beneficiaries selected by Israel, with each receiving $300. TIME noted that it remains unclear how many recipients were affiliated with Hamas or had relatives belonging to the organization.
Qatar says Israel bears responsibility for any funds reaching Hamas
Responding to the investigation, Qatar placed responsibility on Israel for any possible diversion of funds to Hamas.
"All Qatari financial assistance in Gaza was directed to Palestinian civilians through mechanisms coordinated with Israeli authorities and international partners," a spokesperson for Qatar's International Media Office said.
"If any funding reached Hamas, as claimed by individuals and groups with political agendas against Qatar, the responsibility lies with Israel, which supervised the transfers and established the mechanism," the spokesperson added.
The investigation also includes testimony indicating that Qatari officials sought to change the aid distribution system in 2023 to reduce civilians' dependence on both Hamas and the Israeli government. According to several sources, including a senior Israeli official and an international diplomat, Netanyahu's government sought to preserve the existing framework.
Mossad chief requested Qatari funding extension two weeks before October 7
Approximately two weeks before Hamas's October 7, 2023, attack, Mossad director David Barnea traveled to Doha and requested the renewal of Qatari funding, as previously reported by The New York Times. According to additional details published by TIME, Qatari officials agreed but warned that it would be the final extension.
Barnea requested another two months of assistance. Officials familiar with the conversation said the reasoning was that continued financial assistance gave Hamas something to lose, providing Israel with leverage over the terrorist organization.
The arrangement also continued under former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who had been one of its fiercest critics while serving as a minister in Netanyahu's government. After becoming prime minister, Bennett ended the practice of allowing suitcases of cash into Gaza but continued the broader Qatari assistance program.
According to a former senior Biden administration official, Qatar was preparing to terminate the program at the time. An official present during a conversation between an Israeli representative and a US envoy said Israel's message was: "We want to continue this as it is."
Netanyahu rejects claims Qatari funding helped preserve Hamas rule
Netanyahu's critics argue that the policy helped maintain Hamas's rule in Gaza and preserve the political division between the terrorist organization and the Palestinian Authority.
Netanyahu has previously rejected the accusation. In a 2024 interview with TIME, he said the assistance was intended to ensure a functioning civilian administration in Gaza and prevent a humanitarian collapse, including the deterioration of sewage, water, and education systems.
The Prime Minister's Office declined to comment on the latest investigation.
The documents do not prove that Qatari assistance directly financed the October 7 attack. However, they provide additional evidence of a policy based on the assumption that civilian financial assistance would help maintain stability and restrain Hamas.
"It was a policy failure on our part, born out of good intentions and continued by several prime ministers," a former senior Israeli defense official told TIME.
"But Netanyahu was undoubtedly at the center of it. He was the one who promoted and accelerated the program, and his government was responsible for how it was managed."
