‘Wild West’ in southern Israel: illegal gun dealers turn Negev into a firing range
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:35:24 UTC
04:35:24 KST

Gunfire during the day. Gunfire at night. In cities, Bedouin communities and the surrounding countryside. Across a vast stretch of southern Israel's Negev desert, residents say they are suffering from the same relentless problem, from Rahat, Tel Sheva and Omer to Retamim in the Ramat Negev Regional Council and the communities of Nevatim and Givot Bar in the Bnei Shimon Regional Council.
Rahat Mayor Talal al-Krenawi expressed confidence in the police but acknowledged that the gunfire could not be ignored. "There is no doubt that there has been scattered gunfire over the past week," he said. "These are not brawls. These are arms dealers testing weapons. This is a matter for the police, not the municipality or the community."
The practice of arms dealers taking weapons out for a "test drive" for prospective buyers is nothing new. Residents of Nevatim, among others, have long suffered from the phenomenon, with certain areas regularly used by dealers and buyers as makeshift firing ranges. After all, prospective buyers want to test the merchandise before purchasing it.
"There is constant gunfire at night," said a Nevatim resident. "By the time the police reach the more remote parts of the area, the criminals have already disappeared. Over the past year, the gunfire has become more intense and frequent, including shooting incidents in broad daylight. Despite police efforts and the recruitment of volunteers to help protect our homes, we feel as though we've gone backward. All these efforts are just a drop in the ocean."
A resident of one of the Bedouin communities described an atmosphere of fear and lawlessness. "It's the Wild West. It's not like it used to be. Today, you worry about every step your children take. You never know where the danger will come from. We think twice before going out because we're afraid. We used to let our children walk home from school, but now we make sure to drive them there and back because you never know what might happen. Young people do whatever they want, and nobody holds them accountable. They know it, and they don't care. It's a terrible feeling."
Al-Krenawi said local authorities were cooperating fully with the police but argued that more sustained enforcement was needed. "The amount of weapons out there justifies establishing a command center in Rahat for an extended period, not just two weeks or a month. In the meantime, we're purchasing drones through philanthropic donations. I must point out that shooting incidents in the city have fallen by more than 40% since the beginning of the year. But when police forces leave the city, the shooting returns."
Residents of Rahat themselves are increasingly desperate. Just last week, kindergarten and elementary school children had to make their way to school while gunfire could be heard in the background. In such circumstances, it is hardly surprising that many residents feel there is little point even calling the police.
In practice, complaints from residents of Jewish communities tend to attract greater attention, including from the media. Nir Zamir, head of the Bnei Shimon Regional Council, said: "We view the shooting incidents and the harm to our residents' personal security with the utmost seriousness, particularly in recent weeks. The reality in which Negev residents, Jews and Bedouins alike, suffer from the terror of gunfire, violence and a lack of law enforcement is intolerable and demands immediate, fundamental action."
Zamir said local authorities were working continuously to protect residents but stressed that they could not replace the state's law enforcement and judicial institutions. "We call on those responsible at the national level, the government, the National Security Ministry, the police and the justice system, to step up efforts on the ground to tackle gunfire and the breakdown of law and order in the Negev. Our residents' personal security is not a privilege. It is the state's most basic obligation to all its citizens," he said.
Omer Local Council head Erez Badash argued that the latest shooting incident reflected a much broader security threat. "The latest shooting incident in the Negev is not an isolated case. It is further evidence on the ground supporting the warning issued by the head of the Shin Bet during a Cabinet meeting," he claimed. "The processes of radicalization and 'Palestinization' in the Negev are no longer merely a local criminal problem but a strategic and national threat. 
Over the years, the increase in marriages to women from the Gaza Strip and the West Bank has brought extremist influences and ideologies into the Bedouin population. We have been seeing the consequences on the ground for years, from the events of Operation Guardian of the Walls in 2021 to the armed groups operating today."
"Even if this involves a minority of the population, when that minority is driven by a radical agenda and possesses hundreds of thousands of weapons, it dictates the reality and the balance of security on the ground," Badash continued. His claims about the scale of the weapons and the causes of radicalization were not substantiated in the report. 
"The events of October 7 showed us all the price of turning a blind eye. It is time for the Israeli government and the prime minister to move from words to action: determined enforcement, cutting off weapons smuggling and addressing nationalist radicalization at its roots before the next disaster occurs."
Israel Police said in response: "Calls received by the police emergency hotline, 100, were answered and handled immediately, and police forces operated on the ground to stop the gunfire. Israel Police continues determined and sustained operational activity in the area, during which arrests have been made and weapons seized. These operations have led to a reduction in shooting incidents in the region and will continue in order to strengthen residents' security and protect public safety."

The flotilla’s organizers cited a series of mechanical failures, prolonged repairs, and two distressing encounters with the bodies of migrants who died attempting to cross the Mediterranean Sea.
According to the organizers, the delays significantly narrowed the time remaining for the voyage, prompting a decision to postpone the attempt to reach Gaza until spring 2027.
The flotilla embarked on a tour of European ports aimed at mobilizing public and international support for the campaign against Israel's naval blockade of the Gaza Strip.
One of the main vessels in the campaign, the Kate, also known as the Tenacity, departed Bristol, UK, on August 17 and stopped at ports in Ireland, France, and Spain. It was scheduled to arrive in Sicily on October 14, from where it was expected to sail toward the Gaza coast.
However, the two encounters with the bodies of migrants in the open sea were described by participants as a "distressing experience." They emphasized, however, that the technical malfunctions and the need for extensive repairs were what ultimately reduced the time available to complete the voyage.
"We set out for Gaza, and it is painful to end this journey without reaching it," said Frank Romano, a volunteer aboard the Kate. "The commitment that brought us aboard the ship remains as strong as ever. We will carry the solidarity we encountered at every port in Europe into our preparations for the 2027 mission."
Governments worldwide have failed to protect Palestinians, activists say
Huwaida Arraf, a human rights lawyer and member of the flotilla's steering committee alongside Israeli activist Zohar Regev, criticized the international community, arguing that governments worldwide had failed to protect Palestinians.
The organizers stressed that postponing the voyage did not mean suspending their activities. They said they would continue campaigning against Israel and demanding that governments halt arms transfers and military cooperation with the country.
Meanwhile, in the Sicilian city of Catania, flotilla activists and supporters are holding an interfaith conference over the weekend under the title "Faith in a Time of Genocide."
Christian, Muslim, and Jewish religious figures are expected to participate, including Sandra-Laya Ruch of Canada, a former activist with the Isha L'Isha organization in Haifa who is described as a "Jewish priestess."
Participants will discuss the responsibilities of religious communities in light of the war in Gaza and possible courses of action against Israeli policies.
The flotilla organizers also announced their support for international activists traveling to the West Bank to participate in the olive harvest alongside Palestinian farmers. They condemned plans to deport foreign activists arriving in the area.
Next flotilla expected to depart in spring 2027
According to the organizers, they will continue their land activities and preparations for the next flotilla in the coming months.
The next flotilla is expected to depart in spring 2027, although no precise sailing date has been announced.
Israel, for its part, maintains that its naval blockade of the Gaza Strip is a necessary security measure intended to prevent weapons smuggling and remains determined to enforce it.
Separately, the Italian legal team representing the Gaza-bound Sumud flotilla welcomed progress in an investigation by the Rome Prosecutor's Office into senior Israeli officials on Saturday, over suspicions of their involvement in the interception of flotilla vessels in 2025 and 2026 and harm allegedly inflicted on participants.
The investigation, launched following complaints filed by 50 Italian citizens, concerns suspected acts of torture, kidnapping, physical assault, and other offenses.
Among those named on Saturday were Defense Minister Israel Katz, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, and other senior officials in the IDF, Israel Police, and Israel Prison Service.
In a statement, the legal team said the investigation was advancing in the direction it had advocated in its appeals to the authorities, describing the development as "a significant signal against the sense of impunity enjoyed by the chain of command responsible for these serious crimes."
The team said it would continue working to advance legal proceedings in other European countries.

Feeling 'burnt out'? Research suggests your surroundings might be to blame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:31:01 UTC
04:31:01 KST

Survey suggests one-third of us are burnt out
Amlan Sharma says feeling exhausted, less purposeful, less confident and achieving less at a job he loved became normal in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic.
The 38-year-old occupational therapist says he began to recognise what he was experiencing in some of his patients too.
"That's where I started to realise: 'Hang on, I might be burnt out,'" he says.
According to a new survey, more than one in three Australian workers are experiencing burnout, and for those whose workplaces have "high levels of system friction" it is far more likely.
The State of Workplace Burnout Report, published by think tank Infinite Potential in partnership with Beyond Blue and the University of Technology Sydney Business School, collated the responses of 999 Australian survey respondents.
Study author and managing director of Infinite Potential John Chan says there was a big divide between organisations with very low levels of burnout and those with very high rates, and he wanted to "pick out" those differences.
"We're trying to move this conversation away from the individual," he says.
Paula Brough, a professor of organisational psychology and director of the Centre for Work, Organisation and Wellbeing in the Business School at Griffith University, who did not contribute to the survey, says it's important to bear in mind the small sample.
Professor Brough says the levels of burnout reported are a little higher than she would expect, but there's "nothing new" in environmental factors being linked to burnout.
"There's key workplace characteristics … which contribute to high levels of mental ill health, which may or may not lead to burnout," she explains.
Professor Brough says the industries people work in are an important consideration, and are not included in the survey findings.
Higher levels of burnout typically occur in public-facing industries and high-risk industries, from bus drivers and customer-service roles to emergency services, she says.
What is burnout?
The survey relied on the World Health Organization (WHO) definition of what it classifies as an "occupational phenomenon" and "not a medical condition".
According to WHO, burnout is characterised by three dimensions:
- Exhaustion
- Increased mental distance or cynicism toward one's job
- Reduced professional efficacy
To have burnout, Dr Chan says, you need to be experiencing all three.
He says burnout has become a buzzword and while that has helped reduce stigma, the term is often misunderstood.
"If you're just simply exhausted, that's not burnout," he says.
Professor Brough says stress and burnout are also not interchangeable terms.
"Burnout is the extreme end of the continuum [and] stress is the start of it," she says.
Burnout red flags, according to Professor Brough, include sleeping changes, anxiety returning to work after the weekend, abandoning usual hobbies and other changes.
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
'I'm not the problem'
Amlan, who is a father and also has a caring role for a family member, says he became disillusioned with rigid schedules and limited autonomy at his work.
"It was high job demands, excessive workload, time pressure, constant interruptions," he says.
He says issues that were beyond his control felt like they were wearing him down.
While it presented financial challenges, Amlan moved to self-employment and reduced his work hours, which helped with recovery.
"Over time I started to realise that actually I'm not the problem," Amlan says.
Unnecessary meetings, bad systems and red tape
Senior lecturer at the University Technology Sydney (UTS) Business School and researcher at The Ultimo Institute Anna Stephens, who helped design and conduct the survey, says the organisational factors linked to burnout are things "that create unnecessary difficulties in actually completing your work".
Dr Chan says this is the cognitive load or the "friction" involved in doing the job.
According to the survey results, this kind of work friction means you have 84 per cent higher odds of experiencing burnout in Australia.
Dr Stephens lists poorly designed online systems, lengthy bureaucratic processes, unclear instructions and expectations, and pointless meetings as examples.
Professor Brough says workplace stress can be thought about in two ways.
Firstly, "the big stuff". Then there are the small things that happen frequently, known as minor stresses, workplace hassles or red tape.
"They are also a key predictor of occupational stress, [which is] not necessarily burnout," Professor Brough says.
"It's often the workplace hassles which just eat away at you because they're daily."
Workload is also an established factor, and this can look like long work hours for an extended period, a lack of resources, not enough support and a lack of control, she says.
"You might not be able to control your shifts that you work, or your colleagues … or the [hospital] ward you work on," Professor Brough says.
But ideally, Professor Brough says, employers would offset that workload with extra support or independence.
"You can have a high workload, but if you also have high levels of support and control, it doesn't necessarily equate to levels of stress or burnout," she says.
Job security and 'fragmentation'
Dr Chan says job security and fragmentation are also significant factors.
The survey results found 68 per cent of Australians who don't feel secure in their job are experiencing burnout, compared with a burnout rate of 20 per cent for those who feel very secure in their job.
Job insecurity could be caused by restructures, global politics or AI uncertainty, Dr Chan says.
And fragmentation, he explains, is all the switching you do throughout the day without much control. This might be between meetings, tasks and software.
Dr Stephens describes it as the "constant interruption or multiple competing priorities" that divide our attention.
What individuals can do
Dr Chan wants organisations and employers to think about the processes and systems people work within.
Loading...
"The leaders and organisation have the responsibility to create the right type of environment, but then people also need to speak up when something isn't right or they need certain support," he says.
Dr Stephens recommends paying attention to your workload, communicating with your manager often and avoiding (where possible) normalising the frictions and fragmentations.
"They are a drain on our cognitive and our emotional resources, and they leave us with less fuel in the tank, not just for work, but for the important things in our life as well," she says.
Professor Brough says a worker and an employer "have a joint responsibility to look after your mental health".
This article contains general information only. You should consider obtaining independent professional advice in relation to your particular circumstances.

A protester surrounded by tear gas kicks a projectile in front of the tourism office in Lyon, France on Oct. 17, 2026. | Jeff Pachoud/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — President Emmanuel Macron promised that rioters who “destroyed” things will face consequences as he addressed the nation on Sunday after a weekend of massive unrest across France.
Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets nationwide on Saturday, with students joining trade unions and members of the public to protest the cost of living. While thousands protested peacefully, footage of mayhem including public buildings being set on fire, stores being looted and clashes with riot police drew widespread condemnation in France and abroad.
“Those who destroyed must pay; those who looted must reimburse,” Macron said.
Advertisement
The French government has been accused of mismanaging and underestimating the protests, with calls for Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to resign emerging both on the left and the far right.
According to the latest figures from the French interior ministry, some 2,000 people were arrested during the turmoil. Police, firefighters and demonstrators suffered injuries as the situation unraveled.
Serge Papin, France’s minister for small business, will meet with company reps at the Ministry of Economy tomorrow to assess the damage and suggest assistance for businesses that were affected.
Macron said he was awaiting “clear answers” on why the protests turned violent. The French president accused “troublemakers from far-left splinter groups, joined by numerous delinquents” of engaging in “unbridled violence.”
With six months to go before next year’s presidential election in France, the events of Saturday quickly took on a political dimension.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also accused the “ultra-left” of fomenting the violence, alleging that the France Unbowed movement and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon had played an “important role” within a “far-left network” driving the unrest.
Advertisement
Mélenchon, along with left-wing representatives from several other parties, joined Saturday’s protests and encouraged his supporters to attend, although condemning looting and violence. He said accusations that he was responsible for the mayhem were aimed at weakening his presidential bid, and accused Macron of “letting the situation deteriorate” without offering solutions to appease the anger.
Mélenchon is currently in a close race with center-left candidate Raphaël Glucksmann and center-right candidate Edouard Philippe to clinch second place behind far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen in next year’s election. The top two candidates in the election move to a runoff if no candidate wins a majority of votes in the first round.
“At stake, too, are France’s image, its credibility, and its influence around the world,” Philippe said ahead of Macron’s statement. “These images of violence have consequences that extend far beyond our borders.”
Le Pen and her far-right National Rally have brandished the violent footage to pitch herself as the candidate of an “appeased France.” The National Rally accused Macron and his government of being the “party of chaos,” and Mélenchon’s France Unbowed of “legitimizing violence.”
The protesters had “legitimate social demands,” Le Pen said. “The French people are fed up with being caught between the government’s austerity measures and heavy-handed taxation, and the insurrection activists.”
With the U.S. midterms around the corner on Nov. 3, President Donald Trump seized on the violence to blame migration. “France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform Sunday afternoon.

Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:11:27 UTC
04:11:27 KST

Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine’s president says communication between Washington and Kyiv ‘virtually nonstop’, despite a spat with Trump.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the war with Russia “must be brought to an end” and that his country is preparing for the “next steps” of diplomacy to end the conflict.
The Ukrainian leader’s comments come amid a significant diplomatic fallout with US President Donald Trump, who on Friday night waived sanctions targeting Russia’s energy economy.
In a Sunday social media post, Zelenskyy wrote that he had a “conversation with the American president’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner”.
He added that “a lot depends” on the US position, but it’s clear there are “many things that matter to all of us”.
The Trump administration had already eased restrictions on Russian fuel imports on October 9, when it announced a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets in an effort to tackle soaring fuel prices
The US Treasury temporarily authorised the imports despite existing sanctions, prompting criticism that the move could provide Moscow with revenue to sustain its war in Ukraine.
Trump has also criticised recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure as “a disgrace”.
Nonetheless, Zelenskyy said his team is in “virtually nonstop communication” with their US counterparts and said a focus of dialogue is on the results of the talks in Florida and further steps.
US wavers on Ukraine’s access to tech
Zelenskyy also said he was “thankful” that the US had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine after a pause left the country particularly vulnerable to Russia’s regular ballistic missile attacks.
“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side,” Zelenskyy told NBC, adding: “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”
Kyiv has also reported restrictions on the speed of satellite service Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite connectivity network, provided to Ukraine by Musk’s company SpaceX.
Ukraine said its relays were experiencing a limit on how fast receivers could travel while maintaining connectivity, making it almost impossible to intercept Russia’s upgraded jet-powered long-range drones.
Musk had said any restrictions imposed on Starshield connectivity were the responsibility of the US government. The White House quickly rebuked that and in an NBC interview on Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Zelenskyy “very reckless” for accusing the US of throttling connectivity.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that Ukraine is currently blocked from Starshield, and that a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.
US officials defend Russia waiver as Trump orders 60-day review
Meanwhile, in the US, Trump has faced bipartisan pushback for his executive order on Friday night, waiving parts of the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Trump had signed the act into law in September, in honour of the late Senator Graham, a close Republican ally.
But his decision to ease sanctions and tariffs against Russia has prompted backlash even from within his own party. The penalties act was scheduled to take effect on Sunday.
Over the weekend, Trump signalled he has yet to make a final decision on easing the sanctions against Russia.
“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he wrote on Truth Social.
He concluded his post with further criticism directed at Zelenskyy. “He doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump said of the Ukrainian leader.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump wanted up to 60 days to assess the economic consequences of imposing the sanctions and tariffs that were waived on Friday.
Zelenskyy has warned, however, that the waiver could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Rubio also defended the latest deal to import Russian diesel, saying “that diesel is going to be sold one way or the other”. He argued that the fundamental question was how much the US would secure for itself.
In a series of Sunday morning media appearances, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright also backed the arrangement.
Speaking to ABC, he called the deal a “carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline” for Russia.
“If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” Wright told CNN. “He’s putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.”
Long-range attacks continue
Also on Sunday, Ukrainian media reported that Russian strikes killed two people in the western Volyn region, near the border with Poland, and injured at least five others across the country. Overnight attacks by Russia killed a woman and injured a six-year-old in the Zaporizhzhia region.
On Saturday night and in the early hours of Sunday, Ukraine hit Russia’s second-largest city, St Petersburg, with a significant drone attack. It targeted a key oil refinery and depot, a warehouse of Russian online retailer Ozon and a data centre run by Russian social media company, VKontakte.
At least one person was killed in the attack, which Russian state media said was the largest on the city since the start of the war in 2022.

Breadcrumb
Palestinian journalist held in solitary confinement by Israel for nearly two months
Palestinian journalist Bushra al-Taweel has been held by Israel for nearly 50 days in solitary confinement, the Palestinian Prisoners Club (PPC) said in a statement on Sunday.
Al-Taweel, 33, who was previously released by Israel in January 2025 as part of a prisoner exchange deal, was rearrested in February 2026 and has since been subjected to repeated administrative detention orders.
The journalist is facing frequent raids on her cell, during which she is beaten, subjected to tear gas, and verbal abuse from prison authorities, the PPC said, based on al-Taweel's testimony given during a recent visit. The most recent raid took place two days before the visit.
Al-Taweel reported suffering dryness in her eyes, skin, and hands, as well as numbness in her hands due to being handcuffed. She also suffered from scabies prior to being transferred to solitary confinement, where she is being deprived of basic necessities.
The PPC said prison authorities have provided insufficient food for al-Taweel, while forcing her to drink discoloured tap water. She also reported having few clothes to wear, while also being unable to wash what she has.
Al-Taweel indicated that on 4 October, she signed papers for her transfer to Damon Prison, but was surprised to find herself transferred to solitary confinement at the Ohalei Oz Prison in Beersheba, where she remains detained until today. Israeli authorities renewed her administrative detention order for an additional four months.
The PPC described al-Taweel's treatment by Israel as being part of an escalating policy of systematic targeting of female prisoners through administrative detention, solitary confinement, ill-treatment, and the denial of their basic rights.
The Prisoners Club called upon international human rights groups, particularly the International Committee of the Red Cross, to intervene urgently to investigate al-Taweel's detention conditions.
Al-Taweel, a journalist who has campaigned for the rights of Palestinian prisoners, was first arrested by Israeli forces in 2011 at the age of 18, when she was sentenced to 18 months in prison.

Premier Ben Carroll has pledged to cap public transport fares at $30 a week if the Labor government is re-elected in Victoria next month.
The public transport pledge comes hot on the heels of a weekend commitment by Victorian Labor to cap Melbourne freeway tolls at $30 per week.
The Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry has expressed concern over the rising tab associated with cost-of-living pledges during the election campaign.
Victoria Premier Ben Carroll has pledged to cap public transport fares at $30 a week if the Labor government is re-elected next month, the second transport capping pledge in as many days.
Former premier Jacinta Allan introduced half-price fares at the peak of the fuel price crunch in April, after a short period of free public transport statewide in the early months of the US-Iran war.
The half-price fare period was scheduled to expire on December 31.
If re-elected next month, Mr Carroll said a Labor government would introduce the $30-a-week fare cap, which would run for two years until December 2028.
Today the government revealed only Myki cards could be used for the scheme.
Public Transport Minister Vicki Ward said bank cards and Apple Pay would eventually be included in the $30 cap, but was unable to set a date.
"This is real cost-of-living relief that helps a regular commuter save $1,400 a year," Mr Carroll said.
"Everyone can benefit, but full-time workers will benefit most."
Victorian Labor estimated the transport fare cap policy would cost $206 million over its two-year duration, which Mr Carroll said would be offset by savings made elsewhere.
The pledge comes only a day after Labor also committed to a $30-a-week freeway toll cap in an election pledge battle with the Coalition, which only months earlier had committed to a $50-a-week toll cap if elected in November.
Daniel Bowen from the Public Transport Users Association said the scheme would save commuters significant money.
"Currently, if you're travelling every day, five days a week on public transport, the normal fare would be $57. This will bring it down substantially," he said.
"It is a big benefit for public transport users."
He said the government should also look at reducing the fare for short-distance trips, which currently stands at $5.70.
Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry policy and advocacy chief Amelia Bitsis said businesses large and small were concerned about the escalating profligacy of the Victorian election campaign.
"We're asking all major political parties to show some fiscal restraint," she said.
"We simply don't have an accurate enough picture of what the true debt situation is in Victoria.
"What we certainly do know is that business is on the hook for that debt, so are Victorian households," Ms Bitsis said.
"A lot of the election commitments that we are seeing are lovely nice-to-haves but the question becomes: can we afford them?"
Public transport affordability was a key feature of the 2022 Victorian election campaign, with then opposition leader Matthew Guy pledging a $2 a day cap on metropolitan train and tram fares.
During the campaign, the Victorian Coalition also pledged to halve V/Line fares.
A political spat later erupted when Labor and the public service came under fire for undertaking a policy costing of an opposition policy proposal, with Coalition MPs arguing it was outside the remit of public servants.
During the same election campaign, then premier Daniel Andrews pledged to cap regional train services at $9.20 a day for full-fare commuters, and $4.60 for concession card holders.

Suncorp borrower's mortgage payments could spike amid transfer to ANZ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:54:39 UTC
03:54:39 KST

ANZ's Suncorp Bank acquisition could see mortgage payments rise upward of $1,000
In short:
Suncorp Bank mortgage customers have been warned their repayments could increase by $1,000 a month when transferred to ANZ.
ANZ bought Suncorp in 2024.
Consumer advocates say the way Suncorp and ANZ are treating people shows how little power borrowers have in Australia.
Suncorp Bank mortgage customers received an alarming email last week advising them that their monthly mortgage repayments could rise by hundreds of dollars.
ANZ Bank bought Suncorp Bank in 2024 and is now logistically transferring hundreds of thousands of borrowers off Suncorp's books and onto the ANZ loan platforms.
The email sent by Suncorp to Suncorp customers on October 13 said: "If you've made advance payments and have funds available in your Cashback/redraw, your minimum loan repayment at ANZ is likely to increase."
One Suncorp customer who contacted the ABC said Suncorp's email indicated home loan repayments could rise by more than $1,000.
Suncorp had previously allowed customers with redraw and cashback facilities to reduce their minimum monthly repayments.
ANZ does not have this policy, so some customers are being warned their minimum repayments will increase if they do nothing.
"This increase could be significant depending on the loan balance, how much is paid in advance and the remaining loan term," Suncorp's email said.
Consumer advocates say the way Suncorp and ANZ are treating people shows how little power borrowers have in Australia.
"Australians deserve better protections in the mortgage market to give them more certainty about what they will pay and the conditions for their loan," Consumer Policy Research Centre CEO Erin Turner said.
'Unwelcome shock'
The director of data insights at interest rate comparison site Canstar, Sally Tindall, said thousands of Suncorp customers were likely to get an "unwelcome shock" when they learned their minimum repayments were set to rise due to the changeover to ANZ in June next year.
Suncorp told the ABC its customers could avoid any increase in their home loan repayments.
"For most customers there will be no change to their repayments," Suncorp Bank CEO Malcolm Stedman said.
"Those customers ahead on their repayments may see an increase in their minimum repayments, if they choose to take no action."
Ms Tindall agreed with Mr Stedman's claim if customers followed Suncorp's email instructions.
"This is because Suncorp views extra repayments differently to ANZ when they go to calculate a customer's minimum monthly repayments," she said.
The most common practice across the banks, Ms Tindall said, was to exclude or discount any extra home loan payments made, or available cash, when calculating a person's minimum monthly repayments.
For example, if someone has a $600,000 debt owing on their mortgage, and 25 years remaining, but they have $100,000 in extra sitting in the loan, the bank will calculate the minimum repayment amount on the $600,000 debt owing (they will still, however, only charge you interest on the $500,000).
On the average owner-occupier variable rate of 6.49 per cent, the monthly repayments would be $4,047.
However, Ms Tindall said some banks approached this calculation differently by including the extra repayments a customer had added to their loan.
Using the same example as above, the bank calculates how much you need to repay the $500,000 owing over the 25 years remaining.
In this scenario, the person's minimum repayments would be $3,373.
"Most Australians have a home loan that is 'variable at the bank's discretion' where the bank can hike fees or change conditions when it suits them," Ms Turner said.
"This means that most borrowers have little control about how much they are paying for their home."
Banks expected to treat customers fairly
The ANZ Bank's acquisition of Suncorp was originally rejected by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) on the grounds a resulting lack of competition would disadvantage consumers.
"We are not satisfied that the acquisition is not likely to substantially lessen competition in the supply of home loans nationally, small to medium enterprise banking in Queensland, and agribusiness banking in Queensland," ACCC deputy chair Mick Keogh said in August 2023.
"These banking markets are critical for many home owners and for Queensland businesses and farmers in particular.
"Competition being lessened in these markets will lead to customers getting a worse deal."
The Australian Competition Tribunal later set aside the ACCC's decision, leading to the banking acquisition then being approved by both the Queensland and federal governments.
The ABC asked the Queensland Treasury to respond to Suncorp's email to customers asking them to adjust their mortgage repayments to avoid higher costs.
Treasurer David Janetzki told the ABC: "This deal was agreed to by the former Labor government and it is up to former treasurer Cameron Dick to explain why these protections weren't included in the arrangement."
Queensland Labor deputy leader Cameron Dick responded by saying: "As a former banker and as member of parliament who voted to support the merger which saved hundred of Queensland jobs and created hundreds more, David Janetzki should immediately contact the bank to demand answers and action.
"If he is unwilling to act then I am willing to meet with the treasurer, bank chair and CEO to ensure the bank does whatever is necessary to support the bank's new customers."
A spokesperson for federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said: "While these are commercial decisions for ANZ we expect the bank to treat its customers fairly and with respect, otherwise they'll look for better deals from others."

Macron condemns "shocking" scenes of violence across France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:46:00 UTC

‘How can French people do this to France?’: Macron denounces violence as France hit by new clashes
PARIS – President Emmanuel Macron on Oct 18 slammed the “unbridled” violence that erupted in cost-of-living protests across France, as police battled protesters and looters in new clashes in Paris.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested on Oct 17 in unrest that represented some of the worst urban violence in France in years, with almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, seven seriously, the interior ministry said.
In an address to the nation, Macron said the local authorities would be able to ban – “if necessary” – certain rallies in coming days. But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew.
“Tonight, we all feel anger and shame,” Macron said of the devastation brought by the protests that include town halls burned down and hundreds of businesses looted or damaged.
“Looking at these images, we all asked ourselves: what is going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” said Macron, who insisted there must be a distinction between protesters with “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed, and looted”.
He vowed the authorities would be “uncompromising” towards the “agitators from ultra-left fringe groups, joined by numerous delinquents” who “unleashed unbridled violence in our cities”.
AFP journalists said police on Oct 18 fired tear gas and stun grenades at hundreds of people gathered in a Paris square following social media calls for a gathering that the authorities said had not been approved.
Bottles and rocks were hurled at police who made 108 arrests, according to the authorities. At least five stores were looted around Republique square.
Other stores in central Paris also had windows smashed and the city hall told many to close. In the south-eastern city of Lyon, police battled youths who attempted to loot a luxury clothing store.
Macron critics pounce
The unrest came just months from a presidential election where centrist Macron cannot stand again and Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, is riding high in the polls.
Le Pen said the troubles showed that Macron’s administration was “running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented”.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, head of the hard-left France Unbowed party, also running for president, warned that the country could be heading toward “events that will eventually become uncontrollable”.
Macron said “our country deserves a fine presidential election”, marked by debates “with the parties, rather than in the streets with violence”.
The protests on Oct 17 had seen unions, the anti-Macron Yellow Vests movement that rattled the early years of his presidency and school students, who had protested for the last weeks, join forces in a show of anger at the cost of living and prospects for young people.
With images of French town halls burning and shops being looted grabbing headlines around the world, US President Donald Trump waded into the debate, blaming immigration for the unrest.
“France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump said in a social media post.
‘All necessary lessons’
Macron vowed that top officials would “make decisions in coordination with mayors to protect our cities, public buildings, and businesses.”
He said that businesses that suffered would be supported and vowed there would be “full transparency” over the response by security forces to the protests.
Some opposition politicians have already called for the sacking of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez.
Macron said he had asked Nunez to “draw all necessary lessons”, particularly with regard to intelligence gathering and anticipation, adding he expected “clear answers”.
“It’s like we had a war,” a 78-year-old Paris resident Mehmet Ozeden told AFP amid burnt street barricades from the protests on Oct 17.
The city of Limoges lost its 19th-century town hall to a fire that local prefect Maurice Barate told news channel LCI had been deliberately set by “a wild horde”.
In Lyon, a tourist office in the city centre was set ablaze during the protests amid multiple clashes and looting.
A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne. In Mulhouse, a 17-year-old girl lost an eye, according to prosecutors. AFP

GCC condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as Yemen fighting intensifies
Gulf ministers urge action against Houthis as fighting displaces more than 233,000 people across Yemen.
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) has condemned repeated attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi fighters on Saudi Arabia and pledged support for the kingdom.
The political and economic bloc that includes Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates issued a statement on Sunday, shortly after their foreign ministers’ meeting in Manama, Bahrain.
The statement said an attack on any member affected all six, invoking a joint defence agreement and backing Saudi Arabia’s right to protect itself.
The condemnation came as the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis reported shooting down two drones near Riyadh and in Saudi Arabia‘s Eastern Province early on Sunday.
The coalition said another drone had been intercepted near the capital hours earlier, but did not identify who launched it.
Gulf ministers accused the Houthis of carrying out deadly strikes on civilian airports and vital facilities.
They also pressed for tighter enforcement of a United Nations arms embargo against the group and urged countries to formally designate it “a terrorist organisation”.
The ministers welcomed an October 15 statement from the UN Security Council (UNSC), the body responsible for maintaining international peace, which condemned Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and threats to Red Sea shipping.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government separately appealed to the UNSC to act against Houthi attacks on homes and state facilities.
In letters addressed to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and the UNSC’s president for October, Aglaia Balta, the Yemeni government cited an attack on the presidential palace in Aden, where the government is temporarily based.
Separately on Sunday, UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan met Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud in Abu Dhabi to discuss regional security, the UAE’s state news agency WAM reported.
Meanwhile, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press offensives on several fronts.
The Yemeni military said the Houthis fired missiles towards the central city of Marib on Sunday, while government troops reported gains in Taiz, further south.
Government-aligned commanders said eight soldiers died in fighting in Lahij province on Saturday.
Government forces also claimed to have killed 12 Houthi fighters in southern Taiz, figures that could not be independently confirmed.
This latest phase of the war followed Houthi gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces launched a counteroffensive intended to recapture territory from the Houthis, who seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
Civilians face deepening shortages
The fighting has uprooted more than 233,000 people, according to the International Organization for Migration, the UN’s migration agency.
About 121,000 are in Taiz province, where supply routes have been disrupted by the fighting.
Al Jazeera’s Hadeel al-Yamani, reporting from Taiz, said cooking gas was unavailable and food stocks were dwindling as Houthi forces blocked supplies through the city’s western entrance.
A local office tracking the siege said food prices had risen fivefold.
The World Health Organization, the UN health agency, warned that Taiz’s 12 hospitals had fuel for just four more days and had run out of surgical supplies.
Oxygen and medicines were also critically scarce as the city struggled with a cholera outbreak.

A synagogue in Paris's 19th arrondissement was among several Jewish-affiliated sites reportedly broken into or damaged over the weekend amid widespread riots across France, the Jewish community security organization Service de Protection de la Communauté Juive (SPCJ) said in a statement on Sunday.
The SPCJ issued the statement amid concerns about the spread of misinformation surrounding the incidents, urging France's Jewish community to exercise "caution and responsibility," refrain from circulating unverified reports, and rely on official communications from the organization and authorities.
Members of the Ohalei Yaakov congregation discovered that their temporary prayer space on Rue Burnouf had been ransacked when they arrived on Sunday morning. The congregation has been holding services at the location while its permanent synagogue on Rue Henri Murger undergoes renovations.
Prayer books, tefillin, and the contents of lockers and cupboards were found scattered across the floor following the overnight intrusion, according to the French Jewish news outlet IsraJ. The rabbi's office had also been ransacked.
Synagogue officials suspect attempted theft, do not rule out antisemitism
Although the circumstances and motive remain unclear, members of the congregation believe the intruders may have been searching for money rather than seeking to carry out an explicitly antisemitic attack. No antisemitic graffiti or inscriptions were reported at the scene, and the synagogue's Torah scrolls were left untouched.
"It really looks like an attempted robbery; you can see that those who did this were probably looking for money. The Torah scrolls weren't touched; we just found the items that were in the lockers on the floor," Raphael, a member of the Ohalei Yaakov synagogue committee, told IsraJ.
However, Raphael did not entirely rule out an antisemitic motive, raising the possibility that the intruders had deliberately selected the synagogue because it was a Jewish place of worship.
"Of course, it can't be a coincidence that they chose to target a Jewish place of worship. They must have thought that since it was a Jewish place of worship, there would be money there. Because it's a temporary building, there's no sign outside indicating a synagogue. This leads me to believe that those who broke in last night must have scouted the place, seen that Jews went there for prayers."
Raphael said the congregation observed a peaceful Shabbat, with services proceeding normally and no riots nearby. He suggested that an attack motivated primarily by antisemitism would likely have involved more extensive destruction, including damage to Torah scrolls or antisemitic graffiti.
In a message to congregants, the Ohalei Yaakov committee said there were no signs of forced entry and urged members to be more vigilant about securing the premises.
"We noticed that there was an attempted theft, probably by people looking for money. Some lockers were emptied. NOTHING WAS STOLEN OR VANDALIZED. THERE ARE NO SIGNS OF FORCED ENTRY EITHER," the message read.
Jewish-owned businesses damaged amid nationwide unrest
In Marseille, several businesses sustained damage during Saturday's demonstrations, including some owned by Jewish individuals.
However, there was no evidence indicating that the businesses had been singled out because of their owners' Jewish identities or that the damage was motivated by antisemitism.
The incidents occurred as France experienced some of its most serious civil unrest in years, with demonstrations over rising living costs and deteriorating public services escalating into violence, looting, and attacks on public buildings across the country.

Rabbis for Human Rights files police complaint over Rabbi Lior’s Palestinian olive harvest ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:42:11 UTC
03:42:11 KST

Rabbis for Human Rights said Sunday it had filed a police complaint against Rabbi Dov Lior over his religious ruling permitting Jews to harvest olives from Palestinian groves, adding to the rabbinical opposition to the ruling amid violence during the West Bank harvest.
The organization said its acting director, Anton Goodman, submitted the complaint on behalf of its 170 rabbinical members, alleging incitement to racism, incitement to violence, and encouraging the theft of property.
The complaint follows reports that the IDF recommended investigating Lior for suspected incitement.
“I am sorry that I have to file a police complaint against a rabbi in Israel, but reality requires us to stand up for the Torah,” Goodman said in the organization’s announcement.
“Entering other people’s land and taking their crops unlawfully is not what God wants from us in this land.”
Lior argued that olive trees remained property of Jewish people
Lior, the former chief rabbi of Kiryat Arba, published the ruling Friday. He argued that the land remained the property of the Jewish people and that Palestinians prevented from harvesting for security reasons could be presumed to have given up on the olives.
He also argued that past harvests had already provided sufficient compensation for planting the trees. His conclusion extended beyond groves near settlements, permitting Jews to harvest in more distant areas to assert Jewish ownership and fulfill what he described as the religious commandment to conquer the land.
The ruling concerns taking the olives; its text does not explicitly authorize physical attacks on Palestinian farmers. The organization’s allegations that it constitutes incitement are part of its complaint, rather than findings by police or a court.
The dispute turns in part on whether farmers barred from reaching their trees can be treated as having relinquished their crops. Rabbis opposing Lior’s position argue that being prevented from harvesting does not mean owners have abandoned their property.
Earlier in the week, a group of Gush Etzion rabbis issued an opinion prohibiting Jews from taking olives from Palestinian-owned groves near settlements, even where the owners were denied access for security reasons.
They argued that the fruit remained the owners’ property and that taking it constituted theft and a desecration of God’s name. One alternative they proposed was arranging for workers or volunteers to harvest under the permitted security arrangements and return the crop to its owners, with harvesting expenses covered.
Tzohar says theft prohibited regardless of owner's religion
The Tzohar rabbinical organization subsequently rejected Lior’s ruling, stressing that theft is prohibited regardless of whether the owner is Jewish.
Tzohar also disputed the assumption that restricted access amounted to abandonment, particularly where owners expressly said they intended to harvest through arrangements allowed by the military. It cited Lior’s own earlier writings in arguing that individuals could not decide for themselves to confiscate property on security grounds.
The religious dispute comes alongside restrictions on access to some harvesting areas.
Rabbis for Human Rights, which brings together rabbis from different Jewish denominations, said its activists accompany Palestinian farmers during the annual harvest both to help pick olives and to deter violence and document incidents.
The organization’s complaint followed a week of reported attacks on Palestinian harvesters, journalists, and European diplomats participating in the harvest.

West Bank attacks on Washington Post journalist, diplomats may signal dangerous trend - analysis

2026-10-18

The 2023-2026 period is not the first time that a Jewish extremist beat or assaulted a foreign reporter or Western diplomat in the West Bank.
But in the past, when this happened, heads rolled. Whoever was involved was either arrested, fired, or both – and fast.
Often, some of their supervisors were fired or rebuked to make it clear that whoever was managing the area needed to establish a stricter environment to curb such a phenomenon if they wanted to keep their job.
In that sense, the assault on a Washington Post photojournalist in recent days, and what most are reporting as an assault on Western diplomats, is not new.
What is new is that the world assumes that the Israeli government will do nothing other than at most issue condemnations, and that the record of the last three years, and especially the last three months, would suggest they would be right.
Ben-Gvir accused of avoiding crackdown on settler violence
For two years, the IDF and the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) accused National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir of this and of pressuring the police into avoiding cracking down on Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank. Implicitly, they also held Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accountable for not firing Ben-Gvir.
Then, the Shin Bet got quieter for much of 2026 when Netanyahu appointed David Zini, who corralled the agency from involvement against Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank, but the IDF continued its accusations.
And even Zini, after the last few months of a spike in Jewish extremist violence like nothing Israel has seen in decades, recently started to pressure Netanyahu and the government to get more serious about a crackdown.
Yet, despite unanimous, repeated warnings by the defense establishment to Defense Minister Israel Katz and Netanyahu not to suspend the administrative detention of violent extremist Jews, and repeated warnings by the defense establishment to bring it back to get the situation under control, the defense establishment and the prime minister have either said “no” or are waiting until after the elections for any progress.
Their strategy has only encouraged the Jewish extremists to rush to perpetrate more widespread violence in the last three months, as they are concerned that maybe their free hand to attack Palestinians may get rolled back post-elections.
Once the Israeli government does nothing active to truly protect innocent Palestinians for an extended period, such lawlessness was eventually going to impact others in the West Bank, because Jewish extremists realize that the political and defense establishments are intimidated by them.
Netanyahu is afraid that if he confronts Ben-Gvir during election season, he may lose votes to the Otzma Yehudit Party by looking weak.
In this sad state of affairs, enforcing the rule of law in the West Bank has now become associated with looking weak.
Sanctions, US threats have had little effect on Netanyahu, Katz position
What is stunning is that the European and Western sanctions wave in mid-September, and threats from the Trump administration to potentially take some similar actions eventually, have done nothing to change Netanyahu’s and Katz’s position.
Part of this is likely because Netanyahu correctly estimated that Trump would support him in the election. After all, they converge on Iran-related issues, despite their disagreement over the West Bank.
On the same day that US Ambassador Mike Huckabee slammed Israel for mishandling the West Bank, Trump gave Netanyahu a full-throated endorsement because of their joint interests against Iran.
This may or may not decide the election in Netanyahu’s favor.
But whoever is prime minister after October 27, if the situation in the West Bank does not come under control, the defense establishment has warned that violent Jewish extremists, who have already attacked IDF soldiers dozens of times, could become an even greater direct danger to the State of Israel’s ability to function, let alone to its global image.
Palestinian terrorism is still a much bigger threat than Jewish extremist violence and terror. And the West Bank has always been seen as less important than Iran, Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria. But that strategy, or lack thereof, may finally implode with longer-term consequences that will be much harder to fix.

How the weekend’s Jewish extremist violence reverberates through election campaigns - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:42:03 UTC
03:42:03 KST

Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank of the kind witnessed over the weekend is, to the country’s discredit, nothing new. Nor is it unprecedented for journalists or foreign dignitaries to be caught up in it.
What is different this time is the timing.
With elections just a week and a half away, incidents involving Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine and a delegation of European diplomats have become another battleground in the campaign. The violence demands attention regardless of the electoral calendar. But that calendar helps explain how the politicians are responding, and which voters they hope are listening.
The shadow of the election is particularly apparent in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s response. He condemned violence in principle while questioning what happened in these cases. His office said the circumstances remained unclear and that investigators needed to establish the facts.
Demanding an investigation before determining individual responsibility is understandable. But the statements went considerably further.
They highlighted the diplomatic delegation’s failure to coordinate its visit with the IDF, the Communist affiliation of a French mayor accompanying it, and reports of Palestinians and far Left activists confronting Jewish youths near Abu Falah. They also warned of a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria.
“The facts must determine the conclusions. Not the headlines,” his office said.
The effect was to shift attention from the alleged perpetrators to the credibility and motives of those accusing them.
Netanyahu's statements deviate from definitive condemnations by US officials
Netanyahu’s qualified statements do not match the unequivocal response of US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, who can hardly be accused of hostility toward the settlement enterprise. Huckabee condemned the assault on Levine as terrorism by “masked cowards” and demanded an investigation, arrests, and prosecution.
Nor was he alone. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was disturbed by the images and had repeatedly asked Israel to crack down.
Huckabee’s statement is significant. When an outspoken friend of the settlements calls such violence terrorism, it becomes harder to portray it as just another predictable attack on settlers. His response demonstrates that defending Jewish settlement and demanding forceful action against Jewish extremists are compatible.
For Netanyahu, however, the violence puts two political assets in tension: his partnership with the hard Right and his claim to be the indispensable manager of Israel’s relationship with Washington.
Netanyahu has several audiences to satisfy.
Washington expects enforcement. His right-wing partners and voters expect him to resist what they see as efforts to exploit confrontations and provocations to discredit the settlements. And mainstream Israelis, including many on the Right, recoil at images of masked Jews rushing civilians with clubs.
His statements try to satisfy all three by condemning the violence, withholding judgment on the incidents, and rejecting collective blame.
Does Netanyahu's response reflect political spin?
The question is how he can sustain that balancing act. Condemning violence is one thing; going after the perpetrators at the risk of antagonizing elements within his own political camp is quite another. Is Netanyahu’s caution just responsible fact-checking, or does it reflect political dependencies that constrain his ability to impose order?
For the opposition leaders, the answer is obvious. But their responses also reveal different electoral calculations.
Yisrael Beytenu’s Avigdor Liberman made the connection to Netanyahu’s political survival most explicitly.
“Bibi is putting out statements in English,” he wrote, while the prime minister and his defense and national security ministers are “doing nothing to stop this madness.”
The reference to English was pointed: Netanyahu’s concern, Liberman was suggesting, is to reassure foreign audiences while avoiding the confrontation at home that effective enforcement would require.
Liberman’s implicit accusation is that Netanyahu’s political dependence on Otzma Yehudit leader Itamar Ben-Gvir and Religious Zionist Party head Bezalel Smotrich limits his willingness to act.
It also challenges Netanyahu’s diplomatic credentials: What good is privileged access to a sympathetic administration in Washington if his coalition’s conduct keeps generating friction with it?
In his social media post on the violent incidents, Gadi Eisenkot placed greater emphasis on security and leadership. He described the violence as Jewish terrorism under government auspices, warning that a handful of criminals were eroding Israel’s legitimacy, endangering security forces, and damaging national security.
He also, notably, identified the settlement enterprise as a victim, saying these acts harm it. By taking this approach, he appeals to voters who support settlements but reject lawlessness. Eisenkot is arguing that tolerating extremists endangers what those voters value, and that protecting the settlement enterprise requires confronting people committing violence in its name.
His final warning carried a clear post-October 7 resonance: “No one in the leadership will be able to claim that they weren’t woken up in time and that they weren’t warned.”
The language evokes the debate over when Netanyahu was awakened on October 7 and reinforces Eisenkot’s broader campaign argument that Israel needs leaders who recognize danger and act before disaster strikes.
Opposition heads speak to settlers, vow to change tide
Naftali Bennett made a similar appeal, but spoke more directly to the settlers themselves.
He stressed that the perpetrators do not represent half a million residents of Judea and Samaria. “This is an un-Jewish, immoral act,” he said, promising that a new government would confront the criminals and “restore governance.”
Bennett’s message is that the government’s self-proclaimed champions of settlement are endangering its future, and that he would protect it more effectively.
There is considerable overlap with Eisenkot, but their emphases differ. Eisenkot speaks as a prospective national leader sounding a security alarm. Bennett speaks more explicitly as a defender of the settler community who would restore order in its interests.
Democrats Party leader Yair Golan, in his response, provided the most detailed account of what a different government would do.
“Jewish terror must be fought with an iron fist, just as Palestinian terror is fought,” he said.
He called for restoring administrative detention for “dangerous Jewish terror activists,” dismantling centers of terrorist activity, evacuating illegal outposts, and arresting and prosecuting offenders. He also promised full government backing for the military, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and police.
That specificity may energize his voters. It also gives Netanyahu material to portray the prospective government as a threat to the settlement project, particularly his call to evacuate illegal outposts.
In the immediate aftermath of the weekend’s incidents, Netanyahu tried to prevent the violence from becoming an indictment of his government or the wider settler population. Meanwhile, the leaders of the opposition strove to make Netanyahu’s handling of it a test of his fitness to remain in power.
The prime minister and his opponents – with the exception of Golan – describe the perpetrators as a small minority. But that leaves the question his opponents want voters to ask: If the minority is so small, why has his government been unable – or unwilling – to stop it?

The Canadian government said on Sunday that a weekend fire at an Alberta military base killed at least four people and seriously injured 39 more, with 19 in critical condition, according to the Premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith.
Prime Minister Mark Carney called the incident one of the worst peacetime tragedies ever for Canada's armed forces on home soil.
"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost," Carney said Sunday, adding that he had ordered flags on federal buildings across the country to be lowered to half-staff to honor the victims.
CBC, the government-funded national broadcaster, previously reported seven deaths at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, citing unnamed sources. Canadian authorities have said the situation continues to evolve, and that they will not confirm casualty figures until next of kin have been notified.
CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The base, one of Canada's largest, is about 210 km (130 miles) east of Edmonton in Alberta. National Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Sunday he would go to the city for briefings on the situation.
The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Center, which runs training scenarios and exercises for the army. Carney said those affected in Saturday's fire came from military bases across the country.
Cause of military base fire unclear as strong winds hamper response
Few details have been released about the cause of the fire, which took place at about 4 p.m. (2200 GMT) on Saturday in a training area at the base as winds gusted up to 60 miles per hour (96 kilometers per hour).
Military and civilian firefighters fought the fire through the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable," Carney said.
Canadian officials are expected to address the public from Wainwright, which is located in a largely rural area, later on Sunday afternoon.
Air ambulances from Edmonton and Saskatoon, which is about 300 km from Wainwright, flew to the military base on Saturday, Carney said. Patients are being treated in Edmonton, Wainwright, Calgary and Red Deer, he said.
Edmonton hospitals activate mass-casualty response after military base fire
Health staff in Edmonton said a "code orange," or mass-casualty event, was declared to coordinate the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright, CBC News reported.
The town of Wainwright, with a population of about 6,600, is just north of the base.
The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district but no evacuation orders had been issued. It said on Sunday that the fire is not expected to spread beyond its current boundaries.

Egypt's top security body agrees to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against Houthi attacks
Egypt's top security body said Sunday it has agreed to support close ally Saudi Arabia in the major escalation of fighting between the kingdom and Houthi rebels in Yemen, which has marked the latest front in the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia has been pressing allies for military assistance. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked airports and oil infrastructure across the kingdom with drones and missiles that can change direction during flight, posing a challenge to interceptors. At least 19 people have been killed, thousands of flights have been affected and global markets have been rattled.
Also on Sunday, the Saudi defense minister was meeting with the United Arab Emirates president about ways to strengthen cooperation, according to the UAE’s news agency WAM. The countries have had tense relations in the recent past as they backed different factions in the Yemeni coalition fighting the rebels.
The Egyptian announcement on military assistance came a month after a visit by the Saudi crown prince. Chaired by President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, the National Defense Council decided to provide “all possible forms of support” to enable Saudi Arabia to defend its security, according to a presidential statement.
It didn’t provide details. El-Sissi on Saturday called for parliament to grant him the authorization to deploy troops and military equipment abroad.
The surge in fighting has threatened civilians in both Saudi Arabia and Yemen, which has seen a return to civil war. The interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, Aden, has seen its airport and a palace used by the government attacked in the past week.
On Sunday, an airstrike killed at least nine people, including five children and two women, in Yemen’s rebel-held northern province of Saada, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said.
Spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said the strike hit a house in Sahar district and wounded 19 others, including 11 children. Some were in critical condition, he said.
Al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia. There was no immediate comment from the kingdom. The Houthi-run al-Masirah satellite channel aired footage of people clearing debris with their hands and pulling two young people out of the rubble.
The rebels said attacks by Saudi-led forces had killed or wounded over 30 people in the past 24 hours. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, said 110 missiles or airstrikes were carried out against civilian sites in Sanaa and other cities. The Associated Press could not independently verify the claim.
Across the border in Saudi Arabia, a Saudi helicopter gunship crashed near the city of Najran in the southwest, killing its two-member crew, a Saudi military spokesperson said, citing a technical malfunction. The Houthis earlier claimed to have downed it.
Later, Saudi Civil Defense authorities said a projectile fired by the Houthis landed in a residential area of Najran province, wounding six people.
The Houthis have resumed attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks because the kingdom has supported Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The rebels recently seized more territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis’ chief negotiator on Sunday blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation. Mohamed Abdulsalam said on social media that the rebels had warned the kingdom against striking the rebel-held Sanaa airport in mid-July.
That strike prevented the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation returning from the funeral of Iran’s supreme leader, who had been killed in the opening strikes of the war in February.
The Houthis, angry over the longstanding Saudi blockade on them, declared their own blockade on the kingdom.
Oman had offered a five-day truce during which the two sides would meet and settle their dispute, Abdulsalam said. He said the Houthis agreed to stop attacks if Saudi Arabia agreed to “humanitarian demands.” He didn’t elaborate.
He said Saudi Arabia didn’t show “any indication that it is ready to deal positively” with the demands. The rebels shortly after that launched their offensive down the Red Sea coast.
A Saudi diplomat last week in a rare briefing said the kingdom had called for a meeting in Oman with the Houthis in July “to resolve outstanding differences and bring an end to this escalation,” but the rebels refused to participate.
On Sunday, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, Al-Azhar in Egypt, called for the formation of an “urgent mediation committee” to end conflicts across the Arab region.

DR Congo’s fast-moving Ebola outbreak spreads to eighth province

The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to an eighth province in the country’s north, authorities said on Sunday.
The Health Ministry has recorded two cases, including one death, in Nord-Ubangi province, bordering Central African Republic. The ministry said both patients were men in their 20s living in the Wapinda health zone, which borders Bas-Uele province, where Ebola cases have been reported previously.
Authorities have recorded at least 9,400 cases, including more than 4,500 deaths, in the outbreak declared in mid-May, making it the deadliest in DR Congo’s history.
The virus has spilled over into other countries including neighbouring Uganda, which has since declared itself free of the disease, and Kenya, which recorded a seventh case on Saturday. Central African Republic has not recorded any confirmed cases.
