The unexpected crisis facing our expanding cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:35:08 UTC
03:35:08 KST

In brief
- Some metropolitan cemeteries are expected to run out of burial space by the early 2030s.
- Cremation and alternative forms of deathcare are becoming increasingly common in Australia.
Australians are familiar with the housing crisis, but there's a lesser-known land battle occurring right beneath our feet.
Some metropolitan cemeteries are running out of space, and it's raising questions about the accessibility of burial practices and rise of alternative forms of deathcare.
Among them is Rookwood Cemetery in Sydney's west, which is the largest necropolis in the southern hemisphere.
It rivals the size of many suburbs, spanning more than 280 hectares, and has been operating for almost 160 years.
Rob Smart is the acting CEO of Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which manages eight Crown land cemeteries in NSW, including Rookwood.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He said the company maximises operating space and is trying to acquire more land but almost all of their cemeteries are expected to reach capacity by the early 2030s.
"As our larger sites do run out of land, that puts pressure on all of the other sites that might still have land," he told SBS News.
It's not just Metropolitan Memorial Parks, with many cemeteries in major cities predicting they will reach capacity within the decade.
That's in part due to the growth of urban areas, according to Ben Kelly, the CEO of the Australasian Cemeteries and Crematoria Association.
"You look at Rookwood in Sydney, that was right on the outskirts, and now, that's almost an inner suburb," he said.
"It's just our cities have grown, we just haven't continued building cemeteries."
Another challenge, Kelly said, is that some residents don't want to live next them, while governments had other funding priorities.
"They're worried, they'll ... reduce house prices, that type of thing or they just find them spooky and they're not," he said.
The NSW government is considering converting Carnarvon Golf Club in the Sydney suburb of Lidcombe into a new cemetery, a proposal criticised by some community members, including Auburn MP Lynda Voltz.
She addressed NSW parliament in May regarding risks of flooding in the area.
"At first glance, this proposal may be presented as a practical response to the growing demand for burial space but when you take a closer look, a different picture emerges," she said.
"The planning falls short, key risks are being brushed over and yet the environmental consequences are hard to ignore ... flooding here is frequent."
The proposal remains under review.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, last year there were more than 188,000 registered deaths in the nation. Kelly says roughly 75 to 85 per cent of Australians are now cremated.
But some faith groups, including Islam and Judaism, do not permit the practice.
In 2023, the Vatican updated its guidance on cremation, allowing Catholics to request that a small portion of their relative's ashes be preserved in a "place of significance to them".
Smart believes all Australians should be given the option of a traditional burial.
"Australia is a multicultural country and while we do have a broad range of faiths and cultures within Australia, I think, we need to be able to provide choice," he said.
"To say to people, you can't follow your cultural, your faith-based requirements is very restrictive on the individuals, or the families or the communities."
DIY commemorations
While some cemeteries are running out of space for new burials, Hannah Gould, from the University of Melbourne's DeathTech Research Team, said there is often room to keep cremated remains.
She said the way Australians are approaching death and memorial celebrations is also gradually changing, such as with the rise of 'do it yourself' commemorations.
"When it comes to the handling of the body, the vast majority of those processes need to be done by professionals," she said.
"It's not legal in this country to bury somebody or to cremate somebody yourself but kind of everything else now is is increasingly being done by family members and friends.
"You just organise to like get together at the pub with friends, as opposed to having a formal funeral ceremony that's run by a funeral director."
After cremation, ashes can be kept in a permanent place like a cemetery or scattered on private property or certain public areas with permission.
Ashes can also grow into a living memorial tree, be preserved in a memory rock, turned into jewellery, a diamond or even fireworks.
Alternative forms of disposition including sea burials, green or biodegradable burials and full-body human cryonics have taken place around the world.
Upright burials, where the deceased are buried standing, feet first, are also becoming more popular.
Another space-saving measure is renewable tenure, where burial plots are leased for set amounts of time — usually 25, 50 or 99 years — rather than in perpetuity.
If the grave is not renewed after a grace period, the plot can eventually be reused.
It's widely practised in South Australia, while in Western Australia, graves are sold with a 25-year lease known as a grant of right of burial.
Whether a person wants to be cremated or buried, Kelly believes it's important people have conversations about death and disposition while they're still living.
"Trying to plan after the fact of a loved one dying is so difficult," he said.
"So, if they can get in early and have that conversation, you know, put a note on the fridge, a post-it of 'I want to be cremated', it starts a conversation and gets people talking."

The higher-tax proposal experts say could 'secure' Australia’s future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:34:54 UTC
03:34:54 KST

In brief
- Increasing the GST from 10 to 15 per cent would raise about $76 billion a year, according to the Grattan Institute.
- Another recent study found that a GST increase might hurt lower-income households less than commonly thought.
The last time an Australian government owed this much debt, the country was still paying off a world war — except for the COVID-19 pandemic.
As government debt climbs, the Grattan Institute has proposed a controversial solution: hike one tax, cut another, and put more money in welfare recipients' pockets.
In a new report, the think tank argues that raising the country's Goods and Services Tax (GST) and using the money to cut income taxes and boost welfare payments is a solution to the debt issue.
GST is a flat 10 per cent tax applied to the price of most goods and services sold or consumed in Australia.
According to the report, titled Budget reboot: How to fund Australia's future, cost-of-living pressures, growing demand for social services, and higher borrowing costs are the drivers of the Australian government's mounting debt.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It suggests the situation could worsen in the coming years, with factors such as an ageing population, climate change, and high interest rates forcing the government to spend more.
According to the report, raising GST from 10 per cent to 15 per cent and expanding it to include all food would create a more resilient budget.
Why raising GST has become a 'political no-go zone'
Since its introduction by former prime minister John Howard, which came into effect in July 2000, GST has never increased.
"There are no easy paths back to budget sustainability," Aruna Sathanapally, CEO of Grattan Institute and the report's lead author, said.
"But with smarter spending decisions and a tax system that raises sufficient revenue to care for our ageing population, both current and future generations can be better off.
"Reform on this game-changing scale is challenging, but the prize is worth it: a more secure future for Australia's finances, and for all Australians."
A similar 5 per cent increase plan drafted by economist Richard Holden was pitched by Independent MP Kate Chaney in August 2025.
At the time, Holden told SBS News that compared to other "advanced economies", Australia gets about "twice as much of our revenue from income taxes and about half as much of our income from the GST".
At the time, the Greens labelled the plan "lazy", while the Opposition called it "increasingly brave". Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Labor had not considered a possible GST increase.
"Boosting the GST has become a political no-go zone, in part due to disagreements about how to divvy up the revenue, and concerns it would increase the cost of living," the Grattan Institute report stated.
Where should the revenue go?
The GST increase and expansion will raise about $76 billion a year, according to the Grattan Institute.
The think tank suggests using $58 billion to cut income taxes for low- and middle-income earners and boost welfare payments, which could orchestrate the largest personal income tax cuts in nearly 20 years.
"JobSeeker and Youth Allowance should be raised by 20 per cent, Commonwealth Rent Assistance by 50 per cent, the Parenting Payment by 20 per cent, and pensions by about 8 per cent," the report said.
It suggests allocating the remaining revenue to state governments to shore up their budgets and cut inefficient taxes, such as stamp duty.
It predicts that with the GST increase, most households would pay slightly more in taxes, with larger increases for wealthier and older households.
On the other hand, in estimates, a low-income, single-parent family who rents would be about $150 a week better off, while a higher-income working family would pay $162 a week more in tax.
Would an increase in GST be unfair?
For years, the argument against raising GST was that it would be unfair, particularly to lower-income households.
GST is often described as regressive, in that it takes up a larger share of these households' income than that of higher-income households' income.
This is because higher-income households tend to save more of their income while lower-income households generally spend more of what they earn.
In a July 2025 report, the Australian Council of Social Service argued that increasing the GST to fund income tax cuts "would shift resources from those with the least to those with the most".
However, a recent study by e61–UNSW Policy Research Partnership found that GST may be less regressive than commonly thought. It found households that spend more and those that spend less pay roughly the same share of their spending in GST — about 7.3 per cent.
Examining a household's spending in a year doesn't provide the full picture, the UNSW research partnership says.
Instead, it examined the spending of households across a longer time, taking into account changes in people's circumstances, such as studying, taking parental leave or moving between jobs.
Averaging the years, the gap in GST spending between lower-income and higher-income households narrows.
In other words, the perceived fairness of the GST depends not only on how much people earn, but also on how their spending, saving and longer-term financial position are measured, UNSW says.
The research argues that a reform that includes an increase in GST and paying back the revenue to people "through an unconditional income payment" would be "progressive, irrespective of the measure of household resources".

‘They wanted to bring down the Republic’: Macron condemns France riots as violence continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:34:52 UTC
03:34:52 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron delivered a special address to the nation Sunday evening following a weekend of violent riots, declaring that "we all feel anger and shame tonight." Speaking after an emergency meeting with several ministers at the Élysée Palace, Macron said that "those who destroyed must pay, and those who looted must reimburse," promising "full transparency" over how security forces prepared for and handled the unrest.
Macron's speech came shortly after reports of fresh looting in Paris and Lyon, though on a far smaller scale than the violence that swept the country over the weekend. Security forces remained on high alert amid fears of another night of unrest.
Macron spoke shortly after French media reported further looting in Paris. The exact scale of the incidents was not immediately clear, but most were reported around Place de la République, where clashes with police resumed and clothing stores were reportedly targeted. CRS 8, a specialized French riot police unit trained to respond to urban violence, was deployed across the capital, including around the square.
French television network BFMTV broadcast live footage of several people vandalizing and looting a Petite Mendigote store. The shop window was smashed, allowing several men to enter. According to Le Parisien, unmasked youths were later seen walking along the street carrying sweaters. "Would you like a sweater, madam?" one asked a woman riding a bicycle. "No, thank you," she replied.
Just minutes before Macron began his address, fresh clashes were reported in Paris, where police used tear gas and stun grenades on Boulevard Voltaire and Place de la République. A Le Parisien reporter said numerous young people were gathered in the area and could be heard shouting, "Come on, guys, let's go loot something."
Meanwhile, around 50 young people, many wearing masks, attempted to smash the window of a Lacoste store in Lyon. Police intervened before they could break in, dispersing the group with tear gas. In Limoges, where some of Saturday's worst violence occurred, approximately 7,000 people gathered Sunday evening for a demonstration in the city's Place de la République, with no significant disturbances initially reported.
Macron, whose second presidential term ends next May and who is barred from seeking a third consecutive term, has largely limited his response in recent weeks to measured statements acknowledging protesters' anger while condemning violence. Demonstrations by schoolchildren, university students and labor unions have repeatedly descended into serious disorder, but the president has refrained from taking more sweeping measures, including invoking emergency powers that could allow a larger security deployment and tighter restrictions on violent groups.
Seeking to highlight what they described as Macron's detachment from the public, critics circulated footage over the weekend showing him and his wife, Brigitte, dancing and drinking at a Céline Dion concert Friday night, just hours before the riots began. Security forces were already making extensive preparations for Saturday's planned demonstrations, preparations that ultimately proved insufficient to contain the violence. 
The video showed the couple smiling and applauding, prompting accusations that they were completely disconnected from a country increasingly furious over soaring living costs, deteriorating public finances, political paralysis and violence in the streets. Some critics even compared them to Marie Antoinette, the wife of King Louis XVI, who became a symbol of royal extravagance while ordinary French citizens suffered hunger and economic hardship in the years preceding the French Revolution.
Mélenchon's warning to Macron: 'Announce measures or we will lose control'
Even before Macron's address, politicians from both the far right and the far left launched direct attacks on the president and his government. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is running in next year's presidential election, said in a video released shortly before the speech that Macron's administration had "run out of steam" and was exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything beyond commenting on its own impotence and decline.
"We have a government that deplores events without managing to prevent them, control them or even deal with them," Le Pen said. "A minority government that has lost its legitimacy, whose sole concern is no longer governing France but clinging to the last remnants of its fading power." Jordan Bardella, president of Le Pen's National Rally party and her close political ally, said shortly beforehand that Saturday's violence had left "France humiliated" and that "there is no longer any order" in the country.
Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose France Unbowed party (LFI) has been accused by political opponents of inciting protesters and bearing significant responsibility for the violence, also attacked Macron. "I am worried. We had to go through this entire wave of violence before Emmanuel Macron finally made his voice heard," he said. "The government adopted a strategy of letting things deteriorate. Macron is sitting on the fence and playing for time."
Mélenchon has repeatedly accused the government and security forces in recent days of using excessive force against protesters and rioters. On Sunday evening, he again accused the authorities of pursuing a policy of "blind violence." Ahead of Macron's speech, he urged the president to announce concrete measures to address protesters' demands, warning that continuing the political deadlock could cause the situation to spiral out of control.
Édouard Philippe, the former center-right prime minister who also intends to run for president next year and has generally been polling behind Le Pen and Mélenchon, blamed both the far left, particularly LFI, and the current government. He said Saturday's events represented more than a breakdown of public order, describing them as a challenge to the foundations of the French Republic. Philippe also demanded answers about the intelligence assessments and security preparations undertaken before the riots erupted.
The widespread destruction prompted calls from politicians on both the left and right for Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to resign. Members of the Green party also demanded a parliamentary commission of inquiry into both the violence and the policing methods used to contain it. 
"When a day of demonstrations turns into chaos, we must also examine the responsibility of our leaders, particularly the Interior Ministry, which is responsible for public order and everyone's safety," Green senators wrote. Yaël Braun-Pivet, president of the National Assembly, the lower house of the French parliament, also announced plans to propose a parliamentary inquiry.
30,000 people took part in Marseille looting, authorities say
Macron's address followed a Saturday of widespread violence across France, during which large groups of masked rioters attacked police officers and passersby, set dozens of government buildings on fire and looted hundreds of stores. The unrest erupted after a massive afternoon demonstration against rising living costs and deteriorating public services, attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
Politicians on the right in France and abroad have blamed the violence partly on the far left, which they accuse of fueling the unrest as a show of strength ahead of next year's presidential election. Some have also pointed to immigrants and their descendants, alleging that members of those communities participated heavily in the riots. According to the latest figures cited by French authorities in the report, 2,397 people had been arrested and 997 members of the security forces injured, seven of them seriously.
France's Chamber of Commerce estimated Sunday afternoon that at least 1,500 businesses nationwide had been damaged, with losses running into hundreds of millions of euros. Hundreds of stores were reportedly looted in Paris alone, where Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said "entire streets were systematically devastated."
Le Parisien described widespread destruction in several neighborhoods. In the 1st arrondissement, rioters reportedly spared virtually no stores around Les Halles. "Tobacco shops, opticians, beauty salons, pharmacies, clothing stores and more were all damaged," the newspaper reported. In the 10th arrondissement, near Porte Saint-Denis, dozens of additional businesses were vandalized.
The newspaper described piles of garbage and burned bicycles scattered across sidewalks, some still smoldering. Sanitation workers dispatched to the scene told its reporters, "It will take us days to clean all this up."
In Marseille in southern France, Lille in the north, Angers in the west and Bordeaux in the southwest, rioters stormed and vandalized city halls and regional government buildings on Saturday. Authorities in Marseille said Sunday evening that their assessment indicated at least 30,000 people had participated in the looting that swept the city.
In Lyon, southeastern France, the city's tourist information office was set on fire Saturday. Footage from the scene showed one rioter waving a Palestinian flag. Local police said "hostile individuals" had obstructed firefighters sent to bring the blaze under control.
An even more devastating incident occurred in Limoges, central France, where masked rioters set fire to the historic city hall. The ornate building, inaugurated in 1883 and having survived both world wars, collapsed and was "largely destroyed," according to authorities. Its bell tower also came crashing down, in dramatic footage circulated on social media and viewed by millions around the world.
The riots left many French citizens in shock Sunday. "It's disgraceful, terrifying, these gangs of young people we saw here yesterday, looting and destroying things with impunity," said Cécile Rogue, 57, in Paris.
Similar emotions were expressed outside the destroyed Limoges city hall. "My children got married here. It's heartbreaking," said Jean-Louis, a retired local resident. "You can make demands without destroying everything."
Volunteers spontaneously turned out to help clear debris from the devastated streets of several city centers, partly to overcome their sense of helplessness. "I woke up this morning, was left speechless and just wanted to feel useful," said Clémentine, 47, from Lyon, who came to help with the cleanup.
Trump to France: 'Immigration has crushed you, close your borders!'
The weekend riots followed a nationwide day of protest against the high cost of living, deteriorating public services and rising fuel prices. High school and university students, labor unions and members of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 in opposition to Macron's economic policies, all joined the demonstrations.
Many view Saturday's protests as a continuation of student demonstrations that began last month in schools in impoverished suburbs north of Paris, where pupils have complained of teacher shortages and poor learning conditions. Those protests also saw numerous incidents of violence, and similar unrest has since spread to other European countries, including Belgium.
In France and abroad, some commentators and politicians have emphasized the involvement of immigrants and their descendants from Africa, Arab countries and Muslim-majority nations in the demonstrations and violence. Marion Maréchal, the niece of far-right leader Marine Le Pen and a politician in her own right, said Saturday night: "The whole world is watching in astonishment and disbelief as the children of Mélenchon's 'New France' destroy our country."
The term "New France" was coined by Mélenchon to describe his vision of a society in which immigrant communities are an integral part of the nation. Maréchal has used it critically to warn against demographic changes that she and other figures on the French right regard as a serious threat to the country's future.
Claims about the role of immigrant communities in the unrest have circulated since the student protests earlier this month, and U.S. President Donald Trump has also weighed in. About two weeks ago, amid a "day of rage" on French streets, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the protests were not really about schools but were a cover for other aims.
"What is happening in France is nothing more than mass immigration that has gotten out of control," he wrote. "This is not about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country!"
On Sunday, following the weekend's violence, Trump issued another post attacking France's immigration policies. "France is burning!" he wrote. "Immigration of people from a completely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has crushed this once great country. Close your borders and take control before it's too late!"

Get ready to go back in time with this week's history quiz

Italian police arrest 28 after cost-of-living protests turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:17:43 UTC
03:17:43 KST

Italian police have arrested 28 people, including 12 minors, following clashes during cost-of-living protests across several cities.
Tensions continued in central Milan on Sunday after Saturday’s demonstrations, Sky TG24 reported, citing police figures showing 141 law enforcement officers were injured.
Police said 197 people were identified and taken to police stations, while 43 were referred to judicial authorities.
Organised by the Italia in Piazza movement, the protests targeted rising living costs, fuel prices and tax pressures. Police estimated turnout at 5,000 in Milan, 3,000 in Turin, 2,000 in Bologna, 800 in Bergamo and 600 in Brescia.
In Milan, groups threw stones, bottles, firecrackers and barriers at officers, who responded with tear gas and water cannon. Shops in the city centre were damaged and looted, and a Carabinieri vehicle was destroyed.
Police arrested 17 people in the city. Retail association Confcommercio estimated damage to shops and businesses at more than €500,000 ($561,860), according to Sky TG24.
In Turin, officers arrested an adult for resisting police and three minors allegedly carrying Molotov cocktails. A group also entered the Feltrinelli bookstore at Porta Nuova station and threw books onto the floor.
In Bologna, five minors were arrested following clashes near the railway station. Police used tear gas and water cannon after demonstrators threw bottles, stones and barriers.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed solidarity with law enforcement and urged opposition parties to unequivocally condemn the violence, while acknowledging that thousands had protested peacefully.
Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini said his League party would resubmit a parliamentary proposal requiring organisers of demonstrations deemed risky to provide financial guarantees to cover potential damage.
Milan Mayor Giuseppe Sala said protesters’ grievances were understandable, but attacks on officers and extensive damage to the city were unjustifiable.
Bologna Mayor Matteo Lepore also condemned the unrest, urging young people to distance themselves from those using demonstrations as a pretext for violence.

====================================================================================================

Winning the next election could be Labor's undoing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:15:00 UTC
03:15:00 KST

analysis
Without a careful plan, winning the next election could be Labor's undoing
What if the worst thing that can happen to a political party is to win an election?
History is littered with unexpected, sweet victories, but are they really that sweet if they let a party overstay its welcome and trash its political capital and brand?
Scott Morrison's unexpected win in 2019 is an example. The Coalition cycled through three prime ministers and went to the election with a thin agenda. Morrison declared the result a miracle. Three years later, the party had trashed its political capital and lost the 2022 election.
John Howard's victory in 2004 is another example. An aging government secured a thumping win and with it, control of the Senate. The extraordinary power it had been handed gave it the freedom to introduce WorkChoices, an industrial relations overhaul that became a political millstone, leading to Kevin Rudd's win in 2007, an election that also cost Howard his own seat.
In 1993 Paul Keating won what he famously called "the sweetest victory of all", securing a fifth consecutive term for Labor against John Hewson's Coalition. Just three years later, Labor was decimated, languishing in the political wilderness until 2007.
This is not to argue that the voters got it wrong. Voters always get it right. But rejecting the alternative is not the same as endorsing the status quo.
An extra term can delay the reckoning that forces renewal and an autopsy on a loss. Worse, it can breed a sense of invincibility that encourages leaders and senior ministers to believe their own hype, further detaching them from the issues affecting voters.
Reshuffle or revival
Speculation that Albanese is set to reshuffle his frontbench next year raises the question of whether he can avoid the fate of past governments. Another victory risks the government entering a third term without a clear agenda and renewed frontbench.
Albanese is an astute student of politics. He knows the danger of holding onto dead wood for too long.
The prime minister last week told me on Afternoon Briefing he was not "spooked" by the 24-hour news cycle and poor polls. But inside the government there is an emerging view that, unless the government develops a better economic narrative, a reshuffle will not be enough to turn the ship around. Reports of frustration with Treasurer Jim Chalmers inside the Caucus and the prime minister's office are adding to the pressure.
Industry Minister Tim Ayres yesterday downplayed tensions between Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers, denying the prime minister is frustrated with the treasurer amid the fallout over the ATO credit card surcharge ban.
The pair spent last week fending off reports that Albanese rolled Chalmers when he told a business dinner he had agreed to intervene over the ATO credit card ban following a text message from ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar.
Asked on News24 on Sunday whether the two men got along, Senator Ayres said: "This is a cabinet-style government that's working very well. It's stable."
"It's a real contrast to not just what's happening at the other end of the world, but a real contrast to what's happening on the other side of politics, which has been a total mess and has been since 2013," Senator Ayres said.
The credit card fiasco became murkier on Sunday after Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino conceded that the government knew in July that the Australian Taxation Office was considering stopping direct credit card payments in response to surcharge changes.
It gives more life to a story about the failure of the government to address a problem it saw coming but appeared to ignore without reading the obvious political ramifications.
Summer reset
Senior Labor MPs believe the summer provides a crucial opportunity to reset the government.
Feverish speculation that frontbenchers including Andrew Charlton, Jenny McAllister, Daniel Mulino and Kristy McBain may be elevated is not a coincidence. The government needs new energy and to make better use of its talent. There is a view that MPs who have been in the parliament since the Rudd/Gillard years need to step aside from the ministry to allow the government a proper refresh.
On June 17, 2008, retiring Nationals senator Sandy Macdonald reflected on the Howard government's defeat in his valedictory speech: "I do feel that governments sometimes win one election too many." He continued by arguing that Keating should not have won in 1993, before explaining that electorates eventually tire of governments and vote for change.
Political scientists Alfred Cuzán and Richard Heggen examined election results in Australia, Canada, Germany and the United States and identified what they called the cruise-and-crash model. Their finding was that incumbent parties can maintain relatively stable voting support across multiple elections before experiencing a concentrated loss at the election that removes them from office.
For Labor, scraping across the line at the next election can't be the only measure of success. It needs to deliver this term and go to the next election with a clear vision of what it will do next. Simply not being those opposite won't cut it.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

Banned Israeli chess players demand 'world' be stripped from Malaysian championship title
Unknown

2026-10-18
18:06:22 UTC
03:06:22 KST

Malaysian authorities have barred Israeli chess players from representing their country at the upcoming World Amateur Chess Championship, organized by the International Chess Federation (FIDE).
Following discussions with tournament organizers in Malaysia, the official participant list was published without the names of two Israeli players who had registered for the championship, confirming their exclusion from the international competition.
One of the excluded players, Lior Aizenberg, director of the Chess4All organization, criticized the decision.
"Participating with an Israeli passport or even a foreign passport, which doesn't even require an entry visa to the country, makes no difference to them. The Malaysian authorities are simply unwilling to allow Israelis to represent Israel at a World Championship. As far as they are concerned, Israel does not exist. After 78 years of statehood, and especially following October 7, we as Israelis cannot allow such a situation to stand."
Aizenberg and representatives of the Israeli chess community have called for immediate international intervention, urging FIDE to take action against the Malaysian organizers.
“The championship in Malaysia should be canceled and moved to another country, or held in Israel,” the representatives said.
They also called for the tournament to lose its designation as a championship if Israeli players remain barred from competing.
“If the tournament proceeds in Malaysia despite the ban, the word "World" must be stripped from its official title. It cannot be considered a true World Championship if representatives from Israel are barred from participating.”
The Israeli representatives further demanded that international sporting standards be enforced, citing a previous case in which Malaysia lost the right to host a major sporting event over its refusal to admit Israeli athletes.
“With less than three weeks remaining until the event, it is unacceptable that governing bodies have not issued a clear ultimatum to the Malaysian hosts. A direct precedent exists: in 2019, Malaysia was stripped of its hosting rights for the World Para Swimming Championships after refusing to allow Israeli athletes to compete.”
FIDE had invited 'all eligible players' to participate
FIDE's official announcement on the World Amateur Chess Championship stated that "all FIDE member federations and all eligible players are invited to participate."
However, Malaysia's entry restrictions effectively prevent Israeli players from competing, despite the international federation's stated commitment to open participation.
Aizenberg, who has campaigned against boycotts of Israel in sports and culture in recent years, described his initial correspondence with the tournament organizers in an interview with Walla.
"I contacted the tournament organizer with an innocent question about participating, and immediately received a message saying he was sorry, but Israelis would not be able to play because of Malaysia's immigration policy. Right afterward, he deleted the message and added another saying they would get back to me. A place that does not accept Israelis or players from any other country should not be allowed to host a world championship."

According to Fox, the watchlist lawsuit does not establish wrongdoing by Jukaku or El-Sayed.
Michigan Democratic Senate hopeful comes under fire for supposed Muslim Brotherhood ties
El-Sayed, a Michigan-born child of Egyptian immigrants, has recently come under scrutiny for his family's purported ties to the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt.
The Muslim Brotherhood is an Islamist organization that was founded in Egypt in the 1920s and spread quickly through the Middle East and North Africa before splitting into a variety of offshoots, some of which have developed into violent terrorist organizations, including Hamas in Gaza. El-Sayed has sought to mend relations with Jewish voters in the state in recent months, though his opposition to a two-state solution in Israel, along with past controversies involving anti-Israel streamer Hasan Piker and his response to the attack on the Detroit-area Temple Israel, have rendered his candidacy polarizing to the community.

Why Arye Deri's Shas is Israel’s haredi version of woke politics - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:06:12 UTC
03:06:12 KST

The Shas campaign is brilliant. Cynical to the core, and brilliant anyway. It is one of the sharpest campaigns we have seen in the feed, with production values and writing closer to cinema than to a party broadcast, and with delicate family dynamics and real emotion invested in them.
The small moments are executed so well that even while I was tearing my hair out, I could not help admiring the craft.
In the first video, an IDF soldier comes home to a traditional Sephardi family, observant but not ultra-Orthodox, which is precisely Shas’s core electorate.
He arrives at the last second for kiddush, and the film presents the tension between Torah study and military service as something that exists outside the family.
Inside it, there is perfect harmony between the brother who fights and the brother who studies full time. “Did you study a lot this week?” “For you and for all the soldiers.” “I felt it.”
In the second video, that togetherness becomes a havdalah celebration and mutual wishes of “we made it,” tying together prayer, Torah scholars, the army, and, in the voice of Rabbi Ovadia Yosef himself, the Shas movement. Tension? Please.
In the third video, the hidden tension is finally exposed. It runs between the father, who leans toward the ultra-Orthodox position, and his traditional friend, who believes the ultra-Orthodox must enlist. You see the pain, the fight, the frustration, and finally the wordless moment of reconciliation. It settles nothing, but it is full of unity and great love.
The campaign is brilliant because, unlike amateurish propaganda clips, it has real drama, excellent performances, and an emotional pull you cannot stay indifferent to. But you cannot understand the campaign without understanding the size of the trap Arye Deri is caught in.
Shas is the only political phenomenon that manages to take votes from a public that is not ultra-Orthodox and harness them to advance purely ultra-Orthodox interests. The trouble is that in recent years, the unbridgeable gap between the ultra-Orthodox interest and the Zionist interest has risen to the surface.
At the ultimate moment of testing, when combat soldiers were crying out for help, and the number of dead and wounded climbed and climbed, Shas’s elected officials, who take pride in the high rate of service among their own voters, were forced to pick a side. And oh, did they pick.
Rabbi Moshe Maya of Shas’s Council of Torah Sages declared that today no one may enlist, not even someone who is not studying Torah. Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, the former Sephardi chief rabbi, called for draft notices to be thrown in the toilet. And Deri was recorded telling yeshiva students that not one of them should so much as entertain the thought of volunteering or, God forbid, enlisting.
Once you understand that, the newest video in the campaign is astonishing to watch. It really is the cherry on top.
The father attends a parent-teacher meeting at a mainstream state school, where he is confronted with a radical progressive agenda running through the curriculum. It all peaks when he cries out: “What will be left of us if we simply try to be like everyone else?”
Now that is a remarkable moment, because if we are asking about the future, I have a question of my own. What will be left of us if Shas keeps accumulating more power? The answer is simple. Fewer and fewer people will enlist in the army, pay taxes, and obey the law, and the Jewish state will collapse.
That video works the emotions, Jewish emotions, and beyond them the question of whether a Jewish state can survive at all. A state that Shas has refused for many years now to lift a finger for, while working hard to ensure that the ultra-Orthodox public, which it expects to become the majority in Israel, grows up neither Zionist nor economically productive.
Israel's 'woke'
So here is the unpleasant truth. Shas is Israel’s version of wokeness.
Because what is wokeness, at bottom? A complete detachment from reality in favor of self-definitions that everyone is expected to accommodate just so that nobody gets offended. A distortion of the truth in the service of an arbitrary identity.
Shas is the wokeness of the State of Israel, only with a black yarmulke instead of purple hair. A party that quite often acts and speaks in terms more extreme than its Ashkenazi counterpart, United Torah Judaism.
A party whose leaders come out against the IDF and call on young men to defy the institutions of the state if those institutions dare to draft them, and to flush their draft notices down the toilet. A non-Zionist party, through and through.
And yet this same party feels perfectly free to produce a video about the future of the State of Israel and about the return to our land, or to call itself part of “the Right,” for no reason beyond the fact that it can.
And just as wokeness collapses in on itself, simply because the facts do not care about your opinions, the same thing will happen to Shas in the end.
It does not matter how badly you want Shas to be part of the right-wing bloc, the national bloc, or the religious-Zionist bloc. It simply cannot be, because it is not Zionist. Its actions weaken the State of Israel and undermine its very capacity to exist. Those are the facts.
It does not matter how they define themselves, how tightly they cling to their identity, or how many correct words they say. In the end, reality exists, facts exist, and those facts don’t care about anyone’s feelings or Deri’s brilliant campaign.
The writer is the CEO of the Ribo Center.

Israel Railways to reduce service in central Israel 'during peak hours only' for planned work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:06:00 UTC
03:06:00 KST

Israel Railways will reduce service on its Sharon Ring Line in central Israel "during peak hours only" from October 28 to 29, according to an announcement released on the company's website on Sunday.
As part of the service changes, train frequency will be halved to two trains per hour in each direction during peak hours, down from the usual four. Given the line's high ridership and central location, the midweek service reduction is likely to cause significant crowding at stations and onboard trains, as well as increased traffic congestion for those who choose to take private cars instead.
The popularity of the Sharon Ring Line is further evident in its standard peak-hour frequency relative to other popular lines, such as the Herzliya-Jerusalem Line, which runs at a maximum frequency of just two trains per hour, according to the Israel Railways schedule.
Peak hours for the Sharon Ring Line are approximately 6:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., with trains on the line running at a standard frequency of two per hour during off-peak times, according to the schedule.
Service cuts to allow for 'life-saving infrastructure work,' railway says
According to the railway, the service reduction will allow for "life-saving infrastructure work essential for travel safety in the Rishon Lezion area," which the affected rail line traverses along Israel's southern coast, serving Yavne, Ashdod, and Ashkelon. At the time of writing, the update is available only on the railway's Hebrew and Arabic websites, not on its English or Russian websites.
The Sharon Ring Line, named for its loop around the central Sharon region, serves several central Israeli cities, including Tel Aviv, Holon, Bat Yam, Bnei Brak, Petah Tikva, Hod Hasharon, Ra'anana, and Herzliya. The line further serves cities in Israel's northern Negev region, including Sderot, Netivot, Ofakim, and Beersheba.
Peak-hour work planned despite usual practice of off-peak work
The national railway company, overseen by Miri Regev's Transportation Ministry, generally plans major infrastructure work during off-peak hours or on weekends (excluding Shabbat) to avoid serious service disruptions.
For example, similar work planned for this week in the Yavne area will affect trains only from 10:00 p.m. on Tuesday to 4:30 a.m. on Wednesday, according to the Israel Railways website, with no disruptions to peak-hour trains.
It was not immediately clear why the railway chose to do the October 28-29 infrastructure work during peak hours, including rush hour, on two consecutive workdays immediately after Israel's October 27 elections.
The railway noted that some trains on the Beersheba-Herzliya Line will stop at the Holon and Bat Yam stations to alleviate disruptions.

Boeing 737 MAX 10 to be certified despite software glitch, airlines may refuse delivery - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:05:56 UTC
03:05:56 KST

The United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is set to certify Boeing’s new 737 MAX 10 jet as soon as next week, despite the airliner still facing software-related issues, online aviation publication Simple Flying reported on Saturday.
The report follows a successful final type certification board meeting on Friday, according to another online aviation publication, The Air Current, which said the FAA ruled that the software issues do not pose a risk to flight safety.
Specifically, the issues involve a software glitch during the aircraft’s go-around procedure, when a plane aborts a landing, gains altitude, and “goes around” for another attempt.
According to Simple Flying, a flaw in the aircraft’s flight management computer (FMC) software could cause the autopilot to partially disengage during the procedure, leading the aircraft to deviate from its flight path and forcing pilots to suddenly take manual control during a critical phase of flight.
However, since pilots would still technically be in control of the aircraft, the FAA determined that the issue was not substantial enough to delay certification, Simple Flying noted, and issued a non-mandatory Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB), permitting certification with the glitch still unaddressed.
Boeing knew of issue since 2024, did not inform buyers until 2026
Canadian carrier WestJet, the MAX 10 launch customer, informed Boeing of the issue after a November 2024 test flight, Simple Flying reported, though the US aircraft maker did not inform other customers of the problem for nearly two years. Several buyers reportedly told Boeing that they would refuse delivery of any aircraft fitted with the software containing the glitch.
The FMC software, known as U14, updates the previous U13 software, which was introduced alongside the original 737 MAX at its debut in 2017. US carriers United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines, and Alaska Airlines told The Air Current they preferred U13 to U14, calling the older version the “lesser of the two evils.”
The airlines’ preference for U13 comes despite the software having been in place at the time of the 737 MAX’s two fatal crashes in October 2018 and March 2019, killing a total of 346 people. The cause of both crashes was a separate software issue related to the aircraft’s Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), which was addressed amid the grounding of the entire global 737 MAX fleet from shortly after the second crash until December 2021.
The 737 MAX, the latest iteration of Boeing’s 737 aircraft family, also faced additional issues during its seven years in commercial service (accounting for the grounding), ranging from cabin seat flaws and fuselage cracks to a decompression-causing door-plug blowout.
United 'not taking deliveries of new aircraft' with U14 software
United Airlines told Simple Flying in September that it is “not taking deliveries of new aircraft” with U14 installed, meaning the airline will not accept deliveries of the new MAX 10 or MAX 7 variants, with the MAX 7 certified in August. While the new variants currently run only on U14, the older variants, the MAX 8 and MAX 9, can run on both U14 and U13.
United’s statement carries weight for Boeing, as the carrier is the largest buyer of the MAX 10, with 167 firm orders. The carrier has made substantial investments in its current MAX fleet and has recently begun a program to install Starlink internet hardware on its Guam-based MAX 8 fleet, according to the airline’s website.
The company is also expanding its MAX 8 route network, adding a flight from its Newark, New Jersey, hub to Terceira, Portugal, in mid to late 2027, the same year United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby expects the first MAX 10 deliveries, according to an August statement.
Based on the airline’s more recent statement to Simple Flying about the U14 software, the delivery date may change, with a Boeing fix for U14 only expected in 2028.

Israel Election 2026: What does Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud stand for?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:05:54 UTC
03:05:54 KST

The Likud, founded in 1973, is one of many vying for citizens’ votes in the elections for the 26th Knesset, which will be held on October 27.
Led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Likud sits on the political Right and has served as the ruling party for the majority of the past two decades.
The party has historically sat on the Center-Right of the political spectrum, holding a right-wing position on military and defense issues while maintaining a more economically liberal, pro-market approach that favors private enterprise and limited government intervention.
In the 25th Knesset, Likud held 32 seats and is currently polling at 19-21 seats, facing uncertainty over maintaining its status as the largest party in the Knesset.
Netanyahu and the Likud have led the sitting government, hailed as the most right-wing coalition in Israel's history, for four years, leading the country during the judicial reform crisis, the October 7 massacre and the subsequent war in Gaza, escalations across Israel's borders with Lebanon and Syria, and repeated rounds of fighting with the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The Likud's rise from political misfits to Israel's ruling party
Founded in 1973, the Likud brought together several parties, including former prime minister Menachem Begin’s Herut and the Liberal Party, combining nationalist and liberal political traditions. Herut’s roots lay in the Revisionist movement associated with Ze’ev Jabotinsky.
Begin led Likud to power for the first time in 1977, ending nearly three decades of Labor-led government. The victory established the party as a governing alternative and marked a lasting shift in Israel’s political landscape.
The movement’s founding identity included a commitment to individual liberty alongside Jewish national aspirations.
Netanyahu first became Likud leader in 1993 and won the premiership for the first time in 1996, narrowly defeating former prime minister Shimon Peres in Israel’s first direct election for prime minister, a year after the assassination of former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin. His first term ended with defeat at the hands of former prime minister Ehud Barak in 1999, after which former prime minister Ariel Sharon succeeded him as party leader.
He also served as finance minister under Sharon from 2003 to 2005, then regained the Likud leadership in December 2005, winning 44% of the vote against rivals including Silvan Shalom, Moshe Feiglin, and Defense Minister Israel Katz.
Netanyahu returned to the premiership in 2009 and remained in office until 2021, before returning once again following the 2022 election. In 2019, he surpassed David Ben-Gurion as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
During Netanyahu’s leadership, opponents and former Likud lawmakers have accused him of steering the party away from its founding principles and turning it into a vehicle for his personal political interests.
Likud shifts Oct. 7 blame to generals - and highlights Netanyahu's diplomatic role
Following the October 7 massacre, Likud has sought to separate responsibility for the failures that enabled the massacre from credit for the military achievements that followed. Its campaign credits Netanyahu with successes against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran, while arguing that the security establishment bears primary responsibility for failing to provide him with adequate warning of the attack.
Netanyahu has called to dismantle Hamas and for the removal of the terror organization from the governance of Gaza, which serves as one of his government's fundamental war goals. However, Netanyahu has also rejected the Palestinian Authority as a potential post-war governing body, while being accused of stalling US President Donald Trump's peace plan.
Likud's stated position rejects Palestinian statehood. In September 2025, responding to the recognition of a Palestinian state by several Western countries, Netanyahu said, “There will be no Palestinian state west of the Jordan River.”
On settlements, the Netanyahu government’s actions have strengthened and expanded Israeli settlements in the West Bank. It has also pushed for legislation granting tax benefits to qualifying settlements.
Security is central to Likud’s campaign, with Netanyahu presenting his leadership as essential to confronting Israel’s enemies and resisting pressure to limit military action, while portraying his opponents as lacking the resolve to fight Israel’s adversaries and defend its interests abroad.
Likud's campaign messaging is that military achievements must be protected through continued readiness and forceful action, rather than treated as evidence that the threat has disappeared.
On Iran, Netanyahu has presented the toppling of the Islamic regime as an unfinished objective of Operations Rising Lion and Roaring Lion, extending beyond damage to its military capabilities.
On Lebanon, Netanyahu’s policy similarly extends beyond airstrikes to maintaining a security zone and preventing Hezbollah from rebuilding along the border.
The government's defense spending provides another measure of Likud's priorities. The 2026 budget passed by the coalition included about NIS 142 billion for the Defense Ministry, up from about NIS 32 billion during the war.
Netanyahu and Likud have also placed the prime minister’s relationship with the US, particularly Trump, at the center of both security policy and regional normalization.
The US-brokered Abraham Accords agreement with the UAE, Bahrain, and Morocco in 2020 has been touted by the Likud as proof that a Netanyahu-led government could pursue strategic alliances with certain Arab states, arguing that the party’s opponents lack the ability to foster diplomatic relations at Netanyahu’s level.
Beyond the US, Netanyahu faces legal obstacles to international travel. In November 2024, the ICC issued arrest warrants for him and former defense minister Yoav Gallant, exposing him to possible arrest in countries that enforce them.
Likud offers divisive stance on haredi draft, A-G's role - and a free-market approach
Many of the Netanyahu government's domestic policy and legislation have caused a rift within Israeli society, including the hot-button issue of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription into the IDF.
The Likud's position led to recent criticism when contentious legislation to enshrine Torah study as a fundamental value in the country's Basic Law was passed by the government earlier this year. Opponents argued that the legislation would encourage draft evasion amid the military's severe manpower shortage crisis.
Netanyahu’s government has also been under fire for what critics describe as accommodating demands from its haredi partners over enforcement against men who evade military service, which included support from ministers within the Likud faction, including Defense Minister Israel Katz, for a temporary freeze on arrests of draft evaders.
Haredi factions have continually threatened to boycott coalition voting as the contentious legislation they were seeking to advance was being stalled in the Knesset plenum.
The 2026 state budget also raised concerns over the amount of funds transferred to haredi education institutions.
The government's judicial reform served as a key issue during its term, placing the Likud and its coalition partners at the center of a struggle over the powers of the government, Knesset, and courts.
Justice Minister Yariv Levin unveiled his reform package in January 2023, proposing greater political influence over judicial appointments, restrictions on judicial review, and changes to the authority of government legal advisers. Levin argued that courts and legal officials had exceeded their proper role, preventing elected representatives from implementing the policies voters had chosen.
The attempted reform, considered a highly divisive issue in Israeli society, prompted mass nationwide protests across the country before it was shelved by Netanyahu in the months leading up to October 7, and was not renewed due to the war that ensued.
However, the suspension did not end the coalition's legislative effort. In July 2023, Netanyahu’s coalition passed a law to cancel the Reasonableness Clause in a vote boycotted by the opposition. It barred courts from using the reasonableness standard to review decisions by the government and ministers. The High Court struck the amendment down in January 2024 by an eight-to-seven majority.
Amid the government's ongoing rift with the judiciary, the role of the attorney-general also became a major sticking point.
In August 2025, the cabinet unanimously approved Levin’s proposal to dismiss Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara, with the High Court later issuing an injunction blocking its implementation. Levin rejected allegations that the dismissal was connected to his Netanyahu’s criminal trial, while the legal challenge raised concerns about the removal of an independent check on government power.
The prime minister's criminal trials on charges of bribery, fraud, and breach of trust remain ongoing.
The judicial reform remains a part of Likud’s election messaging, with ministers and candidates continuing to call for the A-G's dismissal and for an overhaul of the judiciary.
Likud's socio-economic platform emphasizes lower taxes, competition, and reducing the cost of living. Netanyahu's 2022 plan proposed reducing income and corporate taxes, lowering food import duties, and action on electricity, fuel, water, and municipal charges.
Housing policy has focused on expanding construction and speeding planning procedures. However, The Jerusalem Post’s review of Netanyahu’s 2022 promises found that construction remained behind population growth and that the war disrupted building activity. It also found that universal free childcare for children under three had not been delivered, although subsidies and other support had expanded.
Likud’s record on religion and state is deeply connected to its partnerships with haredi factions Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ). On marriage, conversion, and public transportation on Shabbat, the record similarly points toward preserving existing religious arrangements, also known as the Status Quo, rather than broad liberalization.
What a vote for this party is likely to produce
According to current polling, Netanyahu's sitting coalition, made up of Otzma Yehduit, Religious Zionist Party, Shas, and UTJ is projected to reach 50-55 seats, but lacks a 61-seat majority across most polls conducted by Israeli media.
Despite assumptions that the Likud's partners are set in stone, accusations hurled by coalition partners and speculation ahead of the election suggest that Netanyahu could seek alternative partners in hopes of forming the next government.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has accused the prime minister of attempting to block his Otzma Yehudit party from a future coalition, instead eyeing a partnership with rival for the premiership Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar.
A vote for Likud is most directly a vote for Netanyahu to remain prime minister. Based on existing partnerships, the likeliest starting point would be an attempt to assemble another government with Netanyahu's existing coalition partners. If Netanyahu's bloc falls short of 61 seats, the prime minister would need additional partners or a different coalition arrangement.
A larger Likud faction would strengthen his negotiating position with potential partners, but would not remove the need for compromises.

Speaking on Sunday in an interview with Abu Dhabi-state owned outlet, The National, from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, his head and left arm bandaged, Machchhar said that when the first blow landed, he thought something had gone "horribly wrong with the aircraft structure", before quickly realizing he was being attacked and things had "taken a drastic turn".

"I believe that was the first time when I lost my consciousness."
The aircraft, flight FZ1073, was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a crash axe, typically kept in the cockpit for emergency use.
The incident caused the airliner to plunge 16,000 feet (4,900 meters) in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were on board landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia. The suspect, an Omani national, was transferred to the UAE, flydubai's home country.

"I was not very sure that I'll make it out alive from this. Did I give up? No."

A single dose of psilocybin eased depression within days, but its edge over placebo faded within a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:00:44 UTC
03:00:44 KST

A randomized clinical trial conducted in Sweden found that a single 25-mg dose of psilocybin produced rapid antidepressant effects in patients with moderate to severe recurrent major depressive disorder. On a self-report measure, the effects appeared as early as the second day after dosing and lasted for more than three months, although by one year the difference between groups had faded on the main clinician-rated measure. The paper was published in JAMA Network Open.
Depression, or major depressive disorder, is a mental health condition characterized by persistent low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, and other emotional, cognitive, and physical symptoms that can substantially interfere with daily life. When a person experiences repeated episodes of major depression separated by periods in which symptoms improve or disappear, such a condition is called recurrent depression.
Antidepressant medications such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely used to treat major depressive disorder. However, about two-thirds of patients do not achieve remission with their first SSRI, and some remain depressed despite several treatment attempts. Mainstream antidepressant medications may also take several weeks to produce effects. They frequently need to be taken for years to reduce the risk of relapse, while adverse effects can make long-term treatment difficult. These limitations have increased interest in faster-acting treatments that might produce improvement after only one or a few administrations.
Psilocybin, a classical psychedelic, has attracted particular attention because some studies suggest that a single dose can produce antidepressant effects lasting for several weeks or longer. Researchers are especially interested in whether such effects might also reduce the risk of future depressive episodes and lessen the need for continuous daily medication.
However, evidence for long-term benefits remains limited because many previous studies lacked suitable control groups, used suboptimal designs, or could not fully separate treatment effects from the natural course of depression and other treatments. Psilocybin’s strong effects can also make it easy for participants to tell whether they received the drug, which can undermine blinding.
Study author Hampus Yngwe of the Karolinska Institutet and his colleagues conducted a randomized clinical trial to test the short-term antidepressant effects of a single, oral, 25-mg dose of psilocybin in people with major depressive disorder. They also followed participants for 12 months to examine longer-term effects and tolerability, and tested how well the study’s blinding held up.
Study participants were 35 adults in Sweden with moderate to severe recurrent depression who were in a depressive episode at the time of recruitment and were recruited through social media and online ads. Their average age was 41, and 21 were women. None had used psychedelics before, and none were taking antidepressants or receiving psychotherapy when they entered the study.
Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 25 mg of psilocybin (17 participants) or an identical-looking capsule containing 100 mg of niacin, a form of vitamin B3 (18 participants). Niacin served as an active placebo, a substance that produces noticeable bodily sensations, such as flushing, and was intended to make it harder for participants to tell which capsule they had received. The study was double-blind, meaning that neither participants nor the researchers assessing them were told who received which capsule. Both groups also received five psychotherapeutic support sessions over 17 days, including a preparation session, the dosing session, and three follow-up sessions.
Depressive symptoms were assessed by a clinician using the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) on the dosing day and again on days 8, 15, 42, and 365. Participants also rated their own symptoms using a self-report version of the scale, daily during the first week and then at regular intervals for a year, along with measures of disability, quality of life, and anxiety. Participants who were still depressed at day 42 were referred for standard treatment.
On the clinician-rated measure, depressive symptoms fell by about 7 points more in the psilocybin group than in the niacin group by day 8, the study’s main outcome. The psilocybin group remained ahead on days 15 and 42, but the difference was no longer statistically significant at day 365. On the self-report measure, the psilocybin group showed a greater reduction in symptoms as early as day 2, and the difference persisted through day 102, or more than three months.
By day 8, 8 participants in the psilocybin group had reached remission, compared with 2 in the niacin group, a difference that was not statistically significant. By day 42, remission rates were 53% in the psilocybin group and 6% in the niacin group. After one year, remission rates were 53% and 41%, respectively, a difference small enough that it could reflect chance. Remission in the psilocybin group held steady from the first week onward, while in the niacin group it rose from 12% to 41% over the year, which the authors suggest reflects the episodic nature of depression, including the potential for spontaneous remission.
Similar numbers of participants in the two groups (6 and 7) started antidepressant medication during the follow-up year. Psilocybin was generally well tolerated, with mostly temporary side effects such as headache, anxiety, and hallucinations, and no serious adverse events linked to the drug. However, two participants in the psilocybin group experienced severe anxiety that persisted for weeks after dosing and required medical attention.
“In this randomized clinical trial of MDD [major depressive disorder], a single dose of psilocybin was associated with rapid antidepressant effects, observed by day 2 and persisting for more than 3 months on secondary outcomes; psilocybin was generally well tolerated, but some individuals required additional support after dosing due to anxiety,” study authors concluded.
“These results suggest that psilocybin may provide a rapid and relatively long-lasting antidepressant effect on major depressive disorder, warranting further investigation into repeated dosing or adjunctive treatment strategies.”
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about the antidepressant potential of psilocybin. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a very small group of participants, so any effects needed to be quite large to be detected, and the trial was not designed to draw firm conclusions about long-term effects.
Blinding also largely failed. At the end of the study, 94% of participants in the psilocybin group and all of those in the niacin group who answered correctly guessed which treatment they had received, and the clinicians rating symptoms guessed correctly for most participants as well. Because depression was measured through interviews and self-reports, knowing which treatment they had received may have influenced how participants and raters judged symptoms, and recruitment through social media may have drawn people with high expectations for the treatment.
The paper, “Short-Term and Late-Term Effects of Psilocybin on Symptoms in Major Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial,” was authored by Hampus Yngwe, Pontus Plavén-Sigray, Carl Johan Ekman, Eva Henje, Anders Berglund, Mikael Tiger, Maria Beckman, and Johan Lundberg.

Renters forming larger and multi-family households to cover rising costs
Extended families and friends are teaming up to improve their chances of securing a rental property as tight supply forces prices higher, with experts warning the cohort is being left behind.
For Perth renter Grady Toomath, sharing a home with his brother and another housemate has become a necessity rather than a lifestyle choice.
"I've been living here since 2019. When we moved in, the rent was $315 a week; [after] our latest rent increase it's $715 a week," he said.
That is a 127 per cent increase over seven years that comes as the rental market continues to tighten.
Brisbane real estate agent Avi Khan said multigenerational families and friendship groups accounted for one in five rental applications to his agency.
"The only choice that they have is they come together as a family unit or rent a property with their housemate, their flatmate, their friends, whoever it is. It's the massive shift that we're seeing," Mr Khan said.
"We're seeing multiple couples applying for properties. People are applying with their mums and dads. So we're seeing the changing of the household unit."
Grady Toomath's living arrangement has stretched his budget a little further, but it has come with sacrifices.
"Three guys in a pretty small space, we've had to really adjust," he said.
"It's not entirely the lifestyle any of us wanted, but it's the lifestyle we can afford. So we help each other; we do what we can.
"We work together in this small space and try to just mind each other and be respectful in the way we can, but it's not what any of us really envisioned for our lives."
Mr Khan said the increase in group applications coincided with negative gearing and capital gains tax changes in May's federal budget, which had eaten away at supply.
"Normally for a house, before the budget, we'll get 10 applications. We're [now] looking at 15, 20 applications for those homes,"
he said.
"They [the government] haven't considered the effect these changes will have downstream. So there's no one replacing those investors.
"That's why we're seeing real warning signs in the economy at the moment because where do these tenants go? They've got no other choices."
7.30 has contacted the Federal Housing Minister for comment.
Renters squeezed amid home ownership focus
Federal and state governments offer several incentives to assist buyers to purchase their first home, including the Albanese government's expanded 5 per cent deposit scheme.
But Lyndall Bryant, a senior lecturer in property economics at Queensland University of Technology, said renters have been overlooked.
According to Domain, the national rental vacancy rate was at 1 per cent in the September quarter, with just one in 100 properties available to lease.
Capitals outside Sydney and Melbourne experienced more severe supply shortages.
Agents and property economists said that has pushed the 31 per cent of Australians who rent to be more creative.
"We've been seeing a lot of conversation about how to make housing more affordable for people who have a mortgage or are trying to buy," Dr Bryant said.
"But what we're not seeing is any solutions for the renters and unfortunately for them, the situation is only getting worse."
"We've seen billions of dollars put into social housing and community housing, but social and community housing is only between 3 and 5 per cent of our total housing stock.
"In rough numbers, 25 per cent of all of our people who need housing are renters that rent into the private market. There just isn't enough stock for them."
The federal government increased Commonwealth Rental Assistance payments in 2023 and 2024 and has agreed, along with state and territory first ministers, to move toward more nationally consistent rental rights.
Unions and housing advocacy groups have also called for rental caps and multi-year lease agreements.
But Dr Bryant said the federal budget's tax changes have discouraged investment in housing, disadvantaging renters.
"Our current policy arrangement is that it's dis-incentivising investors from being in residential property and we don't have enough landlords, and they're exiting the market," she said.
"[It's] freeing up housing for first home buyers, which is really wonderful for first home buyers, but we still have this really large portion of the market that are renters and their prices are only going up."
Landlords also feeling squeezed
Sydney accountant Keegan Du Preez has nine investment properties across the country but also rents.
The 24-year-old said he appreciated the challenges of the market from both the landlord and tenant perspective.
"I try and look after the tenant. It's in my best interest, plus it's in the tenant's best interest as well to lock in that rate because the market's only going to go up with rents," he said.
"So them locking in for 24 months helps them budget far better than if you have an increase every 12 months."
He said rent increases were a last resort, but property owners needed to cover expenses.
"Interest rates have spiked significantly; repair costs have gone up. Tradies, there's just a lack thereof, so all the tradies have put their prices up. So you have to compensate somewhere," he said.
"As landlords, we're not an endless pit of money.
"If it means that I go without for a month or two or three in order to look after my tenants, so be it.
"If that is what's required to make sure that the portfolio plus the tenants [are] looked after, that is a sacrifice that landlords sign up [for] the very first day that they buy the property as an investor."
