Forestry agency honors conservation efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:38 UTC
01:42:38 KST

The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency on Saturday held an award ceremony honoring three organizations and 15 individuals for their contributions to sustainable forestry and ecological conservation in Taiwan.
Agency Director-General Lin Hwa-ching (林華慶) said at the ceremony that Taiwan’s conservation efforts depended not only on government agencies but also on local communities and academic researchers.
The agency would continue to bring together resources and expertise from different fields to improve Taiwan’s forest environment, he said.
Photo: CNA
Deputy Minister of Agriculture Huang Chao-chin (黃昭欽) said about 60 percent of Taiwan’s land area is forested, yet only about four percent of the population lives in these areas.
The agency alone cannot protect such vast woodland areas, Huang said, stressing the importance of frontline personnel in forest conservation, law enforcement and disaster prevention.
Forests take decades or even centuries to grow, but illegal loggers can destroy them with a chainsaw in a matter of moments, he said, adding that law enforcement officers, forest rangers and civic groups play important roles in deterring illegal logging.
In addition to forestry and conservation, preventing and mitigating disasters caused by landslide-dammed lakes is another key responsibility of the agency, Huang said. Such lakes can form easily in Taiwan’s mountainous terrain.
He thanked those who took part in disaster response and relief efforts following the overflow of the Mataian barrier lake last year.
The ceremony honored 15 individuals and three organizations for their contributions.
Prosecutors Yen Wei-te (嚴維德), Su Hou-jen (蘇厚仁) and Chang Ya-ching (張雅晴) were recognized for helping dismantle major criminal networks involved in illegal waste disposal and logging.
Police officer Hsieh Jui-hsuan (謝睿軒) was honored for using digital technology to identify leopard cat poaching and the illegal collection of driftwood. Pilot Shih Yu-ping (石宇平) received an award for spotting a newly formed barrier lake and participating in wildfire suppression efforts over many years.
Several award recipients were recognized for their long-standing contributions to conservation research.
Taiwan Forestry Research Institute researcher Lu Sheng-shan (陸聲山) established a specimen database covering more than 200 bee species in Taiwan.
Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute researcher Lin Te-en (林德恩) founded the Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network, which has compiled more than 330,000 records involving more than 600 species of terrestrial vertebrates.
National Dong Hwa University geology professor Liu Ying-san (劉瑩三) completed inventories and assessments of 106 geological sites in eastern Taiwan and helped establish the Fugang and Liji Badlands geoparks.
National Taiwan Normal University life science professor Lin Si-min (林思民) compiled foundational conservation data through research on amphibians, reptiles and raptors. He also actively participated in raptor monitoring, rescue and tracking.
Civic contributions to conservation, sustainable forestry and disaster relief were also recognized.
Society of Wilderness Hualien branch president Chung Hsiu-chou (鍾綉綢) devoted herself to the rescue and conservation of Formosan flying foxes, while Taiwan Etude Education Association president Hu Wen-wei (胡文偉) developed educational materials using wood resources.
Jia Nan Machinery Co. chairman Huang Kuo-pao (黃國寶) has long assisted with major disaster relief efforts. Following last year’s Mataian barrier lake overflow, he led an engineering team in conducting topographical surveys, excavating river channels and carrying out water diversion works.
Environmental Arts Design Co. design director Pan Yi-ju (潘一如) was recognized for incorporating ecological and biodiversity conservation principles into landscape and urban design.
For contributions to institutional development, National Property Administration Director-General Tseng Kuo-chi (曾國基) was honored for promoting afforestation on state-owned land, carbon sink mechanisms and environmental land stewardship in support of Taiwan’s goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.
National Taiwan University Office of International Affairs vice president Yuan Hsiao-wei (袁孝維), a key contributor to the development of Taiwan’s forest therapy industry, helped establish a training and certification system for forest therapists.
Three organizations were also honored for their contributions.
The Chiayi Presbyterian Church Office coordinated efforts among government agencies, private businesses and local volunteers to plant more than 16,000 horsetail trees over the past decade, helping restore four hectares of coastal windbreak forests.
San Hong Wooden Co. used domestically produced Japanese cedar to manufacture more than 17,000 sets of desks and chairs for schools across Taiwan.
The Kaohsiung Wild Bird Society was recognized for its long-standing efforts to conserve critically endangered bird species and restore wetland habitats.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:38 UTC
01:42:38 KST

Palau stands with Taiwan despite severe pressure from Beijing, including Chinese infiltration and the “united front” tactics used to influence the Pacific island nation’s presidential election, President William Lai (賴清德) said yesterday.
Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr has for years shown strong support for Taiwan, even amid Chinese pressure, Lai said at the opening ceremony for a new Shin Kong Wu Ho-su Memorial Hospital building in Taipei on the hospital’s 40th anniversary.
Whipps also attended the event.
Photo: Lin Cheng-kun, Taipei Times
Taiwan has earned international recognition for its commitment to democracy and freedom, its achievements in advanced technologies and its public healthcare services, Lai said.
While the international community needs Taiwan’s participation, Beijing’s efforts to suppress Taiwan remain pervasive, preventing the nation from formally joining many international organizations, he said.
Amid these challenges, Whipps has consistently provided Taiwan with unwavering support, but such backing “has not come without a price,” Lai said.
China in the past few years has exerted severe pressure on Palau and tried to interfere in the country’s presidential election when Whipps was seeking re-election, he said.
Whipps remained steadfast in voicing his support for Taiwan at international forums, including at the UN and the Pacific Islands Forum, he said.
In an interview with US news outlet Politico published on Thursday, Whipps said Beijing had threatened Palau with “consequences” for promoting Taiwanese independence.
The hospital’s contributions toward helping Palau develop healthcare services played a part in the Pacific Island’s support for Taiwan, Lai said.
Since 2007, the hospital has stationed nurses in Palau and implemented emergency and critical care referral support programs cases, he said.
The hospital is supporting Palau’s plans for a new national hospital, demonstrating Shin Kong’s commitment to protecting the health of Taiwanese while supporting the healthcare advancement of the nation’s allies, he said.
“When you reach out your hand, another will always be there to grasp it,” Whipps said.
The hospital has contributed greatly to healthcare in Palau, dispatching more than 450 medical professionals to the country and providing more than 15,000 instances of medical care and services to local residents, he said.
Through clinical knowledge transfer and technical exchanges, the cooperation has significantly improved Palau’s medical standards, he said.
“Behind every number is a family that regained hope,” he said.
The hospital’s partnership facilitated more than 6,500 treatment referrals, Shin Kong Hospital president Hou Sheng-mou (侯勝茂) said.
Palau is one of Taiwan’s 12 diplomatic allies and one of three in the Pacific.
In the Politico interview, Whipps said that Beijing had attempted to bring Palau into its orbit and pushed the government to “sever ties with Taiwan.”
A Chinese ambassador told him that China could give Palau “a million tourists and build all the hotels” he wanted and threatened to retaliate if he did not comply, Whipps said.
However, Palau’s sovereignty should not be threatened because of its recognition of Taiwan, he told Politico.
“If Taiwan can be taken over, then Palau can be taken over and the Philippines can be taken over,” he said, adding that mutual defense is important.

Taiwan says drives away 16 Chinese ships involved in ‘maritime harassment’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:37 UTC
01:42:37 KST

Taiwan said yesterday it had driven away 16 Chinese coast guard, research and fishing vessels involved in simultaneous “maritime harassment” operations.
An “unusually large” number of Chinese vessels took part in the coordinated operations around Taiwan proper and Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands (Dongsha Islands, 東沙群島), the Taiwanese coast guard said in a statement.
The Chinese vessels, including four fishing boats, carried out “simultaneous operations at multiple locations and engaged in hybrid warfare,” the statement said.
Photo courtesy of the CGA
The locations were off Taiwan’s eastern, southern and southwestern coastlines, and around Pratas. Some of the Chinese vessels entered Taiwan’s restricted waters.
China has intensified its maritime pressure on Taiwan in recent months, deploying record numbers of coast guard, research and other vessels around the island.
Yesterday’s operation comes after Taiwan’s coast guard used a water cannon against a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas, in the northern part of the South China Sea, on October 1.
Taiwan’s coast guard said its vessels took “forceful action immediately to effectively neutralise the threats.”
“China is attempting to unilaterally alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait and create the false impression of jurisdiction,” the statement said. “Such actions will only lead to resentment among the people of Taiwan, and the Coast Guard Administration condemns them in the strongest terms.”
China began conducting law enforcement patrols in waters to the east of Taiwan in June, which Taipei branded as “provocative” and “expansionism in disguise.”
Beijing has since dialled up pressure, deploying a record 244 coast guard, scientific research and other ships around Taiwan’s main island in July, Taiwanese official data show.
That compares with 55 ships detected in June and 30 in May, and 58 in July last year. In the first 21 days of August, 152 vessels were detected.
About 60 percent are coast guard ships, with research vessels and other government boats making up the rest.
The figures do not include Chinese warships, which China’s military deploys around Taiwan on a near-daily basis.

Old railway still has stories to tell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:36 UTC
01:42:36 KST

After 16 years of construction, the first section of Tainan’s railway undergrounding project officially opened for business on Saturday. The closure of the level crossings, overpasses, and underpasses the night before is sure to live on in Tainan’s memory and as a milestone for Taiwan’s railway history. With nostalgia and perhaps a touch of sadness, crowds gathered to bid farewell to the last Tze-chiang Limited Express to depart from Tainan Railway Station at about 10pm on Friday.
Railways hold a special place in the hearts of many Taiwanese. When operations ceased for the Tamsui Line in July 1988 and the Western Trunk’s old Mountain Line in September 1998, large crowds also turned out to say their goodbyes.
With the new underground station opening up to the public, the main building of the original station is to be preserved. Built in 1936 during the Japanese colonial era, Tainan’s second-generation railway station is nationally designated as a historic landmark, and has been a part of life in Tainan for 90 years. It has been an important witness to the development of Taiwan’s railways, linking generations of Tainan residents through shared memories. Together, the old and new stations present a harmonious combination of architectural art from the past and the present.
Once restoration is complete, the old station is to be developed into a cultural and artistic space with restaurants and exhibition venues. About 50 years ago, the second floor of the old station housed a famous railway restaurant where many people had their first experiences of dining out. Preserving the old station serves a historical function as it brings scenes from the past back to life. As the opening of the underground railway begins a new chapter for Tainan, we look forward to this historically significant building being fully restored and opened to the public.
For years, the Tainan City Government has spared no effort in restoring a whole array of historic buildings. These include: the National Museum of Taiwan Literature, formerly the Tainan Prefectural Hall; the Tainan Judicial Museum; Hayashi Department Store (林百貨); the Tainan Martial Arts Hall; the Old Japanese Patriotic Women’s Association building; the Tainan City Fire Museum; the Tainan Art Museum Building 1; and now, Tainan Station. These buildings each all possess distinct cultural, architectural and historical value. Their restoration and reemergence in the city make them precious assets of modern urban culture.
Fang Tze-yu is an assistant professor at Southern Taiwan University of Science and Technology.

UNITED STATES
Truck kills 2 on soccer field
A truck drove into a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, leaving a six-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man dead, and 10 others hospitalized with traumatic injuries, police said on Saturday. The injuries ranged from minor to severe, but none appear to be life threatening, Wichita Police Captain Aaron Moses told a news conference. The two people killed were pronounced dead at the scene, he said. A 34-year-old woman was driving the truck, which ended up in a field at the west end of the Stryker Sports Complex, Moses said. “We know what happened, but now we’re working very hard to find out why it happened, and we’re not there yet,” Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan said. The driver had a child playing soccer at the complex, but not on the field where the incident took place, Moses said. The truck involved had two juveniles as passengers, he said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:42:34 UTC
01:42:34 KST

CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) said on Saturday that it would keep domestic gasoline and diesel prices unchanged this week to ease inflationary pressure, even as international crude prices remained high amid military tensions in the Middle East.
Formosa Petrochemical Corp (台塑石化) also maintained its fuel prices at the same levels this week, information posted on the company’s Web site yesterday showed.
It would be the fifth consecutive week that CPC and Formosa have held their fuel prices steady. Concerns over global oil supply disruptions continued to weigh on market sentiment, pushing Brent crude oil prices, the global benchmark, to their highest level since May at one point on Friday.
Front-month Brent crude oil futures last week gained 4.91 percent to settle at US$109.86 per barrel on the Intercontinental Exchange in London, while West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures — the US oil benchmark — increased 10.41 percent to US$101.41 per barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Under CPC’s floating fuel price mechanism, which tracks a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai crude and 30 percent Brent crude, the average international crude oil price fell to US$113.77 per barrel last week from US$114.65 per barrel the previous week, the company said.
However, a weaker New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$32.131 against the US dollar last week, compared with NT$31.810 a week earlier, added financial pressure to CPC.
As a result of their decisions to leave fuel prices unchanged, retail gasoline prices this week are to remain at NT$31.2, NT$32.7 and NT$34.7 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively, at CPC and Formosa stations, while prices of premium diesel would stay at NT$29.9 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.7 per liter at Formosa pumps, the companies said.

Taroko, Yushan national park cabin fees proposed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:34 UTC
01:42:34 KST

Stays at the new Chilai Mountain Cabin (奇萊山屋) in Taroko National Park would cost NT$800 per person per night on weekdays and NT$1,200 on holidays under a proposal released on Friday, which would also raise fees at Paiyun Lodge (排雲山莊) in Yushan National Park.
The Ministry of the Interior’s National Park Service said the proposed fees would be subject to a 60-day public consultation period and that an implementation date would be announced later.
Located at an elevation of 3,345m in Hualien County near the border with Nantou County, the new cabin has 40 beds for hikers tackling some of Taroko National Park’s most challenging routes.
Photo: Taipei Times
It opened on a trial basis on Aug. 21, and stays are currently free.
The National Park Service also proposed raising the fee at Paiyun Lodge, Taiwan’s highest-altitude mountain lodge, from NT$480 per person per night to NT$1,000 on weekdays and NT$1,500 on holidays.
The NT$480 rate has not changed since 2013.
The proposed increase reflects the high cost of maintaining the lodge at 3,402m, where resupply and maintenance is difficult, the National Park Service said.
It also covers the cost of ongoing staffing and facility upgrades, including solar power and energy storage, drying and changing rooms, and communications and charging equipment, the service said.
The new Chilai cabin uses renewable energy and has other green features, its lightweight construction is designed to minimize its impact on the surrounding area, it said.

Heavy traffic expected over the weekend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

The nation’s freeways are expected to see heavy traffic during the three-day Taiwan Retrocession Day weekend, with travel demand expected to be driven mainly by tourism, the National Freeway Bureau said yesterday.
Traffic volume is forecast to reach 106 million to 112 million vehicle-kilometers (mvk) during the holiday, with southbound traffic on the first day expected to reach 61mvk, or 1.3 times regular traffic.
The bureau yesterday released a list of highway sections and time periods expected to experience congestion, based on traffic data from recent holidays, including the Mid-Autumn Festival, Teachers’ Day and the Double Ten National holiday, as well as last year’s Taiwan Retrocession Day.
Photo: CNA
On the Sun Yat-sen Freeway (Freeway No. 1), traffic between Yangmei (楊梅) and Toufen (頭份) interchanges is expected to be congested from 8am to 3pm on Saturday and from 9am to noon on Sunday.
On the Chiang Wei-shui Freeway (Freeway No. 5), heavy traffic is expected between the Nangang System and Toucheng (頭城) from 6am to 4pm on Saturday and from 6am to 3pm on Sunday.
Other expected congestion spots include Formosa Freeway (Freeway No. 3) between the Guansi (關西) and Dasi (大溪) Interchanges, Freeway No. 5 between the Yilan and Pinglin (坪林) Interchanges, and Freeway No. 1 between the Changhua (彰化) and Puyan (埔鹽) Interchanges.
For northbound traffic, the bureau expects congestion on Freeway No. 1 between Siluo (西螺) and the Puyan System from 4pm to 6pm on Saturday and 4pm to 8pm on Monday. Freeway No. 3 between Caotun (草屯) and Wufeng (霧峰) is also expected to be congested during those periods.
The bureau advised southbound travelers on Saturday and Sunday to depart before 6am or after 12pm when using Freeways No. 1 and No. 3, while those using Freeway No. 3 should leave before 5am or after 5pm.
For northbound travelers on Sunday and Monday next week, those in southern Taiwan should depart before 9am, while travelers in central Taiwan should leave before noon. Freeway No. 5 users are also advised to depart before 9am.

Photo: Tsai Ching-hua, Taipei Times

The two agreed that Chen Wei-cheng would pay NT$1 million (US$30,923) toward a violin in exchange for Chen Chi-yuan to arrange another family meeting and standing guard while the couple had sex in a restroom, the ruling said, adding that Chen Chi-yuan did not receive the promised money.

In September 2021, Chen Chi-yuan solicited NT$650,000 from Chiang to buy a violin, who agreed to contribute NT$120,000, the ruling said, adding that Chi-yuan failed to collect the money.
Chen Chi-yuan also instructed colleagues to destroy official video recordings to conceal his misconduct, damaging the integrity of investigation records, the court said. He was convicted of four offenses, including accepting a bribe in the form of an iPhone, agreeing to accept bribes and damaging official property.
In a separate case concerning Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office prosecutor Liu Chung-lin (劉忠霖), Liu tendered his resignation after testing positive for methamphetamine in a urine test following a police stop in New Taipei City on Feb. 27.

British padel boom spurs enthusiasm and pushback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:28 UTC
01:42:28 KST

On a recent weekend, Laura Latham eagerly swung her racket on a padel court celebrating one year playing one of the world’s fast-growing sports, which is now taking hold in the UK.
“I hadn’t ever picked up a racket in my entire life ... and I just fell in love,” said the 42-year-old civil servant, who lives in Stockport in northwest England.
“I know that sounds a bit cliche, but I was just welcomed into this amazing community of fabulous people, all ages, all shapes and sizes,” she said. “It’s just great.”
Photo: AFP
Latham is among a growing number of padel devotees in Britain, where its popularity has exploded after lagging behind European neighbors.
A cross between tennis and squash, played by doubles teams on courts enclosed by glass or wire, enthusiasts see it as an accessible and social sport, while critics say it is an expensive fad for trendsetters.
Other complaints range from the noise to private equity firms funding its expansion, especially in the US.
Tennis legend Rafael Nadal and soccer icon Cristiano Ronaldo are among players as well as high-profile investors in the fast-paced game, created in Mexico in the late 1960s.
As the sport has grown rapidly in parts of the world, it has attracted finance from a growing array of sources, from real-estate firms to specialized institutional investors.
Its recent UK growth has sparked friction in some places, most notably London, where several sites with new or proposed courts have provoked pushback from local communities.
“It’s a kind of hedge fund-backed sport, taking over local spaces and sports,” said Agnieszka Wood, 52, who helped spearhead an unsuccessful campaign to stop a beloved east London skating park becoming padel courts.
“But what happens if there’s too many padel courts? What happens if you’re taking the spaces from the communities, and you’re not replacing them?” Wood asked.
Padel’s growing popularity is unquestioned, with Wood acknowledging even her own children enjoy playing it.
The Lawn Tennis Association, the sport’s governing body in Britain, announced in May that national participation had surpassed 1 million, with about 2,000 courts open nationwide.
That compares with just 400,000 players and 870 courts at the end of 2024.
Globally, active player numbers climbed last year to about 20 million, the 2026 Global Padel Report said, making it one of the world’s fast-growing sports.
Last month it debuted as a medal sport at the Asian Games and harbors hopes of featuring at the Olympics.
Italy, Spain, Portugal and Argentina — so-called “padel heartlands” — lead the way, while Britain has become one of several “demand-led hotspots,” a report by an arm of the consultancy PwC and sport app Playtomic found.
“Padel is tapping into the UK’s deep racquet-sport heritage,” said consultant Ray Algar, who compiled the 2026 UK Padel Report.
His report estimates more than half of UK padel courts are in cities, with about one-quarter in rural places.
Soul Padel is among the companies behind Britain’s boom. It has opened 16 pay-to-play courts across four sites in central and northern England and Scotland, with seven more surfaces to open imminently.
Host towns include post-industrial places such as northwestern St Helen’s and Warrington — a long way from the caricature image of where padel is played.
“Our view was that the sport had landed well in the UK but ... within affluent areas and had been pitched to that kind of crowd,” Soul Padel founder and CEO Mark Hewlett said.
They offer various targeted programs, including “Soul Timers” for people older than 50 years, “Soul Singles” for singletons and its most popular, “Soul Sisters,” for women.
Its court rental costs vary by venue and scheme. In Stockport, Latham said she pays ￡11 (US$15) for her share of some off-peak games, rising by about ￡5 at peak times. However, in London, the cost is typically higher and seen as prohibitive by some.
In Bethnal Green, residents are campaigning against council plans to install a temporary court in an area popular with roller skaters, skateboarders and basketball players.
Meanwhile, displaced skaters remain upset about August’s closure of nearby Barking skatepark.
“There was huge, huge opposition from the people who went there,” said musician and skater Eleanor Dunlop, 29, who co-led the movement against the change. “We’re definitely losing places, like third spaces, where you can be, and there’s not immense pressure to spend money.”

Joseph Wu urges Europe, Taiwan to work together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:28 UTC
01:42:28 KST

National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) has called on Taiwan and Europe to deepen cooperation to safeguard Taiwan’s security and Europe’s prosperity, saying peace in the Taiwan Strait is vital to European security and economic interests.
Wu made the remarks at the Taiwan Forum in Berlin on Thursday, appearing alongside European Parliament Committee on Security and Defence Chair Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann. The forum, hosted by Germany’s Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom, was titled “Taiwan Security, German Prosperity.”
Wu delivered a keynote address and joined a panel discussion with Strack-Zimmermann and Gudrun Wacker, a German specialist on Asian affairs.
Photo: CNA
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and China’s threats against Taiwan show that European and Indo-Pacific security are closely interconnected, Wu said. A conflict in the Taiwan Strait would threaten regional peace and disrupt European industries and global supply chains.
He called for greater Taiwan-Europe cooperation in semiconductors, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to deepen economic resilience.
However, European concern about Taiwan Strait security has yet to translate into a unified policy toward China. Strack-Zimmermann said the EU adopted a recommendation addressing Taiwan’s security and the bloc’s policy toward China. Most member states supported Taiwan during the deliberations, she said, but their approaches differed.
Germany’s past reliance on inexpensive Russian energy, US security guarantees and access to China’s vast market had shaped its approach to foreign policy, Strack-Zimmermann said. Its economic dependence on China had made Germany more cautious on Taiwan-related issues, she added.
Against this backdrop, Wu said Beijing has sought to change the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait through military exercises, maritime operations and hybrid warfare. China has used its “one-China principle” to wage legal warfare internationally, seeking to justify military action against Taiwan, he said.
Asked how Taiwan could respond to Chinese provocations without escalating tensions, Wu said the government faced difficult choices. Countermeasures could heighten tensions, while failing to respond could encourage Beijing to push harder.
Taiwan must carefully weigh the need for a response against possible consequences, while maintaining communication and coordinating actions with like-minded countries, Wu said.
Strack-Zimmermann likewise described the EU’s response to China as “walking a tightrope,” saying that inaction would allow Beijing to tighten its grip on the bloc. China was watching how Europe responded to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and whether democracies had the resolve to defend themselves and support Taiwan, she said.
Wu praised Germany for supporting peace in the Taiwan Strait and Taiwan’s international participation. His public visit to Berlin demonstrated that Germany had not allowed Beijing’s claims over Taiwan to dictate the boundaries of engagement between Taiwan and Germany, he said.
Wu said that Taiwan would not entrust its security to other countries. Defending its freedom, sovereignty and democratic system was Taiwan’s own responsibility, he said.
Taiwan would continue reinforcing its defense capabilities and working with democratic partners to deter geopolitical conflict and maintain peace in the Taiwan Strait, he said.
Founded in 1958, the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom is affiliated with Germany’s Free Democratic Party and promotes democracy, human rights and international exchange. In 2021, it established a Global Innovation Hub in Taiwan focused on digital transformation and democratic innovation to deepen cooperation with Taiwan.

Deadly incident in Alberta sparks major fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

People were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, Canada’s defense minister said, while large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals, reports said.
Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.
It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in Edmonton told Canadian Broadcasting Corp (CBC) that people were being brought to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care.
Photo: AP
“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Royal Alexandra Hospital emergency department doctor Warren Thirsk told CBC News. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster.”
The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident, Canadian Minister of National Defence David McGuinty said, describing the situation as “very, very active and delicate.”
Authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information, he said.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4pm on Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.
Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100kph. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.
By 11pm, the Municipal District of Wainwright wrote on social media that the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected.
There was no evacuation order for residents.
McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but shared no other details.
“I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” McGuinty said.
“We will have more to say in the coming hours and days,” he added.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta, but did not specify what resources were being deployed.
“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on social media.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel.
The Wainwright base is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of today’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.
Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early on Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

GMI Cloud calls CoreWeave’s 15% yield ‘insane’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:26 UTC
01:42:26 KST

The founder of a cloud computing company with a similar business model to CoreWeave Inc said the 15 percent yield on the latter’s bonds is “insane,” compared with the roughly 3.45 percent rate his company secured on a recent New Taiwan dollar loan.
“This is an advantage,” GMI Cloud chief executive officer Alex Yeh (葉威延) said in an interview on Thursday.
He said that cheaper capital and faster execution — helped by proximity to Asian supply chains — give artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure companies that operate in the region an edge as investor jitters raise funding costs for their Western rivals.
Photo: Reuters
CoreWeave bonds last week were trading at deeply distressed levels, sparked by wariness of its plans to take on even more debt after already borrowing tens of billions to finance an unprecedented buildout of AI computing capacity. Meanwhile, companies such as GMI Cloud benefit from being able to borrow in local currencies, which significantly lowers their costs compared with raising debt in US dollars.
CoreWeave and GMI Cloud are so-called neoclouds, which sell computing power generated from advanced computer chips that are used to train AI. Their success is contingent on their graphics processing units (GPUs) coming online on schedule, because the companies have borrowed large sums of money against customer contracts that can only generate revenue once the projects are up and running.
“You have to continue to pay that interest without having revenue come in — that’s one of the biggest issues,” Yeh said.
These types of deals have grown rapidly in the US, but are only beginning to take off in Asia, where GMI Cloud is among the few companies borrowing money to purchase GPUs. Last month, it secured a NT$13.9 billion (US$429.8 million) five-year loan from 14 banks for a data center in Taiwan. The company was also seeking another US$300 million for a facility in Thailand, people familiar with the matter said earlier.
CoreWeave and GMI Cloud have agreements with their supplier Nvidia Corp to purchase unsold computing power, but the deals are structured differently. Such arrangements have raised concerns about circular financing that creates false demand. On Thursday, Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) said that his company did not need to backstop CoreWeave and that its cost of capital “is actually decreasing.”
“From my end, the demand is off the charts,” Yeh said.
GMI Cloud is headquartered in Mountain View, California, and operates in the US, Taiwan, Japan, Indonesia and Thailand. CoreWeave has also begun to move into Asia, with three projects under way in Indonesia.
Yeh said his family’s four-decade-old business in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry has helped GMI Cloud find reliable Taiwanese contractors for construction, electrical equipment and servers. He added that partnerships with conglomerates and prominent families in Asia have also enabled his firm to move more quickly.
“Am I worried?” Yeh asked about the turmoil in markets around AI companies. “Not a single bit, especially [since] our interest rates and customers support us.”

Is China’s Cultural Revolution really over?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:25 UTC
01:42:25 KST

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) announced on Wednesday that United Microelectronics Corp founder Robert Tsao’s (曹興誠) younger brother had been denied entry to Shanghai. TAO spokesperson Chen Binhua (陳斌華) said that Tsao had been placed on Beijing’s list of “die-hard Taiwanese independence separatists,” barring him and his family from entering China, Hong Kong or Macao. One must ask: What did Tsao’s brother do? Is it simply that he must bear the consequences of his brother’s actions because they are related? The TAO cited no specific actions by Tsao’s younger brother, merely invoking the term “family members.”
There is no need to ask what someone has done — if you first consider who their relatives are.
This approach recalls the “family class origin” (家庭成分) system used under People’s Republic of China founder Mao Zedong’s (毛澤東) rule to categorize people based on their family’s economic and social status.
The political classification of people based on their family background predates the Cultural Revolution, but it became a burden for many young people after it began. Being labeled as having a “bad” class background was common and a few words could be enough to close the door on a person’s future opportunities. If a person’s parents were one of the “five black categories” (黑五類) — landlords, rich farmers, counterrevolutionaries, bad elements or right-wingers — they could face discrimination at important junctures in their lives, such as when pursuing an education or seeking employment.
A fundamental principle of democracy and rule of law is that people are responsible for their own actions. Siblings can hold different political views, as can parents and their children. Even when their views align, they should not be held responsible for one another. If someone is to be held accountable, the authorities must present evidence of that person’s actions. Family ties are not proof of wrongdoing, and family relations are no justification for punishment.
Today’s China might be different from the China of the Cultural Revolution, but from labeling people as having a “bad” class background to targeting family members of so-called “die-hard Taiwanese independence separatists,” it is clear that Chinese authorities still extend a person’s political label to their relatives. While claiming to only target a minority of people, they impose restrictions on family members, turning guilt by association into a form of punishment.
In April this year, Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang’s (劉世芳) nephew, Yen Wen-chun (顏文群), was forced to leave his job at Long Time Technology Co (榮炭科技), a Taiwanese firm with Chinese subsidiaries. Beijing cited Yen’s political donations to Democratic Progressive Party candidates running in the legislative elections as the primary reason. Liu said that the donations were made in 2019 and duly reported in accordance with the law, while her nephew did not start his position at the firm until 2023. The TAO said it would not allow “die-hard Taiwanese independence separatists and their relatives” to invest and profit from China, explicitly designating their family members as an excluded group.
From Tsao’s younger brother being denied entry to Shanghai to Liu’s nephew losing his job, political persecution has extended into families, only for the resulting harm to be waved off with victim blaming, portrayed as the fault of those targeted for bringing trouble upon their relatives. Who imposed these restrictions? Who threatened their livelihoods? When even political punishment can spread through family ties, are we really expected to believe that the Cultural Revolution is long over? And who ever said we were one family with the Chinese Communist Party?
Chang Shang-yang is a farmer.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Japan’s brewery ‘cartel’  did not collude enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:25 UTC
01:42:25 KST

Visitors to Japan know the simple joys of a local beer — a mug of lager that, regardless of the brand on the label, is consistently tasty and familiar.
That consistency might be a problem, says the Fair Trade Commission (FTC), which has launched an investigation into the four major brewers. The regulator suspects that they colluded to fix the timing and level of price hikes for wholesalers, Bloomberg News said. Further reports suggest the regulator has been looking at the practice for decades.
The collusion is problematic; if the allegations are true, customers have been paying more than needed for years.
Illustration: Yusha
However, the bigger problem might be that they did not get even closer — and build the scale to compete globally. The four have been fighting over a shrinking domestic beer sector that is about 40 percent smaller than its mid-90s peak while overseas rivals, riding a wave of consolidation, have become substantially larger. A failure to form national champions big enough to take on the likes of Anheuser-Busch InBev and Heineken NV is something Japan might come to regret.
The companies, Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory Spirits, make up an oligopoly that controls 90 percent of the country’s beer sales. Prices and products are largely similar, each shipping one or more flagship variations of the 5 percent or so ABV lager favored by local palates. The firms have, in the past few years, raised prices at similar times as energy and input costs have climbed.
Rather than consistently moving in lockstep, there is a tendency for an innovation by one to be quickly copied by the others.
All four have said they are fully cooperating with the FTC investigation; the president of Asahi Group Holdings Ltd defended the need for price rises citing ￥100 billion (US$632 million) in cumulative cost increases in its business over the past several years.
Kirin dominated for decades until Asahi Super Dry came along in 1987. The innovative lager not only changed the taste profile of Japanese beer, but turned its maker into the industry leader. Rivals have been chasing that high ever since, launching dozens of new products and seasonal variations in an attempt to capture, or just maintain, market share. It is true that this endless variety is one of the joys of life here, from the high-malt Aki Aji autumn beer to brews using regional hops. I do not want to see that go, but we should also consider the alternative.
When Asahi overtook Kirin around the turn of the century, the breweries were among the world’s larger makers. Now, they are distant also-rans to overseas rivals that have become substantially bigger, and operate at a vastly different scale. Combined, the big four have just 20 percent of the production of AB InBev, which controls brands such as Budweiser, Corona and Stella Artois.
Excessive fragmentation is not limited to beer. The country has seven automakers and nearly 100 regional banks. Despite the declining population, they often prefer to compete for a shrinking audience rather than join forces to take on a global one.
Local banks are combining in droves. And, the failed merger of Honda and Nissan aside, the automobile industry is slowly starting to concentrate around two poles. However, when it comes to beer, it is remarkable how little discussion there has been of a broader consolidation despite the broader challenges the sector faces, including a declining population, shifting drinking habits among young people and a trend for cheaper alternatives.
The one exception was the 2009 merger talks between Kirin and Suntory, a potential food-and-beverage behemoth that, at the time, would have been in the world’s top five. However, like many of the proposed combinations of Japanese firms following the financial crisis, talks broke down over control.
As the market has shrunk, each of the big four has attempted a different strategy. For two, beer has become something of an afterthought: Alcohol makes up less than half of annual revenue for Kirin, which has accelerated a push into healthcare, most recently with the US$1.4 billion purchase of Canadian vitamins and supplements maker Jamieson Wellness Inc, while Suntory pushed into liquor with its acquisition of brands including Jim Beam.
Meanwhile, Sapporo made disastrous deals for US craft beer makers Anchor Brewing and Stone Brewing. Subsequently, it was pressured by activist 3D Investment Partners, which accused the company of being “severely mismanaged,” into divesting its real estate holdings. Sapporo is now focusing again on beer, allying with Carlsberg to form a venture to sell in Southeast Asia. Only Asahi has found real success by expanding its portfolio overseas, acquiring brands including Peroni and Pilsner Urquell. Nonetheless, its scale remains well below rivals.
Failure to consolidate on Japanese terms might eventually mean consolidation on someone else’s. In price, taste and format, the consistency of Japanese beer shows that, cartel or not, the country’s brewers knew how to coordinate. It is just a shame they never took that to its logical conclusion.
Gearoid Reidy is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Japan. He previously led the breaking news team in North Asia, and was the Tokyo deputy bureau chief. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

How worried should we be for the economy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

It is difficult to remember a time when economies, financial markets, politics and societies were subject to significant volatility and uncertainty simultaneously, let alone to the degree they are today.
The global economy is entrenched in a cycle of sluggish economic growth, with rates in many countries, particularly the major developed economies, stalling well below 3 percent, the level needed to double per capita income in a generation. While the emerging artificial intelligence (AI) super-cycle could help offset this trend — in the US, annual investment appears set to approach 4 percent of GDP by 2032 — the technology raises serious, even existential, risks. Industry leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have called for frontier-AI development to be paused until labs can credibly control their models.
Meanwhile, many economies continue to struggle with inflation, which remains persistently above the 2 percent headline rate targeted by central banks worldwide. Last month, annual inflation in the eurozone hit 3.8 percent, its highest rate in three years, and the UK’s headline consumer price index reached 3.1 percent in August. In the US, median inflation expectations for the next year rose to 3.9 percent, while holding steady at 3 percent for the five-year horizon.
Some think that inflation is being fueled largely by the Iran war — energy prices have soared since the beginning of this year — and therefore amounts to a temporary challenge. However, concerns about structural unemployment and job diminution, together with arguably unsustainable public-debt burdens (reaching or exceeding 100 percent of GDP in several advanced economies), suggest that current economic woes would not be overcome so easily.
Public-debt risk is compounded by financial-market developments. For starters, the role of institutional investors that could traditionally be relied upon to hold long-term debt, such as pension funds and insurance companies, is being displaced by hedge funds operating on shorter time horizons. Heightening the risks further, particularly for the US, is the large share of public debt held by foreign governments — including those that, as with China, are not politically or ideologically aligned.
The US has another potential problem: The dollar’s longstanding role as the world’s leading reserve currency and a safe haven in times of crisis is increasingly in doubt. If the dollar does become less dominant, the US can expect its global political clout and economic maneuvering room to decline as well.
Growing economic uncertainty is apparent in bond markets. Yields on 10-year US Treasuries are running at more than 5.3 percent, and on 30-year Treasuries have surpassed 5.6 percent — the highest levels since 2002. However, it is not just the US. Yields are elevated across nearly the entire global bond market. In January 2022, just 12 percent of global fixed income yielded more than 3 percent; today, the share is about 84 percent.
The stock market is also making observers queasy. The CBOE Volatility Index — a common measure of volatility expectations — appears rather stable on a five-year historical basis, at about 15.31. However, market concentration has reached extreme levels, with just seven tech firms accounting for more than 30 percent of the S&P 500’s market capitalization. Moreover, the price-to-earnings ratio has reached 26.6 — far higher than the 16 that prevailed for much of the last quarter-century.
Underlying these economic and financial vicissitudes are the eroding foundations of healthy economies and societies. For example, data from the OECD’s Program for International Student Assessment show that education performance continues to decline in core subjects, such as reading, mathematics and science. And infrastructure investment continues to lag. The American Society of Civil Engineers issued US infrastructure — including roads, rails, bridges and ports — a C grade last year.
As the quality and availability of public goods declines, the social fabric starts to fray —and polarization intensifies. A 2022 Pew study showed that 72 percent of Republicans viewed Democrats as more immoral than other Americans, up from 47 percent in 2016, while 63 percent of Democrats held the same view of Republicans, up from 35 percent in 2016. According to a 2024 Gallup poll, 80 percent of US adults believe that Americans are deeply divided on the “most important values.”
This division extends to views of capitalism. In a Gallup poll last year, 54 percent of respondents reported a favorable view of capitalism, down from 60 percent in 2021. That decline is concentrated among Democrats and independents — each group showed an eight-percentage-point drop — with Republicans’ views having remained essentially unchanged.
European politics also make for uncomfortable viewing nowadays, as support for far-right parties continues to grow. Germany’s Alternative fur Deutschland has scored notable victories in state elections. At a minimum, the political fragmentation this trend implies is likely to compound the time-inconsistency problem in policymaking, leading to greater policy volatility, lower investment and weaker economic growth.
All of this is happening against a backdrop of rising geopolitical volatility. As tensions rise and the global balance of power shifts, the institutions that have long underpinned multilateral cooperation are under growing strain, with implications for the global energy transition, trade, capital flows and global commodity prices.
Of course, from a practical perspective, it is not enough simply to restate this growing list of challenges, many of which are already top of mind for global decisionmakers. However, it is worth underscoring just how rare — and dangerous — it is for all of them to be salient at the same time. Those with the power to shape the global economy must never lose sight of the stakes.
Dambisa Moyo, an international economist, is the author of Edge of Chaos: Why Democracy Is Failing to Deliver Economic Growth — and How to Fix It.

Two suspects who went to South Korea after allegedly taking part in a fatal assault in Kaohsiung’s Nanzih District (楠梓) last month have been brought back to Taiwan and taken into custody, police said yesterday.
The suspects, a 25-year-old used-car dealership owner surnamed Lin (林) and a 23-year-old employee surnamed Liu (劉), arrived at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport on Saturday, where they were arrested by a special team investigating the case, the Kaohsiung City Police Department’s Criminal Investigation Corps said.
South Korean police apprehended the two after Taiwan’s Criminal Investigation Bureau requested assistance through its liaison officer in South Korea, the corps said.
Photo courtesy of Kaohsiung City Police Department’s Criminal Investigation Corps
Investigators suspect that Lin orchestrated the assault and that Liu took part in beating the victim. Both men have denied any wrongdoing, and the investigation continues.
The case came to light on Sept. 30, when a 22-year-old man surnamed Mu (穆) called the Nanzih Precinct of the Kaohsiung City Police Department to report that he had accidentally beaten a coworker to death.
Mu later drove the victim’s body to the police station and turned himself in.
Prosecutors said Mu, Liu and several others assaulted a coworker surnamed Chang (張) at Lin’s used-car dealership at about 1am on Sept. 30, striking him with hot glue sticks and clubs.
Mu told police that the attack stemmed from a dispute over NT$100,000 (US$3,079) the victim allegedly owed.
Police had initially questioned Lin and Liu before releasing them on Oct. 1, but investigators subsequently gathered more evidence linking them to the case. Prosecutors later identified the two as key suspects, police said.
When authorities could not locate them for further questioning, they discovered that they had flown to South Korea on Oct. 2. Prosecutors then issued warrants for their arrest.
Mu and three other suspects surnamed Wu (吳), Yeh (葉) and Chen (陳) have been ordered detained on suspicion of murder after prosecutors said that they were flight risks and could coordinate their accounts or tamper with evidence.
A juvenile surnamed Huang (黃) has been referred to juvenile court.

Frozen defense items not on agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:24 UTC
01:42:24 KST

A record-late budget deadlock has left more than 150 requests to unfreeze defense funds stalled, with the legislature’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee yet to schedule a review.
The Executive Yuan submitted the central government’s 2026 fiscal year budget proposal in August last year, but the opposition-dominated legislature did not pass the budget on third reading until Aug. 14, after a record 351-day review.
The Executive Yuan did not receive the approved budget from the Legislative Yuan until Sept. 17, and the Presidential Office the next day promulgated the budget by presidential order.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
However, since the new legislative session began on Sept. 29, Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee conveners have yet to schedule a review session, leaving more than 150 requests to unfreeze Ministry of National Defense funds awaiting review, with none approved.
The army command’s written report to the legislature shows that it had proposed more than NT$1.35 billion (US$41.75 million) for purchasing spare parts from the US for 108 M1A2T Abrams tanks, as the first batch of 38 tanks received in 2024 has reached the end of its two-year warranty period.
The replenishment items were planned in accordance with technical specifications and the list of critical and backup parts provided by US representatives based on their operational experience, the report said.
The army planned to procure 17 types (916 items) of level-2 maintenance parts, 144 types (294 items) of critical components, such as recoil mechanisms, and 86 types (303 items) of war reserve stocks such as AGT-1500 gas turbine engines — totaling 247 types and 1,513 items, it said.
Delaying procurement would adversely affect equipment sustainment, it said.
Citing concerns about restrictive procurement specifications and overlap with existing systems, opposition lawmakers also frozen 10 percent of the budget allocation for the military to use the Taiwan Tactical Mission Network and the Team Awareness Kit to establish a common operational picture for ground forces and enable decentralized command and control capabilities.
However, with little more than two months remaining in this fiscal year and a packed legislative schedule, it is uncertain if these funds can be unfrozen, and even then, there might not be enough time to complete the procurement process, the army command said.
The committee’s conveners are Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) and Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Wang Yi-chuan (王義川).
In the first week of the current legislative session, Hsu set two special report topics — a Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) relocation project proposed by Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the KMT and the alleged misuse of official resources by former Overseas Community Affairs Council (OCAC) Minister Hsu Chia-ching (徐佳青), which she has disputed.
For this week, Wang scheduled two days of inspections and one day for a National Security Bureau operational report.
Hsu Chiao-hsin yesterday said she is in charge of setting the committee agenda for matters involving the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the OCAC.
“The Ministry of National Defense really has nothing to do with me; you have to ask Wang Yi-chuan how he is arranging them,” she said.
Wang said the schedule for operational reports and budget unfreezing proposals was discussed and confirmed with ministries and agencies last week, and meetings would be placed on the agenda in sequential order.

According to the council’s statistics, the number of Taiwanese who went missing, were detained for questioning, or are suspected of having personal freedom restricted while traveling to China this year, as of Friday, stood at 458, an increase of four people from the week before, which covered cases through Oct. 8.
Among them, 175 have been reported missing, up from 173 the previous week, while 41 have been detained for questioning, up from 39 the previous week, and 242 were being held by Chinese authorities, unchanged from last week, the figures showed.
Photo: Reuters
Meanwhile, Straits Exchange Foundation Secretary-General Luo Wen-jia (羅文嘉) on Friday said Taiwanese members of the I-Kuan Tao (一貫道) religious group who have lived in China for years were detained in China each month from April to July, and none of them have been released yet.
The case in April involved a Taiwanese living in Fujian Province who held a China residence permit; the May case is a Taiwanese teacher working in Dongguan, Guangdong Province; the June case involved a Taiwanese businessperson based in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province; and the July case involves a Taiwanese who had moved to Zhangzhou, Fujian Province, after retirement, he said.
The common thread in all four cases is that the detainees are all followers of I-Kuan Tao, he added.
Previous cases of Taiwanese I-Kuan Tao followers detained in China occurred during short-term trips or cross-strait cultural exchange events, but the latest cases involved people who have lived and worked in China for an extended period of time and were detained for religious reasons, Luo said.
“It is evident that just because something was fine in past years does not mean it will be safe now or in the future,” he said, as he strongly suggested they return to Taiwan for their own safety.
As the risks have grown from just short-term travelers to long-term residents of China, he said the travel risk level for I-Kuan Tao followers traveling to China should be raised to a “red alert,” and that they should “return to Taiwan immediately.”
According to Luo, in October 2024, three Taiwanese I-Kuan Tao followers were detained in China and prosecuted under Article 300 of the Criminal Law of the People’s Republic of China, and sentenced to prison terms ranging from two to three years.
One of them is still serving their sentence, another has completed their sentence and returned to Taiwan, and the third has finished serving their sentence, but has not yet been able to return to Taiwan, he said.

Typhoon Champi sea warning possible Wednesday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:20 UTC
01:42:20 KST

A sea warning for Typhoon Champi could be issued as early as Wednesday night, possibly followed by a land warning on Thursday night or Friday, as the storm approaches Taiwan, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
The typhoon is expected to have its greatest impact on Taiwan on Friday and Saturday, bringing heavy rain to central and northern Taiwan and to Yilan and Hualien counties in the east, CWA forecaster Liu Pei-teng (劉沛滕) said.
As of 2pm yesterday, Champi was about 2,470km east-southeast of Oluanpi (鵝鑾鼻), Taiwan’s southernmost tip, moving westnorthwest at 20kph.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
It had maximum sustained winds of 191kph and a storm radius of 200km, CWA data showed.
Forecasts suggest Champi would maintain its strength as it heads toward waters northeast of Taiwan, Liu said.
Some forecast models suggest Champi could make landfall in eastern Taiwan, but its track remains uncertain because the strength of the Pacific high-pressure system could affect its path, he said.
If the high-pressure system weakens sooner than expected, Champi could turn north before approaching Taiwan, Liu said.
If the system strengthens, the typhoon could take a more southerly track or pass through the Bashi Channel, between Taiwan and the Philippines, he said.
International forecast models continue to show divergent tracks, and tomorrow would be key in determining whether Champi turns north, Liu added.
Ahead of the typhoon, the weather would remain relatively stable today and tomorrow, with mostly cloudy to sunny skies across Taiwan, the CWA said.
Brief, isolated showers are possible along the Keelung coast, in northeastern and southeastern Taiwan, and on the Hengchun Peninsula (恆春半島), it said.

Calls for progress on Taichung airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:19 UTC
01:42:19 KST

Taichung International Airport has struggled to keep pace with growing demand for tourism and business travel, while its joint military-civilian use has constrained efforts to expand the airport, legislators said.
The airport is a key gateway for more than 7 million people in central Taiwan. However, of the projects outlined in a development plan five years ago, only improvements to the existing terminal and construction of connecting and apron taxiways have been completed. Plans for a third terminal, remote aprons and an aerospace industry zone remain unrealized.
Taichung airport has more than 30 international routes. Passenger traffic surpassed 2 million in the first seven months of this year, with full-year traffic expected to surpass last year’s 2.75 million passengers.
Photo: Taipei Times
Despite the increase in traffic, the airport has only two baggage carousels, with most international flights arriving in the afternoon. When two flights arrive at the same time, passengers might have to wait about 30 minutes to collect their luggage. Parking is also a major problem, with spaces difficult to find during long weekends and holidays.
Taichung airport is inside the air force’s Ching Chuan Kang Air Base, which is divided by the runway into eastern and western areas. The eastern area is used by the military, while civilian aircraft operate in the western area, although most of the land there is also owned by the air force. Restrictions on military land and difficulties developing the western area have become major obstacles to the airport’s expansion, legislators said.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純), who is also a candidate for Taichung mayor, said that the airport should add more aircraft stands and baggage carousels in the short term.
In the long term, the central government should coordinate with the Ministry of National Defense over the allocation of military land and restrictions on military flight operations at night, she said.
The Ministry of Transportation and Communications and the Civil Aeronautics Administration should submit a development plan for Taichung Airport through 2045 by the end of the year, Ho said.
Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), who is also a candidate for Taichung mayor, said that the third terminal had already been included in the airport’s next phase of construction in 2019.
“The central government must clearly explain what is holding it up,” Chiang said, adding that it should coordinate the competing needs of national defense and aviation safety and present an implementable and trackable construction schedule.
DPP Legislator Tsai Chi-chang (蔡其昌) also said the government should assess options for adding parking spaces, building temporary parking lots or introducing transfer services, while accelerating the Taichung Airport Gateway Project.
Deputy Minister of Transportation and Communications Lin Kuo-hsien (林國顯) said that the civilian airport occupies only 30 hectares of the base’s land, or about 2 percent. The airport would need to expand into the western area to obtain sufficient space, he said, adding that the Civil Aeronautics Administration is working on the airport’s overall development plan through 2045.
Huang Tai-lin (黃泰林), a professor in the Department of Shipping and Transportation Management at Chang Jung Christian University, said that the Civil Aeronautics Administration might be considering a more balanced distribution of airport capacity between northern and southern Taiwan. Taichung and Taoyuan airports have relatively close airspace, while airports in northern and southern Taiwan are farther apart, potentially affecting the order in which projects are developed, he said.
Chaoyang University of Technology Department of Aviation director Lu Yen-liang (盧衍良) said that the development of Taichung airport is also constrained by its role as a regional gateway for central Taiwan, an aircraft maintenance industry cluster and a resilient backup facility, as well as the unique challenges of joint military-civilian use.
He recommended accelerating approval and construction of the Taichung Metro’s orange line, evaluating an elevated access road connecting the airport directly to a national freeway, and building multi-story parking facilities on public land around the airport.
The government should also begin planning and environmental impact assessments for a third terminal and improve operational efficiency, Lu said.
It could also capitalize on central Taiwan’s aerospace and precision machinery clusters to accelerate construction of an aircraft maintenance industrial zone, he said.
Additional reporting by Huang Yi-ching and Ou Su-mei

====================================================================================================

Japan prepares historic Mars mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars’ moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region.
The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies, as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Center tomorrow at 4:41am, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) said.
Photo: AFP
“Being able to be involved in such a grand mission is incredibly exciting,” JAXA’s H3 rocket team project manager Makoto Arita told reporters yesterday.
The spacecraft would arrive near Mars in about August next year, where it would orbit one of its moons, Phobos, before landing and collecting at least 10g of material from the surface during three years of operating within the Martian sphere.
A rover dubbed Idefix — the French name for the comic hero Asterix’s dog — would first conduct surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing.
“The sampling [from] Phobos is of course the world’s first, but it means ... this is the first round trip to the Martian system,” MMX project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu said.
The mission would also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a “natural space station” by establishing the requirements for a round trip to Mars — something “essential for crewed Mars exploration,” JAXA said.
It would also observe the Red Planet’s moon Deimos, although it would not land on it, before returning to Earth.
JAXA hopes the mission would reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the solar system was born.
One theory for the origin of the Martian moons — the “giant impact” hypothesis — is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars.
Meanwhile, the “capture” hypothesis postulates that the moons are asteroids captured by Mars’ gravity.
Determining which theory is correct would help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets,” JAXA said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the Sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
“MMX will shed light on the transport mechanisms that delivered water, volatiles and organic compounds from the outer solar system to the inner rocky planet region — processes that may have played a key role in making these worlds habitable,” said Patrick Michel, a French astrophysicist working on Idefix.
“If Phobos and Deimos are indeed remnants of these early delivery systems, they may hold clues to the origins of life itself, or, to be more correct, to the transport of the materials that were key to the emergence of life on rocky planets,” he said.
MMX is a collaboration with NASA, the European Space Agency, France’s National Center for Space Studies, the German Aerospace Center, and about 20 universities and tech companies.
The development of the spacecraft’s landing legs was particularly difficult, as gravity on Phobos is extremely weak, JAXA scientists said.
Japan’s uncrewed Smart Lander for Investigating Moon — the “Moon Sniper” — tipped over after touching down on Earth’s Moon in 2024, but still transmitted data and survived several two-week lunar nights.
Japan also has experience in bringing back samples from space, including JAXA’s uncrewed Hayabusa-2, which returned 5.4g of rock and dust collected from an asteroid several hundred million kilometers from Earth in 2020.
On the upcoming mission “we have to travel very close to Mars and return,” which means escaping the planet’s heavy gravity, Kawakatsu said.
Phobos orbits about 6,000km above the Martian surface.
“Going deep into what we call the ‘gravity well’ is difficult,” Kawakatsu said.
US and Chinese space agencies have been racing to be the first to return rock samples from Mars’ surface back to Earth.
NASA’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming the Red Planet since 2021, has already collected samples.
However, the mission was effectively canceled by US President Donald Trump’s administration following a vote by the US Congress in January.
Meanwhile, China has announced its Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch in about 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 — potentially before MMX.
Sand and rocks from Phobos might offer a wider variety of samples than those on the planet itself, especially if it was formed by a collision between a celestial body and Mars, JAXA scientists said.
Former British prime minister Rishi Sunak on Wednesday urged so-called middle powers to become a “poisonous shrimp” to carve out strategic economic leverage in a more turbulent global environment. Sunak drew from a metaphor by former Singaporean prime minister Lee Kuan Yew (李光耀): A big fish will eat a smaller fish, and the smaller fish will eat the shrimp. 2026 Elections: Election fraud risk rises as voting draws closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

With the nine-in-one local elections to be held next month, the public should be vigilant against four prevalent types of scams, as fraud rings capitalize on election fever to target voters and businesses, the Criminal Investigation Bureau said yesterday.
The four types of scams are fake giveaways of campaign merchandise, investment fraud involving campaign billboard advertisements, impersonation of candidates and fraudulent political donations, the bureau said in a news release, based on reports received on the 165 anti-fraud hotline.
The first and most common election-related scam involves fake giveaways of campaign merchandise, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Criminal Investigation Bureau
Scammers often pose as merchandise vendors or supporters on social media, offering free campaign items or exchanges among supporters, it said.
Once victims leave comments, they are directed to join Line accounts where scammers request “real-name verification” or “cash-flow verification,” it said.
They would be instructed to use their online banking apps to operate cardless ATM withdrawal services, allowing the scammers to steal their money, it said.
In one case during the Double Ten National Day holiday, a supporter came across a post on Threads offering surplus campaign merchandise, it said.
After clicking a fraudulent link provided by the scammer and following instructions on a fake mobile banking system, the victim gave away over their national ID number, online banking withdrawal code and password, allowing the scammer to withdraw NT$340,000 (US$10,514) from the account within 40 minutes, it said.
The second type of scam involves supposed investments in campaign billboard advertisements, it said.
Scammers claim investors would receive substantial returns once a candidate is elected, or claim to offer insider investment channels with guaranteed profits, it said.
Victims are duped into sending money out of a desire to support the candidate while expecting financial gains, it said.
The third type involves impersonating candidates or public officials on social media, it said.
Scammers first identify staunch supporters on candidate fan pages before impersonating candidates or incumbent officials to send private messages, it said.
Fraud rings claim to be using private accounts and ask supporters to transfer money or provide loans, citing election expenses or the need to raise funds discreetly, it said.
The fourth type involves defrauding businesses under the pretext of political donations, it said.
Scammers place large product orders purportedly to serve as in-kind political donations, paying with post-dated checks, it said, adding that once the merchandise is delivered, the checks bounce.
The bureau urged businesses and the public not to hand over money or goods without first meeting the political figure or campaign team in person and confirming the details.
While the scam tactics are not new and the number of cases reported so far is not high, the public should be vigilant during the final month of the campaign, it said.
People who receive unfamiliar links should verify whether they lead to official Web sites, it said.
If customer service representatives ask them to use online banking apps for real-name or transaction verification, they should immediately halt the process, it said.
Anyone with doubts can call the 165 anti-fraud hotline for assistance, it said.

North, south ports eyed as cruise hubs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

Keelung and Kaohsiung could serve as Taiwan’s northern and southern cruise home ports, with Keelung focusing on routes to Japan and South Korea and Kaohsiung covering the Philippines and Vietnam, the think tank under the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said in a media briefing.
Data collected by the Institute of Transportation (IOT) showed that the number of global cruise ship passengers reached a record-high 37.20 million last year, about 25.3 percent higher than the pre-COVID-19 pandemic level.
Asia had about 3 million cruise ship passengers, about 80 percent of the pre-pandemic level, data showed.
Photo courtesy of Hsieh Chih-huang
However, the number marked a 15 percent increase compared with 2024, the institute said.
IOT deputy director-general Chen Pin-chuan (陳賓權) cited data from the Cruise Lines International Association, showing that Taiwan was the 11th largest cruise ship market from 2016 to 2019 globally, and the second largest market in Asia, preceded by China.
In 2019, Taiwan recorded 671 cruise ship arrivals and 1.06 million cruise ship passengers, Chen said. The Port of Keelung was Asia’s second largest cruise ship port, surpassing the Port of Shanghai and being preceded by the Port of Singapore, he added.
The global cruise ship market was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, with cruise ship passengers in Taiwan reduced to nearly zero in 2022, Chen said.
After the government lifted COVID-19 restrictions in 2023, the number of cruise ship passengers in Taiwan rebounded to 11.57 million last year, surpassing the pre-pandemic level, he said.
However, the number of cruise ship arrivals last year has yet to return to the level in 2019, he said, adding that Taiwan ranked No. 13 in global cruise ship market and No. 4 in Asia.
“This shows the trend toward larger cruise ships, which in turn would optimize the tourism benefits that a cruise ship could bring,” Chen said.
Last year, port-of-call cruises — in which the ship stops at a Taiwanese port as part of its itinerary — accounted for 39 percent, up from 26 percent in 2024, Chen said.
Meanwhile, foreign visitors made up 58 percent of cruise travelers in 2024, with most of them coming from Japan, the US and Germany, he said.
The share of cruise ship passengers arriving through flights and boarding ships in Taiwan — also known as the fly-cruise model — rose to 11 percent by 2023, he added.
More than 64 percent of passengers choose to stay an extra night at the cruise homeport before or after their voyage, generating additional accommodation and tourism spending.
“We recommend that there be more partnerships between the Maritime and Port Bureau and Taiwan International Port Corp (TIPC) to improve port infrastructure and cultivate talents for the cruise ship industry,” Chen said.
International commercial ports in Keelung City and Kaohsiung could take on different roles as Taiwan’s northern and southern cruise homeports, with Keelung covering Japan and South Korea and Kaohsiung expanding routes to the Philippines and Vietnam, Chen said.
“With the increase of fly-cruise travelers, the bureau and the TIPC should work to facilitate the transfer between maritime and air transportation services, including enhancing the baggage handling efficiency,” he said.
TIPC previously estimated that the nation would welcome 605 cruise ships this year, with the number of cruise ship travelers exceeding 1.197 million.
