Netanyahu warns Israel could lose US support, seeks 450 billion shekels in extra defense spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:23:17 UTC
00:23:17 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Sunday that Israel could face a hostile U.S. administration in the future, potentially threatening its military assistance and strategic relationship with Washington, and said the country must develop new international alliances. At the same time, he announced plans to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels in additional defense spending over the next decade.
Netanyahu made the remarks during an event at which he presented his security doctrine, nine days before Israel's October 27 election. Just hours later, U.S. President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu's reelection bid for the first time during the current campaign.
"In two years, a president, man or woman, could come to power who is very hostile to Israel," Netanyahu said. "How would you deal with that? How would you operate in relation to the United States? And beyond that, what solutions would be necessary?"
His remarks came against the possibility that a future U.S. administration could suspend military assistance to Israel or even join international sanctions and an arms embargo against the country.
Netanyahu said Israel must use the remaining years of Trump's presidency to strengthen its position while preparing for a potentially dramatic shift in American policy.
"First, we must do everything we can during these two years, and during the following two years, in the American arena, through good times and bad," he said. "The second thing is to create other alliances. That is what I am working on now with many countries in our region and outside it. India is not a small country, and there are many others."
He pointed to political developments in Latin America as another opportunity to expand Israel's network of allies.
"There is a major shift in Latin America, and there could be an enormous change in Brazil in just a few days," Netanyahu said. "We must expand our pool of alliances and develop capabilities that make us valuable to everyone."
He also addressed Israel's strained relations with European countries, accusing some governments of publicly condemning Israel while continuing to seek cooperation with it.
"Countries that condemn us, and they have some nerve, by the way, condemn us and then come to us," he said. "I tell them: It depends on you. It depends on how you behave."
Netanyahu argued that Israel still possesses diplomatic leverage but would need considerable international expertise to navigate changes in Washington and other capitals.
In a separate social media post Sunday, Netanyahu appeared to acknowledge the possibility of a change in U.S. leadership, describing Trump's remaining time in office as an opportunity to advance Israel's strategic objectives.
"We have another two years of my friend President Trump's term, and this is exactly the time to complete our major missions on every front," he wrote.
On defense spending, Netanyahu said he intended to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels over the coming decade to strengthen Israel's military capabilities. An additional defense spending package of approximately 350 billion shekels had previously been agreed upon, according to earlier reports.
Addressing the future size of the Israel Defense Forces, Netanyahu said the military would have to expand, although technological advances, particularly artificial intelligence, could reduce some of its manpower requirements.
"As for a large army or a small army, the IDF definitely needs to grow," he said. "It will grow, but not at the rate we might have expected because AI reduces many requirements. Still, it needs to grow, and for that, of course, you need to allocate both funding and personnel."
He added: "I am putting about 450 billion shekels into this so that we have the capabilities and the teeth."
Turning to Iran, Netanyahu said the regime remained a threat despite what he described as severe military and economic damage inflicted on it. He warned that Tehran would seek to rebuild its nuclear program, develop other unconventional weapons and restore its regional network of allied armed groups.
"Like cancer, this will not end as long as that regime remains in place," he said. "It will try to recover, renew its nuclear program, renew other unconventional weapons programs and rebuild the axis."
Netanyahu claimed that Israel had already accomplished approximately 90% of its objectives against Iran and described the Iranian leadership as severely weakened.
"Why aren't people taking to the streets? Because right now they are being killed. Simply killed. They are killing or wounding tens of thousands of their own people. That is the nature of this regime," he said.
He then explicitly stated that his policy was aimed at bringing down the Iranian government. "Our plan is very comprehensive and very determined, to bring about the downfall of the regime," Netanyahu said. "That is my plan. That is the directive I have given all the security agencies, and that is what will happen."
Netanyahu also discussed Israel's relationship with Russia, describing it as one based on competing national interests rather than consistent cooperation.
"We speak when necessary," he said. "But Russia has its interests, and we have the interests of the State of Israel, and they do not always overlap. Sometimes they even clash."
He cited Russia's cooperation with Iran during the war in Ukraine as an example of conflicting interests and also raised the issue of anti-Israel bot networks spreading what he described as extreme antisemitic content.
"We raise all these issues, and we do so very clearly," Netanyahu said. "And when there is an opportunity to cooperate, we do that as well."
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the opposition Yashar! party and a former IDF chief of staff, sharply criticized Netanyahu's presentation, describing it as an empty political exercise rather than a serious national security strategy.
"Nine days before the election and three years after the gravest failure and disaster in Israel's history, with every war front still open, Netanyahu decided to present his 'security doctrine' to the public," Eisenkot said.
"Two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing whatsoever to do with a security doctrine, reveal more than anything the strategic vacuum Netanyahu has left the State of Israel in and his disregard for the security of Israeli citizens."
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of attempting to manipulate public opinion and spread fear ahead of the election.
"This is Netanyahu's method: manipulating perceptions, frightening people and trying to divert attention from the parade of lies and racism surrounding his campaign tonight," he said.

Trump endorses Netanyahu in Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

15:16:03 UTC
00:16:03 KST

Trump endorses Netanyahu in Israeli election
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump on Oct 18 endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu as the longtime Israeli prime minister struggles for an edge in next week’s parliamentary election.
Trump praised Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” and peace partner, crediting him with joining the United States in launching strikes on Iran in February.
The conflict, in its seventh month, has disrupted energy markets globally and wreaked havoc across the Middle East, damaging critical infrastructure and destabilising regional economies.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
“Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived! I have watched Bibi under the most trying of times. Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure – But Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today.”
In his message, addressed to “the Great People of Israel,” Trump added, “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
The Trump endorsement is not certain to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party a boost in the Oct 27 national election, as Israeli public support for Trump has diminished amid Israeli-US disagreements over Iran.
Polls have suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel’s prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in Parliament rather than by direct popular vote.
It will be Israel’s first vote since the Hamas attack on Oct 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is defeated by centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era.
Netanyahu promptly expressed his thanks to Trump on X, saying, “Together we will complete the mission!”
Trump has broken with longtime US tradition by endorsing candidates in elections in foreign countries, including Hungary, Colombia, Argentina, Japan and Honduras.
Endorsement might help
Trump’s relationship with Netanyahu has been close but also fractious, with the president at times publicly and privately criticising Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
The war that the US and Israel launched against Iran is unpopular with Americans, who vote Nov 3 in congressional elections, while support for Israel among Americans has also decreased over the Iran war and Israel’s conduct in the three-year war in Gaza that Trump has promised to end. Both leaders on Sunday mentioned finishing the job in Iran.
Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, said Trump’s late endorsement could help win back wavering Netanyahu voters but was unlikely to draw widespread support.
Most Israelis, even those who are critical of Netanyahu and his government, were largely in favour of the Iran war.
In an election this close, “it couldn’t hurt him, and it might help,” said analyst Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show. That could lead to Netanyahu serving as a caretaker prime minister while another election is held.
The US president passed up earlier opportunities to endorse Netanyahu, perhaps because he wanted to see what leverage he could exercise on issues like Gaza or Lebanon, said Miller. In the end, he said, Trump sided with a leader he sees as strong and unfairly persecuted.
“However angry Trump may be at Netanyahu for pushing this Iran war, this in the end was a Trump decision,” Miller added.
A Trump decision not to endorse Netanyahu would have raised “legitimate questions about whether or not the whole Iran venture was in fact something Trump should have done,” he said. REUTERS

Love, loathing and the Zionist underground: A novel in which everything happens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:12:38 UTC
00:12:38 KST

Love, Loathing and the Zionist Underground: A Novel in Which Everything Happens
Early on while reading "Fate," Zeruya Shalev's 2021 novel released in Joanna Chen's English translation this week, I realized that I've read a lot of contemporary literary fiction lately where nothing much happens. This is not a slight against the slightly plotted novel, but a note on the abundant action of Shalev's work, which explodes and melts in your hands.
In "Fate," everything happens: love, secrets, divorce, infidelity, fevered deathbed declarations, guerilla warfare, religious epiphany, Oedipal-adjacent dynamics, momentary necrophilia, spaghetti Bolognese. "Fate" is not for the faint of heart.
The novel begins within the long-ago memories of Rachel, a Jewish freedom fighter – or terrorist, depending who you ask – who has braved sniper fire traveling from Tel Aviv to bang the door of her mother-in-law's Jerusalem home when her young husband, Mano, suddenly leaves her. It is the dawn of Israel's independence, and everything but her convictions are provisional. Moving forward to the present day, elderly Rachel is at her own home in a West Bank settlement, awaiting an introductory visit from Atara, the daughter eventually born to this man who would blockade and divorce her decades earlier. Atara has come because Mano mentioned Rachel – actually, mistook Atara for Rachel – only as he lay dying.
From here the story proceeds, shifting between the poles of these two women, Rachel and Atara, both tied to one another by forces beyond their wills, both facing the vicissitudes of life in Israel from the vantage points of different politics and generations. "This is a different country," Rachel notes of Israel today, "gray and crowded, hiding behind walls and barbed wire fences, a land that has lost faith in its righteousness." She is cranky, tired, a patriot bewildered by her nation's evolution and bitter, still, over the British overlords who killed her friends: "Boaz and Arieh and Yisrael and Uri and Elhanan and Shlomo and Gedalia and Zvi and Haim and Uzi and Yosef and Shmuel and Hemda and Ruth and Meir and Shemesh," a line she recites often, like prayer or meditation.

Lithuania says attempted Starlink arson was Russia-linked sabotage
VILNIUS, Oct 18 - Lithuania is treating an attempted arson attack at a SpaceX Starlink base station on Sunday as a Russia-linked act of sabotage aimed at undermining Ukraine's military capacity, the head of the government's National Crisis Management Centre said.
Lithuanian authorities are searching for suspects who attempted to set fire to a Starlink base station on the outskirts of the capital Vilnius at about 2 a.m. (2300 GMT on Saturday), said Vilmantas Vitkauskas.
The blaze was quickly extinguished, causing only minor property damage and no disruption to operations, he added.
"We understand that this was not a routine arson attack but an act of sabotage," Vitkauskas told reporters in Vilnius.
He said the incident was linked to earlier arson attacks against Starlink stations in Bulgaria and Poland.
"They are part of Russian attempts to disrupt Starlink and influence the success of Ukrainian operations," he said. "Ukraine is the target."
Ukraine uses Starlink terminals extensively for battlefield communications and installs Starlink receivers in many of its drones as part of their guidance systems.
The terminals are used to conduct strikes on Russian targets inside Ukraine and help its interceptor drones defend against Russian drone attacks.
Bulgarian authorities said fire was set to several Starlink antennas in the country on October 10, according to local media reports. And a fire at a Starlink facility in Poland in September damaged its power system and backup generator.
Poland said at the time it believed the fire was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military, and blamed Russia. Four suspects were detained.
Moscow says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. REUTERS

Drones don’t sell on need. They sell on value - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:08:36 UTC
00:08:36 KST

Every sales manual says the same thing: find the pain, sell the cure. In my industry, that advice is half right, and the wrong half is expensive.
A drone produces a dozen different kinds of value. It surveys a highway interchange in an hour, to the centimeter, where a crew once stood in traffic for days. It collects in one day the thermal data on a solar field of 20,000 panels. It patrols a fence at two in the morning without a car, and puts live video in a control room before a guard has found his keys.
Increasingly, it is sold not as hardware but as a service. In drone-as-a-service, the customer buys no aircraft, holds no license, and does not need to know how to fly. The operator installs the station, holds the approvals, trains the dispatchers, maintains the fleet, and carries the responsibility. The customer pays monthly for an outcome: a patrol, a survey, a defect list.
Autonomy is what makes that model work. A drone that lives on site in a weatherproof dock, charges itself, launches on an alarm or a schedule, and lands without anyone beside it turns a drone service from a visit into a utility. Our stations put a drone in the air within 15 seconds of a call; it flies for 54 minutes, recharges in 27, and is directed by a dispatcher who never leaves the control room.
Here is my argument: the urgency of a customer’s need decides how fast he arrives, but only visible value decides whether he signs and whether he stays, and making that value visible, to customers who do not yet feel the need, is the burden of the operators.
One morning near Lod
At about 6:30 a.m. on September 15, 2024, a missile fired from Yemen fell in open ground near Lod, in central Israel. Six weeks earlier, we had installed an autonomous drone at a power station in the area. It was airborne within seconds. The control room had live video of the impact area before anyone had left the gate, and the response teams drove out knowing what was waiting for them.
Nobody in that control room needed to be told afterwards what the drone was for.
That is what need does: it accelerates. But mornings like that are rare. What a customer pays for in every other month is the routine, patrols flown on schedule, alarms verified from the air before anyone is dispatched, every event on video. Need opened the door. Value is the rent.
Now consider a customer with no need at all. This summer, our analysis of an 88-megawatt solar field in the South found dozens of dead strings, rows of panels producing nothing, while the site’s monitoring reported normal operation. The owner felt no pain; the dashboard was green. The loss was invisible, and worth well over $100,000 a year. Need would never have brought that customer to us. Only a number could.
The clearest proof comes from California. Since 2018, police in Chula Vista have sent drones to more than 25,000 emergency calls. The drone arrived first on 17,170 of them, in an average of 97 seconds, and on 4,629 calls, no officer had to be sent at all. A city council does not need to have suffered a slow response to understand that number.
Why the value has outrun the market
None of this is Israeli. In 2016, PwC put the value of business services and labor that drones could replace at more than $127 billion. Nearly a decade later, Drone Industry Insights sizes the entire commercial drone-services market at about $29b. The value was always there. Few customers could see it in their own numbers.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency's figures from November 2025 count 2.5 million registered drone operators across 31 states, and 4,226 operational authorizations, the permits behind serious commercial flying. In the United States, the rule for routine flight beyond visual line of sight, the rule that makes docked autonomy ordinary, was proposed in August 2025 and, as of early October, was still unpublished. Israel has allowed docked flight without a pilot on site since 2022. Regulation is moving; customers are slower.
Who teaches, and who collects
So who makes the value visible? Not the manufacturer, who meets the customer once, at the sale. In a service model, the operator meets him every day. We fly more than 15,000 drone missions a year for more than 200 business customers, and each arrives at a different distance from his own need: defense with the need already sharp, infrastructure security after an event, solar slowly, surveyors on cost. All of them sign for the same reason, a value they can measure. That is why our process starts with the customer’s own baseline, not a demonstration flight: a site visit, a survey, a pilot with metrics agreed in advance, and a decision taken on the data.
It is also why autonomy is the core of our business and the center of its future. A crew-based service sells a day of flying. A stationed drone sells every day. Once the station, the certification, and the control room exist, each additional mission, a patrol, a thermal scan, a check after a storm, costs almost nothing, and each one adds a line to the customer’s baseline. The next step is already visible: control centers running many stations at once under airspace-management systems, and the same network carrying urgent medical supplies and deliveries. We are starting urban delivery work with Israel’s Innovation Authority.
The economic conclusion follows. In drone-as-a-service, value goes to whoever owns the measurement, the company that set the baseline and reports against it every month. Flight hours are already a commodity; the dock is becoming one. The network of stations, and the baseline behind each of them, is not. So the education that builds it has to carry a price: our academy, which trains close to 1,000 commercial operators a year, is a business; dispatcher training is a line on the quote; implementation is a phase with a fee.
What still has to be fixed
Let me name where we got it wrong.
Too often we sold the capability we found impressive rather than the value the customer could measure. A thermal map is beautiful. A site manager wants to know what Monday’s repairs are worth. Every time we led with the technology, the sale got longer.
Early this year, we planned to sell autonomy through security companies, as a back office behind their brands. Within months, we reversed it. A service sold on value needs the operator in the room when the baseline is set. We now sell directly.
And “autonomous” still carries more people than the word suggests. The aircraft flies itself; the service does not run itself. Anyone promising an asset owner a lights-out operation today is selling something.
A customer who needs a drone will eventually find one. A customer who can see what a drone is worth will pay for it every month. The first is a sale. The second is a business, and autonomy is how it scales.
The writer, a colonel in the reserves, is founder and CEO of Propeller Drones Ltd., Israel’s largest drone services provider.
This was written in collaboration with Propeller Drones.

Tirana sees sixth day of violent protests as Albania’s PM refuses to resign
At this moment, no one is clear on what tomorrow will bring, says Albanian journalist Lindita Karadaku.
Violent protests have rocked Albania’s capital Tirana for the sixth consecutive day as Prime Minister Edi Rama, who is serving his fourth term, ruled out resigning.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday in front of the Ministry of Education, chanting “Rama, resign” in a tense standoff with the police, who later used rubber bullets, water cannons and tear gas to hold back the crowds.
Shops and institutions in the centre of the city have secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while city workers removed paving stones to prevent their use by protesters.
Lindita Karadaku, a journalist for Albanian news outlet TV Klan, told Al Jazeera on Sunday that it was difficult to see how the unrest could unfold or how long it could last.
“Prime Minister Rama is determined and has made it very clear that he will not resign, but also the young people who are protesting are determined and make it clear that they will not give up so easily,” she said. “At this moment, no one is clear what tomorrow will bring.”
Rama said during a live social media stream on Sunday that “the government is not being challenged” but implied that ongoing unrest in the country might affect Albania’s path towards European Union membership.
“Albanians need to think very clearly,” Rama said. “Do they want this, or do they want the EU?”
Albania is hoping to achieve membership status by 2030.
Key demands
Protesters are demanding better education, more jobs, a stop to alleged ongoing corruption, and Rama’s resignation.
According to local media reports, demonstrators in Tirana were primarily attacking government institutions and the police, including the Ministry of Education building and the area around Rama’s office.
The prime minister, who has been in office since 2013, blamed the involvement of a “foreign hand” for the surge in protests and said his government is doing its best to address corruption.
At the same time, he said that he was ready to listen to the justified demands of students and discuss the costs of education. But he insisted that those responsible for the destruction of property must be held accountable.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, a political analyst from Tirana, Mentor Nazarko, said Rama does not seem to understand “the depth of the problem, has not found solutions and has lost a lot of time”.
“His legitimacy has melted away. Between him and the citizens there is almost nothing but the police: untrained for protests, poorly paid, with segments that collaborate with crime and corruption,” he said.
According to a Ministry of Health report issued on Sunday morning, 65 people were injured, of which 37 were police officers, while 12 were hospitalised. Since Tuesday, 272 people have been injured in the clashes, including 169 police officers, the ministry said.
Discontent in Albania has been growing for months. The first protests in the country this year were called the “Flamingo Revolution” and began in May. Demonstrators rebelled against the controversial project of a luxury tourist complex in the south of Albania, affiliated with Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.

Israel’s current government is failing. The next one must do better - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

As we approach election day a week from tomorrow, it is worth taking a look at our 37th government, which has probably been the most unstable and malfunctioning government Israel has ever had. Israel’s interest is undoubtedly that its next government will be better, in all respects.
When the government was formed on December 29, 2022, it was supported by the 64 MKs of the Likud, the Religious Zionist Party and Otzma Yehudit union, United Torah Judaism, Shas, and Noam. Soon after being established, it included 32 ministers, some of whom (for example Ron Dermer, who later left the government) were not MKs, while others left the Knesset on the basis of the “Norwegian Law,” to enable other members of their respective parties to enter the Knesset.
In a study about the government soon after it was formed, Prof. Ofer Kenig of the Israel Democracy Institute pointed out that most of the ministers in the new government lacked ministerial experience. In retrospect, we can add that quite a few of the ministers appointed were also unsuitable from a professional point of view, such as Education Minister Yoav Kisch (Likud), and former construction and housing minister Yitzhak Goldknopf (United Torah Judaism).
Several other appointments were of persons prone to be problematic because of their extreme positions and/or conduct, such as Itamar Ben-Gvir (Otzma Yehudit) and Bezalel Smotrich (Religious Zionist Party), who were appointed to the National Security Ministry and the Finance Ministry, respectively (Smotrich was also appointed as an additional minister in the Defense Ministry on Judea and Samaria affairs).
Though there are limits to which a prospective prime minister can decide on the ministers from parties other than his own, and sometimes even on the ministers from his own party, we should at least expect that he will seek to establish the best possible government to serve the state, rather than his own political survival.
In the second half of the government’s term, Netanyahu’s appointment of Israel Katz on November 7, 2024, as defense minister, to replace Yoav Gallant, was undoubtedly based on the latter consideration. Of the eight defense ministers who served under Netanyahu since 1996, Katz is undoubtedly the least suitable from a professional point of view.
When the government was formed at the end of 2022, it was the second largest government Israel had ever had – the largest was the short-lived Netanyahu-Gantz government (Israel’s 35th government), which included 34 ministers. Both governments included many superfluous small ministries.
On October 12, 2023, Benny Gantz’s National Unity Party joined the government following the outbreak of war in the Gaza Strip, and three of its members – Gantz, Gadi Eisenkot, and Gideon Sa’ar – became ministers-without-portfolio. All the components of the National Unity Party resigned on June 9, 2024, against the background of their rejected demand that the government adopt a strategic plan for the war, and delays in bringing back all the hostages.
However, on September 29, 2024, Sa’ar and his newly established United Right party, rejoined the government, with Sa’ar being appointed foreign affairs minister. At this stage, the coalition’s majority rose to 68.
TODAY, MORE than two years later, the coalition includes only 60 members, after Noam left on March 25, 2025, and Torah Judaism left on July 14, 2025. Shas has not formally left the coalition, but has resigned from all its coalition positions in the government and the Knesset.
Noam left because its leader and only MK, Avi Maoz, claimed that most of the promises he had received upon joining were not kept, while the two haredi parties quit against the background of the non-passage of a law for the full exemption of the haredim from military service, which Netanyahu had promised them.
Though Netanyahu failed to give the haredi parties what they demanded, it was another case of Netanyahu putting his own political survival before the national interest.
What this means in practice is that besides being justice minister, Yariv Levin also serves as acting labor minister, Jerusalem and Jewish tradition minister, and religious services minister, while Tourism Minister Haim Katz also serves as health minister, construction and housing minister, and welfare and social security minister.
All these extra ministerial positions were held by the two haredi parties, and Netanyahu decided not to appoint full-time replacements because he needs the haredi parties for his political survival.
One may argue about Levin’s quality as justice minister – depending on whether one supports or opposes the plans he put forward for a legal reform/revolution of Israel’s justice system in January, 2023. But given the major manual labor shortage that Israel is suffering, the absence of a full-time labor minister is no joke.
It could be argued that even though these days, when foreign tourism to Israel is down to a trickle, leaving Israel’s health, construction and housing, and welfare and social security in the hands of Tourism Minister Katz is tantamount to neglect in these fields.
The problem is especially severe in the case of health, which is in a serious crisis due to the results of the unending war, and the vast numbers of physically and mentally injured military personnel. Add to this a growing shortage of doctors and other medical personnel, due to the departure from Israel of over 4,000 doctors in the years 2023-2025.
Experts on Israel’s political system argue that today there isn’t a single ministry that is run efficiently and fulfills its tasks satisfactorily. It is also a statistical fact that coalition funds – money provided by the government to the parties that are members of the coalition for distribution to their specific sectors without Knesset approval – are much higher today than since the system began in the 1980s.
From 2023-2026, coalition funds reached NIS 20.1 billion, while the ministerial budgets for education, health, welfare, and employment for the population at large were cut by NIS 11.7 billion.
Why is this important in regard to the elections to the 26th Knesset?
Because, should Netanyahu once again emerge victorious, the government he will form in its aftermath might be even worse than the outgoing government. Voters should certainly take this into account.
However, at the moment it looks as if the best the Likud and its political bloc can hope for is that the opposing political bloc will fail to form a government like themselves, and Netanyahu will remain the prime minister of a transition government for several months, until new elections take place for the 27th Knesset.
Should the political bloc that opposes the current government, either headed by Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot or someone else, manage to form a new coalition after the elections, constructing a more stable and properly functioning government will undoubtedly be one of its first goals.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

The Israeli blockade constricts the dining tables of Gazans

Breadcrumb
Israel's blockade leaves hungry Gazans facing astronomical prices, unhealthy food choices
Israel's devastating war and blockade on the Gaza Strip have left many Palestinians struggling not only to find food, but also to afford the variety needed to maintain a healthy diet.
Despite the availability of some products in local markets, soaring prices, diminished purchasing power and restrictions on the entry of goods have left families relying on whatever they can obtain to stave off hunger.
For Umm Hadi al-Arja, a displaced mother of four from Beit Lahia in northern Gaza, feeding her children means baking bread in a clay oven fuelled by scraps of cardboard and making do with whatever supplies she can obtain.
The family lives in a dilapidated tent near Gaza City's coastline, relying partly on canned goods distributed through World Food Programme (WFP) food parcels.
Meat, chicken and fish have become unaffordable luxuries, leaving her struggling to provide her children with a balanced diet.
"I have four children, and I try to provide them with whatever food is available to us," al-Arja told The New Arab. "We bake bread and serve it with oil, za'atar or cheese. We do everything we can to ensure they don't go hungry, but I simply cannot provide everything they need."
Israeli restrictions on food supplies and soaring market prices have further narrowed her family's choices, she said.
"Despite the so-called ceasefire, we cannot obtain healthy, nutritious food. Even when items are available in the markets, they are unaffordable," she said. "We eat whatever we can manage to get, not what our bodies actually require."
High prices deepen the food crisis
Mahdi Shomer, who lives with his six children in a tent in Gaza City, faces the same dilemma.
He visits markets where many essential products are displayed, but often returns without buying what his family needs because he cannot afford the prices.
"When I go to the market, I see many of the items we need, but I cannot afford to buy them," Shomer told TNA. "The issue isn't always the availability of food, but rather our ability to pay for it."
His purchases are increasingly dictated by necessity rather than nutritional value.
"I now only buy enough to stave off hunger, rather than what the body actually needs," he said. "Sometimes we make do with just bread and a few simple items. We are forced to go without meat, chicken and fruit because they are too expensive."
The gap between food availability and purchasing power remains a major obstacle for households already dependent on humanitarian assistance.
According to Gaza's Government Media Office, 74,855 humanitarian aid trucks had entered the Strip out of the 219,000 expected under the ceasefire agreement that took effect on 10 October 2025, representing approximately 34 per cent of the agreed total.
A joint food security analysis by the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), the WFP and UNICEF found that approximately 1.4 million people, or nearly 67 per cent of Gaza's population, were facing critical or worse levels of acute food insecurity. This compared with approximately 1.6 million people, or 77 per cent of the population, at the end of 2025.
The analysis also found that approximately 212,000 people were experiencing emergency-level food insecurity.
Although some indicators had improved, the agencies warned that the situation remained fragile and that assistance did not always provide sufficient quantities or diversity to meet nutritional needs.
The destruction and restricted accessibility of agricultural land have further undermined local food production.
According to the analysis, more than 70 per cent of agricultural land was inaccessible, leaving only about 3 per cent usable and limiting farmers' ability to supply fresh vegetables and other produce.
Malnutrition risks extend beyond hunger
Palestinian nutritionist Mahmoud al-Saqqa warns that high food prices and limited choices are forcing Gaza's residents to rely on diets lacking essential nutrients.
"Many families depend on canned food and products high in salt, sugar and fat because fresh produce has become too expensive," he told TNA.
"People may eat enough to satisfy their hunger but still lack the proteins, vitamins and minerals their bodies need to stay healthy," he said, warning that poor nutrition could weaken immunity, particularly among children, older people and those with chronic illnesses.
"Malnutrition does not always mean being underweight. A person can consume enough calories but still lack essential nutrients because their diet is not varied," he added.
Children are particularly vulnerable, with some also forced to take on adult responsibilities.
Fourteen-year-old Mohammed al-Yazji lost his mother during the war, while his father was detained by the Israeli army, leaving him to care for his younger siblings.
"Every day, I think about what we will eat and how I will provide food for my siblings," Mohammed told TNA. "They are young and need many things. I try not to let them feel that we cannot meet their needs, but the situation is extremely difficult."
"We need a variety of food, not just bread and a few basic items. I wish I could provide meat and fruit, but sometimes we have to make do with whatever is available," he said.
Al-Saqqa explained that improving nutrition required access to affordable fresh food, including vegetables, fruits and protein-rich products, as well as targeted support for those at risk of malnutrition.
While humanitarian aid remains essential, addressing the crisis also requires allowing sufficient food supplies into Gaza, supporting local agriculture and making nutritious food affordable for families.

CISF to reorganise eight territorial sectors into specialised functional units from November 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:53:33 UTC
23:53:33 KST

NEW DELHI: Come November 1, the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) will transition from a region-specific administrative and operational control structure to a purely functional one, ensuring that each of its reorganised sectors caters to the specialised requirements of the industries and establishments secured by it.CISF officials said 8 its 11 territorial sectors spread across the country will be reorganised into functional sectors dedicated to govt installations and museums in Delhi, coal industries, power plants, petroleum and natural gas units, and steel industry etc.The National Capital Region (NCR) region, New Delhi will thus become the Govt Buildings, Museums & Monuments and Mass Rapid Transit System (GBMM & MRTS) sector, New Delhi. The North sector, New Delhi will be reorganised as Power-I sector, Delhi and the North Eastern-II sector, Kolkata as Power-II sector, Kolkata. The Eastern sector, Ranchi will be rechristened as Coal Sector, Ranchi and cater to the security needs of the coalfields guarded by CISF.Similarly, the Central sector will become the dedicated Steel sector based at Bhilai. The North Eastern sector at Guwahati has been transformed into the Petroleum and Natural Gas sector, Guwahati.
To fortify India's maritime trade infrastructure, the Western Sector (Mumbai) and South Sector (Chennai) have been respectively transformed into the West Coast Port Sector and the East Coast Port Sector.The existing Department of Atomic Energy and Department of Space sector headquartered at Bengaluru as well as the Airport-I sector, New Delhi and Airport-II sector, Bengaluru, will continue under their respective functional arrangements.“The revised structure, approved by CISF DG Praveer Ranjan with the concurrence of ministry of home affairs (MHA), will come into effect from Nov 1, 2026, a CISF spokesperson said on Sunday. Apart from aligning the supervisory structure of the force more closely with the specific security requirements of different sectors, the new arrangement aims to improve operational oversight, promote sector-specific expertise, ensure greater uniformity insecurity practices and strengthen coordination with the concerned ministries, departments and installation managements.
Over the past 25 years, CISF has progressively adopted a functional approach in selected sectors, including aviation.The experience gained from this approach has highlighted the advantages of specialised supervision, focused training, sector-specific standard operating procedures (SOPs), better utilisation of specialised personnel and closer coordination with the concerned organisations.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

Barricades and clashes in Brussels
Brussels police recorded 118 administrative detentions and 32 judicial arrests, including 15 minors among those arrested under judicial procedures.
The judicial arrests were linked to alleged offences including throwing objects at police officers, resisting arrest and deliberate arson, police said.
Investigators continued identifying suspects, and the figures could change.

Officers repeatedly resorted to tear gas and water cannons during the demonstrations.
Fires and arrests in Liege
In Liege, police reported 40 administrative detentions and five judicial arrests, including 12 minors among those detained, according to the Belga news agency.
Vandalism and fires were reported in public areas on Saturday evening. Around 50 protesters gathered at Place Saint-Lambert and fired pyrotechnic mortars at the Prince-Bishops’ Palace, prompting police to use a water cannon and tear gas to disperse the crowd.
People gathered nearby chanted demands for the release of their friends. Police said calm appeared to have returned by the evening.
The demonstration had begun peacefully, with between 200 and 250 people gathering outside Guillemins railway station at around 10 am before marching to Place Saint-Lambert, where a sit-in blocked bus traffic.
Protesters later blocked roads near Le Cadran, including access to the motorway towards Burenville, with some moving barriers to construct barricades, Belga reported.
Student protests spread from France

Previous protests have led to numerous detentions, with some suspects subsequently remanded in custody.
Saturday’s arrests underline the tensions surrounding demonstrations against education policies and budget reductions, although police said investigations into the latest incidents were continuing.

Putin appeared in military uniform this week and repeated Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The 5th Asian Para Games opened in Aichi-Nagoya on Sunday.
Running from October 18 to 24 under the theme "Imagine One Heart," the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games bring together nearly 3,000 para athletes from 45 countries and regions across Asia, who will compete in about 500 events across 18 sports.
The opening ceremony took place at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium, where delegations paraded into the venue through a handcrafted tree installation symbolizing connection.
Led by flagbearers para taekwondo athlete Li Yujie and para powerlifter Yan Panpan, the Chinese delegation entered the venue to warm applause.

The Chinese athletes, all amateurs from diverse backgrounds including workers, students, office employees and freelancers, will compete in 335 events across 17 sports.
Hideaki Ohmura, president of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games and Asian Para Games Organizing Committee, expressed his gratitude to everyone who had helped make the event a reality.
"I believe the significance of para sports lies not merely in winning competitions, but in fostering awareness and understanding of diversity, and in contributing to the realization of an inclusive society where everyone recognizes and supports one another as we live together," he said.
In his speech, Asian Paralympic Committee President Majid Rashed commended the athletes for the efforts and sacrifices they had made to reach this stage, and hailed their passion, determination and courage.
"Once again, sport can show us another way forward, because sport sees possibility where others may see limits," he said. "Sport brings people together when the world can sometimes pull them apart. Here, our differences do not divide us. They make us stronger."
Seven para-sport participants from various summer and winter sports took part in the final leg of the torch relay inside the stadium. The main flame of the Asian Para Games was then jointly lit by three torchbearers. ■

China Focus: From smart sensors to AI robots, technology transforming China's elderly care
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:42:36 CST
23:42:36 KST

Staff members monitor data at a big data center for elderly care in Luyang District of Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Guo Chen)
HEFEI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A mobile phone alert warns a community worker that no door activity has been detected at an elderly resident's home for more than 24 hours. Another alert reports that a smoke detector has been triggered.
The notifications come from smart devices installed in the homes of over 600 elderly people living alone, mostly aged 80 or above, in Luyang District of Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province in east China. The devices, including door sensors and smoke detectors, help community workers identify potential emergencies and respond more quickly.
The smart early-warning system is part of a government-funded elderly care program launched in 2025, according to Zhao Fei, director of the Luyang district office of the committee on aging.
When an alert is triggered, a three-tier response mechanism involving family members, community workers and community officials is activated to ensure each warning receives appropriate follow-up, Zhao said.
"The combination of smart early warnings and human intervention builds a safety net for elderly people living alone at home," Zhao said.
Around a dozen alerts are generated and handled each day. "It would be nearly impossible to identify such risks through human inspections alone," Zhao said.
The initiative is part of broader efforts to harness intelligent technologies and high-tech products to improve elderly care as China faces a rapidly growing elderly population.
Official data shows that China's population aged 60 and above exceeded 323 million by the end of 2025, accounting for about 23 percent of the national total population.
In addition to smart devices such as millimeter-wave fall detectors, the Shulu Community Service Center in Hefei high-tech zone has introduced a robot to assess the mental health of elderly people, said Liu Li, head of the center's social affairs department.
Equipped with cameras and powered by large AI models, the robot analyzes facial expressions, eye features and subtle body movements, conducts noninvasive screening, and by combining these observations with physiological signals generates a report on a person's mental state.
China's rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced manufacturing are encouraging technology companies to develop products for the expanding elderly care market.
Anhui Sanlian Robot Technology Co., Ltd. has introduced its fourth-generation lower-limb exoskeleton, which uses AI to adapt the level of assistance according to users' movements.
The device can detect when users need extra support as they lift their legs and reduce assistance when they stop moving, allowing people with walking difficulties to move more naturally, said Wu Xianchun, the company's marketing director.
The company's exoskeletons were initially developed mainly for postoperative leg rehabilitation and activities such as mountain climbing. They are now used primarily in elderly care facilities, with demand increasingly shifting toward helping older people exercise their legs and improve everyday mobility, Wu said.
Advances in AI and manufacturing are helping improve the performance and affordability of elderly care products, Wu said. Better algorithms make devices smarter, while improved manufacturing processes and mass production help enhance quality and reduce the cost of components such as batteries and motors.
"Affordable, high-quality elderly care tech products will better serve senior citizens," Wu said.
Smart technologies are also gaining ground in other Chinese cities. In Beijing, intelligent massage and companion robots are being used for physical therapy and companionship. Some nursing homes in Shanghai have adopted smart mattresses to monitor residents' health, while virtual reality devices are being used for rehabilitation training among older people in Shenzhen.
China's market for elderly care service robots is expected to exceed 10 billion yuan (about 1.5 billion U.S. dollars) in 2026, according to a research report released by the China Software Testing Center this year.
The growing market is also driving more young entrepreneurs to tap opportunities in the elderly care industry.
Liu Sizhe, an 18-year-old student at the University of Science and Technology of China, launched a startup this year and led a team in developing an AI-based system for preliminary screening for Alzheimer's disease.
Users can have casual conversations with the system via a mobile phone or a tablet, while the technology analyzes their speech rate and responses to identify potential signs of cognitive impairment.
Liu said his grandparents inspired the project. Watching them grow older prompted him to consider how he could use technology to help elderly people.
"I do not want the elderly to be left behind by technological advances," Liu said. ■
A staff member introduces an intelligent robot for mental health assessment to an elderly person at a community service center in Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua)

China Focus: When family is out of reach, paid companionship fills a gap in China's elder care
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:42:23 CST
23:42:23 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Mrs. Zhou, an 82-year-old widow, lives alone and has no children in Nanjing, the provincial capital of Jiangsu in east China. Her daily life has brightened up since a 24-year-old man began visiting her home to chat, teach her how to use a smartphone and warn her about scams.
The visits are part of a growing practice in China known as "shared children," in which young people are paid to keep elderly people company -- a service seen as filling a gap in emotional support for the country's aging population.
Late last year, the man, Heng Mengyu, first knocked on Zhou's door and soon became a regular visitor. Zhou had no relatives or friends nearby and rarely left her apartment. She was depressed and pessimistic, and had repeatedly mentioned writing a suicide note. After several months, her outlook on life began to change.
One afternoon, Heng arrived at Zhou's apartment as scheduled. He checked for safety hazards -- inspecting kitchen outlets and the gas valve, looking through the refrigerator and clearing out expired food -- while Zhou offered him fruit.
Heng did not try to talk her out of her feelings. Instead, he listened. Over repeated visits, he helped Zhou identify telecom fraud schemes, corrected her health misconceptions, and encouraged a regular routine and a better diet. Zhou gradually opened up, sharing her thoughts and daily life, and regained confidence.
The service is Heng's own venture. He became interested in elder care in college and has worked in the field since graduation. Late last year, he came up with the idea of "doorstep companionship services" and developed a detailed checklist covering home safety inspections, organizing supplies, clearing expired food, smartphone tutorials, anti-fraud education, emotional support, and recording the elderly person's condition.
"Our service isn't just simple care," Heng said. "It focuses on the life and psychological blind spots that the elderly often overlook." After each visit, he records the client's physical condition, emotional state and living situation, and reports back to their children or community.
Heng's visits last at least two hours and start at 200 yuan (about 30 U.S. dollars). His team has grown from one person to nine, including stay-at-home mothers, working teachers, nursing graduates and psychological counselors.
Most "shared children" providers nationwide are young. A post-90s graduate of a Shanghai university, surnamed Qiu, provides weekend visit services, such as chatting with elderly clients, or accompanying them to get haircuts. One client treats him like her own child.
Many individuals and organizations advertise "shared children" services online. Rates are usually hourly, with a single two-to-four-hour visit costing from several hundred to over 1,000 yuan.
The rise of "shared children" reflects a demand driven by population aging. At the end of 2025, China had over 323 million people aged 60 or above, accounting for 23 percent of the population. The figure is projected to surpass 400 million around 2035.
Surveys show the elderly prefer to live at home, and the country has large numbers of empty-nest and disadvantaged elderly, with a high old-age dependency ratio. The fifth sample survey on the living conditions of China's urban and rural elderly found that in 2021, 14.2 percent of elderly Chinese lived alone, while empty-nest elderly -- those living alone or only with a spouse -- accounted for nearly 60 percent.
Mental health needs are equally acute. A blue book on elderly mental health published by the China Research Center on Aging found that 23.76 percent of elderly Chinese experience loneliness to varying degrees, while 26.4 percent show depressive symptoms, including 6.2 percent with moderate to severe depression.
Ye Qing, president of the Wuhan Filial Piety Culture Promotion Association, said increased population mobility has made empty-nest households the norm. Among urban families of only children, the "4-2-1" structure -- four grandparents, two parents and one child -- accounts for 62.3 percent, steadily weakening the traditional family's care-giving role. Children far from home may want to fulfill their filial duties but are constrained by distance and limited energy. The rise of "shared children" responds to this reality, Ye said.
Clients of such services are mostly elderly people who live alone, are socially isolated and emotionally low. Long periods of solitude breed negativity, and with no one nearby to confide in, what they want most is someone to listen to them.
Heng said this is a key difference between "shared children" and ordinary domestic help. "We don't do assembly-line service. We only do companionship with warmth." The core of his team's work is not completing tasks but sensing changes in the elderly person's mood and inner needs, easing loneliness through companionship.
The doorstep model is flexible and customizable to each family's situation, suiting the realities of home-based elder care. Market demand has also created a new employment field, allowing people with a passion for elder care and flexible schedules to work through companionship and care-giving.
Ye and other experts believe the new sector fills part of the gap in emotional elder care, but needs guidance to become standardized and institutionalized. They suggest building efficient supply-demand matching mechanisms through internet platforms, improving user review and credit systems, and refining income distribution and incentive mechanisms -- stabilizing the workforce and ensuring sustainable and quality service over the long term. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Inside China's "unlikely" AI computing hub
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:42:19 CST
23:42:19 KST

* In less than two years, Inner Mongolia's computing capacity has nearly quadrupled, reaching 363,000 petaflops by August 2026, as large-scale data centers have sprung up across the region.
* However, the region is not content to remain a mere "landlord of data centers." It is striving to move up the value chain, reinventing itself not only as a hub for green computing but also for token trading and AI applications.
* With the influx comes new challenges. Computing facilities require enormous amounts of electricity to run and water to keep server racks from overheating. Inner Mongolia, a frontrunner in China's green energy transition, is charting a course of green computing.
HOHHOT, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A four-hour drive northwest of Beijing takes one across the Great Wall and into the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, seemingly a world away from China's booming coastal towns.
Yet here, in a city once known as China's "potato capital," data centers are rising from the grasslands, towering cranes fill the skyline, and some of the country's biggest tech companies are moving in.
The city is Ulanqab, in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, which has emerged as a new frontier in the global race for computing power. Ulanqab is a poster child for this rise. In less than two years, Inner Mongolia's computing capacity has nearly quadrupled, reaching 363,000 petaflops by August 2026, as large-scale data centers have sprung up across the region.
A combination of factors helped fuel this transformation. Its climate allows natural cooling of AI server racks for nearly ten months a year. The windswept steppes offer a massive volume of wind and solar power, driving rates down to as low as around 0.35 yuan (about 5.2 U.S. cents) per kWh. Moreover, its proximity to Beijing ensures an ultra-low latency of under 5 milliseconds, facilitating seamless model training and real-time inference.
However, the region is not content to remain a mere "landlord of data centers." It is striving to move up the value chain, reinventing itself not only as a hub for green computing but also for token trading and AI applications.
RISING ABOVE GRASSLAND
At the Ulanqab Chahar High Tech Development Zone, the epicenter of the city's newfound buzz, an "Apple Boulevard" runs alongside an "Alibaba Boulevard" and a "Huawei Boulevard" -- named after three of the major companies that have set up a presence here. Other tech giants, including ByteDance, Kuaishou and VNET Group, have also moved in.
Vehicles from across China line the roads, and workers speak in accents from every corner of the country. Around lunchtime, food stalls spring up around the construction sites, selling boxed meals, fruit and drinks.
"Within the high-tech zone alone, 22 computing-power projects are currently under construction, involving nearly 30,000 construction workers," said Liu Junping, deputy director of the administrative committee of the development zone.
"When I came here to scout the site in 2022, it was still pretty desolate, and sandstorms would sometimes sweep through," recalled Zhou Yiguang, an executive with the VNET Group's Ulanqab base. The group has planned a computing cluster covering 1,100 mu (about 73 hectares) of land in Ulanqab, and the first phase has been in operation since October 2024.
In fact, it is not just Ulanqab. Inner Mongolia has emerged as a hub for computing power, with its regional capital Hohhot as another high ground. As of the first half of 2026, roughly 20 of China's 30 leading private computing companies had established a presence in the region, with combined investment exceeding 200 billion yuan (around 29.75 billion U.S. dollars). In addition, nine of the country's top 10 computing service providers had also set up operations there.
GREEN COMPUTING
With the influx comes new challenges. Computing facilities require enormous amounts of electricity to run and water to keep server racks from overheating. Inner Mongolia, a frontrunner in China's green energy transition, is charting a course of green computing.
In 2025, the computing industry in Ulanqab alone consumed 4.3 billion kWh of electricity. That figure is estimated to reach 9 billion kWh in 2026 and will continue to surge as more computing centers are expected to start operating over the next two to three years.
Globally, tech giants are moving beyond simply "buying power" to "competing for power" and even "generating their own power." China, however, has leveraged its world-leading power grid, renewable energy and energy storage industries to pioneer the integration of computing power and electricity supply, known as "computing-electricity coordination."
In the Ulanqab Chahar High Tech Development Zone, a zero-carbon industrial park is taking shape. The park will be managed as a unified power distribution unit, with wind and solar infrastructure developed collectively by the government, then distributed to individual computing centers across the park.
Chen Zhigang, deputy director of the Ulanqab municipal development and reform commission, said that the park's surrounding areas have about 10 gigawatts of wind and solar development capacity available. Once tapped, these resources could generate more than 30 billion kWh of electricity annually, enough to cover future increases in demand.
After the zero-carbon industrial park is completed, more than 80 percent of the park's electricity will come directly from renewable energy. In the Horinger New Area in Hohhot, computing centers in operation source 85 percent of their power consumption from green energy.
Water poses another potential constraint. However, widespread adoption of water-conserving cooling equipment, such as waterless fluorine-pump air conditioning systems and closed cooling towers, helped ease the high demand for cooling water.
Moreover, take VNET Group's cloud computing center in Ulanqab for example: here, outdoor cold air is directly used for cooling for nearly 10 months of the year, with spray systems activated only during the hottest summer days.
"All the water used for cooling at the computing center is reclaimed water. It does not affect local natural water resources or groundwater," said Li Yi, technical director of VNET Group's Ulanqab base.
According to the Ulanqab water resources bureau, under the regional regulations, data centers are prohibited from using groundwater as cooling water. In 2025, big data companies across the city consumed 1.54 million cubic meters of water, accounting for only 0.33 percent of the city's total water consumption. Meanwhile, the city produces about 72 million tonnes of reclaimed water annually.
TOKEN HUB
Building computing capacity is one thing, yet turning it into a high-value AI economy is another. "If we rely solely on cheap electricity and low land costs, we risk becoming little more than 'landlords of server rooms,'" Liu Huansuo, deputy director of the Ulanqab big data administration, warned.
The concern is well-founded. The high-value segments of the computing economy -- chips, algorithms and models -- remain largely beyond Inner Mongolia's reach.
According to economic data from Ulanqab, the city's computing-power industry generated 6.835 billion yuan in revenue in 2025, with 368 million yuan in tax revenue. A computing center is estimated to create about 100 jobs per 100 mu (about 6.7 hectares) of land.
Yet these returns remain modest relative to the massive upfront investment in infrastructure and the enormous computing capacity that is being developed.
To address the challenge, Inner Mongolia strives to move up the value chain -- evolving from a "server-room landlord" to a "token capital," and cultivating its own ecosystem of AI applications.
On May 30, Inner Mongolia's Token Trading Platform, billed as the country's first green-computing full-stack AI platform, went into operation in the Horinger New Area, positioning Hohhot to become a major token-trading hub in northern China.
The goal is to turn raw computing power into a tradable commodity that can be measured, priced and ultimately converted into higher-value AI services, said Guo Juying, deputy director of the Horinger New Area Administrative Committee. She described the transition as a shift from "selling electricity" to "selling tokens," as every AI conversation or model inference can ultimately be measured in terms of tokens generated and consumed.
Ulanqab has its own plan. At the end of 2025, the city released a three-year action plan for building a "Token Capital" for 2026-2028, envisioning a new economic chain spanning the production, trading and application of tokens.
The application ecosystem is also expanding. Hohhot has developed nearly 100 application scenarios in sectors such as dairy, new energy and biomedicine. A facial recognition database for cattle is already widely used on smart pastures.
For a region that has built its computing infrastructure at remarkable speed, the next challenge may be harder. But overcoming it will open up a whole new horizon across China's economic landscape. ■
(Video reporter:Zhang Sheng; Video editors: Hong Ling, Zhang Mocheng and Hong Yan)

A timeline of West Bank attacks on Palestinians and foreign officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:42:01 UTC
23:42:01 KST

A timeline of West Bank attacks on Palestinians and foreign officials
Settler pogroms have escalated, coinciding with the annual olive harvest season in the occupied West Bank.
European diplomats and officials were attacked on Saturday amid a surge in settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank in recent weeks, coinciding with olive harvest season.
The settler pogroms have escalated just weeks before Israel heads to the polls on October 27.
The European Union (EU) on Sunday condemned settler attacks on European diplomats and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. A day earlier, a veteran American journalist working for the Washington Post was also brutally attacked.
But this is not the first time Israeli settlers have assaulted foreign officials or prominent Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Here’s a timeline of some of the recent and past attacks:
October 17, 2026
Israeli settlers assaulted European diplomats, including a French mayor, near the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank.
The delegation was visiting Palestinian olive harvesters on Saturday when the Israeli attackers confronted the group.
In Saturday’s incident, the settlers targeted Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats, and Catholic representatives, Belgian Minister of Foreign Affairs Maxime Prevot said.
“A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged,” Prevot said, linking the incident to Israel’s “illegal settlement policy” and pledging to push for further EU sanctions.
Bernard Baudoux, the French mayor who was assaulted, told the AFP news agency the attack suggests that “there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government” towards settler violence.
Video shared by an activist at the scene, Amit Orfali, shows Baudoux leaning against a vehicle while sitting on the dusty ground. Other clips showed young masked men knocking insistently on a driver’s side window and asking for identification, while other masked men carrying sticks advanced in the distance. Orfali said the masked men “threatened to kill us”.
France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called on Israel to arrest the “extremist settlers” who “violently assaulted” Baudoux, and bring them to justice. “They must urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations, as they are compelled to do under international law,” he said in a post on X.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office has, however, appeared to question the reports of the attack on the Europeans, saying on X that they are “alleged” and require “compelling evidence”, despite acknowledging that published footage of the incident exists.
“We take positive note of statements by several Israeli representatives who condemned the attacks,” the EU said in a statement on Sunday. “But we expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists.”
October 16, 2026
Palestinian farmers harvesting olives and veteran American journalist Heidi Levine, 64, who freelances for the Washington Post, were brutally attacked by settlers.
Levine fell to the ground during the assault before she was set upon, witnesses said. “We looked and saw that there was a journalist … on the ground with people surrounding her, beating her, clubbing her, robbing her, pulling her up, beating her again and kicking her,” Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera.
Levine later told reporters that her attackers “just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times”.
Levine was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS” on the front and back. Her cameras and phone were taken from her during the assault, the Washington Post reported.
Nathaniel said he and others managed to reach her when the settlers briefly backed away, but she struggled to stand. “She was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground,” he said.
As they helped Levine towards paramedics, settlers charged again, throwing more stones, he added. The journalist was eventually taken to a hospital in Ramallah.
Nathaniel said Israeli soldiers arrived after the settler assault and opened fire and used tear gas against Palestinians, shooting a man in the leg. “They do nothing to stop the settlers, and they speed into town and start firing their guns and tear-gassing, and they shoot a Palestinian man in the leg,” he said.
“They’re pointing their guns at the paramedics who are helping him, shoving journalists, including myself,” Nathaniel said, adding that the injured man was eventually taken away in an ambulance.
Wafa, the Palestinian news agency, reported that Israeli forces fired live ammunition and tear gas at Palestinians during the attack. After the soldiers left, Palestinians returned to harvesting their olives, Nathaniel added.
Netanyahu’s office has said the facts around the settler attack “remain unclear”, as it offered a conditional condemnation.
“Serious questions remain”, said a post on the official X account of the prime minister’s office, calling for an investigation to “establish the facts, including who initiated the violence”.
October 6, 2026
Israeli settlers beat Palestinian AFP news agency photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, with rifle butts near Aqraba, south of Nablus. He suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken by ambulance to a hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists cited by AFP.
AFP photographer John Wessels was with Ashtiyeh when the incident occurred.
The news agency reported that a quadbike had raced towards the journalists and a man had opened live fire.
“At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists, firing guns,” AFP reported. “As Ashtiyeh attempted to enter a car, which was clearly marked ‘Press’, two men jumped on him and beat him repeatedly with the butts of their rifles. ‘I could hear his screams,’ said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint.”
While Ashtiyeh is now conscious in a hospital in Nablus, the assailants have taken his camera equipment, according to his colleague Wessels.
The Israeli military has yet to respond to the AFP news agency.
July 11, 2026
United States Congressional Representative Ro Khanna said he and his tour group were detained by rifle-wielding Israeli settlers during a trip to Palestine.
In a post on X, Khanna had accused the Israeli army of supporting the settlers.
“When the [Israeli army] arrived, they sided with the settlers and continued our detention,” Khanna wrote.
Khanna, a Democrat who is considering running for US president in 2028, told the Reuters news agency that “hoodlums … with machine guns” had detained his group a day earlier. “They block off the road. And then they call the [Israeli military] and the [Israeli military] is on their side,” Khanna said.
He added that the settlers were armed with US-made assault rifles.
In an interview with DRM News, Khanna said his experience in the occupied West Bank and Israel was the “first time” he had “really been acutely aware of being brown”.
“I saw the arrogance in the eyes of those settlers. Twenty-one and 22-year-olds with guns, laughing that they had detained us. The arrogance of those young [Israeli army] soldiers that my tax dollars are funding. Having no respect for the fact that they were detaining Americans,” he added.
The Israeli military disputed Khanna’s version of the events, saying that it “dispersed” civilians who were blocking the road.
Israeli officials have, however, ruled out apologising to Khanna or holding the settlers accountable.
Three months after the incident, on Saturday, October 17, Khanna called Netanyahu a “liar” after his office released an October 16 statement on X saying that “serious questions remain” about “who initiated the violence” and other details of the attack on Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine.
“Netanyahu called me a liar when settlers detained me, along with a NYT photographer, in Zanuta this past July,” Khanna wrote. “Netanyahu, you are the liar with the blood of Palestinian children on your hands.”
November 2025
One Canadian and three Italian activists were injured by illegal Israeli settlers in the Ein ad-Duyuk village in the Jericho governorate in the central West Bank, local sources told the Anadolu news agency.
Anadolu reported that settlers had stormed into a Bedouin community where the activists were residing and then assaulted them. Three activists sustained moderate injuries, while one was critically wounded, the news agency said and added that their passports, phones, and belongings were also taken.
July 2025
Palestinian activist and English teacher Awdah Hathaleen, who contributed to the Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land, was shot and killed on July 28, 2025, in the occupied West Bank village of Umm al-Khair in the Masafer Yatta region.
The beloved 31-year-old activist and father of three fell to the ground as people rushed over to try to help him. Then an ambulance came out of the nearby illegal settlement of Carmel and took him away.
Footage published by Israeli human rights group B’Tselem appears to show the suspect Yinon Levi opening fire on Hathaleen during a confrontation in the village.
Despite the visual evidence and prior sanctions imposed on Levi by both the EU and the United States over past attacks on Palestinians, Israeli authorities released him to house arrest.
US President Donald Trump also removed the penalties against Levi and other settlers accused of extremist violence after assuming office in January 2025.
July 2024
Israeli settlers attacked a group of foreign volunteers helping Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank.
David Hummel, an American-German in the group, told the AFP news agency that eight mainly American volunteers were working with the farmers in an olive grove near the Palestinian village of Qusra when settlers attacked them.
“They started attacking and beating us all with sticks and metal pipes, and they were throwing rocks as well at us,” he said.
“I was attacked on my legs, on my arms and here on my jaw as well and it was … very violent,” he added.
The Israeli army condemned the violence and said its troops were deployed to the scene and had fired warning shots into the air, causing the Israeli settlers to flee the area.

France was reeling on Oct 18 from widespread damage during protests the day before that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests, piling pressure on President Emmanuel Macron six months before elections to replace him.
Trump’s post comes after similar comments made by Vice-President J.D. Vance on Oct 17.
“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen,” Vance wrote on X.
“I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn,” he added.
Vance, who is seen as a potential presidential candidate in the 2028 election, also drew a connection to upcoming midterm races for congressional seats on Nov 3, where Republicans are not expected to perform well. AFP
