Egypt says ready to give Saudi Arabia necessary support amid Houthi conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:35:47 UTC
23:35:47 KST

Egypt says ready to back Saudi Arabia in war against Iran-allied Houthis
CAIRO, Oct 18 - Regional military power Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, potentially raising the stakes in the Middle East war as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on the kingdom.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend its Gulf Arab ally if the kingdom requested its support.
A parliamentary vote had been expected on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.
Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the north, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Any Egyptian military backing for Saudi Arabia could mark a major escalation in the wider Iran war, which has threatened global energy supplies and sent oil prices soaring since the US and Israel attacked the Islamic Republic in late February.
Hours after an announcement on further discussions by the parliament, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in a post on X that he discussed regional developments and the importance of de-escalation during a phone call with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan.
HOUTHIS RAMP UP ATTACKS ON SAUDI ARABIA
The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with Saudi-backed forces. The Houthi advances threaten the strategic Bab el-Mandeb oil shipping route, following the collapse of a truce.
"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.
The statement followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.
Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.
If Egypt weighs in, it could face attacks by the Houthis, ragtag mountain fighters who have emerged as a deadly force of tens of thousands and whose missiles and drones threaten the region.
Arab countries, especially Gulf states hosting US bases, have faced repeated attacks by Iran and its allies, including the Houthis and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, during the conflict.
Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta came under a drone attack in July with no group claiming responsibility. Egypt has not blamed any party for the attack but said it was taking necessary measures to protect the country's national security.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states including the United Arab Emirates provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013. Sisi became president a year later.
Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role in the civil war.
Riyadh has turned to regional allies and Pakistan after it sought US President Donald Trump's help to fight the Houthis. Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing.
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman visited Abu Dhabi on Sunday and met with UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with talks focusing on regional security, according to the Emirati state news agency.
The talks followed a visit to Riyadh last month by UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the first trip by a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year. REUTERS

'France is burning!': Trump blames immigrants as riots devastate Paris and other cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:31:53 UTC
23:31:53 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump intervened again Sunday in the violent unrest sweeping France, blaming immigration for the destruction and looting that have devastated parts of Paris and other major cities. "France is burning!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!"
His remarks followed a day of widespread violence Saturday in which masked rioters attacked police officers and bystanders, set government buildings ablaze and looted hundreds of stores. The violence erupted following nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services, drawing hundreds of thousands of participants. French authorities reported at least 2,000 arrests and approximately 600 injured police and security personnel, according to the latest figures released Sunday.
The full extent of the destruction remains unclear, but French business representatives estimated that at least 1,500 businesses had been damaged, with losses running into hundreds of millions of euros. In Paris alone, hundreds of stores were looted. Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said "entire streets were systematically destroyed," while Le Parisien described extensive damage in neighborhoods across the capital.
In the central Les Halles district, rioters targeted virtually every type of business, including pharmacies, clothing stores, beauty salons, tobacco shops and opticians. Similar scenes unfolded near Porte Saint-Denis, where dozens of businesses were vandalized. Burned bicycles, broken glass and piles of debris littered the streets. Sanitation workers told Le Parisien that clearing the wreckage would take days.
According to AFP, some looting appeared organized and coordinated. Small groups of masked young people wearing gloves reportedly disabled security cameras before smashing storefront windows and stealing merchandise. In one widely circulated video said to have been filmed in Paris, a woman desperately tried to stop masked looters from entering a supermarket. "Why are you doing this?" she shouted before being pushed aside. "Stop! That's not the point!"
Another video from Nice showed a video game store employee trying to protect a Micromania branch from looters before being kicked in the back and knocked to the ground. In Paris, groups were filmed emptying cellphone stores and passing stolen merchandise to accomplices outside. AFP described scenes resembling an uprising, with protesters shouting "Revolution!" The agency said the scale and intensity of the violence appeared to exceed previous waves of unrest in France, including the 2023 riots following the police killing of teenager Nahel Merzouk and the Yellow Vest protests of 2018 and 2019.
Historic city hall goes up in flames
Some of the most dramatic scenes came from Limoges in central France, where masked rioters set fire to the historic city hall, a building inaugurated in 1883 that had survived both world wars. Flames engulfed the structure, and its bell tower collapsed in footage circulated widely online. Authorities said much of the building had been destroyed.
Government buildings were also attacked in Marseille, Lille, Angers and Bordeaux, where protesters broke into municipal offices and regional administrative buildings. In Lyon, the local tourist office was set ablaze, and police reported that hostile crowds interfered with firefighters attempting to extinguish the flames. Footage from the city showed one rioter waving a Palestinian flag.
The weekend's violence followed weeks of growing frustration over inflation, fuel prices, declining public services and deteriorating conditions in French schools. Students, labor unions and members of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 in opposition to President Emmanuel Macron's economic policies, joined Saturday's demonstrations.
The unrest also follows student protests that began last month in poorer suburbs north of Paris over teacher shortages and inadequate school conditions. Those demonstrations were accompanied by violence that subsequently spread to other European countries, including Belgium.
Macron's government and figures on the French right have accused far-left groups of hijacking legitimate social grievances and turning the demonstrations into violent confrontations ahead of next year's presidential election. The political tensions come as France prepares to choose a successor to Macron, who is barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Polls cited in French political coverage have pointed to a possible contest between far-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party.
Trump and Vance blame immigration
The unrest has also reignited fierce arguments over immigration and integration, with French right-wing politicians and prominent conservative figures abroad blaming immigrants and their descendants for a significant share of the violence. These accusations have become central to the political debate, although the broader demonstrations have involved people from different backgrounds and political movements.
Marion Maréchal, the niece of far-right leader Marine Le Pen, accused supporters of left-wing politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon's vision of a "new France" of destroying the country. "The whole world is watching in astonishment and disbelief as the children of Mélenchon's 'new France' destroy their country," she wrote.
The phrase refers to Mélenchon's vision of a French society in which immigrant communities are an integral part of national identity, but Maréchal and other right-wing figures have adopted it as a warning about demographic change.
Nice Mayor Éric Ciotti expressed outrage over the destruction in Limoges, calling the burning city hall a symbol of a republic in decline. "This is an allegory of our republic going up in flames and dying," he wrote. "We will not allow our country to die without a response. Millions will reject chaos. We will win!"
Trump had already linked the unrest to immigration earlier this month, arguing that student demonstrations were a cover for broader political and cultural aims. In a Truth Social post about two weeks ago, he claimed that the protests had nothing to do with schools and instead reflected mass immigration that had spiraled out of control. He also accused Islam of seeking to take over France.
Vice President JD Vance echoed those accusations Sunday, sharing footage of the destruction in Limoges. "Liberals in the West imported the Third World into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," he wrote, accusing political leaders of ignoring questions about integration and cultural compatibility. He said Western governments had been warned about the consequences but had refused to listen.
Vance also connected the violence to the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, as Trump and Republicans seek to maintain control of Congress. "I hope Americans are paying attention," he wrote. "This is the future congressional Democrats want for your country."
Palestinian flags displayed during some of the demonstrations have drawn particular attention from conservative commentators, who linked them to the broader pro-Palestinian protest movement. American commentator Meghan McCain, daughter of the late Republican senator John McCain, shared footage of the burning Limoges city hall and wrote: "This is what 'globalize the intifada' means."
The slogan, heard frequently at anti-Israel demonstrations in Europe and the United States in recent years, is defended by supporters as a call for Palestinian liberation but criticized by opponents as an endorsement of violence against Jews and Israelis.
Macron faces criticism over response
Macron, meanwhile, was preparing to address the nation at 9 p.m. Israel time Sunday following mounting criticism of his response to the unrest. Opponents of the violence accuse him of failing to take sufficiently decisive action, while supporters of the protests argue that his government has failed to address their demands and restrain police tactics.
In recent weeks, Macron has largely responded with statements acknowledging public anger while condemning violence. Critics have called for stronger measures, including emergency powers that could allow authorities to deploy additional security forces and impose tighter restrictions on rioters. The government has so far avoided declaring a state of emergency.
The president also faced criticism over footage showing him and his wife, Brigitte, dancing and enjoying a Céline Dion concert Friday night, just hours before the unrest erupted. The video circulated widely over the weekend, with critics accusing the couple of appearing detached from growing public frustration over rising living costs, pressure on public finances, political paralysis and violence in the streets.
Some compared the images to Marie Antoinette, the French queen who became a symbol of royal excess during the economic crisis preceding the French Revolution. Critics argued that Macron's appearance at the concert reflected a disconnect between the presidency and the mood of a country facing deepening social and economic tensions.
Macron, whose second term ends next May, cannot run for another consecutive term. The unrest has added to the political pressure on his administration at a time when France is already grappling with economic uncertainty and divisions over immigration, public services and national identity.
With damaged businesses counting their losses, historic buildings in ruins and security forces facing questions about their preparedness, Macron must now contend with both the immediate consequences of the violence and the wider political crisis ahead of France's presidential election.

Syria names Omar al-Halabi as chairman of sovereign wealth fund

Breadcrumb
Syria names Omar al-Halabi as chairman of sovereign wealth fund
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on Sunday appointed Omar al-Halabi as chairman of the country's sovereign wealth fund, created by the transitional authorities but criticised by experts as lacking transparency.
Syria's sovereign fund sits at the heart of the country's efforts to attract foreign capital after 13 years of war, and was created to oversee investment projects and manage state assets.
It also manages assets confiscated from businessmen close to the government of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, whom the new authorities ousted in December 2024.
In a decree published by state media, Sharaa appointed Halabi "as adviser for economic affairs to the presidency of the republic" and as "chairman of the board of directors of the sovereign fund".
According to state news agency SANA, Halabi has "more than 20 years of professional experience working with governments, sovereign institutions and the private sector in the Middle East and international markets in the fields of economic policy and institution building and sovereign investment".
It said Halabi previously headed economics and public policy advisory for the Middle East at accounting firm KPMG and also worked with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.
After establishing Syria's sovereign fund in June 2025, authorities have not announced its director.
But several people who requested anonymity told AFP in July that they met the director and identified him as Abu Maryam al-Australi, a former jihadist whose surname means "the Australian".
Australi is sanctioned by Canberra and was close to Sharaa when the now-president led a rebel group in northwest Syria that went on to spearhead the offensive that toppled Assad.
Syria's authorities, who inherited an economy shattered by years of war and economic sanctions, have been intensifying efforts to speed up reconstruction, with the sovereign fund a key part of the process.
According to official estimates, the fund controls assets whose value exceeds Syria's GDP.
Experts, however, had previously criticised what they said was the fund's lack of transparency, with economist Karam Shaar calling it "a black box".
The fund also manages assets confiscated from businessmen close to the former authorities, including Mohammad Hamsho, who was sanctioned by the European Union and the United States and who has reached a settlement with the new authorities.
Most Syrians live in poverty, while the World Bank has estimated that rebuilding the country will cost more than $216 billion.

Who Owns Iran’s Mining Giants?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:23:09 UTC
23:23:09 KST

Who Owns Iran’s Mining Giants?
Accounting for 44% of Iran’s national iron ore output in 1402, four mining powerhouses reveal two contrasting governance models across the domestic steel value chain: complex cross-shareholding networks driven by institutional funds, and concentrated direct asset control spearheaded by private conglomerates.
An analysis of the ownership structure behind Iran’s iron ore and downstream steel producers highlights two competing operational and capital allocation models:
1. Multi-Tiered Networked Holdings (The Institutional Model):
Institutional investment giants—led by Vamaden (Mines & Metals Development Investment Co.) and Vamid (Omid Investment Group)—serve as the anchor shareholders across key upstream producers, including Gol-Gohar, Chadormalu, Gohar Zamin, and Sabanour. This institutional footprint extends downstream into steel manufacturing, securing 33.4% of Khorasan Steel and 20.0% of Arfa Iron & Steel. The collaborative nature of this network is exemplified by project-based joint ventures such as Tajalli Mining & Metals Development (held 51% by Vamaden, 17% by Chadormalu, and 17% by Gol-Gohar), where Iran's two largest mining competitors act as joint equity partners to pool capital and distribute development risks.
2. Concentrated Direct Control (The Private Conglomerate Model):
In contrast, Mahan Industries & Mines Development Holding, a wholly owned subsidiary of Tourism Financial Group, bypasses interlocking equity webs in favor of centralized asset ownership and direct operational control. Holding a 59.5% controlling interest in Gol-Gohar Mine No. 5 alongside state-owned IMIDRO (40.5%), Mahan Holding functions as an integrated supply engine that channels raw material directly into its Baft and Bonab steel production facilities.
While institutional giants leverage collaborative financial networks to spread risk across the national mining footprint, private groups secure dedicated asset ownership from mine to mill to ensure feedstock autonomy and operational resilience

dennis vanderbroeck creates settings for the moments that bring us together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:15:08 UTC
23:15:08 KST

dennis vanderbroeck creates settings for the moments that bring us together
moving between fashion, theater, and music, the dutch spatial designer treats architecture as a framework for encounter, where the relationship between performers and audiences matters as much as the space itself.
prefer designboom on google
dennis vanderbroeck on designing experiences
A fashion show or a live performance may last only a few minutes, but what happens in the room is harder to capture. For Dennis Vanderbroeck, this temporary collectiveness is at the heart of his work, which moves between fashion, theater, music, and performance. The Dutch spatial designer approaches his work as a way to bring people together and shape how they encounter one another.
With a background in theater, Vanderbroeck focuses on the experience a setting creates. His designs set the scene for encounters between performers and audiences, leaving room for the unexpected. ‘I always say that our designs are just a tool to facilitate the experience,’ he tells designboom. ‘It’s more about the experience of the moment than the space itself.’ At the latest Milan and Paris fashion weeks, the designer developed two distinct approaches to staging fashion, from a scaffolded runway that emphasized collective energy for Diesel to a modular arrangement that suggested movement and change for Miu Miu.
the space between the collective and the individual
Vanderbroeck’s recent collaborations with Diesel and Miu Miu reveal two different ways of exploring this relationship. His work with Glenn Martens at Diesel developed over several shows, with a shared interest in making fashion more inclusive and approachable. Their final collaboration for the brand brought these ideas together through a rigid scaffolding structure and a performative setting shaped by community, presence, and disruption. The contrast between the group and the individual became central to the experience. While people occupied the large scaffolding structure, performers interrupted the scene, and models moved through the space.
For the Miu Miu Spring/Summer 2027 show at the Palais d’Iéna in Paris, Vanderbroeck approached the runway through a different kind of proximity. Working with the brand for the first time, the designer and his team developed a space with tightly arranged bleachers and a narrow catwalk, recalling the intimacy of 1990s runway shows. The audience sat close together, while the models passed directly in front of them.
Although the two projects grew out of different conversations, both explored the relationship between the individual and the group. ‘In our fashion work, we always try to do something with this idea of the collective versus the singular, the individual,’ he highlights. ‘That friction is forever interesting to me.’ At a fashion show, all eyes are on the looks coming down the runway, but the experience is also shaped by the crowd around them. Vanderbroeck plays with this dynamic through the layout of the space, bringing the audience into the experience without prescribing how they should react.
designing movement within a static space
The idea of a space that anticipates its next use also shaped Vanderbroeck’s first collaboration with Miu Miu. The show was developed in relation to Geste de Consolation (Gesture of Consolation), the upcoming exhibition by French filmmaker Alice Diop presented as part of the Art Basel Paris Public Program from October 21st to 25th, 2026. ‘We wanted to create a space that suggests movement and that suggests transition. So for the exhibition, the same venue will be repurposed almost, reframed, and recontextualized,’ the spatial designer explains.
Tracks laid across the floor supported modular bleachers, giving the runway a sense of movement even though the structure itself remained still. The arrangement anticipated the exhibition that would follow, with elements of the fashion show intended to be reconfigured and given a different meaning in a new context. Vanderbroeck describes this approach as a dynamic stage. Drawing on his background in theater, he treats a set not as a finished backdrop but as something that can accommodate different situations over time. The design becomes part of a longer sequence, shaped as much by what comes next as by the event taking place in the room.
from the theater to the live stage
Theater remains an important reference point in Vanderbroeck’s practice, even when he is designing for other forms of performance. For Issey Miyake’s OPEN STUDIO at Tate Modern, he drew on the circular form of the museum’s concrete tanks to explore intimacy and the idea of an embrace. He used the geometry of the architecture to shape different degrees of proximity between performers and audience members. The experience moved from a collective sense of embrace toward a more intimate, one-to-one interaction between a performer and someone watching.
Vanderbroeck also considered the audience’s journey through the museum, from Henri Matisse’s The Snail to the Turbine Hall and into the South Tank. The work formed part of a wider sequence of spaces and encounters, with the architecture and artwork informing the concept. This interest in how a setting shapes a live experience extends to music. For the Lux Tour, Vanderbroeck collaborated closely with Rosalía and her team, bringing together references from fashion, popular culture, theater, and fine art. He describes the project as an accumulation of his practice, with ideas from different disciplines informing one another. ‘With Rosalía, honestly, it was an accumulation of my whole practice in one project, where fashion, music, but also popular culture and theater and the references through fine art all came together,’ Dennis Vanderbroeck comments.
beyond the image
In an era when live events are increasingly documented and circulated online, Dennis Vanderbroeck remains focused on what it means to experience them in person. He recognizes that images matter, particularly in fashion, but does not begin a project by imagining how it will appear on a phone screen. ‘I’m always trying to intentionally design from the physical experience,’ he shares with us. ‘If it then resonates well online or resonates well on your phone or something, then perfect. But it’s never the main intention.’ This thinking carried into the set design for Rosalía’s Lux Tour, where the camera direction followed the energy of the live performance. For Vanderbroeck, filming an event is part of how it is remembered, but it cannot replace the experience of being there.
The Dutch spatial designer also recognizes the impulse to photograph an experience as a way of securing a memory. Taking out a phone can become a means of confirming one’s presence, of holding on to something that would otherwise disappear. Yet the photograph remains separate from the event, which depends on a particular arrangement of people, bodies, movement, and time. That uncertainty is part of what draws Vanderbroeck to theater. Having recently designed the set for Anton Chekhov’s The Seagull, he recalls the first preview in front of an audience as a moment when, despite all the preparation, the response remained impossible to predict. ‘You never can predict how an audience is going to respond,’ he says. For the designer, that first encounter between a work and its audience is a reminder that design can only go so far. He can shape the setting and the conditions for an experience, but what happens once people enter the room is beyond his control.
designer: Dennis Vanderbroeck | @studiodennisvanderbroeck

Why Skilled Mechanics Still Struggle With Vehicle Diagnostics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:06:14 UTC
23:06:14 KST

Why Skilled Mechanics Still Struggle With Vehicle Diagnostics
Modern vehicles combine mechanical components, electrical circuits, sensors, and electronic control systems. Even experienced mechanics can struggle to identify the exact cause of a problem when several faults produce similar symptoms.
Replacing parts without proper testing can increase repair costs and waste time. Developing strong diagnostic skills requires more than experience; it requires technical knowledge, systematic testing, and practical training.
Experience Alone Does Not Guarantee Accurate Diagnosis
An engine that runs unevenly may have an ignition problem, a fuel delivery issue, an air leak, or an electrical fault. Replacing components based on assumptions may not resolve the underlying problem.
A reliable diagnostic process starts with identifying the symptoms, inspecting relevant systems, checking fault codes when appropriate, and performing tests before replacing parts.
Mechanics who understand how different systems interact can make better decisions and avoid unnecessary repairs.
Electrical Faults Require More Than Guesswork
Modern automotive electrical systems include wiring harnesses, relays, sensors, fuses, and electronic control modules. A starting problem, for example, might result from a weak battery, a poor ground connection, a faulty relay, or a damaged wire rather than a defective starter motor.
Tools such as digital multimeters, wiring diagrams, and diagnostic scanners help technicians investigate these possibilities. However, knowing how to interpret measurements is just as important as having the right equipment.
Learning systematic testing methods through automotive electrical training can help aspiring technicians understand circuit operation, identify electrical faults, and make more informed repair decisions.
Mechanical Problems Can Have Similar Symptoms
Mechanical faults also require careful investigation. Poor acceleration, unusual engine noises, overheating, and rough idling can have several possible causes.
For instance, reduced engine performance may be associated with low compression, incorrect valve clearance, restricted airflow, or fuel delivery problems. Each possibility requires a suitable inspection or test.
Understanding engine operation helps mechanics distinguish between symptoms and their actual causes. Practical experience with components, maintenance procedures, and troubleshooting techniques is essential for developing this ability.
A structured automotive mechanics course can help learners build a stronger foundation in mechanical systems and practical fault diagnosis.
Motorcycle Repair Requires the Same Attention to Detail
Motorcycles have their own diagnostic challenges, including compact component layouts, ignition systems, fuel delivery problems, and model-specific maintenance requirements.
A motorcycle that refuses to start could have a battery problem, an ignition fault, insufficient fuel delivery, or a mechanical issue. Replacing parts without testing the relevant systems can lead to recurring failures.
Technicians need to understand motorcycle components, perform appropriate checks, and confirm the cause before carrying out repairs. Practical motorcycle repair training can help learners develop the technical foundation needed to inspect, maintain, and troubleshoot motorcycles.
Why Practical Training Matters
Technical knowledge becomes more valuable when learners can apply it to real diagnostic situations. Practical training helps students use tools correctly, interpret test results, understand component interactions, and follow a consistent troubleshooting process.
When choosing a training program, prospective students should consider the curriculum, workshop equipment, hands-on practice, and opportunities to work with real vehicles or motorcycles.
These factors help bridge the gap between understanding technical concepts and applying them in a professional repair environment.
Conclusion
Accurate vehicle diagnostics depends on technical knowledge, logical reasoning, appropriate testing, and practical experience. Whether working on electrical circuits, mechanical components, or motorcycle systems, technicians who investigate the underlying cause are better equipped to avoid unnecessary part replacements and recurring problems.
For aspiring mechanics, developing these skills through structured learning and practical experience can provide a stronger foundation for a career in vehicle maintenance and repair.

Exclusive breastfeeding for six months linked to fewer ADHD symptoms in children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:00:32 UTC
23:00:32 KST

A new study suggests that infants who receive only breast milk for their first six months tend to show fewer symptoms of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in early childhood. The research indicates that this protective effect holds up even when accounting for a child’s genetic predisposition to the condition. These findings were published in the journal Biological Psychiatry.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a condition involving patterns of hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention that interfere with daily functioning. The behavioral traits associated with the condition exist on a broad spectrum in the general population, with clinical diagnoses given to those experiencing the most extreme symptoms. The disorder often begins in childhood and has a strong genetic component.
Research involving twins and families estimates that genetics account for the vast majority of the risk of developing the disorder. At the same time, environmental factors before and after birth also play a role in how the brain develops. This means that a person’s surroundings, early experiences, and diet can interact with their genetic blueprint over time.
Human breast milk provides a primary food source for many infants and contains components like fatty acids, immune cells, and nutrients that support neurodevelopment. The World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life to maximize these health benefits. This strict definition means an infant consumes no solid foods, commercial infant formula, or even water during that initial period. Previous research has linked infant breastfeeding to a lower chance of receiving an ADHD diagnosis later in life.
It has been difficult to determine whether this relationship is a direct biological result of breast milk or if it stems from other variables in a family’s lifestyle. Mothers who breastfeed longer often have different socioeconomic backgrounds and health behaviors than those who do not. Parents with high levels of ADHD traits themselves might find breastfeeding more challenging, and their children inherit a higher genetic likelihood for the disorder. To separate the specific effects of infant feeding from these shared genetic and environmental traits, scientists needed a large dataset that tracked families over many years. A team of researchers led by Berit Skretting Solberg at the University of Bergen in Norway set out to examine this relationship.
The researchers analyzed data from a large study that tracked thousands of Norwegian families from pregnancy through childhood. The initial analysis included 37,643 children born between 1999 and 2009. When the infants were six months old, mothers filled out questionnaires detailing their feeding practices. They specifically noted how many months the child received full breastfeeding, which the researchers defined as providing breast milk without any formula or solid foods.
As the children aged, their parents completed behavioral assessments to track symptoms of hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention at ages three, five, and eight. The researchers also mapped the genetic profiles of the children to calculate a polygenic risk score for ADHD. A polygenic risk score is a number that estimates a person’s genetic likelihood for a trait based on thousands of tiny variations in their DNA. The researchers found that each additional month of full breastfeeding was associated with a measurable reduction in ADHD symptoms at all three ages.
To refine their analysis, the research team looked at a smaller subgroup of 18,349 mother-father-child units. In this step, the scientists included the polygenic risk scores of both parents alongside the child’s genetic data. They also adjusted the statistical models to account for the mother’s education level, the parents’ ages at the time of birth, the child’s birth weight, and the season of birth. Adding these socioeconomic and perinatal factors provided a more precise view of the relationship between early diet and behavioral development.
Even with the genetic risks of the entire family and various socioeconomic factors factored in, the association remained consistent. Infants who were fully breastfed for longer periods continued to show fewer ADHD symptoms in childhood. The researchers noted that shorter durations of full breastfeeding, or feeding regimens relying on partial breastfeeding, were consistently linked to higher symptom scores. The effect size decreased slightly as the children reached age eight, but the relationship remained present in the data.
The scientists conducted a third analysis comparing 8,209 pairs of siblings within the dataset. By looking at children born to the same mother, they could account for unmeasured environmental and genetic factors that remain constant within a specific household. They focused on over 5,000 sibling pairs where the mother breastfed one child exclusively for a different length of time than the other child. The researchers then compared the behavioral symptom scores of the siblings as they grew up.
The sibling comparison produced results that closely mirrored the main analysis. The sibling who received full breastfeeding for a longer duration tended to exhibit fewer ADHD symptoms than their brother or sister who received less breast milk. This specific finding suggests that breast milk itself, or the act of breastfeeding, might exert a direct biological or psychological influence on behavioral development. However, when the sibling data were analyzed separately by sex, the effects of breastfeeding were attenuated.
While the data points to a potential biological benefit of breast milk, the observed reductions in ADHD symptoms were small on an individual level. The researchers emphasize that these shifts might not translate into clinically observable changes for a specific child. The effect might only become apparent when looking at broad population trends, where a slight overall reduction in symptoms could mean fewer children cross the threshold into a clinical diagnosis. The study relied on parent-reported questionnaires rather than formal evaluations by a doctor, which can introduce personal bias into the symptom scores.
Because participation in the long-term study was voluntary, the sample experienced some loss to follow-up over the years. The research team used statistical techniques to adjust for this missing data, and their results were not substantially altered, but self-selection bias remains a possibility in large health registries. The study was also observational, meaning it tracked natural behaviors rather than assigning diets in a controlled laboratory setting. While the genetic and sibling analyses help rule out many external factors, researchers cannot entirely eliminate the possibility of other hidden variables influencing the outcomes.
Future research will need to explore the exact biological mechanisms that might explain how breast milk influences the developing brain. Human breast milk contains unique components like tryptophan, an amino acid that breaks down in the gut and helps regulate chemical signaling between the digestive system and the central nervous system. Milk also contains specialized complex sugars that promote healthy bacteria, which have been shown to improve working memory and attention in animal models. Scientists also plan to study how the physical skin-to-skin contact required for nursing might influence infant attachment security and long-term emotional regulation.
The study, “Breastfeeding and Development of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Symptoms Across Childhood,” was authored by Berit Skretting Solberg, Anne Lise Brantsæter, Liv Grimstvedt Kvalvik, Catharina A. Hartman, Tian Xie, Kari Klungsøyr, Lin Li, Henrik Larsson, Rolf Gjestad, and Jan Haavik.

The Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Red Sea chokepoint and vital export route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz.

The session was extended into Oct 19 “to give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views”, one of them told AFP.

“I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said on Oct 17. “We are speaking only about defence.” AFP

Why have France’s school protests become a wider political crisis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:48:04 UTC
22:48:04 KST

Why have France’s school protests become a wider political crisis?
France’s school protests have united students and ‘yellow vest’ supporters, exposing deeper anger over living standards.
Protests are sweeping France as anger over conditions in schools meets frustration with high living costs and a government accused of doing little to address problems facing people.
About 550,000 people demonstrated nationwide on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry. Most marched peacefully, while a small minority attacked buildings, looted shops and clashed with police, who fired tear gas and charged protesters.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were injured. Behind the confrontations lies a political crisis, fuelled by anger at deteriorating services and overstretched household budgets, and compounded by a sense that France’s political institutions offer little hope of change.
Here is how school blockades became a nationwide movement – and what that means for President Emmanuel Macron.
How have the protests spread, what are protesters demanding?
The movement began last month in high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where students protested against teacher shortages and poor facilities. School blockades and demonstrations later spread to cities including Bordeaux, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Lille and Marseille.
Saturday brought together students and trade unions, alongside supporters of the “yellow vest” movement that emerged in 2018 to challenge rising living costs and economic inequality.
Emile Chabal, a professor of contemporary history at the University of Edinburgh, told Al Jazeera the demonstrations were “the logical outcome of a series of protests” stretching back to the yellow vests.
That movement was driven by financial pressures and resentment at “the French presidential system”, he told Al Jazeera, alluding to a structure which often leads to the election of a centrist candidate, such as President Emmanuel Macron.
Saturday combined those longstanding grievances with students’ anger at deteriorating state schools. The yellow vests had demanded better public services.
Bringing students’ grievances together with wider social demands, therefore, represented “the worst possible outcome for the French government”, Chabal said.
Students’ immediate demands concern conditions in France’s lycees (public high schools), which generally educate pupils aged 15 to 18. They want smaller classes, enough teachers, better buildings and less exhausting timetables. Their complaints also reflect broader concerns about whether the state can provide the education and opportunities young people need.
But for workers, including school staff, the dispute also concerns wages and the resources available to deliver public services.
The school protests coincided with a nationwide public sector strike against the government’s budget plans. Bringing all these concerns together under one umbrella represented “the worst possible outcome for the French government”, Chabal said.
It comes as the proposed 2027 budget includes a 54 billion euro ($60.8bn) package of cost-cutting and tax measures, which the government says is necessary to reduce France’s deficit. The proposals include freezing the pay scale used to calculate civil servants’ basic salaries, which unions say would be the fourth consecutive annual freeze.
Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, said students were inspiring wider mobilisation around inequality, cuts to public investment and democratic rights, with demands for social welfare spending rather than militarisation.
“They do not want to fight wars; they want a different future,” she told Al Jazeera.
She also linked the movement to young people’s mobilisation over Gaza, with Palestinian flags appearing at demonstrations across several European countries.
How has the government responded?
The government has focused its immediate response on public order, with President Macron saying those responsible for violence would be “prosecuted and punished”.
His comments came as a fire largely destroyed the historic town hall in the city of Limoges, while public buildings and shops were attacked elsewhere.
But those involved in violence represent only a small minority of the much larger mobilisation. Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, has accused the government of repressing school students and allowing the confrontation to intensify.
His argument reflects a wider political dispute about whether the government treats the protests chiefly as a security problem or addresses the grievances that have brought different groups together.
Experts say France’s problems extend beyond disagreement over individual budget measures and reflect deeper discontent. Emile Chabal, from the University of Edinburgh, said political paralysis since the 2024 parliamentary elections, which left no bloc with an outright majority, had created “an environment in which no political party or movement is able to channel social discontent”.
That fragmentation makes it difficult to build a durable agreement on spending, taxation or public services. It also leaves protesters questioning whether changing governments produces meaningful changes in policy.
The protests are also “a tough blow for Macron”, Chabal said, whose promises of youthful energy and a reformed, dynamic France have been undermined by “his inability to articulate his political project and his deeply unempathetic persona”.
Chabal added that the unrest included violence sometimes seen on the fringes of French demonstrations, with direct-action tactics associated with the yellow vests. Targets included shops and, more unusually, public buildings. He described the destruction of Limoges’ town hall as particularly significant because of its place in France’s civic history.
Other researchers emphasise the role of policing. Guya Accornero, a specialist in social movements at Lisbon’s University Institute, said previous confrontations had created lasting tensions between protesters and police.
During the current protests, a 15-year-old lost a hand to a police stun grenade, while a 14-year-old suffered a shattered jaw after being struck by a tear gas canister fired at close range, according to Human Rights Watch. The organisation condemned excessive force against children, saying the demonstrations had been overwhelmingly peaceful.
“Young people have been violently repressed also when using non-disruptive tactics,” she told Al Jazeera.
Who could benefit politically?
There is no clear answer from the experts who spoke to Al Jazeera. Paul Smith, an associate professor in French history and politics at the University of Nottingham, believes far-right leader Marine Le Pen stands to gain.
“I see only one beneficiary and that’s Le Pen,” he told Al Jazeera, suggesting the unrest could also damage Melenchon’s presidential prospects.
Chabal cautioned against assuming a far-right gain, but he said fear of disorder had historically benefited conservative or centrist parties in France, including after the 1968 protests.
Le Pen has not entirely dismissed the protesters’ grievances, describing them on X on Saturday as “legitimate social demands”, while claiming they had been “held hostage by the far left”.
The far-right may seek to reap the rewards of public discontent, but experts say it is more likely to channel that anger towards immigration and the scapegoating of migrants, rather than blaming the structures of neoliberalism and capitalism for the protesters’ woes, as Melenchon has suggested.
With a presidential election due in April 2027, candidates face competing pressures, demonstrating that they can restore order while convincing voters they will address the conditions behind the mobilisation.
The challenge, Chabal said, is how to create change in “an environment in which no political party or movement is able to channel social discontent”.

Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:46:34 UTC
22:46:34 KST

Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt
A soy-derived compound protected mice from high blood pressure and memory problems linked to excessive salt consumption, offering a promising new avenue for research.
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Fujita Health University
- Summary:
- Eating too much salt may do more than raise blood pressure. It could also harm memory and social behavior. In a new study, Japanese researchers discovered that a soy-derived compound called LPC70 helped protect mice from several damaging effects of a high-salt diet. Mice given the supplement had lower blood pressure, better memory, and improved social interactions compared with mice consuming excess salt alone.
- Share:
Consuming too much salt can affect more than blood pressure. Growing evidence suggests that excessive salt intake may also interfere with memory, thinking, and emotional well-being. High salt (HS) consumption is already a major public health concern because of its connection to hypertension, but its potential effects on the brain make finding ways to reduce the damage even more important.
Researchers in Japan have identified a promising possibility in LPC70, a compound derived from soy. Previous research found that this ingredient could reduce high blood pressure and cognitive problems associated with a high-salt diet (HSD) in mice. The latest study takes a closer look at how it works, revealing that the compound influences important chemical signals in the brain and kidneys.
How a Soy Compound May Counter the Effects of Excess Salt
The research centers on prostaglandins (PGs), signaling molecules made from a fatty acid called arachidonic acid (AA). These substances act much like local hormones, helping regulate essential functions throughout the body.
In the cardiovascular system, prostaglandins help control blood pressure by balancing the widening and narrowing of blood vessels. Their effects in the brain are more complicated. Depending on which receptors they activate, they can trigger signals that either protect nerve cells or contribute to harmful processes, potentially affecting memory, thinking, and emotional responses.
LPC70 is a form of soy lysolecithin in which lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) accounts for more than 70% of the phospholipids. Although earlier experiments showed that LPC70 could ease salt-related hypertension and cognitive difficulties, scientists had not fully understood the mechanisms responsible, particularly its influence on prostaglandin signaling.
To investigate, a research team led by Professor Akihiro Mouri and Dr. Hisayoshi Kubota, working with Dr. Kazuhiro Kagotani, examined how LPC70 affected these signaling pathways in mice consuming a high-salt diet.
Dr. Kubota, the study's first author, played a central role in the experiments. He assessed blood pressure, monitored behavioral changes, and analyzed molecular activity associated with prostaglandins. His work helped clarify how LPC70 produces different effects in the organs involved in salt-related cardiovascular and cognitive problems.
Prof. Mouri and Dr. Kubota are affiliated with the Department of Regulatory Science for Evaluation and Development of Pharmaceuticals & Devices at Fujita Health University Graduate School of Medical Science, as well as the International Center for Brain Science (ICBS) at Fujita Health University in Japan. Dr. Kagotani is affiliated with Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd, in Japan and the Tsuji Health and Beauty Science Laboratory at Mie University, Japan.
The findings were released online on May 14, 2026, and published in Volume 197 of Neurochemistry International on July 1, 2026.
"We wanted to understand the role of LPC70 in coordinating changes in PG signaling across organ systems," mentioned Prof. Mouri. "Our study originated from a collaborative research project with Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd, a company that develops naturally derived food ingredients," he added.
Soy Compound Improves Blood Pressure and Memory in Mice
As expected, mice that consumed a high-salt diet developed elevated blood pressure. However, the consequences extended beyond their cardiovascular health.
The animals also became less socially interactive and had difficulty recognizing objects they had encountered before, indicating problems with memory. Interestingly, their general movement and anxiety-like behavior showed no substantial changes. This pattern suggests that excessive salt selectively disrupted more complex cognitive and social functions rather than causing widespread behavioral impairment.
When researchers supplemented the animals' diets with LPC70, several of these effects were reduced. Blood pressure improved, and the mice performed better on tests of social interaction and object recognition memory.
These improvements prompted the researchers to examine what was happening inside the animals' kidneys and brains.
Different Protective Effects in the Kidneys and Brain
In the kidneys, a high-salt diet increased the expression of two components involved in prostaglandin signaling: cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) and the PGE2 receptor EP3. Both may contribute to the development of high blood pressure associated with excessive salt consumption.
LPC70 reduced these salt-related increases, suggesting that the compound helps correct changes in kidney signaling that can interfere with normal blood pressure regulation.
The researchers found a different response in the prefrontal cortex, a brain region essential for thinking, memory, and social behavior.
Excess salt reduced the expression of the PGD2 receptor DP1, which plays a role in protective and anti-inflammatory signaling in the brain. LPC70 restored expression of this receptor without changing DP2, another receptor associated with potentially harmful effects on nerve cells.
This distinction is important because it suggests that LPC70 does not simply increase or suppress all prostaglandin activity. Instead, it may selectively favor signaling pathways that help protect the brain, potentially explaining the improvements in memory and social behavior observed in the mice.
A Surprising Change in Chemical Signaling
The team also discovered an unexpected change involving arachidonic acid, the fatty acid the body uses to produce prostaglandins.
Mice consuming excess salt had lower levels of circulating arachidonic acid. Yet when they received LPC70, levels of prostaglandins derived from this fatty acid, including PGE2 and PGD2, increased.
This seemingly contradictory result suggests that LPC70 may help the body use available arachidonic acid more efficiently to produce prostaglandins under high-salt conditions.
Taken together, the findings reveal a coordinated but highly selective response. In the kidneys, LPC70 appears to suppress signaling changes associated with hypertension. In the brain, it restores signaling linked to protection against inflammation and damage.
The compound's effects therefore depend on both the organ involved and the specific prostaglandin receptors being regulated.
Could Soy-Based Ingredients Help Protect Against Excess Salt?
The results suggest that LPC70 could eventually become a useful functional food ingredient for reducing some of the health consequences of excessive salt intake.
Its ability to improve blood pressure and cognitive performance in mice raises the possibility that it could support cardiovascular and brain health, particularly among people whose diets contain high amounts of salt.
However, the findings come from animal experiments, and further clinical studies are needed to determine whether the same benefits occur in humans.
"Our study elucidates LPC70's role in PG signaling, laying the groundwork for future clinical research and dietary interventions aimed at reducing hypertension-related cognitive decline and promoting healthy aging globally," concluded Prof. Mouri.
The research provides a clearer picture of how a soy-derived compound can influence the body's response to excessive salt, opening new possibilities for nutritional approaches to protecting long-term health.
Research Funding and Support
The study received support through Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research from the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS: 20K07931, 22K07606, 22K11891, and 23H02843).
Additional support came from the Fujita Mind-Brain Research & Innovation Center for Drug Generation (Fujita Mind-BRIDGe) through Japan's Peak Research Universities (J-PEAKS) Program (JPJS00420240019), along with the Japan Science and Technology Agency FOREST Program (JPMJFR215H).
Tsuji Oil Mills Co., Ltd. provided funding for the research. Grants and other support were also supplied by the Education and Research Facility of Animal Models for Human Diseases at Fujita Health University, the Smoking Research Foundation, and the Takeda Science Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fujita Health University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hisayoshi Kubota, Kazuo Kunisawa, Masaya Hasegawa, Hitomi Kurahashi, Kazuhiro Kagotani, Kazuki Nakajima, Yuki Fujimoto, Akihito Hayashi, Ryoji Sono, Takehiko Tsuji, Kuniaki Saito, Toshitaka Nabeshima, Akihiro Mouri. Soy lysolecithin attenuates hypertension and behavioral impairments in mice fed a high-salt diet through receptor-specific regulation of prostaglandin signaling and arachidonic acid-derived prostaglandin production. Neurochemistry International, 2026; 197: 106184 DOI: 10.1016/j.neuint.2026.106184

UN sec-gen frontrunner Rebeca Grynspan’s Jewish roots, record on Israel - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:41:17 UTC
22:41:17 KST

Jewish former vice president of Costa Rica Rebeca Grynspan is leading the straw poll for the next UN secretary-general. If she successfully replaces Antonio Guterres when he finishes his term on December 31, she will become the first Jewish UN secretary-general in the body’s history.
Grynspan, 70, was born to Jewish parents Manuel Grynspan Burstin and Sara Mayufis Schapiro in San José. Her parents fled Poland in 1936, while her maternal grandparents stayed behind and were killed during the Holocaust.
Grynspan’s husband – Saul Weisleder – is also Jewish, and they have two children. Her sister, Frida, lives in Israel, and Grynspan has a niece and nephew who served in the IDF. In a 2014 interview with the Tico Times, Frida referred to herself as a “lifelong Zionist.”
After obtaining a bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of Costa Rica and a master’s degree in economics from the University of Sussex in England, Grynspan became a professor and researcher at the Economic Science Research Institute of the University of Costa Rica.
She served as vice finance minister from 1986 to 1988, and as the second vice president of Costa Rica from 1994 to 1998. She then became the first woman to serve as the secretary-general of the Ibero-American General Secretariat from 2014 to 2021 and then the first woman to become the secretary-general of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) in 2021. She currently holds this position.
In a video explaining why she chose to run for secretary-general, Grynspan said: “Conflicts are going up, trust in international law in the organization is going down, and time is running out.”
“I am a daughter of peace; my parents were refugees of the Second World War. I know what wars take away and what peace makes possible; that’s why I’m running.”
Grynspan's stance on Israel, Palestine
The Jerusalem Post’s research into Grynspan’s Israel and Palestine stances found that she has not maintained a public stance on either matter.
She did not post to social media on or immediately after the October 7 attacks. Her first post was on October 21, 2023, on X/Twitter, when she wrote, “Horrified by the tragic loss of life in Israel & Gaza. All civilians must be protected & we must work for peace in the region so people can have the future they want for themselves & their children. Hatred, terrorism, violence & war are not the way.”
On November 9, 2023, she wrote on Instagram, “I echo the call made by the highest-level humanitarian coordination forum of the @UnitedNations system: Respect for international humanitarian and human rights law; Immediate and unconditional release of civilians held hostage; Civilians must be protected.”
On 21 November 2023, at a UN Trade and Development Board executive session meeting in Geneva, Grynspan “echoed the call of the UN’s Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, condemning the horrific loss of civilian lives on both sides, the attack perpetrated by Hamas on October 7 and the continued bombardment of the IDF hitting civilians, hospitals, shelters, schools, and UN facilities in Gaza.”
“The protection of civilians must be paramount, as you correctly said, dear president, no party to an armed conflict is above international humanitarian law,” she added.
In 2017, she was the keynote speaker at a B’nai B’rith Uruguay memorial event.
Aside from that, the Post could find very few posts where she mentioned Israel, Palestinians, Gaza, Jews, or any related topics.
Grynspan viewed as relatively Israel-friendly candidate
Under Grynspan, the UNCTAD has adopted a seemingly Israel-critical line, publishing several unfavorable reports on the collapse of the Palestinian economy “as a result of the Israeli occupation and bombings.”
Grynspan is nevertheless seen as a more Israel-friendly candidate, given her family ties and relative public neutrality. She is running against outspoken anti-Israel candidates, such as former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet.
In an interview with Reuters last week, Grynspan said “the UN has become too risk-averse” and said the organization must cut jobs, curb bureaucracy and stop agencies duplicating work.
During Antonio Guterres’s tenure as UN secretary-general, the organization has faced renewed criticism over what Israel and pro-Israel watchdogs have described as its disproportionate focus on Israel.
In 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted 17 resolutions concerning Israel, compared with seven addressing the rest of the world combined, according to UN Watch.
Critics also point to UN bodies’ repeated condemnations of Israeli settlement policy and their scrutiny of Israel’s conduct in Gaza.

Tomer Caspi, Tomer Zaltzman crowned Winner Epic Israel bike race champs in Western Galilee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:41:10 UTC
22:41:10 KST

Tomer Caspi and Tomer Zaltzman were crowned the men’s champions of Winner Epic Israel 2026 after four days of demanding mountain biking in the Western Galilee, as Israel’s largest mountain bike race returned to the north for the first time since the war forced trails and forests in the region to close.
The 11th edition of the race, held in partnership with the Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) and sponsored by Specialized, concluded Saturday after bringing approximately 500 riders to Mateh Asher Regional Council and Nahariya for a challenging competition covering more than 300 kilometers and approximately 3,000 meters of cumulative climbing.
Caspi and Zaltzman, competing for Tomer’s team, won the men’s overall title with a combined time of 9:52:12 across the three competitive stages. Their victory capped an event that combined elite competition with a broader message of recovery and renewal for communities that endured years of disruption during the war.
The race, held in memory of its founder’s father, Giora Tzachor, was particularly meaningful this year because of its return to trails that had been inaccessible to the public for approximately three years.
Reopening of routes was made possible in part by KKL-JNF
The reopening of the routes was made possible in part by KKL-JNF’s restoration and upgrading work across the north, including hundreds of kilometers of mountain biking trails in Hanita, Kabri, Yehiam and Matzuba. Several of those routes were incorporated into this year’s course.
For race founder and producer Gal Tzachor, the return was about far more than the competition itself.
“To see hundreds of riders crossing the finish line here in the Western Galilee, after three years in which we could not return to the area, is an especially moving moment for me,” Tzachor said. “This year, the race was much more than a cycling competition. We returned to trails that had been closed, forests that had undergone rehabilitation and an area we all love so much.
“Over four days, we saw competitive sport at the highest level, but also an entire community returning to the north and bringing life back to the region. This race was born out of a love for the land, cycling and people, and it continues the legacy of my father, Giora Tzachor. I am proud of everyone who took part in this special edition.”
The competition began Wednesday, Oct. 14, with a 10.5-kilometer prologue in the Mateh Asher area. Amos Girani and Ronen Shirazi finished first in the opening event before the riders embarked on three demanding stages that determined the overall standings.
On Thursday, the first stage covered approximately 82 kilometers and included 1,150 meters of climbing. Caspi and Zaltzman finished at the top of the standings, establishing themselves as contenders for the overall title.
The pair strengthened their position Friday during the second stage, the most demanding single-day course of this year’s race. The route covered approximately 86.5 kilometers and featured 1,730 meters of climbing, placing significant physical demands on the competitors.
Saturday’s final stage took the riders across another 74 kilometers, with approximately 800 meters of climbing, before the overall champions were confirmed.
While the men’s competition attracted much of the attention, trophies were also awarded across several other categories.
Luba Bernstein and Helen Mora won the women’s division in 15:18:47 for Helen & Luba. Noam Strasnov and Yuval Friedman of NYCC Specialized took the men’s Masters title in 11:08:49, while Abigail Louis Yaavetz and Shahar Tamir of The Buttons-MIX won the mixed category in 12:30:58.
Sharon Pe’er and Erez Shaked of Team Specialized claimed the Grand Masters title in 11:21:44, while Eli Cohen and Eitan Medina of Team Bulthaup won the Super Grand Masters division in 12:36:00.
Race provides an important boost to local economy
The return of the race also provided an important boost to the local economy. Riders were joined by family members, professional support crews and spectators who stayed in the area and visited local hotels, restaurants and businesses.
For communities in the Western Galilee that have faced the consequences of the war, the event offered another opportunity to welcome visitors and restore the region’s sporting and tourism activities.
KKL-JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky described the race’s return as a victory for the entire country.
“It feels like a victory for all the people of Israel,” Ostrinsky said. “At KKL-JNF, we are proud and excited, together with the residents of the north, to see Winner Epic Israel return to the Western Galilee after three years in which the trails were closed because of the war. This is a victory in its own right, another symbol of the return to life in the north, a region that is so dear to every citizen of Israel.
“Alongside our investment in the land, we believe it is important to strengthen communities, tourism and the local economy. We will continue working for and alongside the people of the north to rehabilitate what was damaged and help build and strengthen the region.”
The event also highlighted the role of sport in rehabilitation and community support. Wounded Israeli military veterans from Brothers for Life, an organization that assists injured soldiers throughout their recovery, took part alongside young cyclists from the Bartali Youth Cycling Club, which empowers teenagers through the sport.
Their participation added another dimension to an event centered on perseverance, recovery, and a return to normal life.
Toto Chairman and CEO Meir Bardugo said the organization was proud to support the race as part of its broader commitment to Israeli sport.
“The Toto is proud to partner with Winner Epic Israel again this year, in cooperation with KKL-JNF,” Bardugo said. “The riders and spectators enjoyed a high-quality and moving sporting experience, delivered to particularly high professional standards, that presented Israel in a positive light.
“As we approach the Toto’s 60th anniversary, Winner Epic Israel is another way for us to demonstrate our commitment to supporting Israeli sport in all its forms and to take part in the process of rehabilitation and the return to routine life in Israel.”
Nahariya Mayor Ronen Marley, whose city hosted the competition for the first time, welcomed the opportunity to showcase the area to riders and visitors.
“We were delighted to host Winner Epic Israel for the first time in our city, which is known as the city of bicycles, in partnership with KKL-JNF and the Toto,” Marley said. “The atmosphere was excellent, the riders enjoyed themselves, and the spectators had a great time cheering them on throughout the course.
“Hosting this international competition is part of our municipal efforts to promote sport and tourism, and it allowed us to introduce participants and visitors to our unique coastline and promenade. I am confident that this cooperation will expand in the coming years and contribute to strengthening the north in particular and Israel as a whole.”
Event brought renewed energy to communities still recovering
Mateh Asher Regional Council head and Confrontation Line Forum chairman Moshe Davidovich said the event had brought renewed energy to communities still recovering from the difficult years.
“We are concluding the Epic Israel competition with an enormous sense of pride and excitement,” Davidovich said. “The energy, determination and sporting spirit you brought with you, precisely here and precisely now, after the difficult years we have endured, have breathed new life into Mateh Asher and the entire Western Galilee.
“I congratulate the winners and thank all the participants and the production team for being genuine partners on the road to rehabilitation and growth. We have shown that the Galilee has come alive again. We will continue to rebuild and grow, and we look forward to welcoming you back next year.”
Aviad Friedman, head of the Northern Renewal Administration, also emphasized the significance of restoring major sporting events to the region, describing the race as a meeting point for people, communities and landscapes that demonstrated the north’s potential.
The administration, he said, would continue promoting initiatives that strengthen communities, encourage tourism and create opportunities for local residents and businesses as the region rebuilds.
For Caspi and Zaltzman, the return to the Western Galilee ended with a championship. For the communities that hosted the riders, the event offered a different kind of victory: the reopening of beloved trails, the return of visitors and another step toward restoring the north’s sporting, cultural and economic life.
After three years of disruption, Winner Epic Israel’s 2026 edition demonstrated that the roads to recovery can sometimes be found on two wheels.
