Mamdani, Paris already knows where 'globalize the Intifada' ends up - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:40:21 UTC
22:40:21 KST

Some of the protesters in Paris on Saturday didn’t stay on the ground. They climbed the Monument to the Republic, the bronze Marianne at the center of Place de la République, and stood above a crowd of tens of thousands.
Reuters photographer Jack Taylor caught them up there. In his picture, two flags fly side by side over the square: the French tricolor and the Palestinian flag.
The people below had come to protest the cost of living, worsening public services, and the state of French schools. Those are French problems, and serious ones. So what was the Palestinian flag doing up there next to the tricolor?
Saturday’s demonstrations turned into some of the worst violence France has seen in years. Rioters burned cars, looted shops, and attacked police officers. By Sunday, nearly 1,800 people had been arrested across the country, according to Reuters.
More than half a million people took part in the demonstrations, the overwhelming majority of them peacefully, over real problems: French classrooms are short of teachers, and families are struggling with living costs.
I want to be careful with the answer. The flag proves less than some people were already claiming. It shows that protesters brought the Palestinian cause to a demonstration about French problems. It doesn’t tell us whether anyone carrying it had a hand in the arson or the attacks, and we don’t know that yet.
On Sunday, the Combat Antisemitism Movement shared a video it said showed a Paris synagogue vandalized during the unrest. It opens on what looks like a small prayer room. The Torah scroll is still standing in its wooden ark. Around it, the furniture has been shoved out of place, and things are lying all over the floor.
The synagogue was reported to be in the 19th arrondissement, a district in northeastern Paris. Nobody has independently confirmed what happened there, when the video was filmed, or whether it had anything to do with Saturday’s riots. I’ve watched too many frightening clips get treated as fact before anyone bothered to ask what happened, and I don’t want to add another one.
Still, it bothered me. On Saturday, the Shabbat, a synagogue is a pretty ordinary place. People pray, complain that the rabbi’s sermon ran long, and ask about each other’s kids. Nobody there should have to wonder what happened at a political demonstration earlier that day.
This is how the conflict travels. When it reaches Paris or New York, it rarely finds an Israeli official to shout at. It finds Jews, and it works on them in two steps. First they’re made to stand in for Israel. Then they’re made to answer for it. I learned how the first step works on a Paris street in 2015.
Ten hours in Paris after 2015 terrorist attacks
In February 2015, I spent 10 hours walking through Paris and its suburbs in a kippah and tzitzit, the ritual fringes worn by observant Jewish men. It was a few weeks after the terrorist attacks at the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo and at the Hypercacher kosher supermarket, where four Jews were murdered. A photographer followed me with a hidden camera. A security guard came along and stayed out of sight.
I was covering the Jewish world for the Israeli news website NRG and the newspaper Makor Rishon at the time, and we wanted to see what ordinary Jewish life felt like on the streets of Paris.
We started in the center of Paris, where the worst I got was the occasional stare. Then we headed into other neighborhoods and out to the suburbs, and the mood changed. People cursed at me and threatened me, and some spat. Someone shouted “Viva Palestine” as I walked past. In one neighborhood, our security guard, who had been keeping out of sight, decided it was getting dangerous, and we got out.
I hadn’t said a word about Israel or carried a flag, and nobody asked what I thought of the Israeli government. Apparently my kippah had already answered for me. That’s the first step: to the people shouting at me, a Jew walking down a Paris street had become Israel.
What still gets me is how young some of them were, teenagers barely older than children, who seemed to know almost nothing about Jews except what they’d picked up on the street.
The video went viral. Millions of people watched it, and for a while I was the guy explaining on television around the world what it felt like to walk through Paris in a kippah.
Attacking a synagogue to send a message to Israel
One Saturday morning in August 2024, two cars went up in flames outside the Beth Yaacov synagogue in La Grande-Motte, a seaside town near Montpellier in southern France. One of them had a propane tank inside.
Firefighters found more fires at two of the synagogue’s entrances. Five people were inside, including the rabbi, and none of them were hurt. A police officer who walked up to the scene was injured when the tank exploded.
French prosecutors later said the suspect had admitted carrying out the attack to support the Palestinian cause and to provoke a reaction from the Israeli authorities. He denied wanting to kill anyone, though he acknowledged he had wanted to frighten people.
I still find the logic hard to follow. A man angry at Israel set fire to a synagogue in southern France and expected it to influence decisions made in Jerusalem. The people who prayed there had no say over Israeli policy and no special line to the prime minister’s office. They were Jews, and as far as he was concerned, that was enough. It was the same first step I met on the street in 2015, this time carried out with fire.
After the attack, Yonathan Arfi, president of CRIF, the body that represents French Jewish institutions, spoke to my colleague Michael Starr. He said French Jews lived with the knowledge that some people saw them as legitimate targets in a battle being fought thousands of kilometers away.
French Jews have lived with this since the Second Intifada, which began in 2000, long before October 7, 2023. In those years, attacks on Jewish schools, synagogues, and individuals became common for Europe’s largest Jewish community.
Ilan Halimi was kidnapped, tortured, and murdered in 2006 because he was Jewish. In 2012, a terrorist murdered Rabbi Jonathan Sandler, his two sons, and 8-year-old Myriam Monsonego at a Jewish school in Toulouse. In 2025, France recorded 1,320 antisemitic incidents, according to the Interior Ministry. That was down from the year before and still historically high.
The second step does its damage more quietly. A CRIF study published in July looked at the experiences of 30 Jewish schoolchildren interviewed in 2024. Many said they felt pressured to answer for Israeli policies, sometimes by classmates who barely understood the conflict. Some hid that they were Jewish or avoided talking about Israel at all.
These are teenagers worried about grades and friends, and they’re being asked to defend decisions made by the Israeli cabinet. I’m not sure most of the ministers could explain all of those decisions. A Jewish kid in a Paris classroom is expected to.
What a rabbi told New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani
Early in his campaign, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani resisted calls to condemn the slogan “globalize the intifada.” Intifada, he argued, means uprising, and some activists use the word to describe resistance to oppression.
In September 2025, he told MSNBC’s Al Sharpton that his views had changed. A rabbi, he said, had told him the slogan reminded her of bus bombings in Haifa, and that she feared extremists could terrorize Jews in New York.
She was describing exactly how the intifada travels. He said he now saw a gap between what some people meant by the phrase and its impact on Jewish New Yorkers, and that he would discourage its use.
I’ll give him credit for that. It means he can’t say nobody explained it to him. The rabbi could have added the Park Hotel in Netanya, where a Palestinian suicide bomber walked into a Passover Seder in March 2002 and murdered 30 people.
For Israelis who lived through the Second Intifada, the word means buses blown up in Jerusalem and Haifa and restaurants turned into murder scenes. So when someone calls for that to be globalized, I’d like to know what exactly they’re planning to export.
Mamdani’s supporters may mean demonstrations, civil disobedience, or solidarity with Palestinians. Fine, that’s politics. But we hear the bombings, and calling it an “uprising” doesn’t change what we hear.
Last month, his administration announced a strategy to combat antisemitism, including $6.4 million in grants for hate-crime prevention and support for victims, along with more money for security at synagogues and other houses of worship. I hope it helps.
Earlier this month, I wrote that his security grants and cultural programs would leave a central part of the problem untouched: the hostility Jews face over their attachment to Israel. That part depends on Mamdani himself, and on whether he tells people on his own side when their language or behavior has crossed a line.
On a Wednesday evening in November 2025, two weeks after Mamdani won the election, Nefesh B’Nefesh, which helps Jews move to Israel, was holding an event at Park East Synagogue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side.
Outside, police put up barricades between protesters and a group of counterprotesters. Some of the protesters chanted “globalize the intifada” and “make them scared.” Inside, the event went on.
The next day, his press secretary said he had discouraged the language and would continue to do so. The same statement said sacred spaces “should not be used to promote activities in violation of international law.”
When the news site Jewish Insider pressed his team on what that meant, it said it was referring to the organization’s promotion of settlement activity beyond the Green Line, the pre-1967 armistice line.
So the Jews inside heard a crowd chanting about making them scared, and the next day the mayor-elect’s office suggested they’d misused their own synagogue by promoting settlements.
The protesters had made them stand in for Israel. The incoming mayor’s office then asked them to answer for it. Which part of that evening, exactly, was their fault?
Even the Union for Reform Judaism, whose leaders are hardly automatic supporters of every Israeli government, condemned the intimidation and criticized his response.
Anyone can protest Israel’s policies. Jews going into a synagogue should be able to get there without being threatened, and a mayor should be able to say so without adding a “but.” It isn’t a hard sentence to write.
Young child in Paris understood the presence of antisemitism
The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is part of ordinary life in France now. It comes up in classrooms and neighborhood conversations, and in arguments between people who have never been to Israel.
I have plenty of disagreements with my own government, as regular readers of this column know. A Jew in France or New York should be able to hold any opinion about Israel, or none, without being tested on it before walking into a synagogue.
One moment from those 10 hours in Paris is stuck in my head, much more than the insults.
A young boy saw me walking by in my kippah and asked his mother what I was doing there. Didn’t I know I might be killed?
He seemed genuinely worried about me. The boy knew nothing about the hidden camera or the security guard. All he saw was a Jew walking through his neighborhood. Young as he was, he already understood what that could mean there, and he was afraid of what might happen to me.
He’d be a young man now, and I wonder whether he remembers that afternoon as well as I do.
As for the teenagers who spat at me, I’d like to know whether any of them ever got to know a Jewish person, learned something about Jewish history, or rethought what they had been taught.
Eleven years later, there’s violence in France’s streets again, and French Jews are looking at videos like the one from the 19th arrondissement.
Mamdani has said he wants Jewish New Yorkers to feel safe. I hope he means it. He can show it the next time someone chants “globalize the intifada” outside a synagogue, by condemning it plainly, with no second sentence about the people inside.
People can support Palestinians without reaching for the worst years of the Second Intifada. And kids in Paris and New York deserve to meet Jews as neighbors before anyone teaches them that every Jew is a stand-in for Israel.
I still wonder what that boy’s mother told him. I hope it was something kind.

Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:37:21 UTC
22:37:21 KST

Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Physicists have discovered a strange new state of quantum matter in which ultracold atoms defy familiar organizational rules, forming a highly excited yet surprisingly orderly configuration called a "fractional Fermi sea." The discovery challenges established quantum theories and hints at exotic quasiparticles that scientists have dubbed potential "super-Fermions."
- Share:
Physicists have uncovered a strange new form of quantum behavior in which particles organize themselves in ways that challenge established theories. Even more surprising, the particles maintain a remarkable hidden order despite being driven into an extremely energetic state.
In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers from the group led by Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, working with theoretical physicist Alvise Bastianello of the CNRS and Université Paris-Dauphine, describe how to engineer an exotic quantum state known as a "fractional Fermi sea."
The breakthrough involves pushing ultracold cesium atoms far beyond their normal conditions by repeatedly changing how strongly they attract or repel one another. Rather than simply becoming disordered, the particles rearrange themselves into an unusual configuration that behaves differently from the quantum systems scientists have traditionally studied.
The theoretical findings provide the foundation for recent experimental research conducted by Nägerl's team at the Department of Experimental Physics.
Pushing Quantum Particles Beyond Their Normal Limits
Under ordinary conditions, quantum particles follow well-established rules that determine how they arrange themselves, particularly at extremely low temperatures.
One important example involves fermions, a category of particles that includes electrons. These particles cannot all occupy the same quantum state, so they fill available energy levels according to specific restrictions. At very low temperatures, this arrangement produces what physicists call a Fermi sea.
But what happens when researchers deliberately disrupt the conditions that normally govern how particles behave?
As Alvise Bastianello explains: "Fermions, for instance, stack neatly into the available energy states to form the so-called 'Fermi sea'. But what happens if one forces interacting atoms to continuously cycle through extreme conditions, smoothly shifting them from strongly repelling each other to strongly attracting each other?"
To investigate this possibility, the researchers studied ultracold cesium atoms confined to a one-dimensional system. This means the atoms are restricted to moving along a single direction, creating an environment in which their quantum interactions can be studied with exceptional control.
The team examined what happens when the interactions between these atoms are repeatedly adjusted, cycling between powerful repulsion and attraction.
Their calculations revealed something unexpected. Starting from the ground state, the lowest energy configuration available to the system, the atoms could be driven into a highly excited state without losing their underlying organization.
The researchers call this unusual arrangement a fractional Fermi sea because its particles appear to obey a modified rule governing how quantum states are occupied.
"Instead of simply heating the system, the interaction cycle reorganizes the atoms into a new many-body state," says Yi Zeng, the leading author of this study. "This gives us a controlled way to explore quantum matter beyond the usual equilibrium paradigms."
A Strange New Quantum State With Hidden Order
One of the most intriguing features of the fractional Fermi sea is that its particles remain organized even though the system has been pushed far from equilibrium.
In physics, equilibrium describes a condition in which a system's overall properties have settled into a stable balance. Systems driven far from equilibrium can behave in complicated and unexpected ways, making them particularly challenging to understand.
Yet the fractional Fermi sea is not simply a collection of excited particles behaving randomly. Instead, it contains distinctive mathematical patterns that reveal a deeper structure.
Among these patterns are pronounced ripples called Friedel oscillations. These are wave-like variations associated with the way quantum particles influence one another. The researchers also identified unusual patterns in how correlations between particles weaken with increasing distance, even when the repulsive interactions are relatively weak.
These signatures are important because they differ from predictions associated with Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory, a long-established framework for describing how interacting quantum particles behave in one-dimensional systems.
The findings therefore point toward a previously unexplored type of quantum behavior that cannot be fully described using this familiar theoretical picture.
"This state is highly excited, but it is not random," says Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, the group leader. "It has a hidden order that becomes visible in its correlations."
The strange behavior also raises questions about the effective particles that emerge within the system. Physicists call these collective excitations quasiparticles because they can behave like individual particles even though they arise from the coordinated motion of many interacting particles.
Nägerl suggests that the unusual excitations might eventually deserve a name of their own.
"We are not yet sure how we should name these new quasiparticles. Perhaps 'super-Fermions'?"
Opening a New Frontier in Quantum Physics
The discovery suggests that fractional Fermi seas represent an exotic critical phase of quantum matter, with characteristic patterns of particle correlations that extend beyond existing descriptions of one-dimensional quantum systems.
It also demonstrates the growing power of quantum simulation, a technique that allows scientists to use carefully controlled quantum systems to investigate physical behavior that would otherwise be difficult to reproduce or study.
Ultracold atoms are particularly useful for this purpose because researchers can precisely adjust their interactions and observe how the resulting quantum states change.
Rather than limiting these experiments to recreating phenomena already understood through established theories, scientists can now explore deliberately engineered states that reveal entirely new possibilities.
As Hanns-Christoph Nägerl says: "The discovery of fractional Fermi seas shows how far we can push quantum simulation: not only reproducing known models, but creating and probing states that go beyond established paradigms."
The current publication establishes the theoretical framework for fractional Fermi seas. A companion study describing their experimental realization through quantum simulation is undergoing peer review.
Together, the research points toward new ways of investigating the fundamental behavior of quantum matter, including unusual collective excitations and hidden forms of order that emerge only when particles are pushed far outside their normal conditions.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Alvise Bastianello, Yi Zeng, Sudipta Dhar, Zekui Wang, Xudong Yu, Milena Horvath, Grigori E. Astrakharchik, Yanliang Guo, Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, Manuele Landini. Exotic Critical States as Fractional Fermi Seas in the One-Dimensional Bose Gas. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 136 (23) DOI: 10.1103/j3s5-gjpf
- Yi Zeng, Alvise Bastianello, Sudipta Dhar, Zekui Wang, Xudong Yu, Milena Horvath, Grigori E. Astrakharchik, Yanliang Guo, Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, Manuele Landini. Realization of fractional Fermi seas. arXiv, 19 May 2026 DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.17657

'We are ready for war': Iran's new defense minister threatens US and Israel

Iran appointed Mehrdad Akhlaqi, a longtime senior figure in the Islamic Republic's missile industry, as its new defense minister on Sunday, replacing an acting minister who had served since his predecessor was killed in an Israeli strike in February. Iranian lawmakers approved his appointment by a large majority after he presented a plan to rebuild military-industrial infrastructure damaged during the war, accelerate the development of defense technologies and expand cooperation with private-sector companies. 
The new minister has spent decades in Iran's defense industry, particularly its ballistic missile program, and has been subject to American and European sanctions for his activities. He previously headed the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, a subsidiary of Iran's Aerospace Industries Organization responsible for ballistic missile production. The UN Security Council placed him under sanctions in March 2007, followed by the U.S. Treasury in 2008, which accused him of overseeing the group's daily operations and participating in negotiations to acquire equipment.
In November 2014, Akhlaqi was appointed head of Iran's Aerospace Industries Organization, which operates under the Defense Ministry. European Union documents also link him to senior management roles in Iran's Defense Industries Organization and to the development of missiles, drones and other military technologies. He holds a degree in chemical engineering from Amirkabir University and a master's degree in strategic management from Malek Ashtar University. Despite his extensive career, he has maintained a relatively low public profile, with much of the available information about him appearing in military records and sanctions documents.
'Let's see how many bodies Trump evacuates'
Addressing lawmakers following his appointment, Akhlaqi declared that he had been a potential assassination target for decades. "I have been on the enemy's assassination list for 35 years," he said, warning that if the "American-Israeli enemy makes another mistake," Iran's response would be "surprising and extensive."
He pledged to strengthen Iran's regional network of allied armed groups, known by Tehran as the "axis of resistance," and restructure the Defense Ministry to meet what he described as daily security threats.
Akhlaqi also claimed that Iran had already taken measures to counter a potential American attack involving the GBU-43/B, commonly known as the "Mother of All Bombs," the most powerful conventional bomb in the U.S. arsenal. His remarks followed reports that Trump was considering using the weapon in a future strike against Iran.
"Trump should be thinking about how to get his people out of the region safe and sound," Akhlaqi warned. "Let him try dropping one bomb, and then we'll see how many bodies he has to evacuate."
The new defense minister also claimed that Iran was relocating its military production facilities to more heavily protected locations. "We are not building new factories in their previous locations. Instead, we are building them inside mountains and fortified, secure structures," he said. "With our fingers on the trigger, we are prepared for war against the Zionists."
He further promised that an Iranian-made heavy fighter jet would take flight next year, describing it as an entirely domestically produced aircraft.
Iran says seven-day Hormuz deal remains on the table
Alongside the military threats, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran's proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz under a seven-day framework remained on the table, despite Trump's rejection of the plan last month.
"Our position is completely clear. We presented it to the United States in the form of a seven-day plan," Araghchi said. "If there is any sincerity on the American side, the path forward is clear: If the conditions are met, the strait will reopen on the sixth day and negotiations will resume on the seventh."
Iran's conditions include lifting the U.S. blockade of its ports, removing oil sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds and ending hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. Tehran is effectively seeking a return to the framework of a June memorandum of understanding under which Washington offered significant concessions. Trump, however, has shown no interest in returning to that arrangement and is demanding immediate nuclear concessions that Iran has refused to provide.
Amid the diplomatic deadlock, Iran has intensified attacks this month on oil tankers and commercial vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz under an American-led protection operation, seeking to disrupt traffic through the strategic waterway. Fuel prices have remained elevated despite Trump's statements that the strait is fully open.
The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports also remains in place, further straining an already deteriorating Iranian economy. Trump has signaled that he could resume military strikes after the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, raising the prospect of renewed fighting if negotiations fail.
Araghchi insisted Sunday that Tehran would not surrender in such a scenario. "We are better prepared for self-defense than ever before," he said. "At the same time, we remain open to the diplomatic path, provided it is conducted with respect and dignity and guarantees the rights of the Iranian nation."

Feast of grapes: A harvest tradition and travel experience in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

Feast of grapes: A harvest tradition and travel experience in Iran
TEHRAN - Held between August 21 and September 21 in different grape-growing regions of Iran, the feast of grapes is a traditional harvest celebration with roots believed to date back around 3,000 years.
When grapes reach full ripeness, the festival offers travelers an opportunity to experience Iran’s agricultural traditions, folk culture and living intangible heritage.
The celebration is particularly associated with Urmia and villages across West Azarbaijan province, where the traditional grape feast and Doushab-pazan --the preparation of grape juice and doushab, a thick grape syrup, have been registered as national intangible cultural heritage.
The tradition is believed to have originated in the ancient times as an expression of gratitude for the grape harvest. It later continued among Christian and Armenian communities in the region.
As mentioned by Visit Iran, the festival has been held in villages including Gerdabad, Digaleh, Resimanabad, Ghoshchi, Jamalabad and Goulan, with local communities maintaining their own customs.
Historically, grapes were regarded as a blessing, and some communities avoided eating the first grapes of the harvest before the ceremony. Care was also taken during harvesting to prevent grapes from falling to the ground, reflecting the belief that wasting the fruit was an act of ingratitude.
In the Urmia area, festivities traditionally take place around the vineyards and Lake Urmia. A central figure is the Il Bashi, or tribal leader, who opens the ceremony with words of thanks and a special prayer in Azarbaijani, followed by a Persian translation. Traditionally, the leader is accompanied by four women representing earth, water, air and fire, as well as a young boy and girl symbolizing the continuation of life.
The children distribute grapes to participants as a blessing. Prayers are offered for the protection of vineyards and crops from hail, storms and floods, followed by the traditional extraction of grape juice using specialized tools and equipment.
The festival then becomes a lively community celebration. Local wrestling competitions, Azerbaijani folk songs such as Qushmaja and Bayati, and traditional dances form part of the festivities. The collective Yali dance, performed by participants standing in a line, represents unity and togetherness.
Visitors may also encounter displays and competitions involving dried grapes and other products, including grape juice, vinegar and raisins.
For travelers, the feast of grapes provides more than a seasonal festival. It is an opportunity to enter the vineyards, meet local communities and observe traditions that connect agriculture with music, food, belief and collective memory. Held during the transition from summer to autumn, the celebration offers a distinctive way to discover the cultural landscape of northwestern Iran and the enduring traditions of the communities around Urmia.

New customs instructions drafted to reduce goods stoppage at borders

New customs instructions drafted to reduce goods stoppage at borders
TEHRAN- The Head of Iran Customs Administration announced the drafting of an executive instruction for customs facilitations aimed at speeding up goods clearance, reducing duplicate procedures, and smoothing truck movement at the country’s borders.
According to Mehr News Agency, Foroud Asgari, Head of Iran Customs Administration, speaking on the sidelines of a meeting at the Iran Chamber of Commerce, referred to the issues raised there regarding smoothing the entry and exit of goods, truck traffic at borders, goods valuation, guarantees, and percentage-based clearance of goods. He stated: “During the war period, we obtained a set of customs facilitations from authorized authorities, took them to the government, and had them approved. The President signed these approvals on 16 Mehr, and we are now preparing their executive instruction so that the provisions of the approval are implemented uniformly in customs offices across the country.”
Stating that the main focus of this instruction is preventing goods from stopping at the country’s entry and exit points, he added: “In the export area, we are seeking to have goods assessed using the capacity of inland customs offices so that shipments, after going through assessment procedures, are not stopped again at the borders.”
The Head of Iran Customs Administration, explaining the mechanism envisaged for controlling shipments at borders, said: “Risk management is applied at border entry points, and shipments that require further control based on risk assessment will be directed to the docks for necessary checks; but other goods should pass through the green lane based on mutual trust and the seal affixed by the customs of origin, in order to prevent duplicate controls and unnecessary stoppage.”
Asgari emphasized: “The goal is for customs controls to be carried out in proportion to the risk level of each shipment, and for goods that do not need re-examination to cross the border without imposing extra procedures and stoppage.”
Referring to the envisaged timing mechanism in the import area, he stated: “A specific time has been considered for the various agencies involved in the import process, and the agencies responsible for issuing permits must issue the relevant permits within the set deadline.”
The Head of Iran Customs Administration continued: “The responsible agencies must decide on imported goods and related processes within a specified timetable. If an agency does not act within the stipulated deadline, it must be accountable to the relevant authorities.”
Asgari added: “Customs will also extract information on the timing of processes and permit issuance and will provide performance reports on the agencies to the country’s authorities so that obstacles in the path of goods clearance are identified and followed up.”
Referring to the problems existing in the order registration and goods sampling processes, he said: “In drafting this approval, attention was paid to issues related to order registration, repeated sampling, and measures that were unnecessary but caused rework and increased process time, and we tried to envisage the necessary solutions to resolve these problems.”
The Head of Iran Customs Administration expressed hope that with the implementation of the new instruction, a significant change will occur in the process of goods entering and exiting the country’s customs points, and economic actors will be able to clear their goods more quickly and easily.
Asgari, in response to the issue of truck stoppage and traffic at the country’s borders and the measures taken to resolve this problem, stated: “Part of the existing issues must be followed up by Customs itself. In this regard, we have held border meetings with the heads of customs administrations of neighboring countries to achieve greater coordination for removing obstacles and increasing truck transit capacity.”
He added: “Meetings have been held with the heads of customs administrations of Armenia and the Republic of Azerbaijan, and this week the head of Turkmenistan’s customs administration was present on the soil of the Islamic Republic of Iran and negotiations were held in this regard. The other sides have also announced readiness to cooperate and increase truck transit capacity.”
The Head of Iran Customs Administration, referring to operational visits to important border customs offices of the country, said: “In these visits, problems related to various agencies and obstacles in the process of transit and goods clearance were examined. A significant part of these issues was raised in last week’s meeting with the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, many of which were solvable, and a number have also been resolved.”

Unknown Publisher

Crafting and playing the oud: A living musical heritage in Iran
TEHRAN – With its resonant melodies and distinctive pear-shaped body, the oud has long been part of the musical traditions of Iran and the wider West Aisa. Its craftsmanship and performance, sustained through generations of makers and musicians, received international recognition in 2022 when Iran and Syria jointly inscribed the tradition on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The inscription was approved during the 17th session of the Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, held in Rabat, Morocco, from Nov. 28 to Dec. 3, 2022. At the time, the addition brought the number of Iran’s inscribed intangible cultural heritage elements to 18.
The oud is a lute-like string instrument known for its warm, expressive sound. Musicians play it by resting the instrument on their leg, fingering the strings with one hand and plucking them with the other. Its ability to produce rich melodic and harmonic tones makes it suitable for solo performances as well as ensembles accompanying traditional songs and dances.
Crafting an oud requires patience and specialized woodworking skills. Its most distinctive component is a pear-shaped sound box, commonly made of walnut wood, which plays a central role in shaping the instrument’s resonance. According to the traditional methods described in Iran’s nomination, making an oud can take about 25 days, including stages of wood preparation and treatment. Water and steam are used to improve the wood’s durability and workability.
A typical oud has five pairs of strings, although some versions include a sixth string. Variations in construction and stringing allow musicians to produce a broad range of tones and adapt the instrument to different musical styles.
Beyond its physical form, the oud represents a body of knowledge encompassing material selection, woodworking, instrument construction and musical performance. Its historical presence is reflected in artistic depictions, literary works and miniature paintings, offering evidence of its place in the region’s cultural memory.
In southern Iran, the instrument and related musical traditions have particular significance among some Arab and Bakhtiari communities, especially in Khuzestan, Bushehr and Hormozgan provinces. Oud music is also practiced and appreciated in other parts of the country, including Tehran, Kurdistan, Shiraz, Isfahan and Khorasan.
The tradition continues through formal education and apprenticeship. Music schools, art centres, colleges and universities teach oud performance, while experienced musicians pass on their knowledge through direct instruction. Oud making, traditionally practiced predominantly by men, has also attracted increasing numbers of women, broadening participation in the craft.
Iran included the tradition on its National Heritage List in 2018, before submitting the multinational nomination with Syria for UNESCO recognition.
The inscription adds to Iran’s extensive record of intangible cultural heritage, which includes the Radif of Iranian music, the music of the Bakhshis of Khorasan, the art of crafting and playing the kamantcheh, traditional dotar craftsmanship, carpet weaving, Ta’zieh, Naqqali storytelling and the art of miniature.
The joint recognition of oud craftsmanship and performance highlights the importance of safeguarding living traditions that transcend national borders. Their continuity depends not only on preserving techniques and instruments but also on ensuring that the knowledge, music and cultural practices associated with them remain part of everyday life for future generations.

Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:22:24 UTC
22:22:24 KST

Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
A new study hints that eating blueberries daily could help improve mood in older adults, potentially through surprising effects on the gut microbiome.
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Hebrew SeniorLife Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research
- Summary:
- Eating blueberries every day could have surprising effects on mood, according to a small study that found greater reductions in depressive symptoms among older adults who consumed the fruit for three months. Researchers also detected changes in gut microbial enzymes, suggesting a possible gut-brain connection, although the mood benefits were not statistically significant compared with a placebo.
- Share:
A small pilot study suggests that eating blueberries every day may influence gut bacteria and potentially affect mood in older adults. Participants who consumed blueberries regularly experienced a greater and more consistent reduction in depressive symptoms, along with subtle changes in genes associated with gut microbial enzymes.
However, the improvements in depressive symptoms were not statistically significant when compared with the placebo group. Although the findings do not establish that blueberries can relieve depression, they offer preliminary clues about a possible connection between blueberry consumption, the gut microbiome, and mental health.
"Fiber and anthocyanins in blueberries have potential to modify the gut microbiome and metabolites that are relevant to depression in older adults," said lead author Courtney L. Millar, PhD, assistant scientist II at Hebrew SeniorLife's Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research and assistant professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. "Our objective was to preliminarily determine the effect of blueberry consumption on the gut microbiome, metabolites, and depressive symptoms."
Testing the Effects of Daily Blueberry Consumption
To investigate the potential connection, researchers recruited adults aged 65 and older who were physically inactive and experiencing mild depressive symptoms. The pilot study used a randomized, double-blind, parallel-arm, placebo-controlled design to evaluate whether consuming blueberries could influence gut microbes and mood.
Over three months, participants consumed either 48 grams of blueberry powder each day (approximately two cups of fresh berries) or a matching placebo powder.
Researchers examined the participants' gut microbiomes using metagenomic sequencing, which allowed them to measure the abundance of different microbial species and genes. They also used liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry to analyze gut-derived fecal short-chain fatty acids, compounds produced through microbial activity. Depressive symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires administered before and after the three-month intervention.
Blueberries Linked to Subtle Changes in Gut Microbial Activity
A total of 18 participants completed the study. Most were women, and the group was predominantly white (placebo group, n = 8; mean age: 75 ± 6; blueberry group, n = 10; mean age: 71 ± 4).
Despite the encouraging pattern in depressive symptoms among participants consuming blueberries, the researchers found no statistically significant difference in mood improvements between the blueberry and placebo groups.
The gut microbiome results also revealed a mixed picture. The overall abundance of microbial species, MetaCyc metabolic pathways, and short-chain fatty acid metabolites remained unchanged.
However, researchers identified statistically significant changes within the blueberry group in the abundance of genes associated with several gut microbial enzymes. One of these was EC 3.6.3.31 Polyamine Transporting ATPase, which is involved in the production of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a neurotransmitter that plays a role in brain signaling.
These findings suggest that blueberries may influence specific aspects of gut microbial function even without producing measurable changes in the overall composition of the microbiome. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these changes are connected to meaningful improvements in mood or depressive symptoms.
The study, "A pilot study of daily blueberry intake modulates the gut microbiota enzyme commissions in older, sedentary adults with mild depressive symptoms," was published in the Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging.
Other contributors included Mohit P. Chopra, MD, of the Deanna and Sidney Wolk Center for Memory Health at Hebrew SeniorLife and the Department of Psychiatry at UMass Chan Medical School; Xochitl Morgan, PhD, and Emily A. Green, PhD, of the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; Alex Wolfe of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife; Kerry A. Pierce of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; and Lidan Gao, PhD, and Christopher N. Blesso, PhD, of the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the University of Connecticut.
Additional contributors were Alyssa B. Dufour, PhD, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife and the Department of Medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School; Douglas P. Kiel, MD, MPH, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife, Harvard Medical School, and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; and Lewis A. Lipsitz, MD, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife and professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School.

New corridors help preserve country’s trade capacity: TPO official

Alejandro Davidovich Fokina ended Rafael Jodar's dream run at the Shanghai Masters on Sunday, battling back to beat his fellow Spaniard 1-6 7-6(5) 6-4 and clinch the biggest title of his career.
The 25th-seeded Davidovich Fokina is set to climb 13 places to a career-high world number 13 when the rankings are released on Monday.
Jodar, playing in his first Masters 1000 final and the youngest Shanghai finalist in tournament history, made a blistering start, broke for a 2-0 lead and again to take the opening set.
Davidovich Fokina recovered from a break down in the second set and saved break points in three successive service games before edging a tight tiebreak to force a decider.
The momentum swung decisively in Davidovich Fokina's favour when he broke the 12th-seeded Jodar twice and sealed victory in two hours and 27 minutes.
"I have a blank mind," Davidovich Fokina said. "I don't know what to say and I don't know how I feel. Just a huge relief.
"After the first set I had to keep trying, keep pushing. In the tiebreak, I believed in myself again. In the third set, maybe I had a bit more fitness physically."
It's the third ATP singles title of the 27-year-old's career, adding to his ATP 250 triumphs in Chengdu and Mallorca this season.
The first meeting between the two Spaniards pitted one of the ATP Tour's rising talents against a player enjoying the best season of his career.
The 20-year-old Jodar, who was ranked outside the world's top 900 little more than a year ago, strengthened his bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin in his first full season on tour. (Reuters)

Police pass the buck, IDF can't stop it: why settler violence goes unchecked in the West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

"It is important to understand the situation on the ground. Against Palestinian terrorists, we use every tool available, from M16 rifles to F16 fighter jets, and gather extensive intelligence. But when it comes to the 'blue side,' meaning Jews, the IDF is prohibited from gathering intelligence, and the tools at our disposal are far more limited," a security official told ynet just last week.
Two violent incidents over the weekend once again exposed the difficulties Israeli authorities face in confronting Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank. A Washington Post photographer was attacked during the olive harvest in Abu Falah, while diplomats from France and Belgium visiting the predominantly Christian Palestinian village of Taybeh were attacked on Saturday afternoon. The European Union condemned the incidents, demanding accountability and effective measures to prevent continued violence against Palestinians and journalists.
After months of attacks by Jewish extremists, the latest incidents have renewed questions about who is responsible for preventing the violence, why suspects repeatedly escape before security forces arrive and whether Israeli authorities have the resources and political backing to bring offenders to justice. Security officials sharply criticized the support extremists receive from elected officials. "There are members of Knesset and ministers who visit illegal outposts and give them their full support," one official said.
Police point to jurisdictional restrictions that complicate enforcement. Officers cannot operate independently in Area B of the West Bank, where many confrontations occur, without accompanying IDF forces. The weekend's attacks also took place in areas where Palestinian farmers were not required to coordinate their olive harvest with Israeli authorities, meaning security forces had not been deployed there beforehand. Police said they learned of the incidents only afterward, and no arrests were made because the suspects had fled before officers arrived. Police also cited insufficient cooperation involving the Foreign Ministry and the investigation as an obstacle to progress.
A police official told ynet that several agencies operate in the West Bank, each with different responsibilities. "Responsibility for preventing incidents on the ground is determined according to the law, the area and the missions assigned to each agency," the official said. "The police's responsibility for investigations and enforcement is not in question, but the distinction between that responsibility and the operational responsibility for prevention must not be blurred."
When security forces arrive at confrontations between Jewish extremists and Palestinians, their immediate priority is restoring order. By the time the situation is under control, many of those involved have escaped. Police stress that operational responsibility for Area B rests with the military, but the division of responsibilities has long been identified as a problem. In 2018, Israel's state comptroller urged police and the IDF to clarify their respective duties before and after police arrive at an incident and warned that poor coordination between police, the military and the Shin Bet could undermine law enforcement.
The IDF acknowledges the seriousness of the violence but says it cannot station troops at every potential flashpoint. Military officials estimate that doing so would require at least 10 additional battalions, diverting forces from other operational fronts. The military has already added two regular battalions, the headquarters of the 98th Division and Border Police companies, but officials say significant personnel shortages remain.
Investigations continue as suspects evade arrest
Police say investigations into the attacks on the Washington Post photographer and European diplomats remain in their early stages. Officers are working to identify suspects, collect evidence and prepare arrests. More than 70 indictments have been filed over Jewish nationalist violence in the past year, but security officials say closer coordination is still needed to ensure those responsible face justice. In some cases, arrested suspects have been released to house arrest or without restrictive conditions.
Security officials also criticized the judiciary's handling of certain cases. "There are judges who do not understand the gravity of the situation and release rioters who committed serious offenses, including attacking security personnel or violating orders," one official said. "On the other hand, there are judges who take a much tougher approach."
The latest violence occurred during the annual olive harvest, a period that regularly brings tensions over Palestinian access to agricultural land. Security officials pointed to messages circulated among West Bank residents ahead of the harvest, warning of olive-picking activities and military preparations, which they said were subsequently identified as part of a campaign. Over the weekend, Rabbi Dov Lior also published a letter declaring olive harvesting on Palestinian land permissible and even a religious obligation.
The attacks on a journalist and foreign diplomats have added an international dimension to a longstanding enforcement problem. When foreign nationals and diplomatic representatives are targeted, the consequences extend beyond the West Bank, potentially intensifying criticism of Israel and increasing pressure on its government to demonstrate concrete results.
For Israel, the challenge is twofold: preventing Jewish extremist violence and containing its diplomatic consequences. Without clearer responsibility, better coordination and sufficient forces on the ground, the gap between official condemnations and effective enforcement is likely to persist.

Gaza families fear food shortages as Israel halts commercial shipments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:16:13 UTC
22:16:13 KST

Gaza families fear food shortages as Israel halts commercial shipments
Gaza residents report rising prices after commercial shipments stopped, while families unable to afford extra supplies fear further shortages if the closure continues.
Gaza City, Gaza — Prices of basic goods are rising rapidly in Gaza, where Israeli restrictions on the import of commercial goods are in their fifth consecutive day.
Families already suffering from the siege on the enclave have started stocking up on goods they can still find, for fear of imminent shortages and continued price increases.
The cost of flour, eggs, onions and other staples has sharply increased since Wednesday, when Israel said that commercial goods would no longer enter Gaza. This comes amid a dispute over fees involving Palestinian merchants and Hamas, which still has some authority in the strip.
Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been plunged into poverty since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023. The price of basic goods has soared, as incomes have shrunk due to the war and Israel’s tightened siege.
Residents without the means to buy in bulk will have to continue to purchase food when they can. They will be worst hit by the daily price rises if the border remains closed.
Food shortages
The impact of the Israeli import restrictions is playing out in marketplaces, which are slightly busier than usual.
Ismail al-Barawi, 52, from Jabalia in northern Gaza, noticed a significant rise in prices within two or three days of the crossings being closed on Wednesday.
He described a recurring cycle of uncertainty in Gaza over the status of the crossings, which is usually followed by higher prices.
Al-Barawi said a carton of eggs that had cost 35 shekels ($11.34) was now selling for between 60 and 70 shekels ($18 to $21). The price of a kilogramme of onions had risen from five or six shekels ($1.50–$1.80) to between eight and 10 shekels ($2.40–$3), while a kilogramme of avocados had increased from seven or eight shekels ($2.10–$2.40) to around 15 shekels ($4.50).
“These increases happened in just two or three days,” he said, voicing concern about what prices would be if the crossings remain closed for another 10 to 15 days.
The increases have forced him to buy smaller quantities of what he needs. Instead of a full carton of 30 eggs, he might buy only four or five.
“Today, everyone is trading at the expense of the people. There is no mercy,” he said. He expressed frustration at traders, saying they raise prices as soon as they hear that crossings may remain closed, adding to the problem of real shortages.
Al-Barawi predicted that a 50 kg sack of flour could end up costing 200 or even 300 shekels ($60–$90), if the crossings remained closed.
Al-Barawi is responsible for providing food to his extended family of about 11 or 12 people, including his married daughters and their children. Whenever he has money, he prioritises basic goods such as flour, rice, cooking oil, onions and potatoes.
Given the uncertainty, it makes sense for Palestinians to stock up now before prices increase further. But many families in Gaza have no money to spare, he added.
“Some people cannot even afford to feed themselves for a day. How much can they save or store when they have no money?” he said.
But stockpiling also has its limits. Fresh vegetables can spoil within days, he said. Unreliable electricity supplies make it difficult to store meat for more than a brief period.
Questions on the suspension
Gaza’s Government Media Office on Thursday rejected Israel’s explanation for the suspension, denying that authorities in the territory had imposed taxes or government fees on commercial trucks.
The office said the 10,000-shekel ($3,242) amount cited by Israel was linked to a voluntary community fund intended to support vulnerable families and financial relief projects.
It also said measures requiring a 30 percent rate for cash transactions had been introduced in agreement with the Chamber of Commerce to address a shortage of cash liquidity and the circulation of worn-out banknotes.
The office accused Israel of using the dispute to impose further restrictions on supplies entering Gaza, which has been under an Israeli blockade since 2007.
Gaza authorities were not to blame for the reduction of trucks entering the enclave, it said, and called on mediators and international parties to push for the entry of 600 trucks a day, in line with existing agreements with Israel.
The office warned that continued restrictions would worsen the humanitarian and economic crisis in Gaza.
Food remains unaffordable for many households in Gaza. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that food prices in Gaza in September 2026 averaged 204 percent above pre-October 2023 levels, when the genocidal war on Gaza began and Israel tightened restrictions on goods entering the enclave. OCHA’s October 2 situation report, before the new border restrictions were imposed, documented the wider humanitarian pressures facing residents.
No money
Iman Atallah, a 50-year-old displaced woman living in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, said the suspension of food deliveries has brought back memories of the man-made famine which hit the enclave in 2025.
Atallah said the price of a sack of flour had already risen from between 25 and 35 shekels ($7.50–$10.50) before the closure to about 80 shekels ($24). With little income and a family to support, she said that even buying basic food had become increasingly difficult.
“Before the crossings closed, flour was affordable. We could somehow manage to buy it. Now it costs 80 shekels ($24),” she said.
The flour her family receives through aid distributions lasts less than a month. Fresh fruit and eggs are not completely unaffordable.
“We used to eat more, and we could buy eggs for the children. Now we’ve had to give those things up,” she said.
Her family now relies on rice and lentils, and they can afford only a little bread. Atallah said they sometimes skip breakfast or dinner, with lunch as their main meal of the day.
Atallah’s family is one of the many in Gaza unable to afford extra supplies and facing a bleak outlook if the crisis continues.
“We cannot stock up because we have no income,” she said. “If the crossings remain closed for 10 or 15 days, everything will become extremely expensive. Those who have money will stock up, while those who do not will just have to watch.”

Paris left reeling as student-led protests turn chaotic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:08:06 UTC
22:08:06 KST

Paris left reeling as student-led protests turn chaotic
Some 1,800 people arrested and hundreds injured during nationwide demonstrations attended by hundreds of thousands.
Paris residents tell Al Jazeera they’re dismayed by protest damage
Paris, France – France is counting the cost of a day of unrest after hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets nationwide, in the largest mobilisation since protests over education reforms and rising prices began last month.
At Place de la Republique, in the heart of the French capital, people on Sunday surveyed the previous day’s destruction in dismay: smashed windows, gutted buildings, looted shops.
“I find it unacceptable – absolutely unacceptable,” said Rabah, who has been living in Paris for more than 70 years. “Back in the day, we also demonstrated, but peacefully,” he said.
Staring at the burned skeleton of what used to be a newspaper stand, 56-year-old Claire was also shaken. “I love Paris so much, and seeing it like this makes me furious,” she said. “It’s absolutely appalling. I’m actually quite overcome with emotion.”
Nearby, the statue of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic, was covered in graffiti. “Those who sow misery reap anger,” read one inscription.
The student-led protests began in mid-September, caused by grievances ranging from overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages to systemic inequality and a lack of opportunity.
The movement quickly spilled out of the schoolyards and into the streets, tapping into broader social and economic anxieties.
On Saturday, these complaints converged in a mobilisation that saw a nationwide turnout of 550,000 people, according to authorities; unions and organisers put the estimate at 800,000.
But while the vast majority of demonstrators rallied peacefully, the scale of the violent unrest threatened to eclipse their message. In Paris, there was also heavy use of tear gas and stun grenades by the police, including before the start of the march, which set the tone for a tense day.
“I marched from the 10th arrondissement town hall to Place de Clichy. I was there from start to finish, and it was very peaceful – just all kinds of people, all of them nonviolent,” said Stephanie, a 23-year-old Parisian student.
“But once again, the violence was so spectacular that the actual message – the reasons behind the protesters’ grievances – was never conveyed,” she said.
Macron to address nation
French President Emmanuel Macron, whose second and final term ends next year, will give a televised address to the nation at 18:00 GMT on Sunday after meeting government ministers, his office announced.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said nearly 1,800 people had been arrested – almost half of them in Paris – and more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters had been injured in the unrest.
“Protesting is a fundamental right. Causing disorder through violence and in a concerted manner is not,” he said on Sunday.
During Saturday’s protest in Paris, Al Jazeera saw groups of black-clad, masked young men smashing shop windows with what appeared to be golf clubs before fleeing with bags of stolen goods.
In Marseille, France’s second-largest city, dozens of shops were looted and a group of people broke into the city hall before being forced out.
“Students and others have real claims they want to air which no one is listening to now because idiots are smashing everything,” said Benoit Payan, the city’s mayor.
In Limoges, footage showed flames engulfing the city hall as the fire spread through the historic building. Public buildings were also damaged in Bordeaux and other cities.
Police conduct has also come under scrutiny. France’s police inspectorate, the IGPN, had opened 36 investigations into alleged police violence since the high-school protests began, according to figures released by the Ministry of the Interior on October 13. The figure predates Saturday’s demonstrations.
Human rights lawyers have described some of their clients’ injuries as comparable to those seen in conflict zones. These include a minor who has lost his hand, another with his jaw smashed and a third pupil who lost sight in one eye.
“There is an increasingly systematic use of crowd-control measures that would normally be reserved for much more serious situations,” said Christophe Calvao, president of the Paris Young Lawyers’ Union. “This only serves to inflame tensions and make people even angrier.”
The government now faces the challenge of responding to widespread social discontent while trying to pass a budget aimed at bringing France’s public finances under control.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wants to reduce the country’s deficit through spending restraint and tax measures – a move that will likely deepen public anger. Cuts to France’s generous welfare system have traditionally faced strong public resistance.
All of this takes place in a highly toxic political environment as parties harden their positions ahead of next year’s presidential election.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, the leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party and potential presidential contender who has sought to appeal to young voters, accused the government of fuelling the unrest.
“In Paris, aberrant leadership has opened the door to chaos. Those in charge no longer know what to do; the rank and file are afraid and are running wild,” he said.
Lecornu hit back. “This is YOUR political responsibility,” said the prime minister on social media, accusing far-left groups of orchestrating the violence.

Nearly NIS 800 for a family outing: Israel’s Hanukkah Festigal ticket prices skyrocketing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:06:12 UTC
22:06:12 KST

An Israeli family buying four full-price main-hall tickets to Festigal, one of the country’s best-known Hanukkah children’s shows, would pay NIS 796 this year, after prices rose by up to 7.8%.
That bill covers admission alone, before transportation, food, or other expenses associated with a family outing.
Hanukkah is a busy season for children’s entertainment in Israel. During the school holiday, theaters and entertainment venues stage musicals, plays, and other family performances. Festigal is among the most prominent productions, bringing together Israeli singers and actors in an annual musical built around a new storyline.
This year’s production, Top Secret Festigal, is scheduled to open on November 28 at Expo Tel Aviv. Its cast includes Israeli pop singer Noa Kirel, entertainer Ran Danker, and actress Eliana Tidhar, with Eden Ben Zaken appearing as a guest singer.
According to a price comparison compiled by Shelcha, an Israeli consumer benefits club, Festigal’s full ticket prices increased by NIS 10 in each of its three seating categories compared with 2025.
Main-hall seats rose from NIS 189 to NIS 199, an increase of approximately 5.3%. Lower-tier seats increased from NIS 159 to NIS 169, or 6.3%, while upper-tier tickets rose from NIS 129 to NIS 139, a 7.8% increase.
Holiday attractions becoming financially challenging for families
“Hanukkah is a holiday of light and miracles, but for many families, spending on outings and attractions also becomes a financial challenge,” said Sigalit Cohen-Baruch, CEO of Shelcha.
“When you add the costs of other outings throughout the holiday, you realize that every purchasing decision can affect the family budget,” she said.
The comparison also showed how membership benefits can change the cost of the same show. Consumer clubs and bank-card programs offer eligible customers discounted tickets, with prices and purchase limits varying by program.
Shelcha said its members could buy main-hall tickets for NIS 95 and upper-tier seats for NIS 45. The latter price represented a discount of approximately 67.6% from the full price.
Hever, a benefits organization serving career military personnel and retirees, offered still lower prices in the comparison: NIS 69 for the main hall and NIS 29 for the upper tier.
Bank customers may also qualify for discounts. Mizrahi-Tefahot advertised Festigal tickets ranging from NIS 59 to NIS 119 through its cardholder benefits program, with a limit of two tickets per code and eligibility tied to qualifying card spending.
Holiday children's entertainment shows similar price gaps
Similar price gaps appeared elsewhere in the holiday entertainment market. Motek Forever, a separate production aimed at younger children, was listed at a full price of NIS 159, compared with NIS 59 through Shelcha and NIS 39 through Hever.
In a response published by the Hebrew-language newspaper Israel Hayom, Festigal’s organizers said they offered several price tiers and special arrangements through organizations and workers’ committees to help families afford tickets.
Cohen-Baruch recommended setting a holiday budget before booking and comparing offers across ticket sellers and membership programs. The final cost depends on which performances and seats are available, how many discounted tickets a family is entitled to buy, and whether it meets the program’s conditions.

IRGC profiting from sex trafficking of Iranian women, using children for proxy wars - JCFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:06:03 UTC
22:06:03 KST

Iranian women, undocumented migrants, children, and refugees are being exploited by the Islamic Republic, specifically the IRGC, to finance and support its proxy wars across the region, according to an analysis published last week by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).
Ella Rosenberg, a senior research fellow at the JCFA and a member of the Dvorah Forum, said Iran’s legal framework allows the regime to project an image of compliance with international anti-trafficking regulations while relying on flawed legislation that falls short of international standards and fails to adequately protect victims.
She noted that the Islamic Republic conflates human trafficking with migrant smuggling, and the regime has consistently refused to ratify the 2000 United Nations Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons (the Palermo Protocol).
IRGC directly benefiting from sex trafficking, Israeli study finds
Beyond failing to protect victims, Rosenberg assessed that the IRGC directly benefits from human trafficking. She noted that the IRGC uses the sex trafficking sector, often facilitated by the regime through temporary marriages, as a major source of income.
Rosenberg described Iran as a source, transit, and destination country for the sex trafficking of women and girls, citing widespread poverty, systemic corruption, and economic mismanagement as contributing factors.
She argued that Article 1041 of Iran’s Civil Code, which permits girls to marry at 13 and even younger girls to marry with parental permission and court approval, has helped normalize the sexual exploitation of minors.
Rosenberg also linked the practice of nikah mut’ah, a temporary marriage contract agreed upon for a predetermined period, to the exploitation of vulnerable women and girls for the benefit of organized trafficking networks.
Trafficking networks move victims within Iran and across its borders into neighboring countries, including Iraq, with the alleged support of the IRGC, according to Rosenberg. She said that the scale of cross-border sex trafficking could not be sustained without the IRGC’s complicity, given its role in border control and the intelligence apparatus’s oversight of internal security checkpoints and airports.
Adding more weight to her analysis, human rights groups, including the IHR Monitoring and Evaluation Framework and HRANA, have documented allegations that IRGC commanders accepted bribes to facilitate the passage of trafficking victims.
Rosenberg added that the IRGC profits directly from the exploitation of Iranian women by taxing the commercial sex trade.
IRGC exploiting Afghan, Pakistani refugees
In addition to financially benefiting from human trafficking, the JCFA report said that the IRGC’s Quds Force and the Basij systematically traffic undocumented migrants, refugees, and children to “sustain their proxy wars across the Middle East.”
The IRGC exploits vulnerable populations, particularly Afghan and Pakistani refugees, to recruit fighters through deception, financial coercion, and threats of deportation, she said. Individuals harvested from these communities are coerced into joining proxy militias like the Fatemiyoun and the Zainabiyoun Brigades, for deployment in foreign countries like Iraq.
Additionally, in violation of international law, the Basij systematically recruits and coerces Iranian children as young as 12 into military indoctrination and combat support roles. This was argued to be a severe form of human trafficking, as the recruitment exploits children’s vulnerability to coerce them into hazardous, involuntary servitude in military environments.
Though JCFA warns of the abuse of children aged 12 and up, The Jerusalem Post has previously reported on the death of an 11-year-old Basij member who was killed at a checkpoint in Iran.
Rather than directly profiting from the trafficking of vulnerable individuals into the IRGC, Rosenberg suggested, the financial gain can be categorized as cost avoidance rather than revenue.
She argued that instead of deploying trained members of the IRGC, which the regime would have to pay and has invested in, the system can deploy underpaid or unpaid vulnerable groups who are deemed disposable because of their lack of funded training.
Such deployments were estimated to save the Islamic Republic billions of dollars in military expenditure, freeing funds to be redirected into the IRGC’s domestic corporate monopolies and regional terrorist financing networks.
Again, Iran’s “tax” system also allows it to benefit from migrants transiting from Pakistan and Afghanistan who are hoping to reach Europe through Iran and Turkey.
Such migrants are also routinely subjected to debt bondage, extortion, and forced labor in Iran’s informal agricultural and construction sectors to pay off exorbitant smuggling fees by criminal networks that pay protection money to the IRGC. This alone is estimated to generate billions of dollars for Iran’s shadow economy.
Focus on Iran's nuclear program may distract from IRGC human trafficking
Rosenberg noted that Iran was able to continue to exploit these systems as sanctions from the EU and US have primarily focused on Tehran’s nuclear proliferation, ballistic missile development, support for regional terrorism, and suppression of domestic dissent. Failing to also sanction the IRGC and the front companies it uses for human trafficking continues to provide Tehran a lifeline.
Given that the funds raised by human trafficking are often liquid, Rosenberg also alerted to the fact that it was hard for international systems to monitor how much wealth Iran is accumulating through these sources.
Individuals involved in facilitating or covering for regime-backed smuggling networks can therefore continue to travel, use regional banks, and manage front companies without fear of asset freezes or international arrest warrants.
To prevent Iran from continuing to profit from human trafficking, Rosenberg advised that the US Treasury Department utilize the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act to designate IRGC border commanders, Basij recruitment officers, and complicit Iranian law enforcement officials for their roles in labor and sex trafficking.
She added that the European Commission must also use the Sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (AMLD6) to require European financial institutions to aggressively monitor illicit financial flows generated by Iranian trafficking networks.

Israeli court orders seven to repay NIS 1.85m in misused cancer donations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:05:23 UTC
22:05:23 KST

The Haifa District Court has ordered seven people who ran two linked charities to personally repay NIS 1.85 million after finding that a donation intended to help children and teenagers with cancer was diverted to another organization and spent outside its approved purpose.
Senior Judge Ron Sokol ruled that the officials breached their duties by allowing the transfer, submitting misleading reports and failing to account adequately for the money. His October 8 decision also found that substantial sums were paid unlawfully to the charities’ leading figure, attorney Galit Pauker Shemesh, as salary and rent.
The ruling, announced by the Justice Ministry on Sunday, concerns the charities, Keren L’Chaim and Keren L’Chaim L’Yeladim V’Noar (for children and youth), both ordered by the court to close in 2024.
All seven must repay the money, and any one of them can be required to cover the full amount still owed. Interest and inflation adjustments will be added from April 2019. They were also ordered to pay a total of NIS 20,000 in legal costs.
Donation intended to support children with cancer
The money came from the estate of Helen Hatab. Her estate administrator told the court that she had been a teacher and had suffered from cancer, leading him to propose using part of her estate to support children and teenagers with the disease.
A family court approved the arrangement in March 2019. The program was to provide educational support during illness, guidance for recovering patients and funding for equipment, medicines and treatment through the original Keren L’Chaim charity.
But the bank details supplied for the transfer belonged to the newer organization, Keren L’Chaim L’Yeladim V’Noar. The family court did not approve transferring the donation to a different charity or using it for a different purpose.
The First International Bank of Israel (FIBI) initially refused to transfer the money after identifying the mismatch between the approved recipient and the account. The charities subsequently opened accounts at Bank Mizrahi-Tefahot, where the donation was deposited in the newer charity’s account in April 2019.
Sokol also found that a document submitted to FIBI had been altered to replace the original charity’s registration number with that of the newer organization.
Charity officials defend spending on hostel renovations
The seven argued that the money had supported legitimate charitable work, principally renovations at Beit Keren, a hostel for at-risk girls in Hadera. Pauker Shemesh maintained that the estate administrator had approved redirecting funds, that she had provided evidence of the renovation costs and other expenses, and that her salary and rent payments were justified and approved.
The other six argued that they had volunteered, received no personal benefit, and relied on Pauker Shemesh and professional advisers to oversee the finances.
The court rejected those defenses. The approved cancer-support program could not simply be replaced with another charitable project without the required approval, Sokol found. He concluded that transferring the donation and changing its purpose were intended to evade scrutiny of the original charity and allow the officials to continue handling donations without restrictions.
The officials said that roughly NIS 1m. had been spent on the hostel, but did not provide sufficient invoices, plans or other evidence to establish that expenditure. A promised expert assessment of the work’s value was never submitted.
Sokol accepted that some renovation work had taken place. In calculating the repayment, he deducted NIS 41,621 for that work, using the amount recorded in the charity’s financial report.
Court orders repayment of salary and rent
Pauker Shemesh was separately ordered to return NIS 180,390 in salary and NIS 112,110 in rent, plus interest and inflation adjustments. Any salary and rent she returns will reduce the total amount the seven must repay.
Sokol acknowledged that the officials had genuinely wanted to help people in need and had done so for years. But he found that the money had also been used improperly for personal benefits, mainly for Pauker Shemesh, and that the other officials’ failure to oversee spending had allowed this to happen.
“We cannot accept the respondents’ claim that they are exempt from any duty merely because they acted as volunteers,” Sokol wrote.
Trusting that nobody was pocketing money was no substitute for checking that donations were used for their intended purpose, he added.
