====================================================================================================

Genes linked to educational attainment are also tied to fewer behavior problems in kids, mainly through cognitive pathways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:00:27 UTC
22:00:27 KST

A recent study indicates that genetic variants associated with higher educational attainment are also linked to lower levels of some behavioral and emotional difficulties in children and adolescents, particularly attention problems and stress-related physical complaints. These associations appear to run mainly through the part of the polygenic index tied to cognitive test performance rather than through its non-cognitive part, with the strongest patterns emerging in girls. The findings, published in Behavior Genetics, offer new perspective on how polygenic indices related to educational attainment track with youth mental health and everyday emotional development.
In behavioral genetics, researchers use a tool called a polygenic index, or PGI, to summarize statistical patterns across the human genome. Rather than measuring a fixed internal trait or an inborn biological essence, a PGI is a mathematical summary that adds up a vast number of tiny DNA associations identified in large population studies. When applied to complex outcomes like educational attainment, which reflects total years of formal schooling, these indices capture an intertwined mixture of genetic variation, social structures, and environmental opportunities.
Researchers often classify childhood behavioral challenges into two broad categories: internalizing and externalizing problems. Internalizing problems refer to difficulties directed inward, such as anxiety, sadness, social withdrawal, and physical complaints like stomachaches linked to emotional distress. Externalizing problems refer to outward-directed behaviors, such as rule-breaking and aggression, which disrupt home or classroom settings. Some areas, including attention problems, social problems, and unusual thoughts, fall between these two categories.
Untangling how genes relate to these behaviors within families is complicated because parents provide both their DNA and the home environment. In a 2018 study, researchers demonstrated that parental genetics influence children partly by shaping the rearing environment, a dynamic known as genetic nurture. Because of this environmental pathway, simply linking a child’s genes to their behavior can be misleading unless researchers account for parental DNA to isolate direct genetic associations.
At the same time, educational outcomes reflect many personal qualities beyond standardized test performance, such as persistence, curiosity, and emotional stability. Using a technique called GWAS-by-subtraction (GWAS stands for genome-wide association study, the large genetic surveys used to build these indices), a 2021 study split the genetic signal for educational attainment into two parts: one linked to performance on cognitive tests, and a “non-cognitive” remainder capturing everything else, such as traits tied to motivation or personality. This separation allowed scientists to test whether the genetics of educational attainment operate primarily through cognitive channels or through broader behavioral tendencies.
Separately, a 2020 study demonstrated that a child’s educational attainment PGI was related to having fewer attention and hyperactivity symptoms, even after controlling for parental DNA. Problem behavior is typically grouped with non-cognitive, or socioemotional, skills, which made it a natural test case for whether the decomposed PGIs relate to behavior in expected ways. This prompted the current research team to explore which specific genetic pathways associate with behavioral difficulties and whether these links differ by sex or informant.
“The educational attainment polygenic index (EA PGI) has become a very powerful predictor in sociogenomics, and is also being adopted into other fields like economics and sociology,” explained lead author Lyydia Alajääskö, a Ph.D. researcher in economics at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam in the field of genoeconomics. “I was motivated to better understand what exactly the EA PGI signal contains.”
“From economic theory, we have two types of skills that predict later-life success, cognitive and non-cognitive skills,” Alajääskö told PsyPost. “I was able to test whether the cognitive/non-cognitive distinction holds up when you look at a behavior that should sit clearly on one side of it: childhood problem behavior. This is a novel test of this theory and a novel use of the decomposition approach.”
To investigate these questions, the research team analyzed genetic and behavioral records from the Lifelines study, a multi-generation health project based in the northern Netherlands. The analysis focused on 4,008 unique children and adolescents between 4 and 17 years old who contributed 7,787 total observations across multiple survey waves. All participants were of European genetic ancestry, and most observations relied on at least one parent’s genome being statistically reconstructed rather than directly measured.
Behavioral difficulties were evaluated using standardized surveys from the widely used Achenbach assessment system. Parents completed surveys evaluating their children’s behavior across 4,611 observations, while adolescents aged 13 to 17 completed self-report questionnaires across 3,176 observations. These surveys measured eight specific behavioral areas, ranging from anxiety and physical distress to attention difficulties and aggressive actions.
The authors constructed overall educational attainment PGIs for each participant and separated them into cognitive (Cog) and non-cognitive (NonCog) components. They estimated regression models that controlled for the child’s sex, age, birth year, survey wave, and broad ancestral background, applying a strict statistical threshold to guard against false discoveries. By comparing models with and without parental PGIs, the team separated the child’s direct genetic associations from indirect family-wide effects, calling an association robust if it held up after parents’ PGIs were taken into account.
The findings indicated that youth with higher overall educational attainment PGIs tended to show lower levels of some problem behaviors, but the robust associations were limited to a few areas. These associations ran mainly through the cognitive component of the PGI rather than the non-cognitive component. Specifically, higher values on the cognitive component were robustly linked to fewer attention problems in parent reports and fewer physical complaints tied to emotional distress in youth self-reports. The cognitive component was also associated with fewer anxious or depressed symptoms in parent reports, though this pattern was less consistent across model specifications.
By comparison, the non-cognitive component showed weaker and less consistent associations with youth behavior that were not statistically robust across the main models.
“However, this alone is not enough to conclude the non-cognitive pathway is insignificant or not relevant,” Alajääskö noted. “We could lack power to detect effects, and there are statistical limitations to the GWAS-by-subtraction decomposition in the first place. If anything, our results hint that the cognitive/non-cognitive distinction might partly reflect a shared underlying domain rather than fully separate pathways – though that remains speculative.”
Parents’ own PGIs were not statistically significant predictors of children’s problem behavior in the main models. This suggests the associations were not mainly explained by the home environments that parents’ genetics help shape, though the study had limited power to detect small indirect effects. The authors also note that even these direct associations are not purely biological, since they can include how children’s traits shape the responses they draw from others.
When the authors analyzed boys and girls separately, pronounced differences emerged between the sexes. Among girls, the cognitive component robustly predicted lower levels of anxious or depressed symptoms, unusual or obsessive thoughts, attention problems, and aggression in parent reports. In girls’ self-reports, the overall PGI was robustly linked to fewer physical complaints and internalizing symptoms, while the cognitive component held up only for physical complaints. For boys, several initial associations were present, but none remained statistically robust once parental PGIs were included in the model.
The type of survey respondent also mattered. In the full sample, the link between the cognitive component and fewer physical complaints was stronger in self-reports than in parent reports, while differences between informants were negligible for other behaviors. Among boys, no educational attainment PGI was significantly associated with self-reported behavior.
The authors suggested that cognitive skills and behavioral regulation might share an underlying neurocognitive foundation, such as executive functioning capacities like working memory and self-control. They emphasized, however, that because executive function was not directly measured, this explanation remains speculative.
Martin Fieder, an associate professor of evolutionary demography at the University of Vienna who was not involved in the research, described the work as methodologically sophisticated. “The main message is that the genetic association between educational attainment and childhood problem behavior seems to operate more through the cognitive component of the genetics of educational attainment (i.e., performance on cognitive tests) rather than through the ‘non-cognitive’ component (i.e., the remaining component of genetic variation associated with educational attainment).”
“Accordingly, genetic differences associated with better cognitive performance and higher educational attainment also appear to be associated with fewer behavioral problems, providing evidence for genetic overlap between cognitive performance and childhood behavioral regulation.”
“The study confirms previously reported genetic overlap between educational attainment and childhood problem behavior, but extends this work by showing that the association appears to be driven predominantly by the cognitive component of educational-attainment-related genetic variation,” Fieder observed.
The results are consistent with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that higher intelligence was slightly associated with fewer behavioral and emotional difficulties, a link partly driven by shared genetic factors. While that earlier work evaluated directly tested IQ in seven-year-old twins, the current study examined genome-wide PGIs across children and adolescents aged 4 to 17.
As with all research, there are several caveats to keep in mind, particularly regarding how PGIs are interpreted. “This paper explicitly rejects notions of genetic determinism: our results don’t mean problem behavior is ’caused’ by genes, nor that outcomes are fixed,” Alajääskö emphasized. “PGIs are statistical summaries of genetic associations shaped by and reflecting the environmental and social structures in which genetic differences are expressed.”
“Relatedly, generalizability is a real question: genetic results in general are not representative of the world’s population, as there is a bias toward studies on individuals with European ancestry, partly driven by data availability,” Alajääskö added. “Secondly, genetic studies are also not representative of European country nationals: participants tend to be more educated, healthier, have higher socioeconomic status, and be slightly more female. For instance, our study uses a single cohort from a sub-region of the Netherlands, a country with low socioeconomic inequality and universal access to high-quality education.”
Beyond broad demographic questions, parental ratings introduce an additional layer of complexity, as ratings may partly reflect a parent’s own personality, stress levels, or expectations rather than objective child behavior. These parental perceptions can complicate comparisons across informants, especially when looking at internalizing symptoms like anxiety or physical complaints that children may feel more acutely than parents observe.
Evaluating such intricate genetic models also presents a distinct challenge for non-specialists. “A general reader is unlikely to be familiar with this kind of genetic analysis, and overall, the methods used are not easy to evaluate, even for someone like me who also works in behavioral genetics,” Fieder told PsyPost. “However, some of the authors are leading researchers in the field, which gives me confidence in the quality of the data analysis and the interpretation of the findings.”
Statistical power is another point to consider. While the sample was large enough to detect moderate direct genetic effects, it had more limited power to detect very small associations, which could partly explain why associations with the non-cognitive component were not statistically reliable.
Looking toward future research, Fieder emphasized the need for replication. “As always, I would like to see a replication study using an independent dataset,” he said.
The study, “Genetics of Educational Attainment and Childhood Problem Behavior: Direct Genetic Effects, Cognitive Pathways, and Sex Differences,” was authored by Lyydia Alajääskö, Marina Aguiar-Palma, Abdel Abdellaoui, and Titus Galama.

I’m a journalist. Israel detained me for documenting the olive harvest in the West Bank.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Being detained by the Zionist state was never outside the realm of possibility. As a journalist reporting from Palestine, I considered it as likely as it was foreseeable, and for years I had been making an effort to ensure that, when it happened, I would be prepared. Above all, I wanted to put as few Palestinians as possible at risk.
I have been reporting from Palestine for almost 10 years. The first time I went, in 2017, the fear of being denied entry led me to delete every Palestinian contact from my phone, every possible connection to Palestine from my social media accounts, and every note in my notebooks. It was a waste of time. When I landed at the airport, when I went through security on my way back, and at every checkpoint in the West Bank, I was asked no more than a couple of questions. In the years that followed, I published journalistic reports and opinion pieces, nurtured friendships, and gave press interviews. It was no longer possible, even if I had wanted to, to hide my solidarity with the Palestinian people’s resistance to the Zionist colonial project. Anyone could find it simply by typing my name into an online search engine. Even so, every time I traveled, I continued to enter and leave without being asked many questions.
But over the past few years, everything has escalated, not only in Gaza, with the intensification of the genocide, but also in the West Bank: settler attacks, the expansion of settlements, the militarization of the colony, checkpoints at village entrances, killings, administrative detentions, torture in prisons. The deportation strategy targeting international visitors in the territory has also escalated. Over the past three years in particular, dozens upon dozens of volunteers and journalists from other countries have been detained by the Zionist military and deported from Palestine. Last week, it was my turn.
The morning began early on Thursday, October 8. Together with four other Portuguese companions, I left Ramallah at 6:00 a.m. for the village of Rantis, trying to avoid the many checkpoints being arbitrarily set up to close roads throughout the West Bank. It took us almost two hours to cover 25 miles (40 kilometers), crossing two military checkpoints along the way. When we arrived at our meeting point, a group of 23 people — mostly Palestinians, along with some anti-Zionist Israelis (or Hebrew speakers, as some identify themselves in a deliberate rejection of the Israeli identity) — made their way to an olive grove with around 700 olive trees, according to one of the family members who had planted them. The grove was so close to one of the settlements that, since 2023, the family had been unable to harvest their olives. Whenever they tried, they were attacked by soldiers or settlers.
This time, things were different. Throughout the morning, we picked many pounds of olives from dozens of trees. Although we felt the need to look toward the top of the hill every few minutes to make sure no settlers or soldiers were coming our way, there was no sign of danger for more than four hours. That alone was surprising. Of the roughly 10 days I spent harvesting olives last year, there was only one when our group was not attacked by settlers or soldiers. According to the United Nations, between October 1st and November 10th last year, there were more than 160 attacks from settlers in almost 100 towns and villages. More than 150 Palestinians were injured.
Everything changed at 12:35 p.m. I wrote in my notebook: “A drone is now hovering over our heads. People stop for a moment and look up, but they quickly go back to picking olives.” My experience harvesting olives in 2025 had taught me what would happen next: about half an hour later, an army vehicle arrived near where we were picking. A little while later, three soldiers wearing balaclavas or scarves approached us and informed us that we could not be there. The Palestinian owner of the olive grove refused to leave — it was his grove. The soldiers backed away and stood further away, holding their phones as though they were waiting for orders from their superiors. At 2:03 p.m., I wrote my final note: “Another army vehicle arrives.”
What happened next unfolded in an instant. Six soldiers carrying weapons, with their faces covered, approached the group in an intimidating manner, forcing everyone to leave. There was no resistance whatsoever. Everyone decided to leave the olive grove and head toward the center of the village. It was a long walk, perhaps a mile and a quarter along a dirt road. The soldiers escorted us from their military vehicles until they decided to get out and run toward one of our Portuguese companions, Fred. He had been documenting the Zionist soldiers’ actions on his phone, as almost everyone else had (some of the footage he recorded in the preceding weeks can be seen on the Estórias da Palestina Instagram page). Fred was immediately singled out and detained, without any formal explanation.
“All of you are a danger to my… friends. So take a step back,” said one of the female soldiers, who later introduced herself as Dana. She was 23 years old. She was the oldest person in the entire group. It took dozens of questions before we were finally given a reason for the detention: “This is a military area,” she eventually replied. We asked for documentation proving that the area had officially been designated a military zone and that our presence there had been prohibited. Nothing. But it is hardly relevant whether soldiers produce evidence: arriving at a place where Palestinians are harvesting olives and declaring it a closed military zone on the spot is entirely routine in the West Bank. I have seen it happen more than a dozen times. It is perhaps the military tactic most commonly used to restrict Palestinians’ access to their own land.
I continued doing my job: documenting. Then, when another military vehicle arrived, the soldiers decided they wanted to detain me, too. I showed them my press credentials and explained that I was working, but none of that mattered. I was taken to Fred, handcuffed, and we were both put inside a military vehicle. We were detained for over two days, moving between a military base, a police station, and a prison used to hold immigrants, before being deported to Portugal on Saturday.
Rather than describe the conditions of our detention — which were, from the outset, incomparable to the brutality endured by Palestinians in prison — I believe what matters now is reflecting on why we, and so many other international visitors in recent years, were detained.
One might think the reason for my detention was simply that I had been found in what the military claimed was a closed military zone, the first justification given back in Rantis. One might think it was actually related to my alleged “support for and promotion of support for terrorist organizations,” the accusation leveled against me when I was interrogated for several hours by an investigator of the Zionist state. Or perhaps it had to do with the journalism I had done and the opinions I had published over the years. During the interrogation, I was shown a dossier dated late 2025, containing dozens upon dozens of screenshots collected since October 2023. They included quotations from articles I had written, interviews I had given, descriptions of my work, and many, many posts from my personal Instagram account.
But none of these is the reason for our detention. These are merely narratives the Zionist state invents to try to legitimize detention, imprisonment, and deportation. The reason is much simpler: the Zionist state detained us in an attempt to prevent international observers from witnessing and reporting on the ethnic cleansing project underway in the West Bank, so that it can continue carrying out the genocide of the Palestinian people in the shadows.
It is entirely possible that this text, like the ones I have published before, is being read by the Zionist colony. We are not afraid of you. On the contrary, these detentions make one thing clear: the colonial regime that has occupied Palestine for more than 100 years is very much afraid of people who travel to Palestine to do just one thing — stand alongside the Palestinian people, picking olives, accompanying shepherds as they take their goats and sheep out to graze, staying awake through the night to keep watch over settlers, holding up phones and cameras to document daily attacks, and, above all, returning home to tell the world what they witnessed.
The fact that the Zionist state feels compelled to devote so many resources to this strategy says a great deal about its weakness and about the importance of having people on the ground who have the privilege of holding European passports and having the skin color conventionally referred to as white.
So there is only one response: return, return, and return again. Let the detention of two people lead to dozens more traveling to the West Bank. The olive harvest campaign has only just begun.

Magic mushroom ingredient takes the fight out of aggressive fish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:52:13 UTC
21:52:13 KST

Magic mushroom ingredient takes the fight out of aggressive fish
Scientists discovered that the psychedelic compound in magic mushrooms can calm highly aggressive fish without disrupting their normal social behavior.
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- A psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms appears to have an unexpected effect: calming highly aggressive fish. Researchers discovered that low doses of psilocybin significantly reduced aggressive attacks in mangrove rivulus fish without disrupting their normal social interactions. The findings suggest psilocybin may selectively calm escalating aggression rather than simply suppressing all behavior.
- Share:
Psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, appears to have an unexpected effect on aggressive fish. Most mushrooms containing this compound belong to the gilled mushroom genus Psilocybe. In mammals, psilocybin interacts with serotonin receptors in the brain, influencing emotions and behaviors such as mood, appetite, and aggression. However, scientists still know relatively little about how the substance affects social interactions among animals.
To investigate this question, researchers in Canada examined the effects of psilocybin on the amphibious mangrove rivulus fish (Kryptolebias marmoratus). Their findings, published in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, suggest that even a brief exposure to a low dose can significantly reduce aggressive behavior without disrupting normal social interactions.
"We show that an acute, low dose of psilocybin significantly reduces activity and aggressive attack behavior during social interactions in adult mangrove rivulus fish, a species that is naturally highly aggressive," said first author Dayna Forsyth, a research associate and former MSc student at Acadia University in Nova Scotia.
"These findings provide the first evidence that psilocybin can selectively reduce escalated aggression in a vertebrate model without suppressing social interaction," added senior author Dr. Suzie Currie, a biologist at The University of British Columbia.
Why Scientists Studied Aggressive Mangrove Rivulus Fish
Mangrove rivulus fish are naturally combative, particularly when they encounter another member of their species. Their aggressive responses are easy to recognize and measure, allowing researchers to detect even small changes in behavior.
These fish also have an unusual reproductive ability. They can fertilize themselves, producing offspring that are genetically identical. This makes them especially useful for experiments because scientists can minimize genetic variation and more confidently attribute behavioral differences to psilocybin rather than inherited traits.
For the experiment, the researchers worked with three genetically distinct lines of fish bred in the laboratory. One group received psilocybin, another provided the fish used to provoke social interactions, and the third helped researchers measure how much psilocybin entered and accumulated in the animals' bodies.
The researchers first established a baseline for each fish's behavior. They placed a fish into a tank already occupied by another fish, with the two separated by a fiberglass mesh barrier and an opaque cover. The mesh prevented physical contact while allowing the fish to see and smell each other once the cover was removed.
After allowing five minutes for the fish to adjust to their shared environment, the team removed the opaque cover and recorded their interactions.
The following day, 24 hours after the initial observation, the researchers placed the same fish in water containing dissolved psilocybin. Following 20 minutes of exposure, they returned it to the tank with the same fish it had encountered previously. The opaque cover was then removed again so the researchers could observe any changes in behavior.
Magic Mushroom Compound Reduces Aggressive Attacks
The results revealed a striking change. Fish exposed to psilocybin moved around less and displayed fewer bursts of aggressive swimming than fish that had not received the substance.
To assess these changes, the scientists measured overall activity (time spent moving) and several signs of aggression (including swimming bursts). These rapid bursts are particularly important because they indicate that an encounter is escalating toward an attack, even when the fish cannot make physical contact.
"Swimming bursts are high-energy attack behaviors that represent an escalation of aggression towards the stimulus fish without making physical contact," explained Currie. "Other types of aggressive behaviors, like head-on displays, are more about communication and social assessment and require very little energy."
Interestingly, psilocybin did not suppress every form of aggressive or social behavior. While the fish became less likely to engage in intense, energy-demanding attacks, their less physically demanding social displays remained largely unchanged.
"Psilocybin's calming effect appears to selectively reduce energetically costly, escalated behaviors while lower-energy social display behaviors remained largely unchanged," said Forsyth. "This suggests that this compound can selectively dampen escalated social conflict rather than shutting down behavior altogether."
The compound also reduced general activity. When placed alongside another member of their species, fish treated with psilocybin spent less time swimming than untreated controls.
Together, these findings suggest that psilocybin may influence specific aspects of aggressive behavior rather than simply making animals less responsive to their surroundings.
What the Findings Could Mean for Psychedelic Research
The researchers believe animal studies like this one could eventually help scientists better understand how psychedelic compounds influence behavior and identify possible directions for therapeutic research.
By examining which social responses are most sensitive to psilocybin, researchers may be able to uncover biological mechanisms that are difficult to investigate directly in people. Such insights could ultimately inform studies of potential clinical applications.
However, the team emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a treatment for aggression in humans. The experiment involved fish, did not evaluate any clinical intervention, and cannot establish whether similar effects would occur in people.
There are also important questions about how long the calming effect lasts. The researchers examined only single doses and short exposure periods. They did not investigate repeated treatments, long-term behavioral changes, or whether the fish might adapt to the substance over time.
Additional experiments will be necessary to determine whether psilocybin's ability to reduce aggressive attacks can persist beyond the brief period examined in this study.
"Future studies can build on this work to explore how psilocybin alters neural signaling, which serotonin pathways are involved, and why some aspects of social behavior are affected while others are not," concluded Currie. "These are questions that are difficult or impossible to answer directly in humans."

Journal Reference:
- Dayna Forsyth, Nicoletta Faraone, Simon G. Lamarre, Suzanne Currie. The magic of mushrooms: psilocybin influences behavior in the mangrove rivulus fish, Kryptolebias marmoratus. Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, 2026; 20 DOI: 10.3389/fnbeh.2026.1767175

====================================================================================================

Bonei Zion Prize honors Olim rebuilding Israel after the war as North American Aliyah hits records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:48:37 UTC
21:48:37 KST

When Hamas terrorists tore through the farming communities of the Gaza border on October 7, they left behind burned sheds, wrecked machinery and fields no one could harvest. Within days, Danielle Abraham, a London-born Olah who had spent years bringing Israeli agricultural expertise to countries battling drought and food insecurity, turned her attention homeward and launched ReGrow Israel to get those farms running again.
The initiative has since expanded to farms and communities damaged by the war in the North. This year, it earned Abraham the Global Impact award at the 12th annual Nefesh B’Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize, and her story captures what this year's prize is about.
The Bonei Zion ("Builders of Zion") Prize recognizes Olim from English-speaking countries whose professional achievements and community leadership have made a lasting impact on Israeli society. This year's eight recipients were selected from hundreds of nominees from Australia, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States. They are being honored at a moment when Israel is still rebuilding from war, and when more North American Jews than ever are choosing to follow in their footsteps.
A record year for Aliyah
The Bonei Zion Prize lands in a year that Nefesh B'Nefesh says is shaping up to be one of its strongest since the organization was founded in 2002. More than 1,100 North Americans made Aliyah through Nefesh B'Nefesh in August alone, a monthly record for the organization. "It's record-breaking for us," Marc Rosenberg, Nefesh B'Nefesh's vice president of Diaspora partnerships, told The Jerusalem Post at Ben-Gurion Airport as another 150 Olim landed.
Approximately 2,700 North Americans had made Aliyah by the end of August, and the organization expects the total to pass 4,000 by year's end. Rosenberg said interest in Aliyah has been climbing by three to five percent annually in recent years.
Many of the newcomers are heading to precisely the regions that bore the brunt of the war: around 650 of this summer’s North American Olim moved to the periphery in the North and South. For prize sponsor Sylvan Adams, himself a Nefesh B'Nefesh Oleh who made Aliyah a decade ago, the connection between the honorees and the new arrivals is the point.
"In the wake of the immense challenges Israel and Jewish communities around the world have faced over the past year, these stories of commitment, resilience, and contribution carry even greater meaning," said Adams, president of the World Jewish Congress Israel Region. "At a time when we are working to encourage greater Aliyah and strengthen Israel through the vision of bringing one million new Olim to Israel, these honorees embody the very best of what Aliyah represents."
Builders in every field
Alongside Abraham, this year's Bonei Zion Prize recipients span science, education, social welfare, sport and diplomacy.
In the Community & Non-Profit category, the prize goes to Naomi Stuchiner, founder of Beit Issie Shapiro, one of Israel's leading organizations serving people with disabilities and their families, work whose importance has only grown as Israel confronts the physical and emotional toll of the war.
Rabbanit Chana Henkin, founder and chancellor of Nishmat, is recognized in Education for building one of the country's foremost institutions of advanced Torah learning for women. In Science & Medicine, Dr. Philip Klipstein, senior principal scientist in the R&D division of SemiConductor Devices (SCD), is honored for his contribution to Israel's high-tech and defense-technology base.
Ami Baran, president of the Israel Athletics Association, receives the award in Culture, Art & Sports, while content creator Barak Swarttz, founder of GRIT for Good, is recognized in Young Leadership, representing a new generation of Olim using digital platforms to make an impact.
The Bonei Zion Lifetime Achievement Award goes to Prof. Marta Weinstock-Rosin, the pioneering neuropharmacologist who developed the Alzheimer's drug Exelon. Her research has had a profound global impact on neuroscience and medicine.
This year's Special Recognition Award is presented to Amb. Ron Dermer, former Israeli ambassador to the United States and former minister of strategic affairs, for his decades of public service, including his role in strengthening the US-Israel alliance and advancing the Abraham Accords.
Why they stay
Rosenberg has argued that the bigger Aliyah story is less about what is pushing Jews out of North America than what is drawing them to Israel: family, values, community and a sense of belonging. The Bonei Zion honorees are the long-term proof of that pull. Nefesh B'Nefesh, which works in partnership with Israel's Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, the Jewish Agency for Israel, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael and Jewish National Fund-USA, has helped nearly 100,000 North American Olim settle in Israel and reports a 90% retention rate.
"Each of this year's recipients exemplifies the values of dedication, innovation, and Zionism, and together they are a living embodiment of the vitality and strength that Aliyah continues to bring to the State of Israel," said Rabbi Yehoshua Fass, Nefesh B'Nefesh co-founder and executive director.
For Adams, the message to the thousands landing at Ben-Gurion this year is simple. "Each year, the Bonei Zion Prize reminds us of one of Israel's greatest strengths," he said, "the extraordinary people who choose to build their lives here and, in doing so, help build the future of the Jewish state."

Iran at Nagoya 2026: A smaller squad chasing a strong record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:44:14 UTC
21:44:14 KST

Iran at Nagoya 2026: A smaller squad chasing a strong record
TEHRAN - The Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games opened with Iran’s delegation parading behind flag bearer Rouhollah Rostami.
Iran has entered 166 athletes this time, a noticeably smaller squad than in recent editions. Expectations remain high, though, because Iran’s record at these Games has improved steadily since they began in 2010.
Four editions of progress
Iran debuted at Guangzhou 2010 with 156 athletes and finished fourth with 27 gold, 24 silver and 29 bronze medals, 80 in total. At Incheon 2014 the team again ranked fourth, but its haul rose to 120 medals, including 37 golds and 52 silvers.
Jakarta 2018 brought a podium place in the standings. Iran ranked third with 51 golds and well over 130 medals in total, using a 210-strong team.
The peak so far came at Hangzhou 2022 (held in October 2023). Iran finished second with 44 gold, 46 silver and 41 bronze medals, 131 in all, from a squad of about 209 athletes. It was the first time Iranian para athletes had placed second in the tally. Later doping-related reallocations trimmed Iran’s final count slightly to 129.
What the numbers show
Total medals rose from 80 in 2010 to about 131 in 2022, an increase of roughly 64 percent. The ranking climbed from fourth to fourth to third to second. Gold medals peaked in 2018, but the overall total and the ranking peaked in 2022, which suggests a deeper and broader medal base rather than reliance on a few sports.
Some sports have been constant. Iran’s men have dominated sitting volleyball, winning gold at the first three Asian Para Games, with four titles overall by 2022. The women’s team has regularly reached the final, taking silver in 2018 and again in 2022. Powerlifting has also been a cornerstone of Iran’s success at every edition.
New disciplines have helped too. Para taekwondo and para canoe debuted at Hangzhou, and Iran’s athletes reached the podium in both for the first time.
The Nagoya outlook
The 166 athletes in Nagoya are about 20 percent fewer than the squad Iran sent to Hangzhou. A smaller team has less margin for error, so established strengths such as sitting volleyball, powerlifting, judo and athletics will matter even more. Competition is also stiff. China has dominated every edition, and host Japan will aim to improve on its own record at home.
With the Games only just under way, it is too early to judge whether Iran can hold second place or even improve on it. The history suggests a program that consistently turns its participation into medals, and the coming week will show whether a leaner delegation can keep that run going.

Menopause is normal, suffering through it shouldn't be
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:37:35 UTC
21:37:35 KST

She lies awake at night. The next morning, she struggles to concentrate at work, snaps at loved ones over things that never bothered her before, or wonders why her own body suddenly feels unfamiliar.For some women, menopause arrives quietly; for others, it brings a wave of physical and emotional changes that can leave them exhausted, anxious and searching for answers.And often, the hardest part is not just dealing with the symptoms, but getting someone to take them seriously.Menopause is a natural biological transition, but the symptoms can be disruptive enough to affect everyday life. While some women dismiss them as stress or ageing, others find their concerns brushed aside or are unsure where to turn for help. Despite growing conversations around women's health, gaps in awareness, medical guidance and access to appropriate treatment continue to shape their experiences.A quantitative descriptive survey involving 150 women from urban areas assessed the impact of menopausal symptoms on quality of life. The study, published in the Indian Journal of Preventive & Social Medicine, was authored by Somibala Thokchom and David Ratna Paul Talagathoti.
Participants aged 40 to 55 years completed the 11-item Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) to assess their symptoms and a modified 32-item Menopause-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire (MENQOL) to evaluate how menopause affected their daily lives.The study found that 58.7% of participants were aged 40–45 years, while 75.3% had already experienced menopause. Overall, 92% reported moderate to severe symptoms, 4.7% experienced mild symptoms and 3.3% reported very severe symptoms. Nearly all participants (99.3%) reported changes in their daily routines.
Menopause can bring a range of physical, emotional and urogenital symptoms, affecting women’s sleep, mood and everyday lives.
Although the findings cannot be generalised to all Indian women, given the small, urban sample, they highlight the potential impact of menopause on everyday life.The question is not simply how women experience menopause, but why so many may struggle to recognise their symptoms, seek medical advice or access appropriate care.
When menopause symptoms are dismissed as ‘just ageing’
Many women continue to experience menopause symptoms without seeking medical help, often assuming that fatigue, anxiety, disturbed sleep and mood changes are an inevitable part of ageing.Doctors say this can delay assessment and treatment, particularly when women prioritise family and work responsibilities over their own health.“Menopause is a natural condition, but that does not necessarily imply that symptoms cannot be treated,” said Dr Mitul Gupta, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Cocoon Hospital, Jaipur.Dr Gupta cautioned against attributing symptoms to ageing without proper examination. Fatigue, irritability and poor concentration can also occur with conditions such as thyroid disorders, anaemia, sleep disorders and anxiety, making a detailed medical assessment important.Maya, a Uttar Pradesh native who now lives in Delhi, said, “I started experiencing menopause when I was 51. I did face difficulties, but back then, we didn’t really talk about these things at home. I used to feel hesitant."“I thought it was just a normal part of aging, and no one in my family really knew what I was going through. Even today, many families are unaware of what women experience during menopause, and often, women end up dealing with it on their own,” she adds.Menopause care extends beyond irregular periods and hot flashes. Hormonal changes can affect sleep, mood and sexual health, while the menopausal transition is also an important time to discuss longer-term health concerns, including bone health.
Treatment options for menopause range from hormone therapy and non-hormonal medicines to lifestyle changes
A systematic review titled Menopause Symptoms Experienced by Women in India, examined 23 studies reporting symptoms among menopausal women in India. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and included eligibility criteria, a literature search, screening and data extraction.The review found that somatic symptoms were the most frequently reported category, with an average of 73.66% across the studies. Joint and muscular pain and fatigue were the most commonly reported complaints, followed by hot flashes.Psychological symptoms were reported in an average of 63.03% of women in the studies assessing this category. Eighteen studies reported psychosomatic symptoms, while five did not report psychological symptoms.Urogenital symptoms were reported in 13 studies, with an average prevalence of 51.40%. Ten studies did not report symptoms in this category. Although urogenital symptoms were the least frequently reported, the review noted that women who experienced them reported greater symptom intensity.The findings highlight the range of symptoms associated with menopause and the importance of recognising them rather than dismissing them as an unavoidable consequence of ageing. The percentages are averages reported across the reviewed studies and should not be interpreted as prevalence estimates for all Indian women.
The doctor’s dilemma: recognising symptoms, choosing treatment
Menopause symptoms can vary considerably from one woman to another, making individual assessment essential before deciding on treatment.Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) can help women experiencing troublesome symptoms, including hot flashes and night sweats, but it is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment must take into account an individual's symptoms, medical history, age, time since menopause and potential risks.“HRT is neither universally dangerous nor suitable for everyone. The right treatment is the one that is carefully chosen according to your individual needs, with proper medical guidance and regular follow-up,” said Dr Bharti Soy, consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Fortis O.P. Jindal Hospital & Research Centre.Doctors emphasise that consultations should cover the potential benefits and risks of hormone therapy, as well as non-hormonal alternatives where appropriate. Women should be able to discuss their concerns and make informed decisions with their healthcare providers.Symptoms should not automatically be attributed to menopause, as other medical conditions may require separate investigation and treatment. A thorough consultation can help distinguish between menopause-related changes and other possible causes, allowing care to be tailored to the individual's needs.
Is India’s healthcare system prepared for menopause?
Awareness alone may not be enough if women cannot access appropriate and affordable care. Gaps in menopause-specific knowledge, counselling and healthcare access can leave women without adequate guidance on managing their symptoms.The challenge is not limited to the availability of gynaecologists, but also whether consultations address menopause-related concerns beyond menstrual changes. Symptoms affecting sleep, mood, sexual wellbeing and bone health may require a broader discussion of a woman's physical and emotional health.
Treatments available in India
“Women need a complete evaluation not a consultation for the issues related to menstruation,” said Dr Priyanka Sharma, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Cocoon Hospital, Chandigarh.Barriers such as the cost of travel, time away from work, lack of awareness and limited access to healthcare facilities can make seeking care more difficult. Strengthening primary-level assessment, training healthcare workers and establishing referral pathways could help women receive appropriate support.Education in local languages and more affordable treatment options are also important to ensure that women can understand their symptoms, discuss available choices and access care when needed.Making menopause a routine part of women's healthcare could help shift the focus from simply enduring symptoms to identifying and managing them appropriately.
How social stigma plays a role
Medical care is only part of the picture. Family attitudes and social expectations can influence whether women feel comfortable discussing menopause or seeking help.“In many Indian households, menopause is still not discussed openly because of social stigma, lack of awareness, and the belief that it is simply a natural process. As a result, many women suffer silently rather than seeking medical help,” said Dr Bharti Soy.When symptoms such as disturbed sleep, irritability or discomfort are dismissed as inevitable consequences of growing older, women may begin to question whether their concerns deserve medical attention.
Dr Soy talks to TOI
“If relatives tell her that discomfort, irritability or sleep problems are simply part of growing older, she may question whether her concerns deserve medical attention,” said Dr Swati Sinha, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Rosewalk by Rainbow Hospitals.Families can help by making menopause a subject that can be discussed without embarrassment or judgement. Listening without dismissing symptoms, offering practical support and encouraging medical consultations when problems affect daily life can make the transition easier to navigate.
Partners, children and other family members need not have all the answers. Understanding that menopause affects women differently, and that help is available when symptoms become disruptive, is an important first step.Menopause may be a natural stage of life, but that does not mean women should have to endure its more difficult symptoms without support. Better awareness, informed medical consultations, accessible treatment and understanding families can help ensure that women are heard and their concerns taken seriously.

Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:36:21 UTC
21:36:21 KST

Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Lund University
- Summary:
- A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.
- Share:
A massive volcanic eruption that struck Japan about 7,300 years ago had a devastating impact on prehistoric communities, but its aftermath was far more complicated than scientists once believed. While some populations declined or disappeared from affected areas, others continued to grow despite the destruction.
An international research team led by Lund University investigated how the Kikai-Akahoya eruption changed population patterns across Japan. Their findings challenge the idea that the disaster either completely wiped out nearby communities or left them largely unaffected. Instead, the researchers uncovered a surprising mix of population decline, migration, adaptation, and growth.
A Catastrophic Volcanic Eruption in Ancient Japan
When the Kikai-Akahoya volcano erupted beneath the sea approximately 7,300 years ago, Japan was home to Jomon communities that depended on hunting and gathering for survival.
"This eruption must have been devastating, exploding out of the seabed with little warning. It battered the Japanese islands with powerful earthquakes and enormous tsunamis, and then blanketed the landscape with meters of volcanic ash," explains senior author Peter Jordan, professor in archaeology at Lund University.
For decades, archaeologists have disagreed about what happened to the people living near the eruption. One theory describes an almost complete apocalypse, with human populations abruptly disappearing from areas closest to the eruption. Another suggests that some communities managed to survive even relatively close to the disaster.
The new findings indicate that neither explanation fully captures what happened. The eruption severely damaged ecosystems, forced people from their homes, and made some regions uninhabitable. Yet evidence also points to remarkable adaptability among survivors, with certain populations actually increasing after the catastrophe.
"The disaster caused major loss of life. However, survivors migrated, forged new social relations, innovated new kinds of economy, and appear to have found creative ways to exist and later thrive in the new post-disaster conditions," says lead author Enrico Crema, professor at Cambridge University.
How the Volcanic Disaster Reshaped Japan's Population
The researchers identified striking differences in how communities across Japan responded to the eruption.
In southern Kyushu, Jomon populations had already been shrinking long before the volcano erupted. By the time the disaster occurred, relatively few people remained in the region, which was primarily visited by highly mobile groups of foragers.
Northern Kyushu followed a very different pattern. Its population had been increasing before the eruption, and that growth continued through the catastrophe and afterward, even though the surrounding ecosystems experienced extensive and lasting damage. The researchers suggest that people fleeing the most severely affected regions may have contributed to this unexpected population growth.
Evidence also indicates that survivors who had lived inland relocated toward the northern coast. Marine ecosystems in these areas recovered relatively quickly, providing valuable food resources. By developing new ways to take advantage of the sea's abundance, these communities may have supported further population growth.
Unexpected Effects Far From the Volcano
Perhaps even more surprising, the researchers identified population changes in parts of Japan much farther from the eruption.
These distant regions had experienced population growth before the catastrophe, but afterward, that growth stalled or even reversed. Such widespread demographic consequences had not previously been recognized.
Several possible explanations could account for these changes. The eruption may have caused temporary climate disruptions that affected communities across Japan. Another possibility involves severe tooth wear among deer and wild boar, two important food sources for the Jomon (possibly a consequence of the animals grazing in ash-covered landscapes). Other volcanic effects on human health and living conditions may also have contributed.
Together, these findings suggest that the consequences of a massive natural disaster can extend well beyond the areas experiencing the most immediate destruction.
According to Jordan, the results demonstrate that the effects of catastrophes are rarely straightforward. Even when faced with overwhelming destruction, human communities can respond in different ways, depending on their circumstances and the choices available to them.
"This study helps in creating a deeper understanding of the contingent ways in which cultures and societies cope with sudden shocks and catastrophes. Even in the most impossible situations, survivors and communities have choices, however limited: they need to act and make decisions; they need to adjust, collaborate, and find new connections and social networks," he concludes.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Lund University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Enrico R. Crema, Mitsuhiro Kuwahata, Junzo Uchiyama, Ari Junno, Felix Riede, Peter D. Jordan. Divergent demographic responses to the Kikai-Akahoya volcanic catastrophe in mid-Holocene Japan. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (42) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh7197

Why have settler pogroms surged during olive harvest season in West Bank?
France and Belgium condemn settler attack on diplomats, but critics say the EU needs to act beyond words of condemnation.
The European Union has condemned Israeli settler attacks on EU diplomats and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, amid unprecedented settler pogroms during the Palestinian olive harvest.
“We expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists,” the EU said in a statement on Sunday.
“We urge Israel to fully abide by International Humanitarian and Human Rights Law, and to cease the expansion of settlements.”
Israeli settler attacks during this year’s olive harvest season have already surpassed 2025 totals, with critics pointing out that mere condemnations by the EU and member states without holding Israel to account will not deter settler pogroms, which are granted impunity by the Israeli authorities.
Saturday’s incident is the latest in weeks of intensifying pogroms against local communities in the occupied West Bank by Israelis from illegal settlements who are largely protected – or at least unrestricted – by Israeli forces.
On Friday, Israeli settlers also attacked Palestinian olive pickers and a veteran photojournalist.
Why have settler pogroms surged during olive harvest season in the occupied West Bank?
Here’s what we know:
What has been the response?
Belgium’s Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said the country’s consul general to the Palestinians, as well as French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives, were also among those attacked.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called on the Israeli government to arrest the settlers who assaulted Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, and said on X it must “urgently put an end to this criminal violence and ensure the safety of the civilian population”.
The assault has prompted an Israeli police investigation, as settler pogroms disrupt the Palestinian harvest across the occupied territory.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Trump administration is “very disturbed” by the images of the settler attack on American photojournalist Heidi Levine, 64, who works as a freelance photojournalist for The Washington Post, in the occupied West Bank on Friday.
Speaking to reporters at the Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Rubio said he was yet to receive an official briefing on Friday’s incident, but what he saw “didn’t look good”.
He urged Israel to “crack down” on the violence and said President Donald Trump does not want to see “friction” or “a crisis” in the West Bank.
Ahmed Najar, a Palestinian political analyst and playwright, told Al Jazeera that condemnation without consequences is not accountability.
“Western governments continue to arm, fund and diplomatically protect Israel while treating settler attacks as isolated acts by a few extremists. But this violence flourishes within a wider system of occupation, settlement expansion and impunity,” he said.
“The West cannot claim to oppose settler violence while continuing to support the state and policies that enable it,” he added.
Sven Kuhn von Burgsdorff, former EU representative to the occupied West Bank and Gaza, had a similar view.
“The lame protests issued by the European chancelleries in response to these terrorist acts of Israeli settlers are pathetic since they are not followed up by concrete punitive measures,” he said.
“This is especially disgraceful considering that this settler terrorism has been going on for years with full impunity. At the last Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Brussels on October 12, the EU ministers were still unable to decide on sanctioning the violent settlers and/or its enablers, the annexationist apartheid government of PM Netanyahu,” he added.
What happened on Saturday?
On Saturday, Israeli settlers attacked vehicles belonging to diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland near the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank.
At least seven masked settlers surrounded the vehicles, demanded identification documents, smashed the window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian consulate and assaulted the French mayor, according to witnesses and media reports.
The 78-year-old told the Reuters news agency that he was “a bit shaken” by the event.
“I had my mayor’s sash on, with the blue, white and red colours, which clearly represent the symbol of France, in an attempt to protect the people around me. Well, that was not enough, and I was attacked, violently attacked, protected by the people who were there to try and limit things,” Baudoux said.
He said the settlers threw him to the ground, after which his group rushed back into their vehicles to leave.
“I didn’t think something like this could happen to me coming here as a pacifist to celebrate a ‘twinning’ — friendship between two cities,” he added.
However, refusing to be terrified by the attack, Baudoux said, “I think we need to go back to the olive plantations because they have great significance for the Palestinian people.”
Former EU diplomat Burgsdorff told Al Jazeera these attacks are not new, saying he witnessed “thugs attacking peaceful Palestinian farmers and citizens” during his visits to the occupied Palestinian territory between January 2020 and July 2023.
“Once a settler mob even threw stones at us – but we were already in our vehicles. Since we couldn’t count on protection by Israeli police or military, we left the scene of confrontation as soon as possible,” he added.
Where else have settlers attacked olive pickers?
In recent weeks, Israeli settlers have intensified pogroms against Palestinians picking olives in the region.
Earlier on Saturday, settlers injured six Palestinians as Israeli forces arrested farmers during pogroms across the occupied West Bank.
Four women and a child were among the injured when Israeli settlers attacked residents in Ma’in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS).
In Deir Ammar town, west of Ramallah, Israeli forces opened fire on farmers picking olives, forcing them to leave their land, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Israeli settlers also injured two Palestinians as they opened fire in the area.
In the village of Kafr Malek, northeast of Ramallah, settlers raided a farm at dawn and killed about 20 sheep, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.
Reporting from Ramallah, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said settlers destroyed olive trees across the Beit Furik plain, east of Nablus, in the northern West Bank, while Israeli forces arrested landowners and olive pickers.
In Deir Jarir village, east of Ramallah, she said, settlers under army protection fired live ammunition at farmers in the al-Hariq area to prevent them from harvesting, forcing them off their land.
Settlers also smashed the vehicle of international activist Jonathan Budlak in the village and threw stones at a farmer’s vehicle.
On Friday, dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, throwing stones, using slingshots and setting trees on fire.
Friday’s and Saturday’s attacks follow the killing of Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, during an assault on Palestinians picking olives near Burqa, northwest of Nablus, on October 7. Witnesses reported that settlers and Israeli soldiers attacked the harvesters.
Journalists documenting the violence have also been targeted.
Veteran freelance journalist Levine was attacked near Abu Falah on Friday. She fell to the ground during the attack before she was set upon, witnesses said.
Levine, who was taken to a hospital northeast of Ramallah after the attack, later told reporters that her attackers “just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times”.
Levine was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS” on the front and back. Her cameras and phone were taken from her during the assault, The Washington Post reported.
On October 6, armed settlers beat Palestinian photographer for the AFP news agency Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, with rifle butts near Aqraba, south of Nablus. He was taken to hospital with injuries to his head and torso, according to witnesses, relatives and colleagues.
Why have settler pogroms surged during olive harvest season?
The Israeli settler pogroms have been going on for many weeks and have increased during the ongoing olive harvest season.
Israeli rights group Yesh Din has documented 377 incidents of violence involving occupiers and soldiers in two weeks through October 10.
According to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), “So far this year, nearly 200 settler attacks linked to the olive harvest have caused casualties or property damage. That is already more than the 185 incidents recorded during the entire 2025 season.”
But the attacks are not new. Every year, Israeli settlers and hardline groups use the olive harvest period to assert control over valuable agricultural lands, often blocking Palestinians from reaching their groves, stealing crops, or building illegal settlement outposts and roads on private Palestinian property.
The olive harvest is also a critical economic lifeline for roughly 80,000 to 100,000 Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank. Intimidating, injuring, or barring farmers from picking their olives, as well as uprooting or burning thousands of olive trees, inflict serious financial damage and force families off their land.
“The olive harvest is not simply an agricultural season for Palestinians; it is a vital source of income and a powerful expression of their connection to the land. Settlers target this period because Palestinian families are gathered in exposed groves, often close to settlements and outposts,” Najar told Al Jazeera.
“By assaulting farmers, burning or uprooting trees and stealing crops, they are not merely disrupting a harvest – they are making it increasingly dangerous for Palestinians to reach and remain on their own land,” he said.
“The violence is also intended to deter international campaigners from accompanying Palestinian farmers, standing with them against settler violence and documenting the atrocities being committed … The objective is not only to dispossess Palestinians, but to ensure that their dispossession happens without witnesses,” he added.
According to Al Jazeera’s Odeh, this year, due to the upcoming elections, which are crucial for right-wing parties, Israeli settlers are more emboldened.
“In fact, they have received even a religious edict telling them that stealing the olive harvest was not just permissible; it was the right thing to do,” she said.
What has Israel said about the attacks?
The Israeli military has condemned Saturday’s attack on the EU diplomats and said it has opened an investigation into the incident. It said its soldiers were not present during the attack.
Settler attacks over the years have also occurred under the protection or passive stance of the Israeli army, which often declares Palestinian farming areas “closed military zones” or coordinates with settlers to restrict landowner access.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office has appeared to question the reports of the attack on the Europeans, saying on X that they are “alleged” and require “compelling evidence”, despite acknowledging that published footage of the incident exists.
Al Jazeera’s Odeh noted that while the prime minister downplays violence, Israeli opposition figures are attacking Netanyahu, saying it undermines the standing of Israel.
“They vow to protect the illegal settlements while trying to curb settler violence,” she added.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A sea warning for Typhoon Champi could be issued as early as Wednesday night, with a land warning possible Thursday, according to the Central Weather Administration.
The typhoon could have its greatest impact on Taiwan on Friday and Saturday, bringing heavy to torrential rain to central and northern Taiwan. Forecast models differ on its path, however, and the storm requires continued monitoring, per CNA.
CWA forecaster Liu Pei-teng (劉沛滕) said Champi, the year’s 29th typhoon, was about 2,470 km southeast of Eluanbi on Sunday afternoon, moving west-northwest at 20 km per hour. Maximum sustained winds near its center reached 53 meters per second, with a 200 km radius for winds of at least 7 on the Beaufort scale.
Liu said the storm could approach eastern Taiwan as a strong typhoon, although some forecast models suggest it could make landfall in Hualien or Taitung. Its eventual path will depend partly on changes in the Pacific high-pressure system.
Some models indicate it could turn north before reaching Taiwan, while others suggest it could move farther south through the Bashi Channel.
Liu said the weather would remain relatively stable early in the week, with mostly cloudy to sunny skies and highs of 33–34 C in western Taiwan. As the northeast monsoon strengthens midweek, temperatures in northern and northeastern Taiwan are expected to fall, with scattered showers in some areas.
The typhoon’s outer circulation could bring heavier rain to central and northern Taiwan from Friday. Its subsequent movement and intensity remain uncertain, the CWA said.

Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:19:08 UTC
21:19:08 KST

Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- The Mount Sinai Hospital / Mount Sinai School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Researchers have uncovered three brain pathways linked to lasting improvements in people receiving deep brain stimulation for severe, treatment-resistant depression. They also discovered that patients who failed to improve after two years shared a striking pattern: insufficient stimulation of a crucial brain connection. The findings suggest that millimeters in electrode placement could make a major difference in treatment outcomes.
- Share:
Scientists at Mount Sinai have identified three important brain connections associated with long-term improvement in patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe depression that has not responded to conventional treatments. The discovery could help researchers make this experimental therapy more precise and effective.
Published October 1 in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the research examined the largest group of patients assembled across multiple independent cohorts to date who had received subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (SCC DBS) for treatment-resistant depression.
The researchers found that lasting improvements were consistently associated with electrical stimulation reaching three specific white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.
These findings strengthen the case for using detailed maps of the brain's connections to determine exactly where electrodes should be implanted, rather than choosing their positions based primarily on anatomical landmarks. Known as connectome-based targeting, this strategy has already helped shape the ongoing Abbott TRANSCEND clinical trial, a randomized, controlled study that uses individualized brain connectivity maps to guide SCC DBS treatment.
"This study underscores the importance of individualized surgical targeting for achieving optimal outcomes with deep brain stimulation for depression," said Helen Mayberg, MD, Mount Sinai Professor in Neurotherapeutics and founding Director of the Nash Family Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "In any randomized controlled trial of a neuromodulation treatment, precise lead placement and confirmation that the intended brain target has been engaged are essential first steps. We still have much to learn about which patients are most likely to benefit from stimulation of this particular target, but developing imaging-based signatures that can match patients to their optimal treatment remains a central goal of our research."
How Deep Brain Stimulation Targets Severe Depression
For people with treatment-resistant depression, standard therapies have failed to provide adequate relief. Researchers are investigating deep brain stimulation as a possible treatment for individuals living with severe, persistent symptoms.
The procedure involves surgically placing electrodes inside the brain to deliver controlled electrical signals to circuits involved in depression. However, positioning the electrodes correctly remains one of the greatest challenges.
Electrical stimulation does not simply affect the brain tissue closest to an implanted electrode. It can also influence larger networks through the white matter pathways that connect different brain regions. As a result, two patients with electrodes implanted in nearly identical locations may experience very different outcomes depending on which connections are actually stimulated.
Earlier research from Mount Sinai and Emory University helped establish the importance of these networks. In studies published between 2014 and 2023 in Biological Psychiatry, Molecular Psychiatry, and Nature, the teams identified white matter pathways associated with successful SCC DBS treatment and developed a method for planning electrode placement using brain connectivity maps.
The latest investigation sought to determine whether those connections were also important in patients treated at other research centers. Scientists also wanted to understand whether differences in the pathways reached by stimulation could help account for patients who did not benefit.
Three Brain Connections Linked to Lasting Improvement
To investigate, the researchers examined information from several clinical studies, including the BROADEN trial and a patient cohort at the University of Toronto, where SCC DBS was originally developed.
They used computer models of the electrical fields generated by implanted electrodes alongside maps of brain connectivity. This allowed them to estimate which pathways received stimulation and compare those patterns across different patient groups.
The results showed a consistent relationship between sustained improvement and stimulation of the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.
One finding was especially notable. Across the study sites, patients who had not responded to treatment after two years showed a lack of stimulation engagement with the left cingulum bundle.
The researchers did not investigate whether moving electrodes to reach this pathway would improve those patients' symptoms. Nevertheless, the pattern offers a possible explanation for why apparently similar electrode placements can produce different results. An electrode might be positioned in the correct general region but still fail to activate all the connections associated with lasting improvement.
"This study addresses an important question in DBS: not simply which area of the brain to stimulate, but which connections within that area need to be engaged," said Brian Kopell, MD, Director of the Center for Neuromodulation at Mount Sinai. "For a network disorder such as depression, millimeters can determine whether stimulation reaches the pathways we intend to modulate. Identifying and reproducibly engaging those pathways gives us a more precise surgical target and a framework for understanding why otherwise similar electrode placements may produce different clinical outcomes."
Toward More Personalized Depression Treatments
Although reaching these three pathways appears important, the researchers emphasize that electrode placement alone is unlikely to determine whether a patient improves.
The investigation concentrated on identifying the brain connections that should receive stimulation. Additional studies are needed to determine which individuals are most likely to benefit from SCC DBS and how electrical stimulation should be adjusted as treatment continues.
There were also limitations to the brain imaging data. Individual diffusion MRI scans, which can provide information about a person's white matter connections, were not available for every participant. Consequently, much of the analysis used generalized maps of brain connectivity rather than maps created specifically for each patient.
For the Emory patient group, the researchers were able to compare results obtained from generalized connectivity maps with those based on individual diffusion imaging. Both approaches produced consistent findings, providing further support for the importance of the identified pathways. However, more research is needed to establish the value of patient-specific imaging.
Future investigations will explore whether additional brain imaging measurements, including white matter integrity and functional connectivity, can help identify suitable patients, improve electrode placement, and guide treatment settings.
"Our findings show precisely engaging these white matter pathways is a critical first step toward sustained response," said Ki Sueng Choi, PhD, Associate Professor, Imaging Core Leader at the Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "The next step is to characterize abnormal functional and structural brain states along these pathways to build more detailed models for setting patient-specific stimulation parameters, including amplitude, frequency, and pulse width, for precision medicine."
By combining increasingly detailed brain maps with personalized stimulation settings, scientists hope to better understand why some people experience lasting relief while others do not. The findings represent another step toward developing more targeted treatments for severe depression, although further clinical research is necessary to establish how much these approaches can improve outcomes.
Research Funding and Disclosures
The research received support from the National Institutes of Health BRAIN Initiative through grant UH3NS103550, the Hope for Depression Research Foundation, and the DANA Foundation.
Abbott's Neuromodulation business supplied data from the BROADEN clinical trial but did not participate in designing or analyzing the current study.
Conflict of Interest Disclosures: Dr. Brian Kopell serves as a paid consultant to Abbott Laboratories.
Dr. Helen Mayberg is a named co-inventor of a method that uses deep brain stimulation (DBS) in a particular brain region (the subcallosal cingulate area) to treat treatment-resistant depression. The method was licensed to Abbott Laboratories. Dr. Mayberg has received royalty payments from Functional Neuroscience related to this technology and is eligible to receive additional payments in the future. She also serves as a paid consultant to Abbott Laboratories in connection with its clinical trials involving DBS for depression.
Dr. Ki Sueng Choi and Dr. Martijn Figee are also paid consultants to Abbott Laboratories.
Dr. Mayberg, Dr. Kopell, and Dr. Choi are named co-inventors on a patent application covering a technique for identifying optimal electrode placement in deep brain stimulation for depression. The patent application was filed through Mount Sinai, and the technology remains unlicensed. However, the approach has been used in the TRANSCEND clinical trial.

Hurricane threatens to bring flooding, mudslides to Mexico's Pacific Coast
