Hurricane Trudy weakens to Category 1 storm after bringing heavy rain to Mexico's Pacific coast
Hurricane Trudy brought heavy rain and powerful winds to parts of Mexico's Pacific coast on Sunday, impacting sections of the country's western and southwestern states that were already targeted by Hurricane Simon last week. 
By Sunday night, all hurricane watches and warnings for Mexico's coast had expired. The National Hurricane Center, which is based in Miami, had urged people in coastal regions of Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco to prepare for potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides as a result of impending rain.
As of the hurricane center's latest update, issued Sunday night, Trudy had maximum sustained winds of 80 mph, making it a Category 1 hurricane. The storm had strengthened into a major Category 3 hurricane as it tracked toward Mexico late last week, but it has since weakened. Further rapid weakening was expected Sunday night into Monday, with the possibility of the storm being downgraded to a post-tropical depression by Tuesday night.
On Sunday, Trudy was about 130 miles west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico, and moving northwest at 7 mph.
Trudy's center was expected to turn toward the west-northwest Sunday night into Monday, taking it away from Mexico's coast and south of the Baja California Peninsula on Monday and Tuesday.
The Mexican Navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution earlier Sunday because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.
Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast.
Trudy was expected to bring 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of around 12 inches along and near the coast in Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco. The hurricane center said areas with steep terrain were particularly vulnerable to serious flooding and mudslides.
Other Pacific storms
Also in the Pacific, Typhoon Champi was moving into the Philippine Sea after passing close to Guam 's southern tip, packing sustained winds of 140 mph. By late Sunday, it was 345 miles west of Guam and moving west-northwest at 14 mph, according to the U.S. National Weather Service.
Champi was forecast to weaken before potentially strengthening into a Category 5 typhoon by Monday evening, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, part of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, said.
All tropical cyclone watches and warnings for Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan had been canceled.
The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday.
On Saturday, President Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam authorizing FEMA to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts. FEMA announced that federal disaster assistance was available for the territory of Guam to supplement local response efforts following Typhoon Champi.
Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Relief supplies were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates from FEMA.
The territories are still recovering from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

Feature: Indian-controlled Kashmir's traditional musical instrument makers strive to keep vanishing craft alive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:06:13 CST
21:06:13 KST

A musician examines a rabab before purchasing it at the workshop of Mushtaq Ahmad Dar in the outskirts of Srinagar city, the summer capital of Indian-controlled Kashmir, Oct. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Javed Dar)
by Peerzada Arshad Hamid
NEW DELHI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Inside the courtyard workshop of his two-story home, Mushtaq Ahmad Dar examines each chisel with meticulous attention. Holding one in his left hand, he runs his right index finger along the bevel, then reaches into a water-filled jug for a soaking whetstone. He hones the blade until a faint smile crosses his face, then braces another dull chisel and rubs it steadily across the stone.
"My father says that it is always the tools that work wonders," said Dar, a traditional Kashmiri musical instrument maker.
At 10 a.m., his apprentice places a half-done Kashmiri rabab, an ancient, plectrum-plucked stringed instrument carved from a single piece of mulberry wood, before him. Dar drives a sharpened chisel into the wood, hammering its butt with his adze as shavings curl away, gradually shaping the rabab's deep, concave bowl.
Dar tells Xinhua that he learned the craft as a boy from his father, continuing a tradition dating back to his grandfather, a locally renowned singer.
"Not only am I, but my three brothers are also well-versed in the craft," Dar said. "We live in a joint family, and I am hopeful our children too will carry forward this legacy."
Among his brothers, Dar has perfected the skill and now often discusses the instruments' intricacies with clients on behalf of his father, who, because of his advanced age, can no longer devote himself fully to the trade.
At Dar's workshop in Budgam district, a 25-minute drive northwest of Srinagar city, the summer capital of Indian-controlled Kashmir, traditional string instruments, including the rabab, santoor, sarangi, Kashmiri sitar, and Sikh rabab, are being made.
Dar spends months crafting a single instrument, carefully selecting mulberry and walnut wood and prioritizing quality over speed. His instruments are in demand across India.
"For most of the instruments, we use mulberry wood, but for santoor, we use walnut wood," he said. "I am lucky enough that I have a good clientele. This craft has given us everything we have today. People place orders at my workshop in advance for the instruments of their choice."
"The music runs in our blood, as our forefathers have been associated with it for generations," he said. "I know how to play every instrument that I make. These objects communicate with me."
Dar is seen as one of the torchbearers of a craft many feared would die with the Indian-controlled Kashmir's last santoor maker, 85-year-old Ghulam Mohamed Zaz of Srinagar.
Surrounded by the vibrant walls of his room, Zaz ran his frail fingers across the sharp edges of a newly fashioned, trapezoidal box of walnut wood. He checked its precision with a scale, his movements slow and deliberate.
"A craft doesn't simply die -- it endures," he said. "What kills a craft is the flood of fakes and inferior copies replacing the authentic work. I hold the line for this art today, but I do not know who will carry it into tomorrow."
He is the last of the eighth generation in his family to carve the classical instrument and claims that all the acclaimed artists of the region played on the santoors made by them.
The word santoor in Persian means "a hundred strings." The traditional Kashmiri santoor typically has 100 strings. Worldwide, santoor varieties differ mostly in their string count.
In his uptown Srinagar office, Nazir Ganaie, the founder of Kashmir Rabab Academy, an institute that works to preserve the region's musical heritage, is busy putting the final touches on an upcoming concert schedule. The event offers a rare chance to hear a performance played entirely on traditional Kashmiri instruments.
Driven by a passion to protect these indigenous folk traditions, Ganaie built this platform to bring local artists together and showcase their talents.
"For me, the rabab is not merely a musical instrument. It is an emotion deeply etched into our collective soul. The moment I strike its strings, I am transported to the mountains and valleys of Kashmir, where every note carries a story, a memory and a sense of belonging," Ganaie said.
His love for playing the Kashmiri rabab took him to Dar some years back to place an order in bulk for Kashmiri handmade rababs.
Ganaie often visits Indian-controlled Kashmir's master instrument makers to chronicle their personal histories and the resilient spirit driving them to preserve their craft.
"Today Kashmiri rabab, santoor, and sarangi stand distinct from their global counterparts," said Muzaffar Ahmad Bhat, a Srinagar-based musicologist. "They are now deeply woven into the region's folklore, defining the vibrant rhythm of folk songs and the spiritual depth of classical Sufiana Mausiqi, a centuries-old classical choral ensemble music. Far more than mere tools for performance, these instruments have become inseparable fragments of Kashmiri society, culture, and identity."
The traditional craftsmanship required to make these instruments is rapidly vanishing. At the heart of this decline is the loss of aging master craftsmen, with few apprentices stepping up to fill the void.
"Low financial returns and shrinking demand make it difficult for remaining artisans to earn a living. Ultimately, the shift toward electronic music and cheap, machine-made instruments has severely threatened a legacy that once thrived on human hands," he said.
Ganaie, however, feels the internet and social media have opened up avenues for the musicians as well as makers of the musical instruments to keep the art thriving and prevent it from vanishing into the thin air.
"It is heartening to see rabab and santoor makers and other traditional instrument artisans finding renewed hope as online orders and social media open up new markets for their craft. The growing visibility of these instruments in major productions of Bollywood and music platforms has also helped introduce the region's rich musical heritage to wider national and international audiences," he said.
Meanwhile, a young musical instrument maker Altaf Ahmad Sheikh is hard at work in another Srinagar neighborhood. His hands steady, engraving delicate floral and foliage designs that weave gracefully between the bird motifs on a sarangi. The design has transformed a plain wooden instrument into an ornate work of art.
He has spent months crafting this sarangi, an instrument that represents not just his devotion to the craft, but his very livelihood.
Sheikh, a school dropout, learned the craft from his father, a renowned sarangi maker.
"I am striving hard to keep the craft alive," Sheikh said as his young son sat in front of him, perhaps trying to imbibe the skill. ■

Researchers in Australia develop AI tool to assess stroke risk

SYDNEY, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) model that analyzes DNA to identify genetic risk factors for stroke, paving the way for more personalized risk assessments and prevention.
The study identified 18 genetic variants linked to ischemic stroke, the most common type of stroke. People in the highest genetic risk group had a 22 percent higher chance of stroke than those in the lower-risk group, according to a statement released recently by Australia's University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
The team used a type of AI known as a transformer to train the model on thousands of genetic variations and identify links to ischemic stroke. Researchers tested the AI model using genetic and health data from the UK Biobank and a large U.S. database. The model was more accurate than previous genetic risk tools at distinguishing people who had suffered a stroke from those who had not.
The study also identified the gene EDEM2 in brain cortex tissue as a key contributor to stroke susceptibility, providing a target for further research.
Researchers are now developing a multimodal AI tool that combines genetic assessments with other modes of data, including health and lifestyle surveys, scans and imaging, to improve risk assessment for stroke and other diseases. ■

Two monster black holes could collide in just 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:03:18 UTC
21:03:18 KST

Two monster black holes could collide in just 100 years
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy
- Summary:
- Astronomers have uncovered compelling evidence of two supermassive black holes spiraling toward a potentially spectacular collision at the center of galaxy Mrk 501. A previously unseen jet of particles revealed the likely presence of a second black hole, with observations suggesting the pair completes an orbit every 121 days. Depending on their masses, these cosmic giants could merge in as little as 100 years.
- Share:
Supermassive black holes are thought to exist at the centers of nearly all large galaxies. These enormous objects can weigh millions or even billions of times as much as the Sun, but scientists still do not fully understand how they grow to such extraordinary sizes. Pulling in (accreting) gas from their surroundings is one way they gain mass, although this process alone may be too slow to explain the largest examples. Merging with other massive black holes could provide the missing explanation.
Galaxy collisions are common throughout the universe, making it likely that their central black holes also eventually come together. As two galaxies merge, their black holes are expected to move closer, begin orbiting one another, and gradually spiral inward until they combine into a single object.
Despite this expectation, scientists still struggle to model the final stages of these mergers. Even more puzzling, astronomers have not reliably identified a pair of supermassive black holes orbiting extremely close together, despite abundant evidence of colliding galaxies.
A Second Jet Reveals a Hidden Black Hole
An international research team led by Silke Britzen of the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy (MPIfR) in Bonn has now uncovered direct observational evidence suggesting that such a pair exists at the center of the galaxy Mrk 501. The findings have been accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society and are scheduled to appear in an upcoming issue.
Astronomers have long known that the central black hole in Mrk 501 produces an intense jet of particles that shoots into space at nearly the speed of light. These jets arise from the extreme conditions surrounding black holes, where powerful magnetic fields help accelerate material outward.
To investigate the system, researchers examined detailed radio observations collected at multiple frequencies on dozens of separate days over approximately 23 years. The extensive dataset revealed something remarkable: alongside the familiar jet was a second jet whose movement could also be tracked.
The observations provide what the researchers describe as the first direct imaging evidence of such a system at the center of a galaxy, strongly suggesting that a second supermassive black hole is present. The black holes themselves, however, remain too close together in the sky to be individually resolved.
"We searched for it for so long, and then it came as a complete surprise that we could not only see a second jet, but even track its movement," reports Silke Britzen.
Two Supermassive Black Holes in a Cosmic Dance
The previously known jet is aimed toward Earth, making it appear exceptionally bright and relatively easy to observe. The newly identified jet points in a different direction, which helps explain why it remained hidden for so long.
Over just a few weeks of observations, astronomers noticed dramatic changes in the second jet's position. It appeared to emerge from behind the larger black hole and sweep counterclockwise around it. The movement repeated, suggesting that the entire system was undergoing a regular orbital motion.
"Evaluating the data felt like being on a ship. The entire jet system is in motion. A system of two black holes can explain this: The orbital plane sways," explains Silke Britzen.
The researchers also identified an unusual event in June 2022, when radiation from the system appeared to form a ring. This phenomenon, known as an Einstein ring, occurs when gravity bends light in a way that creates a ringlike appearance.
One possible explanation is that the two black holes and Earth were briefly aligned in just the right way. In that configuration, the gravity of the foreground black hole could have acted like a lens, bending light from the second jet behind it. This effect, called gravitational lensing, offers another potential clue to the nature of the system.
Two Black Holes Could Merge in Just 100 Years
By examining changes in the jets and repeating patterns in their brightness, the team calculated that the two black holes appear to complete an orbit around each other approximately every 121 days.
Their estimated separation is just 250 to 540 times the distance between Earth and the Sun. Although that might sound enormous, it is remarkably small for objects with masses ranging from 100 million to a billion times that of our Sun.
Such a tight orbit could have dramatic consequences. Depending on the black holes' actual masses, their separation may shrink rapidly enough for them to merge in as little as 100 years.
That would be an exceptionally short countdown by astronomical standards, potentially giving researchers an extraordinary opportunity to investigate how supermassive black holes approach their final collision.
Gravitational Waves Could Reveal an Approaching Merger
Unfortunately, Mrk 501 is so distant that even today's most powerful instruments cannot distinguish the two black holes as separate objects. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), which produced the first images of black holes in 2019 and 2022, also lacks the resolution needed to capture this particular pair individually.
As a result, astronomers will not be able to directly watch the distance between the black holes decrease. However, another method could reveal their approach.
As massive objects orbit one another, they generate gravitational waves, tiny distortions in spacetime that travel outward through the universe. The proposed black hole pair in Mrk 501 should produce extremely low-frequency gravitational waves that could be detected using pulsar timing arrays (PTAs).
These arrays use the remarkably regular radio pulses emitted by rapidly rotating neutron stars, known as pulsars, as precise cosmic clocks. By measuring subtle changes in when those pulses arrive at Earth, scientists can search for the influence of passing gravitational waves.
Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) are already considered the leading explanation for the gravitational wave background, a persistent signal thought to arise from many distant sources across the universe. In 2023, the European Pulsar Timing Array and other research collaborations reported evidence of this background.
The discovery in Mrk 501 now makes the galaxy a particularly promising target for connecting a gravitational wave signal to an individual pair of supermassive black holes.
Such a detection could do more than confirm the system's existence. It might allow scientists to measure how the pair's orbit evolves and determine whether the black holes are approaching their final merger.
"If gravitational waves are detected, we may even see their frequency steadily rise as the two giants spiral toward collision, offering a rare chance to watch a supermassive black hole merger unfold," notes co-author Héctor Olivares.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S Britzen, H Olivares, Gopal-Krishna, F Jaron, I N Pashchenko, E Kun, F K Schinzel, J Becerra González, D Paneque, N R MacDonald. Detection of a second jet within the nuclear core of Mrk 501. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 2026; 548 (4) DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag291

In a statement published on the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) social media account on Saturday evening, Netanyahu’s office described the assault as an "alleged" attack and suggested reporting on settler violence was part of a coordinated effort to discredit Israel.
The delegation included representatives from the French and Belgian consulates and the Polish representative to the Palestinian Authority. It also sought to undermine Baudoux’s account by highlighting his support for Palestinians, noting that he had "previously raised the Palestinian flag over his municipal building, prompting French authorities to order its removal". The statement offered no explanation of how that episode cast doubt on his account of the attack.
Speaking after the attack on Saturday, Baudoux said the assault demonstrated Israel’s "tolerance" of settler violence.
"I had on my mayor’s sash with the blue, white and red colours, which clearly represent the symbol of France, in an attempt to protect the people around me. Well that was not enough and I was attacked, violently attacked, and … thrown to the ground," he said.

He added that Washington had "asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff".

Brain iron levels in children with ADHD may depend on when they start medication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:23 UTC
21:00:23 KST

Children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder who begin taking stimulant medications at a younger age may develop different brain iron levels than those who start treatment later. A new analysis of brain imaging data suggests that starting medication by age eight is associated with higher iron concentrations in dopamine-rich brain regions compared to starting at age nine or later. The research was published in the journal Brain Research.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. These symptoms often create challenges with everyday tasks and social interactions. The condition is closely tied to reduced signaling of dopamine, a chemical messenger in the brain that helps regulate movement, attention, and reward. To manage symptoms, doctors routinely prescribe psychostimulants, which work by increasing the amount of dopamine available in the central nervous system.
Brain iron plays an essential role in this process because it is a necessary ingredient for the brain to manufacture dopamine. Tyrosine hydroxylase, the enzyme responsible for creating dopamine, relies entirely on iron to function properly. Iron also aids in the production of myelin, the protective sheath that insulates nerve fibers and speeds up communication between brain cells.
Because of this relationship, iron tends to concentrate heavily in dopamine-rich regions, such as the basal ganglia and the substantia nigra. These deep brain structures are heavily involved in motor control and learning. As a child grows into adolescence, iron levels in these areas typically increase alongside the maturation of the dopamine system.
Prior research has shown that children with ADHD who have never taken medication often have lower levels of brain iron compared to their peers without the condition. At the same time, some brain imaging research suggests that children treated with psychostimulants have iron levels similar to those of neurotypical children. This pattern raised the question of whether stimulant medications directly influence brain iron levels over time.
Hugo A.E. Morandini, a researcher at the Child and Adolescent Health Service in Perth, Australia, along with a team of colleagues, wanted to better understand how psychostimulant treatment relates to brain iron. They designed a study to track iron levels over a two-year period. They specifically looked at how both the duration of treatment and the age a child started taking medication might relate to iron concentrations.
To conduct the research, Morandini and his team used brain imaging data from the Oregon ADHD-1000 dataset, a public repository of clinical information. They identified 29 children with ADHD who were consistently taking psychostimulant medications and 38 neurotypical children with no psychiatric diagnoses. The children underwent magnetic resonance imaging scans at the beginning of the study and again two years later.
The researchers used a specific type of scan called functional magnetic resonance imaging. While this technology is often used to map blood flow, the team analyzed the data using a specialized technique that estimates the concentration of iron in brain tissue based on its magnetic properties. They focused their analysis on several brain regions rich in dopamine and iron, including the globus pallidus, putamen, caudate nucleus, thalamus, and substantia nigra.
First, the team compared the iron levels of the children with ADHD to the neurotypical children across the two-year period. The researchers adjusted their statistical models to account for variables like age, sex, and intelligence quotient. They found that differences in iron levels in the substantia nigra, thalamus, and most of the basal ganglia were not statistically significant between the two groups.
However, the children with ADHD had lower iron content in the globus pallidus. This structure is a key part of the basal ganglia that helps regulate dopamine circuitry and reward behaviors. The authors noted that a shorter average duration of medication exposure in their study compared to past research might explain why globus pallidus iron had not reached the levels seen in neurotypical children.
Next, the researchers looked exclusively at the 29 children with ADHD to see how their medication histories related to their brain iron. They calculated the total time each child had been taking psychostimulants and noted the age at which they first started the treatment. The researchers then tested whether these factors predicted iron levels across the different brain regions.
The length of time a child had been taking stimulants had almost no statistical relationship with brain iron. The researchers found a very small negative association between treatment duration and iron in the thalamus, but they noted this effect was so minor it is unlikely to have any clinical meaning. In all other regions, the models for treatment duration were not statistically significant.
The age at which a child began treatment showed a different pattern. The team split the children with ADHD into two subgroups based on when they started medication. One group began treatment at age eight or younger, while the other began at age nine or older.
The analysis revealed that children who started taking psychostimulants at an earlier age had higher iron content in the thalamus, caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus. The researchers noted that the brain undergoes rapid developmental changes in iron and dopamine during childhood. They proposed that starting medication earlier in childhood might intersect with these developmental windows, making the dopamine system more sensitive to external influences.
The findings come with several limitations that affect how the results should be interpreted. The analysis relied on a relatively small number of participants, meaning the patterns observed need to be confirmed in larger populations. A larger study could provide more precise estimates of how medication timing interacts with brain development.
The researchers also had to rely on parent reports to determine when the children began taking medication and how long they had been treated. Parent recall can sometimes be imprecise, which could introduce errors into the timelines. The study also lacked information on the exact dosages the children were taking and how strictly they adhered to their daily medication schedules.
Because the researchers observed existing medication habits rather than assigning treatments, the results establish an association rather than a direct cause and effect. It is possible that children prescribed medication at a younger age have more severe symptoms, which could be tied to underlying differences in brain biology. The researchers could not measure the children’s brain iron before treatment started, making it difficult to isolate the exact impact of the drugs.
Future research will need to follow patients from before they start medication into adulthood to fully chart the effects of early treatment. Tracking these changes over a longer lifespan could help researchers understand whether the differences in brain iron persist as patients grow older.
The study, “Neurochemical impact of psychostimulants: Longitudinal MRI analysis of brain iron content in children with ADHD,” was authored by Hugo A.E. Morandini, Sjoerd B. Vos, Paola Chivers, Tim J. Silk, and Pradeep Rao.

Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
Akhlaghi’s experience centres on ballistic missiles, aerospace technology and defence-industrial production.
Tehran, Iran – Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi has been appointed Iran’s defence minister at a time when the war with the United States is expected to escalate.
The 68-year-old was approved on Sunday by parliament, which has convened online since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, to assume leadership of the Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics. In total, 237 lawmakers voted in favour of Akhlaghi’s appointment and 15 against.
Former Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed along with a large number of other senior figures, including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, on the opening day of the war.
The position was filled temporarily by Majid Ebn-e Reza, who will now become Akhlaghi’s deputy.
Akhlaghi will be responsible for rebuilding and expanding Iran’s military-industrial infrastructure, which has been heavily targeted by the US and Israel.
The new minister’s defence plans were approved earlier by senior military authorities, President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliament’s Commission on National Security and Foreign Policy.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran will not be the instigator of aggression against any country but will defend the territorial integrity of the country strongly and to the death against any aggression,” Pezeshkian said.
The president said Akhlaghi has more than 42 years of experience in the Defence Ministry and related organisations.
His principal expertise is in ballistic missiles, solid-fuel propulsion, aerospace technology and military-industrial production, according to state media.
Previously, he served as the head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization and the Defence Industries Organization. Akhlaghi and these entities are all subject to sanctions by the US. He is also under United Nations sanctions.
He has been associated with developing several missile types and related weapons-development projects over the past decades, according to Tasnim, a newspaper linked with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),
Akhlaghi reportedly played a role in expanding the major Sejjil and Zolfaghar family of Iranian ballistic missiles as well as precision-guided weapons, such as the Almas missiles and Yasin guided bombs.
He is also said to have expertise in space launchers, research rockets and infrastructure associated with the Imam Khomeini Space Center in Semnan. These have all been critical elements in Iran’s wars against Israel and the US.
This month, Iran’s Defence Ministry spokesman, Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, told reporters that Akhlaghi’s nomination reflected Iran’s need to increase the quantity and quality of strategic weapons, particularly missiles and drones.
“Offensive arms are being actively improved,” the spokesman said.
The US has repeatedly claimed that it has destroyed most of Iran’s military-industrial capacities, but Tehran has maintained it continues to have considerable offensive and defensive capabilities outside the reach of US and Israeli bombs. These weapons have been upgraded based on Iran’s new war experience, it has insisted.
Akhlaghi told members of parliament this month that he had met with senior military commanders, including the commander-in-chief of the IRGC, Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi, to develop a better understanding of their requirements during and after the war.
His priorities as defence minister would be faster military-industrial development, air defences, incorporation of emerging technologies using government and private sector firms, improvements in armed-forces welfare and development of international military cooperation, according to reports.
In his first comments as defence minister on Sunday, Akhlaghi taunted the administration of US President Donald Trump, which this month threatened to use the “mother of all bombs” on Iran’s nuclear and energy infrastructure.
“We have made preparations and continue our work with ease of mind,” he told reporters. “The US president must think of getting his forces out of our region in one piece. If he drops one bomb, he must see how many of his troops he will have to evacuate horizontally.”

Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

Chris Thomas is all-in on AI gadgets.
Thomas, 43, wears a pair of Meta's camera-equipped glasses, a Fieldy note-taking pendant around his neck and a wristband from Amazon's Bee, all of which record his daily life. A Pittsburgh-based business owner and a livestreamer, Thomas relies on the devices to help him stay organized, pay bills on time and set reminders.
"I'm forgetful AF," Thomas said in an interview. "My life is so crazy that not having to remember to remember is fantastic."
Not everyone is on board with his lifestyle. Earlier this week, a bystander at a local bar noticed his Meta Glasses.
"He was like, 'I don't feel comfortable,'" Thomas said. "I don't turn it off, I take it off completely because people don't really believe it's off."
It's the type of interaction users are increasingly navigating as more tech companies introduce AI-powered, always-listening devices and features, which have been marketed as useful tools to transcribe meetings, keep track of conversations, set reminders and offer personalized recommendations.
The latest example of these gadgets arrived Thursday with Amazon's Bee Frontier wearable and Bee Eclipse, a card-shaped device that attaches to a smartphone. Both devices are designed to record, transcribe and analyze a user's day.
Apple's latest Apple Watch Series 12, unveiled in September, will have Siri Recap, which "ambiently" takes notes throughout the day and generates summaries of conversations. Another feature called Live Rewind can recap 15 seconds of a conversation via a text transcription.
Meta's popular smart glasses can take photos, capture video and record voice notes or reminders. Startups including Plaud and Pocket also developed card-sized note-taking devices, while Friend offers an AI necklace.
The devices have fueled concerns that they could erode privacy, by enabling covert recording without obtaining bystanders' consent and collecting sensitive data that's potentially accessible to others.
Amazon, Google and other makers of voice-activated smart speakers faced similar privacy concerns when their devices first hit the market, in some cases leading to lawsuits and regulatory fines.
But this new generation of AI devices is also testing the limits of privacy law.
Unlike earlier smart speakers that were activated via a so-called "wake word" and sometimes stored recordings or sent audio to the cloud, some of these products can continuously listen, interpret speech, and extract its meaning without retaining the underlying audio. This capability has raised a largely untested question about whether that processing itself can amount to an unlawful interception.
"With new technology like this, my statement is always to embrace with caution," Karen Panetta, dean of graduate education at Tufts' School of Engineering and a fellow at the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said.
She added, "If I'm giving permission for myself to be recorded, or for everything I look at to be recorded, that doesn't mean everybody else around you has given that consent."
The gray area
Apple and Amazon appear to have sidestepped some of the privacy concerns that dogged earlier voice assistants.
Apple says the feature does not store audio, send recordings to its servers, or involve human review. Amazon has said it doesn't store audio from Bee devices, and conversations are processed in a secure environment "where no one, including Amazon, can access your data."
But that may not resolve the legal question.
Many state wiretap and eavesdropping laws are written around whether a private communication was intercepted or its contents were acquired — not simply whether a conventional audio recording was created.
Colin Zick, a privacy and data security attorney at Foley Hoag, said Apple appears to have learned from the first wave of litigation over voice assistants. But the new technology raises questions those earlier cases never had to answer: Can a system that is continuously listening, interpreting speech and turning it into a summary still amount to an interception if it never saves the underlying audio?
Some state laws define interception broadly. Massachusetts, for example, defines an intercepting device to include equipment capable of "transmitting, receiving, amplifying, or recording" a communication, while the "contents" of a communication can include its substance and meaning.
In Zick's view, a device that continuously receives speech and produces a written summary could potentially fall within that language even without retaining an audio file.
And in some states, the bigger legal risk may fall not on Apple, Amazon or other AI gadget makers but on the person wearing the device.
"A non-wearer did not buy the watch, agree to Apple's terms, or choose to have their conversation summarized in the app," Zick said.
Daniel Pi, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law, said New Hampshire's statute is broad enough that he believes the Watch's new audio-intelligence features would qualify as an interception. The law covers not only recordings, but the "aural or other acquisition" of the contents of a communication.
That could create an unusual situation in which an ordinary consumer turns on a feature built into a mainstream device and, at least technically, runs afoul of state law by using it during a private conversation without everyone's consent.
Pi said a user in New Hampshire could potentially face civil or criminal liability for doing so, though he stressed that the practical risk of prosecution is far lower. It could be difficult to know whether someone had the feature enabled in the first place, and he said he would be surprised to see prosecutors pursue cases involving a bare statutory violation where no one was harmed.
The legal questions are also different from those raised by earlier smart speakers and voice assistants. Those cases often centered on devices mistakenly activating or capturing speech that was not intended as a command. Here, the feature is designed to acquire and interpret the substance of a conversation — and the user has deliberately opted in.
That changes the analysis, Pi said, and could also shift responsibility toward the wearer rather than the technology company itself.
The bystanders
The broader privacy concern extends beyond who is legally responsible.
Michael Stokes, a former CIA officer and senior vice president of emerging technologies at Veilant, said the bigger shift is that people can be swept into AI-powered surveillance without owning or knowingly interacting with the device doing the collecting.
"I think the bystander problem is really the concern I have — that you can be surveilled without owning the technology," Stokes said.
He pointed to the growing number of cameras, microphones, and sensors embedded in consumer devices, from smart glasses to watches and AI recorders. The difference now, he said, is that AI can rapidly interpret what those devices collect and draw meaning from far larger volumes of information than earlier generations of consumer technology.
For Stokes, that makes the Apple Watch part of a much larger change in the privacy landscape. During his time at the CIA, he helped develop the concept of ubiquitous technical surveillance, describing a world in which everyday devices continuously generate information that can reveal identities, locations, and associations.
The concern is not simply that more data can be collected, he said, but that the cost of making sense of it has fallen dramatically.
In the past, Stokes said, intelligence collection could require thousands of hours of work to gather, sort and analyze information about a person. AI increasingly automates that process, making it cheaper and easier to extract useful information from data that may have been gathered incidentally.
That creates a new kind of exposure for people who never opted into the technology in the first place — whether it is a private conversation picked up by a nearby wearable or information collected by a device they do not own.
"We no longer have these pockets of small privacy that we thought we did in the past," Stokes said.
Aida Baradari, founder of the startup Deveillance, is trying to give some control back to people worried about being recorded without their consent.
The company created a hockey puck-shaped gadget, called the Spectre I, that uses AI to scan for nearby devices and sends out "adversarial signals" that scramble a person's speech before microphones can process it.
Baradari said she watched as more AI wearables hit the market and felt users should have a greater say in how they interact with them.
"We need to be able to use technology while not giving up our core values or rights," she said.

Inside the New York ‘time machine’ racing to save a century of sound and film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Inside the New York ‘time machine’ racing to save a century of sound and film
“I tell my kids I work in a time machine,” said Rhony Dostaly. In a basement beneath Lincoln Center, the media preservation engineer rescues moments from the past. “I go back in time, and I grab elements, and I make them available for people today.”
He and his colleagues at the New York Public Library (NYPL) are working against the clock to preserve the contents of film, tape, discs and cylinders that hold more than a century of sound and moving images.
The records are decaying, and the machines that can play them are disappearing.
Learning from the past
For Mr. Dostaly, it’s not just about technology. He has watched other people’s lives unfold through the archive.
Harry Belafonte, the legendary American singer, actor, civil rights activist – and longtime UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador – filmed his family for decades, from teaching his son to ride a bike in Central Park to trips abroad.
“I’ve actually seen his kids from toddlers all the way to adults,” Mr. Dostaly said.
Films of the African American civil rights leader Malcolm X’s travels, including footage from Mecca, moved him the most. “I’m the one who’s going to be making it available for everyone to see,” he remembered thinking.
By looking through footage like this – he hopes – young people “will realize the importance of events that took place before they were here on Earth.”
Cultural heritage
Next door, Casey McNamara, a media preservation coordinator, bends over a reel of film with a jeweller’s loupe or magnifying glass, checking it frame by frame for tears, splices and shrinkage.
On the white leader she has written “BHARATA NATYAM,” the name of one of the oldest Indian classical dance forms.
Films may reach her “in a rusty tin, on an old projection reel, or in a rag box, in plastic bags.” Without the work she does, some collections “would remain mostly unseen.”
The lab is part of NYPL’s Digital Collections Operations. Once digitized, most of the material will be accessible to anyone with a library card.
“The tapes and the decks are no longer being manufactured, but the history needs to be preserved,” explained lab manager Shahed Dowlatshahi.
Work like this is exactly the kind of project that the UN’s World Day for Audiovisual Heritage, marked annually on 27 October, is designed to highlight and assist.
Preserving UN history
In the audio room, Jeffrey Willens slides a 16-inch disc from a brown paper sleeve marked: A Year To Remember.
The UN Radio Division produced it for broadcast on New Year’s Day 1949, when the Organization was still headquartered at Lake Success on Long Island.
Copies would have been mailed to radio stations and UN offices around the world. Mr. Willens places it on a turntable with a microscope mounted above it, and the voices of actor Fredric March and sportscaster Ted Husing fill the room.
Down the corridor, engineers are digitizing the archive of William Greaves, a pioneering African American documentary filmmaker.
His 2001 film Ralph Bunche: An American Odyssey tells the story of the American diplomat who won the 1950 Nobel Peace Prize for mediating the armistice agreements between Israel and Arab States.
Mr. Bunche was the first Black Nobel laureate and later became UN Under-Secretary-General.
‘Kind of like surgery’
Time is working against all of it.
The acetate film which the New York Public Library is trying to preserve suffers from “vinegar syndrome,” a chemical decay that leaves it brittle, warped and smelling of vinegar.
“Once that process starts, there’s no stopping it,” Ms. McNamara said. “You can slow it down with cold storage, but it will never reverse.”
Audiotape can arrive crinkled or stuck together and must be repaired by hand. “To be able to repair it and then play it and get a successful transfer is kind of like surgery,” said media preservation engineer Victoria Fajardo. “It really is such a privilege to be one of the first people to listen to a lot of this content for the first time since it’s been recorded.”
Even Digital Betacam cassettes, once considered robust, have started to shed. Francis Dougherty, the specialist who originally built the video lab, now has to clean his deck between tapes. “Every year this job gets more difficult,” he said. “Every year physical media degrades.”
The last of the repairmen
“The machines are getting rarer,” Mr. Dougherty added. “The old men who repair the machines are getting even rarer.”
Asked how urgent the work is, he does not hesitate: “It should have been dealt with 20 years ago.”
Universities train young specialists but there are fewer and fewer machines for them to work on.
“Without people to maintain and repair and service them, we won’t be able to do this,” Mr. Dowlatshahi added. “And there’s only a few people that do it now.”
Work in progress
Some solutions are built by hand. The turntable that played the UN disc was made by Nick Bergh, a California engineer who builds playback machines as “sort of a hobby.” The library has one of the first in the world.
It isn’t even finished. For now, its microscope lets engineers inspect record grooves for scratches; eventually, a second arm will read discs optically, without touching them.
Bergh’s earlier machine uses lasers to align warped wax cylinders to within microns and to read broken ones without contact.
The library used it to re-transfer the Mapleson Cylinders, recorded at the Metropolitan Opera in the early 1900s. They hold “unique performances by singers who were never otherwise recorded.”
The paradox according to Mr. Willens is that as playback technology improves, the original recordings keep deteriorating.
Every year of waiting means less heritage left to save.

Türkiye solves 60 cold-case murders in 9 months of this year

Turkish police and gendarmerie forces have solved 60 murders committed between 2004 and 2024 in the first nine months of this year by re-examining evidence from cold cases using modern forensic technology and pursuing new leads, Interior Ministry sources said on Oct. 18.
Of the cases solved, 35 fell under the jurisdiction of the police and 25 under the gendarmerie, with the oldest dating back to 2004, the sources told the Turkish state-run Anadolu Agency.
Re-examinations of evidence from past investigations, assessed alongside newly obtained material, have played a key role in identifying suspects, according to the sources.
Investigators have been analyzing DNA profiles, surveillance footage, telephone records, traffic data, mobile phone base station records and witness statements.
They have also traced physical evidence, including vehicle fragments recovered at crime scenes, while examining similarities between separate cases for potential links.
“Those who think they can commit murder and cover their tracks, believing they will never be found because time has passed, are gravely mistaken,” Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi said.
He stressed that police and gendarmerie units were continuing their investigations in coordination with chief public prosecutors’ offices and relevant institutions.
The Justice Ministry recently established a bureau tasked with investigating several high-profile unsolved cases.
Meanwhile, law enforcement agencies continue to pursue cold cases, including those that have received little or no media attention, in an effort to identify perpetrators and bring them to justice.

There is increased discussion about how Israel might help Saudi Arabia against the Iranian-backed Houthis. How might such help take shape, and what might be most effective?

The context for this latest development is the Houthis’ increased attacks on Saudi Arabia. America has not joined the fighting but may be supporting the Saudis in various ways, such as via intelligence.
The US has so far chosen not to join strikes on the Houthis. The Trump administration carried out strikes on the Houthis in March and April 2025. The administration eventually concluded that it was better to do a deal with the Houthis than continue strikes.
On Sunday, Walla had a piece by Amir Bohbot, asking whether Israeli aid to Saudi Arabia would be an opportunity or a potential powder keg.
“Security sources confirmed to Walla that the quality of Israeli intelligence is improving, but at the same time the Houthis are causing heavy damage. If America continues with the economic sanctions (there is a slim chance of a political agreement without further conflict), this could also lead to escalation in the region.”
Houthis targeted shipping they claimed was linked to Israel after Oct. 7
The overall story now points to potential increased Israeli involvement and support. It’s worth noting that the Houthis began attacks on Israel soon after October 7. The Houthis began by attacking ships they claimed were linked to Israel.
The Iranian-backed group said that it was targeting Israeli ships and vessels linked to Israel, although many of the ships attacked had no direct Israeli ownership or operational connection.
One of the most prominent incidents occurred on November 19, 2023, when Houthi forces seized the Galaxy Leader, a vehicle carrier, in the Red Sea.
Armed men boarded the ship from a helicopter and diverted it to Yemen. A Japanese company operated the vessel and, through its ownership structure, was linked to Israeli businessman Abraham Ungar. None of its 25 crew members were Israeli nationals. They remained detained until January 2025, when the Houthis released them following the Gaza ceasefire agreement.
The seizure marked the beginning of a wider campaign against international shipping. The Houthis subsequently expanded their declared targets to include vessels traveling to Israeli ports and ships associated with American and British interests.
The Houthis also carried out ballistic missile attacks on Israel. Israel responded by striking dozens of Houthi targets in 2025. This shows that Israel has already launched a campaign against the Houthis. The US has also carried out a campaign.
Notably, Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis since 2015. That means that all the players know the Houthi threat and capabilities. The Saudis have worked with Egypt, the UAE, and others in the past against the Houthis.
It appears that Riyadh will work again with Egypt and the UAE. Israel has ties with the UAE and Egypt via peace treaties. Israel also already works closely with the US Central Command.
Any cooperation against the Houthis can strengthen regional defense ties and infrastructure. This helps defend against Iranian-backed threats and Iran’s direct threats. For instance, when Iran carried out large missile attacks on Israel in 2024, many countries cooperated against the threat.

LIMOGES, France – Residents in Limoges recoiled in horror on Oct 18 at the city’s fire-ravaged town hall, an ornate 19th-century neo-Renaissance building that survived both world wars but was torched by a masked mob during the worst unrest to convulse France in years.
Stunned onlookers watched helplessly the previous evening as the blaze tore through the roof, felling the building’s clock tower in scenes that revived haunting memories of the collapse of the Notre Dame cathedral’s spire in a 2019 fire.
“It broke my heart. I saw Notre Dame all over again, except this time it was our town,” said Francoise Faurie, who witnessed the fire consume Limoges’ town hall.
Faurie’s family had been due to celebrate her granddaughter’s baptism at the town hall in a month.
“What kind of country are we living in? What are we leaving our children?” she said. “There’s no reason to touch that building. You can have demands, you have the right to protest, but not the right to violence.”
The local prefect, Maurice Barate, said the roof had caved in to the lower floors, sparing only the west wing and destroying large parts of the exterior.
The destruction of the building – a listed monument opened in 1883 and inspired by Paris’ city hall – was a “heritage catastrophe”, he said.
Its central clock tower and belfry towered 43m over the square below.
“It’s inadmissible to have burned down the town hall!” said one resident, Gilbert. “Those who did this need to be punished. They need to pay out of their own pocket; it’s not for the state to pay.”
The town’s shaken mayor, Guillaume Guerin, described how the local police force had quickly been overwhelmed by a several hundred-strong mob that he said smashed windows and used a battering ram to break down the main door.
“The logistics, the organisation, the premeditation behind the attack on the town hall is something I find unbearable,” he told reporters.
Guerin said there had been insufficient police numbers to protect the building since officers from the national force had been deployed to the street protest.
“I had no single national police officer to protect the town hall,” the centre-right mayor continued. “This country is doing badly. This country is doing very badly, and it’s a small provincial mayor telling you so.”
Crowds gathered under blue skies as specialists surveyed the damage.
Edith Lorcen, a retired nurse, expressed her shock at the malice of those behind the attack.
“I’m disgusted. I’m hurting,” Lorcen said. “But it does nothing to add hate on top of hate.” REUTERS

20:50:15 KST

The government approved on Sunday the allocation of NIS 2.5 billion for “urgent defense procurement,” to be funded through across-the-board cuts to government ministries’ budgets, less than two weeks before the October 27 elections.
The funds will be allocated through across-the-board cuts of 4.9% to government ministries’ budgets, rather than coalition funds.
The cuts will affect key ministries such as the education, health, welfare and social affairs ministries, according to the government proposal.
A legal opinion attached to the proposal warned of the implications of the cuts to government ministries and noted the need for the government to exercise restraint in making decisions during the election period.
The legal opinion also raised concerns that approving the funds so close to the elections could create an irreversible situation for the incoming government and risk prioritizing party interests over the public interest.
However, the document also acknowledged the need for the defense procurement, stating that it was required urgently.
Reason for urgency classified, will be presented to the Ministerial Committee on Procurement
The reasons for the urgency of the classified procurement, as well as the details of the security needs, will be presented as part of the classified proposals submitted to the Ministerial Committee on Procurement, the document added.
The government’s decision on the funds comes after an additional NIS 3.5b. was approved on Wednesday for further urgent defense procurement, including a roughly NIS 1b. deal to purchase Apache helicopters.
The Finance Ministry told The Jerusalem Post that close to NIS 1b. used for the Apache helicopter purchase would be diverted from funds earmarked for a five-year plan to develop Israel’s Arab sector. The remaining NIS 68 million would come from the 2026 state budget.
Lapid criticizes decision to cut government ministries
Opposition leader Yair Lapid on Sunday sharply criticized the defense procurement being funded by making cuts to government ministries.
“Defense procurement is essential, but it can be funded without cutting money for the poor or for our children’s education,” he said.
“There are billions of shekels sitting in coalition funds. Instead of the money going to the corrupt, draft dodgers, and deserters, it could be used to buy Apache helicopters.”
“The cuts to the welfare and education budgets are yet another crime by the government against the productive, serving public,” Lapid added.
MK Oded Forer (Yisrael Beytenu), also from the opposition, accused the government of prioritizing political interests ahead of the elections.
“The Israeli government continues, even in its final days, to put political interests above the public interest,” he said.
“It is cutting the budget for the rehabilitation of the North, as well as health and welfare services in the periphery.”
“But there is always money for draft dodgers and yeshivas. [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich will not touch their funding.”
“Instead of harming essential services for Israeli citizens, it is time to cut the coalition funds that finance draft evasion and buy political loyalty,” Forer added.
